en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then proclaim the *Jaya*. (1)
Possessing a beauty that intensely rivals the splendor of autumn blossoms, served by bees and sages, marked with the signs of the thunderbolt and the lotus,
adorned with shimmering golden anklets, and having shattered the threefold afflictions of his devotees—
I place within my heart the two feet of the Lord of Rādhā, whose radiance is ever-moving. || 2 ||
May he protect my speech— he who is the son of Satyavatī, who sports in the Badarī forest, and who is the foremost of men drinking the primordial nectar flowing from his lotus-like face.
The remover of the sins of those who bow before him, the incarnation of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Once, in the Naimiṣa forest, the radiant Śrī Garga, the best among the wise and a sun of yoga, arrived to see Śaunaka.
Seeing him, Śaunaka rose up suddenly along with the sages and honored him according to the prescribed rites with offerings such as water for the feet.
Śrī Śaunaka said: The wandering of the virtuous is considered blessed for the peace of householders;
it is the saint alone who removes the inner darkness of men, not even the sun.
Therefore, O Lord, dispel this doubt that has arisen in my heart:
how many incarnations (avatāras) of Śrī Hari Viṣṇu are there in total? || 7 ||
The illustrious Garga said: O Brahmin, you have asked well regarding the description of the qualities of the Blessed One;
for indeed, the narration of Him brings peace to those who hear, those who speak, and those who inquire.
In this very context, they cite this ancient history,
by the mere hearing of which great faults are pacified.
Formerly, in the city of Mithilā, there lived the powerful Bahulāśva,
a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa who was peaceful in soul and free from egoism.
Seeing Nārada, the best of sages, arrived from the sky,
he honored him, seated him on a throne, and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Śrī Bahulāśva said:
O high-minded one, tell me why that Lord, the beginningless Self, the Puruṣa who is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), assumes a body.
Śrī Nārada said: Indeed, for the protection of cows, saints, deities, and brahmins,
the Lord Hari himself assumes a body through his own divine play.
Just as an actor is not deluded by his own performance, so he was not; yet others, seeing that illusion, were undoubtedly bewildered. (14)
Śrī Bahulāśva said: O Lord, please tell me out of compassion: in how many ways does the incarnation of Śrī Hari Viṣṇu truly occur for the sake of protecting the virtuous? (15)
Śrī Nārada said: The partial incarnation (aṃśāṃśa), the partial incarnation (aṃśa), as well as the incarnation by entry (āveśa), and the full incarnation (kalāpūrṇa) are proclaimed;
and the sixth, remembered by Vyāsa and others, is the Supreme Perfect One himself (paripūrṇatama).
Marīci and others are partial portions (aṃśāṃśa), while Brahmā and others are likewise portions (aṃśa);
Kapila, Kūrma, and others are parts (kalā), and Bhārgava and others are manifestations (āveśa). || 17 ||
Pūrṇa, Nṛsiṃha, Rāma, Hari the lord of Śvetadvīpa, Vaikuṇṭha, as well as Yajña, and Nara-Nārāyaṇa are remembered [as his forms]. (18)
The most perfect Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the master of countless universes, shines resplendent in his abode of Goloka. (19)
Those who exercise authority over specific tasks are proclaimed as the "parts" (aṃśas) of the Lord; those who bear the burden of His entire work are known as the "sub-parts" (aṃśāṃśas). || 20 ||
O high-minded King, know that Viṣṇu entered within them, performed his task, and emerged again in various guises and incarnations.
He who, having understood and established the Dharma,
then disappears while remaining present in age after age— that is an incarnation of a portion of Hari.
Where there is the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha), where the nine sentiments (rasas) are seen, and furthermore the heroic exploits (vīryas), that alone is declared to be complete. || 23 ||
In whom all splendors are dissolved into his own splendor—
him they call the Supreme, the truly and directly most perfect one.
He whom people perceive individually according to their own characteristics of fullness—even through their own disposition—is He Himself, the Most Perfect One (Paripūrṇatama). 25.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself is indeed the most perfectly complete, and none other;
having come for the sake of a single task, he performed ten million tasks.
He who is the Full, the Ancient, the Supreme among the Supreme Persons, higher than the highest, the Puruṣa, the Lord of all,
who is himself eternally composed of bliss and the source of compassion—
I go for refuge to him, the mine of virtues. || 27 ||
The illustrious Garga said:
Having heard that, the king was thrilled; his hair stood on end and he was overwhelmed with love.
Wiping his eyes which were full of tears, he spoke these words to Nārada. (28)
Śrī Bahulāśva said: For what reason did Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the most perfect Supreme Being in person, come to the land of Bhārata and manifest his glory in Dvāravatī? (29)
O Brahman, O great sage, tell me of that beautiful abode of Goloka belonging to that Lord of Goloka, and of His immeasurable deeds.
When a man, while wandering among sacred fords, becomes supreme through the penance of a hundred births, he shall then quickly attain the company of the virtuous and reach Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
When shall I, with a heart softened by devotion, become a servant of the servant of Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsa— that Supreme Self who is difficult even for the best of gods to attain?
How can that Primordial God be within my range? || 32 ||
Blessed are you, O tiger among kings, beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and dear to Hari;
the Lord of devotees will come here to grant you his vision.
Janārdana, the god of the twice-born, remembers you, the king, and Śrutadeva in Dvārakā; oh, how great is the fortune of the virtuous here!
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Kṛṣṇa," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Even having obtained a tongue, he who does not glorify Kṛṣṇa, who is worthy of praise, is a fool who, though having reached the ladder to liberation, does not ascend it. || 1 ||
Now, O Lord, I shall fully describe to you the arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa on earth; listen to that which occurred during this Vārāha Kalpa.
In ancient times, the Earth, oppressed by the great burden of Dānavas, Daityas, and indeed human kings, assumed the form of a cow.
Wailing like one who is helpless, manifesting her own agony and trembling with her body, she went to Brahmā for refuge. || 4 ||
Then Brahmā, surrounded by all the hosts of gods, immediately comforted her and went together with Śaṅkara to the abode of Hari, Vaikuṇṭha.
Having bowed to the four-armed Viṣṇu, he indeed expressed his own intention.
Then Śrīnātha spoke to that Brahmā and the host of gods who were filled with anxiety.
The Blessed Lord said: [Know] Kṛṣṇa himself, the master of countless universes, the Supreme Lord, manifest, indivisible, beyond the gods, and of exceedingly wonderful pastimes.
Indeed, there will never be any task that can be accomplished without him;
therefore, go quickly to his pure and imperishable abode.
Śrī Brahmā said: I know no one superior to you, who are yourself the most perfect being.
O Lord, if there is indeed another greater than you, show him directly to us.
Śrī Nārada said:
Although thus addressed by all the hosts of gods,
the perfect Hari showed them the path upon the summit of the cosmic egg.
At the summit of the cosmic egg, pierced by the nail of the left big toe of the illustrious Vāmana, within that opening which is filled with the liquid of Brahman; (10)
By way of the water-vehicle, those gods went outside;
they beheld this universe below like the orb of the Kaliṅga fruit.
Other fruits were indeed rolling in the water like the fruits of the *indrāyana* tree;
seeing this, everyone became amazed and as if struck with wonder.
Indeed, extending upwards for eight crores of yojanas, they have reached eight ancient cities,
enchanting with divine ramparts, jewels, and groves of trees.
Beyond that, the gods beheld the auspicious bank of the Virajā,
shimmering like white silk, radiant with stairs, and supremely brilliant as the sun.
Seeing that, they set forth and went to that supreme city,
which was a great orb of light consisting of countless millions of suns.
Having seen it, their eyes were pained and they stood there overwhelmed by its splendor;
then, having offered salutations, Brahmā meditated upon that splendor at the command of Viṣṇu.
Within that circle of light, they beheld a peaceful abode possessing form;
therein they saw the supreme Śeṣa, most wonderful, long, white as a lotus stalk,
and with a thousand faces, and then the gods bowed down.
In his lap is the great realm of Goloka, honored by the worlds,
where Time— the lord of those who calculate— dwells among those who take pride in their own abodes.
O King, māyā cannot prevail over the manas, citta, mati, or the ego (ahaṃkāra);
neither does the transformation (vikāra) enter them, nor the Mahat, so how could the guṇas? || 19 ||
There, the attendants of Kṛṣṇa— possessing the loveliness of Kandarpa and bodies as beautiful as dark sapphire— prevented those who had risen to go to the gate from entering.
The illustrious gods said:
"We are all the world-protectors—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; led by Śakra, we have come here for the sake of beholding Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (21)
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard that intention, the female companions went to the inner apartments and spoke to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the divine gatekeeper, in the supreme [palace].
Then a certain female companion emerged, her face like a hundred moons, wearing yellow garments and holding a staff in her hand; she asked the gods about their desire.
The illustrious Śatacandrānana said:
"O gods, of which cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) are you all the lords who have assembled here?
Speak quickly, for I shall indeed go to that Blessed One."
The glorious goddesses said:
"Aha! Other eggs have been produced, yet they were not shown to us. We know only one egg; O auspicious one, there is no other for us. (25)
The illustrious Śatacandrānana said: "O divine Brahmā, here indeed millions of multitudes of cosmic eggs are rolling about;
just as you are gods among them, so too are there [gods] distinct in every single egg."
"You do not know the collection of names, nor have you ever gathered here;
with dull intellects, you rejoice even without having departed from your homes. (27)
People who are born therein know this single universe alone,
just as mosquitoes dwelling within the fruits of the udumbara tree perceive only that which is inside them.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having thus become objects of derision, the gods remained silent once more;
seeing them as if startled, Viṣṇu spoke these words. (29)
Śrī Viṣṇu said: "O Sanātana, we are situated within that very egg in which the incarnation of Pṛśnigarbha appeared,
[an egg] split open by the toenail of Trivikrama."
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard that and having praised him, she quickly went to the inner apartments; returning once more, she gave her command even to the gods and departed for the city.
Then all the hosts of gods beheld the supreme Goloka;
there, the king of mountains named Govardhana shines resplendent.
Surrounded by cowherd women who consider themselves the pride of spring and by herds of cows, he is adorned by the circle of the rāsa dance amidst clusters of kalpa-tree creepers. || 33 ||
There flows the dark Kṛṣṇā river, adorned with the tips of its embankments,
possessing excellent steps made of beryl, and moving with unrestrained flow.
Vṛndāvana shines resplendent, filled with divine trees and creepers,
adorned with variegated birds and bees, and graced by the bamboo grove and the banyan tree.
On the cool sandy bank, a gentle breeze blows most pleasantly,
repeatedly scattering the pollen of thousand-petaled lotuses.
In its center lies his own grove, endowed with thirty-two forests,
provided with walls and moats, and featuring the courtyard of the Aruṇa and Akṣaya banyan trees.

It was adorned with walls featuring seven rows of excellent lotus-precious stones (padmarāga), and its canopies, shaped like ten million lunar discs, possessed the brilliance of pearls and other gems.
With fluttering banners, divine in appearance, and pathways lined with flower-pavilions, it resounded with the songs of bees and the cries of intoxicated peacocks and cuckoos. (39)
Wearing earrings like the rising sun and possessing the radiance of a hundred moons, these women move at their own will, beholding his beautiful face with their jewels.
Adorned with necklaces and armlets, their jingling anklets and small bells resounded as they ran across courtyards paved with jewels, shining with crest-jewels upon their heads.
By the millions upon millions, enchanting cows, resembling white mountains and adorned with divine ornaments, stood at every door.
They were milch cows, young, endowed with good character, beauty, and virtues; accompanied by their calves, with yellow-tipped tails, they moved along with auspicious forms. (43)
Resounding with the tinkling of bells and anklets, adorned with networks of small bells,
they possessed golden horns and the shimmering luster of golden necklaces and garlands.
Where the cows are of many kinds—pale red, green, copper-colored, yellow, dark, variegated, smoky, and the color of cuckoos. (45)
They yield milk like oceans, are marked by the hands of young women, and are auspicious, adorned with calves that leap about like deer. (46)
And there, among the herds of cattle, great bulls roam here and there—
bulls endowed with long necks and horns, who bear the burden of righteousness.
Some were cowherds with canes in their hands, others were dark-complexioned bearers of flutes, all singing of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes with melodies that enchant the mind.
Having thus bowed to that grove of his own, the gods went into its midst;
there was a lotus adorned with a thousand petals, which was a mandala of lights.
Above that is a sixteen-petaled lotus, and beyond that an eight-petaled lotus;
above that, it is adorned with three shimmering, long stairways.
All the deities beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa together with Rādhā upon a supreme, divine throne inlaid with auspicious Kaustubha gems.
He was accompanied by the divine group of eight friends, beginning with Mohinī,
and was served by Śrīdāmā and others, who were themselves attended by the eight Gopālas.
He was served by white-feathered fans and waving chowries held by those with diamond-hard fists,
and by ten million parasols resembling ten million moons.
His left arm adorned by Śrī Rādhikā, his right foot gracefully bent at will, holding the flute with a beautiful, gentle smile, he bewilders the hosts of Kāmadevas with the play of his eyebrows. (54)
[One should meditate upon] Hari, who possesses a dense radiance, eyes like a thousand lotus petals, long arms, and many yellow garments;
who is resplendent with a beautiful forest garland and the sounds of bees intoxicated by the groves of Vṛndāvana. 55.
He possesses the luster of bracelets, anklets, and girdles made of *kāñcī* beads; His smile is radiant, charming, and exceedingly brilliant;
He bears the beauty of the *śrīvatsa*, the finest jewels, and His locks of hair; and He shines with the splendor of a crown, necklaces, armlets, and earrings. (56)

Seeing him, they were as if submerged in an ocean of bliss; filled with joy, their eyes clouded with streams of tears, the gods then bowed with palms joined and faces bent down to Murāri, the Supreme Person, the ultimate refuge.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Abode of Śrī Goloka," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
O Sage, having seen the high-souled Kṛṣṇa, who is higher than the highest, what did the gods do there before him? Tell me that; please have mercy.
Nārada said: Then, while they were all looking on, Hari Vaikuṇṭha himself,
manifesting with eight arms, rose up and merged into the body of Kṛṣṇa.
At that very moment, Pūrṇa and Nṛsiṃha of fierce prowess arrived;
resembling ten million suns, they merged into the splendor of Kṛṣṇa.
Then the Lord Bhūman, the sovereign of Śvetadvīpa, adorned with a thousand arms, arrived standing upon a brilliant chariot yoked to a hundred thousand horses.
Endowed with splendor, richly equipped with his own weapons, and attended by his attendants,
he too quickly became completely absorbed into the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
At that very moment, the lotus-eyed Rāma arrived in person,
bearing his bow and arrows, adorned by Sītā, and surrounded by his brothers.
In a chariot resembling ten billion suns, fanned by chowries, filled with countless lords of monkeys, and possessing the deep roar of a hundred thousand wheels; || 7 ||
Then, situated upon the golden chariot marked with a hundred thousand banners and yoked with a hundred thousand horses,
he became fully absorbed into the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
At that very moment, Yajña himself arrived in person— Nārāyaṇa Hari—
who resembled the blazing crests of fire at the onset of the dissolution of the universe.
The Lord of the Gods, endowed with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), was visible in a chariot made of light;
he too quickly merged into Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose form is dark-complexioned.
Then the Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa himself arrived,
four-armed, large-eyed, dressed as a sage, and possessing the luster of a cloud.
His matted locks were like millions of flashes of lightning, his radiant orb was shimmering,
he was adorned by divine circles of lordly sages, and his vows remained unbroken.
O King, while all of them were watching with minds filled with wonder,
he too quickly became absorbed in Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the dark and beautiful one.
Recognizing him as the most perfect Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the Lord in person, the gods offered praise, overcome with supreme wonder. || 14 ||
The gods said:

"Obeisances to the Supreme One, to Kṛṣṇa, the perfect Person, higher than the highest, the Lord of sacrifice, the cause of the ultimate cause, the bestower of boons upon Rādhā, the most complete, who is the very embodiment of the abode of Goloka. (15)
The masters of yoga indeed declare you to be the supreme light, and that within that very light you have assumed a form for the sake of the Sātvatas;
today this non-duality of yours has been realized by us—salutations to that supreme Lord, the master of all lights.

Neither by means of the indirect (vyaṅgya) nor by the primary sense (lakṣaṇā), nor even by the "burst" (sphoṭa)—that which the foremost poets do not enter—do we reach You; rather, we go for refuge to You, the Brahman, devoid of qualities, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), and free from all that can be designated as an entity. || 17 ||
Some understand you as Brahman, others as Time, some as the Tranquil, and others as the form of action upon this earth;
some indeed as Yoga, and others as the state of the agent. Having taken refuge in you—who are not known through the words of others—we have come for protection. (18)

Having abandoned the service of the Blessed One’s feet, which brings about the highest good, those who instead perform penance such as visiting sacred fords and sacrificing—do they not become ones who have failed in their purpose, being struck down by hosts of many obstacles through their [lack of] knowledge? (19)
What need is there for me to inform you today, O Lord, who are the witness of all things, shining resplendent within the hearts of all beings?
To that Blessed One, the Supreme Person, whose body is liberated and whose intent is pure, let there be salutation from the gods who bow before him.

You who are the beautiful moon-necklace upon the heart of Rādhikā, the life-giving root-nectar for the eyes of the illustrious gopīs, the banner of the abode of Goloka, and the primordial God—protect, protect the wise ones in times of calamity! 21.
O Lord of Vṛndāvana, O Master of the King of Mountains, O Lord of Vraja, You who perform the eternal play of pastimes in the guise of a cowherd;
O Lord of Rādhā, O Sovereign of those who uphold the Vedas, You who lifted Govardhana, lift up the stream of Dharma upon this earth! 22.
Śrī Nārada said: Thus addressed, you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the Lord of Gokula,
replied to the prostrate gods with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Blessed Lord said: "O eldest of the gods, O Śambhu, O deities, listen to my words:
by my command, you shall take birth among the Yādavas through portions of yourselves and through women."
And I shall descend; I will remove the burden of the earth and accomplish your purpose; I shall be born in the lineage of Yadu.
O Brahmins, the Vedas are my speech, the cows are my mouth, and you gods are my limbs; indeed, the virtuous are the vital breaths within my heart.
And whenever, age after age, Dharma is oppressed by heretical people, I manifest myself directly through my creative power (kratu). || 27 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
When Hari, the Lord of the Universe, had spoken thus, Rādhā— overwhelmed by the separation from her husband who was as dear as her own life—
fainted like a wick of misery consumed by a forest fire, enveloped in a state of trembling, horripilation, and tears.
Śrī Rādhā said: "O Vraja, you are capable of removing the burden of the earth; now hear this supreme oath of mine."
And once you, the Lord of my life, have departed, I shall never again maintain this body here. || 29 ||
Since you do not accept such an oath, I grant you a second opportunity for speech;
my breath is exceedingly agitated, eager to depart from my lips.
The camphor smoke will vanish like a mere speck.
The Blessed Lord said: "I shall go with you; do not grieve, O Rādhikā.
I will remove the burden of the earth and fulfill your word."
Śrī Rādhikā said:
Where there is no Vṛndāvana, where there is no Yamunā river,
and where there is no Govardhana, there my mind finds no happiness.
Śrī Nārada said: Śrī Hari himself sent the serpent Vedanā, a stretch of land measuring one krośa from his own abode, as well as Govardhana and the Yamunā, down to the earth.
Then Brahmā, having bowed again and again along with the hosts of gods,
spoke to Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, who is the most perfect Supreme Being.
Śrī Brahmā said:
Where shall I be, and where will you be?
Where will these others be, and by what houses and by what names? (35)
The Blessed Lord said: "I myself shall become the Supreme Being in Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva;
and a portion of mine shall become Śeṣa in Rohiṇī—of this there is no doubt."
The illustrious Rukmiṇī, daughter of Bhīṣmaka, is Śivā in person; likewise Jāmbavatī, Satyā, and Tulasī on earth, as well as Satyabhāmā, are Vasuṃdharā herself. (37)
Dakṣiṇā, Lakṣmaṇā, Kālindī, and likewise Virajā; Bhadrā, Hrī, Mitravindā, and Jāhnavī, the destroyer of sins. || 38 ||
And Kāmadeva shall become renowned as Pradyumna through Rukmiṇī;
of this there is no doubt, and you too shall become his [wife]. (39)
Nanda is Droṇa and Vasu in person; Yaśodā is remembered as Dharā herself.
Vṛṣabhānu is Sucandra, and his wife is Kalāvatī.
On earth she will be known as Kīrti, and Rādhā shall be her [sister];
I shall always perform the rāsa dance with the gopīs in the circle of Vraja. (41)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Preparations for the Arrival," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
O Creator, Śrīdāmā and his friend Subala were in the abode of Nanda and Upananda; while Stokakṛṣṇa and Arjuna, who is a portion [of Kṛṣṇa], were in the house of Navananda.
Viśāla, Arṣabha, Tejasvī, Devaprastha, Varūthapa, and Pāla—these six among the Vṛṣabhānus shall be my companions in Vraja. || 2 ||
Śrī Brahmā said: Whose station is indeed that of Nanda, and whose is the state of Vṛṣabhānu?
O Lord of the Gods, tell me directly the characteristics of Upananda.
The Blessed Lord said:
Those who always tend cattle in the cowherd settlements and constantly follow the occupation of cowherds are called gopālas by me; hear now their defining characteristics.
Nanda was declared the master of nine hundred thousand cows by the cowherds,
and Upananda was said to be the master of five hundred thousand cows.
He who is the lord of one million cows is called Vṛṣabhānu;
indeed, he whose house contains ten million cows is Nandarāja himself.
He who possesses fifty million cows is Vṛṣabhānuvara;
indeed, there are two such persons in Vraja: Sucandra and Droṇa.
The two kings of the cowherds will be enriched with all auspicious marks and characteristics.
In my delightful Vraja, there will be a hundredfold herd of beautiful cowherd girls, well-dressed and possessing faces like a hundred moons.
The illustrious Brahmā said:
O Friend of the Wretched, O Lord, O Cause of the cause of the universe!
O Supreme Ruler, tell me all the characteristics of the herd.
The Blessed One said: "O Creator, ten koṭis are declared by the sages to be an arbuda;
where there are ten arbudas, that is also called a yūtha."
Some are residents of Goloka, some are indeed gatekeepers,
some are collections of erotic charms, and some are providers of praise.
Likewise, some were known as attendants (*pārṣada*), while others were protectors of Śrī Vṛndāvana; some resided on Govardhana, and others were creators of forest groves (*kuñja*).
They shall become my forest-dwelling companions in Vraja;
and thus shall there be a herd on the Yamunā as well as a herd on the Jāhnavī.
The troop of Māyā will consist of Ramā, Madhumādhavī, Virajā, Lalitā, and Viśākhā. (14)
O Creator, in this way, there shall indeed be sixteen groups of joyful female friends and thirty-two groups of male friends in Vraja.
The Śrutarūpas, the Ṛṣirūpas, the Maithilas, and likewise the Kośalas;
and where the inhabitants of the city of Ayodhyā dwell, along with the Sītā-pulindakas.
To those for whom I have granted a boon in each successive age,
there shall be herds of gopīs in my auspicious Vraja.
Śrī Brahmā said:
O Puruṣottama, by what merit and by what boons will these women come to be in Vraja? For their station is indeed difficult to attain even for yogis.
The Blessed Lord said: In Śvetadvīpa, the Śrutis praised the Supreme Bhūman with yearning words,
and the Thousand-footed One became pleased.
Śrī Hari said:
"Choose indeed a great boon, whatever is desired by your minds;
for what is difficult to obtain for those with whom I am directly pleased? (20)
The Śrutis said: "Because it transcends the range of speech and mind, it cannot indeed be known;
therefore, those who know the ancient truths declare here that it is pure bliss alone. (21)
"Show us that form, if indeed a boon is to be granted to us.
Having heard this, he revealed his own world, which is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
It is the imperishable and immutable state consisting solely of the bliss of pure experience,
wherein lies the forest named Vṛndāvana, filled with wish-fulfilling trees.
It was rich with enchanting jewel-caves and endowed with the pleasures of all seasons;
there stood the mountain named Govardhana, possessed of beautiful waterfalls and caverns.
It is glorious, composed of a mass of jewels, and surrounded by flocks of excellent birds;
there flows the Kālindī, the best of rivers, with its waters free from impurity, its two banks bound with gems, and crowded with swans, lotuses, and other creatures. (25)
There, a multitude of gopīs was intoxicated by the flavors of various sentiments;
standing in the midst of that multitude was Acyuta, in the form of a youth.
Having shown them [the worlds], he said: "Tell me, what shall I do for you?
This world of mine has been seen, for there is no higher boon than this. (27)
The Śrutis said: O You whose beauty equals ten million Cupids, upon seeing You, our minds have undoubtedly attained the state of amorous women and been cast by the God of Love. (28)
By that [power], however, the cowherd women dwelling in your world, considering him to be their lover, worship him with the essence of desire, as do those born of the will to act.
Śrī Hari said:
"Your desire is indeed difficult to attain and difficult to accomplish;
however, being fully approved by me, it shall surely become true."
When the next Viriñci is born and exerts himself for the sake of creation,
after the Sārasvata Kalpa has passed, you shall become gopīs in Vraja.
On the earth, in the land of Bhārata, within my district of Mathurā,
in Vṛndāvana, I shall become your beloved in the circle of the rāsa dance.
Having obtained from me, through the manner of a lover, a very deep, firm, and all-surpassing affection,
you shall all indeed have fulfilled your purpose.
The Blessed Lord said:
"And those gopīs shall be from the boons I granted in a previous kalpa;
now hear, O one of similar nature, the characteristics of other gopīs as well. (34)
For the protection of the gods and for the destruction of the Rākṣasas,
the heroic Rāmacandra, son of Daśaratha, appeared in the Tretā age.
Having gone to Sītā’s svayaṃvara, he broke the bow;
the lotus-eyed Rāma married Sītā, the daughter of Janaka.
Seeing him, O Vidhi, all the women of Mithilā were bewildered;
in secret they said to the Great-Souled One, "O Lord, become our husband! (37)
The Lord of the Raghavas said to them: "O women, do not grieve;
at the end of the Dvāpara age, I shall fulfill your desire. (38)
Practice pilgrimage, charity, austerity, and purity according to their true nature with supreme faith and devotion; then you shall become gopīs in Vraja. (39)
Having thus granted them the boon, Śrī Rāma, the ocean of compassion,
the wielder of the bow who had surpassed Bhārgava in splendor, departed for Kosala.
And on the road, the women of Kosala, seeing Rāma who was exceedingly handsome, chose him as their husband in their minds—he who could enchant even Kandarpa. (41)
Rāma, the knower of all things, granted them a boon even with his mind alone:
"I shall fulfill your desire; you shall become gopīs in Vraja. (42)
Hearing that Raghu had arrived together with Sītā and his soldiers, the inhabitants of the city of Ayodhyā came forth to see him. (43)
Beholding him, they fell into a state of delusion and fainted, overwhelmed with love;
observing vows dedicated to Rāma, they performed penance on the banks of the Sarayū.
Then a voice from the sky spoke to them: "At the end of the Dvāpara age, your desire will be fulfilled in the forest on the banks of the Kālindī; of this there is no doubt. (45)
When Rāma, at his father’s command, went to the forest named Daṇḍaka,
he wandered there together with Sītā and the archer Lakṣmaṇa.
All the cowherd lay devotees dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest were constantly meditating upon me, intent on meditation for the sake of the rāsa dance.
Having reached their hermitage, Rāma— bearing bow and arrows, youthful, and adorned with a crown of matted locks— has entered into meditation upon them.
Seeing him in that different form, their minds were filled with supreme wonder;
rising from their meditation, they beheld him resembling ten million Cupids.
They said, "This Lord Gopāla is without flute or staff";
having reflected thus in their minds, they bowed and offered supreme praise.
"O sages, choose a boon," Śrī Rāma said to them;
they replied, "May we all become exactly as Sītā is. (51)
Śrī Rāma said:
"If a boon is to be requested as much of one's brother Lakṣmaṇa,
then today itself it must be made fruitful by you through my connection."
By Sītā’s words of comparison, the boon [she seeks] is difficult to accomplish and hard to obtain;
for I am indeed one who observes the vow of a single wife, the Supreme Person who is the very limit of righteousness.
Therefore, by my boon as well, you shall come into being at the end of the Dvāpara age;
I shall fulfill your supreme desire and wish.
Having thus granted the boon, Rāma then went to Pañcavaṭī;
having reached the leaf-hut, he indeed began his forest dwelling.
Overwhelmed by love, the Pulinda women, suffering from the pain of longing for the sight of him,
took the dust of his glorious feet and prepared to give up their lives.
Having assumed the form of a celibate student (brahmacārī), Rāma arrived there and said,
"O women, do not abandon your lives in vain."
"Your desire shall be fulfilled in Vṛndāvana at the end of the Dvāpara age";
having spoken thus, the celibate student vanished right there.
Then Rāma, having conquered the night-stalkers such as Rāvaṇa along with the leaders of the monkeys, arrived at Laṅkā; and Sītā went to the city by means of the Puṣpaka chariot.
The lord of kings abandoned Sītā in the forest due to public scandal;
alas, even for the virtuous on this earth, worldly existence brings abundant suffering! (60)
Whenever the lotus-eyed Rāma performed a sacrifice,
at that very time he would fashion a golden Sītā according to the prescribed rites.
In the palace of Rāghava, there was a multitude of sacrificial furrows;
and having become embodiments of pure consciousness, they came to sport with Rāma. (62)
The lord of the Raghus, the Indra among men, said to them, "O dear ones, I shall not accept [this]. Then those women, overcome with love, spoke to Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
And why do you not accept us, the virtuous women of Mithilā, who serve as half of your body during sacrificial rites and are ever the means for accomplishing your tasks? (64)
"You are righteous and a keeper of the sacred scriptures; how can you speak as if you were unrighteous?
Having grasped my hand, you now let it go; therefore, you shall incur sin. (65)
Śrī Rāma said: "What you have spoken to me is indeed correct and true;
for I am a royal sage devoted to the vow of having only one wife, namely Sītā alone."
Therefore, at the end of the Dvāpara age, you shall be in the holy forest of Vṛndāvana;
I shall fulfill your heart's desire.
The Blessed Lord said:
"They shall also be born in Vraja as the sacrificial Sītās and as cowherd women (gopikās).
O lady of that kind, hear now the characteristics of the other cowherd women as well."

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Inquiry on Exertion," in the dialogue between the Blessed One and Brahmā, within the conversation between Nārada and Bahulāśva, in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Those who dwell in Ramā-Vaikuṇṭha, the companions in Śvetadvīpa, those dwelling in the upper Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise those who have taken refuge at the feet of Ajita; || 1 ||
Even the illustrious companions dwelling on Mount Lokācala, who were born from the ocean,
will be surpassed by those cowherd girls in Vraja through their marriage to the Lord of Lakṣmī.
Some will be divine and some non-divine, as well as those whose conduct is governed by the three qualities;
they shall become guardians of the earth through various kinds of meritorious deeds performed.
Deluded by a sense of affection upon seeing the beautiful Yajñāvatāra, the son of Ruci and lord of heaven, the women of the divine folk gazed at him.
And at the word of Devala, they performed austerities on the Himalayas;
"O Creator, by means of supreme devotion, those women shall become my gopīs in Vraja."
When the divine Lord Dhanvantari had vanished from the earth,
the medicinal herbs fell into distress and became fruitless in Bhārata.
For the sake of attaining perfection, those women, having become enchanting, performed austerities;
and when four yugas had passed, Hari became supremely pleased.
Having heard the Ṛgvedic verse, "Choose a boon," the women in the great forest,
seeing him, fell into a state of infatuation and said, "Be our husband here."
"At the end of the Dvāpara age, having become enchanting creepers in Vṛndāvana, you shall become women in the Rāsa dance; and I will fulfill your word."
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Grandfather, these excellent women, endowed with a spirit of devotion and possessed of great fortune,
shall become the vine-gopīs in the forest of Vṛndāvana."
And the women of Jālandhara, having beheld Hari, the Lord of Vṛndā, said: "This is indeed Hari himself; may he become our husband. (11)
A voice from the sky spoke to them: "Quickly take refuge in the Lord of Ramā;
just as Vṛndā is, so shall you become in the forest of Vṛndāvana."
Upon seeing the glorious Fish, Hari, the daughters of the ocean were infatuated;
by the boon of the glorious Fish, they shall indeed become the cowherd girls (gopīs) in Vraja.
There was a king named Pṛthu, who was manifestly a portion of myself and possessed fierce valor;
having conquered his enemies, that best of monarchs milked the earth for all desirable objects.
There, the women of the city of Barhiṣmatī, seeing Pṛthu, approached Atri and, overwhelmed by infatuation, spoke to him. (15)
"But this Pṛthu, the king of kings, possesses vast prowess; how might he not indeed become our suitor? Tell us that, O great sage. (16)
Atri said:
"Perform the milking of the cow this very day; this earth consists of the power of concentration (dhāraṇā).
She will grant you everything, even that which is difficult to attain, including the great ocean of your heart's desires."
And they milked that cow of their desires into the vessel of their minds;
therefore, O Grandfather, they shall become gopīs in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
For the purpose of deluding the army of Kāma, excellent divine Apsarases suddenly appeared before Nārāyaṇa on Mount Gandhamādana.
And to those who desired husbands, he said: "The sage Nārāyaṇa has been perfected;
your heart's desire shall be fulfilled, O gopīs, you shall go. (20)
O Creator, the women dwelling in the region of Sutala, having seen Vāmana and being enchanted,
will perform austerities as gopīs in Vṛndāvana.
Those daughters of the lords of the Nāgas who have approached Śeṣa with devotion out of a desire for a boon,
they shall also be in Vraja for the sake of Saṃkarṣaṇa’s rāsa dance.
Kaśyapa will become Vasudeva, and Aditi will become Devakī; Śūra will become Prāṇa, and he too, Dhruva, will descend as Devaka. (23)
Vasu was Uddhava himself, Dakṣa was Akrūra who is devoted to compassion, Hṛdīka was Kubera, and Kṛtavarman was the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa). || 24 ||
Gada, Prācīnabarhis, the Maruts, and Ugrasena—having bestowed the kingdom upon him according to the prescribed rites, I shall provide his protection. (25)
Yuyudhāna, Ambarīṣa, Prahlāda, and likewise Sātyaki;
the Ocean of Milk, Śantanu himself, Bhīṣma, and Droṇa, the best of the Vasus. (26)
Śala was Divodāsa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra was Bhaga, and Ravi was Pāṇḍu; the best among the virtuous, Dharma, became King Yudhiṣṭhira. (27)
Bhīma is the most powerful Vāyu, Arjuna is Svāyaṃbhuva Manu,
Śatarūpā is Subhadrā, and Savitṛ is indeed Karṇa.
Nakula and Sahadeva are remembered as the two sons of the Aśvins;
Dhātṛ is the hero Bāhlīka, and the powerful Droṇa is Agni. (29)
Duryodhana shall be a portion of Kali, while Abhimanyu shall be Soma himself;
and the son of Droṇa shall become an actual manifestation of Śiva upon the earth.
Thus, by my command, you shall take birth through your own portions along with women in the lineages of Yadu, the Kauravas, and other kings, family after family.
Whichever incarnations of mine occurred in the past, the queens of those [incarnations] were portions of Ramā;
there will be sixteen thousand among the future royal queens.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus there to Brahmā, who is seated upon the lotus, Śrī Hari addressed the divine Bhagavatī Yogamāyā, who possesses a celestial form.
O high-minded one, having drawn out the seventh embryo from Devakī—the wife of Vasudeva—once again, out of fear and terror of Kaṃsa; || 34 ||
"And while Rohiṇī remains in Nanda’s cowherd settlement, you must indeed become the husband of Nanda’s wife after performing this wonderful deed. (35)
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard this, Brahmā, together with the hosts of gods, bowed to Kṛṣṇa, who is higher than the highest;
and having consoled the Earth with his words, he returned to his own abode.
O King of Mithilā, know that Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the most perfectly complete Supreme Being in person; he has arrived upon this earthly realm for the purpose of slaying Kaṃsa and the others. 37.
O King, even when there are as many tongues as there are hairs on the body, even then the great qualities of that glorious Hari cannot be fully described. (38)
O King, just as birds fly through the sky according to their own capacity, so do the wise here describe the divine course of Kṛṣṇa. 39.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Incarnations," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Garga Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Śrī Bahulāśva said: Who is this Kaṃsa, the Daitya of great strength and prowess?
O best of divine sages, tell me of his births and his deeds.
Śrī Nārada said:
Formerly, during the churning of the ocean, the great asura Kālanemi fought with Viṣṇu and was slain by him by force in battle.
Having been restored to life there by Śukra through the *saṃjīvinī* lore,
he again set his mind on exertion, desiring to fight Viṣṇu.
Then the Daitya performed penance in the vicinity of Mount Mandara,
daily drinking the juice of dūrvā grass while worshipping the god Pitāmaha.
When a hundred divine years had passed, the Grandfather (Brahmā) saw him reduced to nothing but bones and an anthill, and said to him, "Choose a boon."
May death not come to me, even though I am full [of pride], from the hands of those mighty gods residing in the cosmic egg who have Viṣṇu as their root.
Brahmā said: "O Daitya, this supreme boon which you have requested is difficult to obtain;
it shall be attained by you at another time, for my word cannot be false."
Śrī Nārada said:
Even in his childhood, he constantly fought with great wrestlers;
furthermore, that asura took birth again from the wife of Ugrasena.
Jarāsandha, the lord of Magadha, set out for the conquest of the quarters;
his camp was established here and there in the vicinity of the Yamunā.
The elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, possessing the strength of a thousand elephants,
broke his collection of chains and, intoxicated with rut, rushed out from the camp.
Toppling tents, houses, and the slopes of mountains,
he arrived at the arena where Kaṃsa was also fighting.
When the Mallas had fled, Kaṃsa,
seizing him by the trunk with his own trunk, threw him down upon the ground.
Seizing him again with both hands and whirling him around,
the son of Ugrasena hurled him a hundred yojanas into the army of Jarāsandha.
Having witnessed that miraculous power, the delighted Lord of Magadha gave to Kaṃsa his two celebrated daughters, Asti and Prāpti.
Jarāsandha gave as a dowry one hundred million horses, one hundred thousand elephants, three hundred thousand chariots,
and ten thousand female slaves.
Then, having fought in duels, the heroic Kaṃsa— proud with the intoxication of his own arm-strength and possessed of fierce valor— went alone to Māhiṣmatī.
Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, Kūṭa, Śala, and Tośalaka—
these were the wrestlers, sons of the lord of Māhiṣmatī, who desired victory in battle.
Kaṃsa spoke to them with conciliation: "O heroes, please enter the arena itself;
if you are victorious, I shall become your slave."
If I am victorious, I shall make all of you my servants in the presence of all those noble citizens as they look on. (19)
Having thus made this vow, he then fought with those seekers of victory;
and when Cāṇūra arrived, the Lord of the Yādavas seized him.
He dashed him against the surface of the earth while uttering a loud cry,
as Muṣṭika, who had come forth for battle, approached with his fists.
With a single fist, he indeed felled him to the ground;
Kaṃsa, having seized Kūṭa who had approached him by the feet, [struck him].
Seizing Śala as he ran with his arm outstretched, he threw him down,
and having dragged him back again, he pulled him across the ground.
Then Kaṃsa, seizing Tośalaka by the strength of his arms,
threw him down to the ground, lifted him up, and hurled him ten yojanas away.
And having made them his servants, the Lord of the Yādavas,
at my word, went quickly with them to the excellent mountain Pravarṣaṇa.
Having informed him of his intention, Kaṃsa fought with that monkey Dvivida for twenty days without ceasing.
Dvivida, having uprooted a mountain, hurled it at his head;
Kamsa, seizing the mountain, threw it back down upon him.
Having struck Kaṃsa with his fist, Dvivida flew into the sky;
but Kaṃsa, running after him and seizing him, threw him down to the ground.
Fainted by that blow, he fell into a state of extreme impurity;
with his vital strength exhausted and his bones crushed, he then became a slave.
Then Kaṃsa went from there to the forest of Ṛṣyamūka;
there dwelt the great Daitya Keśin, who had the form of a horse and a voice like a thundercloud.
Having struck him with his fists and brought him under his control, he mounted him;
thus Kaṃsa, possessed of great heroism, went to the mountain named Mahendra.
The king of the Daityas uprooted the mountain and hurled it a hundred times;
yet Rāma remained there, his eyes bloodshot with rage.
Beholding the sage, who possessed the splendor of the sun at the time of universal dissolution, he bowed his head;
then, having circumambulated him once more, he prostrated himself at his feet.
Then the descendant of Bhṛgu, though pacified, spoke to Kaṃsa with a most fierce gaze:
"O child of a worm and a monkey, you are as insignificant as a gnat."
"Right now I shall slay you, O wicked Kṣatriya who prides yourself on your heroism;
here before me is this great bow, equal to a hundred thousand bhāras. (35)
And this [weapon], given by Viṣṇu to Śambhu in the battle for the three cities, has come here from the hand of Śambhu for the sake of slaying the Kṣatriyas. (36)
If you perform this [task], then it will be well;
but if there is no cultivation of this [field], I shall destroy your strength. (37)
Having heard those words, the Daitya then took up a bow of seven palm-lengths and,
while he looked on, effortlessly made it ready for use.
Drawing it back as far as his ear, he stretched it a hundred times;
by the very snapping of the bowstring, there arose a clanging sound like the roar of lightning.
By that roar, the universe, along with the seven worlds and the subterranean realms, resounded;
the elephants of the quarters trembled, and the stars indeed fell to the surface of the earth.
Having set down that bow and bowed repeatedly, Kaṃsa said to Bhārgava:
"O Lord, I am not a Kṣatriya; I am a Daitya and your servant. (41)
"I am the servant of your servant; protect me, O Supreme Person!
Hearing this, Śrī Rāma was pleased and gave him that very bow.
The illustrious son of Jamadagni said:
"That Vaiṣṇava bow which shall be broken belongs to the Supreme Person;
even He will cause you to be slain."
Śrī Nārada said: Then, having bowed to the sage, Kaṃsa wandered about, intoxicated with pride;
no kings fought with him, and they all paid him tribute.
On the shore of the ocean, Kaṃsa beheld a Daitya named Aghāsura,
who was shaped like a serpent and was licking his lips with hissing sounds.
Seizing him as he approached and bit,
the powerful king of the Daityas fearlessly cast him down and made him into a necklace for his own neck.
In the eastern region of Bengal, there was a great bull belonging to the demon Ariṣṭa;
with him he fought as one elephant fights another.
With his two horns, he hurled high mountains onto Kaṃsa’s head;
Kaṃsa, seizing a mountain, threw it at his [the bull's] head.
Kaṃsa, the preeminent among the Daityas, struck Ariṣṭa with his fist;
having defeated him while he was unconscious, Kaṃsa departed for the northern direction.
Kaṃsa, desiring battle, spoke to the mighty son of the Earth, the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa named Naraka: "O King of Daityas, grant me a fight! (50)
If you, sirs, are victorious, I shall become your slave;
if I am victorious, I shall make all of you my slaves. (51)
Śrī Nārada said: Formerly, the exceedingly powerful Pralamba fought with Kaṃsa,
just as a fierce lion on a mountain fights with another fierce lion.
In the wrestling match, Kaṃsa seized him, threw him to the ground,
and seizing him once more, hurled him toward the city of Prāgjyotiṣa.
One named Dhenuka arrived and, out of rage, seized Kaṃsa;
having displayed his terrible strength, he then hurled him far away.
Kaṃsa urged Dhenuka toward [the mountain] a hundred yojanas away;
having thrown him down, he crushed his body with firm fist-blows.
At the word of Bhauma, Tṛṇāvarta took Kaṃsa and went into the sky;
there, the Daitya fought at a height of one hundred thousand yojanas.
Kaṃsa, exerting his infinite strength, seized the Daitya from the sky and threw him to the ground as he vomited blood from his mouth.
Then Kaṃsa struck down the mighty Daitya Baka as he was swallowing him with his beak, using his fist which dealt blows like a thunderbolt.
Rising up, the powerful Daitya, white-winged and possessing the roar of a cloud,
flew up filled with rage and, with his sharp beak, seized him.
Although he had been swallowed, that Vajrāṅga remained an obstruction in his throat;
with his throat wounded, Mahābaka immediately vomited up Kaṃsa.
Kaṃsa, having seized Baka and thrown him down upon the surface of the earth,
whirled him around with both hands and dragged him about in the combat.
To his own sister named Pūtanā, who stood there desiring to fight, Kaṃsa said, laughing: "Listen to my words, O Pūtanā! (62)
"I shall never engage in battle with a woman;
even if Bakāsura were my brother, you must become my sister. (63)
Then, seeing Kaṃsa possessed of infinite power, Bhauma also, being emboldened,
formed an alliance with Kaṃsa for the purpose of assisting him against the gods.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Kaṃsa’s Army," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Garga Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Then Kaṃsa, together with Pralamba and others, as well as those previously conquered,
went to the city of Śambara and informed him of his intention.
For although Śambara was possessed of exceeding heroism, he did not indeed fight with him;
rather, together with all those of great strength, he established friendship with Kaṃsa.
On the peak of Triśṛṅga lies the powerful asura named Vyoma;
awakened by the foot of Kaṃsa, his eyes became bloodshot with rage.
Rising up, he struck Kaṃsa with powerful and firm fists;
a terrible battle then ensued between the two of them with their mutual blows.
He too became devoid of strength and overwhelmed by dizziness from Kaṃsa’s fists;
then Kaṃsa, having made him his servant, bowed down to me as I arrived.
"O Lord, I am desirous of battle; tell me quickly, where shall I go?
He then said to him, "O Daitya, go to the exceedingly powerful Bāṇa."
And impelled by me, who desired to witness the battle, Kaṃsa—
puffed up with pride in the strength of his arms— went to the city named Śoṇita.
Hearing that vow, Bāṇāsura became greatly enraged;
the powerful one struck her on the middle of the forehead with his palm and roared like a thundercloud.
Having delivered a kick that reached his knees and extended down to the depths of the netherworld (Pātāla), Bāṇa said to him: "First, pull this [kick] back up!"
Hearing these words, Kaṃsa, fierce in his prowess and intoxicated with pride, seized her with both hands, just as one might seize two elephants with a sharp goad.
When she was drawn up and pulled out, the seven firm layers of the worlds were uprooted; many mountains fell and the steadfast world-elephants of the quarters reeled.
Seeing Bāṇa prepared for battle, the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) approached,
enlightened everyone, and spoke to the son of Bali.
No one else on earth besides Kṛṣṇa shall defeat him;
for a boon was granted to him by Bhārgava, as well as the Vaiṣṇava bow.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken these heart-warming words of friendship to Kaṃsa and Bāṇa,
Śiva himself, the Great Lord, immediately established them in supreme peace.
Then Kaṃsa, having heard that the great Asura Vatsa was in the western direction,
that king of the Daityas fought with him who was in the form of a calf.
Seizing that calf by its tail, he dashed it against the ground;
then, having brought that mountain under his control, he proceeded to the lands of the Mlecchas.
Having heard from my mouth about the exceedingly powerful Daitya Kālayavana, he whose beard was red and who wielded a mace went forth to fight him face-to-face. (17)
Kaṃsa, seizing his own mace fashioned from a hundred thousand bhāras,
hurled it at the lord of the Yavanas and then let out a lion’s roar.
Then a terrible mace-duel took place between Kaṃsa and Kālayavana;
the two maces, emitting sparks, were reduced to powder.
Kaṃsa, seizing Kāla, threw him down upon the ground;
seizing him again and striking him down, he rendered him as good as dead.
The powerful Kaṃsa, lord of the Daityas, crushed with his mace that army of the Yavana which was raining down showers of arrows.
Having struck down elephants, horses, excellent chariots, and heroes to the ground,
the hero roared like a thundercloud in the arena of battle during that mace-duel.
Thereupon, the Mlecchas fled, each abandoning his own position in the battle;
however, the wise king did not strike down the Mlecchas who were terrified and fleeing.
He has high feet and long knees; his thighs are pillar-like and his waist is slender;
his chest is broad like a door-panel, his shoulders are fleshy, and he is well-nourished, tall, and possesses long arms. (24)
Lotus-eyed, with long hair, ruddy in complexion, and clad in dark garments;
wearing a crown, earrings, and necklaces, adorned with a garland of lotuses, he is the sun of dissolution.
Equipped with a sword, a quiver, and armor, and armed with a mallet and a bow,
Kaṃsa, intoxicated with pride, went to Amarāvatī to conquer the gods.
He was surrounded by Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, Ariṣṭa, Śala, Tośala, Keśin,
Pralamba, Baka, and Dvivida.
He besieged Amarāvatī with Tṛṇāvarta, Aghakūṭa, Bhauma, Bāṇa, Śambara, Vyoma, Dhenuka, and Vatsa. || 28 ||
Seeing Kaṃsa and the others arrived, Śakra, the self-ruling lord of the gods,
went forth in a rage to fight together with all the hosts of gods.
Between the two of them there occurred a terrible, tumultuous battle that made the hair stand on end,
fought with divine collections of weapons and sharp arrows of flashing luster.
When a darkness of weapons had arisen, Maheśvara, mounted upon his chariot,
hurled at Kaṃsa a hundred-edged thunderbolt with the brilliance of lightning.
The great asura also quickly struck that vajra with a mallet;
the thunderbolt fell in the battle and its edge became shattered.
Then, casting aside his vajra, the wielder of the vajra (Vajrin) seized a sword in rage;
uttering a terrifying roar, he swiftly struck Kaṃsa on the head.
Kaṃsa was not wounded, like an elephant struck by a garland;
he seized a heavy, firm mace made of eight metals.
Kaṃsa, the king of the Daityas, hurled at Indra a mace weighing a hundred thousand bhāras;
seeing it falling toward him, Purandara quickly seized it.
Then the hero, the slayer of Namuci, whose charioteer was Mātali, hurled it at the Daitya; he moved through the battle, shattering his enemies.
Kaṃsa, seizing a heavy iron club, struck the enemy of the asuras on the shoulder;
by that blow, the lord of gods fell into a swoon for a moment.
All the hosts of Maruts covered Kaṃsa with volleys of arrows that flashed with the brilliance of vulture feathers, just as clouds shroud the sun during the rainy season.
Then the heroic and powerful Bāṇāsura, endowed with a thousand arms, repeatedly twanging his bow,
drove them away with his arrows.
And Bāṇa, along with the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Ṛbhus, and gods, having assembled from all sides, struck the mountain with various kinds of weapons. || 40 ||
Then the terrestrial Asura Pralamba arrived, roaring along with other demons;
by that roar, those gods fell down in the battle, unconscious.
Then Śakra, perceiving the truth, rose up quickly and departed;
having mounted his elephant Airāvata, he urged the intoxicated beast toward Kaṃsa.
Enraged by the striking of his goad,
he was felling his enemies with his feet and crushing them here and there with the blasts from his trunk.
[He saw] Śravanmada, possessing four tusks and as difficult to approach as the Himalaya mountain, trumpeting and repeatedly lashing his trunk against its chains. (44)
It was richly furnished with jars, adorned with networks of small bells and jeweled blankets,
and its surface bore designs of cow-urine paste, vermilion, and musk.
With a firm fist, Kaṃsa struck that great elephant;
with a second fist, he struck Śakra on the field of battle.
By that blow from his fist, Śakra fell far away;
touching the earth with his knees, even Gaja became overwhelmed.
Rising up once more, the lord of serpents struck the leader of the Daityas with his fangs,
lifted him with his trunk, and hurled him a hundred thousand yojanas away.
Although he had fallen, that Vajrāṅga, with his mind somewhat agitated,
his lips quivering and his body extremely enraged, returned to the field of battle.
Kaṃsa, having seized the king of elephants and brought it down onto the field of battle,
crushed its trunk and ground its tusks to powder.
Then the elephant Airāvata fled swiftly from the field of battle;
having struck down great heroes, he went to the city of Devadhānī.
Then the king of the Daityas, having taken up the Vaiṣṇava bow and made it ready,
put the gods to flight with floods of arrows and the twanging of his bow.
Then the gods, being struck down by him, fled to the ends of the quarters with cowed minds;
some in the battle had their topknots loosened, speaking thus in the fray: "We are afraid! (53)
Some, with palms joined in reverence, appeared exceedingly wretched; having cast down their weapons in battle, they stood with their waistbands loosened.
Others, utterly overwhelmed, desired to flee from the presence of Kaṃsa, that god among men, on the battlefield.
Thus, having observed those gods who had approached him and having seated them under the royal parasol upon the throne,
that lord of men then returned with all the hosts of Daityas to his own capital, Mathurā.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Kaṃsa’s World Conquest," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Having heard that, O Śaunaka, the illustrious King of Mithilā, endowed with devotion and the foremost among the possessors of knowledge,
bowed again and spoke most wonderfully to the sage.
He was devoted to the worship of Hari and was the most excellent among the celestial sages.
Bahulāśva said:
"O Kausalya, you have purified my lineage with the stainless fame of your own blissful arms."
Even an ordinary person may become a saint through even a momentary association with a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; what need is there to speak further? || 2 ||
O divine sage, O lord of sages, tell me what deeds the Supreme Lord performed after going in person to Vraja with Śrī Rādhā; protect me from the suffering of my threefold affliction. || 3 ||
Śrī Nārada said: Blessed is that lineage which was graced by King Nimi, a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa who was himself higher than the highest.
It is no wonder that you were born from a pearl-oyster shell, for it was already filled with the potential for becoming a pearl. || 4 ||
Now, listen to the most auspicious and holy life of that Supreme Lord,
who appeared on earth for the protection of the virtuous.
Kṛṣṇa did not act solely for the sake of slaying Kaṃsa.
Then, O King, having infused Rādhā— the wife of Vṛṣabhānu— with His own supreme form of splendor,
He descended into that beautiful mansion in a grove on the banks of the Yamunā.
When the sky was thickly covered at midday during the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, on the day of the serpent (the fifth lunar day) and under the Moon constellation,
the hosts of gods showered that palace with shimmering flowers born of the Nandana grove.
Then, through the descent of Rādhā, the rivers became pure, the quarters of the sky grew serene,
and the winds blew coolly, fragrant with the scent of lotuses, moving with a beautiful and gentle motion.
Then, seeing her daughter, who was as delightful as a hundred autumn moons, Kīrti, the cowherd woman, attained great joy;
having quickly performed auspicious rites, she gave two hundred thousand cows to the twice-born, bringing them immense delight.
Swung upon a swing filled with the rays of various jewels, adorned with gold, and anointed with sandalwood paste,
she grew day by day with her companions, like the digit of the moon increasing in its splendor.
That vision which is very difficult even for the best of gods to obtain, and which is attained through sacrifices performed over ten million lifetimes—
[behold] her in embodied form within the temple of Vṛṣabhānu.
People dally with the caresses of women. || 11 ||
In the temple of Vṛṣabhānu, the moonlight of the blossoming Śrī Rāsa-raṅga shines with rows of lamps,
adorning the neck of the crest-jewel of Goloka.
Having meditated upon that supreme [state], I wander upon the earth.
Śrī Bahulāśva said: Oh, what great fortune belongs to Vṛṣabhānu, whose daughter Rādhā has become! What was performed by Kalāvatī and Sucandra in their previous birth? (13)
Śrī Nārada said: O fortunate one, the son of Nṛga was the lord of kings Sucandra; he was a universal emperor, an expansion of Hari, and exceedingly handsome.
The Pitṛs had three mind-born daughters who were captivating;
they were known by the names Kalāvatī, Ratnamālā, and Menakā. (15)

The ancestors gave Kalāvatī to the wise Sucandra, who was a portion of Hari; they gave Ratnamālā to the son of Videha, and Menakā to Himādri, according to the prescribed rites and with wedding gifts, each according to their own desire.
Sītā was born from the Ratnamālā and Pārvatī from Menakā;
O high-minded one, the accounts of both are well-known in the Purāṇas.
Then Sucandra, in the forest on the bank of the Gomatī, performed the penance of Brahmā for twelve divine years with Kalāvatī. || 18 ||
Then Vidhi approached him and said, "Choose a boon.
Having heard this, [the sage] emerged from a portion of the anthill, assuming a divine form.
Having bowed to him, she said, "May there be for me divine liberation, the highest of the high.
Hearing that, the virtuous Kalāvatī, being distressed, spoke to Brahmā.
For it is traditionally held that the husband alone is the supreme deity for women;
if he attains liberation, what then will be my fate? (21)
"Without him I shall not live; if you grant me liberation, I, overwhelmed by the loss of my husband, shall cast a curse upon you. (22)
The illustrious Brahmā said: "Terrified by your curse, I am indeed unable to make my boon false.
Therefore, go to heaven together with the lord of your life."
Having enjoyed pleasures for a time, you two shall be born on earth in the land of Bhārata, between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, at the end of the Dvāpara age.
When Rādhikā, the manifest beloved of the most perfect Supreme Being, becomes your daughter, then you two shall attain liberation.
Śrī Nārada said: Thus, by means of that divine and unfailing boon of Brahmā,
Kalāvatī and Sucandra both became [reborn] on earth.
In Kānyakubja, Kalāvatī was the divine daughter of King Bhalandana; she was born from a sacrificial fire-pit and possessed the memory of her former births.
Sucandra, known as Vṛṣabhānu, was born in the house of Surabhānu;
a preeminent cowherd who remembered his past lives, he was like another Kāmadeva. || 28 ||
The high-minded King Nanda brought about their union,
as those two who remembered their past lives desired it by their own will.
The man who listens to the narrative of Vṛṣabhānu and Kalāvatī,
being liberated from all sins, shall attain union with Kṛṣṇa.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Śrī Rādhikā," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Once, in that excellent city of Śrī Mathurā,
the authoritative sage Garga was appointed as the family priest by all the best of the Yadus at the will of Śūra.
He arrived at the palace of King Sundara. || 1 ||
With its golden panels inlaid with diamonds, resounding with bees struck by the ears of lordly elephants,
and possessing temple-streams flowing like cascading waterfalls from the elephants' cheeks;
It was completely surrounded and adorned with sections of pavilions. || 2 ||
It was well-guarded by great and courageous men clad in armor, wielding bows, shields, and swords in their hands,
and by the strength of chariots, elephants, horses, banners, and troops arranged in circular formations.
The embryo beheld the royal sage Āhuka, the son of Śvaphalka, along with Devaka and Kaṃsa,
seated upon the supreme and lofty throne of Śrī Śakra.
He stood there, surrounded by parasols, canopies, and chowries.
Upon seeing that sage, the king suddenly rose from his seat and prostrated along with the Yādavas.
Having seated him and honored him upon an excellent throne, and having offered praise and circumambulated him, he stood bowed down in reverence. || 5 ||
Having bestowed his blessing upon the king, the sage Garga inquired after the welfare of the monarch and all others;
then the high-minded Ṛṣi spoke to Śrī Devaka, the most illustrious of the Yadus, who was possessed of great power and skilled in statesmanship.
The illustrious Garga said:
"Apart from the daughter of Śūra, there is no one among the kings on earth who could be considered by me as the best choice, even after reflecting upon this here and there for many days."
Therefore, O god among men, give Śrī Devakī, your own daughter, to Vasudeva as his bride; marry her according to the sacred rites.
Śrī Nārada said: Having then made a firm resolve regarding the city,
he who was the most excellent among all upholders of dharma approached Śrī Devaka.
Then, at the desire of Garga, having performed the auspicious rites for the sake of Vasudeva’s boon, he gave his daughter in marriage.
Having performed the wedding, Śauri, together with that daughter of King Devaka, mounted an exceedingly beautiful chariot, well-adorned for the journey and drawn by horses.
He ascended [the vehicle] which was adorned with gold and jewels.
Desiring exceedingly to do what was pleasing to his sister, Kaṃsa grasped the reins of the galloping horses;
yet, surrounded by a fourfold army, he then drove the steeds with a heart devoted to compassion and affection for Śauri.
A thousand female slaves, ten thousand elephants as a noble dowry, a hundred thousand horses,
a hundred thousand chariots, and two hundred thousand cows.
King Devaka indeed gave [her] to his daughter.
A great sound arose from the kettledrums, clay drums, horns, *dhundhurī*, lutes, cymbals, and flutes of the Yadus as they moved about.
And may there be auspiciousness on the path at the time of departure. || 12 ||
At that very moment, a voice from the sky said to Kaṃsa:
"Indeed, her eighth offspring will be your slayer; you do not even know her as she stands upon the chariot."
Having grasped the reins, you carry [the load], yet you are ignorant. || 13 ||
Devoted to evil company and exceedingly cruel, Kaṃsa—shameless, merciless, and of fierce deeds—took up a sharp sword in his hand and resolved to kill his own sister, seizing her by the hair. 14.
The musicians stood before him devoid of their instruments, for they were indeed startled;
while all those with white faces remained there, Śauri, the best among the virtuous, quickly spoke to him.
Śrī Vasudeva said: O Lord of the Bhojas, you alone are the one who brings glory to the Bhoja clan, having [slain] the Asuras Bhauma, Māgadha, Baka, Vatsa, and Bāṇa.
Your virtues are praiseworthy to those who desire to fight you in battle; how then could you, such as you are, slay your own sister here with a sword? (16)
Having recognized that Bakī was indeed a woman intent on fighting you, you did not engage in battle according to the conduct of royal policy;
rather, she was treated by you as a sister for the sake of peace.
But this sister is right here before you; what need is there for deliberation?
Your younger sister has gone there for her wedding; she is a young girl, as pitiable as a daughter, and always auspicious.
O Lord of Mathurā, you ought not to kill her here.
Your mental disposition is fixed upon removing the suffering of the distressed. || 18 ||
Śrī Nārada said: Although thus enlightened, Kaṃsa— being extremely wicked and devoted to evil company— did not heed it.
Then, having considered the course of time for Hari,
Śauri spoke again to Kaṃsa, who had sought his protection.

Śrī Vasudeva said: "O Lord, let there never be fear for her; hear that which was spoken by the voice of the gods. Since it was said, 'I shall give you sons,' let there be no distress for her regarding the birth of her offspring."
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard and deliberated upon the words of Śauri, Kaṃsa then praised them and quickly went home.
Then Śauri, overcome with fear by the daughter of Devaka’s king, returned home. || 21 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Vasudeva’s Marriage," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Śrī Nārada said: Frightened, he did not flee; rather, ten thousand warriors dispatched by Kaṃsa, equipped with weapons, besieged the palace of Śauri. || 1 ||
In due course of time, Śauri begot eight sons upon Devakī,
and then, year after year, he also begot a single daughter, the eternal Māyā.
Indeed, having first brought forth a son named Kīrtimān, Nandagopa,
who knew the highest purpose, approached Kaṃsa and gave him to him.
Kaṃsa indeed felt compassion for Śauri, who was established in truthful speech;
for a virtuous person cannot endure suffering, and who indeed would not have patience for the truth? (4)
Kaṃsa said:
"Let this boy go home; indeed, I have no fear of him.
I shall kill the eighth child of you two, without a doubt. (5)
Śrī Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus, Vasudeva returned home with his son;
he did not believe even slightly in the words of that evil-minded one.
Then, having bowed to me who had arrived from the sky and having worshipped me, the son of Ugrasena asked about the intention of the gods; listen to what I told him.
O lord of kings, all the Vasus beginning with Nanda, the gods beginning with Vṛṣabhānu, and the cowherd women beginning with Vedakā reside upon this earth.
Vasudeva and the other gods, the Vṛṣṇis in Mathurā, and all the women beginning with Devakī—these are certainly deities; this is the certainty.
Indeed, all those who are eighth [in order] from the counting of seven times are to be slain by this [mantra] according to their number; or else, the movement of the gods is from left to right.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus to him, when I had departed and he had set his mind upon slaying the Daityas,
Kaṃsa, suddenly overcome by anger, resolved to kill the Yadus.
Then, having bound Vasudeva and Devakī with firm shackles,
he crushed that infant born from Devakī’s womb upon the surface of a stone.
Remembering his past lives, he killed each creature as soon as it was born out of fear of Viṣṇu;
thus, due to his wicked disposition, he undoubtedly became a malevolent spirit (bhūta) upon the earth.
Then Ugrasena, the lord of the Yādavas and king of men, being enraged,
restrained the one named Kaṃsa, who had acted as Vasudeva’s ally.
Seeing Kaṃsa’s evil intent, the great warriors rose up;
those followers of Ugrasena, swords in hand, provided protection. || 15 ||
Seeing Ugrasena’s followers, Kaṃsa’s warriors rose up;
a battle took place between them in the middle of the assembly hall.
At the gateway as well, a battle broke out among the heroes;
ten thousand people met their death by sword-strokes. || 17 ||
Then Kaṃsa, seizing a mace, crushed his father’s army;
some, struck by Kaṃsa’s mace, had their foreheads split open.
With their feet severed, their faces split, their hopes shattered, and their arms lopped off—with heads turned downward or upward, still clutching weapons—they fell in an instant. (19)
Vomiting blood, the heroes fainted and met their end;
the assembly hall appeared crimson from the flowing of gore.
Thus, having struck down his formidable enemies, the wicked Kaṃsa,
intoxicated with pride and filled with rage, seized his father, the king of kings.
Having seized him from his royal throne and bound him with ropes, that wicked man,
together with his friends and other kings, imprisoned him in a jail.
Having seated himself upon the throne of the Madhus and Śūrasenas— a land possessing every excellence— he himself ruled the kingdom.
All the Yādavas, being oppressed and perceiving the end of time, quickly entered various regions in the four directions under the pretext of visiting their kinsmen.
When Devakī’s seventh pregnancy— which increases both joy and sorrow—
had been transferred by Yogamāyā from Rohiṇī to Vraja, [the Lord became manifest] as Ananta.
"Alas! Where has the child gone? cried the people of Mathurā.
Then, in the month of Bhādrapada, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, under the Svāti asterism, on a Wednesday, after five days had passed since [the birth] in Vraja,
and while he was surrounded by the five planets situated in their exaltations;
When the ascendant is named Libra at midday. || 27 ||
While the gods rained down a shower of beautiful flowers and the clouds released drops of water,
the Lord was born from the wife of Vasudeva.
Illuminating the house of Ānanda with his own radiance. || 28 ||
Nanda, performing the birth-rites for the infant,
gave a million cows to the brahmins and summoned cowherds who were skilled singers.
With its cries, it spreads great auspiciousness. || 29 ||

Dvaipāyana, along with Devala, Devarāta, Vasiṣṭha, and Vācaspati, as well as myself, arrived and took our seats right there; being gratified by the water for the feet and other offerings prepared by Nanda, he remained pleased.
King Nanda said:
"Who is this beautiful boy, whom no one else can equal anywhere?
How is it that he was born only five days ago? Tell me that, O great sage. (31)
Śrī Vyāsa said:
O Nanda, how great is your fortune! This eternal Śeṣa has been born as an infant to Vasudeva in Devakī within the city of Mathurā.
"By the will of Kṛṣṇa, he has been led from her womb to the auspicious Rohiṇī;
O King Nanda, you shall behold him, who is difficult to attain even for yogis. (33)
"I am the great sage Vedavyāsa, come here for the purpose of seeing him;
therefore, show us your form as a child, which is higher than the highest. (34)
Śrī Nārada said:
Then Nanda, filled with wonder, showed him the child Śeṣa;
seeing Him seated upon the swing, the son of Satyavatī bowed and spoke. (35)
Śrī Vyāsa said:
O God of gods, O Blessed One, O Protector of desires, salutations be unto you!
Salutations to Ananta, to Śeṣa; salutations directly to you, Rāma! || 36 ||
Salutations ever to you, Saṃkarṣaṇa, the upholder of the earth, the full one, whose nature is self-effulgence, the wielder of the plow, and the thousand-headed one.
O Revatīramaṇa, you are indeed Baladeva, the elder brother of Acyuta;
O Halāyudha, slayer of Pralamba, O Puruṣottama, protect me! (38)
Salutations again and again to Bala, to Balabhadra, to the one whose banner is the palmyra tree;
salutations to you, the dark-clad, the fair-complexioned, the son of Rohiṇī. || 39 ||
You alone are indeed the enemy of Dhenuka, the enemy of Muṣṭika, and the enemy of Kumbhāṇḍa;
you are the enemy of Rukmin, the enemy of Kūpakarṇa, the enemy of Kūṭa, and the slayer of Balvala.
You are the divider of the Yamunā, the drawer of Hastināpura, the enemy of Dvivida, the lord of the Yādavas, and the ornament of the Vraja region. || 41 ||
You are the slayer of Kaṃsa’s brother, the Lord who undertakes pilgrimages, and the manifest preceptor of Duryodhana; protect me, protect the world, O Lord! 42.
Victory, victory to you, O Acyuta, God, higher than the highest, yourself infinite, whose fame has reached the ends of the quarters;
homage to you, the bestower of boons upon the gods, the lords of sages, and the lords of serpents!
Salutation to the one who is the Musalin, the Balin, and the Halin. || 43 ||
Whoever here constantly recites this hymn shall attain the supreme abode of Hari;
he shall possess all strength in the world and be a crusher of his enemies.
For him there is victory; his own wealth is his true treasure. || 44 ||
Śrī Nārada said: Having circumambulated Balarāma a hundred times and bowed down before him, O Lord, Dvaipāyana, the son of Parāśara, [was honored] by them.
The sage Bādarāyaṇa, possessed of vast intellect, went to the Sarasvatī river, the son of Satyavatī. || 45 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Balabhadra," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Śrī Nārada said:
The most perfect one, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself,
who is higher than the highest, first entered the mind of Vasudeva.
The high-minded Vasudeva, resembling the sun, the moon, and fire,
became exceedingly radiant, like another manifest sacrifice itself.
When Kṛṣṇa, the granter of fearlessness to all, had arrived in Devakī’s womb,
she shone in that house like lightning amidst a thick cloud.
Beholding her so radiant with splendor, Kaṃsa, overcome by fear, said:
"This destroyer of my life has arrived; previously she was not like this."
Saying, "I shall kill him as soon as he is born," he remained overwhelmed with fear,
seeing Hari everywhere and reflecting upon his former enemy.
"Aha! Even Kṛṣṇa himself is seen through the persistence of enmity;
therefore, the asuras cultivate enmity for the sake of attaining Kṛṣṇa."
Then Brahmā and the other gods, together with the lords of sages such as ourselves, arrived above the house of Śauri and, having bowed down to him, offered hymns of praise.
The gods said:

"That which exists as the supreme causeless cause amidst states such as waking and the rest, and upon which the qualities (guṇas) move by taking recourse—into this the great hosts of senses and deities do not enter; salutations to Him, who is like a fire with its widespread sparks."
This one, the most powerful among the powerful, is not able to grasp it;
neither illusion nor sound can make it an object of perception.
Therefore, that Brahman is full, immortal, supreme, and profoundly tranquil.
We have gone for refuge to the pure one, who is higher than the highest. || 9 ||

We bow to that very Kṛṣṇa, who is higher than the full and most perfectly complete, from whom indeed proceed the creation and other cosmic processes through hosts of incarnations—such as portions, sub-portions, sub-sub-portions, and digits—as well as those endowed with the fullness of divine immersion (āveśa). || 10 ||

Throughout the Manvantaras, the Yugas, and the Kalpas that have passed and will come, You assume Your own form through a portion of Your parts; yet even now, You manifest Your most perfectly full splendor.
Having established Dharma upon the earth, you spread auspiciousness everywhere.

O root of bliss, that which is difficult to attain and inaccessible even to the most distinguished yogis becomes accessible to those whose pure hearts melt with the yoga of devotion; as you move slowly, [grant us] that [attainment].
We bear the pollen from the nectar of his lotus feet. || 12 ||
Just as before, here you are, possessing a lovely form,
wondrous and enchanting even to hundreds of millions of Kandarpas,
bearing the splendor of the abode of Goloka.
