We meditate upon the Lord of Rādhā, who bears the weight of the earth as his foremost wealth. || 13 ||
Śrī Nārada said: Then the gods, headed by Brahmā, together with the sages, bowed to Hari;
singing and praising him, they returned to their own abodes with joy.
Then, O lord of the Maithila kings, at the time of Hari’s birth,
the sky became stainless and the ten directions were pure.
The stars became radiant, and the circle of the earth was serene;
the rivers, streams, oceans, and lakes possessed clear waters.
Thousand-petaled lotuses and hundred-petaled ones bloomed on all sides,
their pollen falling as they were stirred by the touch of the breezes.
In them, honeybees hummed and colorful birds sang;
cool, slow-moving breezes, laden with fragrance, blew.
The provinces, villages, and cities became prosperous and auspicious;
the gods, brahmins, trees, and cows were all enveloped in happiness. (19)
Divine drums resounded, filled with cries of victory;
everywhere, O Great King, there was the highest auspiciousness for all.
The Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Kinnaras, and Cāraṇas sang,
while the gods, having excellent leaders, praised him supremely with hymns of praise.
In heaven, the Gandharvas and Vidyādharīs danced with joy,
as did the Pārijātaka, Mandāra, Mālatī, and Sumanā flowers.
The foremost of the gods released [the waters], and the clouds thundered over the water;
on the eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, on a Wednesday, under the Dhātṛ constellation, during the Harṣaṇa yoga, in the Taurus sign,
at midnight, when the moon was in conjunction with the constellation of the Lord of Stars (Śravaṇa).
In a time shrouded in darkness, Hari manifested visibly within Devakī in the house of Śauri, like a fire in a sacrificial altar within a forest.
He who possesses a shimmering, variegated,
and captivating [necklace], who bears the radiant Kaustubha gem, and who is adorned with the luster of a girdle, anklets, and armlets.
Wearing a crown and earrings like the rising morning sun.
Wearing trembling, wonderful fire-bracelets, girdled with a lightning-bright cord,
and adorned with a lotus-garland humming with bees;
Clad in divine garments of fresh Jāmbūnada gold. || 26 ||
The supreme [form], possessing divine beauty like a cloud with lightning, bearing a face with clusters of moving dark locks of hair, dispelling darkness with its shimmering rays.
It was auspicious, beautiful, and lotus-eyed. || 27 ||
Adorned with various ornaments of exquisite craftsmanship, eternally enchanting the minds of millions of gods,
he is the most perfect, higher than the highest.
Intent upon the playing of musical instruments and the sound of the kalaveṇu flute. || 28 ||
Beholding that son, Hari— the best of the Yadus— his eyes blossoming with joy at the festival of his birth,
then quickly [bestowed gifts] upon the assembly of brahmins.
With a devout mind, he gave a million cows.
Having prostrated before him with hymns of praise, Harimānakadundubhi, filled with wonder and with the dawning of great joy, offered his laudation.
Free from fear, he stood in the birth-chamber with palms joined in reverence. || 30 ||
Śrī Vasudeva said:
You who are one, yet appear manifold through the qualities of nature; you are its destroyer, its progenitor, and its protector;
untainted by the colors of the body like a crystal—O Lord of the World, I bow down to you. 31.
Abiding here like fire within fuel, which is both internal and external like the sky,
its support is like the earth— the witness of all.
To you, who pervade all, homage is like the wind [that moves through] space. || 32 ||
You were born solely for the sake of removing the heavy burden of the earth;
you are the protector of the cows, the gods, the twice-born, and your own calves.
You are the most excellent of supreme beings in my home upon this earth.
O Lord of the World, protect me from the sinful Kaṃsa.
Śrī Nārada said: Having recognized Śyāmasundara, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, as the most perfect Supreme Being, Devakī, the goddess of all deities, bowed down to him and then spoke.
Śrī Devakī said: O Kṛṣṇa! O Lord beyond the countless universes! O Supreme Controller! O You whose banner is the abode of Goloka! O Primordial God!
O Lord Pūrṇeśa, O Perfect One, O Most Perfect Lord, protect me from the sin of Kaṃsa, O Supreme God! 35.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard that, the Blessed One Kṛṣṇa himself, the most perfect Supreme Being and the destroyer of all suffering, spoke with a smile to Devakī and Vasudeva.
The Blessed One said:
"This Pṛśni is devoted to her husband, and you were Sutapā, seeking offspring, in a previous creation."
By the command of Brahmā, you two have performed supreme divine penance while subsisting on nothing but water.
When the Manvantara periods had passed,
you two, seeking offspring, performed supreme austerity; then I became pleased with you both.
"Choose a supreme boon; that shall be granted by me," I then said. || 38 ||
"Upon hearing what was said by you both, let there indeed be a son for us who is like you.
Having said, "So be it," when I, Prajāpati, had departed, the couple became [parents] through their own deed.
"Having thoroughly reflected upon that which arose from her [Aditi], the Supreme Lord declared, 'There is no son whatsoever equal to me in this world.
Furthermore, in a second period of time, I became Upendra-Vāmana, renowned on earth as Śrī-Pṛśnigarbha. (40)
Therefore, having led me today to the one who is higher than the highest, please bring me to the palace of Nanda;
thus, there shall be no further fear from Akrūra, the son of Ugrasena.
Having taken your daughter [with you], you two shall become happy. || 41 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having become silent there while the two of them were looking on,
Hari made his visible form unmanifest and became a child, just as an actor does on stage.
Then, as Śauri took him up in his arms and prepared to depart,
Yogamāyā spontaneously entered into the wife of Nanda at Vraja.
While she lay there, and while the universe was asleep and its guardians were slumbering, all the gates were opened, their chains and bolts shattered. (44)
And as Vasudeva departed, his head adorned by Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
darkness was instantly destroyed of its own accord, just as it is at the rising of the sun.
While the clouds rained down in the sky, the self-ruling thousand-faced one followed Śauri,
warding off the torrential downpour with his long hoods.
The Kālindī, the best of rivers, whose turbulent currents were filled with whirlpools and who carried lions, serpents, and other creatures, immediately gave way for him. 47.
Having reached Nanda’s cowherd settlement, which was entirely fast asleep,
he quickly placed the infant upon Yaśodā’s bed and beheld her.
Taking her daughter with him, Śauri departed from the house again;
having crossed the illustrious Yamunā, he remained in his own abode as before.
Having failed to recognize whether it was a son or a daughter who had been born, the cowherd woman Yaśomatī,
being exhausted, fell asleep upon her own bed in a sleep of bliss.
Then, hearing the sound of crying, the guards arrived;
having gone to the royal palace, they spoke to the heroic Kaṃsa.
Terrified with fear, Kaṃsa went quickly to the lying-in chamber;
then his sister, weeping and distressed for her child, spoke to her brother.
Śrī Devakī said:
"Since my sons have all perished, grant me at least one daughter;
you ought not to kill a woman, O brother, for you are compassionate toward the distressed. (53)
"O auspicious one, I am their younger sister, my son has been killed, and I have been cast into prison;
you ought to grant me your auspicious daughter as well. (54)
Śrī Nārada said:
While the tearful and deluded mother repeatedly covered her son with her garment,
that wicked man rebuked her, snatched him from her lap, and carried him away.
Devoted to evil company, wicked, and the lowest of the Yadu clan,
that villain seized his sister’s daughter by the feet and dashed her against the surface of a stone.
Leaping up from Kaṃsa’s hand, she quickly ascended into the sky upon a divine hundred-petaled lotus chariot drawn by a thousand horses.
Seated upon a white, swaying chowrie, the divine-eyed Māyā appeared,
possessing eight arms equipped with weapons and attended by her attendants;
resembling a hundred suns in brilliance and possessing a voice like a thundercloud, she spoke to Kaṃsa.
Śrī Yogamāyā said:
"The most perfect Supreme Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, has appeared in person.
Where indeed is your slayer? You are grieving in vain for one who is already gone. (59)
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus to him, the Goddess then departed for the Vindhya mountain;
the Blessed Yogamāyā indeed assumed many names.
Then Kaṃsa was struck with wonder upon hearing Māyā’s supreme words;
he released Devakī and Vasudeva from their bonds.
Kaṃsa said:
"I am a sinner, a doer of evil deeds, a rogue, and the lowest of the Yadu clan.
Forgive me for my actions on this earth, I who have been the slayer of your sons."
"O sister, listen to me, O Śauri; I believe this has been brought about by Time, by which I am being driven away like a mass of clouds by the wind. (63)
I have placed my trust in the words of the gods, yet those gods themselves speak falsehoods;
I do not know where my enemy has arisen, nor in which place he was mentioned by her.
Śrī Nārada said: Thus Kaṃsa, weeping with a tearful face,
fell at their feet and performed supreme service, demonstrating his affection for them both.
Aha! On this earth, what could not be accomplished by the side-glances of the most perfect Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, which are so skilled in bestowing gifts?
Then, at dawn, the wicked Kaṃsa summoned the great asuras, headed by Pralamba, and spoke to them through his illusory power (māyā).
Kaṃsa said:
"Indeed, one who will bring about my end has been born on this earth, as told by Yogamāyā.
You shall kill infants, both those less than ten days old and those more than ten days old."
The Daityas said:
"When you, a duelist, stand ready with your bow in battle, the gods are terrified by its twang; how can you imagine that they cause you any fear? (69)

Cows, Brahmins, virtuous people, the Vedas, the gods, Dharma and the others, as well as Viṣṇu—these are indeed his manifestations; it is taught that upon their destruction, the strength of the Daityas perishes.
If that enemy of yours, Mahāviṣṇu, has been born upon the surface of the earth, this is the means for his destruction: the slaughter of cows and other such beings. (71)
Thus, the exceedingly fierce and wicked Daityas, incited by Kaṃsa,
rushed toward the sky from the cows and other animals, and they struck down the newborn infants.
Entering every house across the land as far as the ocean,
the Daityas, assuming forms at will, moved about like serpents.
There, moreover, the fierce Daityas sent by Kaṃsa—like those on a wrong path—were struck down by the monkey;
he became like one intoxicated with wine or possessed by a spirit.
O Vaideha, O Maithila, O lord of men, O devotee of Upendra, O foremost among the righteous, O Janaka of great asceticism and majesty!
O King, this [conduct] is indeed a reproach upon the virtuous on earth.
It cuts through all fourfold objects of meaning, O Bahulāśva. || 75 ||

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 11 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Then, having heard that the festival for the birth of his son had occurred, Nanda summoned the brāhmaṇas at the hour of dawn and caused auspicious rites to be performed.
Having performed the birth-rites according to the prescribed rules, the high-minded King Nanda joyfully gave a hundred thousand cows as sacrificial fees to the Brahmins.
Bowing low, he gave to the brahmins mountains one krośa in extent, with peaks of gold and ridges of jewels, as well as lakes filled with the seven kinds of grain.
Mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, conchs, and other instruments, as well as kettledrums, resounded repeatedly;
singers sang at the gate, and courtesans danced.
With banners, golden pitchers, canopies, and auspicious archways,
variegated and of many colors, the palace of Śrī Nanda shone brilliantly.
The streets, lanes, doorways, walls, courtyards, and altars, as well as the towers,
pavilions, and assembly halls, shone with fragrant waters and silken cloths.
The cows had horns of gold and necks adorned with shimmering golden garlands;
they were decorated with red blankets and resounded with the tinkling of bells and anklets.
With yellow tails, accompanied by their calves, marked with the signs of young women, smeared with turmeric and saffron, and variegated with various minerals. || 8 ||
At the gate of Śrī Nanda, the bulls— upholders of the dharma of bulls— shone here and there, captivating the mind with their bushy tails and scented waters.
White calves, adorned with golden garlands and resplendent with pearl necklaces,
wandered here and there with their feet jingling with anklets.
Having heard of his son’s festival, Vṛṣabhānuvara likewise arrived at Nanda’s palace mounted upon an elephant together with Kalāvatī.
Nanda, the nine Upanandas, and likewise the six Vṛṣabhānus,
all arrived as well, bringing various offerings with them.
Adorned with garlands upon their uṣṇīṣas, beautified by yellow tunics, their hair bound with peacock feathers and guñjā berries, they are decorated with forest garlands. || 13 ||
Those cowherds also arrived—carrying flutes, holding staffs in their hands, adorned with beautiful leaf-shaped tilakas, and wearing bound hair-locks as part of their attire. 14.
Dancing, singing aloud, and shaking their garments,
others were bearded children accompanied by various offerings.
Taking many offerings of fresh butter, milk, curd, and ghee,
the elderly women, carrying staffs in their hands, arrived at the palace of Nanda.
Speaking to one another about the festival for the son of the Lord of Vraja, they were overwhelmed with states of love and agitated by tears of their own bliss. (17)
When the festival for the birth of his son occurred, Nanda, his eyes overflowing with tears of joy,
honored them all according to the prescribed rites with tilaka and other offerings.
The cowherds said: "O Lord of Vraja, O Nanda! A festival for the birth of a son has occurred for you who were childless and longed for one; what greater auspiciousness than this could there be? (19)
This day has been shown to you by destiny after many days;
we have become fulfilled by beholding the son of the Delight of Śrī.
When you take that most wicked one and lead him away, saying "He is a deluder," and when we are left in a state of being cherished, only then will there be happiness for us.
Śrī Nanda said:
"By virtue of your auspicious blessings, this beautiful happiness has arisen;
for I am indeed a servant following the commands of the cowherds who dwell in Vraja. (22)

Having heard of the wonderful birth of the son of King Nanda, the gopīs immediately abandoned their household chores and quickly went from the houses of the kings of Vraja to the palace of the King of Vraja, their hearts filled with rising joy and the great limbs of their bodies brimming with emotion.
All of them, departing from their own homes in the city of Ānandamandira, were hurrying here and there;
their garments, ornaments, and hair-ties were loosened by their carriage.
On the king's path, pearls were released by the earth once more. || 24 ||
They shone with the tinkling of anklets, new armlets, golden robes, sandals, necklaces, jeweled earrings, and girdles;
with the sacred thread upon their shoulders, bracelets, and forehead-marks, they possessed the flawless radiance of the full moon’s orb. (25)

O King, having performed the ritual of lifting the child onto their laps with auspicious powders of *rājikā*, salt, and special night-herbs, along with wheat, mustard, and barley, they bestowed all those blessings upon his face; they sang and proclaimed the fame of Yaśodā.
The gopīs said:
"Excellent, excellent, Yaśodā! By good fortune, by good fortune, O Queen of Vraja!
Blessed, most blessed is that supreme womb by which this son was begotten. (27)
"Indeed, after a long time, your desire has been fulfilled by the Lord;
protect this lotus-eyed child, who possesses a beautiful smile and is dark and handsome. (28)
Śrī Yaśodā said:
By the blessings of your compassion, supreme happiness has been born for me;
by good fortune, may it likewise be supreme for you all as well from this moment forward. (29)
"O highly intelligent Rohiṇī, perform the worship of the residents of Vraja and of the noble families who have arrived, according to their desires and wishes. (30)
Śrī Nārada said: Rohiṇī, though she was a princess, had hands inclined toward giving;
even when prompted there, that highly noble-minded woman gave.
Fair-complexioned, clad in divine garments, and adorned with jewel ornaments,
Rohiṇī herself wandered about, honoring the inhabitants of Vraja.
When Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the most perfect Supreme Being, arrived in person at Vraja, while human musical instruments resounded, a great cry of "Victory! arose.
Delighted, the cowherds and cowherd women there sprinkled Him with curd, milk, and fresh butter from the previous day's milking, and they sang loudly to one another.
When the entire city, both inside and out, was covered on all sides with a mire of curd, the elderly and those of stout bodies fell down, and were mocked by others. (35)
The Sūtas are said to be experts in the Purāṇas; the Māgadhas are those who proclaim the genealogies; and the Vandins are those of pure intellect whose speech is appropriate to the occasion. (36)
To each of them, King Nanda gave a thousand cows individually, as well as garments, ornaments, jewels, horses, and elephants— all of them.
Like a rain-cloud, King Nanda, the lord of Vraja, showered abundant wealth upon all the bards and panegyrists.
Treasure, accomplishment, prosperity, enjoyment, and liberation are as if rolling about in every house and on every street; indeed, no one has any desire for them.
Sanatkumāra, Kapila, Śuka, Vyāsa, and others, along with Haṃsadatta, Pulastya, and the rest, went to Brahmā together with me.
Mounted upon a swan, golden-hued, wearing a crown and earrings that shimmer,
four-faced and the creator of the Vedas, he illuminates the circle of the quarters.
Likewise, Maheśvara, richly adorned, followed him mounted upon his bull;
Ravi himself was mounted upon his chariot, and Purandara was mounted upon his elephant.
Vāyu is mounted upon a Khañjana bird, Yama has a buffalo as his vehicle,
Dhanada is mounted upon the Puṣpaka chariot, and Kṣapeśvara (the Lord of Night) is mounted upon a deer.
Vītihotra (Agni) is mounted upon a goat; Varuṇa is seated upon a crocodile;
Kārtikeya is seated upon a peacock; and Bhāratī has a swan as her vehicle.
Lakṣmī, mounted upon Garuḍa; she known as Durgā, borne by a lion; Pṛthivī, assuming the form of a cow; and [the goddess] seated in a celestial chariot all arrived.
The sixteen principal Mother-goddesses (Mātṛkās), possessing divine complexions, were mounted upon swings;
and Ṣaṣṭhī was mounted upon a palanquin, wielding a sword and holding a staff.
Maṅgala is mounted upon a monkey; Budha is remembered as being mounted upon a partridge; Gīṣpati is seated upon a black antelope; and Śukra has a gavaya for his vehicle.
Saturn, mounted upon a crocodile, and Rāhu, the son of Siṃhikā, seated on a camel— resembling ten million rising suns— arrived at the palace of Nanda.
Having approached Nanda’s palace, which was filled with a great clamor and crowded with hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses, the gods stood there for a moment and then departed.
Having bowed down to and beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, who was the most perfect and in the form of a child, the gods then offered him supreme praise.
Then, having beheld Kṛṣṇa, all the gods, led by Brahmā and accompanied by the sages,
departed for their own abodes, filled with joy and overwhelmed by love.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Great Festival of Śrī Nanda," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
When Nanda had gone to the glorious Mathurā to inquire after Śauri, to pay tribute to the king, and to report the festival of his son’s birth.
Sent by Kaṃsa, the wicked Pūtanā, a bringer of death,
wandered through cities, villages, and cowherd settlements with a gurgling sound.
Then, having reached Gokula, which was crowded with hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses,
she assumed a divine form with the body of a sixteen-year-old.
Neither the cowherds nor the cowherd-wives could restrain that beautiful woman,
who was like Śacī, Vāṇī, Ramā, Rambhā, and Rati, as she cast them aside.
And while Rohiṇī and Yaśodā were being assailed, she, with her throbbing breasts,
took that child onto her lap and fondled him again and again.
She gave the infant her breast, which was enveloped by the most terrible Kālakūṭa poison;
Hari, overcome with rage, drank the bitter milk along with his own life-breaths.
Saying "Release me! Release me! as she ran with her breasts oppressed by pain, she led him outside and indeed became free from her illusory power.
With her eyes rolling, her body white, and weeping as she fell to the ground,
she caused the entire universe, along with its seven worlds and subterranean realms, to resound.
The earth with its islands trembled, and that was like a marvel;
she [the chariot] struck down firm, long trees that stood six krośas behind her on the surface of the ground.
O lord of kings, seeing that terrible and massive body, those cowherds cried out as he crushed [the mountain] with his diamond-hard limbs.
A child held by her fingers never lives;
yet she gazes with joy upon that smiling infant playing blissfully upon her breast. (11)
Seeing him yawning after drinking the milk, the women,
along with Yaśodā and Rohiṇī, were struck with wonder and placed him upon their breasts.
Taking the boy with them from all sides, they performed protective rites according to the prescribed rules,
using the meritorious, nectar-like waters of the Kālindī and by waving the cow's tail over him.
Having bathed him with cow urine and cow dust, they sang this: || 14 ||
The gopīs said:
May Śrī Kṛṣṇa protect your head; may Vaikuṇṭha protect your neck; may the Lord of Śvetadvīpa protect your ears; and may He who assumes the form of sacrifice protect your nose. (15)
May Nṛsiṃha protect your pair of eyes, may the son of Daśaratha protect your tongue, and may the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa protect your two lips.
May the kalās (parts) of Hari, Sanaka and the others, protect your cheeks directly; may Śvetavārāha protect your forehead, and Nārada protect your two eyebrows.
May Kapila protect the chin; may Dattātreya protect the chest;
may Ṛṣabha protect both shoulders; and may Matsya protect your hands. 18.
May Pṛthu, of vast prowess, constantly protect your staff-like arms;
may Kamaṭha protect your belly, and Dhanvantari protect your navel.
May Mohinī protect your private parts, and may Vāmana protect your hips; may Paraśurāma protect your back, and Bādarāyaṇa your thighs.
May Bala protect your two knees; may the Buddha protect your shanks;
and may Kalki, the Lord and Master of Dharma, protect your feet along with your ankles.
This divine and supreme armor of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which provides all protection,
was bestowed by the Blessed One upon Brahmā from the lotus of his navel.
Brahmā gave it to Śambhu; Śambhu gave it to Durvāsas;
and Durvāsas bestowed it upon the illustrious Yaśomatī in the palace of King Nanda.
Having performed this protection for him along with the cowherd women, Śrī Yaśomatī suckled him at her breast and gave great gifts to the Brahmins.
Then the cowherds, headed by Nanda, arrived from the city of Mathurā;
upon seeing the terrible one named Pūtanā, they became overwhelmed with fear.
Having cut that body with axes on the bank of the illustrious Yamunā,
the cowherds prepared many funeral pyres and indeed cremated her.
The fragrance of cardamom, cloves, sandalwood, tagara, and agaru rose from the burning of the pure body as smoke ascended. (27)
Alas, in the absence of Kṛṣṇa, to whom indeed shall we go for refuge here?
For He who purifies the fallen has granted the path of liberation even to Pūtanā.
Śrī Bahulāśva said:
Who was this Rākṣasī Pūtanā, the slayer of infants in the past, who possessed a wicked nature and poisoned breasts; how did she attain supreme liberation? (29)
Śrī Nārada said: Having seen the supreme form of Vāmana at Bali’s sacrifice,
Bali’s daughter Ratnamālā felt affection for him as if he were her own son.
If such a child, with that pure smile, should come to be, I shall indeed suckle him at my breast; by that, my mind will then be satisfied.
To the daughter of Bali, who was his supreme devotee, Hari, in the form of Vāmana,
granted her a boon, saying, "May your heart's desire be fulfilled even within your mind."
Whoever hears this liberation of Pūtanā by the divine Kṛṣṇa, who is higher than the highest,
shall possess devotion accompanied by love for him.
O Lord of Mithilā, is there not even the purification of the three aims of life? 34.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Pūtanā," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 13 ||
Thus has been narrated this divine and excellent account of the life of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
he who hears it with devotion and humility has achieved his life's purpose, without a doubt. (1)
Śrī Śaunaka said:
O Sage, having heard from your own lips the auspicious life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which is sweeter than even a fragment of nectar, we have truly attained our purpose.
O ascetic, tell me that: what did Bahulāśva—the devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the peaceful-souled, and the best among the virtuous—then ask the sage?
Śrī Garga said:
Then the righteous King, the lord of Mithilā, joyful and overwhelmed with love,
spoke to Nārada while remembering the Supreme Perfection.
Śrī Bahulāśva said:
I am blessed and I have achieved my life’s purpose through you, O performer of great deeds;
for indeed, association with the devotees of the Lord is difficult to attain and hard to accomplish.
O Sage, tell me what wonderful deed Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is himself a child, the manifest wonder, and affectionate toward his devotees, performed before me.
Śrī Nārada said:
Well asked by you, O King, who are devoted to the dharma of Kṛṣṇa!
Indeed, the company of the virtuous bestows peace upon everyone. (7)
Once, on the lunar mansion of Kṛṣṇa’s birth, Yaśodā, the wife of Nanda,
summoned the cowherds and cowherdesses and performed auspicious rites with the twice-born brahmins.
Clad in red garments, his limbs adorned with golden ornaments, holding a child whose lotus-eyes were smeared with collyrium,
dark-complexioned, and wearing a moon-shaped necklace encircled by shimmering emerald nails—
Having prostrated before the gods, he bestowed Sudhana upon the twice-born.
Having quickly placed her own son upon the swing on that auspicious day and honored all those cowherd women,
the gopī did not hear even the slightest sound from her son who had been born.
Amidst the cowherds going to and fro at their auspicious dwellings.
Right there, a demon named Utkaca, who had been incited by the wicked Kaṃsa and possessed a body like the wind, approached the cart and set about hurling it onto the head of the child.
Kṛṣṇa, for his part, indeed struck him with his fierce foot.
When the Daitya had been reduced to powder and his chariot had fallen, Vimala abandoned his body as the Wind-god and became pure;
then, having bowed to Hari, he was joined with a chariot yoked to a hundred horses.
He went to his own pure realm, the abode of Goloka.
Then Nanda and the other inhabitants of Vraja, along with all the cowherd women of Vraja, gathered together and spoke simultaneously to the children:
"How indeed has this cart fallen down by itself?"
"O sons of Vraja, you know that you are all well."
The children said:
"He was sitting on the swing, crying for milk while kicking his feet;
he struck the cart with his foot, and that is surely why it has fallen."
The cowherds and cowherd women, filled with wonder, placed no faith in the words of the child:
"Where is this three-month-old infant, and where is this bearing of such a burden? (15)
Taking the child onto her lap, Yaśodā, fearing the influence of evil planets,
had a sacrifice performed according to the rules by well-satisfied Brahmins.
Śrī Bahulāśva said: Who was this Daitya named Utkaca who was formerly so skilled?
Oh, great sage, how did he attain liberation through the touch of Kṛṣṇa’s feet? (17)
Śrī Nārada said:
O King of Mithilā, a Daitya named Utkaca, the son of Hiraṇyākṣa,
while going to the hermitage of Lomaśa, crushed the trees along the way.
Seeing that immensely powerful man named Utkaca, who was endowed with a gross physical body, the Brahmin, filled with rage, cursed him: "O evil-minded one, become bodiless! (19)
Due to the ripening of his karma, his body fell like the sloughed skin of a serpent;
immediately falling at his feet, the king of the Daityas spoke.
Utkaca said:
"O Sage, O ocean of mercy, show compassion toward me!
I do not know your power; O Lord, grant me a body. (21)
Śrī Nārada said:
Then that sage became pleased, having seen the hundredfold policy of Brahmā;
for even the anger of the virtuous bestows boons, so what need be said of him who is the supreme granter of the boon of liberation?
Śrī Lomaśa said:
"When this Cākṣuṣa Manvantara has passed, may you possess a body of wind;
and in the Vaivasvata Manvantara, there shall be liberation at the feet of Hari."
Śrī Nārada said:
Therefore, the Daitya Utkaca was liberated by the splendor of Lomaśa;
let there be salutations to the virtuous who are truly capable of both granting boons and pronouncing curses.
O King, once while she was fondling the child playing on her lap,
Śrī Nanda’s wife was unable to bear the weight of the mountain.
"Ah! How could this child be like a mountain?"—thus amazed, she immediately set him down upon the ground and said to no one: "This is not so! (26)
Urged on by Kaṃsa, the exceedingly powerful Daitya Tṛṇāvarta carried off the beautiful child as he was playing with a whirlwind.
There in Gokula, a blinding darkness arose accompanied by a terrible sound,
and for two ghaṭikās, the eyes became filled with dust.
Then Yaśodā did not see her son in the courtyard of the house;
deluded and weeping, she beheld terrible portents upon the rooftops of the dwelling.
And when she did not see her son and fell to the ground in a swoon,
she wept piteously and loudly, like a cow that has lost its calf.
Then the cowherd women, overwhelmed by love and affection,
wept as they looked here and there at the son of Nanda with tearful faces.
Tṛṇāvarta reached the sky at a height of a hundred thousand yojanas;
though he was oppressed, he considered the boy to be like Mount Sumeru upon his shoulder.
Then the Daitya prepared himself there to strike down Kṛṣṇa;
but the Supreme Lord Himself seized his throat.
When the Daitya cried out, "Release me! Release me!", the wondrous child Kṛṣṇa seized him by the throat with great force and deprived the Daitya of his life.
That light merged into the dark-complexioned Śrīghana like a flash of lightning;
the demon fell from the sky onto a rock along with the child. (35)
Even as his limbs were shattered and he fell, a great sound indeed arose;
all the quarters resounded with it, and the circle of the earth trembled.
Then all the cowherd women, seeing the child sitting upon his back while they were weeping silently, took him up simultaneously, gave him to their mother, and sang.
The cowherd women said:
"O Yaśodā, you are not at all fit to fondle this child;
no compassion has ever been seen in you, for you indeed become angry when spoken to. (38)
For when darkness has fallen, someone indeed abandons a child from their own lap;
yet by you, merciless as you are, the child was cast upon the ground in the midst of great terror.
Śrī Yaśodā said:
"I did not know how this child had become like a mountain, a heavy burden;
therefore, I placed him on the ground during a great and terrifying whirlwind. (40)
The gopīs said:
"Do not speak falsely, O auspicious Yaśodā, you who are free from distress!
This child has a mouth like milk; he is as light as a tuft of flowers. (41)
Śrī Nārada said: Then,
when the child had returned, the cowherd women and the cowherds, headed by Nanda, attained extreme joy, conversing with the people about his well-being.
Having taken the boy and repeatedly suckled him at her breast, Yaśodā smelled him on her chest and, being deluded, spoke to Rohiṇī with her garment. (43)
Śrī Yaśodā said:
"This one was granted to me by fate; I do not have many sons.
Yet, even for this one, many calamities indeed arrive in an instant. (44)
Today I have been released from the jaws of death; what will happen beyond this? What shall I do? Where shall I go? And where might my dwelling be hereafter? (45)
"O child, those Daityas who possess the essence of vajra, being merciless and terrible to behold, harbor enmity toward me; O Fate, O Fate, where is there happiness? (46)
Wealth, body, home, mansion, and various kinds of jewels—all these are indeed beyond one's control; may my child, however, remain well. (47)
"When I am victorious over my enemies as a youth, I shall then perform worship of Hari, give gifts, perform sacrifices, carry out works of public utility, and build a hundred temples. (48)
"O beloved Rohiṇī, my happiness depends on you alone, like a blind man relies on a staff; taking our son with me, I shall go to a land free from fear. (49)
Śrī Nārada said:
At that very moment, learned brāhmaṇas arrived at Nanda’s house;
they were honored by Yaśodā and Nanda and took their seats upon thrones.
The brāhmaṇas said:
"Do not grieve, O Nanda, O Yaśodā, Queen of Vraja!
We shall perform the protection rite for the infant; may he live long. (51)
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, those foremost of the twice-born [honored him] with tips of kuśa grass, fresh sprouts,
purifying jars, water, and hymns born of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Having caused the sacrifice to be performed according to the rules with auspicious rites by others,
they worshipped the fire according to the injunctions and established protection for the child.
The Brahmins said:
May Dāmodara protect the feet; may Viṣṭaraśravas protect the knees;
may Hari protect the thighs; and may Paripūrṇatama himself protect the navel. (54)
May the Lord of Rādhā protect your waist; may He who wears yellow garments protect your belly;
may Padmanābha protect your heart, and Govardhanoddhara your two arms. (55)
May the Lord of Mathurā protect my face, and may the Lord of Dvārakā protect my head; may the Destroyer of Asuras protect my back, and may the Blessed One himself protect me from all sides.
Whatever person should always recite these three verses of praise, great happiness shall be his, and no fear shall exist for him anywhere. (57)
Śrī Nārada said: Nanda gave them a hundred thousand cows, ten million pieces of gold, a thousand of the nine precious gems, and an excellent hundred thousand garments.
When the foremost of the twice-born had departed, Nanda, having restrained the cowherds,
honored them with beautiful garments and ornaments and fed them.
Śrī Bahulāśva said:
Who was this man Tṛṇāvarta in former times, this performer of meritorious deeds, who attained absorption into Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the most perfect Supreme Being? (60)
Śrī Nārada said: There was a powerful king born in the land of Pāṇḍu named Sahasrākṣa;
he was a devotee of Hari, steadfast in dharma, a performer of sacrifices, and intent on charity.
On the most divine bank of the Revā, thick with creepers and cane reeds,
he wandered about, sporting with a thousand women.
He did not bow down to the sage Durvāsas when he arrived in person;
then the sage pronounced a curse: "O evil-minded one, become a Rākṣasa! (63)
Then the sage granted a boon to the king who had fallen at his feet;
indeed, through the touch of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s form, he attained supreme liberation.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Asuras Śakaṭa and Tṛṇāvarta," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.

Yaśodā beheld Hari reclining on a swing made of gold and jewels— the dark-complexioned infant, whose gentle smile enchants the hearts of people, who dispels the pain of her gaze, and who bears a dot of ink upon his forehead.
He placed upon his own lap the one whose lotus-eyes were smeared with collyrium.
Drinking from his foot with faces whose hair-ties are dark blue, fresh, and soft; possessing wondrous limbs and extreme agility;
and adorned with the shimmering crescent moon upon the claws of the glorious man-lion.
Caressing him with great affection, the cowherd girl experienced supreme joy.
O King, as the infant, having drunk milk, yawned,
all the principles (tattvas) shone forth within his entire mouth;
and his mother [beheld] everything, including the Lord of the Gods (Indra) and ten million others.
Having seen him, she attained supreme fear and closed her eyes.

O King, she who had previously deceived the entire universe through her artifice before Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme and Most Perfect, became once again possessed of her wits when overcome with compassion for her own son; how can I describe the great ascetic power of Nanda’s wife? || 4 ||
Śrī Bahulāśva said:
What great austerity did Nanda perform together with Yaśodā, by which even Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra became their son? || 5 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Among the eight Vasus, Droṇa was the chief and lord of the earth;
though childless, he was a devotee of Viṣṇu and ruled the kingdom of the gods.
Once, O King, desiring a son and urged by Brahmā,
he went to Mount Mandara with his wife Dharā to perform austerities.
Then they subsisted on bulbs, roots, and fruits; after that, they ate only leaves;
then they drank only water; and finally, they remained in a desolate place without even water.
When an arbuda of years had passed while those two were performing that austerity,
Brahmā became pleased and, approaching them, said, "Choose a boon."
Emerging from the anthill together with his wife Dharā, Droṇa bowed to Brahmā,
honored him, and, filled with joy, spoke to that Lord.
Śrī Droṇa said:
O Brāhmaṇa, may we both possess constant devotion characterized by love for Kṛṣṇa, the most perfect Janārdana, who has become our son. 11.

"O Creator, by means of this [knowledge] we easily cross over the ocean of existence which is otherwise difficult to traverse; for us two who are performing penance, no other boon should be desired. (12)
The illustrious Brahmā said: "That boon which has been requested by you two from me is difficult to accomplish and hard to obtain;
nevertheless, let it bear fruit for you both in another birth."
Śrī Nārada said:
Droṇa became Nanda on earth, and she who was Dharā is remembered as Yaśodā.
Kṛṣṇa arrived at the cowherd settlement from his father’s city in order to fulfill the word of Brahmā.
The auspicious life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is sweeter than a fragment of nectar;
it was indeed heard from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa on the peak of Mount Gandhamādana.
And by the grace of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, I have achieved my purpose;
I have related this to you—what more do you wish to hear?
Śrī Bahulāśva said:
O great sage, tell me what the eternal Hari did while in the form of a child in the house of Nanda, along with Balarāma as well. 17.
Śrī Nārada said: Once, the great sage Garga Ācārya, accompanied by his disciples and urged by Vasudeva (Śauri), came in person to the palace of Nanda.
Having duly honored the best of sages with water for the feet and other offerings,
Nanda then circumambulated him and prostrated himself before him with his eight limbs touching the ground.
Śrī Nanda said: Today our ancestors, the gods, and our sacred fires have been fully satisfied;
our abode has become purified by the dust of your feet.
"O twice-born one, O great sage, perform the naming ceremony for my son;
O Lord, your arrival is difficult to attain even through meritorious pilgrimages. (21)
The illustrious Garga said: "I shall perform the naming ceremony for your son, of this there is no doubt;
I will relate the ancient account. Go now, Nanda, to a secluded place."
Śrī Nārada said:
Having raised them up with Nanda, Yaśodā, and the two children, Garga went to a secluded spot in Govraja and bestowed names upon them.
Having worshipped Gaṇanātha and the other deities, and having diligently purified the planets,
the great sage Garga-ācārya, his limbs radiant with joy, spoke to Nanda.
Listen also to the recitation of the name of this son of Rohiṇī:
for yogis indeed delight in him, or rather, he delights everywhere.
Because he delights his devotees with his qualities, the supreme ones know him as Rāma;
and because he draws forth [the world] from the womb, he is remembered as Saṃkarṣaṇa.
They know that the first [portion] is the remainder of all that remains, while the [subsequent] portion is strength due to its abundance of power;
O Nanda, listen now with vigilance to the names of your own sons as well. (27)
The syllable *ka* is the beloved of Kamalā (Lakṣmī), and the syllable *ṛ* is Rāma; these are instantly purifying to living beings and auspicious for the worlds. (28)
The letter *ṣa* is the Lord of the six qualities (*ṣaḍguṇapati*) and the dweller in Śvetadvīpa;
the letter *ṇa* is this Nārasiṃha, and the letter *a* is indeed the imperishable consumer of fire.
Likewise, these two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, as well as the two Visargas,
are completely merged within that pure Great Self (mahātman) in which the six perfections reside.
Because he is manifest as the most perfect one, he is proclaimed as Kṛṣṇa;
yet he assumes the colors white, red, and yellow according to the respective yugas.
At the end of the Dvāpara age and the beginning of the Kali age, this boy attained a dark complexion;
therefore, this son of Nanda became famous by the name Kṛṣṇa.
The Vasus are indeed the sense organs, and their deity is the mind itself;
and he who acts within that [mind] is also remembered as Vāsudeva. (33)
Rādhā, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, was born in the temple of Kīrti;
he is her manifest husband, and for that reason he is remembered as Rādhāpati (the Lord of Rādhā).
The most perfect one, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the master of countless universes, shines resplendent in his abode, Goloka. 35.
Thus, this child of yours has been born for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden, for the sake of slaying Kaṃsa and others, and for the protection of the devotees. (36)
O Bhārata, his names are infinite and secret even to the Vedas;
they will manifest through his divine sports, and one should feel no wonder at those deeds.
O Nanda, how great is your good fortune that this Supreme Person, higher than the highest, dwells in your house in the form of an infant! 38.
Having spoken thus, when Garga had departed, the high-minded King Nanda, together with his wife, considered himself filled with blessings and was greatly rejoiced. (39)
Then Garga, the best of sages, the foremost among the wise and the giver of knowledge, went to the city of Vṛṣabhānu, which was richly adorned by the banks of the Kālindī. (40)
The Brahmin was adorned with an umbrella like a second Indra, and graced by a staff as if he were the King of Dharma himself standing manifest. || 41 ||
With his splendor illuminating the quarters like another manifest sun,
he held a book and wore a girdle, appearing like a second Brahmā.
Adorned with white garments, standing like the god Viṣṇu himself—
seeing that tiger among sages, he rose up suddenly and respectfully.
Having immediately bowed his head, he stood facing him with palms joined in reverence;
and having seated the sage upon a throne, he, being skilled in ritual service, honored him with water for the feet and other offerings.
He worshipped Śrī Garga, the best among the wise, according to the prescribed rites;
thereafter, the great Vṛṣabhānu circumambulated him. 45.
Śrī Vṛṣabhānu said: "The peaceful wandering of the virtuous is remembered as a means for the peace of householders;
it is the saint alone who removes the inner darkness of men, not the sun."
O Lord, by the sight of you we cowherds have become sacred pilgrimage sites;
for such holy men as you make even ordinary places into sacred shrines upon this earth.
"O sage, this daughter of mine named Rādhikā is the source of my auspiciousness;
tell me with certainty, to which bridegroom should she be given? (48)
"Wandering through the three worlds like the sun, you possess divine vision;
I shall give this maiden to whoever is truly her equal. (49)
Śrī Nārada said:
Taking Vṛṣabhānu’s hand, the great sage Śrī Garga went to the banks of the Yamunā, to a secluded and beautiful place.
Having seated the Lord of the Gopas there amidst the tumultuous roar of the waves of the Yamunā’s waters, the lord of sages, who knows the dharma, spoke.
Śrī Garga said:
O cowherd, this secret narrative must not be told by you;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself is the most perfect Supreme Lord in person.
The Lord of Goloka, the master of countless universes, higher than the highest—there is no superior boon greater than him, who was born as the Lord in the house of Nanda. (53)
Śrī Vṛṣabhānu said:
O great sage, how wonderful is the good fortune of Nanda!
Tell me the entire reason for the incarnation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The illustrious Garga said: At the request of Brahmā, for the purpose of removing the earth's burden and for the slaying of Kaṃsa and others, Kṛṣṇa appeared upon the surface of the world.
She who is the illustrious Queen Consort of Kṛṣṇa, known as Rādhikā in Goloka, has also been born in your house; yet you do not recognize her as the Supreme.
Śrī Nārada said:
Then the cowherd Vṛṣabhānu, greatly delighted and filled with wonder,
summoned Kalāvatī and consulted with her.
Having realized the power of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, that supreme and excellent cowherd,
shedding tears of joy, spoke again to the great sage.
Śrī Vṛṣabhānu said: "O brāhmaṇa, I shall give my lotus-eyed daughter to him;
you have shown me the path, and this marriage must be performed by you."
The illustrious Garga said:
"O King, I shall not perform the marriage of these two;
their wedding shall take place at Bhāṇḍīra on the bank of the Yamunā."
And near Vṛndāvana, in a secluded and beautiful place,
Parameṣṭhin will arrive and cause the marriage to be performed.
Therefore, O best of cowherds, know Rādhā to be the half-body of the Supreme Lord;
she is the crest-jewel of the world and the queen in the palace of Goloka.
All of you cowherds have come from Goloka to this earth;
likewise, the hosts of cowherd girls and the cowherds remain in Goloka by the will of Rādhikā.

The sight of you, which is indeed difficult to obtain and hard to achieve even through the gods, sacrifices, or births— how much more so is it now that you stand with a physical form in the courtyard of your temple?
Many cowherds and cowherd girls perceive her as she remains concealed.
Śrī Nārada said:
Then, O King, the couple, filled with wonder and exceedingly joyful upon hearing the power of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, spoke to Śrī Garga.
The couple said:
"O Brahmin, tell us the true explanation of the word 'Rādhā.
O great sage, there is no one else on earth besides you who can sever our doubt. (66)
Śrī Garga said:
On Mount Gandhamādana, I heard the essential meaning of the Sāmaveda from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa even while I was still his disciple.
The letter *ra* comes from Ramā; the letter *ā* is the first Gopikā;
the letter *dha* comes from Dharā; and the letter *ā* is the river Virajā. (68)
From the fourfold splendor of the Supreme Śrīkṛṣṇa, there arose four wives: Līlābhū, Śrī, Virajā, and [the fourth]. Indeed, these were his consorts. (69)
And they all merged completely into Rādhā within the bower-dwelling;
therefore, the wise call Rādhā the most perfect one (paripūrṇatamā).
Śrī Nārada said:
O cowherd, for those who repeatedly chant "Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa," what need have they for the four goals of life? Even Kṛṣṇa Himself is obtained by them directly.
Then, O King, Vṛṣabhānu, accompanied by his beloved, was greatly amazed;
having realized that power of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, he became filled with bliss. (72)
Thus Garga, the best of the wise, the lord of sages, the all-knowing seer, being honored by Vṛṣabhānu, went to his own home.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Vision of the Universal Form by Nanda’s Wife and the Naming Ceremony of Śrī Kṛṣṇa," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Śrī Nārada said: While tending the cows in the Nandana grove, he was fondling them from a great distance away.
Nanda also went to the Bhāṇḍīra forest, which was shaken by the breezes from the banks of the Yamunā.
Then, by the will of Kṛṣṇa, a wind more swift than before arose,
and the sky became thick with clouds and the sprouts of tamāla and nīpa trees.
With those falling and shimmering intensely, what splendor! || 2 ||
Then, when a great darkness had arisen and the child, having fallen into his lap, was crying in extreme fear, Nanda became terrified; carrying the infant, he sought refuge in Hari, the Supreme Lord.
At that very moment, a radiance like a multitude of ten million suns appeared as if approaching and moving through the quarters;
within that light, the King of Navananda beheld Rādhā, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu.
She possesses the splendor of ten million moons, wears blue garments, and has a beautiful, primordial complexion;
she bears anklets whose deep-sounding jingling produces an exceedingly charming melody.
Mixed with the sounds of her girdle, waist-bands, and bracelets, shimmering with necklaces, rings, and armlets, and accompanied by the swans that are the pearls from her glorious nose-ornament—
Adorned with the crest-jewel and earrings of Śrīkaṇṭha.
Overwhelmed by her splendor, Nanda quickly bowed and, with palms joined in reverence, said to her:
"This one is indeed Puruṣottama himself; you are [his mother]."
O Rādhā, you have always been the foremost among those dear to him.
I know this secret through the mouth of Garga; O Rādhā, take your own Lord from your lap and lead him,
who is afraid of the rain-clouds, to his home.
And in this regard, I speak thus concerning that which is enriched by the qualities of primordial nature.
"I bow to you; protect me on this earth according to my desire, which is difficult for all people to attain.
Śrī Rādhā said:
"O Nanda, I am pleased with your devotion; indeed, a vision of Me is very difficult to obtain."
Śrī Nanda said:
"If you are pleased, then may my devotion be firm toward the lotus feet of you two."
May I have devotion to the virtuous, association with those who share my devotion, and [this] always in every age. (10)
Śrī Nārada said: Having spoken thus, "So be it," Rādhā then took her own Lord Hari from his lap with both hands.
Then, after Nanda had departed and the Lord of Vraja had bowed down, he indeed went to Bhāṇḍīravana.
Long ago, the Earth arrived from the world of Goloka, assuming her own natural form,
which was composed of gold inlaid with rubies and other gems.
At that very moment, she became entirely so.
Vṛndāvana, possessing a divine form together with excellent wish-fulfilling trees,
as well as the daughter of Kalinda and golden mansions—
It became composed of auspicious jeweled stairways. || 13 ||

O King, Govardhana, composed of jeweled stones, appeared like a woman with uplifted arms, with its golden peaks shimmering on all sides and its caves— beautiful with waterfalls— filled with intoxicated bees.
Then Nikunja also assumed his own form, which was joined by a divine pavilion in the courtyard;
it possessed the sweetness of spring and resounded with the songs of bees, peacocks, pigeons, and cuckoos.
It was covered with cloths inlaid with gold, jewels, and other precious materials, and it shone with rows of fluttering banners;
the lake was adorned with beautiful golden lotuses that sparkled as they were pecked by swarms of bees.

At that very moment, the Supreme among the Supreme Persons appeared in person, possessing the form of a youth and a deep, cloud-like luster; He was clad in yellow garments and adorned with the Kaustubha jewel.
The bearer of the flute, who enchants the multitude of the god of love. || 17 ||
Taking his beloved by the arm, Hari went smiling into the midst of the wedding pavilion,
which was furnished with all the requisites for the marriage ceremony and adorned with the girdle, sacrificial grass, soft water-pots, and other articles.
Right there, upon that exalted and supreme lion-throne,
the couple shone as they met one another,
speaking most sweetly to each other.
And they were like lightning and clouds in the sky, flashing with radiance. || 19 ||
Then the Lord Brahmā, the best of gods, descended from the sky and appeared before that Supreme One;
having bowed at his feet, he addressed him with radiant words.
With palms joined in reverence, the beautiful four-faced one sang.
Śrī Brahmā said:
[I bow to] Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, who is without beginning, the primordial one, the highest of the high among persons, and who is affectionate toward his own devotees.
I myself take refuge in you, the lord of countless universes, the one higher than the highest, the husband of Rādhā. || 21 ||
When you are the Lord of Goloka, you are exceedingly playful,
and this Līlāvatī is the play of your own world; when you are the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, you are indeed that very same one.
For this very Lakṣmī is indeed the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu.
You are Rāmacandra and I am the daughter of Janaka; you are Hari on earth and I am Kamalālayā.
Whenever you are an incarnation for the sake of sacrifice, then so am I.
The illustrious Dakṣiṇā is the foremost wife and principal consort. || 23 ||
You are Nārasiṃha, and this Ramā is his; you are Nārāyaṇa when joined with Nara, and then this Śānti is truly manifest as your very own corresponding shadow. || 24 ||
You are Brahman and this Prakṛti standing aloof; they know you as Time when this is the Pradhāna,
and at other times you are the Great One (Mahat), the sprout of the universe.
This Rādhā is that very Māyā endowed with qualities (saguṇā). || 25 ||
When the inner self is known by these four, then this is the functioning of the nature of characteristics;
when you yourself assume the body of Virāṭ, then this entire earth is held [by you]. 26.
O Supreme among the best of Persons, your two-fold majesty is known as both dark and fair;
I go for refuge to you, the Lord of the abode of Goloka, the Supreme Ruler, higher than the highest. || 27 ||
Whoever constantly recites this supreme hymn to the Divine Couple attains the most excellent abode of Goloka; even in this very world, they achieve beauty, prosperity, and supernatural powers.
Furthermore, these qualities also arise in him by his very nature. || 28 ||
Although you two are a couple filled with love, supreme beyond the Supreme, and endowed with perfectly matching forms,
nevertheless, for the sake of upholding worldly convention, I shall perform the marriage rite for you.
Śrī Nārada said: Then that Creator (Brahmā), having arisen and kindled the sacrificial fire in the pit before those two who were standing there, spoke.
Having duly performed the ritual of taking Śruti by the hand, the Creator stood ready. || 30 ||
He caused Hari and Rādhikā to circumambulate the seven sacrificial fires;
then, having made them bow down before him, he, who was learned in the Vedas, had them recite the seventh mantra.
Then, having placed Rādhikā’s hand upon Hari’s chest and Hari’s hand upon Śrī Rādhikā’s back, he [pressed them together].
Having established the mantras, he taught the ritual procedure.
With both her hands, Rādhā placed a golden-pollen garland, humming with bees, around Kṛṣṇa’s neck;
and from Hari’s hands, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu [placed one] upon his neck.
Then, having caused the fire to bow down, the knower of the Vedas—
The Grandfather (Brahmā) made them sit upon two excellent seats with their palms joined in reverence and observed by silence;
he then taught them the five mantras.
And having entrusted Rādhā to him like a father giving away his daughter, || 34 ||
O King, at that time the gods rained down flowers;
the celestial damsels danced with the Vidyādharīs,
while the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Cāraṇas sang melodiously.
The Kinnaras sang the auspicious song of Kṛṣṇa.

Mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, murujas, flutes, conchs, ānakas, and dundubhis, accompanied by cymbals, resounded repeatedly; and by the best of gods stationed in heaven, the auspicious cry of "Victory! was raised loudly. (36)
There, Hari himself spoke regarding the ritual procedure:
"O Brahmin, state whatever sacrificial fee you desire. Then Brahmā said to Hari: "O Lord, [grant it] to me."
Grant me the fee for my devotion to your feet. || 37 ||
"Let it be so," said the voice of Lord Hari and Śrī Rādhikā;
bowing again and again with his two hands and head to their auspicious pair of feet, he departed for home, prostrate and filled with great joy.
Then, in the groves, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, laughing, ate the four kinds of divine and delightful food offered by his beloved.
And Rādhā was given a betel nut by Kṛṣṇa. || 39 ||
Then Hari, taking his beloved’s hand with his own, proceeded into the grove;
he went along, speaking sweetly and gazing about him.
Vṛndāvana, the auspicious Yamunā, and the creepers. || 40 ||
Seeing him smiling and hidden within the dense thickets of the beautiful forest of creepers, concealed by the branches, Rādhā—
She seized the yellow garment as she was approaching.
Radha, whose lotus-like hands were held by Hari, ran away while making a tinkling sound with her anklets;
she hid herself within a grove on the banks of the Yamuna.
Again she went forth, [measuring] only the length of Hari's hand.
Just as a Tamāla tree shines with a streak of gold,
or as a dark cloud gleams with a flash of lightning, so does the blue king of mountains shine with a vein of touchstone.
But he is the first [of all] with Śrī Rādhā, that delightful woman. || 43 ||
In the supreme arena of the Śrī-rāsa, devoid of other people, Hari took delight with Rādhā through the essence of the rāsa-dance;
in Vṛndāvana, where the creepers resound with the humming of bees and the cries of peacocks, that Supreme Lord of Love continues to sport.
Accompanied by Śrī Rādhā, Kṛṣṇa Hari, the Supreme Soul, danced in the caves of Govardhana,
which were graced by lakes flowing with streams, intoxicated bees, and radiant flowering creepers.
Having approached the Yamunā, Kṛṣṇa engaged in excellent pastimes with the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu;
from Rādhā’s hand, he received a hundred-thousand-petaled lotus.
Having taken up the flute in the waters of the Yamunā. || 46 ||
Rādhā, laughing, suddenly seized Hari’s yellow garment, his flute, and his staff,
as Hari said to her, "Give me the flute!"
Rādhā said, "Please give me a lotus. || 47 ||
Then the best of gods gave her a lotus, and Rādhā gave him a yellow-edged flute; and he gave a staff to Hari.
Again, the pastimes of the two of them took place on the banks of the Yamunā.

Then, in the Bhāṇḍīra forest, the jewel of the cowherds of Vraja performed a most beautiful adornment for his beloved with leaf-designs, red lac, collyrium, and other such things, as well as flowers and fine jewels. (49)
When Rādhā was indeed intent on fully preparing the amorous adornment for Hari,
at that very moment Kṛṣṇa became a child.
Having indeed abandoned his youthful body himself. || 50 ||
Seeing the infant Hari, who had been brought by Nanda exactly as he was— rolling on the ground and crying— Rādhikā immediately burst into tears.
O Hari, how is it that you spread out this illusion toward me? 51.
To Rādhā, who was thus suddenly weeping in despondency, a voice from the sky spoke at that very moment:
"O Rādhā, do not grieve here; your heart's desire shall indeed be fulfilled later."
Having heard this, Rādhā indeed took Hari and went quickly to the house of the wife of the King of Vraja;
and having given the child to the wife of Nanda, she departed.
And he said, "They were given to you on the road by your husband."
O King, the wife of Nanda said to Rādhā: "O Rādhā, daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, you are blessed!
By you my infant was protected from fear when the sky was covered with clouds and he was terrified in the forest. (54)
Having been fully honored and praised for her excellent virtues, that daughter of Śrī Vṛṣabhānu was greatly delighted;
then, having indeed taken leave of Yaśodā, she—
Rādhā then slowly went to her own home. || 55 ||
Thus has been described the secret narrative of Hari, adorned with the most auspicious account of Rādhā’s wedding;
by those who have heard it, or read it, or caused it to be read.
Multitudes of sins never touch them. || 56 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Marriage of Śrī Rādhikā," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Śrī Nārada said: Then the two boys, Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, fair and dark respectively, enchanting to the mind,
made the beautiful house of Nanda exceedingly delightful through their playful pastimes.
And crawling on their knees and hands together, O King of Mithilā,
they moved through Vraja in a short time, speaking sweetly.
When did those two infants, cherished and nourished by Yaśodā and Rohiṇī, ever emerge from their laps or remain seated upon them? (3)
Making the sound of their anklets and small bells as they moved here and there,
those two, possessing the illusory forms of children, enchanted the three worlds.
Taking the child as he played, rolling about in Yaśodā’s courtyard with the boys of Vraja,
his limbs greyed and covered by the dust of that place, she indeed performed a thorough sprinkling over him with great care.
Moving again with both knees and hands level, Kṛṣṇa reached the courtyard and then returned once more to a spot near his mother.
He shone in Vraja with the playful charm of a young lion;
he was adorned everywhere with various winter ornaments,
wearing yellow garments and a tunic.
Seeing her son wearing a crown made of jewels with shimmering radiance, Yaśodā attained great joy.
Seeing the child Mukunda engaged in most beautiful childhood play, the gopīs attained supreme joy;
and King Nanda, leaving his home, arrived at the cowherd settlement of Vraja.
But all of them had forgotten their homes; they were embodiments of happiness.
O King, having seen the artificial lion-form in the house of the illustrious King Nanda, he who fled back, crying out like one terrified,
and [saw] her returning home after taking her own son—
The cowherd women, filled with compassion, spoke thus to Yaśodā in Vraja.
The gopīs said:
"O auspicious one, do not send this restless child out from the courtyard for play;
he is a milk-faced infant engaged in childish frolics, still wearing the side-locks of hair."
"The two upper teeth that appeared first portend trouble for your maternal uncle;
yet, O Yaśomatī, your son has no maternal uncle at all."
Therefore, one should indeed practice charity for the sake of destroying obstacles,
as well as perform the worship of cows, Brahmins, gods, holy men, and the Vedas.
Śrī Nārada said:
Then Yaśodā and Rohiṇī, for the sake of their son’s auspiciousness,
constantly gave gifts of clothing, jewels, and various kinds of new food.
Then, in Vraja, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who gazed with the look of young lions,
began to move about on foot through the cowherd settlements, growing in stature.
Together with their companions Śrīdāma, Subala, and other boys of Vraja, they were rolling about on the bright sandbank of the Yamunā, full of curiosity.
In the forest grove on the banks of the Kālindī, which was covered with dense, dark tamāla trees and enriched by the beauty of kadamba thickets, Rāma and Keśava wandered.
Producing joy for the cowherds and cowherd-maidens through his childhood play,
Hari stole butter and ghee along with his companions.
Once, Upananda’s wife, a cowherd woman named Prabhāvatī, arrived at the house of Śrī Nanda and spoke to Yaśodā.
Prabhāvatī said:
"O Yaśomatī, through your grace, butter, ghee, milk, curd, and buttermilk have become indistinguishable from one another for us two. (19)
I do not say that he has learned theft anywhere; you yourself have failed to provide instruction to your son who steals butter. (20)
"When I gave him instruction, your son became insolent;
having uttered insults, he runs away from my courtyard. (21)
"Having become the son of the lord of Vraja, he would commit theft;
yet, out of respect for you, Yaśodā, I have said nothing. (22)
Śrī Nārada said: Having heard the words of Prabhāvatī, Yaśodā, the wife of Nanda,
rebuked the boy and then spoke to her with gentleness, being devoted to love.
Śrī Yaśodā said:
"I have ten million cows in my house, and the mountains are moistened by my dairy products;
yet I do not know why this boy never eats curd or yogurt here."
"Whatever has been stolen from my cow, take that same amount from me;
O powerful one, there is no difference at all between those calves and my calf. (25)
And when you bring him here with butter on his face, then I shall administer instruction, as well as reprimand and imprisonment. (26)
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard those words, the gopī returned home with a joyful heart.
Once, Kṛṣṇa went to her house for the purpose of stealing curd.
Together with his young companions, Kṛṣṇa slowly entered the side wall of the house, moving from hand to hand as they supported one another.
Seeing the cow's milk situated in a hanging basket within reach of his hand, Hari himself placed the cowherd boys on a wooden mortar and a small stool, and then climbed up it.
Even that milk, suspended in a swing, was reachable by the tall Śrīdāman;
yet Subala struck it with his staff as well.
From the broken vessel, Mādhava, together with his companions and the boys, joyfully ate all the cow-products, which were beautiful on the vast ground. || 31 ||
Hearing the sound of broken pottery, the cowherd girl Prabhāvatī arrived;
while the boys fled, she seized the hand of Hari.
Having led away the timid woman who was shedding false tears, she went to Nanda’s house;
seeing Nanda standing before her, she placed a cloth over his mouth.
Thinking thus, "The mother will inflict punishment," the Lord Hari,
whose movement is independent, assumed that form of a child.
Approaching Yaśodā quickly, that cowherd woman, filled with rage, said:
"All the vessels have been broken and the curds have indeed been stolen by this boy."
Seeing her son, Yaśodā smiled and spoke to the cowherd woman;
the cowherd woman, removing the edge of her garment from his face, spoke to him who was free from sin.
When blame must be assigned, banish it from me to another;
let the theft committed by your son be considered as committed by my son. (37)
Overcome with shame before the people, she drew her veil away and,
her mind filled with wonder upon seeing her own child, spoke to him.
"Where have you come from, you who are without feet? The essence of Vraja is in my hand.
Speaking thus, they took him and departed from Nanda’s house. (39)
Yaśodā, Rohiṇī, Nanda, Rāma, the cowherds, and the cowherd-maidens laughed as they said, "A great injustice has been witnessed in Vraja! (40)
But the Blessed One, the joy of Śrī Nanda, having come to the outer path, spoke with a smile to the gopī, his limbs bold and his eyes flickering. (41)
The Blessed Lord said:
"O cowherd girl, if you should ever take me up again,
then I shall undoubtedly appear in the form of your husband."
Śrī Nārada said:
O King of Mithilā, having heard this, that cowherd girl was struck with wonder and returned home;
at that time, out of shame, the cowherd girls in every house would not accept Hari.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Theft of Curd," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the Śrī Garga Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Śrī Nārada said:
Wandering among the houses of the cowherd women, He was a stealer of butter—
dark-complexioned, with a captivating form and eyes like fresh lotuses.
Like the illustrious Bālacaṃdra, having attained full growth, he captivated the hearts of men and brought splendor to Vraja. || 1 ||
Having taken up the exceedingly restless Śrī Naṃdanandana and placed him in their home, the cowherds of Navananda were enchanted;
they constantly protected him with excellent balls.
Singing with intense joy, they did not remember the world.
The king said:
O divine sage, tell me the names of the nine Nandanās;
oh, what great fortune is theirs, for they have previously come here! || 3 ||
Likewise, [he described] the deeds and auspicious rites of the six Vṛṣabhānus.
Śrī Nārada said: Gaya, Vimala, Śrīśa, Śrīdhara, and Maṅgalāyana. (4)
Maṅgala, Raṅgavallīśa, Raṅgoji, and Devanāyaka—these nine Nandas are said to have been born in Gokula, in Vraja. || 5 ||
Vītihotra, Agnibhuk, Sāmba, Śrīkara, Gopati, Śruta, Vrajeśa, Pāvana, and Śānta are proclaimed as the Upanandas. || 6 ||
O King, six Vṛṣabhānus were born in Vraja: Nītivit, Mārgada, Śukla, Pataṅga, Divyavāhana, and Gopeṣṭa.
In Goloka, those who reside at the gateway of Kṛṣṇacandra’s bower,
holding canes in their hands and possessing dark-complexioned limbs, are known as the Navanandas.
In the grove there were millions of cows, and those intent on their protection,
adorned with flutes and peacock feathers, are remembered as the Upanandas.
In the protection of the forest thickets and fortresses, they stood bearing staffs and nooses;
stationed at the six gates, these six were indeed declared to be the Vṛṣabhānus.
By the will of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they all came from Goloka to the earth;
indeed, even the four-faced Brahmā is not capable of describing their power.
What indeed shall I say of their great and exalted fortune, upon whose lap Hari shone while engaged in childhood play? (12)
Once, on the bank of the Yamunā, the child was seen licking clay; the boys said to Yaśodā, "The boy is eating your clay! (13)
While Balabhadra was speaking, Nanda’s wife then took her son by the hand and, with eyes full of fear, said to him: || 14 ||
Śrī Yaśodā said:
"O Knower of the Great, why did you eat clay? Tell me, for your companions say so directly."
This elder and powerful one speaks what is well-known; he does not abandon this purpose, nor is it undesirable to him.
The Blessed One said:
"O Mother, all these children have mounted the chariot of falsehood; I have never anywhere eaten earth."
When you have correctly mastered this path of speech,
then look directly upon my face.
Śrī Nārada said:
Then, as the gopī gazed upon the beautiful face of the child, she beheld the expanded universe constructed from the [three] qualities (guṇas). 17.
The seven islands, the seven oceans, the regions with their divisions, the firm mountains,
and the three worlds up to the realm of Brahmā, together with his own selves and his cowherd settlements.
Having seen him on the bank of the illustrious Yamunā, she closed her eyes and became filled with the realization: "This child is indeed Hari himself. (19)
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa laughed, as if deluding her with his illusory power (māyā);
Yaśodā, her memory lost, did not remember the greatness she had witnessed.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Vision of the Cosmic Egg," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Śrī Nārada said: Once, in Gokula, the cowherd women churned curds everywhere in every house, singing aloud the supreme deeds of the cowherd boy.
Yaśodā also, having risen in the morning at the house of Śrī Nanda,
placed the curds in a vessel and churned them, O beautiful one.
Making the sound of his anklets ring out, the child, the delight of the joy of Lakṣmī,
danced for the sake of the butter, out of curiosity for the sound of the word "rāya" (wealth).
Dancing and wandering about his mother’s side, he shone with childhood play,
repeatedly causing the cluster of beautiful bells and small tinkling ornaments to ring out.
Constantly requesting fresh *haiyaṅgavīna* from his mother while speaking sweet words,
the wise Kṛṣṇa took a stone in his hand and, out of anger, smashed the vessel for churning curds.
Yaśodā Prabhāvatī did not catch her fleeing son even at the distance of a cubit’s length—
he who is difficult to attain even for the lords of yogis.
How does he proceed toward seizing his mother? || 6 ||
Nevertheless, O lord of kings, Śrī Hari has demonstrated his subjection to his devotees even toward those who are devoted;
for he took Yaśomatī’s young son as his own child.
Then, out of rage, he bound her with a rope to the mortar.
Whatever many ropes Yaśodā took, each one became very small in the presence of her son;
for how could he who is beyond material nature and not bound by its qualities be bound here by a rope?
O King, when Yaśodā, desiring to release him from his bonds, sat down dejected with a weary mind,
then he, out of compassion, [bound himself] in his own bonds.
Kṛṣṇa, though independent and self-controlled, [acts] according to his own will. || 9 ||
This grace was not for those of heroic deeds, nor for the wise, much less for those whose intellect is fixed on ritual action;
O King, it was as it was with these [devotees] toward their mother, therefore Mādhava granted them liberation, which is sufficient for devotion.

At that very moment, the cowherd women arrived in haste; seeing the vessel for churning curds shattered, and beholding the infant bound tightly with ropes to the mortar, they spoke, overcome with compassion.
The gopīs said:
"In our houses, this child constantly breaks the vessels;
yet out of compassion, O wife of Nanda, we do not say anything to him."
O Yaśodā, devoid of compassion and free from distress, O Queen of Vraja, this child was threatened by you with a staff and bound for the exhaustion of his [stolen] pots. (13)
Śrī Nārada said:
While Yaśodā was thus addressed and occupied with household chores,
Kṛṣṇa, dragging the mortar along with other boys, went to the beautiful Yamunā.
And on that bank were two ancient great trees, twin *arjuna* trees;
between them went the Lord Kṛṣṇa Dāmodara, smiling. (15)
Kṛṣṇa suddenly dragged the mortar sideways;
by that pulling, both [the demons] fell to the surface of the earth along with their roots.
Even with that falling, a sound arose as fierce as a thunderbolt;
and from the two trees, two gods emerged like fires from a sacrificial altar.
Having circumambulated Dāmodara and touched his feet with their crowns,
and having bowed to Hari with palms joined in reverence, the two stood before him.
The two gods said: "O Acyuta, we have been instantly liberated from the Brahminical curse by the sight of you.
O Hari, let there never be any slighting of our own devotees by you. (19)
Salutations again and again to you, the treasure-house of compassion, whose nature is the auspiciousness of the world—to Dāmodara, Kṛṣṇa, and Govinda. || 20 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having thus bowed to Hari, those two departed toward the northern direction;
at that very moment, Nanda and all the others arrived, overwhelmed with fear.
"O children of Vraja, how did these two trees fall without wind?
At that, all the young boys, residents of Vraja, spoke quickly. || 22 ||
The children said:
"By this [wind], two trees were felled, and from them two men emerged. Having bowed to him, they have now departed toward the north, their splendor quivering. (23)
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard these words of theirs, they did not believe them;
consequently, Nanda released his own boy, who had been bound by a rope to the mortar.
O King, while fondling the infant on his own lap and smelling its head,
Nanda rebuked the beautiful woman and gave a hundred cows to the brahmins.
Śrī Bahulāśva said:
"O best of divine sages, tell me who these two divine persons are;
by what fault were the Yamalārjuna trees reduced to the state of being trees?"
Śrī Nārada said: The two supreme sons of the king of kings, Nalakūbara and Maṇigrīva,
went to the Nandana grove while staying on the bank of the Mandākinī.
Singing with the Apsarases,
the two youths, intoxicated by the wine of Varuṇa and arrogant because of their wealth, wandered about divested of their garments.
Once, a lord of sages named Devala, who had mastered the Vedas, saw those two naked, evil-natured, and deprived of their senses, and said to them: ||| 29 ||
Devala said:
"You two appear like trees, shameless and arrogant because of your wealth;
therefore, you shall both become trees upon this earth for a hundred years. (30)
At the end of the Dvāpara age, in Bhārata, within the district of Mathurā in the Vraja region,
on the bank of the Kaliṃdā river near the Mahāvana forest.
Having beheld that Kṛṣṇa Dāmodara Hari, who is most perfectly complete,
the Lord of Goloka, you two shall return to your former forms.
O King, having thus been reduced to the state of trees by the curse of Devala,
Nalakūbara and Maṇigrīva were liberated by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Breaking of the Yamalārjuna Trees," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 19 ||
Śrī Nārada said: Once, for the sake of beholding the Supreme Kṛṣṇacandra,
Durvāsā, the tiger among sages, arrived at the district of Vraja.
On the holy sandy bank near the Kālindī,
in a delightful spot close to a great forest, he beheld Kṛṣṇa.
The glorious Madanagopāla, rolling about with the boys and engaging in mutual wrestling, performs a charming childhood pastime.
Seeing Hari running along with the boys— his entire body grey with dust, his hair disheveled, and naked— he was struck with wonder.
The venerable sage said:
"How can this Lord, the Blessed One, be rolling on the ground like a child?
This is merely the son of Nanda; he is not Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is higher than the highest. (5)
Śrī Nārada said:
While the great sage Durvāsas was thus fallen into delusion,
Kṛṣṇa, playing nearby, came of his own accord into his presence and onto his lap.
Having emerged once more from the syllable Aṃ, Kṛṣṇa returned facing him again, laughing softly and gazing like a lion upon a child.
As he was laughing, the sage entered his mouth along with the breaths;
there he beheld another great world, containing forests and devoid of people.
While wandering there in the forests, asking "From where have you come?",
the great sage was swallowed at that very moment by a python.
There he beheld the supreme cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) along with its worlds and its shell;
wandering through the continents, that sage came to rest upon a white mountain.
Worshipping the Lord, he performed austerities for ten billion years;
meanwhile, the dissolution known as the Naimittika, which brings terror to the entire universe, arrived.
Those oceans, coming forth and flooding the surface of the earth,
carried Durvāsas within them, yet he did not reach the end of the water.
When a thousand yugas had passed, he became submerged and lost his memory;
then, moving again within the waters, he beheld another cosmic egg.
Having entered that opening, he then proceeded to the divine creation;
moving upon the summit of that egg amidst the worlds for a duration equal to the lifespan of Brahmā.
Thus, perceiving an opening there, he entered while remembering Hari;
having indeed emerged from the cosmic egg, he quickly beheld a vast expanse of water.
