In that water, indeed, millions of multitudes of cosmic eggs were perceived;
then the sage, looking at the water, beheld the river Virajā.
Having reached the further shore of that, the sage directly entered Goloka,
[specifically] Vṛndāvana, Govardhana, and the auspicious banks of the Yamunā.
Having seen this, the sage became filled with joy and then entered the bower,
which was surrounded by hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses and accompanied by tens of millions of cows.
Then, within a circle of light consisting of countless millions of suns,
he beheld Hari, the Lord of Rādhā, seated upon a divine lotus with a hundred thousand petals.
He beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, in His most perfect and manifest form, the Lord of countless universes, who is Goloka itself.
As Śrī Kṛṣṇa was laughing, the sage entered his mouth;
emerging again, he beheld the child, the delight of the Goddess of Fortune.
On the holy sandy bank near the Kālindī, a place for recreation,
Kṛṣṇa was wandering in the great forest together with the boys.
Then the sage Durvāsas, having recognized Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme beyond the supreme,
the delight of Śrī, bowed down again and again and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
The sage said:
[I beheld] the boy, with large eyes like fresh lotus petals, with lips like the bimba fruit, possessing the luster of a water-laden cloud, and enchanting.
I bow in my mind to the son of Śrīnaṃdana, who possesses a gentle smile, who is sweet and beautiful, and who is full of slow-moving compassion. 24.
[He] whose waist is adorned with a girdle of ever-sounding jewels, anklets, and bracelets; who possesses a multitude of locks of hair, necklaces, and lion-like nails that rival [the sun];
and who, removing all distress with His glance, is resplendent with drops of musk.
I bow to the childhood play upon the banks of the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā). || 25 ||
Upon his face, as beautiful as the full moon, his hair— curled at the tips and resembling the deep blue of fresh clouds— shines,
adorning his head which is like a blooming night-lotus.
Salutations, salutations to you, the son of Nandā, who possesses great strength. || 26 ||
Whoever, having risen at dawn, recites this hymn to Śrīnaṃdanandana,
the Delight of Nanda, shall find that the Delight of Nanda joyfully comes within the range of his vision.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having thus prostrated before Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Durvāsas, the best of sages,
departed for the excellent Badarī hermitage while meditating upon Him and chanting His name.
Thus was the life of Kṛṣṇa narrated by the high-souled Nārada, the foremost of divine sages, to the wise Bahulāśva.
O Brahman, I have related to you this divine narrative which destroys the impurities of the Kali age and bestows the four goals of human existence; what more do you wish to hear?
Śrī Śaunaka said:
O ascetic, tell me that— what did Bahulāśva, the lord of the Maithilas, ask the great sage Nārada, the peaceful bestower of knowledge?
Śrī Garga said:
Having bowed down to Nārada, the bestower of knowledge, the King of Mithilā, who honors his guests,
again questioned him regarding the auspicious life-story of Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Bahulāśva said:
O Lord, tell me of some wonderful deed performed by the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is the manifest embodiment of supreme bliss. (33)
The deeds performed in his previous incarnations are indeed auspicious;
however, what else [could there be]—the supreme and purifying life-story of Kṛṣṇa? (34)
Śrī Nārada said: Excellent, excellent! You have asked about the auspicious life-story of Hari;
I shall relate to you that fame which He possesses in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
This Goloka-khaṇḍa is a supreme secret and most wonderful;
it was narrated by Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the circle of the Rāsa dance at Goloka.
In the bower, Rādhā gave this to Rādhikā, and I have narrated it to you; it is the supreme bestower of all goals.
By reciting this, a Brahmin shall become one who has mastered the meaning of all scriptures;
by hearing this, a Kṣatriya shall become a universal monarch of fierce prowess. (38)
The Vaiśya shall become a lord of treasures, and the Śūdra shall be released from bondage;
even one who is free from desire in this world becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
He who recites this constantly and correctly, endowed with a spirit of devotion,
shall go to Goloka, beyond primordial nature, to the moon-like Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Birth, the Demonstration of Māyā by Durvāsas, and the Description of the Hymn to Śrī Nandanandana," in the Goloka-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.

May Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa—whose necks are like conch-shells, who cast their arms around one another, and who move together on the banks of the Yamunā where cuckoos sport, where clusters of guñjā berries grow, and where there are groves of celestial flowers and the like—grant me auspiciousness. (1)
Salutations to that illustrious Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the applicator of the collyrium of knowledge. || 2 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Once, having observed the distress, Nanda [summoned] his joyful assistants, as well as Vṛṣabhānu, Upananda, and the excellent Vṛṣabhānus. || 3 ||
Having summoned the other elders into the assembly hall, Nanda spoke to them:
"Tell me, what should be done? For great portents exist in the vast forest."
Śrī Nārada said: Having heard them, the joyful elder cowherd, who was highly skilled in counsel,
took Rāma and Kṛṣṇa onto his lap and spoke to King Nanda.
Sannanda said:
"We must all rise from here together with our attendants and go to other lands where indeed no portents exist."
To you, Kṛṣṇa is but a child, yet he is as dear as life itself; he is the very life of the inhabitants of Vraja.
In Vraja, he is their wealth and the lamp of their lineage, enchanting them with his childhood play.
Alas! This boy has been spared even by Baka, by Śakaṭa, and by Tṛṇāvarta, as well as by the falling tree; what calamity could possibly exceed this? (8)
Therefore, everyone, including the children, must go to Vṛndāvana;
once the calamities have passed, you may return again.
Nanda said:
O best among the wise, tell me how many krośas that forest of Vṛndāvana extends in breadth, and describe its characteristics and its bliss.
Sannanda said:
They know the Mathurā region to lie to the northeast of Barhiṣad, to the south of the city of Yadu, and to the west of Śoṇitapura. || 11 ||
The wise call the divine district of Mathurā, Vraja, twenty and a half yojanas in extent.
In Mathurā, at the house of Śauri, I heard from the mouth of Garga Ācārya that the divine district of Mathurā is worshipped by the King of Tīrthas.
Among all those forests, Vṛndāvana is the most excellent;
it is the enchanting playground for the pastimes of even the Most Perfect One.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, another world superior to Vaikuṇṭha;
yet Vṛndāvana alone is higher than even that supreme realm.
There, where the king of mountains named Govardhana shines resplendent,
and where, near the Kālindī, lies a sandbank that is an abode of auspiciousness.
There is the mountain Bṛhatsānu, where the mountain Nandīśvara is located;
it is surrounded by forests extending for twenty-four krośas.
Beneficial to cattle, worthy of being frequented by cowherds and cowherdesses, and charming to the mind—
that forest, covered with bowers of creepers, is indeed known as Vṛndāvana.
Nanda said:
O Saṃnanda, when was this Vraja honored by the king of holy places?
I wish to know this, for my curiosity is indeed great. (19)
Sannanda said:
In ancient times, during the periodical dissolution (naimittika-laya), while Brahmā was sleeping, that great Daitya Śaṅkhāsura, the preeminent among demons and a subverter of the Vedas, [arose].
Having conquered the gods, he took the Vedas from the world of Brahmā and went to the ocean;
when those Vedas had departed, the strength of the gods also vanished.
Then the perfect Lord Hari himself, assuming the form of a fish in the ocean at the time of dissolution,
fought with that king of sacrifices.
The mighty Daitya Śaṅkha hurled a spear at Hari;
with his own discus, Hari himself shattered that spear into a hundred pieces.
Śaṅkha struck Hari on the chest with his head;
yet by that blow to his crown, the Supreme beyond the supreme did not waver.
Then Hari, assuming the form of a fish,
took up his mace and struck that mighty Daitya, who was in the form of a conch, on the back.
Pained by the blow of the mace and with his mind somewhat agitated,
he rose up again and struck the Lord of All with his fist.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu himself, the lotus-eyed Bhagavān, being enraged, struck off that firm head along with its horns using his own discus.
O Lord of Vraja, having conquered Śaṅkha along with the best of the gods, Viṣṇu,
that Hari, arrived at Prayāga and gave those Vedas back to Brahmā.
He performed a sacrifice according to the prescribed rites together with all the hosts of gods,
and having summoned Prayāga, he made it the king of holy places (tīrtharāja).
Then, the eternal banyan tree was made by them into a play-umbrella for the sage, the son of the Sun; and it shone with the waves of the ocean as fly-whisks.
At that very moment, all the holy fords situated in Jambūdvīpa brought their offerings and arrived before the wise King of Tīrthas.
Having fully worshipped the King of Tīrthas and having bowed down to all the sacred fords on every side, O Nanda, they departed for their own abodes once Hari had gone with the gods.
At that very moment, Nārada, the lord of sages who is fond of quarrels,
arrived and spoke to the King of Tīrthas, who was resplendent upon his throne.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King of Tīrthas, you of great austerity are indeed honored by all holy places;
and here, all the principal tīrthas have offered oblations unto you. (34)
Vraja, Vṛndāvana, and other such places have not come before you;
though you are the king of kings among holy sites, you have been disregarded by those who are heedless. (35)
Having spoken thus as that best of celestial rishis departed visibly before his eyes,
the King of Tīrthas then became enraged and went to the world of Hari.
Having bowed to Hari, circumambulated him, and stood before him with palms joined in reverence,
the King of Tīrthas, surrounded by all the sacred waters, spoke to Śrīnātha.
The King of Tīrthas said: "O God of gods, I have arrived; I have been made the King of Tīrthas by you.
All the tīrthas have offered tribute to me, with the sole exception of the Mathurā region. (38)
I have been insulted by those negligent ones who visit sacred fords;
therefore, I have come to your residence and have told this to you.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Earth, you have been made the King of all holy places by me;
however, even for your own home, you yourself have not been made the sovereign. (40)
"Why do you speak words like a madman, desiring my abode?
O King of Tīrthas, go to your own home and listen to my auspicious words. (41)
The Mathurā-maṇḍala is my own manifest temple, higher than the highest;
it is divine, beyond the three worlds, and is not destroyed even at the time of universal dissolution.
Sannanda said:
Having heard this, the king of holy places (Prayāga) was struck with wonder, yet his pride vanished;
he arrived, bowed down, and worshipped the Mathurā region, the circle of Vraja.
Then, having circumambulated her, he returned once more to his own abode.
This was previously displayed by me for the purpose of shattering the pride of the Earth; I have now related this before you—what more do you wish to hear? 44.
Nanda said:
"O Lord of the Gopas, tell me this: by whom was the Māthura region and the circle of Vraja previously shown for the purpose of breaking Dharā’s pride? (45)
Sannanda said:
In the beginning of this Vārāha-kalpa, the Lord Hari, assuming the form of a boar,
shone forth as he lifted the earth from the subterranean realm (rasātala) with his tusk.
As the Blessed Lord Rameśvara was walking amidst the masses of water, the Earth, adorned upon the tip of his tusk, spoke to the god Janārdana: || 47 ||
Dharā said: "O Lord, in which place will you indeed establish me?
O Master, tell me, for the entire world is seen filled with water. (48)
Vārāha said:
"When trees indeed become visible, appearing as if agitated in the water, then your installation shall take place; go along, observing the trees."
Dhara said:
"The arrangement of the stationary beings rests upon me;
is there any other earth? For I am indeed composed of the power of support."
Sannanda said:
Speaking thus, he saw before him beautiful trees upon the water;
having observed the earth, Hari spoke to her, his wonder vanished in every respect. (51)
Dhara said:
"O Lord, in what place do these trees with their sprouts exist? This is a wonder in my mind; tell me, O Lord, Master of Sacrifice. (52)
Vārāha said:
O slender-waisted lady, this divine region of Mathurā is seen before you;
it is joined with the land of Goloka and is not destroyed even at the time of universal dissolution.
Sannanda said:
Having heard that, the earth was struck with wonder and became free from pride;
therefore, O mighty-armed Nanda, this Vraja is superior to everything else.
Having heard this majesty of Vraja, a man becomes liberated while living;
know that the Mathurā region of Vraja is superior even to the king of holy places.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Effort to Go to Vṛndāvana," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 1 ||
Nanda said: O Sannanda, O one of great wisdom, you are omniscient and deeply learned;
from your own mouth I have heard the majesty of the circle of Vraja. || 1 ||
Tell me also of the origin of that mountain named Govardhana;
why indeed do they call this best of mountains the king of mountains?
From which world has this river Yamunā come directly?
Tell me its greatness, for you are the best among the wise. (3)
Sannanda said:
Once, in Hastināpura, Pāṇḍu questioned Bhīṣma, the best among the upholders of dharma, while the people were listening.
The most perfect Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the master of countless universes, the sovereign of Goloka, and the Lord. || 5 ||
As Lord Janārdana was departing to descend from the burden of the earth, he said to Rādhā: "O beloved, O timid one, you too must go to the surface of the earth."
Rādhā said: Where Vṛndāvana is not, where the Yamunā river is not,
and where Govardhana is not— there my mind finds no happiness.
Sannanda said:
Śrī Hari himself sent the serpent Vedanā, Krośa, Bhūmi,
Govardhana, and Yamunā from his own abode to the earth.
Vedana-gakrośa-bhūmi also arrived there;
she is endowed with twenty-four forests and is saluted by all the worlds.
To the west of Bhārata, from the midst of Śālmalīdvīpa,
Govardhana took birth from the wife of Droṇācala.
Upon Govardhana, the gods rained down a shower of flowers;
all the mountains, beginning with Himālaya and Sumeru, arrived there together. (11)
Having bowed down, circumambulated, and performed worship according to the prescribed rites,
the great mountains offered the supreme hymn of praise to Govardhana.
The mountains said:
"You are the direct manifestation of the most perfect Kṛṣṇacandra,
in Goloka, which is joined by herds of cows and filled with cowherds and cowherdesses."
For you, named Govardhana, shine resplendent in the Vṛndāvana forest;
you are now the king of all mountains for us. (14)
Salutations to you, who bear the mark of Vṛndāvana and wear Goloka as your crown;
salutations to the umbrella of the perfect Brahman, and salutations to Govardhana as well. 15.
Sannanda said:
Having thus offered praise, the mountains then departed for their respective homes;
that mountain, the best of peaks, is known as Girirāja himself. || 16 ||
Once, the excellent sage Pulastya, while traveling on a pilgrimage,
[reached] the beautiful mountain Govardhana, the dark-hued son of Mount Droṇa.
The Mādhavī creeper’s flower, accompanied by the essence of meat, resounded with waterfalls; it was peaceful and served as an auspicious abode within the mountain cave.
It was a hundred-peaked mountain, worthy of asceticism, made of jewels, and enchanting;
its body was variegated with diverse minerals, it was adorned with peaks, and it was teeming with birds.
The great sage beheld that place, filled with deer and monkeys, adorned with the cries of peacocks, and bestowing liberation upon those seeking release.
Desiring to obtain [the weapon], that tiger among sages approached the side of Droṇa;
honored by Mount Droṇa, Pulastya spoke to that mountain.
Pulastya said: O Droṇa, you are the king of mountains, honored by all the gods; endowed with divine medicinal herbs, you are the eternal bestower of life upon men.
"O Great Sage, I am a seeker who has come into your presence from Kāśī;
grant me your son Govardhana, for I have no need here for anything else. (23)
The great city named Kāśī belongs to the Lord Viśveśvara;
for even a sinner who dies there immediately attains supreme liberation.
Where the Gaṅgā herself has arrived and where Viśvanātha truly resides, there indeed I shall establish [the image]; this desire of mine has been fulfilled.
Sannanda said:
Having heard the words of Pulastya, Droṇagiri, overwhelmed by affection for his son and with eyes full of tears, spoke these words to that sage. || 27 ||
Droṇa said:
"O great sage, I am indeed overwhelmed by affection for my son; this son of mine is exceedingly dear to me. Fearing your curse, I speak thus to him. (28)
"O son, go to the auspicious land of Bhārata where the sage dwells;
there, men obtain the three aims of life and even liberation in an instant. (29)
Govardhana said:
"O sage, why do you carry me suspended eight yojanas [above the ground],
when my body is two yojanas high and five yojanas wide?"
Pulastya said:
"Sit upon my hand, my son; go as you please.
I shall indeed carry you on my hand until we have reached Kāśī."
Govardhana said:
"O Sage, on whichever spot of earth you shall establish me, I shall not rise from that ground; this is my solemn oath."
Pulastya said:
"Having established Kausala as the boundary up to the Āśālmalidvīpa, I shall not establish [any other] residence; you too must swear this oath to me on the path."
Sannanda said:
That great mountain ascended onto the palm of the sage;
having bowed to his father Droṇa, his eyes were overwhelmed and filled with tears. (34)
Holding him by the right hand, the Sage proceeded very slowly,
manifesting his own splendor to the people, and arrived at the district of Vraja.
Thereupon, the mountain Jātismara, reflecting upon this while on the path, said:
"The Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself is manifest as the Most Perfect One. (36)
The Lord of the entire universe will descend here in Vraja,
performing childhood pastimes and youthful activities with the cowherd boys.
"Lord Hari will perform his pastimes of generosity and his pastimes of honor here;
therefore, I must not go, for this ground is the daughter of Kalinda. (38)
"Śrī Kṛṣṇa will come here from Goloka together with Rādhā;
having obtained that supreme vision, I shall have fulfilled my life's purpose. (39)
Having reflected thus in his mind, he placed a heavy burden upon his hand;
then the sage became exhausted and lost his former memory.
Having lifted that mountain from his hand and placed it within the circle of Vraja,
he, oppressed by the weight, departed quickly for the sake of conquering his fear.
Having performed his purifications and bathed in the water, Pulastya, the best of sages, spoke to the supreme Mount Govardhana: "Arise! (42)
The Great Sage attempted to seize with both hands that [elephant], which was heavy with a vast burden and had not yet risen,
by means of his own splendor and strength.
Although the king of mountains was addressed with gentle words by the Sage, the son of Droṇa did not move even a single finger. || 44 ||
Sannanda said:
"Go, go, O best of mountains; do not bear the burden, do not bear it!
You have been recognized by me; you are angry, so tell me your intention at once. (45)
Govardhana said:
"O sage, there is no fault in me here; you yourself established me.
I shall not rise up, for I have previously made a vow."
Sannanda said: Pulastya, that tiger among sages, his senses agitated by anger,
with quivering lips and his resolve shattered, cursed the son of Droṇa.
Sannanda said: "O mountain, because you were so insolent, my desire was not fulfilled;
therefore, you shall indeed undergo constant emaciation by even a sesame seed's measure. (48)
Sannanda said:
O Nanda, once the sage Pulastya had gone to Kāśī, this Govardhana mountain diminished daily by the measure of a sesame seed.
As long as the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā flows and as long as Mount Govardhana stands, so long shall the influence of the Kali age never prevail.
I have related before you this wondrous, sacred, and purifying account of Govardhana, which removes the great sins of men.
O Kaurava, it is not surprising that this beautiful [act] grants perfect liberation. || 51 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Origin of the King of Mountains," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Sannanda said: Commanded by Hari in Goloka, Kālindī, the best of rivers,
circumambulated Kṛṣṇa and prepared to depart.
At that very moment, Virajā herself, the Gaṅgā born from the flow of Brahman, became merged into the Yamunā;
thus the two rivers became one.
Therefore, O King Nanda, people know Kṛṣṇā as the most perfect [expansion] of Kṛṣṇa,
and the chief queen of even the most perfect one.
Then, with great speed, Kālindī, the best of rivers,
having emerged from the gateway of the grove, broke through the force of Virajā.
Having touched the multitude of countless cosmic eggs and turned into the liquid of Brahma,
that great river, by its own force, flows far along, piercing through those waters.
At the tip of the big toe of his left foot, which had pierced the summit of the cosmic egg,
there was the cavity of the venerable Vāmana, filled with the fluid of Brahmā.
Into that [lake], the best of rivers entered together with the glorious Gaṅgā;
and having reached Vaikuṇṭha, the station of the Unconquerable, she remained within the sphere of Dhruva.
Pervading the world of Brahmā as she fell from the sphere of Brahmā,
she then went from world to world through the hundreds of worlds of the gods.
Then it fell with great force upon the summit of Mount Sumeru,
having surpassed the mountain peaks and shattered the surfaces of the massive boulders.
She rose up to go toward the southern direction of Sumeru;
then the illustrious Yamunā herself issued forth from the illustrious Gaṅgā.
The great river Gaṅgā then proceeded toward the Himavat mountain,
while the Kṛṣṇā, having reached the Kalinda mountain, then set forth.
When she originates from the Kaliṅda mountain, she is celebrated as Kālindī;
[she flows] along the firm slopes of the boulder-cliffs of the ridges of Mount Kaliṅga.
Breaking through and rolling over the surface of the earth, the swift and virtuous Kālindī,
purifying the lands as she flowed, reached the Khāṇḍava forest.
Desiring the most perfect Śrī Kṛṣṇa as her husband in person, the daughter of Kalinda assumed a supreme, divine form and performed austerities. 14.
Having taken refuge in the water within the house built by her father, she then swiftly reached the region of Vraja as the Kālindī river. || 15 ||
Near Vṛndāvana, close to Mathurā,
in an auspicious place on the shore of the Śrī Mahāvana forest, at a delightful sandy spot.
And in Śrīgokula, the most beautiful Yamunā, having become a herd of cows,
made her own dwelling for the sake of the rāsa dance with Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra.
Then, moving from one cow-pen to another, overwhelmed by the sight of Vraja,
she became drenched in tears of the bliss of love and flowed toward the west.
Then, having bowed three times with speed in the circle of Vraja,
she departed for Prayāga, the most excellent of holy places, purifying the lands as she went.
Once again, she went with the illustrious Gaṅgā to the Ocean of Milk;
in the heavens, the gods rained down flowers and raised shouts of victory.
Kṛṣṇā, the illustrious Yamunā herself, Kālindī, the best among rivers,
having reached the ocean, spoke to Śrī Gaṅgā with a faltering voice.
Yamunā said:
O Gaṅgā, you are indeed blessed, the purifier of the entire universe;
born from the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, you are the sole object of veneration for all the worlds.
I am going upward to the world of Hari; you too go, O auspicious one!
For there has never been, nor will there ever be, anyone divine equal to you.
Gaṅgā said: "Gaṅgā consists of all sacred fords; therefore, I bow down to you.
Whatever has been spoken [inappropriately], forgive that, O most auspicious one. (24)
O Kṛṣṇā, you alone are blessed, the purifier of the entire universe;
born from the left shoulder of Kṛṣṇa, you are the embodiment of supreme bliss.
She is the most perfectly complete, directly worshipped by all the world as the one and only;
she belongs to the high-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is himself the most perfectly complete. || 26 ||
O Kṛṣṇa, I bow down to you, the supreme Queen, who are yourself Kṛṣṇā;
you are difficult for even the holy places and gods to attain, and you are hard to find even in Goloka. (27)
"O auspicious one, by the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, I shall go to Pātāla;
for, afflicted by separation from you, I am truly unable to drink. (28)
"I shall become a member of the herd in Śrī Vraja within the circle of the Rāsa dance;
O beloved of Hari, forgive whatever I have said. (29)
Having thus bowed to one another, the two rivers departed swiftly;
purifying the worlds, the celestial river entered the nether regions.
She too shone in the forest of Bhogavatī by the name Bhogavatī;
for Śeṣa, along with the three-eyed Lord, indeed bears her waters upon his head.
Then Kṛṣṇā, having pierced through the seven concentric circles with great force,
rolled upon the surface of the earth consisting of the seven continents with even greater speed.
Having reached the golden ground and arrived at the Lokāloka mountain,
the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā) broke through the slopes of its peaks and ridges.
And it quickly flew up over her head with a vast stream of water;
rising upward from there, it went to the heaven of the gods.
Having pervaded those worlds up to the realm of Brahmā, she reached the abode of Hari, the aperture of the cosmic egg,
which was filled with the essence of the venerable Brahman.
While the gods rained down a shower of flowers and bowed down in reverence,
the best of rivers ascended once more to Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s Goloka.
If this auspicious account of the fresh movements of the daughter of Mount Kalinda is heard or recited on earth, it bestows excellent blessings;
and if any person indeed retains it or reads it constantly, [the same result follows].
He goes to the supreme abode, which is encompassed by the pastimes of his own private grove.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of Kālindī’s Arrival," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nanda and Saṃnanda.
Having heard the words of Sannanda, Nanda prepared to depart;
together with all the hosts of cowherds, the high-minded one became joyful. || 1 ||
Accompanied by Yaśodā, Rohiṇī, and all the hosts of cowherd women,
he was adorned with horses, chariots, heroic men, and circles of brahmins.
Drawn by oxen and yoked with carts, followed by the elderly and children alike,
he was accompanied by singers and the sounding of conchs and drums.
O King, the high-minded King Nanda, having mounted his chariot with his two sons Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, went to the forest of Vṛndāvana.
The eminent cowherd Vṛṣabhānu, having mounted an elephant with his wife,
carried his daughter Rādhā on his lap while being sung to by singers.
Accompanied by the sweet sounds of mṛdaṅgas, cymbals, lutes, and flutes,
he went to the Vṛndāvana forest together with cowherds and herds of cows.
Likewise, the Upanandas, the Nandas, and the six Vṛṣabhānus went to the forest of Vṛndāvana together with all their attendants.
Having entered Vṛndāvana, all the cowherds, together with their followers,
established their camps and took up residence here and there.
It was provided with an assembly hall and pavilions, possessed strong fortifications and moats,
extended for four yojanas, and was equipped with seven gates.
Vṛṣabhānu constructed a charming city with a royal highway surrounded by lakes and containing a thousand groves.
In the city of Nanda, the city of Vṛṣabhānu, Śrī Kṛṣṇa wandered about intent on play with the boys, bringing joy to the gopīs.
Then, O King, in Vṛndāvana, with the approval of all the cowherds,
Rāma and Kṛṣṇa became charming keepers of calves.
Rāma and Keśava drove the calves along with the boys to the sacred sandy bank near the Kālindī at the edge of the village.
Completely absorbed here and there in groves and bowers, crawling about and playing, they wandered through the forest.
Adorned with networks of tinkling bells, their feet were graced by splashing anklets and ornaments;
they wore blue and yellow garments and were decorated with necklaces and armlets.
While the children were throwing [stones] at them with slings, they remained intent on playing the flute,
accompanied by other children who made the sound of tinkling bells with their mouths.
Running along, Rāma and Keśava shone with the shadows of birds;
they were adorned with peacock feathers and decorated with flowers and sprouts.
O King, once, having learned that the demon Vatsāsura had arrived among the herds of calves,
sent by Kaṃsa, he went there slowly.
Running about everywhere among the cowherds and repeatedly wagging his tail,
the demon struck Hari on the shoulder with his two hind legs.
When the boys had fled, Kṛṣṇa seized him by both feet,
whirled him around, and threw him down upon the ground.
Taking him up again with both hands, Hari hurled him at a wood-apple tree;
then, as the Daitya met his death, that great wood-apple tree [was shattered].
He caused the wood-apples to fall, and that was like a marvel; while the boys were struck with wonder, they cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! (22).
In the heavens, the gods raised shouts of victory and let fall a rain of flowers;
that great light of the Daitya then became absorbed into Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Bahulāśva said:
O Sage, who was this Vatsāsura in his previous life that he performed such meritorious deeds,
that he attained absorption in Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme beyond the supreme, who is full of all splendor?
Śrī Nārada said: The great Daitya named Pramīla, the son of Mura and conqueror of the gods,
arrived at the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha and beheld the cow Nandinī.
Desiring to obtain [the cow], Vasiṣṭha became a Brāhmaṇa and begged for the beautiful cow;
while Vasiṣṭha, who possessed divine vision, remained silent, the cow spoke.
Nandinī said:
"Having become a brahmin, you came here to seize the cow of the sages;
therefore, O evil-minded one, you are a demon born from a drum—become a calf of the cows! (27)
Śrī Nārada said:
At that very moment, the great asura, the son of Mura, assumed the form of a calf;
having circumambulated Vasiṣṭha and bowed down, he cried out, "Save me! (28)
Gaurī said:
"O great Daitya, at the end of the Dvāpara age, when you have gone among the cows and calves in the Vṛndā forest, then your liberation will occur. (29)
Śrī Nārada said:
Since Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the most perfect Supreme Being in person and the purifier of the fallen,
it is no cause for wonder that the demon Vatsāsura was absorbed into Him.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Demon Vatsāsura," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Once, while tending the calves with his companions, Lord Hari,
accompanied by Balarāma, beheld the Daitya Baka who had arrived near the Yamunā.
Resembling a white mountain, with massive feet and a thunderous roar,
Vajratuṇḍa seized Hari as the young boys fled.
All the children, weeping, became as if lifeless;
then, raising a cry of "Alas! Alas!", all the gods assembled.
Then Indra, taking up his thunderbolt, struck that one of great strength;
by that blow he fell down, yet he did not die and rose up again.
Brahmā also struck that Mahābaka with the Brahma-staff;
by that blow, he fell down unconscious for two ghaṭikās.
Shaking his own body and yawning with force, the powerful Daitya rose up again; he did not die then, but roared like a thundercloud.
Trilocana struck that great asura with his trident;
though one of his wings was severed, the exceedingly terrifying Daitya did not die.
Then Vāyu struck that Baka with the Vāyavya weapon;
Baka wavered because of it, but then he stood firm there once more.
Yama struck him in front with the staff of Yama;
yet Baka, who possessed fierce prowess, did not die by that staff.
The staff too was broken, yet the crane was not wounded;
at that very moment, the sun of fierce prowess arrived before them.
The wielder of the bow struck the demon Baka with a hundred arrows;
however, Baka did not die from those sharp shafts that had entered his wings.
And he struck Dhanada with an exceedingly sharp sword;
though his second wing was severed, that bull among the Daityas did not die.
With the frost-weapon, Soma struck that great demon;
afflicted by the cold and rendered unconscious, the Daitya did not die, but rose up again.
With the Āgneya weapon, Agni struck that great Baka;
the Daitya's hair turned to ash, yet the great villain did not die.
The Lord of Waters bound him with a noose and dragged him across the earth;
from that dragging, the great sinner was torn apart, yet he did not die. || 15 ||
The powerful Bhadrakālī struck him with her mace;
stunned by that blow, he fell into a state of extreme exhaustion.
Rising up with his head wounded and shaking his body again,
the heroic Baka, that great and wicked Daitya, roared like a thundercloud.
Then Śaktidhara quickly hurled his spear at him;
by it, one foot of that best of birds was broken, but he did not die.
Then, suddenly rushing forward in a rage with a sound like lightning,
the Daitya put the gods to flight with his own beak, which had a sharp tip.
Baka pursued the gods who had fled ahead through the sky;
then that Daitya returned there, making the circle of the quarters resound.
Then all the celestial sages, all the Brahman-sages,
and the twice-born quickly bestowed a fruitful blessing upon the joy of the Śrīs.
At that very moment, Kṛṣṇa expanded his radiant body within him;
Mahābaka, his throat wounded, suddenly vomited up Kṛṣṇa.
Again, having arrived with a sharp beak to seize Kṛṣṇa,
he was caught by the tail and dashed against the ground by Kṛṣṇa.
Rising again, Kṛṣṇa stretched out his beak and, as an elephant tears a branch, he tore at the crane’s beak with both hands. || 24 ||
Then, as the Daitya died, his light entered into Kṛṣṇa;
the deities showered flowers, accompanied by shouts of "Victory! (jaya). || 25 ||
All the cowherds, filled with wonder, embraced Kṛṣṇa from all sides and said, "O friend, you have become safe; you have been liberated from the jaws of death!"
Thus Kṛṣṇa, having slain Baka, returned to the royal palace with his army, accompanied by the boys and the calves, singing joyfully.
Having heard this, the young girls went to the house of this great-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the most perfect one, and sang; they were exceedingly amazed. || 28 ||
Śrī Bahulāśva said:
Who was this Daitya in former times, and for what reason did he become a crane? And how did he attain absorption into Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman and Lord of All? (29)
Śrī Nārada said: O King, there was a Daitya named Utkala, the son of Hayagrīva;
having utterly defeated the immortals in battle, he seized the parasol of Indra.
Likewise, having seized the kingdom from men and kings, the one of great strength ruled for a hundred years a sovereignty endowed with every prosperity.
Once, while wandering at the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean, the Daitya approached the vicinity of the leaf-hut of the sage-siddha Jājali.
Casting his hook into the water and repeatedly pulling up fish,
that evil-minded man paid no heed even though he was forbidden by the sage.
To him, the perfected Jājali, the best of sages, pronounced this curse:
"O evil-minded one, since you devour fish like a crane, become a crane yourself! (34)
At that very moment, he became a crane, his luster vanished and his pride gone;
falling at his feet and bowing with palms joined in reverence, he spoke.
Utkala said:
"O sage Jājali, I do not know of your fierce austerity; protect me!
The wise know that association with holy men like you is the supreme gateway to liberation. (36)
Those who are equal toward friend and foe, in honor and dishonor, and toward gold and a clod of earth; those who are indeed the same in pleasure and pain—they are the virtuous ones such as you.
O Sage, what great thing has not been attained by men through the sight of the Great Ones?
One may obtain the sovereignty of Brahmā, universal empire, or even the station of Indra. (38)
O Jājali, tiger among sages, what need have people for the three aims of life?
Through the grace of the virtuous, even the complete Brahman is directly attained. (39)
Śrī Nārada said:
Then that sage Jājali, being pleased, spoke to him:
"Indeed, by him sixty thousand years of austerity have been performed."
When the twenty-eighth yuga of the Vaivasvata Manvantara had arrived,
at the end of the Dvāpara age, in the land of Bhārata, specifically in the district of Mathurā within the Vraja region.
The most perfect Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself will personally wander about in Vṛndāvana, tending the calves of the cows. 42.
Then you will attain absorption in Kṛṣṇa, of this there is no doubt;
even Daityas such as Hiraṇyākṣa and others reached the supreme state through enmity alone. (43)
Thus the Daitya Bakāsura became Utkala through the boon of Jājali and attained absorption in Śrī Kṛṣṇa; what cannot be achieved through the company of the virtuous? (44)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Bakāsura," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Once, while tending the calves together with the boys,
Hari engaged in childhood play near the beautiful banks of the Kālindī.
A great Daitya named Aghāsura was stationed there;
having made his body one krośa in length, he stretched out the circle of his mouth.
Having seen from afar that form resembling a mountain in the forest of Vṛndāvana,
the cowherds went toward its mouth, making the sound of *añjali* gestures with their calves.
And for the sake of protecting them, Hari entered its mouth with his army; meanwhile, the children along with their calves were swallowed by the one in the form of a serpent.
There was a cry of "Alas! from the gods, while the Daityas indeed experienced great joy;
then Kṛṣṇa expanded his own Vairāja body within the belly of Agha.
His vital breaths, being obstructed, emerged after piercing through his head;
O King of Mithilā, Kṛṣṇa then issued forth from his mouth along with the calves and the boys.
Seeing the calves along with their mothers, Mādhava restored them to life;
that light then merged into the dark-complexioned Śrīghana, just as lightning dissolves into a rain cloud.
At that very moment, O King, the gods rained down showers of flowers.
Having heard these words of the sage, the King of Mithilā spoke these words.
Who was this Daitya who, in former times, attained absorption into Śrī Kṛṣṇa? Oh, through the persistence of his enmity, the Daitya quickly went to Hari! (9)
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, the son of the demon Śaṅkha was named Agha, possessed of great strength;
he was a youth exceedingly handsome, like a second Kāmadeva in person.
Seeing the sage Aṣṭāvakra, who was deformed, walking on Mount Malaya,
that sinner laughed at him, saying, "This man is ugly."
He cursed that great evildoer: "O evil-minded one, become a serpent!
Be ugly, with a crooked gait, born among serpents upon the circle of the earth. (12)
Seeing the Daitya fallen at his feet, dejected and stripped of pride,
the sage was pleased and granted him a boon once again.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"When Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose beauty is like ten million Cupids, comes to your womb in the form of a serpent, then your liberation will occur."
Śrī Nārada said:
By the curse of Aṣṭāvakra, Aghāsura indeed became a serpent;
yet, by virtue of that very boon, he attained supreme liberation, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Having heard that Kṛṣṇa had been released from the mouth of the calf-eating demon and subsequently freed from the demon Aghāsura, Yaśodā became overwhelmed with fear after only a few days.
[He saw] Kalāvatī and Rohiṇī, the cowherd women and the cowherds older than himself,
the excellent cowherd Vṛṣabhānu, King Nanda, and the Lord of Vraja.
Having summoned the nine Upanandas, the Nandas, and the Vṛṣabhānus, the lords of subjects, Yaśomatī spoke these words in their presence.
Yaśodā said:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How may prosperity be mine? For many portents of ill fortune come upon my son moment by moment. (19)
"Previously, having left the great forest, we went to Vṛndāraṇya;
now, having abandoned this as well, where shall we go? Tell us of a place free from fear. (20)
"This boy of mine is restless; while playing, he indeed wanders far away.
All children are fickle; they do not heed my words. (21)
The powerful Bakāsura, with his sharp beak, swallowed my infant; but Aghāsura seized the child who had been released from him, though he was distressed by the other children.
The demon Vatsāsura, who sought to kill him, was himself slain by fate;
for the sake of my calf, I do not allow the child to go outside from his own home. (23)
Śrī Nārada said: Seeing Yaśodā thus speaking and constantly weeping, Nanda spoke to her.
He, the best among the upholders of dharma and the knower of dharma and artha, comforted him with the words of Śukra.
King Nanda said:
"O Yaśomatī, you have forgotten all the words of Garga;
the speech of Brahmins is true and never becomes false. (25)
Therefore, one should practice giving, which wards off all calamities;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a blessing greater than giving.
Śrī Nārada said:
Then, O King, Yaśodā gave to the brāhmaṇas nine jewels of great value,
as well as her own ornaments for the child and Balarāma.
Then Nanda gave as a gift ten thousand bulls, a hundred thousand charming cows, and two hundred thousand loads of food. (28)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Aghāsura," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Now listen further, O Indra among kings, to this account of the childhood play and the youth of the high-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa, just as it was proclaimed. (1)
Having protected the calves and cowherds from death at the mouth of Agha, Śrī Kṛṣṇa went to the bank of the Yamunā and spoke these words that increase one's joy.
"Oh, how exceedingly beautiful is this dear sandy bank, with its soft sands and filled with the pollen of autumn-blooming lotuses! (3)
It was perfumed by a threefold wind of sweet fragrance;
it resounded with the humming of bees and was filled with groves of trees and creepers.
Having sat down here, O cowherds, since one watch of the day has passed, it is now time for food;
therefore, take your meal.
Here the ground suitable for eating is seen, with its soft sand;
having drunk water, the calves will graze upon the lush grass.
Having heard these words of Kṛṣṇa, the boys said, "So be it," and they all sat down on the riverbank to take their meal.
Then some boys who had no food with them spoke into the ear of Kṛṣṇa with piteous voices: || 8 ||
"But what shall we do? There is no food by our side;
indeed, we must go to the distant village of Nanda with the calves. (9)
Having heard this, Hari said: "O dear ones, do not grieve;
with great effort, I shall provide food for everyone."
"Therefore, all you children, remain intent upon my words.
At these words of Kṛṣṇa, they stood by Kṛṣṇa's side;
having set aside their carrying-slings, all the others ate together with Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa indeed formed a royal circle with the cowherd boys gathered before him;
he stood in the center, adorned with a yellow cloth, while they were arrayed in garments of many colors.
Then he was surrounded on all sides by those excellent cowherd boys, just as the Lord of the Immortals is surrounded by the gods;
and again, O Vaideha, he was like a golden pericarp in the midst of soft lotuses.
Having eaten mouthfuls of flowers, sprouts, shoots, leaves, and fruits, Kṛṣṇa looked at them all and spoke this: kṛṣṇastu kavalaṃ bhuktvā sarvān paśyannidaṃ jagau || 15 ||
Pointing to other [fruits], he said, "I truly do not know what is sweet, my friend.
Having said, "So be it," the boy took other mouthfuls and gave them to him. (16)
Having eaten, they spoke to one another while laughing;
once again there, Subala gave a morsel to Hari.
Kṛṣṇa, having eaten a few morsels there, laughed;
and all those children who had already eaten their morsels laughed aloud.
The children said:
"Listen, O son of Nanda! He whose maternal grandfather is a fool has no knowledge of food; therefore, sweetness is not found in it. (19)
Then Śrīdāmā gave a morsel to Mādhava as well;
and all the boys of Vraja praised him as the most excellent among them all.
Furthermore, the protector of the herd gave a morsel to Kṛṣṇa,
and with some effort, he gave small portions to all the other boys as well;
having eaten, Śrī Kṛṣṇa and all the children of Vraja laughed together.
The children said:
"And his food was just like that of Subala."
Having eaten, all of us were indeed extremely distressed in mind; therefore, we each showed him our own food individually. (23)
Laughing and making others laugh, they played with one another;
they held flutes, canes, and horns against their bellies and tucked them under their armpits.
In his left hand he holds a morsel of food, and on his fingers he wears fruits;
upon his head he bears a crown, and likewise a yellow cloth upon his shoulder.
Wearing a forest garland on his chest and a girdle likewise upon his waist,
he bore anklets on his feet and the Śrīvatsa mark and Kaustubha gem upon his heart.
Standing in the midst of the assembly of cowherds and making them laugh with his own jests, Hari,
the enjoyer of sacrifices, partook of the sacrificial food while the world of heaven looked on.
While the children, whose protector was Kṛṣṇa, were thus eating,
the calves entered deep into the cave out of greed for grass.
Seeing those cowherds terrified with fear, Kṛṣ�na said:
"You all go; I, however, will not bring the calves back here."
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa rose up, took a morsel in his hand,
and searched for his own calves within the mountain caves, thickets, and abysses.
At that very moment, the Lotus-born Brahmā arrived;
having witnessed the liberation of the demon Aghara,
he beheld Kṛṣṇa with his mind according to his own desire.
He was eating food together with the cowherd boys. || 31 ||
And having seen Kṛṣṇa, he said in his mind:
"This is surely a cowherd and not the God of gods; for if Hari were he, he would not eat such highly contemptible food."
Or how was he delighted with the cowherd boys of Vraja? || 32 ||
Having spoken thus, O King, Brahmā was deluded by the Māyā of the Supreme Self; indeed, he then set his mind upon beholding Mañju’s greatness—how wonderful! (33)
Having previously led all the calves away from the cowherds and stationed himself in the sky,
the unborn Lord, filled with wonder upon seeing the liberation of the demon Aghāsura, vanished from sight.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Abduction of the Calf and the Cowherd Boys," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
The venerable Nārada said:
Once, Kṛṣṇa, together with Balarāma, was tending the charming cows.
Accompanied by all the cowherds, he went to the fresh palm grove. || 1 ||
Out of fear of Dhenuka, those cowherds did not go into the interior of the forest.
Kṛṣṇa did not go there either; Balarāma alone entered.
The immensely powerful Baladeva had a blue garment tied around his waist.
For indeed, he wandered through that forest for the sake of ripening fruit.
Shaking the palm trees with his two arms, he caused a multitude of fruits to fall.
And roaring fearlessly, he was manifestly Ananta himself, possessed of infinite prowess.
Hearing the sound of the falling fruits, Khara was overcome with anger.
At midday, the wicked and powerful Bhīma, a friend of Kaṃsa, fell asleep.
Dhenuka came forward to fight with Baladeva.
He swiftly struck him on the chest with the strength of his two hind legs.
Running about repeatedly, he made his own harsh sound.
Having quickly seized Dhenuka by his two hind legs, Balarāma—
And with one hand, he effortlessly cast down the palm tree.
By him even the palm tree was broken, along with many other palm trees standing nearby.
O Indra among kings, he caused it to fall; that was like a marvel.
Rising up again, the lord of the Daityas seized Bala with fury.
He urged him forward for a league, like one elephant driving against another.
Then Balarāma, having seized Dhenuka, immediately whirled him around.
He dashed him against the surface of the earth; he fell unconscious with his head shattered.
In an instant, rising up again with a body joined by wrath, ||11||
Having placed [it] upon his head, he assumed a four-peaked and terrifying form.
He drove away the cowherds with his sharp and terrifying horns.
Intoxicated with pride, he swiftly pursued the cowherds who had fled ahead.
Śrīdāmā struck him with a staff, and Subala likewise with his fist.
Stoka struck that mighty Daitya with his noose.
With a throw he struck Arjuna, and with a kick he struck the Daitya Khara.
Viśālarṣabha quickly approached with his foot and by means of his own strength.
For Tejasvin was struck with a crescent-headed arrow, and Devaprastha with javelins. ||15||
Varūthapa struck the great donkey with a ball.
Then Kṛṣṇa also, having seized that demon Dhenuka with both his hands, [crushed him].
Having whirled it rapidly, he hurled it upon Mount Govardhana.
By the blow of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he remained unconscious for two ghaṭikās.
Rising again, he shook his body and tore at his face.
Carrying Śrī Hari on his two horns, the Daitya ran, not out of devotion.
He moved through the sky with that [weapon], fighting at a height of one hundred thousand yojanas.
Having seized the demon Dhenuka, the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself—
He threw him down into the midst of the earth; with his bones crushed, he fell unconscious.
Rising up again, he let out an exceedingly terrifying roar with his two horns.
Having uprooted Govardhana, the donkey hurled it at Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having seized the mountain, Śrī Kṛṣṇa did not hurl it at his head.
Then the powerful Daitya, seizing a mountain, hurled it at Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa, having lifted Govardhana, set it back down in its original place.
Running again, the great Daitya tore up the earth with his two horns.
Striking with his two hind legs, he roared;
by that roar, the entire circle of the earth's regions and the cosmic egg trembled.
Grasping him with both hands, the exceedingly powerful Baladeva—
He dashed him, unconscious and with his head shattered, against the surface of the earth.
Then Acyuta’s elder brother struck that Daitya once more with his fist.
By that blow of the fist, he indeed met his death instantly.
At that very moment, the gods showered flowers born of the Nandana grove.
Having emerged from the body, he too possessed a dark and beautiful form.
The Lord wears a garland, is clothed in yellow garments, and is adorned with a forest wreath. ||27||
Accompanied by a hundred thousand attendants and adorned with a thousand banners.
He bore the sound of a thousand wheels and was accompanied by ten thousand horses.
Abounding in the splendor of a hundred thousand chowries, it was crimson in color and filled with exceedingly precious gems.
It was a hundred thousand yojanas wide, moving as fast as thought, and captivating to the mind. ||29||
It was equipped with a network of small bells and joined with the tinkling of water-pots and anklets.
Having circumambulated Hari along with his army, he assumed a divine form.
Having ascended his divine chariot, he illuminated the circles of the quarters.
O King, the Daitya went to Goloka, which is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). || 31 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, together with his companions and the boys, having slain Dhenuka, [departed].
The fame of that [cowherd] shone forth as the herds of cows in Gokula sang it aloud.
The king said:
O Sage, how did you previously attain liberation? Who was that Dhenukāsurasura?
Tell me this in truth: how did he come to attain such harshness?
The venerable Nārada said:
The son of Vairocanerba was the powerful one named Sāhasika.
He indeed took delight with ten thousand women on Mount Gandhamādana.
A great sound of musical instruments and anklets arose in that forest.
Even though he was staying in a cave, the sage remained mindful of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then, by that [act] as well, the meditation of Durvāsas was indeed interrupted.
Durvāsas, emaciated in body, went forth wearing his wooden sandals.
With a long beard, holding a staff, and possessing a splendor like a mass of blazing fire.
He, by whose curse this entire universe trembles, spoke thus.
Durvāsas said:
Arise, you who have the form of a donkey! Be a donkey, O evil-minded one!
When four hundred thousand years had passed in Bhārata once again, || 38 ||
In the divine and meritorious region of Mādhura, in the Tāla forest grove.
O Asura, your liberation shall come through the hand of Baladeva.
The illustrious Nārada said:
Therefore, Śrī Kṛṣṇa struck him with Bala’s hand.
A boon was granted to Prahlāda: "The lineage of yours shall not be slain by me."
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Asura Dhenuka," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Brahmā said: To Kṛṣṇa, who possesses a cloud-like body, whose garment is the lightning, who speaks words as sweet as nectar, and who is higher than the highest;
Salutations be to that Lord who holds the flute, who is endowed with the moonlight of his crest-lock, and who is accompanied by his brother. || 1 ||
But Kṛṣṇa is himself the Supreme Person, the manifest, the perfect, the Supreme Lord, Hari who transcends primordial nature;
we gods are but portions of the digits of his incarnations.
We create the universe through the powers of his strides. || 2 ||
You, who are the manifest incarnation of Kṛṣṇacandra,
have come here in Vṛndāvana as the son of Nanda, assuming the guise of a cowherd to tend the calves.
Tending [the cattle] with the chief cowherds, you truly shine forth.
Hari, who is enchanting with the playfulness of ten million Cupids,
radiant with the Kaustubha gem, dark-complexioned, clad in yellow garments,
the Lord of Vraja, the flute-bearer, and the Lord of Rādhikā— [I meditate upon Him].
I bow to that most beautiful one in the grove. || 4 ||

Worship that Kṛṣṇa, Hari, the primordial God, who is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) in this world, like a cloud-free sky; whose limbs are pure, who is the supreme intellect, and whose form is the consciousness of the sacrificial altar.
Through devotion and other qualities, together with a multitude of states of pure dispassion. || 5 ||
O learned one, as long as the mind is dominated by powerful passion, it remains nothing but conceptualization and mental construction.
From these two arises the god of love through the union of egoism; and by that means, people gradually undergo a transformation of their intellect.
Like a flash of lightning, like the seasonal quality of water, like a line in the midst of water, like a firebrand on the ground, and like the beast of a deceitful traveler—
so too is the happiness of this world false.
Enveloped by suffering, reeling amidst sense objects, it is like a whirling firebrand. || 7 ||
Just as trees appear to move here even when the water is moving, and the earth appears to move when the eye is shaken,
so too do the qualities born of material nature affect the person who wanders within it.
One should speak the truth, which is the source of virtue and happiness; this alone, O Kṛṣṇa.
Suffering and happiness arise from the mind; while they may seem real during sleep, alas, upon waking on this earth, they are seen to be false.
Thus, for a person whose intellect is refined by discernment, everything [is seen as such].
For the world, perceived through the delusion of a dream, would indeed exist eternally [as such]. || 9 ||
The man of knowledge, having abandoned the sense of "mine" and the bond of egoism, constantly relishing the state of dispassion and remaining free from desire,
is like a lamp that produces hundreds of other lamps.
One should likewise perceive the manifestation of the Self as the single reality upon the earth.
A devotee should worship Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Unborn, within his heart, having shaken off the nature of qualities like a smokeless fire;
just as one perceives the single moon reflected in various jars filled with water.
Such is the excellent Paramahaṃsa, who has accomplished his purpose. || 11 ||
The Vedas constantly praise him who indeed knows but a sixteenth part of Hari’s greatness;
they never know it, even within the three worlds.
Who else is there among people capable of describing his virtues? || 12 ||
With four faces, I am indeed the god Śrī Pañcavaktra with five faces;
and with a thousand heads, I am indeed he with a thousand faces.
[The merit] belongs to him who praises [him] and performs service. || 13 ||
Viṣṇu is the dweller in Vaikuṇṭha,
and Hari himself is the resident of the Ocean of Milk;
he is Nārāyaṇa and likewise the son of Dharma.
He worships you, the Lord of Goloka. || 14 ||
Oh, how exceedingly blessed is the majesty of Murāri! Neither sages nor humans on earth know it;
nor do gods, demons, Manus, or even the wise behold those two feet even in their dreams. (15)
I bow down to Hari, the mine of virtues, the bestower of excellent liberation, the Supreme beyond the supreme; the Lord of Ramā, the Lord of qualities, the Lord of Vraja.
His face was made beautiful by betel-leaf; he spoke sweetly with his bimba-like lips, accompanied by a smile and teeth as white as kunda flowers;
his cheeks were enchanting, framed by dark locks of hair.
I bow to him who is worthy of the ornament of swinging golden earrings.
Indeed, your beautiful form,
which utterly captivates the mind of the God of Love, may it ever manifest before my eyes.
Dark-complexioned and adorned with crocodile-shaped earrings. || 18 ||
I worship Him who is the most excellent of the pastimes of Vaikuṇṭha, the captivating one, the supreme boon-granter saluted by the hosts of gods,
and who is endowed with the pastimes of a cowherd boy.
I bow my head to Golokanātha. || 19 ||
Vṛndāvana is joined with cuckoos and birds of the spring season,
united with fragrant flowers and trees with sprouting branches, and graced by the play of gentle, steady breezes.
Victorious Hari, who goes [thus], may he always protect his devotees. || 20 ||
It steals away the pride of the lotus, the conceit of the trembling pearl, and the gift of the earth's lover; it is the arrow of the God of Love,
whose path is known by the ear and whose departure is marked by the pair of eyes.
Worship, therefore, that side-long glance which is skillful in bestowing gifts right before one's eyes.
I worship Him who has the form of the autumnal moon, whose multitude of jewel-like nails is delightful and deep red, whose heart is full, who manifests the shattering of darkness,
and who destroys all the sins of men within the universe.
The gods in heaven have sufficiently praised Hari-Viṣṇu in the land of Bhārata.
"Does this appear like the rim of a great lotus, or does it constantly resemble the wheel of the sun's flashing chariot? Such is the bearer of sound,
appearing just like the wheel placed by Hari, joined with a hundred rays."
The shimmering, glorious anklet has been placed upon your lotus-like foot by Hari.
I worship the divine yellow garment on the waist of Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless, which captivates the mind and is adorned with tiny bells. 24.
I worship the feet of the sage Bhṛgu upon Kṛṣṇa’s chest, which are a perfect abode of splendor;
likewise, I worship the Śrīvatsa mark, which possesses the luster of a touchstone and is endowed with supreme radiance;
and I worship the diamond necklaces and the rows of golden gems and pearls adorning His throat.
[He saw] masses of bees, shimmering like stars, making a humming sound. || 25 ||
Adorned with a flute, habitually giving gifts to the twice-born,
the color of vermilion, with the graceful movement of a very tall bamboo, possessing a multitude of golden rings, and endowed with moon-like nails.
Remember those two hands, permeated by the sweet fragrance of the kadamba flower. || 26 ||

I eternally worship His neck, which moves slowly like the neck of the royal swan of Lake Mānasa and rises high; and I worship His two hands, which eclipse the pride of the clouds and possess the side-locks of hair like the feathers of a crow.
The king, as bright as a mirror of black steel, bestowing happiness, possessing the form of fresh youth,
and radiant with jeweled earrings and locks of hair—
Adore her pair of cheeks, which possess the luster of the sun and the moon. || 28 ||
Adorned with gold and pearls, clothed in red lapis lazuli,
she is the playful beauty of Madana’s face, the essence of all loveliness;
resembling the reddish moon, she possesses the brilliance of ten million suns.
I bow to the crown of Viṣṇu, which has a beautiful crest fashioned from fire. || 29 ||
O Lord of Guha, in this region of the river,
neither Gaṇeśa, nor Tārīreśa, nor Divākara can enter the circle of the forest groves without [your] command.
I worship that Kṛṣṇacandra, the Lord of the World. || 30 ||
Having thus offered praise to the high-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā,
with palms joined once more, made his formal petition.
Forgive the transgression of your son as you would your own;
O Lord of the Universe, I am born from the lotus of your navel.
Where am I, a mere lord of the world, and where are you, the leader of millions of universes?
Therefore, O Lord, Master of Vraja, O Madhusūdana, protect me!
"By whose illusory power gods, demons, humans, and others are deluded, I, a fool, have indeed exerted myself to be deluded by his own māyā. (34)
"You are Nārāyaṇa, O Govinda; I am not Nārāyaṇa, O Hari.
Having fashioned the cosmic egg in the past, you lay upon it as Nārāyaṇa. (35)
In that very abode of Śrī Brahmā where yogis go after giving up their life-breath, Pūtanā has gone together with her entire family.
O Mādhava, O Lord, having assumed the forms of calves and cowherds, you indeed wandered in the forest because of my offense. (37)
Therefore, O Govinda, forgive me and be gracious toward me, disregarding my offense just as a father disregards that of his son. (38)
For those who are not devoted to you but are intent on knowledge, their affliction is especially great, like that of farmers seeking chaff in the field after much toil. (39)
Many who were devoted to the state of devotion to you have attained your own state—
namely, the yogis, the sages, and likewise those who dwell in Vraja.
The supreme delight is twofold: from hearing and from seeing.
Alas, O Hari, by your illusory power (māyā), no delight at all has arisen within me! 41.
Having spoken thus, with a tearful face and bowing at his lotus feet,
Brahmā spoke again to Kṛṣṇa with devotion, seeking forgiveness for everything.
When, having become one of those dwelling in the cowherd settlements, I worship Your lotus feet, may I then attain a happy rebirth, and not otherwise. (43)
But we, Śiva and the others, abide within the bodies of cowherds;
therefore, those who behold Kṛṣṇa even once in Bhārata are truly blessed. (44)
O Lord, how great is the good fortune of Kṛṣṇa, of you, his mother and father, and likewise of the cowherds and cowherd-maidens, that you are seen in Vraja in such a complete form! 45.
May the pearl necklace— the benefactor of the entire universe, the support of all, the creator of the world— protect me;
he who is the abode of divine play and the playground for the daughters of the sages.
The incarnation of Kṛṣṇacandra is the perfection of play. || 46 ||
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, lotus of the Vṛṣṇi clan, son of Nanda,
Lord of Rādhā, Madanamohana, God of gods!
O Lord of Vraja, you have utterly deluded me on this earth with your unconquerable power.
O Govinda, Lord of Gokula, protect me, protect me! || 47 ||
Whoever performs a circumambulation of Kṛṣṇa-Hari shall obtain the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites;
they shall go to the world of Kṛṣṇa, which bestows happiness and is higher than the highest.
He shall go to Goloka, the most excellent world. || 48 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having thus praised Govinda, the glorious Lord of Vṛndāvana,
and having bowed down three times, the Lord of the World performed a circumambulation.
There, having become unobserved, Hari gave a command with his eye;
then, having bowed again, the Self-born One returned to his own world.
Then Kṛṣṇa quickly brought the calves from the forest to that sandy bank where, O King, the circle of cowherd leaders was gathered.
And the cowherd boys, deluded by Kṛṣṇa’s illusory power upon seeing Śrī Kṛṣṇa returned together with the calves, thought it had been but half a moment.
They said, "O Kṛṣṇa, you have arrived quickly with the calves;
O Lord, please take your meal here, for no one has prepared any food."
Then, laughing, Kṛṣṇa, having finished his meal together with the children,
showed them both the hide and the python.
In the evening, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Rāma and surrounded by the cowherds,
slowly returned to Vraja, leading the herd of calves before him.

[He saw] the son of the protector of Vraja, surrounded by a circle of cowherds and accompanied by calves of various colors— white, black, dark, and yellow, as well as red, smoky-grey, and green— possessing many temperaments and forms.
I bow to him who comes from the forest to the pleasant assembly hall.
O King, there was indeed great joy for the cowherd women at the sight of Kṛṣṇa; for without him, even a single moment had become like an eon for them.
Having separated the calves from the herd in the cow-pen, the children went each to their own home; and they sang of Hari’s slaying of the demon Aghāsura and his protection of themselves.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Hymn of Brahmā," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārada said:
By the will of the cowherd, those two, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, became cowherds;
tending the cows with their companions, the other cowherds, they wandered in the forest.
Then the cows, grazing in front, behind, and on both sides,
were beholding the beautiful faces of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma.
Moving here and there, they made the tinkling sound of bells and anklets;
they were adorned with networks of small bells, and their necks shone with golden garlands.
With clusters of pearls and peacock feathers, their tails and pure manes were radiant; they shone with networks of garlands made of shimmering new jewels. || 4 ||
O King, between the two horns were the head-ornaments, enchanting with their crest-jewels, which,
flashing with the brilliance of golden rays, wound themselves around the sides of the horns.
Some had slightly reddish forehead-marks, with yellow tails and ruddy feet;
they resembled Mount Kailāsa and possessed great virtues of character and form.
O King of Mithilā, there were cows with their calves moving slowly under the weight of their udders;
some were white as jasmine, others were pale-red, all possessing auspicious forms and yielding abundant milk.
Some were yellow, variegated, dark, and green;
others were copper-colored, smoke-colored, or as dark as a rain cloud, with their eyes fixed upon the one who was as dark as a rain cloud.
Those with short horns, long horns, or high horns, together with bulls;
those with deer-like horns or curved horns—these tawny cows are the refuge of auspiciousness.
Even as they gaze upon the tender and lovely meadows in forest after forest,
millions upon millions of cows graze at the sides of Kṛṣṇa.
The meritorious bank of the Śrī Yamunā is a forest dark with *tamāla* trees,
and filled with *nīpa*, *nimba*, and *kadamba* trees, as well as *pravāla*, *panasa*, and other trees.
It was adorned with plantains, kovidāras, and mangoes; with charming rose-apples and bilvas; and with aśvatthas, kapitthas, and mādhavī creepers.
The divine Vṛndāvana shone, enchanting with the spring season;
it surpassed the Nandana grove, the Sarvatobhadra, and the Caitraratha forest on every side.
There is a mountain named Govardhana, endowed with beautiful waterfalls and caves, composed of jewels and minerals, glorious, and filled with groves of Mandāra trees.
It was surrounded by śrīkhaṇḍa, badarī, raṃbhā, devadāru, and vaṭa trees,
as well as palāśa, plakṣa, aśoka, ariṣṭa, arjuna, and kadambaka trees.
It was adorned with *pārijāta*, *pāṭala*, and *campaka* trees;
it abounded in groves of *karañja* thickets and was surrounded by dark *indrayava* shrubs.
Accompanied by sweet-voiced cuckoos, male cuckoos, and peacocks, Kṛṣṇa wandered from forest to forest there, tending the cows.
In Vṛndāvana, in Madhuvana, beside Tālavana, in Kumudvana, in Bāhula, and in another, the divine Kāmavana; || 18 ||
On the side of Mount Bṛhatsānu and Mount Nandīśvara,
in the beautiful Kokila forest, which was filled with the warbling of cuckoos.
O King, [he dwelt] in the delightful and auspicious Kuśa forest, endowed with networks of creepers,
in the highly meritorious Bhadravana, and in the grove of Bhāṇḍīra.
At Lohārgala and on the banks of the Yamunā, in forest after forest,
he was dressed in yellow garments, surrounded by his retinue, wearing the attire of a dancer, and enchanting to behold.
O King, Kṛṣṇa shone forth, holding a cane and playing his flute to bring joy to the cowherd girls; he wore a crown of peacock feathers and was adorned with garlands.
Placing the herd of cows at the front, Hari himself entered the village of Śrī Nanda in the evening, playing his flute with various melodies.
Having heard the sound of the flute from the path of Śrī-vaṃśīvaṭa and seeing the sky pervaded by the dust of the cows, they emerged from their homes.
To distance themselves from the affliction of mental anguish and to obtain supreme bliss, the cowherd women came to see him, for they were unable to forget him. (25)

Moving slowly through the narrow streets crowded with herds of cattle, he— whose eyes were like lotus petals— was not obstructed by the womenfolk who watched him with sidelong glances like lions and moved with the playful grace of young elephants.

Adorned with the dust from the cows of Mithilā, bearing a magnificent dark-blue topknot, wearing golden armlets and a resplendent crown, he drew his arrow-like glances back as far as his ears. || 27 ||

Adorned with a necklace of jasmine flowers covered in pollen, with a blooming *karṇikāra* flower shimmering above his ear, wearing yellow garments and producing the sound of the flute, may the Lord, who has removed the heavy burden [of the world], protect you. (28)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s Tending of Cattle," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārada said:
Once, while tending the charming cows together with Balarāma and all the cowherd boys, Kṛṣṇa went to the fresh Tālavana forest.
Out of fear of Dhenuka, the cowherds did not go into the interior of the forest;
Kṛṣṇa also did not go there, but Balarāma alone entered.
Having tied his blue garment around his waist, the exceedingly powerful Baladeva wandered through that forest for the sake of ripe fruits.
Shaking the palm trees with his two arms and causing their clusters of fruit to fall,
he roared fearlessly like the manifest Ananta of infinite prowess.
Hearing the sound of the falling fruits, the powerful Khara—terrible, wicked, a friend of Kaṃsa, and overcome with anger—was asleep at midday. (5)
Dhenuka came forward to fight Baladeva;
he swiftly struck Bala on the chest with his two hind legs.
Running about repeatedly, Balarāma quickly seized Dhenuka by his two hind legs and let out a loud braying sound.
And with one hand, he effortlessly hurled the palm tree;
by that blow, the palm tree was shattered along with many other palms standing nearby.
O king of kings, he caused him to fall; it was like a marvel.
Rising once more, the lord of the Daityas seized Bala with fury.
Like one elephant attacking another, Balarāma hurled Dhenuka a distance of one yojana;
then, seizing him, he immediately whirled him around.
He dashed him against the surface of the earth; he fell unconscious with his head shattered.
In a moment, rising again, his body was filled with rage.
Placing his four-horned form upon his head and assuming a terrifying appearance,
he put the cowherds to flight with his sharp and fearsome horns.
Intoxicated with pride, he quickly ran after the cowherds who had fled ahead;
Śrīdāmā struck him with a staff, and Subala likewise with his fist.
Stoka struck that mighty Daitya with a noose;
Arjuna and Aṃśu struck the Daitya with a sling and a kick, respectively.
Viśālarṣabha quickly approached with his foot and by his own strength;
the radiant Devaprastha [struck] with a half-moon [arrow] and with slaps. || 15 ||
Varūthapa struck the great donkey with a ball;
then Kṛṣṇa also seized that demon Dhenuka with both his hands.
Having whirled him around, he quickly hurled him over Mount Govardhana;
by Śrī Kṛṣṇa's blow, he remained unconscious for two ghaṭikās.
Rising again, shaking his body and tearing at his face,
the demon seized Śrī Hari with his two horns and fled into the sky.
Having seized the demon Dhenuka himself, the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa engaged in a battle with him in the sky at a height of one hundred thousand yojanas.
He threw him down into the midst of the earth with his bones crushed; he fainted, but rising again, he let out an exceedingly terrifying roar with his two horns.
Having uprooted Govardhana, he challenged Śrī Kṛṣṇa to a contest of strength;
seizing the mountain, Śrī Kṛṣṇa hurled it onto his head.
Then the powerful demon, seizing the mountain, hurled it at Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
Kṛṣṇa, however, took Govardhana and cast it back to its original place.
Running again, the great Daitya tore the earth with his two horns;
striking Bala with his two hind feet, he let out a roar.
By that roar, the entire universe, including the circle of the earth's regions, trembled;
then the exceedingly powerful Baladeva seized him with both hands.
He dashed him, unconscious and with his head broken, against the surface of the earth;
then the elder brother of Acyuta struck that Daitya again with his fist.
By that blow of the fist, he immediately met his end;
at that very moment, the gods showered him with flowers born of the Nandana grove.
Having emerged from the body, he too possessed a dark and beautiful form;
the Lord was adorned with a garland, clad in yellow garments, and embellished with a forest wreath.
Accompanied by a hundred thousand attendants, adorned with a thousand banners,
resounding with the noise of a thousand wheels, and joined by ten thousand horses.
Abounding in the splendor of a hundred thousand yak-tail whisks, crimson in color, and laden with exquisite jewels,
it was a divine chariot a yojana in extent, moving as fast as thought, and captivating to the mind.
Adorned with a network of small bells and equipped with tinkling bells and anklets, he,
assuming a divine form, circumambulated Hari along with his army.
Having ascended a divine chariot and illuminating the circle of the quarters,
O King, the Daitya went to Goloka, which is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
Having slain Dhenuka along with his army, Śrī Kṛṣṇa shone together with the boys and the herds of cows in Gokula, who were loudly singing his glory.
The King said:
O Sage, how did he previously attain liberation? Who was that Dhenukāsuras, and how did he come to possess the state of a donkey? Tell me this in accordance with the truth.
Śrī Nārada said: The son of Bali, Virocana, was a powerful man named Sāhasika;
he indeed took delight with ten thousand women on Mount Gandhamādana.
A great sound of musical instruments and anklets arose in that forest, even for the sage who remained in his cave while remembering Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (35)
Then, because of him as well, Durvāsas’s meditation was interrupted;
Durvāsas, whose body was emaciated, emerged mounted upon his sandals.
With long beard, holding a staff, and possessing the brilliance of a mass of blazing fire,
he whose curse makes this entire universe tremble spoke.
Durvāsas said:
"Arise, you who have the form of a donkey! O evil-minded one, become a donkey again once four hundred thousand years have passed in Bhārata. (38)
O Asura, in the divine and meritorious region of Mathurā, in the Tālavana forest, your liberation shall come about by the hand of Baladeva.
Nārada said:
Therefore, Śrī Kṛṣṇa struck him with the hand of Bala; for a boon had been granted to Prahlāda: "Your lineage shall not be slain by me."
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Asura Dhenuka," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Then, without his companions, Hari himself, while tending the cows with the cowherds,
went to the bank of the Kālindī and proceeded toward a place enveloped by water and poison.
There, the water was defiled by Kāliya, the lord of serpents;
having drunk it, the Vasus, the cows, and the cowherds fell down near the water’s edge.
Then Hari, the manifest Lord, the destroyer of suffering, with a compassionate heart, restored them to life with a glance full of nectar.
Having tied a yellow cloth around his waist and climbed a *nīpa* tree, Mādhava fell from its lofty branch into that water polluted by poison.
The wicked water, churned by the mass of Kṛṣṇa, surged forth;
it became like a swarm of bees in the river at the serpent's abode.
At that very moment, O King, the enraged serpent Kāliya, covered with a hundred hoods, bit Mādhava with his teeth and covered him with his coils.
Kṛṣṇa, having assumed a massive body, emerged from his bonds; seizing that lord of serpents by the tail, he whirled him about here and there.
Having cast him down into the water, he quickly hurled him a hundred bow-lengths away with his two hands;
then the lord of serpents rose up again, licking [his lips], terrifying.
The serpent seized Mādhava, Hari, with his left hand in a rage; Hari, having grasped that great villain with his right hand, [acted].
He dashed him against that water as Suparṇa strikes a serpent;
the serpent, having extended his hundred long mouths, returned once more.
Seizing him by the tail, Kṛṣṇa quickly dragged him for a distance of a hundred bow-lengths;
emerging from Kṛṣṇa's hand, the serpent bit him once again.
He who possessed the strength of the three worlds struck the serpent with his fist;
by Kṛṣṇa’s blow from the fist, the serpent fainted and lost consciousness.
Having bent his hundred faces, he stood facing Kṛṣṇa,
having ascended those hundred hoods which were enchanting with their clusters of jewels.
Dressed as a charming dancer, Kṛṣṇa danced like an actor,
singing melodies and performing music with the seven notes and rhythmic beats.
While the gods showered flowers as he danced like the King of Dancers (Śiva),
