he joyfully played the lute, the drum, the kettle-drum, and the flute.
With the placement of his steps, Kṛṣṇa shattered the many radiant hoods of the great-souled Kāliya as he hissed. || 16 ||
At that very moment, those wives of the Nāgas arrived, overwhelmed with fear;
having bowed at the feet of the divine Kṛṣṇa, they spoke with voices faltering with emotion.
The wives of the Nāgas said:
"Obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, obeisance to the Lord of Goloka; obeisance to You, the sovereign of countless universes, the most perfect Supreme Being. (18)
Salutations to You, the Lord of Śrī Rādhā; salutations to You, the Sovereign of Vraja.
Salutations to You, the son of Śrī Nanda; salutations to You, the delighter of Yaśodā. (19)
Protect me, protect me, O Supreme God!
There is no refuge other than you in the three worlds. You are Hari himself, far superior even to the feet [of the Lord].
Indeed, you manifest a physical form through your divine play.
Śrī Nārada said: Praised by the wives of the serpent, Kṛṣṇa— Hari himself, the most perfect Supreme Person— dismissed Kāliya, whose pride had vanished.
To that Kāliya who was crying out "Protect me! as he approached before Him, the Lord Hari, the divine Janārdana, spoke to him as he stood bowed down in His presence.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Go to the island of Ramaṇaka, accompanied by your wife and friends;
for Suparṇa shall not devour you once you are marked with my footprint."
Śrī Nārada said: Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa, circumambulated him, and bowed down to him, the serpent,
accompanied by his wife and sons, went to the island of Ramaṇaka.
Then, having heard that the son of Nanda had been seized by Kāliya,
all the people, including Nanda and the hosts of cowherds, arrived at that place.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa emerged from the water, the people rejoiced;
and Nanda, embracing his own son, attained supreme joy.
Having obtained her son, Yaśodā,
her breasts overflowing with milk out of affection, gave gifts to the twice-born for the sake of her son’s auspiciousness.
Right there, O King, near the Kālindī, all the cowherds, together with the groups of cowherd girls and cowherds, made their bed due to exhaustion. (28)
A forest fire, produced by the friction of bamboo stalks, like the fire of universal destruction,
came flashing from all sides at midnight to burn the cowherds.
The cowherd companions, having sought refuge with Śrī Kṛṣṇa along with Balarāma, bowed down and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to him while trembling with fear. (30)
The cowherds said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge! Protect, protect your own people from the misery of the forest fire, O Lord! (31)
The illustrious Nārada said:
"O your own eyes, do not fear; close them," saying this, Mādhava, the Lord of the masters of yoga, drank the fire.
In the morning, the son of Nanda, accompanied by the astonished groups of cowherds and the herds of cows,
arrived at the illustrious circle of Vraja.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Subduing of Kāliya and the Drinking of the Forest Fire," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
The King of Videha said:
That lotus-foot of Hari, which is difficult even for yogis to attain in this world after many births, has now visibly appeared upon the heads of Kāliya.
Who was this Kāliya, the best of serpents, who formerly performed meritorious deeds?
I wish to know about him; please tell me, O most excellent of divine sages.
Śrī Nārada said: Formerly, during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara, a sage named Vedaśiras,
born of the lineage of Bhṛgu, performed austerities on the Vindhya mountain.
Then the sage Aśvaśiras arrived at that hermitage to perform penance;
seeing him, Vedaśiras, his eyes red with rage, spoke: ||| 4 ||
Vedaśiras said:
"O Brahmin, do not perform penance in my hermitage, for it does not bestow happiness.
O you whose wealth is austerity, there is no other ground suitable for your penance."
Śrī Nārada said:
Having then heard the words of Vedaśiras, the sage Aśvaśiras,
filled with wrath and with blood-red eyes, spoke to that bull among sages.
Aśvaśiras said:
"O best of sages, this ground belongs to Mahāviṣṇu; it is not yours, nor mine.
How many sages have not performed supreme penance here?"
O sir, hissing like a serpent, you indeed indulge in vain anger;
therefore, become a serpent yourself, for then you shall have cause for fear of Garuḍa.
Vedaśiras said:
"You are of wicked intent and exert great effort toward a trivial injury; you are like the god of love seeking his own ends. O evil-minded one, become a crow on this earth!"
Then, as the two of them were thus cursing each other, Viṣṇu appeared;
and seeing them distressed by their respective curses, he consoled them with his speech.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O sages, you two are equally devoted to me, like my two arms upon my body;
yet, O lords of sages, I am capable of making my own word false."
I do not wish to make the devotee’s words false; this is my solemn oath.
O Vedaśiras, my two feet shall rest upon your head.
Then you shall never have fear of Garuḍa;
listen to my words, O Aśvaśiras, do not grieve, do not grieve! (13)
Even in the form of a crow, you will certainly possess excellent knowledge—the supreme knowledge of the three times—endowed with the perfections of yoga. (14)
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, after Viṣṇu had spoken thus and departed, the sage Aśvaśiras became the manifest Kākabhuṣaṇḍa,
a lord of yogins, on Mount Nīla.
A devotee of Rāma of great splendor, who illuminated the meaning of all the scriptures,
he indeed sang the Rāmāyaṇa to the high-souled Garuḍa.
O King, when the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara had arrived, Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas,
gave eleven beautiful daughters to Kaśyapa.
Among them, she who was the eldest, Kadrū, is remembered today as Rohiṇī;
she was the beloved of Vasudeva, and from her Baladeva was born as a son.
And that Kadrū gave birth to crores of great serpents—mighty, powerful with poison, fierce, and possessing five hundred faces. (19)
Some were bearers of great hoods, unbearable and possessing hundreds of faces;
among them was the great-hooded serpent named Kāliya, whose head was the Vedas.
Among them, at the beginning, there was Śeṣa, the lord of serpents, Ananta, who is higher than the highest;
he is today indeed Baladeva, the infinite Rāma, the elder brother of Acyuta.
Once, the glorious Lord Hari himself, the Supreme Person beyond material nature,
being pleased in spirit, spoke to Śeṣa with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Blessed Lord said: "Indeed, no one possesses the power to sustain the circle of the earth;
therefore, lift up this terrestrial globe upon your head. (23)
"You indeed possess infinite prowess, which is why you are remembered as Ananta;
this task must be performed for the sake of the welfare of all beings."
Śeṣa said:
"O Lord, set a limit for me regarding the lifting of the Earth;
at your word, I shall bear the burden of the world here for that duration."
The Blessed Lord said: O Lord of Serpents, constantly recite my names, which flash forth with my own qualities, individually and in their entirety from your thousand mouths.
And when the divine names of men reach their end,
then, having relieved the burden of the earth, may you, O Serpent, be at perfect ease.
Śeṣa said: "I shall be the support; but who will be my support?
O Lord, tell me how I can remain in the water without a support."
The Blessed Lord said: "And I, having become a tortoise, shall support your body, which is long and composed of a great burden; do not grieve, O my friend. (29)
Śrī Nārada said: Then, O King, Śeṣa arose, bowed to the Lord whose banner is Garuḍa,
and went from Pātāla down to a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas.
Having grasped this most weighty circle of the earth with his own hand,
Śeṣa, possessed of fierce prowess, supported it upon a single hood.
Then, when Saṃkarṣaṇa had gone to Pātāla, which is beyond the supreme Ananta,
the other lords of serpents entered after him at the command of Brahmā.
Some reached Vitala, some Sutala and Mahātala,
while others likewise reached Talātala and Rasātala.
Brahmā granted them the island of Ramaṇaka on earth;
there, the serpents headed by Kāliya dwelt, enveloped in happiness.
Thus, O King, has this narrative of Kāliya been told to you; it bestows enjoyment and liberation, and is the very essence. What more do you wish to hear? (35)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Śeṣa," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Vaideha said:
"O Brahmin, how did the king [behave] on the island of Ramaṇaka, other than toward the serpents?"
Tell me all of this: what was the cause of Kāliya’s fear? || 1 ||
Śrī Nārada said: There, the destroyer of serpents constantly slaughtered the hosts of nāgas.
Once, when they were free from agitation, those [nāgas], overcome by fear, spoke to Tārkṣya: || 2 ||
The Nāgas said:
O Garuḍa, salutations to you; you are the manifest vehicle of Viṣṇu.
When you devour us serpents, how shall there be life for us? || 3 ||
Therefore, quickly accept an offering from each house every month,
according to the prescribed ritual, with the services of trees, nectar, and various foods.
Garuḍa said:
"Either one serpent must be given to me by you, or something other than that from your house;
for how else shall I cook that supreme offering like a betel-roll?"
Śrī Nārada said: Having been told "So be it," O King, they all gave a perpetual divine offering to the high-souled Garuḍa for his protection.
O King, when the time for Kāliya’s own meal arrived,
Kāliya would forcibly devour the entire offering intended for Tārkṣya.
Then Garuḍa, of fierce prowess, arrived with great speed and, being enraged, cast his foot down upon Kāliya.
Struck by the blow of Garuḍa’s foot, Kāliya fell unconscious;
rising again, he hissed as he licked the [Garuda's] face with his tongues.
Spreading out his hundred hoods, Kāliya, the best of serpents,
powerfully bit Garuḍa with his swift, venomous fangs.
And seizing him with his beak, Garuḍa, the divine vehicle,
dashed him against the surface of the earth, striking him repeatedly with his two wings.
The serpent, having emerged from his mouth, seized his wings;
writhing and biting his feet, it repeatedly hissed.
But the sight of them is meritorious, bestowing the fruit of all desires;
O Lord of Mithilā, that occurs on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina.
Enraged, Garuḍa seized Kāliya with his beak,
threw him suddenly to the ground, and tore at his body.
Then Kāliya, trembling with fear, fled from its beak;
and the king of birds, possessed of fierce prowess, suddenly pursued him.
Then the serpent went through the seven islands, the seven regions, and the seven oceans;
wherever he went, there he beheld Tārkṣya.
The serpent went to Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, and Svarloka;
then, running from there, he reached Maharloka and proceeded to Janaloka.
As soon as Garuḍa arrived, he went again to the lower worlds;
out of fear of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, no one provided him protection.
When no happiness arose anywhere, even Kāliya, overcome with fear,
went to the presence of the feet of Śeṣa, the God of gods.
Having bowed down and prostrated before Śeṣa, and having circumambulated him with palms joined in reverence, Dīrghapṛṣṭha, distressed and overcome with fear, spoke while trembling. (20)
Kāliya said:
O supporter of the earth, O Lord of the world, O Infinite One, you are indeed the remover of the earth's burden, possessing manifold divine sports.
Protect me, protect me! You are the omnipotent, the full, the one beyond the supreme, the ancient Puruṣa. || 21 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Seeing Kāliya distressed and overcome with fear,
the divine Janārdana, the lord of the illustrious serpents, spoke, pleasing him with sweet words.
Śeṣa said: O highly intelligent Kāliya, listen to my supreme words;
there shall be no protection for you anywhere, of this there is no doubt. (23)
In ancient times, there was a perfected sage known by the name Saubhari;
he performed austerities in the waters for ten thousand years in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
He of great intelligence, who once felt a longing for home upon seeing the Mīnarāja monastery, bore the hundred daughters of Māndhātṛ.
To him, Hari personally bestowed supreme, divine prosperity;
and upon seeing that, O King, Māndhātṛ was struck with wonder, yet his pride vanished.
While the son of Subhara was performing long penance within the waters of the Yamunā,
Garuḍa struck down the king of fish as he looked on.
Seeing the fish in extreme distress, the compassionate Saubhari, that best of sages, being unable to endure their suffering, became enraged and uttered two curses upon them. (28)
Saubhari said:
"O Virāṭa, if you eat fish from this day forward by force, then at that very moment, let there be a destruction of your life through my curse immediately. (29)
Śeṣa said:
From that day forward, Garuḍa did not come there, being overwhelmed by the curse.
Therefore, O Kāliya, go quickly to Vṛndāvana, the forest of Hari.
And, urged by my word, take up your own residence in the Kālindī;
you shall be free from fear, and no danger shall ever arise for you from Tārkṣya.
Śrī Nārada said: Thus addressed, O King, the terrified Kāliya, together with his wives and sons,
was expelled from his residence in the Kālindī by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Legend of Kāliya," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārada said:
This meritorious account of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s deeds, including the subduing of Kāliya, has been narrated by me to you. What more do you wish to hear?
Bahulāśva said:
Indeed, having heard the story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, a devotee never reaches satiety,
just as an immortal does not after drinking nectar, nor a bee after reaching the pericarp of a lotus.
When the Great Soul Hari had assumed the form of an infant to perform the rāsa dance, a divine voice spoke to Śrī Rādhā, whose mind was distressed, at the Bhāṇḍīra tree. || 3 ||
"Do not grieve, O auspicious lady, in the enchanting Vṛndā forest;
your heart's desire shall be fulfilled by the high-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa."
Thus addressed in the language of the gods, [he asked: "How did the Lord become the great ocean of desires in the enchanting forest of Vṛndā? (5)
How did He, the most perfect Supreme Person Himself, perform the enchanting rāsa-dance together with Śrī Rādhā in the forest of Vṛndāvana? (6)
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, you have asked well regarding the auspicious deeds of the Blessed Lord. I shall relate to you this captivating narrative of His divine play, which is kept secret even from the gods. (7)
Once, two auspicious and principal companions, Viśākhā and Lalitā, having reached the house of Vṛṣabhānu, approached Rādhā in private.
The two friends said:
"O Rādhā, he about whom you think and whose virtues you yourself describe—he too constantly comes to the city of Vṛṣabhānu along with other boys. (9)
O Rādhā, you must behold him who is worthy of being seen, most beautiful to look upon, having gone out to tend the cattle during the final watch of the night. (10)
Rādhā said:
"Having painted his charming portrait, show it to me quickly; then I shall behold him, of this there is no doubt. (11)
Śrī Nārada said:
Then the two friends painted a beautiful picture of the child of Nanda; they quickly presented it to Rādhā, displaying His sweetness in the bloom of fresh youth.
Seeing that, Rādhā, longing for the sight of Kṛṣṇa, was filled with joy;
gazing at the painting in her hand, she fell asleep, overwhelmed with bliss.
Lying in her chamber, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu beheld Kṛṣṇa dancing nearby.
At that very moment, Rādhā, overwhelmed by the separation from the Supreme Kṛṣṇa, rose from her bed while meditating upon Him of lovely form.
The King of Videha regarded the three worlds as if they were a blade of grass.
Then, as the Lord of Vraja was returning from his own forest along the narrow path toward the city of Vṛṣabhānu,
she quickly went to a window, where he was pointed out by her friend.
Upon seeing this, Sundarī fell into a swoon.
Kṛṣṇa too, seeing the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu— who was endowed with beauty and skill and was the abode of all virtues—
Mādhava’s mind became exceedingly intent on enjoying her company.
He, whose body was his divine play, departed for his own abode. || 17 ||
Thus, having observed Rādhā, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, overwhelmed by separation from Kṛṣṇa and her mind distressed by the intense fever of passion;
The excellent friend Lalitā spoke these words.
Lalitā said:
O Rādhā, why are you so distressed, fainting and overcome with intense pain?
O lady of beautiful eyebrows, if you desire Hari, then fix your love upon him firmly.
O auspicious one, even all the happiness currently available to the world now burns the heart with the fire of suffering, like the fire of a potter’s kiln.
Śrī Nārada said: Having heard the charming words of Lalitā, the Queen of Vraja opened her eyes and spoke to Lalitā with a voice faltering with emotion.
Rādhā said:
"If indeed my feet, which are the ornaments of Vraja, have not been attained by You, then I shall certainly no longer maintain this body. (22)
Śrī Nārada said: Having heard her words, Lalitā, overwhelmed with fear,
went to the side of Śrī Kṛṣṇa on the enchanting bank of the Kṛṣṇā.
In a secluded spot at the foot of a Kadamba tree, filled with clusters of Mādhavī creepers and resonant with sweet sounds, she spoke to Hari, who was alone.
Lalita said:
On that day when Your wonderful form was seen by Rādhā, You became paralyzed from that moment; why do You not speak, like a young girl? (25)
Her ornaments are like fire, her garment is like the dust of ashes;
though fragrant, it is as pungent as poison; and her home is a desolate forest. (26)
O friend, know that the flower is an arrow and the moon's orb is a root of poison;
grant to Rādhā a sight of him that shall destroy her suffering.
O Witness, do you not already fully know what occurs upon the earth? Are you not the one who creates, protects, and then withdraws the world? For you are equal toward all people in every respect.
Nevertheless, O Supreme Lord, you favor those who are devoted to you.
Śrī Nārada said: Having heard these charming words of Lalitā, the Lord Hari himself,
the Blessed One, spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Blessed One said:
"O beautiful lady, every state of mind arises from another; indeed, it is never produced from itself alone."
Therefore, love alone should be spontaneously offered to me; there is nothing on earth equal to love. (30)
For just as her heart's desire was fulfilled in the Bhāṇḍīra forest, so indeed shall it come to pass;
for selfless love is that which is relied upon by the virtuous.
And even that, it is said, the wise know to be devoid of qualities. || 31 ||

Those who do not perceive even the slightest difference between Rādhikā and myself, Keśava— just as one does not see a distinction between milk and its whiteness— they alone attain my state of Brahman.
These are characterized by devotion that manifests spontaneously and without cause. || 32 ||
Those people of wicked intellect on earth who perceive a difference between Rādhikā, myself Keśava, and Hari,
fall into the Kālasūtra hell, suffering in misery.
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, as long as the moon and sun indeed exist— || 33 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard all these words and having bowed to him, Lalitā’s friend approached Rādhā in private and, with a smiling face, spoke to her. (34)
Lalitā said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, as you desire him, so does Madhusūdana desire you;
the splendor of you two is indivisible, though it appears as one to people in two forms. (35)
Nevertheless, O Goddess, perform this disinterested service for Kṛṣṇa with supreme devotion, O virtuous lady, so that your desire may be fulfilled.
Śrī Nārada said: O King, having heard these words of her friend, Rādhā, the Queen of the Rāsa dance,
spoke to her moon-faced companion, who was the best among those who know all dharmas.
Tell me of some worship that grants one's desires, which is highly meritorious, increases supreme good fortune, and is for the purpose of pleasing Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (38)
"O auspicious one, you have heard the Dharmaśāstra from the mouth of Gargācārya;
therefore, O high-minded lady, tell me of the vow or the worship. (39)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ardent Effort of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa's Love," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārada said: O King, having then heard the words of Rādhā, the moon-faced one, the best among all her companions,
reflected for a moment in her heart and replied.
Candrānanā said:
"O Rādhā, the service of Tulasī is considered the bestower of supreme good fortune, highly meritorious, and a granter of boons; it is intended for the sake of attaining even Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (2)
Whether seen, touched, meditated upon, glorified, saluted, praised,
planted, watered, or constantly worshipped, Tulasī grants one's desires.
O auspicious one, those who perform the ninefold devotion to Tulasī day after day attain the merit of thousands of millions of yugas.
As long as the Tulasī planted by mortals on the surface of the earth flourishes with its branches, twigs, seeds, flowers, and auspicious leaves, [so long does it bestow merit]. || 5 ||
Those who are born in their lineages, those who will be born, and those who have passed away—
for a thousand kalpas of yugas, they shall dwell in the abode of Hari.
O Rādhikā, whatever fruit is obtained from all leaves and all flowers is always attained by means of a single tulasī leaf.
The man who worships Hari with leaves produced from the Tulasī plant is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
One obtains that same fruit by protecting a grove of Tulasī as one would by [giving] a hundred loads of gold and four times as much silver.
O Rādhā, that house in which a grove of Tulasī stands is indeed of the nature of a sacred pilgrimage site; the servants of Yama do not go there.
Those excellent men who plant a grove of tulasī— which removes all sins, bestows merit, and grants desires— do not behold the son of the Sun (Yama).
Through planting, protecting, sprinkling, seeing, and touching,
Tulasī destroys the sins accumulated by men through speech, mind, and body.
The holy places beginning with Puṣkara, the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā,
and the gods beginning with Vāsudeva all dwell upon the Tulasī leaf.
He who gives up his life-breaths while holding a Tulasī blossom—
even if he is burdened with hundreds of sins— Yama himself is not able even to look upon him.
If a man wears sandalwood paste produced from Tulasī wood,
no sin shall touch his body, even that which is being committed here in this world.
Wherever there may be the auspicious shade of a grove of Tulasī trees, there one should perform the Śrāddha; what is given to the ancestors there becomes inexhaustible.

O friend, even the primordial four-faced god Brahmā would not be capable of describing the greatness of Tulasī, just as he is not capable of describing the greatness of the Lord who wields the Śārṅga bow.
Whether it be a man or a woman, whoever offers Tulasī together with sandalwood paste at the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra shall obtain the fruit as described.
O daughter of the cowherd, perform the service of Tulasī daily;
by this means, Śrī Kṛṣṇa shall indeed always come under your control.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, having thus heard the words of the moon-faced one, the Queen of the Rāsa dance immediately began the service of Tulasī, which directly pleases Hari.

And in the midst of a forest of *ketakī* flowers, there was a beautiful, auspicious structure a hundred cubits long and perfectly circular, with high walls inlaid with gold and terraces made of rubies.
It shone brilliantly with a wall made of turmeric, diamonds, and pearls; it was furnished with turrets on all sides and beautifully adorned with wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi).
It was adorned with golden banners and graced by lofty arches;
with its golden canopies on all sides, it shone like the Vaijayanta palace.
Such is the beautiful and enchanting temple of Śrītulasī; having installed Tulasī within it, adorned with green sprouts. (24)
Under the constellation Abhijit,
that virtuous woman performed her service according to the rite prescribed by Garga, who had been summoned.
For the sake of pleasing Śrī Kṛṣṇa, that virtuous woman, with supreme devotion,
undertook this vow beginning from the full moon of Āśvina until the full moon of Caitra.
One should worship Tulasī with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) separately month by month,
beginning the concluding rite (udyāpana) on the first day of the month of Vaiśākha.
O King, according to the rite prescribed by Garga, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu [bestowed] two hundred thousand Brahmins with fifty-six kinds of enjoyments.
Having gratified them with garments, ornaments, and other gifts, Rādhikā gave a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
the King of Videha gave one hundred thousand bhāras of divine, large pearls.
She gave ten million gold pieces to Garga Ācārya,
as well as a hundred bhāras of gold and the same amount of pearls.
With supreme devotion, Rādhā gave [gifts] to every single brāhmaṇa.
The celestial drums resounded and throngs of apsarases danced;
above her palace, the gods showered down a rain of flowers.
Then Tulasī, the beloved of Hari, appeared,
seated upon a splendid throne atop a golden pedestal;
she was four-armed, with eyes like the petals of a lotus.
Dark-complexioned, she wears a shimmering golden crown and earrings.
Wearing a garland of fresh Vaijayantī flowers, with her serpent-braid concealed by yellow garments,
Raṅgavallī descended from the bird.
He kissed Rādhā, embracing her with his arms. || 34 ||
Tulasī said:

"O daughter of Kalāvatī, I am well-pleased with you, for I have been constantly conquered by the spirit of your devotion. O beautiful lady, you have performed this all-encompassing vow in accordance with the conventions of worldly conduct."
May your desire here be fruitful;
may the intellect, senses, consciousness,
and mind be ever perfectly favorable to their Lord.
Thus should good fortune be celebrated. || 36 ||
Having bowed to Tulasī, the beloved of Hari, who was speaking thus, Rādhā, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu,
replied regarding the two lotus-feet of Govinda.
For my devotion to you is indeed known to be without cause. || 37 ||
"Let it be so," said Tulasī, the beloved of Hari; then, O best of kings, O ruler of Mithilā, she vanished from sight.
At that very moment, Rādhā, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu—
With a serene mind, she became present in her own city. || 38 ||

O King, whoever on this earth, being devoted to bhakti, hears this wonderful narrative of Śrī Rādhikā while mentally attaining the state of the three goals of life (traivargya), [attains the highest goal].
Then the man goes, having accomplished his purpose. || 39 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Worship of Tulasī," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Śrī Bahulāśva said: O sage, as I listen to the life-story of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa,
my mind finds no satisfaction, just like a bee among autumn lotuses.
O Brahmin, rich in asceticism, tell me what occurred when the mistress of the rāsa dance, the wife of Kṛṣṇa, performed service to Tulasī.
Śrī Nārada said: Having learned of Rādhikā’s penance in the service of Tulasī,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa went to the city of Vṛṣabhānu to test her love.
The wondrous form of the cowherd girl, with her moving jingling anklets, the sound of small bells and tinkling ornaments, and adorned with finger-rings; || 4 ||
Adorned with jeweled bracelets, armlets, and pearl necklaces,
her beautiful mass of hair was graced by a circlet shining like the rising sun.
Having assumed a divine luster like a pearl from the nose-ornament and a mass of dark locks of hair,
he beheld the palace of Vṛṣabhānu.
It was provided with walls and moats, endowed with four gates,
and at every gate it was enchanting with lordly elephants resembling swans.
With horses possessing the speed of the wind and the speed of thought, and adorned with various colors,
necklaces, and chowries, the courtyard of the shimmering pavilion was filled.
O King, there the cowherds, bearing flutes and canes, sing amidst herds of cows with their calves and bulls who bear the burden of righteousness.
Thus beholding the architectural splendor of Vṛṣabhānuvara’s palace, he,
assuming the guise of a young woman, entered the inner apartments.
Where rows of pillars with resplendent door-panels shine at the extremities in jeweled courtyards, accompanied by jewels among women.
Playing enchanting lutes, cymbals, drums, and other instruments,
and adorned with flower garlands, they sang of the virtues of Rādhikā.
Within that inner apartment was a great, divine, and radiant grove,
covered with tall trees such as pomegranate, kunda, mandāra, and citron.
It is resplendent with clusters of ketakī and mālatī flowers and with mādhavī vines;
there lies Rādhā’s bower, filled with the fragrance of kalpa-trees.
O Lord of Kings, where bees intoxicated by honey fall down, a cool breeze, scented with fragrance, blows gently and most pleasantly. (15)
Repeatedly scattering the pollen of thousand-petaled lotuses, the male cuckoos, female cuckoos, peacocks, cranes, and parrots [filled the air]. (16)
They warble sweet sounds upon the treetops of the groves;
there are thousands of flower-beds and thousands of water-courses.
In that palace of clouds, they indeed move about with wide, quivering splendor,
wearing earrings like the rising sun and faces adorned with variegated garments.
There, millions of female friends skilled in various arts were present;
in their midst, Queen Rādhikā was wandering in the courtyard of the palace.
It was adorned with fine cloth combined with Kashmiri saffron paste,
and filled up to the ankles with petals from the ground of *śirīṣa* flowers.
Surrounded by falling droplets of *mālatī* and *makaranda*, she was slender with a delicate form, resembling ten million moons;
she moved her tender lotus-feet very slowly. (21)
Rādhā, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, saw her arrived upon the courtyard of the jeweled palace;
by her splendor, the luster of those women was eclipsed.
They were born as quickly as stars appear with the moon.

Recognizing that supreme and great honor, Rādhikā rose and embraced him with both arms; then, having seated him upon a divine throne according to the custom of the virtuous world, she began the auspicious ritual of hospitality, beginning with water and other offerings.
Rādhā said:
"Welcome to you, O auspicious friend; tell me your name quickly.
By your coming here of your own accord, great fortune has come to me today. (24)
Indeed, a divine form equal to yours is not seen anywhere on the surface of the earth;
O fair-browed one, that city where you reside is truly blessed. (25)
"Speak, O Goddess, in detail the reason for your arrival;
whatever task is suitable for me must certainly be told by you. (26)
"By her sidelong glance, her radiant luster, her speech, her gentle smile,
her gait, and her actions, she is now seen by me to be truly like the Lord of Śrī."
O auspicious one, come to meet me constantly;
if not, then establish a private tryst,
so that our union may indeed occur according to destiny.
That rule must always be observed by you. || 28 ||

O Goddess, my very self and that which is most dear to me is your own form—the son of the King of Vraja—by whom my heart has been stolen; therefore, O Mother, I offer him to you as your brother-in-law.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having thus heard the words of Rādhā, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, wearing the guise of a young woman through his illusory power, spoke to the lotus-eyed Rādhā.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, in the city of Nandana, to the north of Nanda’s house, my residence is in Gokula; I am known by the name Gopadevatā."
"I have heard of the sweetness of the qualities of your form from the mouth of Lalitā;
O lady with tremulous glances, I have come to your house to behold it. (32)
O lotus-eyed one, the dense clusters of groves where the bees hum amidst the Guñjā thickets— groves that clearly delight the beautiful Mallikā vines— have been seen and heard by you ever anew.
Which is not equaled even in the city of Purandara in its divine splendor. || 33 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus, O Lord of Mithilā, their meeting took place;
having established mutual affection, they both shone brightly there in the forest. (34)
Laughing and singing while playing with a flower-ball, and gazing at the forest trees, they wandered about, O Lord of Mithilā. (35)
O King, the goddess of the cowherds addressed these words in a sweet voice to the lotus-eyed Rādhā, who was endowed with skill in the arts: 36.
The deity of the cow-pasture said: "Nanda’s city is indeed far away, and twilight has fallen, O Queen of Vraja;
I shall come to your presence at dawn, without a doubt. (37)
Śrī Nārada said: Having heard those words of his, the Queen of Vraja immediately shed a continuous stream of tears from her eyes.
Overwhelmed by the emotion of rising horripilation and joy,
she fell to the ground like Rambhā when struck down by the wind-god.
There, groups of female friends, overcome with apprehension, stood quickly fanning her with fans;
she was dressed in garments smeared with sandalwood paste and flower-essence.
O King, the goddess of the cowherds spoke to Rādhā.
The deity of the cow-pasture said:
"I shall come at dawn; do not grieve, O Rādhikā!
By my word, I swear this by the cow, my brother, and the cowherds—if it be not so. (40)
Śrī Nārada said: O lord of kings, having spoken thus and consoled Rādhā, Hari,
assuming the guise of a young woman through his illusory power, went to the cowherd settlement of Śrī Nanda.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Union of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa," in the Vṛndāvana Section of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā. || 17 ||
Śrī Nārada said: Then, when the night had passed, Hari, assuming the form of a woman through his illusory power (māyā),
went to the house of Vṛṣabhānu for the sake of pacifying Rādhā’s sorrow.
O King of Mithilā, seeing him arrive, Rādhā rose up with great joy and worshipped him according to the ritual procedure involving the offering of life-breath.
Śrī Rādhā said:
"O friend, without you I was distressed at night; now that you have arrived, I am like one who has found a lost treasure."
O beautiful lady, just as there is initially pleasure from that which is unwholesome, yet subsequently suffering follows, so it shall be for you through my attachment.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard those words, the deity of the cowherd settlement became despondent;
she said nothing to Śrī Rādhā, remaining as if overwhelmed by sorrow.
Having perceived that Rādhikā, the goddess of the cowherds, was overcome with distress,
she consulted with her friends and, intent on affection, spoke.
Rādhā said:
"O blessed goddess of the cowherds, tell me, why are you dejected? Have you been rebuked with anger by your mother, your husband, your sister's husband, or your mother-in-law? (6)
"O Manoharā, are you despondent because of some offense committed by a co-wife, or due to separation from your husband, or because your heart is fixed elsewhere? (7)
"O illustrious lady, has she perhaps become overwhelmed by the fatigue of the journey, or by illness?
Tell me quickly, O noble one, the cause of her suffering."
"O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, whatever has been said by anyone to disparage this brahmin who is a devotee of Kṛṣṇa— I shall now provide the remedy for that."
Take elephants, horses, and other jewels, as well as garments and wealth, and various wonderful mansions, if you so desire. (10)
One should protect one's body by giving wealth; having given one's body, one should preserve one's sense of shame.
Indeed, for the sake of a friend's purpose alone, one may give wealth, body, and even shame.
Having given wealth, one must always and constantly protect one's life.

He alone is most blessed who practices friendship without guile and without motive; fie upon that lecherous actor, skilled in pretexts, who practices deceit after having established a bond of friendship! 12.
Having heard her words of love, O King of kings, the Blessed One, the deity of the cowherds, smilingly spoke to Śrī Rādhā, the delight of Kīrti.
The deity of the cow-pen said:
"O Rādhā, as you walk with your attendants upon the mountain ridges and the enchanting narrow paths,"
As I was going of my own accord for the purpose of selling curds, the son of Navananda blocked me on the road. (14)
Holding a flute and a staff in his hands, Vaṃśīdhara,
bold and shameless, quickly seized me by the hand and gave this gift to me for the sake of a tax-payment.
Crying out "Give me! in the forest, he was a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor. || 15 ||
"I will never give alms to you, a self-born one who is greedy for cow's milk.
When these words were spoken by me, then the vessel—
Having led it away, he shattered that [vessel] of curd. || 16 ||
Having broken the vessel and drunk the curd,
he took my upper garment and went toward the intermediate direction from Mount Nandīśvara.
Therefore, I have become dejected and ill-at-ease. || 17 ||
By birth he was indeed a cowherd, dark-complexioned, poor, neither a hero nor possessed of virtuous character;
yet you, O lady of excellent conduct, have placed your love in him.
Quickly abandon Kṛṣṇa today, who is free from delusion.
Having heard those words, so full of enmity and harshness, Rādhā, the delight of Vṛṣabhānu,
was greatly astonished; her speech faltered at every word.
Smiling, she spoke these words to her: || 19 ||
Rādhā said:
"For the sake of attaining whom Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods perform supreme penance in the fire according to their own respective methods of yoga,"
Datta, Śuka, Kapila, Āsuri, and Aṅgiras—those who touch the pollen of the nectar from the lotus-feet of Him [the Guru]. || 20 ||
To that Kṛṣṇa, the primordial person, the perfect God, the unborn one who descends through divine play to remove the suffering of people,
and who acts for the welfare of the virtuous in order to remove the heavy burden of the earth—
"How can you, O ill-behaved friend, revile one who has been born? (21)
They constantly tend the cows of the dust [of the earth] and touch the Gaṅgā of the cows;
they mutter the auspicious names of the cows and gaze day and night with great joy upon the beautiful face of the cows.
No birth on earth is known to be superior to that of the cow-born.
Beholding that beautiful digit shining upon his dark form, the peacock, with his mind fixed intently upon it,
abandons all great pleasure and wanders and runs about like one intoxicated.
He bears a matted lock, a bull, ashes, a skull, and serpents.
The guardians of the hosts of gods, siddhas, munis, yakṣas, and maruts, as well as all the lords of the nāgas, kinnaras, and humans,
constantly prostrate with devotion at his lotus feet.
Having indeed obtained prosperity, they offered tribute to him.

What need is there to mention the slaying of Vatsa, Aghaka, Kāliya, Baka, Arjuna, Dhenuka, Āka, Cakravāta, Śakaṭāsura, and Pūtanā? What glory belongs to Murāri, who is the cause of the creation and destruction of millions of cosmic eggs? (25)
Neither Śambhu, nor Brahmā, nor Ramā, nor the son of Rohiṇī is known to be as dear to Puruṣottama as a devotee;
with his heart bound by devotion, he follows after his devotees.
Kṛṣṇa is the crest-jewel for all people in the world. || 26 ||
Moving about, the Great-Souled One reveals His own delight to the people of Hari, making Himself known to the worlds and drawing near to His own folk.
Therefore, for those who worship Him intensely, the Blessed Mukunda grants liberation, yet never ceases to grant the yoga of true devotion.
The goddess of the cow-pasture said:
"O Rādhā, your intellect mocks the intellect of Bṛhaspati,
and your speech, through its great skill, imitates the Vedic revelation."
O Goddess, I believe that when Hari, the Supreme Lord, comes here, he will truly grant your word.
Rādhā said:
"Tell me, O fair-browed one, when Hari, the Supreme Lord, shall come today, what shall I have you do?"
If there were no sacred scripture [to the contrary], I would indeed give you my entire wealth and my palace, O wearer of the forest garland. || 29 ||
Śrī Nārada said: Then Rādhā, having risen and bowed to the son of Śrī Nanda,
sat upon her seat and meditated with eyes motionless in concentration.
Beholding his beloved longing, perspiring, with a throat choked by tears and a face filled with weeping, Hari assumed his own male form.
While his friends were looking on, the Lord, who is affectionate toward his devotees, suddenly spoke to Rādhā with a gracious soul and a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhā, beloved queen of the beauties of Vraja, with thighs like plantain stalks, face like the moon, and possessing the pride of fresh youth!
Open your eyes and behold me, who have arrived quickly, summoned by you with sweet words. (33)
"Come, Kṛṣṇa!"— this was the word I heard from there, and immediately, leaving behind my own herd of cows and cowherds,
I ran forth from the bamboo grove near the Yamunā.
Therefore, O lady with beautiful eyes, I have come for your pleasure. || 34 ||
Now that I have arrived, who was it that departed in the form of a female friend—was she a Yakṣī, an Asurī, a celestial woman, or perhaps a Kinnarī?
Or was it Māyāvatī, come to deceive you? Therefore, one must never place trust in the wife of a serpent. (35)
Śrī Nārada said:
Then, O King, having seen Hari and bowed at His lotus feet, Rādhā immediately attained supreme joy, her heart’s desire being fulfilled. (36)
Thus, that man who listens with devotion to these wonderful deeds of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra shall become one who has achieved his life's purpose. || 37 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Vision of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. || 18 ||
Bahulāśva said:
Having granted Rādhā his vision and having performed the test of her love,
what pastime did the Blessed Lord next perform through his own divine play?
Śrī Nārada said: In the month of Mādhava, which is filled with mādhavī vines, Mādhava himself,
the Lord of the Rāsa dance, commenced the rāsa in Vṛndāvana.
On the auspicious fifth day of the month of Vaiśākha, when the moon had risen,
the enchanting Lord took delight in the Yamunā grove with the Queen of the Rāsa dance.
O King of Mithilā, in ancient times, that earth which had come from Goloka to the world of mortals quickly became entirely composed of gold and rubies.
Vṛndāvana, possessing a divine form with desire-yielding trees and mādhavī creepers,
surpassed even the Nandana garden;
it was endowed with jeweled staircases and shimmering golden pavilions.
O King, the Yamunā shone, crowded with swans, lotuses, and other such creatures.
Consisting of a treasury of jewels, it possessed the shimmering splendor of glorious jewel-peaks;
it was filled with flocks of birds and was enchanting with flowering creepers.
Surrounded by beautiful waterfalls and caves filled with female bees,
the king of mountains named Govardhana shone like a lordly elephant.
All the groves all around shone, possessing divine forms,
along with the assembly halls, courtyards, and rows of pillars.
O King, with golden jars possessing divine luster and fluttering banners, and with white and reddish flower-petals situated within the flower-pavilions; || 10 ||
Bearing the sweetness of spring, with cuckoos and cranes warbling,
they were filled here and there with the cooing of pigeons and peacocks.
All the groves shone brilliantly with honey-bees, intoxicated by nectar, who were singing the meritorious stories of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa as they hovered about.
On the riverbank, a cool breeze blows gently and pleasantly,
repeatedly scattering the pollen of thousand-petaled lotuses.
Some were inhabitants of Goloka, some were attendants at His bedchamber;
some were collections of erotic charms, and some were indeed doorkeepers.
The companions known as the pārṣadas held parasols and chowries in their hands;
they were the guardians of Śrī Vṛndāvana who fashioned flower ornaments. 15.
Some were inhabitants of Govardhana who constructed groves;
others dwelt in those very groves as dancers intent upon playing musical instruments.
O King, all of them indeed had moon-like faces and were of youthful age; twelve groups of these maidens went into the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (17)
In that very manner, Yamunā herself arrived, having become a leader of a herd;
she was white-complexioned, dressed in white garments, and adorned with ornaments of pearls. (18)
Likewise came the wife of Kṛṣṇa, known by the name Madhumādhavī;
she was lotus-colored, adorned with flowers, wearing beautiful garments, and accompanied by her female companions.
In that very manner, Virajā herself arrived, having become the leader of the herd;
she was dressed in yellow garments, fair-complexioned, and adorned with jewel ornaments.
The troop of Māyā arrived with Lalitā and Viśākhā;
thus, there were indeed sixteen troops of her own chosen friends and companions. (23)
And thirty-two groups of companions all arrived together;
O King, the Blessed One shone amidst the throngs of women in the circle of the rāsa dance.
In Vṛndāvana, like the moon in the sky surrounded by hosts of stars,
he was dressed in yellow garments, adorned with a garland, and captivating in his dancer’s attire.
Playing the flute with a cane staff, bringing joy to the cowherd girls, he wore a crown of peacock feathers, was adorned with garlands, and decorated with earrings. (26)
Just as the Lord of Rati shines with Rati in the rāsa dance,
so did Hari himself shine in the rāsa, surrounded by a multitude of beautiful women, while singing.
Accompanied by Rādhā, he went to the holy bank of the Yamunā,
holding with his hand her lotus-like foot and her own beloved hand.
Hari sat down on the charmingly tranquil bank of the Kṛṣṇā,
speaking again most sweetly while gazing upon his beloved Vṛndāvana.
Moving and laughing, he wandered from grove to grove with Rādhikā; leaving his beloved’s hand in haste as he hid himself within a grove.
Seeing Mādhava hidden behind a branch, Rādhā seized him;
then, making a "jhaṅkāra" sound at every step, Rādhā ran away from his grasp.
While Mādhava was watching her as she hid in the groves,
as soon as Hari ran away, Rādhā likewise departed from that place.
At the side of the tree, she ran hither and thither for the space of a cubit,
like a Tamāla tree entwined by a golden creeper, or like a dark cloud with a flickering lightning flash.
On the Blue Mountain, Hari shone with Rādhikā as if on a golden mine;
Madanamohana gleamed with Rādhā, the enchantress of the universe.
Just as Madana [the god of love] was absorbed in Rati on the stage of the rāsa dance in Vṛndāvana, so too did He assume as many forms as there were women of Vraja.
He danced upon that stage of the rāsa dance like an actor on a theatrical stage;
and all the charming gopīs also sang and danced. (36)
They shone like the celestial nymphs with Śakra and Kṛṣṇacandra;
Madhusūdana then engaged in water-sports in the Yamunā.

Together with all the hosts of gopīs, Kṛṣṇa shone like the king of the yakṣas with his yakṣī consorts; he was resplendent with the beautiful, variegated flowers fallen from their braided locks of hair, appearing as if sealed by a crest-jewel.
To the sweet-sounding resonance of mṛdaṅga drums and cymbals, they sang the glory of Madhusūdana;
with their desires fulfilled, wearing garlands of swaying flowers, they attained joy, freed from all suffering by Hari.
With drops of water struck by his glorious hand, which shine with the splendor of vast and peerless sprays,
the Lord of Vṛndāvana [is served] by the beauties of Vraja.
He himself [advanced] with his weapons, like a king of elephants with its tusks. || 40 ||
The Vidyādharīs and the wives of the gods and Gandharvas, standing in the sky and beholding that stage of the Rāsa dance,
together with the gods, let fall a rain of flowers.
They fell into a state of delusion, their garments and waistbands slipping loose. || 41 ||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Rāsa Dance," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Then Kṛṣṇa Hari, the enchanting one, having performed his sport in the water,
went with all the hosts of gopīs to Mount Govardhana.
On Mount Govardhana, in a cave on a ground of jewels,
Hari himself performed the rāsa dance together with Rādhā, the Queen of the rāsa.
There, upon that beautiful lion-throne strewn with flowers, Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa shone resplendently, like lightning and a cloud upon a mountain. || 3 ||
There, the friends, filled with joy, performed the adornment of their mistress with sandalwood paste, saffron, and the like, as well as with lac-dye, agallochum, and collyrium.
Having worshipped the daughter of Kīrti according to the prescribed rites with nectars, Śrī Yamunā herself gave many anklets to Rādhā.
The divine Śrī Gaṅgā, daughter of Jahnu, is the ornament of the anklets;
Śrī Ramā is the cluster of small bells; and Śrī Madhumādhavī is the necklace.
Virajā wore a beautiful moon-necklace as pure as ten million moons,
Lalitā wore a jeweled bodice, and Viśākhā wore a neck-ornament.
Then Candrānanā gave jeweled rings,
and Ekādaśī gave two gem-studded bracelets to Rādhikā.
Śatacandrānanā gave her armlets and gems,
while Madhumatī herself gave her two shimmering jeweled arm-bands.
The bard offered a pair of earrings, two joy-bestowing pendants,
and that chief companion who brings delight presented a jeweled arch for Rādhā’s forehead.
Padmā gave him the auspicious tilaka on his forehead and the crescent moon as a dot;
the virtuous Padmāvatī gave him the swaying pearl from her nose.
O King, the auspicious friend Candrakāntā gave to Śrī Rādhā a charming forehead-flower, endowed with the brilliance of the rising sun. 12.
Śiromaṇi, Sundarī, Ratnaveṇī, and Praharṣiṇī are the ornaments,
resplendent like ten million flashes of lightning, known as the Moon and the Sun.
The goddess Vṛndā, the sovereign of Vṛndāvana, gave [it] to Rādhikā;
thus Hari was with Rādhā, whose form was radiant with amorous passion.
O King, O Ruler of Mithilā, on that king of mountains the sacrifice shone like one accompanied by sacrificial fees, where indeed Rādhā performed her amorous play in the rāsa dance. 15.
There on Govardhana is the place known as Śṛṅgāramaṇḍala;
then Kṛṣṇa went with his beloveds to Candrasarovara.
He sported in those waters like a lordly elephant with female elephants;
and there, the Moon arrived, bringing two auspicious moonstones (candrakānta).
He gave two thousand-petaled lotuses to the Mistress and to Hari;
then Kṛṣṇa, Lord Hari himself, beheld the splendor of Vṛndāvana.
She went to the Bāhula grove, which was filled with networks of creepers;
there she saw all her female companions covered in perspiration. (19)
Vaṃśīdhara himself sang the Rāga Meghamallāra;
immediately, the clouds there rained down droplets of water.
At that very moment, a cool breeze, enchanting with its fragrance, blew;
by it, O King of Videha, all the groups of cowherd women attained happiness.
There, joined together, they loudly sang the glory of Śrī Murāri;
from there, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Rādhikā, went to the Tālavana forest.
Surrounded by the women of Vraja, he began the rāsa-maṇḍala while singing;
there, all the groups of gopīs were covered in sweat and afflicted by thirst.
The gopīs said: With their palms joined in reverence, they spoke slowly to the Lord of the Rāsa dance:
"O God, the Yamunā is indeed far away, and we have become intensely thirsty. (24)
"O Hari, you must perform right here in this rāsa a divine and enchanting sport in the water and drinking; we shall do so as well. (25)
Śrī Nārada said:
"You are the creator of the world, its protector, and also the leader of its destruction.
Upon hearing that, Kṛṣṇa struck the ground with his staff.
At that very moment it issued forth and is called the Vetragangā stream;
by the mere touch of its water, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having bathed there, O King of Mithilā, any man goes to Goloka,
where the Lord Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, dwells together with Rādhā and the gopīs.
The Lord Madanamohana performed his pastime in the waters;
thereafter, he reached the grove of water-lilies, which was enchanting with its clusters of creepers.
Accompanied by the humming of bees, she performed the rāsa dance with her companions;
there Rādhā indeed manifested amorous passion for Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
While the residents of Vraja were looking on with various flowers and offerings, He appeared with a girdle of blooming campaka flowers and armlets of golden yuthi blossoms.
Hari is one whose ears shine with the filaments of a thousand-petaled lotus,
and who wears garlands of Mohinī, Mālinī, Kunda, and Ketakī flowers as necklaces.
The Lord was radiant with a crown and armlets shimmering with kadamba flowers;
he wore a mantle of mandāra blossoms and held a lotus-stalk.
Adorned with a forest garland joined with *tulasī* blossoms,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa thus attained a state of amorous passion together with his beloved.
O King, he shone in the lily grove like a joyful springtime,
accompanied by the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, vīṇās, vaṃśīs, murus, yaṣṭis, and sweet-sounding cymbals.
Accompanied by rhythmic clapping of their palms, the gopīs sang enchantingly in the *bhairava*, *meghamallāra*, *dīpaka*, and *mālakośaka* melodic modes. (36)
Likewise, Śrīrāga and Hindola—these two rāgas [should be performed] individually with eight tālas, three grāmas, and seven notes (svaras) preceding them. || 37 ||
Delighting Hari with various kinds of beautiful dances endowed with gestures and expressions, the cowherd women of Vraja gladdened him with their side-long glances. || 38 ||
Singing, he went to Madhuvana surrounded by a multitude of beautiful women;
there, the Lord of the Rāsa himself performed the Rāsa-līlā with the Queen of the Rāsa.
By means of the moonlight of the Vaiśākha month, by the breeze fragrant with *mālatī* flowers, and indeed by the mass of pollen from the shimmering, sweet-smelling *kahlāra* lotuses; || 40 ||
In that secluded forest, beautified by clusters of blooming mādhavī creepers,
Kṛṣṇa took delight with the groups of gopīs, just as Indra does in the Nandana grove.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rāsa Dance," in the Vṛndāvana Section of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus, in the delightful Kuṇḍavana, in the auspicious grove of Mālatī flowers, and in the dense forest of mangoes, oranges, and citrons; (1)
And in that forest, O King, were pomegranates, grapes, and walnuts,
as well as kadamba trees, bilva trees, and likewise kuṭaja trees.
In an auspicious forest of banyan, jackfruit, and holy fig trees, and in a grove of tulasī, kovidāra, ketaka, and plantain trees; || 3 ||
O King, Hari, wandering through the forest of Karīra, Kuñja, Bakula, and Mandāra trees,
proceeded toward Kāmavana, surrounded by the women of Vraja.
On that very mountain, Kṛṣṇa played his flute melodiously;
by that sound, the women of Vraja became faint and overwhelmed.
O King, with their limbs pierced by the arrows of the mind, the celestial women in their aerial chariots, along with the gods, fell into a state of dejection as their waist-knots became loosened.
The fourfold assemblies of living beings have fallen into delusion regarding the immobile;
rivers and streams have become solid, and mountains have attained a state of fluidity.
The mountain in Kāmavana became marked with the impressions of his feet;
by the mere sight of it, a person attains the fulfillment of their purpose. || 8 ||
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Rādhikā, together with the hosts of gopīs,
performed the rāsa dance on the broad slopes of Mount Nandīśvara,
O Lord of Mithilā; there, the gopīs became exceedingly proud.
Having abandoned them, Hari vanished right there along with Rādhā.
And all the gopīs, O King of Mithilā, being deeply distressed by separation from Kṛṣṇa in the lonely forest,
wandered about with their eyes clouded by a flood of tears.
Just as startled does deer flee hither and thither. || 11 ||
For not seeing Kṛṣṇa, the women of Vraja have fallen into distress, just as female elephants in the forest do when they lose their mate,
or as female ospreys when they lose their male.
All of them were weeping, being intensely distressed by separation.
Like madmen, all the clusters of trees and creepers gathered together and, in forest after forest,
asked from nearby about the son of the king’s son.
"O trees, tell me quickly where he is staying."
Uttering the words "Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa," with their minds fixed upon the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
those women became one in form with Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Like a worm reaching a variegated cloth made by a weaver. || 14 ||
The cowherd girls who dwell beneath the pedestal of the Śrīpādukā have taken refuge in the lotus of the Śrīpādukā. || 15 ||
Then, by his grace and through the sight of the worship of his feet,
the gopīs beheld the earth marked with the footprints of the Blessed One.
Śrī Bahulāśva said: The Lord of Rādhā entered the Saṃketa-vaṭa tree together with Rādhā;
he indeed arranged the flowers in his beloved’s braid of hair. (17)
Śrī Nārada said:
Śrī Kṛṣṇa entered the Saṃketavaṭa grove together with Rādhā;
on Kṛṣṇa’s full-moon-like countenance were painted decorative leaf-designs.
Thus Kṛṣṇa, beholding the Bhadravana forest, the great forest of Khadira trees,
and the forest of Bilva trees, proceeded to the forest named Kokila.
Searching for Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd girls saw his footprints,
marked with barley-corns, wheels, banners, umbrellas, svastikas, goads, and dots.
They are joined with an eight-pointed vajra and a lotus,
as well as blue conch shells and jars, along with fish and upward-pointing triangles within the triangular sections.
Then the gopīs followed those footprints of the Great Soul, which were adorned with a bow, a cow's hoofprint, and a half-moon.
Having constantly taken that dust and held it upon their heads, the women of Vraja saw other footprints marked with different signs.
They were adorned with banners, lotuses, and parasols, as well as with barley, upward-pointing lines, wheels, half-moons, goads, and dots.
And the King of Videha [adorned it] with various *lavaṅgalatikā* creepers,
with clubs, *pāṭhīna* fish, conch shells, the King of Mountains, and spears.
Seeing the two lion-thrones marked with two dots, they said, "The son of Nanda has gone together with Rādhikā."
Having gone to the forest named Kokila, they beheld his lotus feet;
then, hearing the clamor of the gopīs, Mādhava spoke to Rādhikā.
O Rādhā, who resembles ten million moons, O beloved, move quickly!
All the gopīs have arrived and will surely carry you away from every side.
Then Rādhā, having become possessed of pride and filled with the arrogance of her beauty, youth, skill, and character, spoke to the Lord of Ramā.
Rādhā said: "I am unable to move, having not even stepped out from the palace;
being so delicate and now covered in perspiration, how can you carry me, my beloved? (31)
Nārada said: Having heard these words, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Rādhikā,
then created a breeze for her with his divine yellow garment.
Taking her by the hand, he said to her, "Go, O Rādhā, as you please.
Although she was addressed thus by Kṛṣṇa, she did not go back with him.
Then, having turned her back toward Hari, Rādhā stood silent once more;
Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of the virtuous, spoke to his dear and proud Rādhā.
The Blessed Lord said: O proud lady, leaving behind the cowherd girls who desire me here, I shall worship you alone with my heart.
"O Rādhā, I shall do whatever is pleasing to you;
climb onto my shoulder and walk quickly and comfortably."
Śrī Nārada said: O King, having thus left his beloved wife— who desired to be carried on his shoulder—
the Lord Kṛṣṇa, whose movement is according to his own will, vanished from sight.
Her pride gone, the daughter of Kīrti, distressed by separation from the Blessed One,
wept aloud, O King of kings, in that other forest named Kokila.
At that very moment, O Lord of Mithilā, the groups of cowherd women arrived;
hearing that most piteous weeping, they went there overcome with shame.
Some bathed the Goddess with nectars,
using sprays of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron juice.
They fanned his limbs with moving whisks and chowries,
and comforted him with words of supreme excellence, skilled in various forms of persuasion.
O Lord of Mithilā, having heard from his mouth the pride of Kṛṣṇa, the proud Gopīs became filled with supreme astonishment.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Rāsa-dance," in the Vṛndāvana-section of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārada said:
Then all the women, having gathered together, sang of the beautiful qualities of Kṛṣṇa with charming rhythms and melodies for the purpose of bringing Kṛṣṇa there.
The gopīs said:
O delight of the worlds, ornament of men, lamp of the universe, enchanter of Kandarpa, remover of the suffering and afflictions of the world!
O root of bliss, delight of the Yadus, son of Nanda,
nectar of the self-willed lotus— salutations, salutations unto you!
O banner of victory for cows, brahmins, and the virtuous; O God worshipped by the gods; O Lord who has taken incarnation for the purpose of slaying Kaṃsa and other demons;
O Sun to the lotus of King Nanda’s lineage!
O mirror for the faces of liberated beings, beginning with the gods, may victory be yours! || 3 ||
O Supreme Soul, who assumes the form of the supreme pearl of the ocean of cowherds; O sapphire of the mountain that is the lineage of the cowherds;
O you whose form is the lotus in the lake of the circle of cowherds!
In the sandalwood forest of the cowherds, O chief among the swans! || 4 ||
You are the bee upon the lotus-face of Śrī Rādhikā;
you are the cakora bird for the moon of Śrī Rādhikā’s face;
you are the beautiful moon-necklace upon the heart of Śrī Rādhikā.
O Śrī Rādhikā, you are the flower-bearing tree for the honey-vine of Madhu. || 5 ||
He who possesses abundant pastimes through the natural majesty of his own splendor, who is the life-giving necklace for the eyes of the gopīs,
and who indeed displayed pride before the proud woman in secret—
May this very Hari come before our eyes.
He who adorned the entire herd of cowherd girls and the mountain of Vṛndāvana with the dust of his own feet,
and who appeared upon the earth for the prosperity of all the worlds.
We worship Him, whose arms are like the lord of serpents and who possesses manifold divine sports.
The moon blazes with scorching rays;
the entire forest becomes like entering a forest of sword-leaves; and the wind blows with extreme force, rendering movement exceedingly difficult.
Indeed, we consider ourselves to be afflicted with pain without you. || 8 ||
The sorrow born from separation from the queen of King Saudāsa was already a thousandfold for Nala’s principal consort; that of Janaka’s daughter, however, was ten million times greater than that.
Therefore, O Hara, remove this endless and extreme suffering of ours.
Śrī Uddhava is the crest-jewel of all devotees and the one who holds the foremost authority over Your excellent lotus feet;
therefore, we too have come for refuge to Your feet.
O glorious one, show mercy toward this refuge that is free from suffering.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, while the gopīs were thus weeping, the lotus-eyed Lord suddenly appeared of his own accord, like the very object of their desire.
Adorned with a shimmering crown, armlets, earrings, and bracelets,
he possessed glossy, pure, fragrant, dark, and curly locks of hair.
Seeing him arrive simultaneously, the women of Vraja rose up together,
just as the organs of perception rise upon seeing their respective objects.
O King, Hari, intent on playing the flute, danced in their midst together with Rādhā, just as the Lord of Rati dances with Rati.
Assuming as many forms as there were all the cowherd girls, Hari went with them in Vraja and took his pleasure, just as the mind delights in its own various states.
The women of Vraja, their sorrows dispelled, approached Kṛṣṇa as he stood in the forest region;
with palms joined in reverence, they addressed Hari with voices choked with emotion.
The gopīs said:
"O Hari, tell us, where have you gone, leaving behind this great multitude of gopīs whose minds have been fixed upon your feet, having treated the entire world as mere straw? (17)
The Blessed Lord said: O gopīs, on Puṣkaradvīpa, a great sage named Haṃsa performed penance while remaining within the ocean of curd-cream (dadhimaṇḍoda).
Devoted to meditation upon me, he practiced causeless devotion;
two manvantaras passed while he was performing those austerities.
On that very day, a fish possessing a body half a yojana in length swallowed him;
however, the demon Pauṇḍraka, assuming the form of a fish, devoured that fish as well.
Thus, even though the swan had fallen into such distress,
I went quickly and, having severed the heads of those two with my sword, [rescued] the sage.
Having liberated them, O women of Vraja, he then departed for Śvetadvīpa;
meanwhile, I took my rest upon the couch of Śeṣa in the Ocean of Milk.
Knowing that you, my beloveds, were suffering, I, who am subject to the power of devotion, suddenly abandoned sleep and have returned here once more. (23)
The wise who perceive with equanimity, the self-controlled and great ones who are indeed free from dependence, know this:
for me, freedom from dependence is the supreme happiness.
Just as the sense organs [perceive] taste and so forth. || 24 ||
The gopīs said:
"O Mādhava, if you are pleased with us, grant us the vision of that form which was assumed by you upon the couch of Śeṣa in the Ocean of Milk."
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, while the assembly of gopīs looked on, the Blessed One assumed an eight-armed form as well as the form of Śrī Rādhā.
There, the ocean of milk appeared, adorned with surging waves;
and there arose divine jeweled palaces and auspicious objects. (27)
Therein, Śeṣa is white as a lotus stalk, situated in a coiled form,
resplendent with a parasol formed by the thousand hoods that serve as his crown, like the rising sun.
Upon that very couch of Śeṣa, Mādhava slept happily;
Rādhā, in her form as Śrī, performed service at his feet.
Seeing that beautiful form, which resembled ten million suns,
all the hosts of gopīs bowed down and were filled with supreme wonder.
O King of Mithilā, the place where Kṛṣṇa granted his vision to the gopīs became a most meritorious field that destroys all sins.
Then Mādhava, having approached the Yamunā together with the groups of cowherd girls,
engaged in water-sports amidst the swift currents of the Kālindī's waters.
From the hand of Rādhā, Mādhava himself, laughing, went running through the waters toward a hundred-thousand-petaled lotus and a yellow garment.
Taking hold of Hari’s yellow garment, which shone with the brilliance of a flickering cane, Rādhā proceeded into the waters of the Yamunā, pressing him down as she went.
To the high-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa who was saying, "Give me the flute," Rādhā replied, "O Mādhava, give me a lotus and a garment."
Kṛṣṇa gave a lotus and a garment to Rādhikā; Rādhā gave a yellow cloth, a staff, and a flute to the Great-Souled One.
Then Kṛṣṇa, singing sweetly and wearing a Vaijayantī garland that hung down to his knees,
went toward the glorious Bhāṇḍīra tree.
There, the Lord of the Skilled performed an adornment for his beloved with leaf-designs using the tips of lac-dye,
flowers, kohl, and saffron.
With sandalwood, agallochum, musk, saffron, and other substances, Kīrtinandinī prepared a beautiful decorative mark upon the face of Hari for his adornment. (39)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Rāsa-dance," in the Vṛndāvana-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārada said:
Then, O King, Kṛṣṇa went with the gopīs to Lokajaṅghavana,
which was filled with springtime mādhavī creepers.
Then, with clusters of those flowers, radiant and possessing a pervasive fragrance,
Hari braided the tresses of all the women there.
Accompanied by his beloved, Kṛṣṇa wandered near the Yamunā, which resounded with the humming of bees and was perfumed by fragrant breezes.
Kṛṣṇa, Hari, the Lord of the Rāsa dance, went to a most meritorious forest crowded with trees such as Karīras, Pīlus, dark Śyāmas, and Tamālas.
There, accompanied by the Mistress of the Rāsa dance, he began the Rāsa;
being sung of by the gopīs as if by apsarases, like Indra himself.
In that regard, O King, listen from my mouth as I relate what was wonderful:
the powerful Yakṣa Śaṅkhacūḍa, a follower of Kubera, was filled with pride. (6)
On this earth, there is no one equal to him who is so skilled in mace-fighting;
having heard of the exceedingly fierce strength of the lord of the Ugrasenas, who is my mouthpiece.
Taking up his heavy mace, which weighed a hundred thousand bhāras, the king of the yakṣas,
possessed of fierce prowess, went from his own abode to the city of Madhupurī.
Bowing down in the assembly hall, one arrogant with pride said to Kaṃsa:
"You are a conqueror of the three worlds; grant me a duel with maces."
"If you are victorious, I shall indeed become your slave;
but if I am victorious, I shall quickly make you my slave. (10)
Having said, "So be it," Kaṃsa took up his great mace and fought with Śaṅkhacūḍa on the arena floor, O King of Videha.
And between the two of them, a battle with maces occurred that was truly terrible in form;
from their striking one another, there arose a *caṭ-caṭ* sound like the roar of lightning from the clouds of doom.
The two wrestlers shone in the middle of the arena like two actors in a dance;
they were like two lordly elephants with long limbs, and as formidable as two lions.
And as the two fought, O King, each desiring victory over the other,
their two maces, emitting sparks, were reduced to powder.
Kaṃsa struck the enraged Yakṣa with his fist,
and Śaṅkhacūḍa also struck Kaṃsa with his fist.
For twenty-seven days there was a hand-to-hand struggle between those two,
whose strength remained undiminished and who were filled with wonder.
Having seized Śaṅkhacūḍa, the powerful Kaṃsa, lord of the Daityas,
suddenly hurled him by force a hundred yojanas into the sky.
Śaṅkhacūḍa, his mind somewhat agitated,
seized Kaṃsa and hurled him through the sky to a distance of ten thousand yojanas.
Falling from the sky with a somewhat agitated mind, Kaṃsa suddenly seized the yakṣa and dashed him to the ground.
Śaṅkhacūḍa seized him and dashed him against the ground;
as the battle thus proceeded, the circle of the earth trembled.
The Lord of Sages, the omniscient Garga Ācārya himself, arrived;
having been saluted by the two of them in the arena, he spoke to Kaṃsa with words of victory.
The illustrious Garga said:
"O Indra among kings, do not wage war; this battle here will surely be fruitless.
For this hero Śaṅkhacūḍa is of great strength and is indeed your equal."
By the blow of your fist, the elephant Airāvata struck the earth with his knees and fell into a state of extreme distress. || 23 ||
Other powerful Daityas as well met their death by his fist;
yet Śaṅkhacūḍa did not fall—of this there is no doubt, so listen to that.
He who is indeed most fully perfected will also slay you;
likewise, he known as Śaṅkhacūḍa, who is empowered by the boon of even Śiva.
Therefore, O scion of the Yadu dynasty, you must show affection toward Śaṅkhacūḍa;
and you must certainly maintain affection for Kaṃsa as well, who is the king of the Yakṣas.
Śrī Nārada said: Then, having met with one another after being addressed by Garga, those two—
the bearer of the conch (Śaṅkhacūḍa) and the leader of the Yadus— exchanged supreme affection.
Then, having taken leave of Kaṃsa, he prepared to go home;
while traveling on the road at night, he heard the enchanting song of the rāsa dance.
Following the sound of the cymbals, he arrived at the circle of the rāsa dance;
there, in the rāsa, he beheld Hari, the Lord of the rāsa, together with the Mistress of the rāsa.
His left arm adorned by Śrī Rādhā, His right foot gracefully bent at His will,
holding the flute, beautiful, and possessing a gentle smile.
With the circles of their eyebrows, they deluded the mass of Kāma. || 30 ||
Recognizing Kṛṣṇa— the leader of the cowherd women’s throng, the lord of Vraja, well-served by millions of chowries and umbrellas— to be indeed an exceedingly delicate infant;
He set his mind upon abducting the cowherd girl. || 31 ||
Bahulāśva said:
What occurred thereafter in the Rāsa dance when Śaṅkhacūḍa had arrived?
Tell me this, O best of Brahmins, for you are the most knowledgeable in all things high and low.
Śrī Rādhā said:
Seeing him with the face of a tiger, black in color, ten palm trees high, terrifying, and with a lolling tongue, the gopīs were utterly terrified. (33)
The cowherd women fled in all directions and a great clamor arose;
at that very moment, a cry of "Alas! Alas! broke out when Śaṅkhacūḍa arrived.
Taking the cowherd girl Śatacandrānanā, the wicked king of the Yakṣas,
tormented by lust and free from fear, quickly fled toward the northern direction.
As she was weeping and crying out "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!
overwhelmed by fear, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, with a śāla tree in his hand, pursued her in great rage.
Seeing him approaching like the invincible God of Death, the yakṣa, desiring to live, abandoned the cowherd girl and fled, trembling with fear. (37)
Wherever the great villain Śaṅkhacūḍa went running,
there Kṛṣṇa followed with a tree in his hand, filled with intense rage.
Having reached the slopes of the Himalayas and uprooting a śāla tree, O King, the king of the yakṣas stood facing him, especially desirous of battle. (39)
Against him, the Blessed One hurled a śāla tree with the strength of his arms;
by that blow, the tree fell like one struck down by the wind.
Rising up again, he struck Vaikuṇṭha with his fist;
the wicked one suddenly roared, making the entire circle of the quarters resound.
Seizing him with both arms and whirling him around by the strength of his limbs,
Hari threw him down upon the surface of the earth, like a lotus uprooted by the wind.
Śaṅkhacūḍa seized him and dashed him against the ground;
thus, as the battle proceeded, the circle of the earth trembled.
Having severed his head with his fist, Mādhava, Hari himself, took the crest-jewel from it, just as a virtuous man takes possession of a treasure.
O King, that light emerged as a long beam, illuminating the circle of the directions,
and became absorbed into Śrīdāman, the friend of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, in Vraja.
Having thus slain Śaṅkhacūḍa, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana,
with the jewel in his hand, quickly returned once more to the circle of the Rāsa dance.
Having given that jewel to Candrānanā, Hari himself, who is compassionate toward the distressed, again performed the rāsa dance together with the leaders of the gopīs.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa," in the section on Vṛndāvana within the Rāsakrīḍā of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārada said: Then, beholding the banks of the Śrī Yamunā together with the hosts of gopīs,
Kṛṣṇa went to sport in the enchanting Vṛndāvana forest.
By the boon of Hari, the medicinal herbs became absorbed in Vṛndāvana;
they all turned into women and arrived there, forming a multitude.
O King of Mithilā, Lord Hari, the sovereign of Vṛndāvana, took delight in the forest of Vṛndāvana with the multicolored multitude of vine-like gopīs. || 3 ||
On the auspicious bank of the Kālindī and Nandinī rivers, shaded by kadamba trees and made fragrant on all sides by the three kinds of breezes; || 4 ||
Accompanied by Rādhā and overcome with the fatigue from the rāsa dance, he remained upon a beautiful, shimmering sandbank adorned with bamboo and banyan trees.
Vīṇās, cymbals, mṛdaṅgas, and other instruments, as well as murus and flutes,
resounded in the sky, played by the gods together with the hosts of gopīs.
While the gods rained down flowers accompanied by shouts of victory,
the cowherd women, gladdening Hari, sang his supreme glory.
Some indeed [sang] Meghamallāra, others likewise Dīpaka;
some Mālakośa and Bhairava, and similarly Śrīrāga. || 8 ||
O King, some sang the *hiṃdola* melody along with the seven notes;
among them, O monarch, some women were deeply intoxicated and others were charmingly innocent.
Some mature gopīs, devoted to love with their minds fixed on Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
indeed worship Govinda according to the manner of a paramour.
Some, accompanied by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, were engaged in playing with balls;
others played with one another using flowers along with Hari. 11.
Some, running among the creepers with their anklets and girdles tinkling,
others constantly drink the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s lips by force.
One woman, having grasped Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who is difficult even for yogis to attain—with both her arms, laughed and embraced him closely with a great embrace. (13)
The charming King Yadu and Lord Hari,
the Lord of Vṛndāvana, took delight in the forest of Vṛndāvana, which was sealed with saffron from the Gopīs.
Some were playing the lute in harmony with the flute-player,
while others played the mṛdaṅga drum and sang of the Lord's virtues.
Some, indeed, beating a sweet rhythm before Hari and holding a mridanga drum in their hands, [danced] on the surface of the earth with Hari, O Madhavi.
Some, singing while remaining perfectly steady on the ground, forgot the happiness of the world; others, having placed their arms around Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s arm upon the creepers, [did the same]. (17)
O King, they wandered here and there beholding the splendor of Vṛndāvana,
where the clusters of necklaces belonging to the gopīs were entwined within the lattices of creepers.
Govinda, having touched the chests of those gopīs, himself separated their pearl necklaces from their noses and their hair from them. (19)
Gradually, the son of Śrīnaṃdana made it beautiful;
then, having taken half of the chewed betel, the cowherd girls immediately [departed].
Chewing that which was rich in fragrance, their asceticism became great;
some [women] slowly, with two fingers, [rubbed] upon the cheeks of Śyāmaka.
Laughing and striking them apart by force among the kadamba trees,
some of those women, adorned with crowns and earrings, assumed the dress of men and acted as leaders.
O King of Mithilā, dancing before Kṛṣṇa like Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself,
the gopīs assumed the dress of Rādhā, their faces possessing the splendor of a hundred moons.
And pleasing Rādhā as well as the Lord of Rādhā, some among them sang, endowed with ecstatic emotions (sāttvika-bhāvas) and overwhelmed with love. || 24 ||
Like yogis established upon the ground, they were immersed in supreme bliss;
some were indeed upon creepers, in trees, on the earth, and in the intermediate directions.
Beholding the Lord, the Consort of Śrī, or else maintaining silence within themselves, thus all the cowherd women in the Rāsa dance had their desires fulfilled. (26)
They all approached Govinda, the Lord of All, who is affectionate toward his devotees;
by whose grace, O high-minded King, the gopīs obtained [this state]. (27)
Even for the possessors of knowledge this is not so; how much less so for those engaged in ritual action?
Such is the case with the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, Hari, the husband of Rādhā. (28)
O high-minded one, hear that wonderful event which occurred at the rāsa dance:
there was a lord of sages named Āsuri, a great ascetic who was dear to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (29)
