While that brahmin was looking on, [the messenger] arrived to bring him;
when that divine chariot arrived, the brahmin and the god bowed to it.
Then, having ascended the chariot, that perfected one,
O King of Mithilā, illuminating the regions of the earth,
departed for the world of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which is higher than the highest.
It was charming and captivating, with the playful grace of a forest grove. || 23 ||
The brahmin also, having returned from there to Govardhana Hill— the deity of all the lords of mountains—
circumambulated it and bowed down to it once more.
O King of Mithilā, he went home, illuminated by her splendor.
I have related to you this formidable section concerning the King of Auspicious Mountains (Śrīgirirāja), which bestows excellent liberation;
by hearing it, even a person who has committed sins shall no longer be formidable.
Even in a dream, one would see Yama with his fierce staff.
O King of Mountains, he who hears this glorious secret of the new pastimes of the King of Cowherds attains here a status equal to that of the King of the Gods.
Like King Nanda, he shall attain peace in the hereafter. || 26 ||

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Siddhas," in the section on the Girirāja-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva, describing the exposition of the majesty of the King of Mountains. || 11 ||
Thus ends the illustrious Girirāja-khaṇḍa, the third [section].

May the wearer of the forest garland—whose beauty is comparable to the flax flower, who dwells amidst the *kadamba* trees on the banks of the Yamunā, and who is radiant with the playful charm of the young cowherd women—grant us auspicious blessings. 1.
Hari, who has made his yellow garment his girdle, whose neck is bowed by the crowns of the crested deities,
who holds a staff and a flute in his hands, and whose earrings sway.
I worship him who is exceedingly clever and wears the garb of an actor. || 2 ||
Bahulāśva said: O sage, how did Śrutidevī, Rūpavatī, and the other gopīs— who were previously celestial nymphs due to their boons— become fulfilled in their desires through Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra?
O one of great intelligence, you who are the best among those who know both the higher and the lower, please tell this most wonderful and purifying account of the deeds of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.

Śrī Nārada said: O King of Videha, those gopīs who were personifications of the Vedas took birth in the noble family of the cowherds in Vraja by virtue of the boon they had heard from the Lord reclining upon Śeṣa.
Beholding the lovely son of Nanda in Vṛndāvana, they took refuge in Vṛndā,
the Mistress of Vṛndāvana, with the desire for her blessing.
Having swiftly become pleased by the boon granted by Vṛndā, the Lord Hari,
who is affectionate toward his devotees, goes daily to their house for the sake of the rāsa dance.
Once, O King, when two watches of the night had passed,
the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa arrived at her house for the sake of the rāsa dance.
Then the longing gopīs, having performed that supreme worship,
questioned the Lord with supreme devotion and sweet speech.
The gopīs said:
O destroyer of sins, why have you not come quickly to our homes, while we gopīs long for you as cakora birds long for the moon? (10)
The Blessed Lord said:
Whoever dwells within another's heart is never far away.
O beloveds, having seen the sun in the sky and a lotus on the ground, this [lotus] blooms.
"My preceptor, the venerable sage Durvāsā himself, is at Bhāṇḍīra;
he arrived today, and I have gone there for the sake of serving him. (12)
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru is the manifest Supreme Brahman—salutation to that illustrious Guru. 13.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, who with the collyrium-stick of knowledge has opened the eye blinded by the darkness of ignorance. (14)
One should recognize my own guru as myself and never treat him with contempt;
one should not serve him with the notion that he is a mere mortal, for the guru embodies all the gods. 15.
Therefore, O beloved ones, having performed that worship and bowed at his lotus feet, I have come to your houses with some delay.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard those supreme words, all the gopīs were struck with wonder;
with palms joined in reverence and necks bowed, they spoke to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (17)
The gopīs said:
"O Lord, even for the most perfect one, Durvāsas is remembered as your preceptor;
oh, our minds are now impelled to behold him."
O Lord, when two watches of the night have passed today, O Supreme Ishvara, how may we behold him? (19)
Likewise, in the middle, the long river Yamunā stands as an obstacle;
O Lord, how will its crossing be possible without a boat? (20)
The Blessed Lord said:
"O beloved ones, you must certainly go;
having reached the Yamunā, this very thing must be told for the sake of finding the path."
"If Kṛṣṇa, the child of the Yadus, is indeed free from all faults, then grant us a path, O Kālindī, best among rivers."
When these words have been spoken, Kṛṣṇā will herself grant you the path; by that way, all you women of Vraja may proceed with ease. (23)
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard those words, all the women of Vraja then took fifty-six types of enjoyments individually in long vessels. (24)
Having reached the Yamunā, they sang [of Hari] with their necks bowed;
O Lord of Mithilā, Kṛṣṇā immediately gave way to the gopīs.
Then all the gopīs, filled with great wonder, went to Bhāṇḍīra;
thereafter, they circumambulated the sage Durvāsas.
Having bowed down, they presented him with a great quantity of food before them, saying:
"O Sage, you must first eat my food, and again my food before anyone else. (27)
Having understood the characteristic of devotion among the cowherd women who were thus disputing, that tiger among sages spoke these pure words.
The sage said:
"O gopīs, I am a paramahaṃsa, for I have accomplished my purpose and am free from ritual action;
therefore, you should place your respective food into my mouth with your own hands."
Śrī Nārada said:
When his mouth was thus opened by him, all the gopīs, filled with great joy,
each thrust in her own fifty-six kinds of enjoyments.
While the cowherd girls were casting glances at him, the Lord of Sages,
as if afflicted by hunger, devoured millions of Māras and all their enjoyments.
While the astonished cowherd women were looking at one another,
O best of kings, the vessels thus became empty.
Then all the cowherd women, their desires fulfilled, bowed down to that peaceful sage who is kind to his devotees; filled with wonder and prostrate before him, they spoke.
The Gopīs said:
O Sage, before our arrival, we crossed the river at Kṛṣṇa’s word and came into your presence with the auspicious desire for a vision of you.
"How shall we go from here? A great doubt has arisen.
Therefore, salutations to you; please provide that by which the path may become easy. (35)
Therefore, you should proceed from here with ease;
when you reach the Yamunā yourself, this indeed must be said for the sake of the path. (36)
If Durvāsas, having drunk the juice of dūrvā grass, remains on the earth as a practitioner of vows, subsisting on nothing but the ground, without food and without water; || 37 ||
"Then, O Kālindī, best of rivers, grant us a path indeed.
When these words were spoken, the Kṛṣṇā will herself grant you a path.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard these words, O King, the gopīs bowed to that bull among sages; then, having gone to the Yamunā and spoken what the sage had told them, they crossed the river.
Filled with wonder and seeking auspiciousness, they approached the side of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. || 40 ||
Then, in the rāsa dance, having beheld Śrī Hari in private and their desires being fully realized, the cowherd women asked him about the doubt that had arisen in their minds. (41)
The gopīs said:
"O sirs, we have already had a vision of Durvāsas;
yet, because of your words, this doubt has arisen within us. (42)
As is the teacher, so is the disciple; there is no doubt that you are a speaker of falsehood.
O Lord, from your very childhood, you have been a lover of the cowherd girls and a connoisseur of their rasa.
"O crusher of sins, tell us how you truly became a child;
and how the sage Durvāsas, having drunk the juice of dūrvā grass, became a great eater?
This doubt has arisen in us as we watch, O Lord of Vraja. (44)
The Blessed Lord said:
"I am free from possessiveness, free from egoism, equal, all-pervading, supreme, eternally devoid of partiality, and beyond the qualities (nirguṇa); of this there is no doubt. (45)
Nevertheless, I indeed honor those devotees who worship me in whatever manner they do;
likewise, the virtuous man of knowledge is always free from partiality. (46)
One should not create a disturbance in the minds of the ignorant who are attached to action;
rather, the wise man, being disciplined, should encourage them by performing all actions himself.
The wise call him a learned man whose every undertaking is free from desire and purposeful intent, and whose actions have been consumed by the fire of knowledge. 48.
With his mind and self free from desire, having renounced all possessions, he who performs action solely for the sake of the body incurs no sin. 49.
Indeed, there is nothing in this world as purifying as knowledge;
one who is perfected through yoga finds that within oneself in due course of time.
He who performs actions by dedicating them to Brahman, having abandoned attachment,
is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Therefore, the sage Durvāsas, though a great eater, is intent on your welfare;
since his food consists of nothing more than the juice of dūrvā grass, he would have no desire for other meals.
Śrī Nārada said:
O Lord of Mithilā, having heard these words, all those gopīs had their doubts severed; they became embodiments of the Vedas and were filled with knowledge.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Narrative of Śrutirūpā," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 1 ||
Hari Oṃ. May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is Tat-Sat.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King of Mithilā, listen to the narrative of the gopīs who took the form of sages;
it is meritorious, it removes all sins, and it increases devotion to Kṛṣṇa. (1)
In Vaṅga, there was a high-minded cowherd named Maṅgala;
he was prosperous, endowed with learning, and the master of nine hundred thousand cows.
O King of Mithilā, he had five thousand wives;
once, by the turn of fate, all his wealth went to ruin.
Some of his cows were carried off by thieves, and others were forcibly seized by the king;
when such misery had thus arrived, Maṅgala became distressed. (4)
Then, by the boon of Śrī Rāma, the sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest attained womanhood and became his daughters. ||5||
Seeing that multitude of maidens, the cowherd Maṅgala then became sorrowful;
filled with the misery of wretchedness and overwhelmed by mental and physical afflictions, he spoke.
Maṅgala said: "What shall I do? Where shall I go? Who will dispel my sorrow?
At present, I possess neither fortune, nor prosperity, nor noble lineage, nor strength. (7)
Without wealth, how indeed will their marriage take place? Alas! Where there is doubt regarding food, what can one expect regarding wealth? (8)
If there were any girls in my house by mere chance, they would have been reduced to a state of wretchedness;
therefore, I belong to some king who is both wealthy and powerful. (9)
"I shall give these maidens for the sake of the happiness of the daughters";
having thus resolved in his mind, he remained intent upon making those maidens suffer.
At that very moment, a certain cowherd arrived from the region of Mathurā.
Nārada said: A traveler to sacred fords named Jaya, an elder and the best among the wise,
heard of the wonderful majesty of King Nanda from his own mouth.
For the sake of Nandarāja’s strength, Maṅgala, afflicted by dejection,
reflected and sent forth beautiful-eyed maidens.
Those maidens, adorned with jewels, became cow-dung gatherers in the cow-pens of King Nanda’s household.
Having beheld the beautiful Śrī Kṛṣṇa, those maidens, who remembered their former births,
performed the service of the Yamunā daily for the sake of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then once, the dark-limbed Kālindī, with her long eyes,
granted them her sight and prepared to bestow a boon upon them.
They chose [this boon]: "May he become the son of the Lord of Vraja and may he be our husband.
Having said, "So be it," Kālindī vanished right there.
Having arrived in the forest of Vṛndaka on the full moon day of Kārtika at the circle of the Rāsa dance, Hari took delight with them, just as the king of the gods does with the celestial nymphs.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Sage's Form," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||2||
Hari Om. May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is Tat-Sat.
The Third Chapter of the Section on Sweetness:
The Narrative of Maithilī and the Multitude of Gopīs.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King of Mithilā, listen to the narrative of the Gopikās of Mithilā;
it bestows the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices and increases devotion.
Those who were born in the houses of the nine Nandas by virtue of Śrī Rāma’s boon became infatuated upon seeing the lovely son of Nanda. || 2 ||
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, they performed the Kātyāyanī-vrata,
having fashioned an image of the Goddess out of clay with the sixteen modes of service.
Having bathed daily in the waters of the auspicious Yamunā at the time of dawn,
they gathered together and arrived singing the virtues of the Blessed Lord.
Once, those women of Vraja, having placed their garments on the bank,
sported in the waters of the Yamunā, sprinkling one another with their hands.
Having gathered their clothes, the Blessed One arrived in the morning;
quickly climbing a kadamba tree, he remained silent like a thief.
O King, seeing their own garments there and then beholding him standing beneath the Nīpa tree, the cowherd girls were struck with wonder; yet, feeling bashful, they laughed.
"Let all of you come here and receive your own garments;
otherwise, I shall not give them," Kṛṣṇa said.
Shining in the cool water, they laughed and spoke while bowing down.
The gopīs said:
O delight of Nanda, O enchanting one, O jewel among cowherds, O swan of the cowherd lineage, O dispeller of great suffering!
O Śrī Śyāmasundara, how can we, who are indeed naked, carry out the words spoken by you today, even though we are your maidservants? (10)
Having become a thief of the cowherd women’s garments, butter, and curds, you have indeed become a great libertine in Vraja; you are truly fearless!
Give back the clothes, otherwise the village elders will surely beat you.
We shall speak of this; you have indeed acted excessively in this matter.
The Blessed Lord said:

"O Daityas, if these women with beautiful, gentle smiles desire only me here at the foot of this Kadamba tree, then I shall take all their garments and return them to their homes; therefore, you must act upon my word without delay."
Śrī Nārada said: Then all those gopīs emerged from the water, trembling violently;
overcome by the cold, they bent down and covered their private parts with both hands.
All the women born in Vraja gave garments bestowed by Kṛṣṇa;
enchanted, they stood there with their eyes cast down in modesty.
Having understood their intention, which was characterized by supreme love,
Kṛṣṇa, looking at them all around with a gentle smile, spoke these words.
The Blessed Lord said: "O ladies, the vow to Kātyāyanī was observed by you in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa;
for my sake, that shall become fruitful, of this there is no doubt."
And on the day after tomorrow, in the forest on the charming bank of the Kṛṣṇā river,
I shall perform with you the Rāsa dance that fulfills all desires.
Having spoken thus, when Kṛṣṇa, the most perfect Hari, had departed,
all the gopīs, filled with bliss and smiling softly, went to their homes.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Narrative of Maithilī," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī-Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Hari Om. May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is Tat-Sat.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King of Mithilā, listen to the description of the cowherd girls of Kośala;
it is meritorious, a destroyer of all sins, and the nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s life-story.
Born in the houses of Upananda’s nine sons in Vraja by virtue of Rāma’s boon,
they were married by the cowherd folk and adorned with ornaments of jewels.
Resembling the full moon, endowed with fresh youth,
they were like lotus-women (padminīs) with the gait of swans and eyes like lotus petals.
In the manner of lovers, they formed an exceedingly firm and intense affection toward Kṛṣṇa, the son of Nanda, who was most desirable and great-souled, surpassing all others.
Together with them, Mādhava constantly engaged in laughter upon the streets of Vraja,
using smiles, the seizing of their yellow garments, and playful tugging.
Going about for the purpose of selling curd, O Kṛṣṇa, they cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!
as they wandered through the circle of forest bowers, filled with love for Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, Kṛṣṇa was perceived by them in the sky, in the wind, in fire and water, on the earth, in the luminaries, in the quarters, in the trees, and among the throngs of people.
Those women were endowed with the characteristics of divine love, their minds captivated by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and they were possessed of the eight types of sattvic emotions (sāttvika-bhāvas).
O King, out of love for the paramahaṃsas, those daughters of Kṛṣṇa’s joy ran along the paths of Vraja, having attained their station.
Being inert, they do not perceive what is inert, like the insane or ghosts; whether remaining silent or speaking, they are devoid of shame and free from distress.
Thus having attained their goal, those gopīs who were absorbed in Him forcibly drew Kṛṣṇa toward them and kissed his lotus-like face.
O King, what can I say of their austerity toward Vāsudeva, the supreme Brahman, who is complete?
They fixed their love upon Him with their hearts and senses, having abandoned the path of worldly conduct.
Placing their arms upon the shoulders of Kṛṣṇa on the stage of Rāsa, their hearts pierced by love,
they brought Kṛṣṇa under their control through such intense austerity that even the Lord of Serpents is unable to describe it with his many mouths.
That state which is attained through yoga, through the auspicious Sāṃkhya, through virtuous action, and by those who are the best among the knowers of the principles of Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika—
that very state is attained by the King of the Vedas.
It is attained solely through the state of devotion. || 14 ||
Lord Hari, the primordial God, is indeed brought under control by devotion alone;
in this matter, the Gopīs are truly the eternal authority,
for they never practiced Sāṃkhya or Yoga.
By love alone, they would have returned to their natural state. || 15 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Kauśala," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the Śrīgargasaṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Hari Om. May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is Tat-Sat.
Śrī Nārada said:
Listen now to the description of the gopīs residing in Ayodhyā;
it directly bestows the four goals of human existence and grants the supreme attainment of Kṛṣṇa. (1)
O King of Mithilā, there was a city named Campakā in the lands of Sindh; in that city lived a king named Vimala, who was devoted to righteousness.
Rich in a treasury like Kuvera, wise like the king of beasts, a devotee of Viṣṇu with a tranquil soul, he was like Prahlāda incarnate. || 3 ||
That king had six thousand wives,
beautiful and lotus-eyed, yet they all became barren.
"O King, by what merit might I have offspring here? May there be auspiciousness for me.
As he was thinking thus, many years passed away.
Once, Yājñavalkya, the lord of sages, arrived there;
having bowed to him and worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, the king stood before him.
Seeing the king overwhelmed with anxiety, the great sage Yājñavalkya—
omniscient, all-knowing, and tranquil— replied to that best of kings.
The venerable Yājñavalkya said:
"O King, why are you emaciated? What anxiety dwells in your heart?
At present, prosperity is seen among all your subjects."
Vimala said:
"O Brahmin, do you not know this through your penance and divine vision?
Nevertheless, I shall speak because of the weight of your words."
"O best of sages, I am overwhelmed by the suffering of childlessness;
tell me, what austerity or gift should I perform so that offspring may be born? (10)
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard this, Yājñavalkya, the best of sages, with eyes motionless in meditation, reflected deeply, contemplating the past and the future.
The illustrious Yājñavalkya said:
"O Indra among kings, in this birth you shall have neither son nor daughter at all;
yet, O best of monarchs, you shall have daughters by the millions."
The king said:
"O Lord of Sages, on this earth no one is ever liberated from the ancient debt [to ancestors] without a son.
Indeed, there is always suffering in the home of one who has no son; moreover, there is no happiness for him either in this world or the next. (13)
The venerable Yājñavalkya said:
"Do not grieve, O Indra among kings; you must indeed give your daughters to the future Śrī Kṛṣṇa, along with supreme gifts and other offerings. (14)
By that very deed, O tiger among kings, you are indeed released from your debt to the gods, sages, and ancestors, and you shall attain supreme liberation.
Śrī Nārada said: Then, having heard the words of the great sage, the king was exceedingly delighted;
he again questioned the great sage Yājñavalkya regarding his doubt. (16)
The King said:
In what lineage and in what land will Śrī Hari himself appear? Of what form and what complexion will he be, and after how many years have passed? (17)
The venerable Yājñavalkya said: O mighty-armed King, in this Dvāpara age,
when one hundred and fifteen years remain of your reign, O Monarch (18).

In that year, in the Yadu clan, in Mathurā, the city of Yadu, during the month of Bhādrapada, on a Wednesday in the dark fortnight, under the Dhātṛ constellation, in the Harṣaṇa yoga, and in the sign of Taurus; || 19 ||
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight at midnight, when the moon was in its great exaltation in the constellation Rohiṇī,
and at a time shrouded in darkness, [the Lord was born] from Devakī in the house of Vasudeva.
Hari will manifest in person within the forest at the sacrifice like a fire;
marked with the Śrīvatsa, dark as a rain-cloud, and exceedingly beautiful with a garland of wild flowers. (21)
Clad in yellow garments and lotus-eyed, he shall become four-armed;
you must give your daughter to him, for his life remains—of this there is no doubt. (22)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Resident of Ayodhyāpura," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā. || 5 ||
Hari Om. May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is Tat-Sat.
Śrī Nārada said:
When the great sage Yājñavalkya had thus spoken and departed, [the king]...
Vimala and the lord of Campaka were both filled with extreme joy. || 1 ||
The inhabitants of the city of Ayodhyā, who [attained their status] by the grace of Śrī Rāma.
To all his wives, those auspicious maidens were born.
Seeing that they were suitable for marriage, the lord of Campaka began to reflect.
Recalling the words of Yājñavalkya, the lord of kings spoke to the messenger.
Vimala said:
"O messenger, go to Mathurā; having gone there, [enter] the auspicious house of Śauri."
"You must behold the handsome son of Vasudeva. || 4 ||
Marked with the Śrīvatsa, dark as a rain cloud, wearing a forest garland, and four-armed.
If that were so, then I would give all my excellent daughters to him. || 5 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard these words, that messenger then went to Mathurā and inquired about the intentions of all the great men of Mathurā.
Having heard those words, the wise citizens of Mathurā, fearing Kaṃsa,
spoke to that messenger in private, whispering into his ear with soft voices.
The people of Mathurā said:
"Many sons of Vasudeva were slain by Kaṃsa;
the one daughter who remained as the youngest has also gone to heaven."
"Vasudeva is also right here, indeed sonless and dejected in mind;
you must certainly not speak of this in the city out of fear of Kaṃsa."
If anyone speaks news concerning the lineage of Śauri in the city of Mathurā,
that Kaṃsa— the enemy of the eighth child of Śūrasena— punishes him.
Śrī Nārada said:
Then, having heard the words of the people, the messenger went to the city of Campakapura and related that wonderful cause to the king.
The messenger said:
"In Mathurā there is Śauri, who is childless and exceedingly wretched;
it has been heard that his sons born previously were slain by Kaṃsa."
The one remaining maiden also departed from Kaṃsa's hand into the sky;
having heard this, I slowly emerged from the city of the Yadus.
While wandering in the beautiful and auspicious Vṛndāvana near the Yamunā,
I suddenly beheld a certain child amidst a thicket of creepers.

O King, he possesses the marks of a great man, stands in the midst of a multitude of cows and cowherds, bears the Śrīvatsa mark, is dark as a rain cloud, and is exceedingly beautiful with a forest garland. (15)
Furthermore, this son of a cowherd has two arms, whereas you have described Hari, the son of Vasudeva, as having four arms; thus, he is quite different from that.
"Tell me, O King, what should be done? For the word of a sage is never false. O Lord, send me wherever you desire. (17)
Śrī Nārada said:
While the king was thus reflecting in amazement,
Bhīṣma arrived from the land of Sindhu to conquer Hastināpura.
Having honored him and offered him a great sacrificial gift (bali), King Vimala questioned Bhīṣma, the best among the upholders of dharma, regarding his entire intention.
Vimala said:
"As previously stated by Yājñavalkya, Hari himself will be born in Mathurā from Vasudeva and Devakī; of this there is no doubt. (20)
"The supreme Hari has not been born today from Vasudeva;
the word of the sage must not be false. To whom shall I give my daughters? (21)
"You are a great devotee of the Lord, the knower of the higher and the lower, one who has conquered his senses, a hero, an archer, and the best of the Vasus even from childhood.
O one of great intelligence, tell me this: what indeed should be done by me in this matter?"
Śrī Nārada said: The great devotee of the Lord, the wise Gāṅgeya (Bhīṣma)— who possessed divine vision, knew the essence of dharma, and understood the majesty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa— spoke to Vimala.
Bhīṣma said: O King, listen to this secret narrative heard from the mouth of Vedavyāsa; it is meritorious, a destroyer of all sins, and an increaser of joy. (24)
For the sake of protecting the gods and for the destruction of the Daityas,
Hari, the most perfect one, was born in the house of Vasudeva.
O King, at midnight, having taken him away in haste out of fear of Kaṃsa, Śauri went to Gokula and placed his son upon the bed.
Having taken Māyā, the daughter of Yaśodā and Nanda, he went to the city.
Kṛṣṇa grew up in Gokula, protected and unrecognized by any men.
This very day, Hari, assuming the guise of a cowherd, shall dwell in concealment for eleven years in the forest of Vṛndāvana;
having caused the death of the demon Kaṃsa, he will become manifest.
Those auspicious maidens who were the inhabitants of Ayodhyāpurī by virtue of Śrī Rāma’s boon all became the wives of your sons. (29)
"Indeed, these maidens must be given by you to the hidden God of gods;
no delay should ever be made, for this body is subject to time. (30)
When the omniscient Bhīṣma had spoken thus and departed for Hastināpura,
Vimala dispatched his own messenger to the son of Nanda.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Resident of Ayodhyā-pura," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Hari Oṃ! May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is Tat-Sat.
Śrī Nārada said:
Then the messenger, having returned from the Mathurā region of Sindhu and wandering along the banks of the Yamunā in Vṛndāvana, beheld Kṛṣṇa.
Having bowed down to Kṛṣṇa in private with palms joined in reverence,
the messenger circumambulated him and slowly spoke the words of Vimala.
The messenger said:
He is himself the Supreme Brahman, the Highest, the Supreme Lord, invisible to others, the perfectly complete God.
Homage to him who is the domain of the virtuous, and who is indeed ever distant from the multitudes of merit. || 3 ||

For the sake of protecting cows, Brahmins, gods, the Vedas, the virtuous, and dharma, you, who are unborn, have been born this very day in the lineage of Yadu for the purpose of slaying Kaṃsa and others.
Salutation to him, the ocean of infinite qualities.
Oh, what supreme fortune for the inhabitants of Vraja! Blessed is the lineage of your father, the noble Nanda;
blessed are the cowherds of Vraja, and blessed is this forest.
Wherein the supreme Hari is directly manifest.
That very jewel upon the beautiful throat of Rādhikā, that very root-form of the life of the gopīs— may He appear before the path of my eyes.
How can I describe my own good fortune? || 6 ||
You are protected in Vraja by the army of cowherds and are renowned like the fragrance of musk;
and your stainless fame quickly makes all white.
It acts everywhere, pervading the three worlds.
You know all that people regard as sacred shrines; you are the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the Self, the witness of the multitude of forms.
Nevertheless, I shall speak the words uttered by the king.
The supreme secret, one's own duty, in private.
In the lands of Sindhu, there is a famous and auspicious city named Śrīcampakā, which is like the city of Indra;
its protector is Vimala, who is like Indra himself.
With the functions of my mind fixed upon your lotus feet. || 9 ||
For your sake, hundreds of sacrifices have always been performed,
as well as acts of charity, austerity, service to Brahmins, pilgrimage to sacred sites, and the chanting of mantras— by means of these excellent spiritual disciplines.
To him, grant the supreme vision itself. || 10 ||
Those maidens, with large lotus-like eyes, seek you, their perfect husband, nearby;
they are always established in restrictive vows for your sake, their bodies purified by service to your feet. (11)
O Lord of Vraja, having granted them the supreme and wondrous vision of Yourself, take their hands;
depart quickly and purify the rivers.
For you must indeed act after due reflection. || 12 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard those words of the messenger, the blessed Lord Hari became pleased;
accompanied by the messenger, he traveled to the city of Campakā in a mere moment.
During Vimala’s great sacrifice, which was filled with the sound of the Vedas,
Kṛṣṇa suddenly descended from the sky along with his messenger.
Hari, marked with the śrīvatsa, dark as a rain cloud, beautiful, wearing a forest garland,
clad in yellow garments, lotus-eyed, who had arrived at the sacrificial enclosure.
Seeing him, Vimala rose up suddenly, overwhelmed with love;
with his hair standing on end and palms joined in reverence, he fell at the feet of the Lord. || 16 ||
Having placed [the image] upon a divine pedestal whose feet were inlaid with gems and gold, and having praised and worshipped it according to the prescribed rites, the king stood before it. (17)
Seeing the beautiful women gazing out from the windows, Mādhava Kṛṣṇa spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud to Vimala.
The Blessed One said: "O Mahāmati, choose a boon, whatever dwells in your mind.
By the word of Yājñavalkya, this vision of me has been granted to you."
Vimala said:
"O God of gods, may my mind, having become like a female bee, always dwell within the lotus of your feet; I have no other desire whatsoever."
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, King Vimala offered his entire great treasury of wealth,
along with elephants, horses, and chariots, as a self-surrender.
O King, having offered all the maidens to Hari according to the prescribed rite, the pure Vimala, intent on devotion, paid obeisance to Kṛṣṇa.
Then a cry of "Victory! Victory! arose among the circles of people;
the deities stationed in the sky rained down showers of flowers. (23)
At that very moment, he attained a form identical to Kṛṣṇa, with a radiance flashing like that of the bodiless god of love,
resembling a hundred suns as he illuminated the circle of the quarters.
Having mounted Vainateya and bowed to the Lord whose banner is the glorious Garuḍa,
the pure Vimala, together with his wife, departed for Vaikuṇṭha while the people looked on.
Having personally granted liberation to the king, the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa took his beautiful daughters and returned to the district of Vraja.
There, in the delightful Kāmavana, filled with divine mansions,
all those auspicious beloveds of Kṛṣṇa stood playing with balls.
Assuming as many forms as there were beloved and principal women, the Lord Hari, the King of Vraja, shone resplendently in the rāsa dance, his mind fixed solely upon them. 28.
In the Rāsa dance, from the drops of tears of joy shed by the daughters of Vimala,
the Vimalakuṇḍa was formed— the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
O Lord of Kings, having seen, drunk from, bathed in, and worshipped it,
a human being destroys sin as vast as Mount Meru and goes to Goloka.
The man who hears the story of the inhabitants of Ayodhyā shall go to the supreme abode, Goloka, which is difficult even for yogis to attain. (31)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Resident of Ayodhyā," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the Śrīgargasaṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Hari Om. May this be offered to the True Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Om Tat Sat. Śrī Kṛṣṇārpaṇam astu.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King of Mithilā, listen to the narrative of the gopīs who were the sacrificial Sītās;
it is meritorious, a destroyer of all sins, a granter of desires, and a source of auspiciousness. (1)
There was a country named Uśīnara situated in the southern direction;
once, the rain-god did not send rain there for ten years.
There, wealthy cowherds, afflicted by the fear of drought, arrived at the circle of the settlement with their families and their cattle-wealth. ||3||
O King, they made their dwelling in the auspicious and delightful holy forest of Vṛndāvana, near the Kālindī river, with the assistance of King Nanda.
Born in their houses were the cowherd girls,
who were the sacrificial furrows of Śrī Rāma— divine, endowed with excellent and celestial youth.
O lord of kings, having seen the beautiful Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they were enchanted;
they approached Rādhā to ask about a vow for the sake of obtaining Kṛṣṇa’s grace. ||6||
The gopīs said:
O divine daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, O Rādhā with eyes like lotus petals, please tell us of some auspicious vow for the sake of obtaining the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (7)
The son of Nanda is under your control, though he is difficult even for the gods to approach;
O Rādhā, you are the enchantress of the world and one who has reached the further shore of the meaning of all the scriptures. 8.
Śrī Rādhā said:
"For the sake of obtaining the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, observe the Ekādaśī vow;
by that, Hari will become directly submissive to you, without a doubt. (9)
The gopīs said: O Rādhikā, tell us the names of the twelfth days (dvādaśī) of the year;
by what disposition should her vow be observed month after month?
Śrī said:
In the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the excellent Ekādaśī tithi was born from the body of Viṣṇu for the purpose of slaying the demon Mura. (11)
Month after month, she appears in distinct forms; she alone is the supreme among all vows.
Out of a desire for your welfare, I shall declare her twenty-six names.
Likewise, Utpatti and Mokṣā, followed by Saphalā;
then Putradā, Ṣaṭtilā, Jayā, and Vijayā. (13)
Then follows Āmalakī, truly named Pāpamocanī;
after that, Kāmadā is mentioned, and then indeed Varūthinī. (14)
Mohinī is proclaimed as another, and thereafter Nirjalā is mentioned;
then Yoginī, Devaśayanī, and after that Kāminī. ||15||
Then Pavitrā, Ajā, Padmā, and Indirā;
after that, Pāśāṅkuśā, Ramā, and then Prabodhinī. 16.
And the two [Ekādaśīs] occurring in the intercalary month are said to bestow all prosperity;
thus, whoever recites these twenty-six names of Ekādaśī— (17)
He indeed obtains the fruit of twelve years of the Dvādaśī fasts;
now listen, O women of Vraja, to the rule for Ekādaśī as well.
Sleeping on the ground, eating but once a day, and having conquered his senses, he [attains] the tenth stage.
Having drunk water once and wearing freshly washed, perfectly clean garments,
he rose during the Brāhma-muhūrta on the eleventh lunar day and bowed to Hari.
Bathing in a small well is the lowest; bathing in a large pond is middling;
bathing in a tank is excellent; and bathing in a river is superior to that. (20)
Having bathed in this manner, the best of men, free from anger and greed,
should not speak with base people or heretics on that day.
Those who delight in false speech, as well as those who revile Brahmins, and others of wicked conduct who take pleasure in approaching women who should not be approached. (22)

That man observing the vow should not speak with those who steal the property of others, those who approach the wives of others, those of evil conduct, or those who have transgressed the bounds of propriety. (23)
Having worshipped Keśava, one should there present an offering of food (naivedya);
with a mind endowed with devotion, one should offer a lamp in that house. ||24||
Having heard the discourses from the Brahmins, one should further give them excellent sacrificial fees;
at night, one should keep a vigil while singing the names of Kṛṣṇa’s feet.
Bell-metal, meat, lentils, kodrava grain, chickpeas, as well as leafy vegetables, honey, food belonging to others, eating a second meal, and sexual intercourse—[these should be avoided]. (26)
When the vow of Viṣṇu is to be performed, one should avoid ten things for ten days:
gambling, play, sleep, betel, and the cleansing of the teeth.
On the eleventh day, one should avoid slandering others, backbiting, theft, as well as delighting in violence, and speech full of anger or falsehood. (28)
On the twelfth lunar day, one should avoid bell-metal, meat, liquor, honey, oil, false speech, [flesh of] fattening animals, and lentils. (29)
One should perform this supreme Dvādaśī vow according to the prescribed rite. ||30||
The gopīs said:
O high-minded one, tell us the proper time for this Ekādaśī vow;
tell us what its fruit is, and describe its greatness according to the truth. (31)
Śrī Rādhā said:
If the tenth lunar day is seen to have fifty-five ghaṭikās, then that eleventh day must be abandoned, and one should fast on the twelfth day. (32)
The eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) must be abandoned even if it lasts for only a single pala [of time] after the tenth;
just as a jar of Ganges water is abandoned by the falling of a single drop of liquor.
When the eleventh day increases and the twelfth day has likewise increased, then the latter (the second Ekādaśī) should indeed be observed for fasting; the former is for the vow of Dvādaśī.
O women of Vraja, I shall describe the fruit of this Ekādaśī vow, by the mere hearing of which one obtains the merit of a Vājapeya sacrifice. (35)
A man who observes the vow of Dvādaśī obtains the same fruit as one who feeds eighty-eight thousand twice-born brahmins. (36)
Whoever gives away the earth together with its oceans and forests,
the merit of that is multiplied a thousandfold by the great vow of Ekādaśī.
For the sake of uplifting those who are submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, which is thick with the mud of sin, there is this supreme vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī-vrata).
A man who observes the Ekādaśī vow and keeps a vigil at night does not see the fierce Yama, even if he is burdened with hundreds of sins.
He who worships Hari with devotion on the twelfth lunar day using tulasī leaves is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (40)
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices are not worth even a sixteenth part of the fast on the eleventh lunar day. 41.
Indeed, ten on the mother’s side, likewise ten on the father’s side, and ten on the side of his beloved—such men does a man rescue from [rebirth]. ||42||
As is the white, so is the black; the fruit of both is the same.
A cow that is white and one that is black—the milk of both is equal. (43)
O Gopīs, even sins as vast as Mount Meru and Mandara accumulated over a hundred lifetimes are consumed by a single Ekādaśī, just like a heap of cotton.
Whether performed according to the rules or devoid of them, even a gift given on the twelfth day,
or any small virtuous deed, O Gopīs, shall become equal to Mount Meru.
He who listens to the story of Hari, Viṣṇu, on the day of Ekādaśī, obtains the same fruit as that from the gift of the earth consisting of seven continents. ||46||
Having bathed at Śaṅkhoddhāra and beheld the god Gadādhara, a man does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of fasting on the Ekādaśī day. 47.
At Prabhāsa, Kurukṣetra, Kedāra, and Badarikāśrama;
at Kāśī and Sūkarakṣetra, during the eclipses of the moon and the sun. ||48||
The gift given by men at four hundred thousand solar transits (saṅkrāntis) does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of fasting on the Ekādaśī day. 49.
Just as Śeṣa is among the nāgas, as Garuḍa is among the birds, as Viṣṇu is among the gods, and as the Brāhmaṇa is among the social classes; ||50||
Just as the Aśvattha is among trees and Tulasī is among leaves, so too is the Ekādaśī lunar day the most excellent among vows and the Gopīs among women. 51.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by performing austerities for ten thousand years,
a man who observes the vow of Dvādaśī attains an equal result.
"Thus, O women of Vraja, the fruit of the eleven Ekādaśīs has been declared.
Perform the vow yourselves quickly; what more do you wish to hear? (53)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Ekādaśī," within the narrative of Yajñasītā, in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva, in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā. ||8||
Hari Om Tat Sat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The gopīs said:
O daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, O fair-browed one, you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures, with your speech you mock the very words of the sage Vācaspati! || 1 ||
O Rādhā, by whom and by whom was the Ekādaśī vow performed in ancient times?
Tell us that in detail, for you are the personified treasure-house of knowledge.
Śrī Rādhā said: O gopīs, in the beginning, the gods performed the vow of Ekādaśī for the sake of regaining their lost kingdom and for the destruction of the demons. (3)
In former times, King Vaiśaṃta performed the Ekādaśī vow for the sake of delivering his father who had gone to the realm of Yama.
Even the sinner Luṃpaka, who had abandoned his kin,
obtained a kingdom because he observed Ekādaśī by chance.
In Bhadrāvatī, Ketumā, who was childless, performed the Ekādaśī vow; by virtue of the virtuous words [of the sage], that man obtained a son.
The Brahmin woman was given the Ekādaśī vow by the wives of the gods;
by that, she obtained heavenly bliss, wealth, and grain as a human being.
Puṣpadanta and Mālyavān attained the state of Piśācas due to Śakra’s curse;
having performed a vow, they both returned to the state of Gandharvas.
In ancient times, the vow of Ekādaśī was observed by Śrī Rāmacandra for the purpose of building a bridge across the ocean and for the slaying of Rāvaṇa.
And at the conclusion of the dissolution, the gods were born beneath the Dhātṛ tree;
they observed the vow of Ekādaśī for the sake of all auspiciousness.
The wise one observed the vow of the twelfth day according to his father’s word;
freed from the fault of contact with the apsarases, he became radiant and pure.
The Gandharva Lalita had fallen from his state due to a curse along with his wife; may he be protected!
By the vow of Ekādaśī alone, he regained his status as a Gandharva once again. (12)
By the vow of Ekādaśī alone, Māndhātṛ attained the heavenly state, as did Sagara, Kakutstha, and the high-minded Mucukunda. (13)
Likewise, there were many other kings such as Dhundhumāra and others;
thus the Lord Bhava became liberated from the skull of Brahmā.
Dhṛṣṭabuddhi, the son of a Vaiśya, who was a great rogue abandoned by his kinsmen, went to Vaikuṇṭha after performing the Ekādaśī vow. || 15 ||
King Rukmāṅgada also observed the Ekādaśī vow;
having enjoyed the entire circle of the earth, he went to Vaikuṇṭha along with his city.
King Ambarīṣa also observed the vow of Ekādaśī;
even the curse of a brahmin, which had never before been thwarted anywhere, did not touch him.
A Yakṣa named Hemamālī, who was afflicted with leprosy due to the curse of Kubera,
became as radiant as the moon after performing the Ekādaśī vow.
King Mahījit also observed the Ekādaśī vow;
having obtained an auspicious son through that merit, he departed for Vaikuṇṭha.
King Hariścandra also observed the Ekādaśī vow;
by that merit, having obtained sovereignty over the earth, he went to Vaikuṇṭha along with his city.
In former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, one named Śrīśobhana was the son-in-law of King Mucukunda;
he who, having fasted on the Ekādaśī day in Bhārata, [attained such merit].
He was indeed encountered by the gods on Mount Mandara.
Even today, he rules the kingdom like Kubera, accompanied by the queen Candrabhāgā;
O gopīs, you should know that Ekādaśī is the supreme sovereign of all lunar days, for there is no other equal to her.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard this from the mouth of Rādhā, the Gopīs, including Yajñasītā,
being eager for Kṛṣṇa, performed the Ekādaśī vow according to the prescribed rules.
Pleased even by the vow of Ekādaśī, Śrī Hari himself performed the rāsa dance with them on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Ekādaśī," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Hari Om Tat Sat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Nārada said: Hereafter, I shall indeed provide a description of the Pulindaka cowherdesses;
it is meritorious, wondrous, a destroyer of all sins, and an increaser of devotion.
Certain Pulinda tribesmen, fierce dwellers of the forests of the Vindhya mountains,
were plundering the wealth of kings, yet they never harmed the poor.
Enraged at them, the powerful and mighty lord of the Vindhya region besieged all those Pulindas with two akṣauhiṇīs.
They also fought for several days with swords, spears, tridents, axes, javelins, double-edged swords, bhṛśuṇḍīs, and arrows.
They sent a letter to Kaṃsa, the lord of the Yadus;
then the powerful Daitya Pralamba was dispatched by Kaṃsa.
His body was two yojanas tall, with a luster like a dark rain-cloud;
he wore a crown and earrings, and was adorned with a necklace of serpents.
With his feet bound by chains, mace in hand, wearing earrings,
with a lolling tongue and a terrible form, he was casting down the lords of mountains and trees.
Seeing him shaking the earth with his speed, hanging low, and intoxicated by the pride of battle,
the king, along with his army, was overwhelmed on the field of combat.
Having abandoned them, he fled suddenly like an elephant upon seeing a lion;
then Pralamba, having gathered them together, returned again to Mathurā.
O lord of kings, those Pulindas also, having entered into the service of Kaṃsa,
took up residence on Mount Kāmagiri together with their families.
Born in their houses by virtue of the supreme boon of Śrī Rāma,
there were divine Puliṇḍī maidens, possessed of beautiful forms and honored like the Goddess Śrī herself.
The Pulindya women, overwhelmed with love and suffering from the pain of longing for the sight of him,
held the dust of his glorious feet and meditated upon him day and night.
And they too, having arrived at the rāsa dance, beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord,
the most perfect one in person, the sovereign of Goloka and the Master.
The dust of the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is extremely difficult even for the gods to obtain;
oh, how great is the fortune of these Pulinda women that they have attained it in such abundance! (14)
He who desires neither the entire sovereignty of Brahmā, nor the celestial abode of Mahendra, nor constant universal kingship, nor lordship over the netherworlds,
nor the perfections of yoga, nor even liberation from rebirth;
That devotee desires nothing more than the supreme dust of Your feet. || 15 ||
Free from possessions, detached from the fruits of their own actions,
those great sages who are devotees of Hari take refuge in the dust of Hari’s feet; for that is the state which the people of Hari, devoted to it, enjoy.
Others say that indeed there is no happiness in independence.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Pulinda's Anger," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the Śrīgargasaṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 10 ||
Hari Oṃ. May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is Tat-Sat.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King of Mithilā, listen now to the description of the other gopīs as well;
it is meritorious, removes all sins, and increases devotion to Hari. (1)
O King, six descendants of Vṛṣabhanu were born in Vraja: Nītivit, Mārgada, Śukla, Pataṅga, Divyavāhana, and Gopeṣṭa. || 2 ||
Born in their houses from the boon of Lakṣmīpati, these offspring—
residents of Vaikuṇṭha and companions of Śrī— were likewise born from the ocean.

Those residing above in Vaikuṇṭha, as well as those who have taken refuge at the feet of the Unconquerable (Ajitapada), the companions of Śrī residing on the Mountain of the World of Prosperity (Śrīlokācala), and even the female friends of Śrī born from the ocean; || 4 ||
Constantly meditating upon the glorious lotus feet of Govinda,
they performed the Māgha vow for the sake of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s grace.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, at the beginning of spring, Hari himself—
Kṛṣṇa indeed— went to their homes for the purpose of testing their love.
Wearing a tiger-skin garment, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
grey with sacred ashes, he plays the flute, enchanting the world.
Seeing Him arrive at their pathways from all sides, the gopīs too,
deluded and overwhelmed with love, came to behold Him.
Beholding the exceedingly beautiful yogin, all the cowherd maidens,
overwhelmed with the bliss of love, spoke to one another.
The gopīs said:
"Who is this infant? Is he the son of Nanda, or the son of some wealthy man or king?"
With his vital organs pierced by the arrows of a woman’s wicked words, he became dispassionate and ceased all worldly activities. || 10 ||
Exceedingly beautiful, with a delicate body, as swift as thought, and enchanting to the whole world—
oh, how does his mother live?
And his father, wife, and sister [are not superior] to him. || 11 ||
Thus, all those women of Vraja, having gathered together in groups from every side,
being struck with wonder and overwhelmed with love, questioned that best of yogis.
The gopīs said:
"Who are you, O yogin? What is your name? Where is your dwelling, O sage?
What is your livelihood and what is your perfection? Tell us, O best among speakers. (13)
The Siddha said:
"I am a master of yoga; my dwelling is always at Mānasa-sarovara.
By name I am Svayaṃprakāśa, and I am eternally independent of food through my own power."
"O women of Vraja, I am going with the company of the supreme *paramahaṃsas*;
possessing divine vision, I know the past, the future, and the present. (15)
I know how to perform exorcism, killing, deluding, and likewise paralyzing, as well as subjugation, by means of mantras and vidyās. || 16 ||
The gopīs said:
"O Yogi, if you know the news arising from the three periods of time, then tell us, O high-minded one, what is currently in our minds. (17)
The Siddha said:
"This speech must be told into your ears;
either by your command I shall speak it here while everyone listens."
The gopīs said:
"It is true that you are the Lord of Yoga, the knower of the three periods of time; of this there is no doubt.
[This is so] by the power of the subjugation mantra, merely through its recitation. (19)
O sage, if he whom we have indeed been thinking of comes right here,
then we shall truly consider you the foremost among counselors.
The Siddha said:
"O women, the state you have described is difficult to attain and hard to accomplish;
nevertheless, I shall do it, for the word of the virtuous does not waver."
Close your eyes, O women; do not grieve.
There is no doubt that your purpose shall be accomplished.
Śrī Nārada said: When the gopīs had thus closed their eyes, the Blessed Lord Hari,
the delighter of Śrī, abandoned that form of a yogi and shone forth as the son of Nanda.
Opening their eyes, they beheld the Joy of the Nandana grove with delight;
struck with wonder at his majesty, they were filled with joy and then fell into a swoon.
In the month of Māgha, during a great festival in the holy forest of Vṛndāvana,
Hari took delight with them, just as the king of the gods does with the celestial nymphs.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Friends of Śrī Residing on Ramācala, the Ajitapada, the White Island (Śvetadvīpa), and Upper Vaikuṇṭha," within the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 11 ||
Hari Om. May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is Tat-Sat.
Śrī Nārada said:
This auspicious account of the gopīs has been told by me to you;
now hear, O King of Mithilā, the description of other gopīs as well.
Vītihotra, Agnibhuk, Sāṃba, Śrīkara, Gopati, Śruta, Vrajeśa, Pāvana, and Śānta—these are the Upanandas born in Vraja. || 2 ||
They were wealthy, handsome, possessed of sons, and deeply learned;
endowed with virtues such as good character, they were all devoted to the practice of charity.
Born in their houses by the word of the gods were daughters—
some divine, some non-divine, and likewise those whose conduct was governed by the three qualities (guṇas).
O King of Videha, by means of various merits performed, they were born as protectors of the earth and became the companions and friends of Rādhikā.
Once, during the great festival of Holikā, all those gopīs of Vraja, seeing that Hari had arrived, spoke to the proud Rādhā.
The gopīs said:
O Rādhā, whose thighs are like plantain stalks, whose face is like the moon, and who are the mistress of those proud with youth; O graceful woman, listen to these sweet words:
this ornament of Vraja is coming to your city-grove to fully perform the festive pastimes of the Śrī Holi festival.
With eyes rolling from the intoxication of youth and beauty, his cheeks adorned with dark locks of hair, he approached from nearby,
completely enveloped in the dense darkness of a fine yellow bodice.
Not shaking [it], with his own feet that were red and possessed of sound.
Victorious is he, whose limbs are adorned with armlets and necklaces as pure as the rising morning sun, who wears shark-shaped earrings that surpass flashing lightning,
and who, clad in yellow garments, stands upon the earth like a cloud in the sky, a circle of splendor accompanied by his bow.

O friend Rādhā, having seen you nearby with your body smeared with the juices of *ābīra* and saffron, holding a new sprinkling-vessel in your hand, the garden will immediately become a sight to behold.
He remains intent on the playful enjoyment of the aesthetic flavor of your dramatic performance. || 10 ||
Depart under the pretext of the Phālguna festival, casting aside your pride; for today, fame must indeed be bestowed upon Holi.
And let the thick paste of sandalwood and the nectar of camphor be quickly prepared for the festive arena of your own palace. 11.
Arise and go at once with your own circles, O high-minded one, to where he indeed is;
for such an occasion as this will never be found again, like a palm already washed away by the current.
Śrī Nārada said: Then Rādhā, full of pride, cast aside her resentment and arose,
surrounded by throngs of her friends, to celebrate the festival of Holi.
Those women of Vraja were accompanied by leather bags filled with the juices of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, turmeric, and saffron.
With blood-red hands and yellow garments, their anklets and girdles jingling, they sang Holikā songs with abusive words and humorous interludes. || 15 ||
With handfuls of red *ābīra* powder, they made the earth, the horizons, and the sky alike crimson on every side.
There, fistfuls of fragrant, reddish powders flash forth by the millions and millions, and likewise by the millions and millions more.
The cowherd women of Vraja grasped Kṛṣṇa from all sides with their two hands,
just as flashes of lightning seize a cloud during the twilight of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Then, smearing his face with handfuls of red *abīra* powder and using flasks filled with saffron, the women moistened him according to the prescribed ritual.
O lord of kings, the Blessed One also assumed as many forms as there were women in Vraja and sported with them right there.
There, during the great festival of Holi, Kṛṣṇa shone with Rādhā like a cloud with lightning at the moment of the evening twilight of the rainy season.
Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, having had His eyes anointed by their hands and having given them His own new upper garment,
departed for the home of Nanda.
And the gods rained down a shower of flowers. || 22 ||

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Gopīs on the Ground of the Divine Threefold Function during the Holi Festival," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the Śrīgargasaṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Hari Om. May this be offered to the True Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Om tat sat. Śrī Kṛṣṇārpaṇam astu.
Śrī Nārada said:
Now listen to the description of the celestial damsels and the cowherd women, which bestows the four goals of human life upon men and is the supreme increaser of devotion. (1)
In the land of Mālava, there was a cowherd named Nanda, who was like a lord of the day;
he was endowed with a thousand wives, wealthy, and supremely wise in ethics.
In the course of a pilgrimage, he arrived at Mathurā;
having heard that Nanda Rāja was the lord of Vraja, he went to the glorious Gokula.
Having assembled and beheld the king of the cowherds and the splendor of Vṛndāvana,
that high-minded one took up residence there by the command of King Nanda.
O King, having established the cowherd settlement over an area of two yojanas,
that lord of the day (the Sun) attained great joy in Vraja along with his kinsmen.
By the word of Devala, all the women of the divine race became great celestial maidens, resembling the blazing crests of fire.
Upon seeing the beautiful Śrī Kṛṣṇa, those maidens were infatuated;
for the sake of attaining Dāmodara, they performed the supreme Māgha-vow.
At the time of the sun's half-rise, the women of Vraja, having bathed daily in the Yamunā,
sang loudly of Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes, overwhelmed with the bliss of divine love.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, being pleased with them, said, "Choose a boon.
Bowing low to him, they spoke slowly to him with their palms joined in reverence. (9)
The gopīs said:
You are indeed difficult to attain even for the masters of yoga; you are the Lord of all, the cause of all causes.
May you, the bearer of the flute whose body is the destroyer of the god of love, always be present before our eyes.
Having said, "So be it," Hari, the primordial deity,
who extended his vision toward them, may he always abide in your heart through the path of your eyes.
In that way, he quickly [arose] in the mind as if summoned. || 11 ||
The most perfect Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself is indeed none other;
having arrived for the sake of a single task, he performed ten million tasks.
Hari, who has made his yellow garment his girdle, whose neck is bowed by the crowns of peacock-feathered ones,
who holds a staff and a flute in his hands, and whose earrings sway.
I worship him who assumes a most clever disguise for the sake of bowing down. || 13 ||
Lord Hari, the primordial God, is indeed always submissive to devotion alone; in this matter, the gopīs are truly the authority,
for they never practiced Sāṃkhya or Yoga.
By love alone, they would have returned to their natural state. || 14 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Celestial Women," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 13 ||
Hari Om. May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is Tat-Sat.
Śrī Nārada said: O Maithila, O great king, hear now of the births and the deeds of the Jālandharī gopīs, which always destroy the sins of men.
O King, on the bank of the Saptanadī is the excellent city of Raṅgapattana,
endowed with every prosperity, long and two yojanas in circumference.
There lived a cowherd named Raṅgoji, a powerful lord of the city,
who was endowed with sons and grandsons and possessed great abundance of wealth and grain.
To Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of Hastināpura and the ruler of the earth,
he always gave a hundred arbudas of gold as his annual tribute.
Once, O King of Mithilā, when the rainy season had passed, that man,
intoxicated with pride, did not pay the annual tax to the king.
Ten thousand heroes, dispatched by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, did not come to meet Raṅgoja, the leader of the Gopas.
Having bound that cowherd with ropes, they brought him to the place called Gaja;
for how many years did Raṅgoji remain in prison? (7)
Though bound and beaten, the greedy man did not become afraid;
he did not give even the slightest wealth to King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Once, having escaped from that most terrifying prison,
Raṅgoji, the leader of the cowherds, arrived at Raṅgapura during the night.
Furthermore, O King, three akṣauhiṇīs, complete with capable forces and vehicles, were dispatched by Dhṛtarāṣṭra to collect him [Duryodhana].
Armored for battle, he fought with him using floods of sharp-edged arrows flashing with brilliance,
repeatedly twanging his bow.
With his armor shattered by enemies, his bow broken, and his own men slain,
Raṅgoji returned to the city and waged war for several days.
Helpless and seeking refuge, Raṅgoji, oppressed by fear, dispatched his own messenger to Kaṃsa, the king of the Yadus.
The messenger, having arrived at Mathurā and entered the assembly hall with his face bowed down,
paid homage to the son of Ugrasena with joined palms and spoke with a voice full of emotion.
In the city of Raṅgapattana, there was a king named Raṅgoji,
a cowherd who was the supreme master of statecraft and the ruler of the city; his capital was besieged by his enemies, and he bore great mental anguish.
Having found no protector, I have come to you for refuge. || 15 ||

On this earth, you are the remover of the suffering and pain of the wretched; you possess great strength, with virtues sung by Bhauma and others, and you subdue the gods, asuras, and formidable rulers of the land.
Having conquered in battle, he stood like the king of the gods. || 16 ||
Just as the cakora bird [longs for] the moon, the lotus for the sun, and the cātaka bird for the autumnal spray,
so does one oppressed by hunger long for food, and one oppressed by thirst for water.
In the same way, he remembers you when there is fear of an enemy. || 17 ||
Having heard these words of his, Kaṃsa, who was compassionate toward the distressed,
resolved in his mind to go accompanied by ten million Daityas.
His face bore vermilion from the accumulation of cow-urine and musk as decorative leaf-designs;
he was dark-complexioned like the Vindhya mountain and endowed with cascades of ichor.
And having mounted the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, who was intoxicated with rut and whose feet were bound by a network of chains that rattled loudly like thunderclouds, he set forth.
Armed with Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, and others, as well as Keśin, Vyoma, and the Asura Vṛṣa,
Kaṃsa hurriedly went to the arena city.
And between the two armies of the Yadus and the Kurus,
a terrible battle took place with arrows, swords, and tridents.
When the darkness of arrows had arisen, Kaṃsa, taking up his great mace,
entered the Kuru armies like a fire in a forest.
With his mace, which was like a thunderbolt, he felled certain armored heroes to the surface of the earth,
just as Indra strikes a mountain with his vajra.
He crushed chariots with his two feet and struck horses with the heels;
having struck elephant against elephant, he raised his feet high upon the elephants.
Seizing some by their shoulders and armpits, the powerful one violently whirled those who were closely huddled together on jeweled blankets and hurled them into the sky.
O King, lifting elephants adorned with dangling bells by their trunks,
the powerful Vyomāsura hurled them into the midst of the battle.
Seizing chariots along with their horses and repeatedly whirling them like horns,
the powerful and wicked Daitya Vṛṣāsura hurled them in all directions.
O Indra among kings, the powerful Keśī, lord of the Daityas, forcibly struck down the heroic horses here and there with his two hind legs.
Having seen such a terrifying battle, the remaining Kuru soldiers,
those heroes overcome with fear, also fled in the ten directions.
Then the heroic Kaṃsa, the king of the Daityas, taking Raṅgoji along with his family,
proceeded toward Mathurā while slowly sounding the kettledrums.
Having heard of their own defeat, the Kauravas were overwhelmed with anger;
yet, seeing the resolve of the Daityas, they all maintained a vow of silence.
In the vicinity of Vraja, Kaṃsa, the powerful lord of the Daityas, gave to Raṅgojaya a charming city named Barhiṣada.
There, Raṅgoji, the leader of the cowherds, made his dwelling;
by the boon of Hari, Jālandharīs became his wives.
Married by the cowherd folk and adorned with beauty and youth,
they established a deep affection for Śrī Kṛṣṇa through the practice of lovers.
In the month of Caitra, during the great festival, Hari himself, the Lord of Vṛndāvana, took delight in the beautiful and holy Vṛndāvana together with them.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Jālandharī," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the Śrīgargasaṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 14 ||
Hari Om Tat Sat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Nārada said: O King of Mithilā, in Vraja there was a wealthy and great cowherd named Nanda, the lord of Śoṇapura;
he had five thousand wives.
O King, from that excellent fish were born the daughters of the cowherds in the ocean,
as well as others, through the milking of the earth with the threefold speech.
The excellent celestial nymphs who were born in the city of Barhiṣmatī as those possessing the memory of their former births became others [in this life] by virtue of a boon from Nārāyaṇa. || 3 ||
Likewise, by the boon of Vāmana, women came to dwell in Sutala;
and similarly, the daughters of the lords of the Nāgas were born there by the supreme boon of Śeṣa.
To them, Durvāsas gave the wonderful *kṛṣṇāpañcāṅga* [fivefold black ointment];
having worshipped Yamunā with that, they chose the Lord of Śrī as their boon.
Once, Śrī Hari was with them in the enchanting Vṛndāvana forest,
near the Yamunā, in a divine grove of trees resounding with the cries of male cuckoos.
In the month of Madhu, when the air was filled with the humming of bees and the warbling of cuckoos and cranes, when gentle breezes blew and the land was covered with spring creepers; || 7 ||
Hari, the enchanter of Madana, commenced the Dolotsava festival in secret beneath a beautiful Kadamba tree that resembled a Kalpa tree.
In that place, which was filled with the tumultuous roar of the waves of the Yamunā's waters,
those gopīs, overwhelmed with love, engaged in the sport of swinging.
In Vṛndāvana, Kṛṣṇa shone with Rādhā, the daughter of Kīrti, who was as radiant as ten million moons, just as the Lord of Rati shines with Rati.
Thus, for all those who have attained Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the joy of the gods,
who is the most perfect Supreme Being in person— how can their austerity even be described?
All those auspicious daughters of the Naga kings reached Balabhadra Hari on the banks of the Kṛṣṇā during the enchanting month of Caitra.
This auspicious account of the cowherd girls, which removes all sins and is meritorious, has been told by me to you. What more do you wish to hear?
Śrī Bahulāśva said:
O Sage, tell me, O Lord, how the five-limbed [mantra] of Yamunā was given by Durvāsas to the gopīs, by which Govinda was attained. (14)
Śrī Nārada said: In this very context, they cite this ancient history, by the mere hearing of which the destruction of sins becomes supreme. (15)
The illustrious Māndhātṛ, the best of kings and lord of Ayodhyā,
while wandering on a hunt, arrived at the auspicious hermitage of Saubhari.
Having bowed down to his son-in-law Saubhari, who was staying in person at Vṛndāvana on the charming bank of the Kṛṣṇā river, the king, the bestower of honor, spoke to him.
Māndhātṛ said:
"O Blessed One, you are the omniscient one in person, the best among those who know both the higher and the lower;
you are like another divine sun for the worlds blinded by darkness. (18)
Tell me quickly that by which one may possess a kingdom in this world endowed with all perfections, and in the hereafter, attain the same form as Kṛṣṇa.
Saubhari said:
I shall describe before you the five-fold [pilgrimage] of the Yamunā,
which eternally bestows all perfections and brings about identity of form with Kṛṣṇa.
From the time the sun rises until it sets, this [place] bestows sovereignty here and brings one under the control of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. || 21 ||

O Lord of the Solar Dynasty, the wise know the five limbs [of this scripture] to be the armor (kavaca), the hymn (stava), the thousand names (nāmasahasra), the chapter (paṭala), and the manual (paddhati). || 22 ||

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Daughter of the Serpent King, a Resident of Sutala and an Apsarā Married to the Householder of Barhiṣmatī," within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva, and the dialogue between Śrī Saubhari and Māndhātṛ, in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. || 15 ||
Hari Oṃ. May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is Tat-Sat.
Māndhātṛ said:
O illustrious one, grant me the stainless armor of Yamunā, the black queen; I shall wear it forever.
Saubhari said:
O high-minded King, listen now to the armor (kavaca) of Yamunā, which provides complete protection for men and directly bestows the four goals of human existence.
Having meditated upon the beautiful goddess Kṛṣṇā— dark-complexioned, four-armed, with eyes like lotus petals, and seated upon a chariot— one should then wear the armor.
Having bathed, facing east, observing silence, and having performed the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā),
the Brahmin, with his topknot tied with kuśa grass, should recite [the mantra] while seated upon a kuśa mat in the svastika posture.
May Yamunā protect my head, may Kṛṣṇā always protect my two eyes, may Śyāmā protect the region of my eyebrows, and may Nākavāsinī protect my nose.
May she who is the manifest embodiment of supreme bliss protect my two cheeks;
may she who was born from the left shoulder of Kṛṣṇa protect both my ears.
May Kālindī protect my lips, the daughter of the Sun (Yamunā) my chin, Yama’s sister (Yamunā) my neck, and the Great River (Gaṅgā) my heart.
May Kṛṣṇapriyā protect my back, O river; may Suśroṇī protect my two arms, and may Cārudarśanā protect the slope of my hips and my waist.
May Raṃbhoru protect my two thighs, Aṅghribhedinī my knees, Rāseśvarī my ankles, and Pāpaprahāriṇī my feet. || 9 ||
May she who is most dear to the Supreme Fullness protect the world on all sides—within, without, below, above, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions. 10.
This most wonderful armor (kavaca) of Śrī Yamunā—
one who recites it with devotion ten times shall become wealthy even if he was previously destitute.
The wise person, practicing celibacy and eating moderately, should recite this for three months;
he will attain sovereignty over all kingdoms—of this there is no doubt. (12)
For one who, having become disciplined, recites this constantly for one hundred and ten [verses] with devotion over the course of three months, what is there that does not come to pass for him? (13)
Whoever recites this upon rising in the morning shall obtain the fruit of all sacred fords;
in the end, they shall go to the supreme abode, Goloka, which is difficult even for yogis to attain.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Armor of Śrī Yamunā," within the dialogue between Śrī Saubhari and Māndhātṛ, which occurs in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva, in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. || 16 ||
Hari Oṃ! May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is Tat-Sat.
Māndhātṛ said:
O tiger among sages, Saubhari, please tell me quickly out of compassion this supreme, divine hymn to Yamunā, which bestows all spiritual perfections.
Śrī Saubhari said:
O high-minded one, listen to the hymn of praise to the daughter of Mārtaṇḍa,
which bestows all perfections upon earth and grants the fruits of the four aims of human life.
Constant salutations to Kṛṣṇā, who has become the left shoulder of Kṛṣṇa;
salutations to you, O Kṛṣṇā, whose form is Śrī Kṛṣṇa—salutations again and again.

To him who is defiled by the mire of sin, the water of worldly desire, and the stain of wickedness, and who indeed instigates strife among the virtuous— that fool and lustful one— Vṛndāvana bestows its own abode.
The daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā), together with the flowing Milinda and others.
In Kṛṣṇa you yourself abide as the manifest form of Kṛṣṇa;
in the whirlpool of the flood you abide in the form of a fish;
and in every wave you always abide in the form of a tortoise.
In every single drop, Lord Govinda shines forth.
I bow to you, Līlāvatī,
who resemble a dark rain cloud, who have become the left shoulder of Kṛṣṇa,
and who possess the power known as Vairaja.
Violently shattering the entire mass of waters by her own power,
she has recently split the cosmic egg and the mountains of the city of the gods, which are as formidable as boulders from mountain slopes.
Having pierced through the middle of the land,
she proceeds with a garland of waves resting against her banks.
O Yamunā, where have you heard this divine name? For it punishes the entire, unbroken mass of sins as if they were mountains.
Let that [truth] dwell for a moment within the circle of my words:

that fierce and excessive punishment of your brother, the son of the Sun, which punishes those who deserve it and fails to punish those who do not, and which is harsh even when his speech is once interrupted—this very thing resounds loudly in the city. (7)
Or it is a rope for crossing the dark well of sense-objects; a wicked female serpent in a pit; and the bamboo-flute and the *uṣṇih* meter upon the head of the form of *virāj*.
Or perhaps the beautiful Mālā exists;
beyond this, what greater fortune for men on earth could there be than one where the Primordial Creator is beloved?
Even in Goloka, this peerless river shines forth, exceedingly auspicious and extremely difficult to attain.

O Kālindī, you who are radiant with the splendor of Kṛṣṇa and engaged in the playful pastimes of the cowherds, cows, and cowherd girls; on your banks, [there is] the swaying of balls tossed about by the water.
A tumultuous roar of billowing waves;
a clamor of warbling peacocks mingled with the humming of swarms of bees eager for the delights of your forest.
May the vine of Vraja, filled with the warbling of cuckoos and bearing ornaments, protect me. || 9 ||
Even when tongues become as numerous as the fine hairs on the body and voices as swift as the sands of the earth,
they still do not reach the end of your virtues.
Truly, the virtuous are great, being equal to Śeṣa himself. || 10 ||
Whether this hymn to the daughter of Mount Kalinda be heard or recited at dawn on earth, it bestows auspiciousness;
indeed, any person who constantly retains it in memory or recites it shall likewise attain it.
He goes to the supreme abode, which is enveloped by the pastimes of his own forest groves.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Śrī Yamunā," within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva, and the dialogue between Śrī Saubhari and Māndhātṛ, in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. || 17 ||
Hari Om. May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is Tat-Sat.
Māndhātṛ said:
O tiger among sages, you who are the manifest treasure-house of knowledge, tell me the meritorious chapter on Kṛṣṇā as well as the ritual manual (paddhati) that grants all desires. || 1 ||
Saubhari said:
O high-minded one, I shall declare the chapter and the ritual manual of Yamunā;
by performing, hearing, or reciting it, a man becomes liberated while living.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, then the Māyā-bīja, then having placed the Ramā-bīja, and then the Kāma-bīja according to the prescribed rule; || 3 ||
After the word "Kālindī" ending in the dative case, one should then place the word "Devī," followed by "namaḥ"; having thus arranged it, a person should recite this mantra. || 4 ||
Having recited the mantra eleven lakhs of times, the attainment of mantric perfection shall occur on earth;
and whatever desires are sought by people, all of them shall be obtained spontaneously.
Having fashioned a sixteen-petalled lotus upon an auspicious throne,
one should place Kālindī, united with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, within the pericarp.
The Jāhnavī, Virajā, Kṛṣṇā, Candrabhāgā, Sarasvatī,
Gomatī, Kauśikī, Veṇī, Sindhu, and likewise the Godāvarī.
The best of men should worship the Vedasmṛti, the Vetravatī, the Śatadru, the Sarayū, as well as the Ṛṣikulyā and the Kakudminī.
Having pronounced their names individually according to the prescribed rite upon those petals—
namely Vṛndāvana, Govardhana, Vṛndā, and Tulasī—
one should quickly perform worship in the four directions with their respective names.
Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, the daughter of Kalinda, the daughter of the Sun, the sister of Yama, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who has become a troop [of companions]; svāhā!
With this mantra, one who is composed should offer the sixteen services beginning with invocation (āvāhana). || 10 ||
Know that this indeed is the chapter; I shall now declare to you the ritual manual (paddhati) until the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) reaches its completion.

For that long, the twice-born man should remain a celibate student; he should recite prayers while observing a vow of silence, subsisting on barley, sleeping on the ground, eating from leaves, and having his mind fully conquered.
Having cast aside desire, anger, greed, delusion, and hatred, O King, that teacher dwelt there with supreme devotion. (13)
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and meditated upon the Goddess born of the Yamunā,
one should perform a bath in the river at the time of dawn.
O King, intent upon the twilight worship at both midday and evening,
he remained on the bank of the Kālindī during that seventh observance.
Having honored one million high-souled Brahmins along with their sons with perfumes and flowers, and having given them excellent food; (16)
