One should give garments, ornaments, golden vessels, and radiant auspicious sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā); from that, success will surely be attained. || 17 ||
Thus, O high-minded King, this manual has been declared by me to you; perform every prescribed observance. What more do you wish to hear? (18)

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Sequence of Chapters," in the dialogue between Śrī Saubhari and Māndhātṛ, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva, in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. || 18 ||
Hari Oṃ. May this be offered to the True Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Māndhātṛ said:
O tiger among sages, you who are omniscient and free from all affliction, please tell me the supreme thousand names of Kṛṣṇā, which bestows all spiritual perfections. (1)
Saubhari said:
O Māndhātṛ, I shall recite to you the thousand names of the Kālindī,
which bestows all perfections, is divine, and brings Kṛṣṇa under one's control.
Oṃ. Of this mantra of the *Śrī Kālindī Sahasranāmastotra*, Saubhari is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the venerable Yamunā is the deity (*devatā*), the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandaḥ*),
the seed-syllable of Māyā is the pin (*kīlaka*), and the seed-syllable of Ramā is the power (*śakti*).
The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining the grace of the illustrious daughter of Kālinda through recitation (*japa*).
Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*):
[I meditate upon her] who is dark-complexioned, with lotus-eyes, possessing the luster of a dense rain-cloud, and whose jeweled anklets tinkle.

One should meditate upon the daughter of the Sun, who is beautiful and charming, wearing two earrings made of gold and jewels along with a golden armlet; she is adorned with shimmering, beautiful blue garments and a weight of pure, sparkling, moving necklaces, her feet lovely as they are illuminated by a mass of slender rays of light.
Thus is the meditation: Oṃ! Kālindī, Yamunā, Kṛṣṇā, eternal in form as Kṛṣṇa, born from the left shoulder of Kṛṣṇa, she whose form is supreme bliss. || 4 ||
She is the dark-complexioned dweller of Goloka, who delights in Vṛndāvana;
she is the friend of Rādhā, the Rāsa-dance play, and the ornament of the Rāsa circle.
The beautiful Raṅgavallī, a Mādhavī creeper in the forest bower, has become the Śrī Rāsa-maṇḍalī; she is a herd of Hari’s beloveds.
The divine river of Goloka dwells within the depths of the forest groves;
she is profound with the force of her long waves and carries along flowers and tender sprouts.
She who is dark as a dense cloud, a garland of clouds, and a flight of cranes; she who wears a garland of lotuses;
she who is the most perfectly full, the full, the supreme beloved of the perfect Brahman.
Possessing great speed, she has emerged directly from the door of the bower;
she is the great river of slow gait, free from passion, who shatters all velocity.
Extending through many Brahmā-eggs, filled with the essence of Brahmā,
mingled with the Gaṅgā, appearing waterless yet pure— she is the best of rivers.
With both its banks adorned with jewels, crowded with swans, lotuses, and other creatures,
the river possesses pure water and sanctifies the entire universe.
The moat that forms the boundary of Vaikuṇṭha is a destroyer of sins;
it reaches the world of Brahmā as the Brāhmī river, and as the Svargā, she dwells within heaven itself.
The brilliantly radiant crest of the Ganges' waters, shimmering and leaping upward like a garland of Mount Meru, breaks through the massive boulders of the mountain.
Purifying the lands as she flows, carrying her waters while situated within the earth,
the holy daughter of the Sun, the delight of Mount Kalinda, proceeds on her way.
The sister of Yama, with a gentle smile, possessing beautiful teeth and well-fashioned garments, clad in blue robes, lotus-faced, moving about, and of lovely appearance. || 15 ||
The lotus-eyed Mādhavī, the best of women with thighs like plantain stalks and beautiful hips,
was performing penance, her girdle and anklets tinkling.

Staying in the water, her limbs dark-complexioned, with a luster like that of sugar-cane, sporting playfully, speaking to the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, she was a forest-dweller who desired Śrī Kṛṣṇa as her husband. || 17 ||
The queen, the chief consort who had reached the highest state, traveled to Dvārakā;
the great queen, adorned with jewels, wandered along the banks of the Gomatī.
She is his own, bringing him happiness, intent on her own purpose, and accomplishing the tasks of her devotees;
she is a fresh-limbed maiden, charming, beautiful of form, and lovely-eyed.
Her youth was unknown; she was dejected, yet her splendor, radiance, luster, and complexion were supreme in beauty;
she was the highest fame and auspiciousness, with her youth remaining unrecognized.
The newlywed, the one in her middle years, the mature, and the fully developed;
the steadfast, the unsteady, and the one who maintains her composure; the elder, the most excellent, and the noble lady of the family. (21)
The flash of a moment, the flickering flame, the lightning, the cloud-burst, and the bolt;
the self-dependent Lakṣmī, and the well-nourished woman who has her husband under her control. (22)
Separated by a quarrel, timid, agitated by longing and desire, lying upon her bed with her mind stolen by Govinda, she rests upon a celestial couch. 23.
A woman whose beauty is impaired yet remains rich with unbroken splendor is called a *vipralabdhā* (one deceived);
one who is distressed by separation is a *virahiṇī* (one suffering from separation); and one whose husband is away on a journey is a *proṣitabhartṛkā* (one whose husband is abroad). || 24 ||
Proud, bestowing honor, wise, dwelling in the Mandāra forest;
making the sound "jham," making the sound "jhaṇat," with tinkling anklets and foot-ornaments.
Mekhalā, Amekhalā, Kāñcī, Kāñcīnī, and that which consists of gold; Kañcukī, Kañcukamaṇi, Śrīkaṇṭhāḍhyā, and Mahāmaṇi. || 26 ||
She wears a garland of lotuses that steals away all splendor, adorned with pearls and precious gems; she possesses jeweled bracelets and armlets, and her fingers are graced with shimmering ornaments.
She is the mirror, having become a mirror for all; she is the destroyer of the pride of the wicked.
She has a neck like a conch shell, wears ornaments of conch shells, and is resplendent with a jeweled necklace.
She wears earrings, is adorned with golden kundalas,
decorated with a crest-jewel, has flowers upon her forehead, and is beautified by a pearl in her nose.
The Goddess resides upon the jeweled ground, she sports on Mount Raivata;
she is Vṛndā in Vṛndāvana, dwelling in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
She is the honey of the creepers of Vṛndāvana, the ornament of the Vṛndā forest;
she is the wave of beauty, Lakṣmī, who dwells at the sacred ford of Mathurā. 31.
The great river of the vast forest is the dwelling place of the rested, desirable, and beautiful; it resides in Gokula and is rich with the splendor of the grounds for amorous play.
She is bowed to, she is uplifted, she is nourishing, and she is the speech honored by Bharata;
she has her course in the king of holy places, she is the lineage, and she is the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Dividing the seven oceans, restless, and forcefully traversing the seven continents,
she rolled over the mountains, splitting them, quivering, and exceedingly swift.
She is golden, the golden ground, and she is cultivated by the golden ground;
she is the vision of the world, the play of the world, and she is worshipped by the mountain that illuminates the world.
She who has emerged from the mountain, she who has gone to heaven, she who is praised in heaven, she who is worshipped in heaven;
she who belongs to Vṛndāvana, she who is the presiding deity of the forest, she who is protection, she who is the inner chamber, and she who is the slope and the path.
Kacchā resides within the cauldron of the sword; Ādijā has surged forth according to her own will; Rathaprasthā dwells in the mountain caverns; and Prasthā is exceedingly peaceful yet afflicted.
She is like a spray of water droplets, she is the female frog who bears the male frog;
she is the goad for sin, the lioness of sin, and the axe for the tree of sin.
She is a mass of merit, of meritorious fame, the giver of merit, and the increaser of merit;
she is the preeminent river of the Madhu forest, incomparable, and situated in the Tāla grove. (39)
The river Kubjā is a grove of night-lotuses that increases both lilies and lotuses;
she is the form of a raft, she is impetuous, and she carries lions, serpents, and other creatures.
Bahulī, Bahudā, Bahvī, Bahulā, she who is saluted by the forest, she who is worshipped by the artistic Radhakuṇḍa, and she who rests upon the waters of Kṛṣṇakuṇḍa. || 41 ||
Ghaṇṭā resides in Lalitākuṇḍa, adorned by Viśākhākuṇḍa;
she dwells in Govindakuṇḍa and flows through Gopakuṇḍa.
Śrīgaṅgā, Mānasīgaṅgā, Kusumāmbaramāvinī, Govardhinī, Godhanāḍhyā, Mayūrī, and Varavarṇinī. || 43 ||

She has the luster of a crane and a blue-throated peacock; she is like a young female cuckoo warbling; she is the mother of the king of mountains; she possesses abundant royal umbrellas and is herself the bearer of the parasol.

She is marked by Govardhana, she is Godantī, the treasure-trove of divine herbs, and the path; she is Pāradī, composed of mercury (pārada), she is Nāradī, and she is the autumnal abundance (śāradī-bhṛti).
She who rests upon the lap of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet, who is adorned by the forest of desire, who is the forest of desire, who is Nandinī, and who is the mountain of Nandagrāma. 46.
Possessing the splendor of a vast summit, she is celebrated as being accompanied by Nandīśvara;
she is like the soft warbling of a cuckoo and is skilled in the arts of Bhāṇḍīra and Kuśa.
Lohārgalapradā, Kārā, and she who is clothed in garments from Kaśmīra;
Barhiṣadī, Śoṇapurī, and she who is preeminent among the cities of Śūrakṣetra. 48.
Richly adorned with various ornaments, endowed with diverse colors,
abounding in various women and lotuses, the arenas were like trees of delight.
She possesses rays of light reaching various worlds, she is endowed with various waters;
she is a jewel among women, an abode of jewels, and one who delights in the jewel of womankind.
She is the colored one, rich in the stage of performance, the colors themselves, and the trees of the theater;
she is the royal science, the royal secret, the world-renowned fame, and the cloudless rain-cloud.
With swaying bells and a dark-limbed body, she was born from the dark-bodied one;
she possessed the luster of a blue lotus and captivated with the beauty of a blue lotus.
She possesses blue splendor, is rich with blue lotuses, and dwells within the blue water-lily;
she is the betel vine, the city of the serpents, and is worshipped with the leaves of the betel vine.
Her discourse is adorned with betel, enchanting like nectar;
she is like a lioness possessing a mane, graced by her mass of hair. (54)
She has the luster of collyrium, is smeared with collyrium, and is adorned with kohl;
her feet are red with lac-dye, she is copper-hued, and her saliva has turned her garments copper-colored. || 55 ||
Her speech was adorned with vermilion, her beauty was graced by sandalwood paste;
she wore garments of fragrant wood-paste and was clothed in the fine raiment of jaṭāmāṃsī.
Her mass of hair, adorned with the fragrance of agaru and guru, scented by the breeze carrying the scent of tagara, and beautiful with fragrant oil, was like a swarm of bees. 57.
Śakuntalā is free from the dust of worldly passion and devoted to her husband;
she is Sūryaprabhā, the daughter of the Sun, born from the very body of the Sun.
Resembling ten million suns, born of the Sun, the delight of the Sun;
she is Saṃjñā, the daughter of Saṃjñā, autonomous will, and the bestower of joy upon Saṃjñā.

She is the daughter of Saṃjñā, she is the shimmering shadow, she is Tapatī who causes heat; she is the altar through the experience of Sāvarṇi, she is the submarine fire, and she is the bestower of happiness.
She is the younger sister of Śanaiścara, the Kīlā who increases the lunar dynasty,
the bride of the lunar dynasty, Candrā, and the companion of Candrāvalī.
Candrāvatī, Candralekhā, Candrakāntānugāṃśukā, Bhairavī, Piṅgalāśaṅkī, Līlāvatī, and Āgarīmayī. (62)
Dhanaśrī, Devagāndhārī, Svarmaṇi, Guṇavardhinī, Vrajamallā, Bandhakārī, Vicitrā, and Jayakāriṇī. || 63 ||
Gāndhārī, Mañjarī, Ṭoḍī, Gurjaryā, Sāvarī, Jayā, Karṇāṭī, Rāgiṇī, Gaurī, Vairāṭī, and Gauravāṭikā. || 64 ||
Catuścandrā, Kalā, Herī, Tailaṅgī, Vijayāvatī, Tālī, Talasvarā, Gānā, and Kriyāmātraprakāśinī. || 65 ||
Vaiśākhī, Cācalā, Cārurmācārī, Ghūghaṭī, Ghaṭā, Vaihāgarī, Soraṭhīśā, Kaidārī, and Jaladhārikā. (66)
Kāmākaraśrī, Kalyāṇī, Gauḍakalyāṇamiśritā, Rājasaṃjīvinī, Helā, Mandārī, and Kāmarūpiṇī. || 67 ||
Sāraṅgī, Mārutī, Hoḍhā, Sāgarī, Kāmavādinī, Vaibhāsī, Maṅgalā, Cāndrī, and Rāsamaṇḍalamaṇḍanā. || 68 ||
She is the wish-fulfilling cow, the vine of desire, the bestower of wishes, and the most desirable one;
she is the site of the Kalpa-tree, the vast one, and the dweller in the palace of nectar.
The fair-browed resident of Goloka, the female gatekeeper holding a staff, the abundance of erotic sentiment, the source of passion, the pure one, and the attendant at the bed. 70.
She is served by her attendants and dear friends; she is the protectress of Śrī Vṛndāvana; she possesses clusters of bowers and groves; and she is adorned with ornaments of guñjā berries.
She who dwells in the forest bower, who stays away from home, who is born on the slopes of Govardhana;
she is Viśākhā, Lalitā, Rāmā, Nīrujā, and Madhumādhavī. (72)
She is both one and many, a fair-complexioned friend in the midst of her companions, high-minded;
she is the personification of the Vedas and the form of the seers—the women of Mithilā and Kośala.
The Pulindakas, who were Sītās at their sacrifices, were residents of Ayodhyā;
they were inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha with Ramā and companions of the Śvetadvīpa.
They dwell in the upper Vaikuṇṭha, resting at the feet of the Divine Unconquered One;
they reside on the mountains of the world of Śrī, are the friends of Śrī, and are born from the ocean. (75)
Celestial and non-celestial, with celestial limbs, pervaded by the functions of the three qualities;
they are the protectors of the earth, divine women, creepers, medicinal herbs, and shrubs.
The women of Jālandhara, the daughters of Sindhu, those born of Pṛthu and Barhiṣmatī, the celestial Apsarases, the Sautalas, and the daughters of the Nāgas; || 77 ||
The supreme abode, the supreme Brahman, the primordial nature (prakṛti) of the Puruṣa;
she is described as both transcendent and immanent, consisting of both qualities and the absence of qualities, and composed of the gunas themselves.
The mass of consciousness, the garland of existence and non-existence, the vision, the visible, and the source of qualities;
the principle of Mahat, ego, mind, intellect, and pure awareness. (79)
The activity of the mind is her inner self; she is the fourth [state], consisting of four syllables, possessing four manifestations (vyūhas), and having four forms: ether, air, fire, and water.
Earth, sound, taste, smell, touch, and form in its many varieties;
the organ of action, that which consists of action, knowledge, and the organ of knowledge—these are the two-fold [categories]. (81)
The internal self is established in three ways: as the elemental, the personal, and the divine;
she is the power of knowledge, the power of action, and the supreme deity of all deities.
She is the embodiment of the assembly of truths, the form of liberation, the power of concentration, and that which consists of concentration;
she is the sacred revelation, the traditional law, the personification of the Vedas, the Saṃhitā, and the Garga-saṃhitā.
That very creation is the Pārāśarī, the Pārahaṃsī, and the Vidhātṛkā;
it is the Yājñavalkī, the Bhāgavatī, and is worshipped by the Śrīmadbhāgavata. (84)
Consisting of the Rāmāyaṇa, she is delightful and dear to the Ancient Puruṣa;
she is the ancient embodiment with meritorious limbs, the highly exalted embodiment of the scriptures. (85)
Manīṣā, dhiṣaṇā, buddhi, vāṇī, dhī, śemuṣī, mati; Gāyatrī, Vedasāvitrī, Brahmāṇī, and she who possesses the characteristics of Brahman. || 86 ||
Durgā, Aparṇā, Satī, Satyā, Pārvatī, Caṇḍikā, Ambikā, Āryā, Dākṣāyaṇī, Dākṣī, and the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. || 87 ||
Pulomajā, Śacī, Indrāṇī, Devī, the one bestowed by the best of gods, the supporter by means of Vāyu, the blessed one, Vāyavī, and she who moves with the speed of Vāyu. 88.
Yamānujā, Saṃyamanī, Saṃjñā, Chāyā, Sphuraddyuti, Ratnadevī, Ratnavṛndā, Tārā, and Taraṇimaṇḍalā. || 89 ||
Ruci, Śānti, Kṣamā, Śobhā, Dayā, Dakṣā, Dyuti, Trapā, Talatuṣṭi, Vibhā, Puṣṭi, Santuṣṭi, and Puṣṭabhāvanā. || 90 ||
The lady has four arms, beautiful eyes, or two or eight arms;
she holds a conch, a lotus, a discus, and a mace in her hands.
She carries a quiver, holds a shield and sword in her hands, and wields a bow;
she is the twanger of the bowstring, a warrior, and the destroyer of the fierce Daityas.
Seated upon a chariot, mounted on Garuḍa, and dwelling within the heart of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
she holds a flute, wears the attire of Kṛṣṇa, is adorned with garlands, and wears a forest-wreath.
Wearing a diadem, she moves with a very slow gait upon her vehicle;
she resembles ten million moons, slender, and possessed of a delicate form. (94)
Bhaiṣmī, the daughter of Bhīṣma; the formidable Rukmiṇī, whose form is golden; Satyabhāmā, Jāmbavatī, Satyā, Bhadrā, and Sudakṣiṇā. || 95 ||
Mitravindā, Sakhīvṛndā, she who rises above the banner of the Vṛndā forest;
she who creates erotic passion, Śṛṅgārā, the source of the horn, the giver of the horn, and she who moves through the sky.
Forbearance, vision, memory, rivalry, longing, faith, self-contentment, lordship, thirst, division, affection, violence, begging, fatigue, and agriculture; || 97 ||
She is hope, sleep, the sleep of yoga, the Yoginī, the bestower of yoga, and the one beyond the ages;
she is the culmination, the foundation, tranquility, and the supreme nature of pure being.

One of a *tamas* nature is difficult to endure; one of a *rajas* nature is prone to bowing down; while the *sattvic* disposition consists of action, inaction, performance of deeds, and freedom from exhaustion—this is the spiritual state of the bull-like man. 99.
She is the crest-jewel of service, the prosperity born from the invocation of Piṅgalā;
she is the speech of the Nāgas, adorned by the Nāgas, the lady of the city, the city itself, and the mountain.
The boat of the state of existence (bhavanau) should be conceived as a vessel that serves as a bridge across the ocean of worldly existence;
it may be made of mind, wood, or sand. || 101 ||

It may be written, it may be molded, made of jewels, or fashioned from refined gold; it may be made of stone, produced from a mountain, or of clay; it may have the luster of spray, and it may be mobile or immobile. (102)
The brush is unfixed yet well-established; the method is both medical and tantric.
She is the twilight, clothed in the clouds of twilight, the junction of the Vedas, and composed of nectar. (103)
The evening crest-lock (śikhā) is to be pierced; it is subtle, having the form of a spark of life, become one with the Self, meditated upon as minute, humble, and like the pericarp of a lotus.
The Nīrājanī is the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), the Kaṃdalī that accomplishes all tasks;
it is vast worship and installation, purifying and pertaining to the world beyond. || 105 ||
She is the pure oyster shell, the pearl-like cognition, and the Supreme Goddess;
she is the stainless Uṣṇih meter, the Virāj, the Veṇī river, the flute, and she who resounds through the flute. || 106 ||
She who causes one to revolve, the giver of livelihood, the news, the means of subsistence, and she who dwells in celestial chariots;
she who is rich in aesthetic delight, the one who possesses abundance, the aesthetic delight itself, and she who moves within the circle of the rāsa dance.
The sovereign of the cowherds and cowherdesses, the cowherdess herself, she who is praised by cowherds and cowherdesses;
she who wanders among the cattle, the river of the cowherds, and the bestower of bliss upon the cowherds. || 108 ||
It is beneficial for cattle, frequented by cowherds, surrounded by millions of herds of cows, followed by cowherds, abounding in cows, and bearing the footprints of Govinda. 109.

Rādhā, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, who brings Śrī Kṛṣṇa under her control, is dearer to Kṛṣṇa than his own life; she is eternally full of aesthetic relish (rasika) and the sovereign of all who possess such relish. 110.
The Avaṭodā, Tāmraparṇī, Kṛtamālā, Vihāyasī, Kṛṣṇā, Veṇī, Bhīmarathī, Tāpī, Revā, and Mahāpagā; || 111 ||
The Vaiyāsakī, the Kāverī, the Tuṅgabhadrā, the Sarasvatī, the Candrabhāgā, the Vetravatī, the Ṛṣikulyā, and the Kakudminī. (112)
Gautamī, Kauśikī, Sindhu, Bāṇagaṅgā—the bestower of great perfection;
Godāvarī, Ratnamālā, Gaṅgā, Mandākinī, and Balā. (113)
The Svarṇadī, Jāhnavī, Velā, Vaiṣṇavī, Maṅgalālayā,
Bālā, Viṣṇupadī, and Sindhusāgarasaṃgatā are thus described.
The river Sāmudrī, rich with the splendor of the Ganges and the ocean, is a stream that bestows jewels;
she is the Bhāgīrathī, the celestial river, the very earth fallen from the foot of Lord Vāmana.
Lakṣmī, Ramā, the delightful one, Bhārgavī, the beloved of Viṣṇu; Sītā, Arcirjā, Janakī, Mātā, the stainless one, and Kalā. 116.
Born from the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, she flows through all three paths;
she is Dharā, Viśvaṃbharā, Anantā, Bhūmi, Dhātrī, and is composed of forbearance (Kṣamā). || 117 ||
The earth is firm, the bearer, the vast expanse, resting upon the hoods of Śeṣa;
Ayodhyā is the city of Rāghava, and Kauśikī is born of the Raghu lineage. 118.
Mathurā, Māthurī, Paṃthā, Yādavī, Dhruvapūjitā, Mayā, Āyurbilva, Nīlodā, and the Gaṅgā that has issued forth from Gaṅgādvāra. || 119 ||
Kāśī, the city of Śiva, is composed of Kuśāvarta, it is eternal, situated in the center of the Dhruva-maṇḍala, and is the supreme, auspicious Vārāṇasī. 120.
The city of the gods, Avanti, has been conquered by the radiant Ujjayinī;
likewise Dvārāvatī, which was once desirous of being Dvārakā, and Kuśasthalī, which had become Kuśabhūtā. || 121 ||
Mahāpurī is situated in Saptapurī at the site of Nandigrāma;
Śālagrāmaśilādityā is located in the midst of Śambhalagrāma.
Vaṃśagopālinī was cast down and came to dwell in Hari’s abode;
Barhiṣmatī became Hastināpura, and she who resided in Śakraprastha [became] Indraprastha. 123.
Dāḍimī, Saiṃdhavī, Jambū, Pauṣkarī, Puṣkaraprasū, Utpalāvartagamanā, Naimiṣī, and Naimiṣāvṛtā. || 124 ||
The land of Kurujāṅgala is Kālī; the region of Arbuda is known as Haimavatī by the wise; and the field of Śūkara is Śvetavārāhadhāritā. || 125 ||
She embodies all sacred fords, she is the ford among fords, and she is the one who makes even fords holy;
she is the remover of all defects and the bestower of all prosperity.
She is the direct increaser of splendors, the destroyer of the latent impressions of the womb,
the mistress of the wealth of the realm of Goloka, and her own blossom within the forest groves.
She is the most excellent of all, the embodiment of all merit, the chain of all beauty;
she stands above all sacred fords and is the presiding deity of all sacred fords.
Śrīdā, Śrīśā, Śrīnivāsā, Śrīnidhi, Śrīvibhāvanā, Svakṣā, Svaṅgā, Śatānandā, Nandā, and Jyotirgaṇeśvarī. (129)
This supreme thousand names of Kālindī bestows fame and fulfills desires;
it is meritorious, a destroyer of great sins, and the most excellent increaser of longevity. (130)
If one recites it once at night, there shall be no fear of thieves;
if one recites it twice on a road, there shall be no fear of bandits anywhere.
Starting from the second [verse], the twice-born should recite until the end,
having meditated with devotion ten times upon the Goddess born of the Yamunā.
The sick shall be freed from disease, the bound shall be released from bondage;
the pregnant woman shall give birth to a son, and the seeker of knowledge shall become a scholar. (133)
Delusion, paralyzing, constant subjugation, as well as eradication, destruction, withering, and likewise kindling. (134)
Whether it be enchanting, scorching, or even the discovery of hidden treasure—whatever a person desires in their heart, that very thing they obtain. (135)
Upon hearing this, may the Brāhmaṇa become endowed with spiritual luster, the Kṣatriya become the lord of the world, the Vaiśya become the master of treasures, and the Śūdra become stainless.
But he who always recites this at the time of worship with a spirit of devotion is not stained by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. (137)
One should recite it daily a hundred times for a period of one year;
having prepared the chapter (paṭala), the manual (paddhati), the hymn (stava), and likewise the armor (kavaca).
One shall obtain sovereignty over the earth with its seven continents; of this there is no doubt. || 139 ||
He who recites this without motive, yet endowed with devotion to Yamunā, being virtuous, shall attain the three aims of life and become liberated while living in this world. (140)
Charming with the playful grace of its groves, captivating, and filled with clusters of creepers on the banks of the Yamunā,
Vṛndāvana resounds with the humming of intoxicated bees.
He who reads this [work] shall go to that Goloka. || 141 ||

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Thousand Names of Śrī Yamunā," within the dialogue between Śrī Saubhari and Māndhātṛ, which occurs in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva, in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. || 19 ||
Hari Om Tat Sat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Nārada said: Having heard this hymn of praise to Kṛṣṇa, the heroic Māndhātā, the best of kings,
bowed to the sage Śrī Saubhari and departed for Ayodhyā.
This auspicious account of the cowherd girls, which removes great sins and is meritorious, has been narrated by me to you. What more do you wish to hear? || 2 ||
Bahulāśva said:
O Brahmin, I have heard from your mouth the supreme description of the cowherd girls and the five-limbed [stotra] of the Yamunā, which destroys great sins. (3)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Balarāma, the Lord who is the manifest sovereign of Goloka,
first performed his charming pastimes within the circle of Vraja.
Śrī Nārada said: Once, while tending his own cows along with the cowherd boys and his companions on the banks of the Yamunā at Bhāṇḍīra, he engaged in childhood pastimes.
While having a monastery built by the fools, Kṛṣṇa sported in the forest, displaying his charming cowherd-girls, who were characterized as both the carriers and the carried.
Having arrived there in the form of a cowherd, Pralamba, sent by Kaṃsa, was not recognized by the boys; yet he was known by Hari.
No one agreed to take Vijaya Rāma to the monastery;
instead, that Pralamba carried him from Bhāṇḍīra to the bank of the Yamunā.
Descending from there, the Daitya prepared to go to Mathurā;
he assumed a form like a dense cloud, as difficult to traverse as the king of mountains.
Balarāma shone upon the back of the Daitya, handsome with his swinging earrings,
like the full moon in the sky accompanied by lightning and clouds.
Beholding the terrifying Daitya, the exceedingly powerful Baladeva struck him on the head with his fist in rage, as Indra strikes a mountain with his thunderbolt.
With his head shattered like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt, the Daitya suddenly fell to the earth, shaking the surface of the ground.
That light, having emerged, became absorbed in Bala;
at that very moment, the gods showered flowers born of the Nandana grove.
O Lord of Kings, there arose a cry of "Victory! Victory! in heaven and on earth.
Thus, O King, I have related to you this most wonderful account of Śrī Baladeva; what more do you wish to hear?
Bahulāśva said:
Who was this Daitya named Pralamba in former times, who was so intoxicated with pride in battle?
O Sage, how did he attain liberation by the hand of Baladeva? (15)
Śrī Nārada said: Indeed,
for the purpose of worshipping Śiva, the king of the Yakṣas had the protection of the flowers ensured by Yakṣas here and there within his auspicious grove.
They seized even those radiant flowers from him;
thereupon, the powerful Dhanada, the king of the Yakṣas, became enraged and pronounced a curse.
Those gods and other humans who seize his flowers shall all suddenly become asuras on earth due to my curse. (18)
Then Vijaya, the son of Hūhū, wandering through sacred pilgrimage sites,
reached Caitraratha forest while singing the virtues of Viṣṇu along the way.
Indeed, the Gandharva Vīṇāpāṇi, unaware that he was holding flowers,
became an Asura after abandoning his status as a Gandharva.
At that very moment, he sought refuge with the high-souled Kubera;
having bowed down, he slowly made his request with palms joined in reverence.
O Indra among kings, Kubera too, being pleased with him, granted him a boon:
"You are a devotee of Viṣṇu and one whose soul is tranquil; do not grieve, O giver of honor! (22)
And at the end of the Dvāpara age, your liberation will take place at the hands of Baladeva on the banks of the Yamunā at Bhāṇḍīra; of this there is no doubt.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, that Gandharva Hūhū became the great Asura Pralamba;
yet, by the boon of Kubera, he attained supreme liberation.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Pralamba," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the Śrīgargasaṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 20 ||
Hari Oṃ! May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is Tat-Sat.
Śrī Nārada said: Now, while the cowherds and Balarāma were engaged in their play,
all the cows entered the great forest out of greed for grass.
To bring them back, the cowherd boys reached the distant Muñja forest;
there, a great forest fire arose, equal to the fire of universal destruction.
Those cowherds, gathered together with their cattle and afflicted by fear, cried out "Save us! Save us! and sought refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Hari, who was accompanied by Balarāma. || 3 ||
Seeing the danger from fire for his own people, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the lords of yoga,
closed [their] eyes and said, "Do not be afraid."
O King, while the cowherds remained in that state, the Blessed Lord drank up that terrifying fire even as the gods looked on.
Having thus drunk the great fire and led the cowherds and the herd of cows,
Hari arrived at the auspicious Aśoka grove on the bank of the Yamunā.
There, the cowherds, afflicted by hunger, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Hari along with Balarāma: "O Lord, we are distressed by hunger."
Then Hari sent them to the sacrifice of Aṅgiras;
having gone there, they bowed to that excellent sacrifice and spoke these pure words: ||| 8 ||
The cowherds said:
"Accompanied by the cowherd boys and Balarāma, the joy of the King of Vraja has arrived while tending the cows."
O gods on earth, grant food and sustenance to him and his retinue, who is afflicted by hunger, for he is not subject to delusion.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, having heard those words, all the twice-born remained silent;
but the cowherds, having returned despondent, spoke thus to Hari along with Balarāma.
The cowherds said: You are the sovereign lord of this circle of Vraja, the powerful one in Śrīgokula, the foremost leader who holds the staff before Nanda’s city.
The fierce heat of your sun-like splendor does not prevail in the city of Madhu; it shines only upon the impurity of the rod of punishment.
Śrī Nārada said:
Hari himself sent them back again to his wives;
having returned once more to the sacrificial enclosure, they then bowed down to the beloved wives of the brahmins.
With their palms joined in reverence, the cowherds, impelled by Kṛṣṇa, spoke.
The cowherds said:
"Accompanied by his cowherd companions, the son of the illustrious King of Vraja has arrived, tending the cows."
"O Aṅganā, who deludes even Ananga, give food and nourishment to him and his retinue, for they are overcome by hunger. (13)
Śrī Nārada said: Hearing that Kṛṣṇa had arrived, all the wives of the twice-born, longing for a sight of Kṛṣṇa, prepared food in vessels and brought it forth.
Immediately casting aside all worldly shame, they approached the side of Kṛṣṇa in a beautiful and charming forest of Aśoka trees on the bank of the Kṛṣṇā. 15.
Just as it was heard, so was the wonderful form of Śrī Hari seen;
having attained bliss, they all reached the fourth state (turiya), just like yogis.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O twice-born ladies, you are blessed who have come for the sake of seeing Me. O goddesses of the earth, return quickly to your homes without any fear."
But by your power, your husbands, the twice-born, shall immediately obtain the fruit of sacrifice and become stainless along with you. (18)
They shall go to the supreme abode, Goloka, which is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
Then, having bowed to Hari, they all returned to the sacrificial arena.
Śrī Nārada said:
Seeing them, all the brāhmaṇas reproached themselves, saying, "Fie upon us!
Desiring to see Śrī Kṛṣṇa, we did not come because we were afraid of Kaṃsa. (20)
O King of Mithilā, having eaten his food and being full of strength, Kṛṣṇa returned with the cowherds to the enchanting Vṛndāvana forest while tending the cows.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Liberation from the Forest Fire and the Sight of the Brahmin’s Wife," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the Śrīgargasaṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 21 ||
Hari Oṃ! May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, that which is Truth (Sat).
Śrī Nārada said: Once, having observed the vow of Ekādaśī,
King Nanda entered the waters of the Yamunā with the cowherds on the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) to bathe.
Having seized him, the servant of Pāśi went to the world of Pāśi,
O Lord of Mithilā, while a great clamor arose among the cowherds.
Having consoled them all, the Blessed One departed for the city of Varuṇa;
Hari himself suddenly reduced the fortress of that city to ashes.
Seeing Hari enraged and resembling ten million suns, Varuṇa, having bowed with palms joined in reverence and circumambulated him, spoke while being overwhelmed [by his power]. || 4 ||
Varuṇa said:
Salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, the most perfect Supreme Being;
salutations to the Lord of Goloka, who sustains countless universes.

Salutations to you, the Great One consisting of the fourfold manifestation; salutations to you, the embodiment of all splendor. Salutations to you, the essence of all existence; salutations to the Supreme Brahman.
Some fool among my followers has committed a great offense against me this very day;
therefore, O Lord, please forgive me who have come to you for refuge.
O Supreme Lord, O Infinite One, protect me, protect me! || 7 ||
Śrī Nārada said: Thus, the blessed Lord, having made Nanda live a truly fulfilled life and manifesting happiness upon his kinsmen, returned to the region of Vraja.
Having heard from the mouth of King Nanda that power of Śrī Hari,
the hosts of gopīs and gopas spoke to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the son of Nanda.
O Lord, if you, the Blessed One, have been truly well-honored by the world-protectors,
then, O Master, quickly show us the supreme realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
Then, having led them all to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, Kṛṣṇa revealed his own form situated in the midst of a circle of light.
Endowed with a thousand arms, blazing with a crown and bracelets, and resplendent with a conch, discus, mace, lotus, and a forest garland; || 12 ||
Resembling countless millions of suns, seated upon Śeṣa,
possessing a divine luster from the waving of chowries, and attended by Brahmā and the other gods.
At that very moment, those attendants bearing maces made the groups of cowherds stand upright, maintained their posture with reverence, and placed them at a distance with great care.
Seeing them as if startled, the attendants spoke with their voices: "Ho there!
Be silent, forest-dwellers; nothing more should be said! (15)
"Do not speak; have you not seen the assembly of Hari?
Even while the Lord himself, the Supreme Master, is present here, the Vedas themselves are speaking. (16)
Having received this instruction, the cowherds were delighted and maintained silence;
yet in their minds they said, "This Kṛṣṇa is seated upon a lofty throne. (17)
Having cast us far below, he never speaks with us;
therefore, there is no world better than Vraja, and none that bestows such happiness.
"Where there might indeed be mutual news even with his own brother"—
saying this to them, O King, the Blessed Lord Hari, the most perfect Master, led them away and returned to Vraja.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Vision of Vaikuṇṭha by Nanda and Others," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the Śrī Garga Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 22 ||
Hari Oṃ. May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is Tat-Sat.
Śrī Nārada said: O King, once the cowherds, headed by Vṛṣabhānu and Upananda, arrived at Ambikāvana with carts filled with jewels.
Having worshipped Bhadrakālī and Paśupati according to the prescribed rites,
they gave gifts to the twice-born and slept there on the riverbank.
There, one snake emerged at night and seized Nanda by the foot;
overwhelmed by extreme fear, Nanda cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! (3).
O King, the cowherd boys then prodded the python with firebrands,
yet that serpent did not relinquish its position, just as one does not give up one's own jewel.
The Blessed One, the purifier of the world, struck the serpent with his foot;
immediately abandoning its serpentine form and becoming a perfected Vidyādhara, he bowed to Kṛṣṇa, circumambulated him, and spoke with palms joined in reverence. || 5 ||
Sudarśana said: "O Lord, I am a preeminent Vidyādhara named Sudarśana;
having seen the sage Aṣṭāvakra, I, who possess great strength, laughed."
"He also gave me a curse, saying, 'O evil-minded one, become a serpent!
By your grace, O Mādhava, I am now liberated from that curse."
By the touch of the particles of pollen from the nectar of your lotus feet, I have suddenly attained the divine state;
salutations to that Blessed One, the Lord of the World.
He who is the incarnation of the Earth for the purpose of removing its heavy burden. || 8 ||
Śrī Nārada said: O King, having thus bowed down to Hari-Kṛṣṇa, that Vidyādhara went indeed to the world of Viṣṇu, which is free from all calamities.
Nanda and all the others, filled with wonder upon realizing that Kṛṣṇa was the Supreme Lord,
quickly departed from Ambikāvana and returned to the district of Vraja.
This auspicious account of the deeds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa has been narrated by me to you;
it is meritorious and removes all sins. What more do you wish to hear?
Bahulāśva said:
"Oh, how most wonderful is the life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra! Having heard it, my mind remains unsatiated and desires to hear it yet again. (12)
O best of divine sages, tell me what supreme pastimes did Hari, the Lord of Vraja, perform effortlessly in the circle of Vraja? 13.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Narrative of Sudarśana," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the Śrīgargasaṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 23 ||
Hari Om. May this be offered to the True Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Tat Sat.
Śrī Nārada said:
Once, in the mountain regions, the Blessed Lord Hari, accompanied by his companions,
engaged in the game of hide-and-seek, characterized by the roles of thief and herdsman.
There, the Daitya Vyomāsura repeatedly seized many boys who had turned into rams,
carried them away, and cast them into a mountain cave again and again.
The mighty son of Maya blocked the door with a stone;
and knowing him to be a thief of truth, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana [acted].
Having seized him with both arms, he threw him down upon the circle of the earth.
Then, O King, when the Daitya had met his death, that radiant light emerged and,
wandering through the ten directions, became absorbed into Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then, indeed, a cry of "Victory! Victory! arose in heaven and on earth;
the gods, filled with supreme bliss, rained down flowers.
Bahulāśva said:
Who was this one named Vyoma who formerly performed meritorious deeds? Tell me that, by whom he became merged into Kṛṣṇa, who is dark as a rain-cloud, like a flash of lightning. (7)
Śrī Nārada said: In Kāśī there was a king named Bhīmaratha, who was devoted to charity,
a performer of sacrifices, a bestower of honors, an archer, and entirely dedicated to devotion for Viṣṇu.
Having installed his son in the kingdom, he went to the Malaya mountain;
there he began a penance for exactly one hundred thousand years.
Pulastya arrived at his hermitage accompanied by a multitude of disciples;
seeing him, the proud royal sage neither rose nor bowed.
Pulastya also pronounced a curse: "Become a Daitya, O great villain!
Then he fell at his feet, having come for refuge.
The tiger among sages, Pulastya, who is compassionate toward the distressed, said: "At the end of the Dvāpara age, in the holy region of Mathurā within the sacred circle of Vraja..."
By the power of the arms of Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the Lord of the Yadu dynasty, the liberation desired by yogis will be attained; of this there is no doubt. (13)
Śrī Nārada said:
This very King Bhīmaratha was the son of the Daitya Maya;
through the force of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s arms, he, the king of Videha, attained liberation.
Once, while the cowherd boys were there, the exceedingly powerful demon Ariṣṭa arrived,
making the sky and the earth resound and tearing up the banks with his horns.
Seeing him, the cowherd women, the cowherds, and the herds of cows fled in fear;
the Lord, the slayer of demons, granted them freedom from fear, saying, "Do not be afraid."
Taking him by the horns, Mādhava pushed him away;
he, in turn, pushed Śrī Kṛṣṇa for two yojanas.
Seizing him by the tail, Kṛṣṇa whirled him around with the strength of his arms and dashed him against the surface of the earth, as a child might throw a water-pot.
Then Ariṣṭa, rising up again with eyes bloodshot with rage,
that great villain uprooted Mount Rohita with his horns.
Roaring like a cloud, the hero hurled [the mountain] upon Kṛṣṇa;
Kṛṣṇa, seizing a rock, hurled it back upon him.
His mind somewhat agitated by the blow from the mountain, he struck the earth with the tips of his horns; water then issued forth from them onto the ground.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, seizing him by the horns and whirling him around repeatedly,
dashed him against the surface of the earth like a lotus uprooted by the wind.
At that very moment, having abandoned his bull-form and assumed the body of a brahmin,
he bowed at the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and spoke with a voice choked with emotion.
The twice-born said: "I am Varatantu, the best of the twice-born and a disciple of Bṛhaspati;
I went to Bṛhaspati’s presence in order to study."
Placing my feet [upon him], I stood before him as he looked on;
then, in anger, that sage said, "You stand before me like a bull."
"O evil-minded one, because you have committed an offense against your guru, become a bull!
Due to his curse, O Mādhava, I became a bull in the lands of Vaṅga.
Through association with the Asuras, I attained the state of an Asura;
by your grace, I am now liberated from that curse and from my demonic nature.
Salutations to you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa; salutations to you, Vāsudeva.
Salutations again and again to Govinda, who destroys the afflictions of those who bow before him.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus and bowed to Śrī Hari, the direct disciple of Bṛhaspati,
O King, departed for heaven by means of a celestial chariot, illuminating the world.
This wonderful section on sweetness has been narrated by me to you;
it is meritorious, it removes all sins, and it brings about the supreme attainment of Kṛṣṇa. || 30 ||
For those who constantly recite this *Kāmada*, what more do you wish to hear? || 31 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Asuras Vyoma and Ariṣṭa," in the Mādhuryakhaṇḍa of the Śrīgargasaṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 24 ||
Hari Om. May this be offered to the True Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Nārada said: I bow to Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudeva, the God who crushes Kaṃsa and Cāṇūra, the supreme joy of Devakī, and the Teacher of the World.
Bahulāśva said:
O Sage, what deeds did the Blessed One perform in Mathurā?
How did he slay the one named Kaṃsa? Tell me this in accordance with the truth.
Śrī Nārada said: O lord of kings, once I came to behold the supreme city of Mathurā.
Impelled directly in his mind by Hari, the Supreme, he resolved to undertake the supreme effort to slay the Daityas. || 3 ||

When the lion-throne had been offered by Indra, along with a white parasol and shimmering, beautiful chowries, I spoke thus to King Kaṃsa—who was difficult even for the gods to endure—as he sat there, having been honored by him: "Listen to that."
The daughter born of Yaśodā, who ascended to heaven from your hand, has been born as Kṛṣṇa in Devakī; and Balarāma, the delight of Rohiṇī, has been born [there].
Out of fear of you both, O King of Daityas, Vasudeva has placed his two sons, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, with his own friend, King Nanda, who is your enemy.
Indeed, those Daityas beginning with Pūtanā and ending with Ariṣṭa, who were arrogant due to your strength, were slain by you two in the forest region; they are truly known as Death itself.
Thus addressed, the lord of the Bhojas, his body trembling with rage,
seized a sharpened sword on the floor of the assembly hall to slay Śauri.
Having been restrained by me, he too was bound with broad and firm shackles;
having thus bound him along with his wife, he confined them in a prison.
Having spoken thus to him as I departed, the king of the Daityas dispatched Keśin,
the foremost of the Daityas, for the purpose of slaying Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
Having summoned Cāṇūra and the others, as well as the elephant-keeper and those people capable of bearing the burden of the task, the powerful King of the Bhojas spoke this.
Kaṃsa said: "O Kūṭa, O Tośalaka, O mighty Cāṇūra!
Nārada has indeed shown me that Rāma and Kṛṣṇa are my death."
"When you two have arrived here, they should be slain with the ease of wrestlers;
and quickly prepare the wrestling arena, making it auspicious. (13)
"O Mahāmātra, having stationed the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa— intoxicated with rut— at the entrance of the arena, my two enemies are to be slain by him."
On the fourteenth day, however, the Dhanuryāga should be performed for the sake of pacification;
on the new moon day, there shall be a wrestling match here among the people.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus to his own kinsmen, Kaṃsa quickly summoned Akrūra and,
O Indra among kings, spoke in private a counsel that was pleasing to his ministers.
Kaṃsa said:
"O master of charity, O counselor, listen to my supreme words!
Go to Nanda’s cowherd settlement at dawn and perform your task, O high-minded one! (17)
"Those two sons of Vasudeva are indeed my enemies;
they were pointed out to me very clearly even by Nārada, the celestial seer. (18)
"Bring them to Mathurā without delay by means of a chariot, under the pretext of seeing the city, together with the groups of cowherds led by King Nanda and accompanied by gifts."
"Or with an elephant, or with great wrestlers, I shall have those two children killed; after that, I will kill King Nanda along with Vasudeva as his helper."
"Afterwards, I shall slay Vṛṣabhānu, the best of men, then Navananda and Upananda, and thereafter Śauri and his ally Devaka."
And after that, I shall kill my aged father Ugrasena, who is eager for the kingdom, and all the Yādavas thereafter; of this there is no doubt.
O minister, all these hosts of gods have been born upon the surface of the earth;
Śakuni, the lord of Candrāvatī, is my great friend and powerful ally.
Bhūtasaṃtāpana, Hṛṣṭa, Vṛka, and Śambara;
likewise Kālanābha, Mahānābha, and Hariśmaśru. (24)
"These are my friends who have forcibly given up their lives for my sake;
even my father-in-law Jarāsandha is remembered as my friend, as is Dvivida. (25)
And Bāṇāsura and Naraka have likewise formed a friendship with me alone;
these two, having conquered the entire earth and bound the gods along with Indra, [rule over it]. (26)
Having cast Kuberu, the lord of wealth, into the inaccessible cave of Mount Meru, they will undoubtedly always exercise sovereignty over the three worlds. || 27 ||
On this earth, you are like a poet among poets and like Bṛhaspati in speech;
O Lord of Generosity, this task must be performed by you with haste.
Akrūra said:
O Lord of the Yadus, this great ocean of desires has been created by you;
yet by the will of fate, that very ocean becomes a mere cow’s footprint in your absence. (29)
Kaṃsa said:
The powerful man acts by casting aside destiny, while the weak indeed relies upon destiny.
Let the practitioner of action remain undisturbed by the power of Time and the Self, both of which are eternally moving.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus to the chief minister, Kaṃsa rose from the assembly hall and, somewhat provoked, slowly departed for the inner apartments.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Counsel of Kaṃsa," in the Śrī Garga Saṃhitā, within the Mathurā-khaṇḍa, in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 1 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Then the great demon Keśī, in the form of a horse, intoxicated with pride,
arrived at the beautiful Vṛndāvana and roared like a thundercloud, being full of strength.
By the trampling of his feet, sturdy trees fell;
by the strike of his tail, the clouds in the sky were shattered into pieces.
O Lord of Mithilā, seeing him of unbearable speed, the hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses were greatly overcome with fear and went to Śrī Kṛṣṇa for refuge.
Having granted fearlessness by saying, "Do not fear," the Blessed One, the destroyer of afflictions,
tied his yellow garment around his waist and proceeded to slay the Daitya.
O King, the great asura, shaking the earth and making the vault of the sky resound, struck Hari with his two hind legs.
Seizing the Daitya by the feet, Kṛṣṇa whirled him about in the sky with his arm and hurled him a yojana away, like a lotus uprooted by the wind.
He too returned, his body filled with rage,
and struck Lord Śrī Hari on the courtyard of Vraja with his tail.
Seizing him by the tail, O King, Kṛṣṇa whirled him about with the strength of his arms and forcefully hurled him a hundred yojanas into the sky.
Having fallen from the sky, that powerful Daitya, his mind somewhat agitated,
rose up again and roared like a thundercloud.
Shaking his mane and repeatedly tossing his tail in the sky,
tearing up the earth with his feet, he sprang forward before Hari.
The Blessed One Madhusūdana indeed struck him with his fist;
by that blow of the fist, he remained unconscious for two ghaṭikās.
Having uprooted Hari from the region of his throat with its head,
the horse leaped from the earth's surface into the sky to a distance of a hundred thousand yojanas.
O King, a terrible battle took place between those two in the sky for two watches,
fought with feet, tusks, manes, tails, and sharp hooves.
Seizing him with both arms and whirling him here and there,
Hari cast him down from the sky as a child might throw a water-pot.
The Blessed Lord Hari thrust his arm into his mouth;
having entered his belly, the arm grew exceedingly like a disease.
Then, having suppressed his vital breaths, the great asura assumed the form of a horse and passed dung; his belly instantly burst apart and he died.
Having immediately emerged from his body, adorned with a crown and earrings,
he prostrated with joined palms before Kṛṣṇa, who possessed a divine form.
Kumuda said: "O Mādhava, I am indeed a follower of Śakra, named Kumuda;
I am radiant, handsome, and heroic, victorious while wielding a whirling umbrella. (18)
Formerly, for the sake of pacifying the sin of killing a Brahmin incurred during the slaying of the demon Vṛtra,
the Lord of Heaven performed the horse sacrifice, the most excellent of rituals.
Desiring to mount that auspicious horse of the Aśvamedha sacrifice— dark-eared and swift as thought— I, being wicked, stole it and went to Tala.
Then, while that great villain was being led away by the hosts of Maruts bound with nooses, the enemy of Bala cursed me: "O evil-minded one, become a Rākṣasa! (21)
"Having taken the form of a horse, I was born upon the earth for two Manvantaras;
today I am liberated from that curse immediately by your touch, O Lord. (22)
O Lord, make me your servant, my mind fixed upon your feet;
salutations to you, the Blessed One, the sole witness of all the worlds. (23)
Śrī Nārada said: Having circumambulated Hari, the Supreme Lord,
he ascended a most radiant and supreme celestial chariot.
O King of Mithilā, Kumuda went swiftly to the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, illuminating the regions of the quarters.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Slaying of Keśin," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 2 ||
Śrī Nārada said: O Lord of Mithilā, having mounted his chariot to perform the king’s business, Akrūra, filled with great joy, set out for Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
Having attained supreme devotion for Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person,
the high-minded one traveled along the road while reflecting thus with his intellect.
Akrūra said:
"What meritorious deed have I performed in Bhārata, or what selfless gift, or even the highest of sacrifices?"
Or rather, let there be auspicious wandering to sacred fords and service to the twice-born,
so that today I may behold Hari, the Supreme Lord.
What great penance was performed by me in the past, or what service to the virtuous was rendered with devotion,
that today I have obtained this vision so difficult to attain?
It will take place before the divine Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Their existence on this earth is indeed fruitful, since the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of the Gods, has come within the range of their vision; for having now obtained that sight which is so difficult to attain—
I shall immediately become one who has achieved his purpose in every respect. || 5 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus reflecting upon Kṛṣṇa and beholding that most auspicious omen,
the son of Gāndinī, seated in his chariot, arrived at Gokula at the time of twilight.
On the earth, he beheld footprints marked with the lotus of Kṛṣṇa’s feet, complete with barley-corns and goads, and covered with pollen imbued with his passion.
Overwhelmed by the joy of the emotion of devotion and the eagerness born from seeing them,
he leaped down from his chariot, rolled upon the ground before them, and shed tears.
O King of Mithilā, for those in whose hearts there is devotion to the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
all the happiness of the world, from Brahmā down to the lowest level, is like a blade of grass.
Then Akrūra, mounted on his chariot, reached Nanda’s city in an instant;
he beheld Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Balarāma, arriving at the cowherd settlements.
The two ancient gods, the supreme persons,
lotus-eyed and of dark and fair complexions,
like a sapphire banner and a diamond mountain.
Rāma and Kṛṣṇa both took refuge on that path. || 11 ||
Seeing them wearing garments as radiant as lightning and possessing the luster of autumnal clouds, with the rising sun upon their crests,
he quickly descended from his own chariot.
Bowing down to them with devotion, he prostrated himself.
Then, seeing his face with eyes clouded by teardrops and his body covered in horripilation, Hari, the Supreme Lord, overcome with compassion,
raised him up with both arms and shed tears.
Mādhava released his devotee after embracing him. || 13 ||
Having thus assembled with his army, Hari immediately brought him forward, offered him an excellent seat,
presented him with a cow, and served him a fine meal as a guest.
Filled with love, he indeed offered it, covered with the juice. || 14 ||
Nanda embraced him with both arms and said: "Aho! How do you live in the kingdom of King Kaṃsa?
How can he, who is shameless and who slaughtered the children of his own sister, be deluded regarding other people?"
When Nanda had returned home, Hari asked him about the welfare of his parents,
as well as that of the Yadus and his kinsmen.
[He perceived] all of Kaṃsa’s perverted understanding. || 16 ||
Akrūra said:
"O Lord, on the day after tomorrow, the King of the Bhojas was prepared to slay Śauri with a sword in hand, but he was dissuaded by Nārada. (17)
All the Yādava kinsmen were distressed and overwhelmed by fear;
along with their families, they departed for other lands on this earth out of fear of Kaṃsa.
This very day, the powerful king of the Daityas has prepared to slay the Yādavas and conquer the gods; what else does he wish to do on this earth?
Therefore, you two must go to perform an imperishable act of merit; for without you two, O lords of the virtuous, no purpose whatsoever would be accomplished.
Śrī Nārada said: Then, having heard his words, the Blessed Lord Hari, accompanied by His army, spoke thus to the cowherds who were to carry out the task, in accordance with the opinion of King Nanda.
The Blessed Lord said:
King Nanda also came with his forces and groups of elderly cowherds;
likewise, the nine Nandas, the Upanandas, and the six Vṛṣabhānus.
Having risen early in the morning, they will all go to Mathurā;
and from there, they will all take dairy products such as curd, milk, ghee, and so forth.
Having gathered them together, they must then be prepared with offerings;
furthermore, quickly make the chariots capable by equipping them along with wagons.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard this, all the cowherds who were performing their duties told everything exactly as it had been spoken to the cowherd women who were listening in every house.
Hearing that, their hearts agitated and overwhelmed by the pangs of separation, all those gopīs spoke these words to one another in every house.
O lord of kings, this news of the departure of the high-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa has also reached the house of the noble Vṛṣabhānu.
Hearing the news in the assembly that her husband was about to depart, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu became exceedingly distressed and suddenly fell into a swoon.
She fell upon the ground like Rambhā, struck down by the Maruts. || 28 ||
Some had the beauty of their faces withered away;
their finger-rings became mere ornaments for their hands,
as their jewelry and hair-braids suddenly grew loose.
They remained as if they were merely the beginnings of figures depicted in a painting. || 29 ||
In their own homes, some women, extremely overwhelmed, cried out, "Śrī Kṛṣṇa! Govinda! Hari! Murāri!", abandoning all their household duties on every side.
And like a yogi, O lord of kings, they have attained bliss.
O King, some who were capable, having gathered together, spoke simultaneously to their circle of friends with voices faltering and choked in their throats.
With eyes carrying drops of tears flowing spontaneously. || 31 ||
The Gopīs said: "Oh, how extremely shameless is this person! It is wonderful; his conduct is not fit to be spoken of.
One thing is on his lips, while another is in his heart; even a god does not know [the truth], so how could a human being? (32)
Even regarding the Rāsa-līlā, he has now resolved to depart, setting aside everything that was spoken there.
Alas! When this Lord of our lives has gone to the city, what suffering indeed would not have befallen us? (33)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Arrival of Akrūra," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 3 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, perceiving the intense separation of the gopīs as they spoke thus,
the Lord, the Divine One, quickly went to their homes.
O King, Hari assumed as many forms as there were women and personally enlightened them all individually with his words.
Having gone to the temple of Śrī Rādhā and seeing Rādhā unconscious while staying in private with her circle of friends, he sweetly sounded his flute. || 3 ||
Hearing the sound of the flute, Rādhā suddenly rose up in agitation;
opening her eyes, she beheld Śrī Govinda who had arrived.
Like a lotus pond whose joy had departed upon seeing the sun, the lotus pond,
having risen at his sight, approached him and respectfully offered him a seat.
To the lotus-eyed Rādhā, who was distressed, her face filled with tears,
and grieving, the Blessed One spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Why are you dejected, O blessed one? Do not grieve, O Rādhikā.
Or perhaps, having heard that I am desirous of departing, you have become distressed by the thought of separation."
Requested by Brahmā for the purpose of removing the earth's burden and for the slaying of Kaṃsa and others, I have indeed been born together with you.
"I shall indeed go to Mathurā; I will remove the burden of the earth.
I will return here quickly and bring you auspiciousness."
Śrī Nārada said:
To Hari, the Lord of the Universe, who had spoken thus,
Rādhā, overwhelmed by the pangs of separation, replied:
Like a forest vine scorched by a forest fire, she was fainting, trembling,
and covered with horripilation.
Śrī Rādhā said: "Go to the city of Vraja; you are capable of removing the burden of the earth.
Now hear my solemn vow from you."
And once you, the Lord of my life, have departed, I shall never again maintain this body here. || 11 ||
Since you do not believe the oath I have sworn to you, I grant you a second opportunity for speech;
my breath is exceedingly agitated to depart from my lips.
It will vanish like a particle of camphor dust.
The Blessed Lord said:
O Rādhā, I am indeed capable of setting aside my own scriptural injunctions, but I am not capable of setting aside the words of my devotees. (13)
"O Śrīdāman, due to my previous curse resulting from our quarrel in Goloka, you shall suffer separation from me for one hundred years; of this there is no doubt. (14)
"Do not grieve, O auspicious Rādhikā; remember my boon:
month after month, during our separation, you shall have a vision of me."
Śrī Rādhā said:
"O Hari, if you do not come to grant me your vision at the end of every month during our separation, then I shall give up my life out of grief. (16)
O delight of the world, ornament of the people, lamp of the universe, enchanter of Kandarpa, remover of the suffering and afflictions of the world,
root of bliss, joy of the Yadus, son of Nanda!
Today, in my presence, take an oath regarding your arrival.
The Blessed Lord said:
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, if I do not return to you at the end of every month during our separation, then let this be my oath by the cows.
O Rādhā, know that these words spoken by me are beyond doubt and free from deceit.
He who practices friendship without guile and without motive is indeed most blessed;
having established a bond of friendship, he would not then practice deceit.
Fie on that lecherous actor, who is a mere puppet of causes! || 19 ||

Just as the organs of action [perceive] tastes and other objects, so too do sages possessed of desire experience pleasure here; for they do not know even slightly that supreme, hidden state of indifference which is characterized by being beyond the gunas.
The virtuous who perceive with equanimity, who are self-controlled, great, and indeed free from worldly dependence— they know that supreme happiness for me lies in that very state of non-dependence.
Just as the sense organs [perceive] taste and the other objects. 21.
For every state of mind arises from another, O beautiful lady, and not from itself; therefore,
you must spontaneously bestow your love upon me.
There is nothing on earth equal to love. || 22 ||
Just as there was a longing for Rādhā at the Bhāṇḍīra fig tree, so indeed shall it come to pass;
for such causeless love is embraced by the virtuous.
And indeed, the wise know that even this is devoid of qualities. || 23 ||
Those who indeed perceive no difference between Rādhikā, you Keśava, and myself— just as there is no distinction between milk and its whiteness—
they alone attain my state of Brahman.
These are characterized by devotion that manifests spontaneously and without cause. || 24 ||
Those men of wicked intellect on earth who perceive a difference between Rādhikā, you, Keśava, and me,
fall into the Kālasūtra hell, suffering in misery.
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, as long as the moon and sun indeed exist— || 25 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having thus consoled Rādhā as well as the entire assembly of gopīs,
the Blessed One, who is skilled in policy, went to the abode of Nanda.
Then, when sunrise had occurred, Nanda and the others took the sacrificial offerings on carts and,
mounting their chariots, all went to the illustrious Mathurā.
O King, having mounted his own chariot with Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, the son of Gāndinī set out,
intent on seeing Mathurā.
Millions upon millions of cowherd women stood by every path,
watching his departure, filled with rage and overwhelmed by delusion.
Crying out "Cruel! Cruel! and uttering harsh words, they blocked his chariot from all sides, just as clouds obstruct the sun along with its chariot.
O King, overcome by the agony of separation from the Blessed One, they struck Akrūra’s chariot violently with their staffs, as well as his horses and his charioteer.
There, the horses, being struck, bolted hither and thither;
by the blow of the cowherd’s two fingers, the charioteer fell from the chariot.
Casting aside all shame for the world, he forcibly dragged Akrūra from the chariot by his bracelets while Kṛṣṇa and Rāma looked on.
Seeing the strength of the cowherd girls' group, the Lord Hari, accompanied by his own forces,
protected the son of Gāndinī and then addressed the cowherd girls.
"I shall return at twilight; do not grieve, O women. Let the inhabitants of Vraja not see my smile while I am looking upon them. (35)
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Baladeva and his chariot, arrived together with Akrūra,
drawn by swift and captivating horses.
He went to the city adorned by the multitude of Yādavas.
As long as the chariot, its banner, and the dust raised by the horses could still be perceived,
those women stood upon the path, utterly bewildered, like figures in a painting.
Having remembered the words of Hari, they returned with their hopes extinguished.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Departure for Śrī Mathurā," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārada said:
Hari went to the grove of Mathurā with Akrūra and Mā;
having stayed near the Yamunā and drunk its water, he proceeded toward his chariot.
Having taken leave of them, Akrūra went to the auspicious Yamunā to bathe;
to perform his daily and occasional rites, he entered the pure water.
In that water, which was bottomless and deep, and filled with great whirlpools,
the son of Gāndinī beheld Rāma and Kṛṣṇa as they were speaking.
Having forgotten them, O King, he saw those two again standing in the water upon his chariot;
there he beheld the lord of serpents stationed there, coiled into a circle.
In his lap [he saw] the great realm of Goloka, honored by the worlds,
as well as Mount Govardhana, the Yamunā, and the enchanting Vṛndāvana forest.
The Lord, the most perfect Supreme Person, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, who is the orb of light consisting of countless millions of suns.
There Akrūra beheld the Lord, who possesses the beauty of ten million Cupids, situated in the midst of the Rāsa circle together with Rādhā.
Having realized Kṛṣṇa to be the Supreme Brahman and bowing down again and again,
Akrūra, with palms joined in reverence, offered a hymn of praise, filled with great joy.
Akrūra said:
Salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, the most perfect Supreme Being;
salutations to the Lord of countless universes and the Lord of Goloka.
Salutations to You, the husband of Śrī Rādhā; salutations to You, the Lord of Vraja. Salutations to the son of Śrī Nanda, and to the one who delights Yaśodā.
O son of Devakī, O Govinda, O Vāsudeva, O Lord of the universe!
O best of the Yadus, O Lord of the world, O Supreme Person, protect me! 11.

May my speech always be engaged in describing Your virtues; may my ears be intent upon Your story and my hands upon Your service; may my mind ever dwell upon the lotus feet of You, and my eyes upon the vision of Your extraordinary, radiant splendor. (12)
Śrī Nārada said: While he was thus offering praise and looking on in amazement,
the Lord Kṛṣṇa, the Sovereign, vanished right there along with his world.
Having bowed to him and performed the prescribed rites for the occasion, Akrūra recognized Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Brahman; filled with wonder, he approached the chariot.
At the end of the day, the son of Gāndinī brought Rāma and Kṛṣṇa on a chariot that moved with the speed of the wind and resounded with a smooth, deep roar.
Seeing Nanda there in the city’s grove, the best of the Yadus smiled and spoke to Akrūra with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O giver of honor, you must indeed go to Mathurā by means of your own chariot;
I shall come later together with the cowherds."
Akrūra said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Govinda, Supreme Person!
O Lord, come to my home together with your elder brother and the cowherds.
Purify my home with the dust of your lotus feet;
O Lord of the Universe, I shall not go to my own abode without you. (19)
The Blessed Lord said:
"Having slain those who are hostile to the Yādavas, I shall come to your home with my army and kinsmen; I will do what is pleasing to you."
Śrī Nārada said:
Then, while Kṛṣṇa remained there, Akrūra went to Mathurā;
having reported this to Kaṃsa, he then departed for his own home.
Then, in the afternoon, seeing Govinda approaching the city with his companions and the boys to see him, Nanda spoke these words.
"You must indeed come to the city with straightforwardness;
do not consider this Gokula to be within the kingdom of King Kaṃsa, which is filled with great danger. (23)
Having said, "So be it," the Blessed One, accompanied by his army, went to the city together with the elderly cowherds urged on by Nanda and with the young boys.
Adorned with palaces that touch the sky and houses inlaid with gold and jewels, it was fortified with strongholds and stood like the city of the gods.
The Kālindī, with its jewel-stairways and the curiosity of its surging waves,
was as rich in splendor as Alakā, filled with divine women and men.
Beholding the splendor of Śrī Mathurā and the mansions of the wealthy, Kṛṣṇa entered the royal highway together with the cowherd boys.
Having heard that the son of Vasudeva had arrived,
the highly learned women of the city of Mathurā abandoned their tasks and left their infants behind.
They rushed toward the ocean to see him, just as rivers flow toward the sea. || 28 ||
Some indeed emerged from the latticed windows of the palace, some from the walls, some from the curtains, some from the casements,
and others from the openings of the door-panels.
The matrons beheld him at that crossroads. || 29 ||
He wears a single lock of hair dangling over his face; was this done merely to captivate the minds of those walking ahead, while leaving it behind on the surface of his crown?
What is the second [offense], the seizing of those following behind? || 30 ||
Wearing yellow garments on one half of his body and possessing powerful, quivering hips on the other half— like lightning upon a cloud on his shoulder—
he was the son of Vasudeva, holding a lotus in his hand and the Vaijayantī garland against his chest.
Beholding him, with his earrings swinging as he walked and his arms adorned with golden armlets like the rising sun, all the women of the city were struck with wonder.
O King, [he is] the Lord of countless eggs, the Supreme beyond the supreme.
The matrons said:
"Aho! How beautiful is Vṛndāvana, where he is indeed present! Blessed are all the cowherds who behold this enchanting one."
Blessed are those supreme cowherd girls; what meritorious deed have they performed, that they repeatedly drink the nectar of His lips upon the stage of the rāsa dance?
Śrī Nārada said: On the royal road, Madhusūdana, with the permission of Gopāla, spoke to a washerman who was walking along, intoxicated and acting as a performer.
"O friend of great intelligence, give us these beautiful garments;
for there will be the highest welfare for you, the giver, of this—of this there is no doubt. (36)
Blazing intensely like a fire fueled by the words of Kṛṣṇa, that most wicked servant of Kaṃsa spoke thus to Mādhava on the road: || 37 ||
The washerman said:
"Such clothes as these were worn by your fathers and grandfathers; why then have you become so arrogant that you now wear only rags? (38)
"Depart quickly from the city, all of you, out of a desire for life; I shall have you, those who stole my clothes, imprisoned in a jail. (39)
Śrī Nārada said:
Even as the washerman was speaking thus, the best of the Yadus instantly and effortlessly severed his head with the very tip of his hand.
That light merged into Śrīghanaśyāma, O King of Videha;
immediately thereafter, all his followers indeed cast off their garments and inner chambers.
O King, they fled in all directions like clouds in the autumn season,
having seized the garments dear to themselves while Rāma and Kṛṣṇa stood there.
The cowherd boys and even the people on the royal highway—
those children who knew how to wear them— put on those beautiful garments in a haphazard fashion while Śrī Kṛṣṇa looked on.
Seeing those two, Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Baladeva, a certain weaver fashioned for them a divine attire with garments of variegated colors.
Having likewise performed what was appropriate for the other children,
O King, he beheld Kṛṣṇa once more with supreme devotion.
The Lord, being pleased, granted him his own form;
furthermore, Baladeva bestowed upon him strength, prosperity, and sovereignty.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Entrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa into Mathurā," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Śrī Nārada said:
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the son of Nanda, together with the cowherd boys and Balarāma,
went to the house of Sudāmā, who was adorned with a garland of flowers.
Seeing them, he rose up, paid homage with palms joined in reverence,
placed them upon a flower-throne, and spoke with a voice faltering with emotion.
Sudāma said:
"My lineage, my home, and my very birth are blessed now that you, O venerable one, have arrived; seven generations of my family are purified."
I believe that seven [generations] of my mother’s and father’s lineages have gone to the realm of Vaikuṇṭha along with their beloveds. || 3 ||
O Supreme Lords, born in the lineage of Yadu, you two are fully capable of removing the burden of the earth;
salutations to you both, for my most wretched self.
The two supreme Lords of the World went to their home.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the gardener presented flower arrangements, ornaments, the humming of bees, and drops of nectar,
and then he bowed down.
Having gathered that mass of flowers, the Blessed Lord Hari, accompanied by his army,
gave them to the cowherds nearby and spoke with a smiling face.
May you always possess a devotion even greater toward my lotus feet;
may you have the company of my devotees, for in this very life you shall indeed attain my own nature.
Baladeva gave him prosperity that increases one's lineage;
then, O King, having risen from there, the two of them proceeded to another street.
On the road, Mādhava questioned a young woman who was walking along— a lotus-eyed, hunchbacked lady carrying a vessel of sandalwood paste.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Who are you, O fair-browed one? Whose beloved are you? And for whose sake is this sandalwood paste? Give it to us two, so that your long-term welfare shall be secured."
The maidservant said:
"O best of handsome men, O high-minded one, I am a hunchbacked woman named Sairandhrī; this sandalwood paste produced from my own hands is dear to the Lord of Bhoja."
Even now, I am still a servant of Kaṃsa; yet my mind is set upon these two staff-like arms of yours, which are like the trunks of elephants.
Who else besides you two would be worthy to apply this ointment?
Indeed, an equal beauty to yours does not exist in the three worlds. (13)
Śrī Nārada said: Delighted, she gave both of them a thick ointment;
then Rāma and Kṛṣṇa shone brilliantly with that body-paste.
The cowherd boys each took a little of the divine sandalwood;
then Kṛṣṇa set his mind upon making Trivakrā straight.
Stepping upon his two forefeet with his two feet, the all-pervading Supreme Lord,
while being gazed upon by men, seized them by the chin with his upturned hand.
Hari straightened that crooked body.
At that very moment, she— her form resembling a staff and her beauty as if surpassing Rambhā herself in embodied splendor—
having appeared and seized Hari by the garment, spoke.
She of the pure smile became overwhelmed by the passion that had arisen. || 17 ||
The Sairandhrī said:
"Go quickly, O best of handsome men, to my house; indeed, I cannot bear to let you go."
Be gracious, O Omniscient One, O Knower of Flavors, O Giver of Honor; my mind has been utterly agitated by you. (18)
Śrī Nārada said:
At that very moment, the cowherds laughed among themselves, exclaiming, "Aho! What is this? amidst the sound of their clapping hands.
While Rāma was looking on, Hari, smiling and being entreated by them, spoke these further words.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Oh, how exceedingly blessed is this city of Mathurā, where indeed such gentle people dwell!"
I shall come to your city, that abode where they lead unknown travelers into their own homes upon seeing them.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa drew the edge of his upper garment toward him with a tender voice; while proceeding along the royal road, he beheld wealthy Vaiśyas.
Having worshipped Hari with fruits rich in flowers, betel, and fragrance, as well as milky fruits,
and having established him upon his own seat, the people of foremost intellect bowed down.
The Vaiśyas said:
"If your sovereignty should be established here, then you must protect your own people.
O Lord, we are your subjects; once the kingdom is attained, who would not remember [this obligation]? (23)
Śrī Nārada said:
With a gentle smile, Acyuta asked the Vaiśyas about the location of the bow;
yet those wise men did not tell him, fearing that the bow might break.
And those people of Mathurā, enchanted by the sweetness of his form and virtues, cried out, "O Prince, come and see Dhanu! desiring to behold him.
Following the path shown by them, Kṛṣṇa entered the grounds of the bow-pit,
cultivating friendship with his companions, the boys of Mathurā.
Just as Indra’s bow, richly adorned with gold, measuring seven palm trees in length and possessing great weight, was fit to be carried by five thousand men; (so too was his own).
Consisting of eight metals, defiled, weighing a hundred thousand bhāras at most,
it was worshipped by the citizens on the fourteenth day in the sacrificial pavilion.
Mādhava beheld that which had been given long ago by Bhārgava to Yadu-rāja,
appearing like Śeṣa himself standing there in person, coiled into a circle.
Though being restrained by the men, Kṛṣṇa forcibly took up the bow;
while the citizens there looked on, he then made it ready with ease.
Drawing the bow back to his ear with his two staff-like arms,
O King, Hari broke it in the middle, just as an elephant breaks a stalk of sugarcane.
