As the bow was being broken, there arose a twanging sound like a flash of lightning;
by that sound, the entire cosmic egg, along with the seven worlds and the subterranean realms, resounded.
The elephants of the quarters trembled, the circle of the earth’s regions shone brightly,
and at that very moment, the multitude of people on earth was rendered deaf.
The sound tore Kaṃsa’s heart for two ghaṭīs;
his guards, enraged, rose up as assailants.
Desiring to seize Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they said to him, "Let him be bound!
Then, seeing those who had arrived armed, Balarāma and Keśava [prepared for them].
Having taken up fragments of their bows, they struck the arrogant ones violently;
by that excessive blow from the fragments, some heroes indeed fainted. (36)
With their feet severed and their nails split, some with their shoulders and arms cut off,
five thousand heroes fell upon the surface of the earth.
All the people of Mathurā were agitated and ran out, desiring to see that;
when a tumult arose in the city, a great fear came upon the men. (38)
O King, the royal umbrella of Bhojarāja suddenly fell down. Running from Cāpasthala with his cowherds and his army, Kṛṣṇa arrived near Nanda at the time of twilight, appearing as if terrified.
Beholding the wondrous and beautiful form of Govinda,
the women of the city of Mathurā were utterly infatuated; their garments and hair became disheveled as they were tormented by the pangs of love.
They said this to one another among their circle of female friends. || 40 ||
The matrons said:
"Hari, possessing the splendor of ten million Kandarpas, moving at his own will and acting with haste, is being beheld by us as he truly enters into every limb of ours. (41)
The virtuous ones said:
"Are there not indeed cruel women in this city, by whom Anaṅgamohana is being gazed upon?"
Although he is most beautiful in every limb, we do not see him filled with joy. (42)
In whose single part is sweetness observed?
There, the eye is like a moth falling [into a flame].
But he, O friend, who is enchanting in every limb—
How can that very same thing be perceived by the eye? || 43 ||
For wherever the eye falls upon each and every beautiful limb of the son of Nanda,
from that very spot it obtains a joy equal to his name.
With his mind fixed as if submerged in an ocean of loveliness. || 44 ||

Śrī Nārada said: O King of Mithilā, how could the women of the city— who beheld that delight of the king of Vraja during the day, and who even saw him before them in their dreams— not remember that sweet one by whom the circle of the rāsa dance was performed with the gopīs?
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Vision of Śrī Mathurā," in the Śrī Garga Saṃhitā, within the Mathurā-khaṇḍa, in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Śrī Nārada said: Having heard of the decapitation of the washerman, the slaughter of the guards, and the breaking of the bow, Kaṃsa indeed fell into a state of supreme terror.
From that very moment, beholding ill omens and the throbbing of his left limbs, as well as a breaking sensation in his body, the king of the Daityas could not obtain sleep.
In a dream, joined by hungry ghosts (pretas), smeared with oil, and naked,
he went toward the southern direction mounted upon a buffalo, carrying a rosary of *japā* flowers.
Having risen at dawn, he summoned the men charged with the burden of affairs and caused a great festival of wrestling matches to be held.
In the front part of the assembly hall, which possessed a spacious courtyard and was adorned with pillars of gold, there was indeed a performance arena.
O King, the stage shone with canopies resembling gold, with hanging strings of pearls,
and with stairways and golden platforms.
Upon that auspicious royal throne made of jewels and honored with *makaranda* flowers,
there was the throne of Śakra, complete with a circular cushion of fine upholstery.
He was accompanied by a divine parasol as beautiful as the orb of the moon,
and by whisks with diamond-studded handles that resembled swans.
Having ascended that [palace] which was ten cubits high and eternally fashioned by Viśvakarman,
Kaṃsa shone like a lion upon a mountain peak.
There the singers sang, the courtesans danced, and the mṛdaṅgas, paṭahas, tālas, bherīs, ānakas, and other instruments resounded.
O King, the monarchs, provincial rulers, and citizens from the countryside,
seated upon their respective platforms, watched the wrestling match.
Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, Kūṭa, Śala, and Tośala,
equipped with clubs for exercise, fought with one another.
The cowherds, headed by King Nanda, having been summoned by Kaṃsa, stood with downcast faces;
after offering him a great tribute, they took their places upon a single platform.
O King, from the cities of Bāṇāsura, Jarāsaṃdha, and Naraka,
as well as from those of other kings such as Śambara and others.
And the Bālakhilyas, O King, went there indeed to Yadurāja;
then those two, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, were in the form of illusory children.
To witness the sport of the wrestlers, they went to the arena pavilion,
which was filled with faces adorned with vermilion and musk-leaf patterns like the urine of a cow,
with great elephants intoxicated by flowing rut and decorated with jeweled earrings.
Seeing the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa stationed at the entrance of the arena, Kṛṣṇa spoke to the mahout in a deep voice.
"O King of Serpents, draw me out; make a path for me according to my desire!
Otherwise, I shall cast you along with the serpent down upon the surface of the earth. (18)
Then the enraged mahāmātra urged that elephant toward the son of Nanda, who was letting out a fierce trumpeting sound in all directions.
Seizing that Hari immediately with his trunk, the king of elephants lifted him up from there;
then Hari, bearing the weight, emerged from it.
He became dissolved at His feet, falling here and there, just as Hari [is absorbed] in the groves and trees of Vṛndāvana. || 21 ||
The elephant seized him by the feet with its trunk;
Hari, having squeezed the trunk with his two hands, emerged from behind.
And the serpent, having turned horizontal, proceeded to seize him;
but Mādhava, striking him with his fist, fled ahead.
The king of the Nāgas pursued him, as did the King of Videha in Mathurā;
when a great clamor arose at that time, Hari departed from there.
Seizing that serpent by its tail, the exceedingly powerful Baladeva dragged the hooded creature with his two staff-like arms, just as Garuḍa would do.
Laughing, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa seized him by the hand with force and dragged him with his two staff-like arms, as a man might pull a rope attached to an elbow.
O lord of kings, because he was pulled by two [elephant-keepers], the elephant became agitated;
then seven mahāmātras forcibly mounted that elephant.
Likewise, three hundred other elephants were led by others to kill Kṛṣṇa;
yet the infuriated, intoxicated elephant returned again, goaded by the striking of its hook.
The Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa [did this] in the very presence of Baladeva.
Seizing him by the trunk and whirling him here and there,
he threw him down upon the surface of the earth like a child throwing a water-pot.
His mahouts fell far away here and there;
even as the virtuous looked on, the elephant suddenly met its death.
That light became merged in Śrīghanaśyāma, O King of Videha;
and then the two mighty ones, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, having uprooted his tusks,
slaughtered the mahāmātras just as lions slay deer.
When Dvīpa was slain, the other high officials who were here and there fled in all directions, like clouds when the rainy season has passed.
Having thus slain the elephant with the remaining cowherds who were eager for the spectacle,
Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, marked by sweat and rut-fluid, were greeted with shouts of victory.
With faces reddened by exertion, the two entered the arena in haste, holding their teeth in their hands, possessing great speed like the wind and fire acting according to their nature. || 35 ||
The wrestlers [long for] the wrestler, men [long for] the lord of men,
women [long for] Smara, the cowherds in Vraja [long for] the Lord of the Cowherds, and the wicked fathers [long for] their sons who are the wielders of the staff.
And Kaṃsa [will become] Death, O gods, while Virāja [will become] the Sovereign. || 36 ||
Then the supreme reality, the Bhojas, and the best of yogis beheld the Lord who had entered the arena with his power;
indeed, all the people saw that perfect God through their respective individual meditations.
Seeing the elephant slain, those two of great strength caused the wise Kaṃsa to feel fear in his heart,
while those seated upon the dais were delighted in their minds.
Like cakora birds toward the moon, they went happily.
Placing ear to ear,
those citizens, filled with great eagerness, said to one another:
"These two are indeed the supreme Lords in person."
Indeed, they both became the sons of Vasudeva.
Oh, how exceedingly beautiful is this supreme district of Vraja, wherein Mādhava himself has now personally wandered;
for today we have beheld that which is otherwise difficult to obtain!
May we, however, become successful in every respect. || 40 ||
Śrī Nārada said: O King of Mithilā, while the citizens were speaking and the musical instruments were sounding,
Cāṇūra approached Rāma and Kṛṣṇa and spoke to them.
Cāṇūra said:
"O Rāma, O Kṛṣṇa, you two who possess great strength, perform a wrestling match by force before the king!"
When the King, the best of the Yadus, is thus gladdened, what auspicious thing will not come to pass for us here? 42.
The Blessed One said:
"O King, by the grace of the Lord of Prosperity, we were already children at that time, as were they; thus our combat was with children of equal strength.
Let it be so that there may be no unrighteous battle here, which would be improper for those who are powerful."
Cāṇūra said: You are neither a child nor a youth; you are Balarāma himself, the mightiest among the mighty.
An elephant possessing the strength of a thousand elephants has been slain by you two with ease.
Śrī Nārada said: Having heard these words of his, the Lord, the destroyer of suffering,
the mighty Balarāma fought with both Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika.
While the people looked on, they performed the drawing back and the thrusting with their arms and long forearms, like two elephants desiring victory.
Lifting Cāṇūra’s body with both hands, Hari himself weighed the burden of his frame, just as Brahmā weighs the burden of merit.
The great hero Cāṇūra effortlessly lifted up that Lord Hari with a single hand, just as the king of serpents supports a fragment of the earth.
Seizing Cāṇūra by the neck with the strength of his arms and lifting him up by the waist, Mādhava suddenly threw him down upon the ground. 49.
With their hands, knees, feet, arms, thighs, fingers, and fists,
Kṛṣṇa and Cāṇūra struck each other, as did Bala and Muṣṭika.
Seeing the faces of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa covered with drops of perspiration, the king’s wives, standing at the windows, then spoke with compassion: (51)
The women said:
"Alas! A most great injustice has occurred in the assembly while the king is still present."
Where indeed are the two wrestlers with limbs as hard as adamant, and where, alas, are Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who are like flowers? 52.
"Alas, what misfortune for us, the citizens, that we have witnessed those two today in battle!
Oh, how exceedingly blessed and great is our fortune!"
It was produced by the forest-dwellers through the essence of their joy.
"O friends, while this king of wicked mind remains, no one at all is able to speak;
therefore, if by the power of our merit those two— "
Hasten indeed to conquer your own enemies in battle! || 54 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Kuvalayāpīḍa," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Śrī Nārada said:
Remembering King Nanda’s moistened heart and the desire of the women, Hari, wishing to slay his enemies, waged war by force. (1)
Seizing Cāṇūra with his two staff-like arms,
Kṛṣṇa suddenly hurled him into the sky by force, like a lotus uprooted by the wind.
Having fallen from the sky like a star with its face turned downward,
he rose up and struck Kṛṣṇa with his fist with great force.
By that blow of his fist, the Supreme Being beyond the supreme did not waver;
instead, seizing Cāṇūra instantly, he threw him to the ground.
O King of Mithilā, Cāṇūra, his teeth shattered, filled with rage and intoxicated by pride,
struck Śrī Kṛṣṇa on the chest with both fists.
Taking him up with his own two hands, O King, the Blessed One whirled him around in front of Kaṃsa while everyone looked on.
With a blow from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Cāṇūra’s head was split open, and he fell upon the surface of the earth like a child dropping his water-pot.
O King, vomiting blood, he indeed met his death instantly;
likewise, [he struck] the wrestler Muṣṭika, who was difficult to overcome in combat with his fists.
Seizing his feet and whirling him in the air, the mighty Baladeva dashed him down upon the surface of the earth, just as Garuḍa strikes down a serpent;
Muṣṭika met his death, vomiting blood from his mouth.
Seeing the mountain peak approaching, the exceedingly powerful Baladeva struck it down with his fist, just as Indra strikes a mountain with his thunderbolt.
O King, having caught Śala, the son of Nanda struck him with a sharp whip,
just as Garuḍa strikes a serpent with his sharp beak.
Having seized Tośala and torn him asunder in the middle, Kṛṣṇa cast him down before Kaṃsa's couch, just as an elephant casts down a tree branch.
These were struck down on the stage and immediately met their end;
their lights entered Vaikuṇṭha while the virtuous looked on. (13)
Thus, when the wrestlers had been slain by Śrī Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, the remaining wrestlers fled in terror, desiring to save their lives. 14.
Drawing in his companions Śrīdāma and the other cowherds, Mādhava began a battle with them while all the virtuous ones looked on.
Seeing Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, wearing crowns and earrings, sporting with their companions in the arena, the city-dwellers were filled with wonder.
Except for Kaṃsa, the cry of "Victory! issued from everyone's mouth;
there was a clamor of "Well done! Well done!", and then the kettledrums resounded.
Seeing his own defeat, Kaṃsa, overwhelmed with great rage,
silenced the sound of the musical instruments and spoke with his lips quivering.
Kaṃsa said:
"Quickly and by force, expel these two sons of Vasudeva, who are possessed of evil intent, from my city!"
"Seize all the wealth of the inhabitants of Vraja and suddenly bind the exceedingly wicked Nanda! (19)
"Quickly, cut off, cut off the head of my father Ugrasena, that evil-minded Śauri!
Wherever they may be, even there, as well as here, you must surely slaughter these Vṛṣṇis who are portions of the gods! || 20 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
While Kaṃsa was thus boasting, the delighter of the Yadus,
filled with rage, suddenly leapt up and ascended that dais.
Seeing Death arrived, he rose quickly from his couch;
arrogant with pride, he brandished his sword and shield while threatening him.
He suddenly seized Kaṃsa with both arms, together with his shield and sword,
just as a majestic serpent seizes a venomous snake with the two divisions of its mouth.
Wielding a falling sword and a brandishing shield, the powerful Puṇḍarīka emerged from the grip of his arms by force, like a serpent from the beak of Garuḍa.
Those two powerful ones, crushing each other with great force, shone exactly like two lions on a mountain peak. (25)
As Kaṃsa was leaping up with force toward the great sky with a hundred arms,
Kṛṣṇa, leaping up as well, seized him in the sky just as one hawk seizes another.
Seizing that fierce bull among the Daityas with his two staff-like arms,
the God, who wields the strength of the three worlds, whirled him hither and thither.
Filled with rage, he caused it to fall from the sky onto the couch;
the couch, its staff broken, became like a tree struck by a bolt of lightning. || 28 ||
O Vajrāṅga, although he had fallen, his mind was somewhat agitated;
rising up suddenly, he fought with the high-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having led him by his two staff-like arms and cast him upon the couch,
the Lord Mādhava again ascended his chest and seized his crown-lock.
Suddenly seizing him by the hair, Hari himself threw him from the platform onto the arena floor, like a boulder from a mountain.
Above him, the eternal Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the support of all,
himself descended with speed— the infinite one of infinite prowess.
Thus, O King, by the falling of the two [mountains], the low-lying circle of the earth's surface suddenly trembled like a cooking pot for two ghaṭikās.
O King, he dragged the deceased Bhojarāja across the ground while everyone looked on, just as a lion drags a lordly elephant.
At that very moment, O King, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the running monarchs;
for the mighty Kaṃsa was worshipping the Lord of Gods out of a spirit of enmity.
He attained a form identical to that of Bhṛṅgin, just as a worm becomes like its host;
and seeing Kaṃsa fallen, his eight exceedingly powerful brothers— Sunāman, Sṛṣṭi, Nyagrodha, Tuṣṭimat, Dṛṣṭi, and Pālaka— [fled].
With their lips quivering in rage, some bearing spears and stakes, and others wielding swords and shields, they advanced toward Kṛṣṇa to fight. || 37 ||
Seeing them, Balarāma, the delighter of Rohiṇī, took up his club and let out a roar from afar,
like a lion toward deer.
O King of Mithilā, by the mere sound of "huṃ," weapons fell from their hands out of fear, like mango fruits dropping at the stroke of a staff.
Weaponless, those great heroes struck the army from all sides with their fists,
just as elephants strike a mountain here and there with the trunks of their tusks.
In that manner, Bala struck Sṛṣṭi and Sunāmā with his mace;
he struck Nyagrodha with the force of his arm and Kaṅka indeed with his left hand.
Mādhava struck Śaṅku, who was full of joy, with his left foot,
and he struck Rāṣṭrapāla with his right foot.
Eight trees fell suddenly, like those struck down by the wind;
their light merged into the Blessed One, O King of Videha. (43)
Then the celestial drums resounded and a cry of victory arose;
immediately the gods rained down flowers born of the Nandana grove.
The Vidyādharīs and Gandharvīs danced, overwhelmed with joy;
and the Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras sang his glory. (45)
Brahmā and other sages and perfected beings (siddhas), having arrived in celestial chariots to behold them,
praised Rāma and Kṛṣṇa with words dedicated to the Vedas.
Beating their breasts with their hands, the women, headed by Astiprāpti,
emerged and wept, distressed by the grief of having become widows.
The women said: "O Lord! O Master of battle! Where have you gone, O one of great strength, you who were the conqueror of the three worlds and truly invincible even to the gods? (48)
As soon as they were born, your own sister’s sons were slain by you without mercy; others, some less than ten days old and others already ten days old, were likewise killed by force. 49.
Due to that terrible sin, he has fallen into such a state as this.
Śrī Nārada said: Having thus consoled the distressed wives of the king, whose faces were bathed in tears,
he prepared funeral pyres on the bank of the Yamunā, adorned with sandalwood.
Having caused the funeral rites for the deceased to be performed for the sake of the next world,
the Blessed One, the creator of the worlds, enlightened them all.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Kaṃsa," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Śrī Nārada said:
Then the two gods, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by the Vṛṣṇis, went directly into the presence of Devakī and Vasudeva.
O King, upon seeing that Garuḍa had arrived, the bonds of those two became loosened of their own accord, like the coils of a serpent's noose.
Seeing his parents, who were experts in their own supernatural powers, Hari, accompanied by Bala,
immediately and forcibly spread his own illusion that deludes the entire world.
Knowing Rāma and Kṛṣṇa to be his sons, Vasudeva, overwhelmed by delusion and filled with tears, rose up together with Devakī and embraced them.
Having consoled them, Hari, immediately surrounded by the Vṛṣṇis,
made his maternal grandfather Ugrasena the lord of Mathurā.
Having summoned the Yādavas who had fled to other lands out of fear of Kaṃsa,
he affectionately settled them with their families in the city of Yadu.
To King Nanda, who was preparing to go to his own home with the groups of cowherds,
he (Kṛṣṇa), accompanied by Balarāma, bowed down and spoke as if bewildering him with his illusory power.
O dear one, make your dwelling right here in this city; if the desire to go should arise in your mind,
then later I, along with my forces or the Yadus, shall surely follow.
Having placed [him] at your side, I shall return.
Śrī Nārada said: Thus honored by Śrī Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, King Nanda embraced Śauri (Kṛṣṇa) and, overwhelmed with love, departed for Vraja along with the cowherds.
In former times, on the occasion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s birth-star, Śauri gave a million cows,
adorned with garments and garlands, to the Brāhmaṇas.
Śauri, the knower of dharma, having summoned Garga, caused the sacred thread ceremony (yajñopavīta) to be performed for Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Baladeva according to the prescribed rites.
Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, intent on studying all branches of knowledge,
went to the presence of their preceptor Sāndīpani like ordinary men.
Having performed supreme service to their guru, the two Mādhavas, the best among all knowers of every science, mastered all branches of knowledge in a short time.
As the two of them, with palms joined in reverence, were prepared to give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor,
the brahmin preceptor chose their deceased son as that fee.
Having mounted a chariot adorned with gold,
those two self-controlled ones of terrible prowess went to Prabhāsa, near the ocean.
Immediately shaken, the ocean brought an excellent offering of jewels and,
with palms joined in reverence, fell at his feet.
The Blessed One said to him: "Quickly give back my son;
it was by you that he was seized amidst the surging masses of fierce waves."
The Ocean said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, this child was not taken by me;
he was indeed carried off by Pañcajana, the asura in the form of a conch."
O Lord, that most powerful bull among the Daityas, who causes fear to the gods, dwells perpetually within my belly; he is fit to be conquered by you. (19)
Śrī Nārada said: Thus addressed by him, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa tied his garment firmly around his waist and leapt with great speed into the ocean that roared with a terrible sound.
At the descent of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who bears the burden of the three worlds,
the ocean trembled violently, like King Videha at the stroke of the thunderbolt's peak.
Then the heroic Daitya Pañcajana suddenly came before Śrī Kṛṣṇa to fight and hurled a trident at Mādhava.
Seizing that trident in his hand, he struck him with it;
by that blow, he fell down unconscious upon the surface of the water.
Rising suddenly with his mind somewhat agitated, he struck the Lord of Gods on the head with his hand, just as a serpent strikes the king of birds with its hood.
The most perfect, manifest Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Blessed Lord Hari,
being enraged, struck him forcefully on the head with His fist.
By the blow of Kṛṣṇa’s fist, he immediately met his end;
that light merged into the dark splendor of Śrīghana, O King of Videha. (26)
Having thus slain Pañcajana and taken the conch shell born from his body,
he emerged suddenly from the great ocean and approached his chariot.
By means of a vehicle swift as the wind, the two charming ones, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
went even to the long city of Saṃyamanī belonging to Śamana.
The fierce sound of the Pāñcajanya conch, like the roar of clouds, filled the world;
hearing it, Yama trembled along with his assembly.
Those sinners who heard your voice have gone to liberation, even though they had been cast down into eighty-four hundred thousand hells.
Yama, having immediately brought the offering, fell at the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Baladeva, humbled and with palms joined in reverence.
Yama said: O Hari, O ocean of mercy, O Rāma, Rāma of great strength!
You two are the lords of countless universes and the most perfect beings.
The two ancient gods, the two great Puruṣas, the lords of all, the sovereigns of all beings in the universe—
verily even today they abide at the very summit of all.
"O Supreme Lords, speak your own command with your voice. || 33 ||
The Blessed One said: "O Lokapāla of great intelligence, bring the son of the preceptor;
rule the kingdom according to justice, honoring at all times what I have spoken."
Śrī Nārada said:
At that very moment, Hari himself took the preceptor’s son who had been brought by him,
went to Avantikā, and gave the child to the venerable Guru.
Accompanied by the guru’s blessing, the two of them, having bowed to him with palms joined in reverence,
mounted their chariot and arrived at Mathurā, honored by the Yadus.
Once, Kṛṣṇa, the cause of all causes, accompanied by Balarāma,
went to the house of Akrūra while remembering his devotees, the Pāṇḍavas.
O King, Akrūra rose up suddenly and, filled with joy, embraced them both; he then honored them with the sixteen modes of worship.
Standing before him with palms joined in reverence, his desires now fully realized, the king spoke while shedding drops of tears born of joy. (39)
Akrūra said:
"Constant salutations, repeated salutations, to you both, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa!
O Lords, that which was promised by you both on the road has been fully accomplished."
The two delights of the world, the supreme ornaments of humanity, and the lamps illuminating the entire universe both within and without,
have this very day entered the lineage of Yadu for the sake of protecting cows, brahmins, the virtuous, the Vedas, dharma, and the gods.
For the purpose of destroying Kaṃsa and the other lords of the Daityas,
those two of perfect splendor descended from the realm of Goloka to the circle of the land of Bhārata.
I am constantly bowing down to you both, the Supreme Lords. || 42 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
"You are a noble elder and steadfast, while I am but a child before you;
for the virtuous, O high-minded one, praise themselves only in the presence of their own selves."
"Go to Hastināpura indeed to see the welfare of the Pāṇḍavas;
O Lord of Generosity, having seen them all, return quickly. (44)
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus to Akrūra, the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees and the accomplisher of all tasks, went with Balarāma to the residence of Vasudeva.
Having gone to the city of the Kaurava lord and seen the Pāṇḍavas, Akrūra returned and related the entire news to Kṛṣṇa.
Akrūra said:
"O Kaurava, without you two, no one else can be a helper to the Pāṇḍavas who are now enduring such suffering."
And when Pāṇḍu has died, those sons of Pṛthā whose hearts are indeed attached to the lotus-feet of you two [will follow]. (47)
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard this from the mouth of Akrūra, the Blessed Lord Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, forcibly gave half the kingdom to the Pāṇḍavas from the Kauravas. 48.
Then, remembering the words that had been spoken,
he went to the palace of Kubjā accompanied by Uddhava and surrounded by great auspiciousness.
Seeing from afar that Śrī Hari had arrived, the beautiful Kubjā quickly honored her beloved of life with devotion, offering water for his feet and other services.
In that excellent mansion of Kubjā, whose walls were inlaid with gold and jewels,
Hari shone like he does with Rāmā in Vaikuṇṭha, together with that beautiful woman.
O King, how great was her ascetic merit, since her husband was the most perfect Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself! 52.
Having stayed there for eight days, the divine Hari, the king of Videha,
who had assumed a playful human form, returned to the abode of Śauri.
Thus, O King of Videha, this sacred account of the deeds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa in Mathurā removes all sins, increases longevity, and is most excellent. (54)
This which bestows the four goals of human life upon men and brings Śrī Kṛṣṇa under one's control has been told by me to you as requested; what more do you wish to hear? || 55 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Happiness of the Yadus," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Bahulāśva said:
"I have heard the meritorious life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa from your mouth; yet my mind desires to hear it again today, like one who has gone for water while still thirsty. (1)
The birth and deeds of Kaṃsa have been told by you and heard by me;
I have also heard what was done in previous births by the foremost Daityas, such as Keśin and others.
Who was this washerman who formerly slew him [the king], and how did Hari [do so]?
Oh, how his great light has now become absorbed into Kṛṣṇa! || 3 ||
Śrī Nārada said: In the Tretā Yuga, during the reign of Rāma in Ayodhyā,
a certain washerman spoke to his beloved while the spies were listening.
I do not maintain you, a wicked woman who desires another's house;
Rāma may maintain Sītā out of lust for a wife, but I shall never again associate with her.
Having thus heard these words from many quarters of the world, Rāghava then suddenly abandoned Sītā in the forest due to public censure.
The best of the Raghavas did not wish to inflict punishment upon him;
at the end of the Dvāpara age, he became a washerman in Mathurā.
To pacify the fault of his evil speech, Hari himself slew him;
yet even so, the ocean of compassion, Śrī, granted him liberation.
O King, I have narrated to you this most wonderful life-story of the compassionate Kṛṣṇacandra; what more do you wish to hear?
Bahulāśva said:
O best of sages, who indeed was this weaver in former times to whom the Blessed Lord Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, granted the same form as His own? (10)
Śrī Nārada said:
Formerly, in the city of Mithilā, there was a weaver who was a devotee of Hari;
at the time of Śrī Rāma’s wedding, by the command of King Sīradhvaja—
While preparing garments for the purpose of dressing Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, he,
being skilled in the craft of tailoring, was indeed sewing them with fine threads.
O King, seeing those two beautiful ones, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, who possessed the loveliness of ten million Cupids, the noble-minded weaver became infatuated. (13)
"I shall personally, with my own hands, cause them both to be clothed on all sides of their bodies"; thus did he form this desire in his mind.
Rāma, the knower of all things, granted him even by his mind a boon:
"At the end of the Dvāpara age, your desire shall be fulfilled in Bhārata. (15)
By the boon of Śrī Rāma, he indeed came to Mathurā;
having caused them both to assume their dress, he attained their very likeness.
Bahulāśva said:
O Brahmin, tell me what meritorious deed was performed by Sudāmā Mālin, that the enchanting Rāma and Kṛṣṇa themselves came to his house? (17)
Śrī Nārada said:
There is a beautiful and auspicious grove belonging to the king of kings, known by the name Caitraratha;
in it dwells a flower-gatherer named Hemamālī.
Devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, peaceful, charitable, and great through his association with the virtuous,
he performed the worship of the Lord for the sake of attaining the divine Śrī Viṣṇu.
Having daily brought five thousand and three hundred lotuses and placed them before Dhūrjaṭi, he bowed down.
Once, Tryambaka, the ocean of compassion, became exceedingly pleased;
he said to the highly intelligent garland-maker, "Choose a boon."
Then Hemamālī, having bowed to the God with palms joined in reverence,
circumambulated him and, standing before him with his face bowed down, spoke.
Hemamālī said:
"By your boon, may this come to pass: that I behold with my own eyes the most perfect Kṛṣṇa, who has never before entered our home. (23)
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"O high-minded one, at the end of the Dvāpara age in Mathurā in Bhārata, your desire shall be fulfilled; of this there is no doubt."
Śrī Nārada said: By virtue of a boon from Maheśvara, that high-minded garland-maker Hemamālī was born as Sudāmā at the end of the Dvāpara age.
Therefore, Rāma and Keśava went directly to his house to fulfill the nectar-like words of Śiva. What more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Washerwoman, the Weaver, and Sudāmā," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Bahulāśva said:
What supreme and most difficult penance was performed by Sairandhrī in the past, by which Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who is very hard to attain even for the gods—was pleased? (1)
Śrī Nārada said: Beholding Rāma, who resembled ten million Cupids, stationed at Pañcavaṭī,
a Rākṣasī named Śūrpaṇakhā became intensely infatuated.
Then, seeing Rāghava free from delusion and established in his vow of devotion to a single wife,
the sister of Rāvaṇa rushed forward in anger to devour Sītā.
Filled with rage, Lakṣmaṇa, the younger brother of Rāghava, immediately severed her ears and nose with his sharp-edged sword.
With her nose cut off, she went to Laṅkā and reported it to Rāvaṇa;
then, deeply dejected, she went once more to the Puṣkara tīrtha. || 5 ||
Śūrpaṇakhā performed austerities in the water for ten thousand years,
meditating upon the three-eyed god Śrī Rāma, desiring him as her boon.
Then the blessed Lord, the god of gods and husband of Umā, being pleased,
came to that holy site of Puṣkara and said, "Choose a boon."
Śūrpaṇakhā said:
"May Śrī Rāma, who is dear to the virtuous, become my husband; grant me this boon.
You are the supreme God of gods, the Lord of all blessings. (8)
Śrī Śiva said:
"O Rākṣasī, listen; your boon shall not be fruitful this very day;
it will come to pass in Mathurā at the end of the Dvāpara age, of this there is no doubt."
Śrī Nārada said:
That very same Rākṣasī named Śūrpaṇakhā, who could assume any form at will,
became known by the name Kubjā in the illustrious city of Mathurā, O high-minded one.
Even by virtue of a boon from Mahādeva, she became the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
This has been told by me to you; what more do you wish to hear?
Bahulāśva said: O Nārada, who was this Kuvalayāpīḍa in his previous birth?
How did he attain the state of an elephant and yet reach absorption in Śrī Kṛṣṇa? (12)
Śrī Nārada said:
The son of Bali was of massive body, powerful, and known by the name Mandagati;
he was the best among all wielders of weapons and possessed strength equal to a hundred thousand elephants.
Once, he too went out among the people for a festival procession,
forcefully crushing the folk with his two arms like a rutting elephant.
Falling on the path due to the force of his arm, the aged sage Trita became enraged and cursed that intoxicated son of Bali, who was endowed with great strength.
Trita said:
"O evil-minded one, because you wandered about during the festival procession like an elephant, intoxicated with pride and crushing the people, become an elephant! (16)
Thus cursed at that time, the powerful Daitya named Mandagati became like a falling cloak, his body shorn of its splendor.
Immediately recognizing the power of the sage, the Daitya, with palms joined in reverence,
bowed down, circumambulated the sage Trita, and spoke to him.
Mandagati said:
"O Sage, O ocean of compassion, you are the lord of yogis and the best of the twice-born;
tell me quickly, when will my liberation from this state as an elephant come to pass? (19)
O sage, let there never be any slight against virtuous beings such as you;
for sages like you, O Brahmin, are capable of both boons and curses. (20)
Śrī Nārada said: Thus propitiated by him, the great sage named Trita,
that best of brāhmaṇas, being compassionate and free from anger, spoke to the daitya.
Trita said:
"My word shall not be false; I am delighted by your devotion. I shall grant you a divine boon, difficult even for the gods to obtain. (22)
Do not grieve, O Lord of Daityas, in Mathurā, the city of Hari;
liberation from the hand of Śrī Kṛṣṇa shall be yours, of this there is no doubt. (23)
Śrī Nārada said: This very Daitya, moving slowly, became an elephant on the Vindhya mountain named Kuvalayāpīḍa,
equal in strength to ten thousand serpents.
This very elephant, which was seized by force in the forest from the Lord of Magadha along with a hundred thousand elephants,
has now been given as a dowry to Kaṃsa by the King of Videha.
By the word of Trita, his abode attained dissolution into Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
This has been told by me to you; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of Kubjā and Kuvalayāpīḍa," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 11 ||
Bahulāśva said:
Who were those wrestlers, Cāṇūra and the others, who previously came here?
Oh, they had a battle with the illustrious Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra!
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, in ancient times there was a great sage named Utathya in Amarāvatī;
he had five sons whose splendor was equal to that of Kāmadeva.
Having abandoned their knowledge, study, and recitation, along with that very [teacher], those men,
arrogant with pride, went and constantly practiced wrestling with Bali.
To those who had fallen away from the duties of Brahmins and were devoid of Vedic study,
Tathyu, the best of sages, spoke in anger to those intoxicated ones.
Utathya said:
Tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, purity, forbearance, and uprightness; knowledge, realization, and faith—these are the duties of a Brahmin, born of his own nature. (5)
Valor, majesty, fortitude, dexterity, and not fleeing in battle,
as well as generosity and lordliness— this is the duty of a Kshatriya, born of his own nature.
Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the duties born of the nature of the Vaiśya;
likewise, service is the duty of the Śūdra, born of his own nature. (7)
"Having abandoned the duties of a Brahmin, you sons of Brahmā—
how is it that you, O wicked ones, engage in fist-fighting and the combat of a Kṣatriya?"
Therefore, O sirs, you Mallas should listen in the arena of the Bharatas;
for by association with the Asuras, you have quickly become wicked men.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, those sons of Utathya were indeed born as wrestlers on the surface of the earth;
yet, by the mere touch of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s body, they attained supreme liberation.
Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, Kūṭa, Śala, and Tośala—this account of their deeds has been told; what more do you wish to hear?
Bahulāśva said:
O sage, tell me who were those eight younger brothers of Kaṃsa, Kaṅka, Nyagrodhaka, and the others, who previously attained supreme liberation?
Śrī Nārada said: Formerly, in Alakā, there was a Yakṣa known as Devayakṣa;
he was wise, devoted to knowledge, venerable, and possessed of great luster due to his devotion to Śiva. (13)
And eight sons were born to him: Devakūṭa, Mahāgiri, Gaṇḍa, Daṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Khaṇḍadaṇḍa, and likewise Pṛthu.
Once, at dawn, urged by Devayakṣa during the worship of Śiva, they set out to fetch a thousand white lotuses.
Having brought flowers from Lake Mānasa, which were called out by bees,
they indeed gave them to Janaka, having smelled them out of a longing for their fragrance.
By the fault of rendering [the deity] impure with remnants, the worship of Śiva was desecrated;
those fools entered an asuric womb for three births. (17)
O King of Videha, through their two auspicious hands, those [servants] of Baladeva indeed attained supreme liberation, being freed from all defects.
O King, I have related to you this account of the previous births of Kaṃsa’s younger brothers;
what more do you wish to hear?
Śrī Bahulāśva said:
Who was this Daitya Pañcajana of old who bore the form of a conch? O Brahmin, how did his conch come to shine upon the lotus-hand of Śrī Kṛṣṇa? (20)
Śrī Nārada said:
O King of Videha, even before this, these secondary emblems, beginning with the discus,
had been rendered powerless by the splendor of Hari, the Lord of the three worlds.
O King, among them, Śaṅkha Pāñcajanya attained a great station;
clinging to the mouth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he drank the nectar of His lips.
And once, pride arose in his mind, and the king of conchs said:
"Indeed, I, who possess a luster like that of a royal swan, have been seized by Hari."
While I was victorious, Śrī Kṛṣṇa blew his conch, the Dakṣiṇāvarta;
and that nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s lips, which is difficult even for the daughter of the ocean to obtain.
"Therefore, I am the foremost of all; I shall drink [the nectar] day and night.
Thinking thus, the King of Videha honored the conch Pāñcajanya with ten million [offerings]. (25)
In her anger, Lakṣmī cursed him: "O evil-minded one, become a Daitya!
Thus he became that Daitya named Pañcajana in the lord of rivers (the ocean).
Out of a spirit of enmity, the Lord of the Dānavas again approached the Lord of the Gods;
yet his body shone within the hand of the Lord of the Gods, absorbed in light.
Know that his fortune is truly marvelous—what more do you wish to hear? (27)

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Cāṇūra and the Other Four Brothers of Kaṃsa," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 12 ||
Bahulāśva said:
O best of sages, tell me this: what was the first deed performed by that foremost of the Yadus in Mathurā after he had settled his kinsmen there?
Śrī Nārada said: The most perfect Supreme Lord himself, who is affectionate toward his devotees,
remembered the distressed Gokula, which was teeming with cowherds and cowherd boys.
Once, having summoned his friend Uddhava, the devotee, into private,
the Blessed Lord spoke with a voice faltering with love.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Go quickly to Vraja, O friend; it is beautiful, adorned with clusters of auspicious creepers, groves, and other such delights."
Vṛndāvana, beautiful with the luster of dark mountains, was filled with Gokula, crowded with hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses. || 4 ||
O friend, let one vessel indeed be given to Nanda,
or a second to Yaśodā,
and let this third be for Rādhikā.
Having gone there, indeed, to that beautiful temple.
Or rather, O friend, let this auspicious and skillful letter be given separately to the fourth group, to the young companions; and likewise, O friend,
to the hundreds of groups of gopīs.
And leaves should be given to those who have been freed from delusion. || 6 ||
My father, King Nanda, is compassionate, and my mother Yaśodā, whose mind is fixed on me, remembers me quickly; you,
who are skilled in policy, [should comfort] them both with many auspicious words.
Bring about supreme joy for both of us.
My beloved Rādhikā, distressed by separation from me, perceives the entire world as empty due to her delusion;
release her from the agony of my absence by means of the words spoken by me.
You are skilled in the path of speech.
The cowherd boys, Sudāmā and others, who are dear to Me, have become afflicted by delusion without Me, their friend;
grant them happiness as you would to a friend, O Śrī Vraja.
I shall arrive there in a very short time.

Those cowherd women, distressed by the intense agony of separation from me, whose minds were fixed on me, and who had surrendered their bodies and lives for my sake— those women who abandoned the world for my cause.
O minister, how could I not maintain this myself? || 10 ||
O Uddhava, they were prepared to give up their lives here,
yet even now their lives have been held back with great difficulty;
release them from the agony of separation from me by means of the words I have spoken.
You are Dakṣiṇa on the path of speech.
O friend, that very chariot from which I previously returned from Vraja— along with its horses, its charioteer, and its tinkling bells—
is today indeed identical to me, clad in yellow garments.
A lotus with a thousand Vaijayantī petals. || 12 ||
The two earrings adorned with the luster of divine jewels,
the Kaustubha gem blazing like ten million rising suns,
and my auspicious, great-sounding, beautiful flute.
And a flower-adorned staff that deludes the world. || 13 ||
O Uddhava, O Aṅgada, take this crown, which is beautiful with sandalwood paste, covered in divine fragrances, adorned with peacock feathers and other ornaments, and resounds with tinkling anklets.
Go, go this very day quickly at my word! || 14 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having been addressed thus, Uddhava quickly bowed down with palms joined in reverence;
after circumambulating Kṛṣṇa, he mounted his chariot and departed for Vraja.
In every place where there were charming cows by the millions upon millions,
they resembled white mountains and were adorned with divine ornaments.
They were milch cows, young, endowed with good character, beauty, and virtues; accompanied by their calves, with yellow-tipped tails, they moved along with auspicious forms. (17)
Adorned with networks of small bells, they resounded with the tinkling of large bells and anklets;
resembling gold, they possessed golden horns and were garlands of necklaces shimmering with radiance. (18)
Where the cows are of many kinds—pale red, green, copper-colored, yellow, dark, variegated, smoky, and the color of the cuckoo. (19)
They yield milk like oceans, are adorned with the marks of young women's hands, and are auspicious, graced by calves leaping about like deer. (20)
And there, among herds of cattle, great bulls—
long-necked and richly endowed with horns— wander here and there, bearing the burden of righteousness.
Some were cowherds with canes in their hands, while others held dark bamboo flutes; they sang the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa with melodies that enchant the mind.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa arrive from afar and recognizing him, the boys of Vraja,
eager for a sight of Kṛṣṇa, spoke among themselves.
The cowherds said:
"This is surely the son of Nanda who is coming as a friend; of this there is no doubt.
He is dark as a rain-cloud, dressed in yellow garments, wearing a garland, and adorned with earrings. (24)
Wearing the Kaustubha gem and earrings, he bore a lotus with a thousand petals;
he wore that very lotus as a crown, which resembled ten million suns.
Those very horses and this chariot adorned with a network of tinkling bells are here;
yet there is no strength in this chariot, for the Son of Nandana is alone.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King of Videha, while speaking thus, Śrīdāmā and the other cowherds approached from all sides the chariot containing the form of Kṛṣṇa and the friend of Kṛṣṇa.
To those who were saying, "Kṛṣṇa is not here," who was this person appearing in his very form?
Having paid homage to them and embraced them on the road, the son of Upagu (Nanda) spoke.
Uddhava said:
"O Śrīdāman, take this letter given by Kṛṣṇa; of this there is no doubt.
Do not grieve; Hari himself is well with the cowherds."
Having accomplished the great task for the Yādavas, the Lord, accompanied by his army,
will also return here in a short time.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having read that document on palm-leaf, Śrīdāmā and the other boys of Vraja shed profuse tears and spoke with voices choked with emotion. (31)
The cowherds said:
"O delusion-free one, in the son of Nanda, who is like a traveler, there is neither body, nor opulence, nor wealth, nor strength."
Without Kṛṣṇa, all our thoughts are fixed on Vraja; indeed, the entire world has become empty for us. || 32 ||
O Mahāmati, for the inhabitants of Vraja, a moment becomes a yuga, a ghaṭī becomes a manvantara,
and a watch as well as a kalpa becomes a day— without Hari.
It has reached the state of two parārdhas through the sorrows of separation.
Day and night we do not forget him, O Uddhava; for that wicked hour has passed by which he,
stealing away the minds of us forest-dwellers, departed.
Always acting with the affection of a friend toward those who have committed offenses. || 34 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Arrival of Uddhava," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 13 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
To the cowherds who were thus overwhelmed with love and distressed by separation from Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
Uddhava, filled with affection and free from astonishment, spoke as follows.
Uddhava said:
"I am the servant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, His beloved, and His confidant. I have been sent in haste by Hari to see that you are well."
Then, having gone to the city and informed Hari of your separation from him,
I shall please him by bathing his feet with the tears from my eyes.
"O inhabitants of Vraja, after bathing, I shall indeed come quickly to your presence; my oath is not false."
Be joyful and do not grieve;
O cowherds, you shall behold Hari, the Lord of Śrī, even here in this Vraja.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having thus consoled the cowherds, the joy of the Yadus, seated upon his chariot and filled with delight, set out accompanied by Śrīdāmā and the other cowherds.
When the sun had entered the western ocean, he entered the city of Nanda.
Hearing that Uddhava had arrived, the high-minded King Nanda quickly embraced him with joy and, being delighted, honored him.
To Uddhava, who was seated upon a couch, composed and having finished his meal,
King Nanda, also seated upon a couch, spoke with a voice faltering with emotion.
Nanda said:
"O high-minded one, is my friend in the city of Śūrasena well, along with his sons?"
O friend, after Kaṃsa was slain, supreme happiness arose on earth for those bulls among the Yādavas.
I wonder if Mādhava,
together with his army, ever remembers his mother Yaśodā, or the cowherds, Govardhana, the herds of cattle, and Vraja?
Or Vṛndāvana, or the sandy bank of a river.
Alas, O Fate! At what time shall I behold my own son, with lips like the *bimba* fruit, beautiful and with eyes like lotuses, upon the courtyard of the palace?
[He saw him] rolling repeatedly on the ground with force along with the children. || 11 ||
The groves, the thickets, the Yamunā, the great river, Govardhana, this forest, and these woods,
together with houses, creepers, trees, and herds of cows—
Without Mukunda, this world is like poison.
Fie upon my life, my sleep, and my food, without Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals!
Like a cakora bird on the earth without the moon, I live only with the intense hope for his arrival.
O high-minded one, the Supreme Being, who was fervently entreated by the gods to remove the excessive burden of the earth,
has himself been born, intent upon the protection of the virtuous.
For I consider Kṛṣṇa, together with Balarāma, to be the Supreme beyond the supreme.
Śrī Nārada said: Constantly remembering Hari, the Supreme Lord,
King Navananda became silent.
Even while resting his head upon his own pillow, his limbs became overwhelmed with horripilation and longing.
Then, as the friend of Kṛṣṇa looked on, the continuous streams of water from the lotus-eyes of Śrī Nanda drenched the bed,
complete with its cloth and pillows.
Having moistened the courtyard, he set forth. || 16 ||
Hearing that Uddhava had arrived from the city of Śrī Mathurā,
the virtuous Yaśodā quickly went to the door and listened intently to the description of her own son.
With her breasts and lotus-eyes streaming with affection.
Casting aside her shame out of affection for her son, she then asked Uddhava about all his welfare,
after wiping away the flow of tears from his eyes with her garment.
And while Nanda remained there, overwhelmed by the emotion of love for Hari.
Śrī Yaśodā said:
Does Kṛṣṇa ever remember me, or perhaps King Nanda, or even Sannanda, the brother of King Nanda, who is eager for a sight of him? (19)
And there were Nanda, Anupa, and Nanda, along with six Vṛṣabhānus in the cow-pens,
upon whose shoulders he mounted to engage in childhood sports in forest after forest.
The delight of the Nandas played joyfully with a ball; at times, he would spontaneously remember those cowherds who were filled with affection for him.
"This is my only son who has arrived; I have no other sons. Yet even he has gone away to some distant land, abandoning me, his wretched mother. (22)
"Alas, what a tragedy! O Great-minded One, the affection of those who possess love is difficult to restrain. What shall I do without my son? How shall I live, O giver of honor? (23)
"Mother, give me curd; Mother, give me fresh butter-milk!
Speaking thus sweetly, he would always make a persistent demand at home. (24)
How can that Kṛṣṇa take his meal at midday?
This Śrī Kṛṣṇa is my own son, the very life of the residents of Vraja;
he is the wealth of Vraja, the lamp of his lineage, and enchanting with his childhood play. (25)
Through his fondling and protection, my day passed like a mere moment;
yet that day, without the son of Nanda, became like an entire kalpa.
To restrain the calves at the edge of the village on the riverbank, Kṛṣṇa was not permitted by the boys to go; instead, he went to Mathurā. || 27 ||
Crying out "O Mohan! and taking him to his lap from afar, King Nanda then began to fondle him, having become distressed without him.
"Alas! Once, while I was binding a child with a rope, the vessel of curd was broken; I grieve for that deed. (29)
That courtyard, the entire assembly hall, the temple, the gate, the pathways, the palace rooftops, and my very life—all are empty; fie upon this world without Mukunda, for it is like poison! (30)
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, having witnessed the supreme manifestation of love between Yaśodā and Nanda, Uddhava became utterly amazed, his pride completely gone.
Uddhava said:
O Great Lords, even if a tongue as small as a single hair were to grow upon my body, it would still not be sufficient for me to offer praise to you both.
Such devotion, characterized by love, has been shown by you both toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, who is directly present and most perfect.
That eternal devotion characterized by love, which is difficult to attain even through pilgrimage to sacred fords, ascetic penance, charity, Sāṅkhya, and Yoga, has been obtained by you both. 34.
"Do not grieve, O Nanda! O Yaśodā, Queen of Vraja!
Take these two leaves immediately given by Kṛṣṇa; of this there is no doubt. (35)
The elder brother of Sahasrajit, the son of Nanda, is well in the city of the Yadus;
having then accomplished a great task for the Yādavas, that powerful lord, accompanied by his army, [departed]. (36)
And even here, the Blessed One will arrive in a short time;
know that Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the delight of the Nandas, is most perfectly complete for the sake of slaying Kaṃsa and others, and for the protection of his devotees. (37)
Requested by Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa descended into your house;
as soon as he was born, Hari, together with Balarāma, performed wondrous deeds.
The taking of Pūtanā’s life, the overturning of the cart, the felling of Tṛṇāvarta, and the breaking of the twin Arjuna trees. || 39 ||
And he showed his own universal form to Yaśodā within his own mouth;
and in Vṛndāvana, the Lord, the Master, was tending the calves.
He carried out the slaughter of the cowherds while Bakas and Vatsa looked on;
he also performed the slaying of Aghāsura and the crushing of Dhenuka.
Baladeva indeed performed the crushing of Kāliya and the drinking of fire; thereafter, he carried out the slaying of Pralamba.
Having effortlessly uprooted Govardhana with a single hand while you were looking on, he held it aloft like a lordly elephant bearing a lotus.
The Lord of the worlds took the crest-jewel from Śaṅkhacūḍa;
having slain Ariṣṭa, he indeed struck down Keśin.
He indeed crushed that great Daitya, Vyomāsura, with his fist;
likewise, O high-minded one, he performed a marvel in Mathurā.
He struck the boasting washerman with his hand and broke that fierce bow of Kaṃsa in the middle,
just as an elephant breaks a stalk of sugarcane, while all the men were looking on.
Seizing the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, who was equal in strength to ten thousand elephants,
by its trunk-staff, he cast it down upon the ground.
Through wrestling, Mādhava threw Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, Kūṭa, Śala, and Tośala down upon the surface of the earth.
Seizing the Daitya Kālanemi, who was intoxicated with pride and equal to a hundred thousand serpents in strength,
from the platform, Kṛṣṇa whirled him around by the power of his arms.
He cast him down upon the surface of the earth like a child throwing a water-pot;
he fell upon him just as a lion falls upon an elephant.
And the exceedingly powerful Baladeva quickly crushed Kaṅka and the other younger brothers of Kaṃsa with his mace, just as a lion crushes deer.
In order to give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to his preceptor, Hari himself leaped into the great ocean and slew Pañcajana in the form of a conch shell.
O Mahānanda, who other than Śrī Hari could perform such wonderful deeds? Salutations to that Śrī Hari! (53)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Meeting of King Nanda and Uddhava," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 14 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, while Nanda and Uddhava were thus recounting the stories of Hari,
the night that increased their joy passed away as if it were a single moment.
Having risen during the Brāhma-muhūrta, all the cowherd women, in every house,
smeared the thresholds and courtyards and placed lamps there.
Having washed their hands and feet and placed the vessel upon a clean spot,
they all worked together and churned those thick curds.
Their armlets and tiny bells jingled as their arms moved while drawing back their eyes; flowers fell from their braids, and they were adorned with shimmering earrings.
With moon-like faces and lotus-eyes, they were captivating with their variegated colors;
they [sang] the auspicious deeds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Baladeva. || 5 ||
In every house and in every cow-pen, auspicious cows were lowing here and there, while women filled with love sang songs.

Hearing the song of the cowherd girls mixed with the sound of curds everywhere, in every street, Uddhava was filled with wonder and said: 7. Hearing the song of the cowherd girls mixed with the sound of curds everywhere, in every street, Uddhava was filled with wonder and said:
"Aha! Indeed, devotion dances where there is the city of Nandana. Speaking thus, he went out from the village to bathe in the waters of the river.
The cowherd women said:
Whose chariot has arrived here today? Or has the cruel Akrūra come again?
By whom the son of Śrī Nanda, whose eyes are like fresh lotuses, was led to the great city of Mathurā.
At what ill-fated time did his mother give birth to him,
who brings torment even to the virtuous and the affectionate, just as Kadrū gave birth to the multitude of serpents enveloped in poison?
To kill people here and there in vain. || 10 ||
"He who acted for Kaṃsa's sake, who was a friend to Kaṃsa, and who was exceedingly cruel—has he now returned to the district of Vraja?
For even for our deceased husband, he will surely perform the rites for the next world this very day."
Śrī Nārada said: Speaking thus, the young wives of the cowherds of Vraja struck the charioteer on the face with their fingers.
They asked the one whose intellect had reached its limit: "Tell us quickly, for whom is this vehicle? || 12 ||
He of dense radiance, with eyes as broad as lotus petals,
possessing a dark form that enchants millions of mind-born beings,
clad in yellow garments and surrounded by swarms of bees.
Wearing a fresh Vaijayantī garland.
Holding a thousand-petaled lotus that quivers in his hand, bearing a flute and a staff, and enchanting;
adorned with a crown possessing the brilliance of ten million rising suns.
[They saw] those adorned with great jewels and earrings. || 14 ||
O King, having beheld Uddhava— who possessed a form identical to Śrī Kṛṣṇa through his gait, appearance, graceful body, smile, and melodious voice— all were then struck with wonder.
Having recognized him as the friend of Govinda, they went before him.
Then, having learned of the messenger of Lord Hari, he [Yudhiṣṭhira],
the lord of the virtuous, with great respect and through the propriety of excellent speech, inquired after his welfare in private.
Having led Uddhava away, they went to the plantain grove.
Right there on the bank of the Kṛṣṇā, in a beautiful bower-mansion, Rādhā— the delight of Vṛṣabhānu—
remained situated, deeply distressed by the pain of separation from Him.
But she considers the world to be empty without Hari.
With plantain leaves and heaps of sandalwood paste,
it was like a vast, shimmering, and cool temple of clouds,
where the spray from the beautiful, moving waves of the Kṛṣṇā river fell.
From itself, it was a mass of nectar dripping from the moon.

That very grove of plantain trees, which was of such a nature, was completely and constantly reduced to ashes by the brilliance of the fire of separation from Rādhā; for it protected its own body only out of the hope for Kṛṣṇa’s arrival.
Hearing that Uddhava, the friend of Kṛṣṇa, had arrived, Rādhā, together with her companions, showed him honor by offering water for his feet,
a seat, and other auspicious madhuparka offerings.
They repeatedly cried out, "Śrī Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! again and again.
Then Uddhava, with palms joined in reverence, [approached] Rādhā, who was distressed by separation from Govinda, emaciated in limb, and bowed down like a digit of the moon on the new-moon night.
Having circumambulated him, he spoke, filled with joy. || 21 ||
Uddhava said:
Kṛṣṇa is eternally the perfect God,
and O Rādhā, you are eternally the perfect Goddess.
Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra has performed eternal pastimes;
you, O Līlāvatī, have performed eternal pastimes.
Kṛṣṇa is the Infinite, and you are always Indirā;
Kṛṣṇa is Brahman, and you are always Svarā.
Kṛṣṇa is Śiva, and you are Śivā, whose purpose is Śiva.
"You are indeed the Lord Viṣṇu, and you are the supreme Vaiṣṇavī."
You alone are Hari, the primordial deity who created the world of children; you indeed are the auspicious Smṛti, consisting of pure knowledge.
You alone are Hari, intent on sporting in the waters of dissolution; you are the Sacrifice, the Boar, and the Earth itself.
The best of divine sages, Hari himself, was there in person with his own hand holding a lute;
Nārāyaṇa was indeed the son of Dharma along with Nara, and you were Śānti, the bringer of peace to the people.
Kṛṣṇa is indeed the great lord Kapila himself; you alone are Siddhi, served by the Siddhas;
and Kṛṣṇa is Datta, the supreme lord of great sages.
O Rādhā, you alone are indeed eternally composed of knowledge.

You are indeed the sacrifice, Hari; you are the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), Hari; for you are always victorious as the Wide-Striding One (Urukrama). When Pṛthu was the lord of all kings, O Hari, you were then his radiant queen, the beloved of the royal crown.
When Hari appeared as the Fish incarnation to slay the demon Śaṅkha, you were that very Fish;
and when the ocean was churned with Mount Mandara, Hari was the Tortoise.
For you, Vāsukī, have been made the leader and are indeed the bestower of auspiciousness.
Dhanvantari is Hari, the supreme remover of suffering; you are the divine medicinal herb composed of nectar, O auspicious one.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa became Indra, while you became Mohinī, the enchantress who deludes the world there.
When Hari was Nṛsiṃha, you were that very Līlā through the play of Nṛsiṃha; for when Kṛṣṇa became Vāmana, you likewise became so, O you who are affectionate toward your own devotees.
Then you shall be Kīrti, renowned throughout your own world.
When Hari, the Supreme Person, assumed the form of Bhārgava,
you were indeed the stream of his axe; when he was Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, you were the moon of the Raghu dynasty.
At that time, you were the daughter of Janaka. || 31 ||
The venerable Bādarāyaṇa, whose bow is the Śārṅga,
is indeed the author of the Vedānta; you are the very embodiment of the Vedas, while Saṃkarṣaṇa is Mādhava himself among the Vṛṣṇis.
You are Revatī, established equally in the state of Brahman. || 32 ||
When the Buddha was the one who deluded the demons, you were the one who deluded people;
when Kalkī becomes the Lord of Dharma, [you shall likewise act].
Then you shall become Hari, the performer of virtuous deeds. || 33 ||
O Rādhā, Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra indeed resides eternally in the lunar orb as the moonlight known as Candramukhī,
while Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the sun in the solar orb in the heavens.
You are the radiance of the sun, established within the halo.
Indra indeed always resides there as the lord of the Yādavas; O Rādhā, Śacī herself is the sovereign lady there,
and Hari, the supreme lord, is indeed Hiraṇyaretas.
For you are always the supreme golden weapon.
For Śrī, the king of kings, is indeed resplendent as Hari; but you, O Mistress of Treasures, shine forth as the treasury itself.
Hari is indeed in the form of the Ocean of Milk, while you are the river with its white, rippling silken ripples.
Whenever the Lord of All assumes a body, at that very time you manifest in a form corresponding to it; Hari himself is composed of the universe and composed of Brahman.
For you alone are indeed identical with the world and identical with Brahman.
Thus, O Rādhā, you have become this very daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, the joy of the King of Vraja;
by both of you, she who is composed of pure goodness was brought forth for the sake of peace.
By means of her playful deeds, such as the sport of Lalitā and others. || 38 ||
Kṛṣṇa himself is the supreme, ancient Brahman; you alone are his sport, his will, and his primordial nature (prakṛti),
through the mutual union and separation of the two.
Obeisance to you both, Hari and Rādhikā. || 39 ||
Take this letter given by your own lord;
do not grieve excessively, O Rādhikā.
Having accomplished your task in a short time, [you shall return].
I shall go there; such are the words he spoke.
"Accept this very day these hundreds of most auspicious leaves given by Kṛṣṇa;
and let the hundredfold herd of cows belonging to the beautiful women of Vraja, the beloveds of Kṛṣṇa, be returned. (41)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Vision of Śrī Rādhā," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 15 ||
Śrī Nārada said: Taking the letter of Rādhā and placing it upon his head, eyes, and heart,
he read it and meditated upon her lotus feet.
O King, overcome with excessive love and shedding a stream of tears, Rādhā fell into a deep swoon while the Yādava looked on. || 2 ||
Worshipped with liquid pastes of saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood, as well as with the juices of flowers, and fanned by the waving of chowries, she once again attained consciousness. || 3 ||
Beholding the lotus-eyed Rādhā submerged in the ocean of separation, Uddhava and the gopīs likewise shed a continuous stream of tears.
O King, by the flow of their tears in the forest of Vṛndāvana,
the Līlā-sarovara lake was instantly formed, filled with white lotuses.
O King, having seen, drunk [the water], bathed well, and heard this narrative, a man is liberated from the bondage of karma and attains Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then, having heard from the mouth of Uddhava once again of the arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
they inquired after the complete welfare of the high-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Rādhā said: "At what time shall I behold the son of the King of Vraja, the giver of bliss, who possesses the luster of a dark cloud?"
She was intensely eager for him like a peahen for a rain-cloud,
and longing to behold him like a cakorī bird for the moon.
At what ill-fated time did our separation occur, by which each single moment became for me like an eon?
This very night has become as long as two parārdhas.
He performs [all this] except for the two feet of Govinda. || 9 ||
Will Hari ever come to Vraja? What does he do there? Tell me quickly!
For today, indeed, my life-breaths have been held fast with effort.
Afflicted by false speech, they depart by force.
Upon seeing you for a moment, my heart has become cool; I am delighted that you have arrived,
just as Janaka’s daughter was delighted in the past.
When the son of the Wind-god arrived at the city of Laṅkā. || 11 ||

I do not consider even the nectar written upon his letter to be of value for him who, having formed a hope, abandoned his own wealth of delusion, and having forgotten what was spoken by his words, went to Mathurā.
And bring him here, O best among those who know the mantras.
Uddhava said:

"O Rādhā, having gone to Your city and reported Your supreme separation, and having offered an oblation with the tears from my own eyes, I have brought Hari back before You; I have returned. Do not grieve today—this is my oath upon Your feet."
Śrī Nārada said: Then,
O King, the gracious Śrī Rādhā gave to Uddhava two auspicious moon-lustrous gems that had been bestowed upon her by the Moon during the Rāsa dance.
In ancient times, the Moon-god gave two thousand-petaled lotuses;
then Rādhā, pleased and affectionate toward her devotees, gave them to Uddhava.
The beloved of Hari gave him a divine parasol, a lion-throne, and two enchanting fly-whisks, all produced from the mind of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Your sovereignty, endowed with perfect knowledge and being the teacher of all teachers, as well as the power to effect union with Kṛṣṇa, shall be yours forever. (17)
She further bestowed upon him devotion enriched by the state beyond the gunas and characterized by love,
as well as knowledge accompanied by realized wisdom and detachment.
And Śaṅkhacūḍa, the king of Videha, gave that auspicious crest-jewel brought by Hari to him, Uddhava; she who has a moon-like face.
Likewise, O King, all the groups of gopīs, being delighted, gave a collection of auspicious ornaments to the high-souled Uddhava. (20)
Śrī Nārada said: Having heard the auspicious words of the son of Upaguva, Rādhikā indeed attained a state of bliss.
The cowherd women of Vraja spoke individually to him, who was seated in the assembly as a friend of Kṛṣṇa, from a distance.
The gopīs said:
"Tell us quickly what was written on the leaf; however, that which was spoken by Hari is truly wonderful."
"You are the knower of the high and the low, the friend of Hari, the most skilled in mantras, and the great one who possesses his very form. (22)
Uddhava said:
"O wives of the cowherds, as you remember the Lord of Gods, so does he remember you at every moment; this is my observation, of which there is no doubt. (23)
Once, having summoned me and called you to mind in private, that secret-keeper,
the delighter of Nanda, spoke the message residing in his heart.
The Blessed One said: "The mind attached to the qualities (guṇas) leads indeed to bondage; when it is devoted to the Supreme Person (puruṣa), it leads to liberation.
They say the mind is the cause of both; therefore, having conquered it, one should move about free from attachment. (25)

When the discerning one, through the mature practice of spiritual yoga, knows me—Brahman, who is higher than the highest and all-pervading—then he shall abandon the impurity of the mind. As long as the firewood remains in the midst [of the fire], the eye arising from it does not perceive its own nature as smoke. || 26 ||
I am far removed from the gross body, not in reality am I a woman; therefore, indeed, practice the yoga of spiritual discipline here.
For that state which is reached through the categories of Sāṃkhya is likewise reached spontaneously through the states of Yoga.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Consolation of Rādhā and the Gopīs," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, having heard the message of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the beloveds of the cowherds became joyful; with tearful faces and voices choked with sobs, they spoke to the daughter of Upagu (Akrūra).
The residents of Goloka said:
"Kṛṣṇa has gone to a foreign land, abandoning his former beloved people;
alas, he has practiced yoga upon that, through the power of his freedom from delusion."
The female gatekeepers said:
"Just as the moon [gives joy] to the cakora bird, the sun to the lotus, and the lotus to the bee, so too the cloud never brings delight to the cātaka bird. (3)
The Śṛṅgāraprakaras said:
"O friends, the cakora bird has the moon as its friend, and the spark of fire is always [the friend] of the sun;
whatever has been inscribed by the Creator cannot be diminished in this world. (4)
The attendants of the bedchamber said:
"Even a hunter, having killed deer, remembers them while afflicted by haste;
oh, how strange it is that one who has slain his own beloveds with a mere glance remains free from delusion and does not remember them!"
The attendants said:
No one else has ever known the sorrow born of separation as it is felt by one whose body is pierced by a thorn, or by a wise man who himself has been pierced by a thorn. (6)
The guardians of Vṛndāvana said:
"One who is free from motives indeed experiences the bliss of love, which is itself motiveless;
one who possesses motives does not know that rasa, just as the organ of action [cannot perceive taste]."
The residents of Govardhana said:
"He who indeed became the leader of the *sairandhrīs*, creating love even among the matrons—what need is there for much speaking about him by those dwelling on the mountain? (8)
The women who had fashioned the bower said:
"Alas! In this cluster of mādhavī bower where intoxicated bees hum, this very story is heard concerning him who was indeed made the object of your own eyes."
The residents of the forest bowers said:
"In Vṛndāvana, amidst swarms of intoxicated bees in the kadamba thickets on the banks of the Yamunā,"
We worship the son of Nanda, who moves slowly, yet is accompanied by his army, his cowherds, and his wealth of cattle. || 10 ||
The host of Jāhnavī said: "When will our time come,
such that it may be seen as the time of householders?"
O women of Vraja, do not grieve excessively;
for at all times, neither victory nor defeat belongs to anyone. (11)
Yamunāyūtha said:
The Creator has no compassion whatsoever; he joins together and separates all beings just as a child plays with his toys. (12)
Ramayūtha said:
"A maidservant who formerly had a body as straight as an arrow has now attained the status of one born of noble lineage."
Alas, in just four days, she who was ill-formed became beautiful, making the sound of a celestial drum.
The Virajā-yūthas said:
"The arms of no one are always dear upon another's shoulder;
one does not remain eternally young."
Like Indra, he does not exercise sovereignty forever;
let him adorn his pride for only four days. || 14 ||
Lalitāyūtha said:
Having prevented the consecration of Rāma, Mantharā indeed created an obstacle in the city of Kosala.
This very same hunchback has gone to the city of Mathurā; O cowherd girls, what indeed will this hunchback not do? (15)
Viśākhāyūtha said: [I remember] him wandering to the cow-pastures with his attendants for grazing, awakening his own city with his resonant sounds.
Indeed, we do not forget the son of Śrī Nanda, who was mimicking an intoxicated elephant. || 16 ||
The group of Māyās said:

"When, having seized him by the cloth in the narrow alleys and forcibly placing that Hari upon our hearts with our arms, shall we indeed lead him home amidst the mutual joy and fear of being drawn toward one another? (17)
The eight friends said:
"O dear one, having beheld the son of Nanda, so beautiful that today our eyes see nothing else in the world,"
"Since the son of King Nanda remains in the city, what will happen? Tell us quickly, without delay! (18)
The sixteen companions said:
Having heard in the forest that sound as sweet as the resonance of a flute, which increases the power of the flower-arrowed god of love;
May our pair of ears here hear that which is sung everywhere by us, or even the supreme glory.
The thirty-two friends said with affection: "One should win over one's enemy through kindness,
a greedy person through wealth, and a brahmin with respect."
By what means does one subdue the Guru—who is full of aesthetic relish, who acts with passion, yet remains free from delusion—through prostrations? || 20 ||
The personified Vedas said:
"Salutations to Him who is the supreme cause of this world throughout its states such as waking and the rest, and by whom the qualities (guṇas) move;
to Him, the Great One, into whom the hosts of sense-deities do not enter, just as sparks cannot enter a spreading fire. (21)
The sages said: "This one is not capable of being controlled by the most powerful, for he is the master of illusion; nor does our word reach him as an object of perception.
We have gone for refuge to that Brahman which is full, immortal, supreme, profoundly peaceful, pure, and higher than the highest. (22)
The celestial nymphs said:

We bow to that very Kṛṣṇa, who is more complete than the complete, the most supremely perfect one, from whom indeed proceed the creation and other cosmic processes through hosts of incarnations—such as the portions, sub-portions, and minute fractions—as well as those filled with his direct spiritual presence. || 23 ||
The sacrificial furrows said:
"This is the blossoming grove of creepers for the glorious one;
this is the ornament for the heart and neck of Śrī Rādhikā."
He is the Lord of the Śrī Rāsa-maṇḍala, the Sovereign of the Vraja-maṇḍala,
and the protector of the earth within the sphere of the cosmic egg.
The residents of Ramā-Vaikuṇṭha said:
"He who adorned the entire multitude of cowherd girls and Vṛndāvana with the dust of his own feet..."
We worship Him who appeared on earth as the source of terror for all the worlds, He whose arms are like the lord of serpents and who possesses manifold divine sports. || 25 ||
The companions from Śvetadvīpa said:
"Just as a young elephant effortlessly [uproots] a śilīndhra tree with its own trunk, or [lifts] Mount Puṣkara."
Holding it, the son of the King of Vraja shone;
for that compassionate one has never been forgotten by anyone.
The residents of the upper Vaikuṇṭha said:
"What is the use of their practice of yoga, they by whom no duality is seen—those whose dark-hued eyes behold the entire world as dark? (27)
Those who had taken refuge at the feet of the Unconquered One said:
"The firm bond of affection has been severed, yet it could not be severed without Hari;
having cut it, he went to Mathurā, just as a bird escapes from a serpent's coil. (28)
The women dwelling on the mountain of the world said: "O Kṛṣṇa, our pair of eyes is fixed upon you, running through the ten directions;
alas, it is not fixed anywhere else, just as a bee is fixed upon a lotus. (29)
The noble friends said:
"Through miserliness one destroys fame; through anger, the arising of a multitude of virtues;
through vices, one's wealth; and through deceit alone, one's friendship. (30)
The Maithilas said:
"One should protect one's body by giving wealth; having given one's body, one should preserve one's modesty.
Indeed, for the sake of a friend's purpose alone, one should give wealth, body, and even modesty. (31)
The women of Kauśala said:
"No one knows the state born of separation except for Jīva; even she is not able to describe it.
May we never, at any time, suffer the pain of separation from our beloved, like a deer pierced by a distant arrow. (32)
The inhabitants of the city of Ayodhyā said:
"Having rendered us hopeless and having cast away our hope,
he has gone toward the region of the city of Mathurā."
And he placed his yoga upon him; oh, how wonderful is the mind of those free from delusion! 33.
The Pulindakas said:
