"How can there be compassion for you from that son of Sumitrā, who formerly in the forest forcibly deformed Śūrpaṇakhā— who had come to him utterly overwhelmed with desire to choose him as her husband— into one of hideous appearance?"
The inhabitants of Sutala said:
"He who, having taken Bali— who was devoted, truthful, and a giver of much— bound him in anger."
"Oh, how can he perform service for that deceptive dwarf who has assumed the form of a Vāmana? (35)
The Jālandharīs said:

"Formerly, when the best of asuras, Kāyādhu—the most excellent devotee—had departed to a state of extreme suffering, this one became Nṛsiṃha and rendered him assistance; alas, supreme cruelty is now observed!"
The guardians of the earth said:
"Oh, how strange is this supreme conduct of people utterly devoid of delusion! It is not fit to be described;
one thing is on their lips and another is in their hearts—neither God nor any human being knows it. (37)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Words of the Gopīs," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the Śrī-Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 17 ||
The inhabitants of Barhiṣmatī said:

"Aho! When the Great-souled Hari, assuming the form of a boar, compassionately lifted her up from the ocean of dissolution, the merciful Pṛthu, the first king, followed after her, having taken up his bow and arrows. (1)
The forest-creeper maidens said:
"In former times, the high-souled Dhanvantari, the physician of the universe, did not distribute the nectar himself."
Then, while the gods and asuras were bound in enmity toward one another,
he who is fond of strife assumed the form of a woman and gave her away.
The daughters of the serpent-king said:
"Alas! Hari, accompanied by the son of Sumitrā, saw Śūrpaṇakhā arrive in the great forest desiring him as her husband; he then made her ugly. Oh, what unpleasant thing had she done to him?"
The daughters of the ocean said:
"How is it that she who constantly goes to hundreds of houses, bestowing both suffering and happiness upon people,
is her own wife, virtuous, and yet remains so fickle in this world?"
The Apsarases said:
"Out of affection for him, the ears and nose of Rāvaṇa’s sister were indeed removed;
let that story be abandoned, for he too showed mercy toward you."
The celestial beings said:
"The Lord of All, the compassionate Master of Liberation, having led Bali away and bound him, cast him down; that it happened thus is truly wonderful. (6)
The Ādityas said:
"In ancient times, when Manu was performing peaceful austerities for ten thousand years with Śatarūpā, that ocean of compassion later protected him when he was being harassed by the Daityas. (7)

The beings said: "O you who are compassionate toward the distressed, why did you not first protect Dhruva and Kāyādhava, your devotees who had previously fallen into hardship, out of mercy? Why was it later? (8)
The descendants of Raju said: Hari, testing the truthfulness of the virtuous Rukmāṅgada, Hariścandra, and Ambarīṣa,
bestowed upon them once again the fortune of a devotee.
The attendants of Tamas said:
"By whom Vṛndā was previously deceived through trickery by that powerful deceiver,
even he has now been deceived by this deceitful and powerful Kubjā."
For even a single-edged sword, though curved, slays many people;
how much more so Kubjā, who is triple-curved and possesses a three-fold bend like Śrī Kṛṣṇa?
While they were watching the path of Kṛṣṇa, their eyes became intensely distressed;
indeed, Vāmana made them take a step toward the limit.
Our skin has turned yellow, our feet have become weak,
and our minds have fallen into intense delusion in this month of Mādhava, without Mādhava.
"Alas, O Fate! At what time shall we behold the Son of Nanda, who has arrived at the hour of dawn adorned with the marks of his rival's theft? (14)
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus meditating upon Kṛṣṇa, the gopīs, overwhelmed by love and filled with longing, wept; they fainted and fell to the ground. (15)
Having consoled each of them individually with skillful words and having awakened all the cowherd women to understanding, Uddhava then spoke to Rādhā.
Uddhava said: O Kṛṣṇa, the most perfect one, son of Vṛṣabhānu’s best daughter; O Queen of Vraja, I bow to you; grant me permission to depart.
"O auspicious lady, give a letter to the high-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
having bowed down to him, I shall quickly bring him back to your presence. (18)
Śrī Nārada said:
Then Rādhā, taking her pen and the ink-pot, quickly began to reflect upon the news; meanwhile, tears flowed forth from her eyes.
Whatever leaf, accompanied by a pen, was brought by Rādhā, each one became moistened by the waters from her lotus-like eyes. || 20 ||
Seeing Rādhā, whose lotus-eyes were eager for the sight of Kṛṣṇa and who was shedding a stream of tears, Uddhava spoke with wonder: 21.
Uddhava said:
"O Rādhā, why do you write? Why indeed do you cause such distress?
I shall tell him of all my agony, even without your letter. (22)
Śrī Nārada said: Having heard these words of Rādhā, who was now free from all distress,
Uddhava was then honored by her and by all the gopīs.
Having bowed down and circumambulated the supreme Rādhā, the mistress of the rāsa dance,
and having repeatedly bowed again and again to the assembly of gopīs, he took his leave.
Having mounted a divine chariot adorned with jewel ornaments, he,
having abandoned his pride as a servant, went to Nanda at twilight.
When the sun had risen, Uddhava, having bowed to the cowherd woman Yaśomatī and having taken leave of King Nanda and the nine Nandas, [departed].
Having taken leave of the world from Vṛṣabhānu and Upanandā,
as well as all the friends of Kṛṣṇa, he mounted his chariot and departed.
All the cowherds and the groups of cowherd women followed him for a long distance;
then Uddhava, turning back out of affection for them, went to Mathurā.
In a secluded spot at the Akṣaya-vaṭa on the charming bank of the Kṛṣṇā, Uddhava—
the most excellent in intelligence— having bowed to Kṛṣṇa and circumambulated Him, spoke with a voice faltering with love, his lotus-eyes overflowing with tears. (29)
Uddhava said:
O Lord, what can be told to me by You, the witness of all things?
Bestow welfare upon Rādhikā and grant Your vision to the gopīs.
"I shall bring Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the gods of gods, into your presence;
O ocean of mercy, protect, protect this word of mine! (31)
Just as [you heard] the vows of Prahlāda and Rukmāṅgada,
and directly those of King Bali, Khaṭvāṅga,
as well as those of Ambarīṣa and Dhruva, so [may you hear] mine.
And it has been performed, O Lord of Devotion; protect, protect! || 32 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Arrival of Uddhava," within the Dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva, in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, specifically in the words of the Gopīs.
Śrī Nārada said: Having thus heard the words of the devotee, Acyuta, who is affectionate toward his devotees,
remembered the words he himself had spoken and resolved to depart.
Having entrusted Baladeva with all the burdens of state affairs, [he mounted] a chariot richly adorned with gold, covered with a network of tinkling bells, and yoked to fleet horses.
Mounting a chariot that shone like the sun, he, filled with impetuous joy,
set out for Nanda’s cowherd settlement to grant an audience to his devotees.
Beholding Govardhana, Gokula, and the forest of Vṛndāvana,
Kṛṣṇa arrived at the charming sandy bank on the shore of the Yamunā.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa, the lord of Vraja, by the millions upon millions, the cows ran toward him from all sides,
their udders overflowing with milk out of affection.
With their ears and tails raised and hanging down, accompanied by their calves, they had morsels of food in their mouths; with tearful faces, they were free from distress.
O King, as Uddhava looked on, they obstructed that chariot— along with its driver, its horses, and its banner— as clouds shroud the sun in autumn.
Śrī Gopāla, calling each of their names individually and touching their limbs with his auspicious hand, experienced great joy.
Seeing a herd of cows that had gone near him,
Śrīdāma and the other boys of Vraja were amazed and spoke to one another from a distance.
The cowherds said:
[Behold] that chariot, with its banner bearing a water-pot and the speed of the wind, resounding with the sound of its well-crafted bell-metal plates.
How did you friends obstruct the cows, which were yoked to a hundred horses and possessed the splendor of a hundred suns? || 10 ||
Indeed, no one else comes here with these joyful greetings for the cows, but rather the son of the King of Vraja;
our right limbs are throbbing, and Śrī Nīlakaṇṭha is stretching out the archway.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having deliberated thus in their minds, all the cowherds gathered together and beheld Mādhava, their friend, as people see a vanished object.
Leaping down from his chariot, Kṛṣṇa himself, the most perfect one,
overwhelmed by their love, placed them all before him with his two arms.
Shedding tears from his lotus-eyes, he embraced each of them individually.
Oh, who on this earth is able to describe the greatness of devotion? 14.
O King of Mithilā, all those cowherds wept, shedding tears;
overwhelmed by the agitation caused by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they were unable to speak. 15.
The most perfect Lord himself, with a sweet voice,
consoled those who were bowed down and overwhelmed with the bliss of love.
Uddhava, who had been sent along with the boys by Śrī Kṛṣṇa to deliver a message,
reported that Śrī Kṛṣṇa had arrived at Nanda’s city.
Having heard that Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the son of Nanda and beloved of the cowherds, had arrived, they all went out to welcome him, their desires completely fulfilled. (18)
With the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, and tabors, with sweet-toned instruments, with full water-pots, and with the chanting of the Vedas by the twice-born;
with perfumes, unbroken grains of rice, and auspicious parched grain—King Nanda, accompanied by Yaśodā, proceeded forth in splendor.
Then, placing at the head of the procession an elephant exalted with rut, its trunk bearing vermilion and a golden chain,
Śrī Vṛṣabhānu and the other leaders arrived.
The dispositions therein are associated with the digit of Kṛti. || 20 ||
Nanda and Upananda, the Vṛṣabhānus, and the cowherds— both old, young, and children—
all adorned with garlands, flutes, guñjā berries, and peacock feathers.
They have departed with their desires fulfilled. || 21 ||
Singing from afar of the son of the king’s son, they danced,
shaking their yellow garments; holding flutes, they carried staffs and horns in their hands.
They were greatly delighted and intensely longing for the sight [of him]. || 22 ||
Having heard from the mouths of her friends that Hari had arrived,
Rādhā rose from her bed;
filled with great joy, she gave her own ornaments to them.
She was as delighted as a fresh lotus pond with its own fragrance. || 23 ||
O King of Mithilā, the gopīs of the cowherd community, numbering thirty-two, eight, sixteen, and two, accompanied by their respective groups,
mounted a beautiful palanquin for Rādhā.
He arrived for the purpose of beholding Śrīdhara. || 24 ||
For indeed, O Lord of Kings, it is said that millions of cowherd women,
having abandoned all their household duties and with their garments and ornaments disarrayed, [came to the forest].
They arrived, their bodies and minds agitated by love. || 25 ||
Seeing the entire settlement of Vraja— including its trees, cattle, deer, and birds— arrived there overcome with love,
as well as his father, King Nanda, and his mother;
Kṛṣṇa bowed down with his palms joined in reverence at his head.

King Nanda, having finally attained his long-held desire, took his son—who had returned after a long time—into his arms and pressed him to his heart; he then bathed him with the waters of his own beautiful eyes, while Yaśodā looked on.
Having paid homage to Nanda, Upananda, Vṛṣabhānu, and all the elders, and having received the blessings bestowed by them,
as well as mutual greetings with his companions;
And he stood there, lifting the small ones by seizing them with his hands. || 28 ||
Then Hari himself, having mounted the chariot and placed Nanda upon the elephant along with Yaśodā,
set out accompanied by Nanda’s kinsmen and herds of cattle.
He entered the city of the illustrious King Nanda.

At that very moment, when Hari had arrived at his home, the gods indeed rained down flowers, the women of the city scattered parched grain as a traditional offering, and the cowherds raised auspicious cries of "Victory! there.
"Blessed is this supreme friend of yours, Uddhava, for he has indeed been made manifest here before our eyes.
Thus spoke the cowherds, the protectors of the people, their voices choked with emotion as they lamented in this way. (31)
O Lord of Men, I have thus related to you the return of Hari to Vraja;
what more do you wish to hear concerning the gods and asuras?
The supreme conduct is auspicious and wonderful.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Festival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s Arrival," in the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Bahulāśva said: What did the Lord do first in person within the circle of Vraja?
How indeed did He grant His vision to Rādhā and the cowherd girls? (1)
Having fulfilled the desire of the gopīs, he indeed returned to Mathurā;
tell me this, O best of brahmins, for you are the most knowledgeable of both the higher and the lower.
Śrī Nārada said:
Summoned by Rādhā at the time of twilight, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself went to a secluded, eternally cool plantain grove. (3)
A vast, shimmering mansion of clouds, anointed with *raṃbhā* and sandalwood,
emitting sprays of black aloe-wood, and dripping nectar from the rays of the moon.
Such a forest, constantly reduced to ashes by the brilliance of the fire of separation from Rādhā, is indeed protected by Kṛṣṇa’s hope for her.
Right there, all the hundreds of groups of cowherd girls assembled and informed her of Mādhava’s arrival.
Rising suddenly, the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu herself,
surrounded by her friends, came to bring Kṛṣṇa.
Offering a seat, water for the feet, and the arghya— delightful services—
the one who excels in virtue spoke words of auspicious inquiry with great respect.
Upon seeing Hari, who captivates the sweetness of ten million youthful Cupids, Rādhā abandoned her sorrow, just as one abandons the notion of material qualities upon realizing the Absolute Brahman.
There, the daughter of Kīrti, being delighted, prepared for amorous dalliance;
yet, now that the traveler Kṛṣṇa has departed, she has performed no such dalliance.
Neither sandalwood paste nor betel-leaf, nor food equal to nectar, was enjoyed;
neither a celestial bed was prepared, nor was any laughter ever indulged in.
To Kṛṣṇa, who was most perfectly complete, his most perfectly complete beloved,
shedding tears of joy, spoke with a voice faltering with emotion.
Rādhā said:
"How far away is the city of the Yadus? Why have you not arrived, and what are you doing?
What secret sorrow shall I speak of to you, the witness of everything? (13)
There is neither the queen of King Saudāsa, Damayantī, nor Maithilī; whom here can I name as having placed separation before her as an enemy? (14)
The gopīs, who share my very same refuge, are never able to describe [Him], just as the cakorī bird cannot describe the autumn moon, nor the peahen the new rain-cloud. (15)
I long for you, Śrī Vṛndāvana-candra, who are dark as a rain cloud;
you were quickly revealed to me by your fortunate friend Uddhava.
There is no one else in Vraja by whose love you have come.
Śrī Nārada said:
Seeing his supreme beloved speaking thus and constantly weeping, his limbs were overcome with compassion.
With tears flowing from his eyes, he immediately comforted him with wise words while clasping him with both arms.
The Blessed Lord said: "Do not grieve, O Rādhā; I have come here because of my love for you.
Our splendor is one and indivisible, though it appears as two to people."
Just as there is whiteness in milk, so are we always united in auspiciousness;
wherever I am, you are always there, for there is indeed no separation between us.
I am the full Supreme Brahman, and you are the source of the universe, standing as its boundary;
perceive through true knowledge that the separation between us is unreal.
Just as the great wind, omnipresent, is eternally situated in space,
so too is water in its subtle form, and fire pervades the fuel.
O fair-faced one, just as the earth exists separately within and without,
so am I free from modification, unlike the three qualities which are like impurities.
In that same way, you should perceive my true nature; then you will become eternally blissful.
O fair-faced one, by the notion of "I" and "mine," a duality exists.

Just as long as one remains in the midst of the forest, the eye does not perceive its own form, the sun that has arisen; likewise, as long as this [individual] is within the qualities born of primordial matter (pradhāna), he does not see the Supreme Self, but when those [qualities] have passed away, he sees it.
The mind attached to the qualities (guṇas) leads indeed to bondage, while the mind colored by devotion to the Supreme Person (puruṣa) leads to liberation.
They say the mind is the cause of both; therefore, having conquered it from afar, one should move about free from attachment.
For all states of mind arise from one another and not from a single source, O beautiful lady; therefore,
you must naturally bestow your love upon me alone.
There is nothing on earth equal to love. || 26 ||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard these words of Hari, Kīrtinandinī became delighted and,
together with the gopīs, worshipped Kṛṣṇa Mādhava.
Then, on the full moon night of Kārtika, Hari himself went to the circle of the rāsa dance and played his flute together with Rādhā and the gopīs.
O King, near the Yamunā, the Lord of Rādhikā shone resplendently upon the stage of the rāsa dance with Rādhā and beautiful women. 29.
Assuming as many forms as there were gopīs at the rāsa dance, Hari,
the Lord of Vṛndāvana, took delight in the divine Vṛndāvana.
With jingling anklets and girdle, adorned with a forest garland,
wearing yellow garments, holding a lotus, and bearing a crown like the rising sun.
Adorned with shimmering golden earrings that flash like streaks of lightning, holding a staff and playing a flute, he is dressed as a dancer and possesses the luster of a rain cloud.
Enriched by the shimmering Kaustubha gem and with his glistening earrings swaying,
he shone with Rādhā in the Rāsa dance, like the Lord of Rati with Rati.
Just as Śakra is with Śacī in heaven, or as a cloud is with lightning,
so is the Lord of Vṛndāvana with Vṛndā in the forest of Vṛndaka.
Beholding Vṛndāvana, the riverbanks, the forests, and the groves, he went with the hosts of gopīs to Mount Govardhana.
Observing the pride of the hundreds of groups of gopīs, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of Vraja,
vanished right there along with Rādhā.
Then, three *yojanas* distant from Govardhana, he went to the beautiful Rohitācala mountain, which was permeated with the fragrance of sandalwood.
Beholding the bowers and thickets of creepers while conversing with her,
he wandered upon the delightful mountain, which was a dwelling place for golden vines.
There lies the beautiful Devasaras lake, created by Badrinātha,
teeming with pāṭhīna fish, tortoises, crocodiles, swans, and cranes.
It was adorned here and there with thousand-petaled lotuses,
filled with the humming of bees and the warbling of male cuckoos.
On that shore, rich with the fragrance of blooming lotuses and stirred by a gentle breeze,
Mādhava sat down together with Rādhā.
On that shore, he saw the great sage named Ṛbhu performing penance,
standing perpetually on one foot, entirely absorbed in meditation upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
For sixty thousand and six hundred years,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa beheld him who was peaceful, without food, and without water.
Beholding him, Rādhā asked, and smiling, she said to Mādhava:
"O Lord, manifest Your majesty; behold the devotion of this great sage."
Those auspicious words loudly uttered by Ṛbhu, "O Ṛbhu!", were not heard at all by him who had indeed reached the end. || 45 ||
Then Hari quickly vanished from his heart;
seeing Hari gone from his meditation, the lord of sages was greatly amazed.
Opening his eyes, he beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa arrived with Rādhā,
like a dark cloud accompanied by lightning, delighting the ten directions.
Rising immediately, devoted to the service of Hari, he circumambulated Hari together with Rādhikā;
bowing with his head, he fell at their feet and spoke to Kṛṣṇa with many faltering syllables.
Śrī Ṛbhu said: Salutations to Kṛṣṇa and to Kṛṣṇā, to Rādhā and to Mādhava;
to the Most Perfect Female and to the Most Perfect Male. (49)
Constant salutations to the Lord who is dark as a rain-cloud, and to Śyāmā; constant salutations again and again to the Lord of the Rāsa dance, and to the Mistress of the Rāsa. || 50 ||
Salutations again and again to the one whose divine play transcends Goloka, the playful consort; salutations to the presiding goddess of countless universes and the storehouse of countless universes.
To remove the burden of the earth, they have descended to the world; for my peace, they have come together here,
having made peace with one another after their conflict.
Salutations to you both, Hari and Rādhikā.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the great sage, his eyes overflowing with tears and filled with the bliss of divine love, gave up his life at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa. (53)
At that very moment, a light emerged, possessing a radiance equal to ten suns;
it circled through the ten directions and became absorbed into Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Beholding the devotion of his devotee, which was characterized by love, Śrī Kṛṣṇa shed tears of joy and called out to him with affection.
Again, from the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the sage emerged, possessing a form identical to Kṛṣṇa's, resembling ten million gods of love, with an exceedingly beautiful countenance. (56)
Taking him by both arms and placing him against his heart, the Compassionate One comforted him and laid his divine, auspicious hand upon him.

Having circumambulated Hari and prostrated before Rādhikā, the sage Ṛbhu ascended his beautiful chariot and departed for the realm of Goloka, illuminating the region of Mithilā and the quarters of the earth, O King.
Seeing the supreme liberation of the great sage Ṛbhu, Śrī Rādhikā was filled with intense wonder;
for a long time, she shed tears of bliss.
The daughter of Vṛṣabhānu spoke to Kṛṣṇa.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Ṛbhu," in the Rāsa festival section of the Śrī Nārada-Bahulāśva dialogue within the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Śrī Rādhā said:
This tiger among sages is blessed; he was a great devotee full of love for you, and he attained your very form because even you had tears upon your face.
O destroyer of evil, you are worthy to perform the funeral rites for this body;
moreover, through his ascetic power, this body shines with a stainless form. (2)
Śrī Nārada said:
While Rādhā was speaking there, her body also became a river;
carrying [the waters] and destroying sins, it is seen on Mount Rohita.
Seeing that his body had also become a river, Rādhā was greatly amazed;
the daughter of the excellent Vṛṣabhānu spoke to the son of King Nanda.
Śrī Rādhā said:
"O Great Sage, how did this body attain the state of water?
O Lord, you ought to sever this doubt of mine completely. (5)
The Blessed Lord said:
"O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, this lord of sages is endowed with devotion characterized by love;
therefore, his body has reached a state of melting."
Upon seeing me, the bestower of boons, the great sage became filled with joy;
his body attained the state of water, just as I previously attained the state of fluidity.
Śrī Rādhā said:
O God of gods, O ocean of mercy, how have you come to this state of melting?
This has indeed become a wonder to me; tell me everything in detail.
The Blessed Lord said: In this very context, they cite this ancient history,
by the mere hearing of which the supreme destruction of sin occurs.
Long ago, Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, who was born from my navel-lotus,
empowered by my boon, constantly created Prakṛti through austerity.
The auspicious Nārada was born from the lap of Brahmā as he was engaged in creation;
intoxicated by devotion, he wandered the earth singing of my footprints.
Once, the god Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, said to Nārada:
"O one of great intelligence, create progeny; abandon this aimless wandering."
Having heard those words, Nārada, intent on knowledge, spoke this:
"O Father, I do not create the world, which causes sorrow, delusion, and the like. (13)
"I shall practice devotion to Hari, accompanied by the chanting of His glories;
you too, being exceedingly afflicted by suffering, should abandon the creation of the world. (14)
Enraged, Brahmā, his lower lip quivering, cursed him and said:
"O evil-minded one, become a Gandharva devoted to singing for an entire kalpa!"
Thus, O Rādhā, by virtue of that curse,
Upabarhaṇa became the lord of the Gandharvas for the duration of a single kalpa in the abode of the gods.
Once, having gone to the world of Brahmā surrounded by women,
he set his mind upon those beautiful ones and sang without keeping time.
Brahmā cursed him again: "O evil-minded one, become a Śūdra!
Then, by that curse of Brahmā, he indeed became the son of a maidservant.
O Rādhā, in former times, through association with the virtuous, he attained the status of being a son of Brahmā;
intoxicated by devotion, he wandered the earth singing of my own footsteps.
The Lord of Sages, the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, my beloved, the sun of knowledge,
is the supreme Bhāgavata, Nārada himself, whose mind is always fixed on me.
Once, Nārada, who wanders everywhere, intent on singing while observing the worlds, went to the region named Ilāvṛta.
Where the river Jambū flows, dark with the juice of jambū fruits, there,
O beloved, the gold known as Jāmbūnada is produced.
In that region, the yogi Nārada beheld the city of Veda, constructed with palaces of jewels and surrounded by divine women and men.
Some indeed were devoid of feet, lacking ankles and shorn of knees; they were without calves, with deformed hips, or had emaciated thighs and crooked waists.
He beheld women and men with their teeth loose, their shoulders hunched, their faces bent down, their necks twisted, and their limbs broken.
"Aha! What a wonder this is! Having seen them all, the sage said:
"All of you have lotus-like faces, divine bodies, and auspicious garments. (26)
Are you gods or secondary deities, or perhaps the best of sages? For all of you are accompanied by musical instruments and devoted to beautiful singing. || 27 ||
"How is it that your limbs are broken? Tell me this quickly!
When he had spoken thus, they all replied with dejected minds.
The Passions said:
"O Sage, a great suffering has arisen within our very bodies;
it must indeed be told before Him who is capable of removing it. (29)
"O Sage, we are the Passions (Rāgas) who always dwell in the city of the Vedas;
O giver of honor, hear the reason why we have become broken-limbed. (30)
Born as the son of Hiraṇyagarbha, he bore the name Nārada;
intoxicated with love, he sang the verses of Dhruva at an unseasonable hour.
That great sage wandered this earth at his own will;
and because of his singing at the wrong time— discordant, devoid of rhythm, and lacking melody— we all became broken in our limbs.
Having heard those words, Nārada was struck with wonder;
his pride departed, he spoke as if mocking Rāga.
The sage said:
"By what method indeed may the knowledge of both time (kāla) and the ender of time (tālaya) arise here, endowed with its vowels? Tell me this quickly."
The Passions said:
When Sarasvatī herself, the foremost beloved of the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha,
gives instruction to him, then the sage shall become a knower of Time.
Then, having heard their words, Nārada, who is compassionate toward the distressed, went quickly to the bright mountain for the sake of obtaining the grace of Sarasvatī. || 36 ||
O Queen of Vraja, for a hundred divine years he constantly performed most difficult penance,
abstaining from food and water, absorbed in meditation upon the Goddess of Speech.
Then, having cast off that [portion] named Śubhra, which purified the mountain, it became the mountain named Nārada through the ascetic power of Nārada. (38)
At the conclusion of his austerities, the sage Nārada beheld Śrī Sarasvatī, the goddess of speech in person—the beloved of Viṣṇu, possessed of divine complexion—approaching him. (39)
Rising suddenly, bowing to her, and circumambulating her with his face bowed low,
the lord of sages offered a hymn of praise for the beauty, virtues, and sweetness of her form.
Śrī Nārada said:

I bow to Sarasvatī, whose face is like ten million moons; she is resplendent with earrings, armlets, a crown, and bracelets possessing the brilliance of the rising sun’s orb, and she is delighted by the sound of her shimmering, tinkling anklets.
I always pay homage to the rising Kalahaṃsa bird,
whose feet move gracefully and whose trembling beak is like a cluster of pearls from a necklace washed clean.
[He beheld] the auspicious Sarasvatī, who sustains [all beings]. || 42 ||
I bow to you, Sarasvatī, the bestower of auspiciousness, who holds in her two stainless hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, along with a book and a lute.
She who consists of the universe, who consists of Brahman, and who is captivating to the mind. || 43 ||
O Supreme One, clad in shimmering white silken garments,
grant me the knowledge of the eternal sound, which is exceedingly auspicious,
so that I may indeed become non-dual within the Imperishable.
May I be at the very summit in the circle of supreme passion. || 44 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
"Whoever, having risen at dawn, recites this divine hymn spoken by Nārada which removes dullness, shall become possessed of learning in this world. (45)
Then the goddess of speech, being pleased, gave to the high-souled Nārada the lute Devadattā, which was adorned with the essence of the sacred sounds.
Together with men of passion and women full of passion, as well as their sons,
and in accordance with the distinctions of place and time, along with rhythmic beats, measures, and musical notes.
With fifty-six crores of divisions and countless internal subdivisions, along with villages, auspicious dances accompanied by musical instruments, and melodic modulations (mūrchanās). || 48 ||
Sarasvatī herself, the foremost beloved of the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha,
taught Nārada by means of perfected words that could be easily understood.
O Rādhā, having made that assembly circle free from any rival passion,
Vāgdevī, the beloved of Viṣṇu, departed for Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nārada," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Mathurā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. || 21 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
"To whom should this secret, which is the form of passion and captivating to the mind, be given?
Reflecting thus with his intellect, he went to the city of the Gandharvas.
Having made the Gandharva named Tuṃbaru his disciple, that Nārada,
devoted to the playing of the lute, sang sweetly of my virtues.
Seeking those before whom he might sing this captivating song of passion,
Nārada approached Śakra to find a worthy listener.
Seeing him thus unextinguished, Nārada, the best of sages,
went to the world of the Sun together with his friend Tumburu.
Seeing Sūrya rushing toward him on his chariot, the great sage,
the best of divine seers, quickly went to the side of Śiva.
O Rādhā, having beheld that Lord of Beings, the knower of the reality of knowledge, whose eyes were motionless in meditation, Nārada departed for the world of Brahmā.
Seeing Brahmā busily engaged in the creation of the world,
the sage went to Vaikuṇṭha, which is saluted by all the worlds, the abode of Viṣṇu.
Seeing the Lord of Devotees, who is affectionate toward his devotees, going somewhere for the sake of food, the lord of yogis then proceeded from there together with Tumburu.

O daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, for those who are masters of yoga, it is said that there is no distinction between the interior and the exterior of the three worlds; they do not attain [rebirth] through their past actions.
Having transcended millions upon millions of cosmic eggs, the Lord of Sages proceeded to Goloka, the supreme abode beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
Having swiftly crossed the dustless river filled with billowing waves,
he went to the beautiful Vṛndāvana, which resounded with the humming of bees.
Having beheld Mount Govardhana, which was always endowed with the six seasons and possessed groves of creepers and pavilions for the Maruts, he arrived at my bower.
"Who are you two? From where have you come? And tell us, what is your purpose?
Thus questioned by their friends, the sage and Tumburu spoke. (13)
"We two are skilled singers; we shall [sing of] the most perfect sound of the lute, which is Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the husband of Rādhikā. (14)
The two best of bards have come to cause the supreme Kala to hear;
this message must be spoken to the high-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (15)
Having heard this, my female companions informed me accordingly;
then, by my command, they came and with gentle words gave permission for the two bards to depart.
In the courtyard of the mango grove, filled with the brilliance of ten million shining suns,
enriched by the embedded Kaustubha gem, and adorned with waving, beautiful chowries.
Under a parasol of shimmering pearls and accompanied by millions of female companions,
they both beheld me standing there in person upon a great lotus.
Having bowed, circumambulated, and stood there by my command,
he praised me and proceeded to speak of my virtues.
Striking his musical instrument, the lute Devadattā, which was like the nectar of sound,
Nārada sang a sweet, peerless melody together with Tumburu.
Satisfied, shaking my head at that praiseworthy sound, and being intent on love, I gave myself over and attained the state of water. (21)
That water which has arisen from my body is indeed known as the fluid of Brahman;
for heaps of cosmic eggs by the millions upon millions are indeed rolling therein.
O Rādhā, like the fruits of the indrāyaṇa tree at its end within that auspicious water,
this universe, the womb of Pṛśni, is clearly my own abode.
Having pierced through that [layer] and arrived manifest in this auspicious Manvantara,
the ancients know her as the celestial river, the illustrious Gaṅgā, the remover of sins.
In heaven she is called Mandākinī; on earth she is Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī;
and below, she is called Bhogavatī—thus the triple-pathed river flows in three ways.
For a man who goes to bathe and bows down at every step, the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices is not difficult to attain. (26)
Whoever should utter "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā," even from hundreds of yojanas away,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
In the Kali age, the Gaṅgā destroys the sins of a hundred births by being seen, those of two hundred births by being drunk,
and those of a thousand births by being bathed in.
Truly, their birth is fruitful for those who behold the Jāhnavī;
the birth of those who do not behold the Jāhnavī has passed in vain.
For just as Virajā attained a state of melting out of fear of you,
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, so too did the daughters of Virajā attain that same state of liquefaction.
Just as the Kṛṣṇā river is Viṣṇu, as the Veṇī is the god Śiva, as Brahmā is the Kakudminī, and as the Gaṅgā and the Gandakī are Apsarases; || 31 ||

And while the mṛdaṅga drums resounded, shimmering with the dance of courtesans.
The great lord of Vidarbha settled the two princes there. ||43||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Journey to the City of Kuṇḍina," in the Śrīdvārakākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gargasamhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 4 ||
The venerable Nārada said:
The lotus-eyed daughter of Bhīṣma meditated upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa.
Or he thought to himself, "Alas, my labor is in vain," as he meditated upon him who is dark as a rain cloud.
Rukmiṇī said:
"Alas! My marriage has been postponed; Kṛṣṇacandra himself does not come."
O Creator, I do not know what the reason is here that the lord of the earth still does not return even today. ||2||
For this best of Yadus, the foremost of gods, has seen some slight impurity in me, O Creator.
Having surely exerted himself excessively, he is coming to seize me by the hand; what shall I do? ||3||
Alas! For me, an unfortunate woman, neither the Creator nor even the moon-crested Lord Śiva is truly favorable.
Neither was the one-tusked elephant nor Gaurī averse [to him], for neither the cows nor the brahmins were unfriendly.
The venerable Nārada said:
Thus reflecting, that daughter of Bhīṣma wandered through the courtyards and terraces of the house.
Wandering about, she beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa from the pinnacle of her house.
At that very moment, her left side throbbed as she spoke.
By that, the illustrious Bhaiṣmī, who knows the proper time and is all-auspicious, was pleased. ||6||
Urged by Kṛṣṇa, the brāhmaṇa then arrived immediately;
he slowly related everything regarding Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s arrival to her.
Then, being pleased, the illustrious daughter of Bhīṣma prostrated at his feet.
"O Brahmin, I shall not go from your lineage; this is my word," he said.
Having heard that Rāma and Kṛṣṇa had arrived, eager to witness the wedding.
Bhīṣmaka went out, accompanied by Brahmins, to lead her away, being empowered by that [rite].
And [he placed them] abundantly in auspicious vessels filled with fragrances and unbroken grains of rice.
Having taken up a heap of garments and jewels, accompanied by auspicious songs and instrumental music.
And having prepared crores of honey-mixtures arranged in arrays of jars.
Then, having worshipped Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, the supreme lords, according to the prescribed rites.
And thinking, "Alas, she does not give this to him," he became deeply distressed in mind.
Having established [him] in Ānandanavana and bowed down, he returned to his own home. ||12||
Having heard that the son of Śrī Vasudeva, the supreme lord and treasury of beauty in the three worlds, had arrived.
The citizens, having arrived with their hands cupped in reverence, drank the supreme nectar from the lotus of his face.
"Indeed, Rukmiṇī alone is worthy to be his wife, and no other," so said the city-dwellers.
Having bestowed their own merits for the sake of marriage, they became the very embodiments of the digits of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s loveliness. ||14||
Perhaps at some time we people have actually come to the house of our father-in-law.
Then we shall behold the state of having accomplished our purpose; what is the use of a long life in this world?
And while the worlds were speaking thus, O King, for the purpose of worshipping the daughter of Bhīṣma as a mountain goddess.
Accompanied by all her female companions, she departed from the inner apartments, her mind captivated by Kṛṣṇa.

With the sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, and many cymbals, along with excellent singers, bards, and panegyrists, and the charming gestures of the dancing courtesans, there arose the loud, auspicious cry of "Victory! (Jaya).
She who possesses the splendor of ten million lunar orbs, wearing the rising sun as her ear-ornament—that very Goddess Śrī.
The attendants at his side served him with shimmering sunshades, fans, and beautiful whisks. ||18||
Drawing white-sworded blades from their scabbards, heroic foot-soldiers rushed here and there.
Likewise, chariot-warriors on horses and elephants, with weapons raised, guarded her from afar.
Having reached the temple of the Goddess, she stood in the beautiful courtyard—tranquil, pure, and with her lotus-like hands and feet washed clean.
Having approached her, with speech restrained and palms joined in reverence, he worshipped Bhavānī, who removes the fear of worldly existence.
O Durgā, who are endowed with your own lineage, O Śivā, O Auspicious One, I bow to you perpetually, O Bhavānī.
May the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, the Supreme Sovereign who is himself beyond primordial nature, become my husband. (21)
O Śubhā, do not speak thus; utter the name of Kṛṣṇa with reference to the King of Cedi, and choose a boon.
While her friends were speaking thus, the daughter of Bhīṣma spoke further in the abode of Bhavānī.
Thus spoke Bhaimī to her friends while they were speaking, though this young girl of yours was unaware.
With perfumes, unbroken grains of rice, incense, ornaments, and the like; with garlands, wreaths, rows of lamps, offerings, and garments. || 23 ||
And with cakes, betel, fruits, and sugarcane, he worshipped Bhavānī with supreme devotion.
Then, having bowed to them and honored those auspicious women with many ornaments and other gifts, he prostrated before them.
All those women bestowed excellent gifts and most auspicious benedictions upon her.
O Lord, your form is always equal to Śatarūpā, and your conduct is always equal to the Daughter of the Mountain.
Service to her husband may be equal to that of Arundhatī, and indeed, her forbearance may be like that of the daughter of Janaka.
O daughter of Bhīṣma, such good fortune, equal to a sacrificial fee, and great splendor like that of Śacī is yours.
May you have devotion to Sarasvatī and to your husband equal to that which the virtuous have for Hari. || 26 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Departure of Rukmiṇī," in the Śrīdvārakākhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus congratulated by the auspicious blessings of the brahmin wives,
she bowed down again and again to the Goddess, who was herself surrounded by the brahmin women.
Then, having abandoned her vow as a sage, the daughter of Bhīṣma slowly emerged from the cave of Girijā along with her female companions and friends.
The heroes suddenly beheld Bhaiṣmī, whose eyes were like lotuses and who resembled ten million moons, just as poor men might behold a great treasure.
The horsemen, chariot-warriors, elephant-riders,
and foot-soldiers who had assembled as guards were bewildered upon seeing Rukmiṇī.
Then, by her side-long glances and smiles—sharp arrows discharged from the bow of Kāma—the soldiers, abandoning their weapons, fell down, tormented by desire. || 5 ||
On a chariot with the speed of the wind, resounding with the tinkling of bells and anklets, yoked to horses capable of securing the highest bliss, and adorned with many banners.
With the swift impact of his own army, he shattered that host,
just as the wind disperses a lotus grove— Hari, with Dāruka as his charioteer.
While his enemies were looking on, the Lord, the son of Tārkṣya, quickly approached the group of women and placed the daughter of Bhīṣma upon his chariot, as if she were nectar.
While the gods looked on, O King, he carried off the princess,
repeatedly twanging his divine Śārṅga bow, the best of weapons.
Then, as Hari returned to his own army with great speed,
the celestial drums resounded, and at that time the drums of the Yādavas also rang out.
The Siddhas and Siddha-kanyās, as well as the gods, being filled with joy, showered flowers born of the Nandana grove upon the chariot of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then Hari, accompanied by Rāma, proceeded slowly amidst shouts of victory,
like a lion emerging from the midst of a pack of jackals.
Then, when a great clamor arose and Rumiṇī was being carried away,
there occurred a mutual clash of weapons among the guards.
All those proud and most excellent kings under Jarāsaṃdha’s command could not endure their own humiliation and the supreme loss of their glory that had occurred.
"Alas! Woe to us, for our fame has been snatched away by cowherds, just as lions' pride is taken by jackals; what else could this be but defeat? (15)
Having spoken thus, overcome with anger, they cast aside their gaming pieces and other such things; then, clad in armor and joined by their armies, they seized a multitude of weapons.
Filled with rage, Pauṇḍraka came with two akṣauhiṇīs,
and the great hero Vidūratha with three akṣauhiṇīs.
The exceedingly fierce Dantavakra was accompanied by five akṣauhiṇīs,
while Śālva, the lord of Rājapura, arrived swiftly with three akṣauhiṇīs.
The mighty Jarāsandha, with ten akṣauhiṇīs, came forward to fight against the high-souled Yādavas. (19)
And other partisans of the King of Cedi also arrived by the thousands to fight in the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, making their bows twang.
Beholding the army resembling the ocean at the time of universal dissolution, the best of the Yadus approached nearby to cross it, with Kṛṣṇa as their helmsman and his boat as their vessel.
A tumultuous, wonderful, and hair-raising battle took place between the two armies,
one's own and the enemy's, like that between the gods and the dānavas.
There, chariot-warriors fought with chariot-warriors, infantrymen with infantrymen, elephants with elephants, and horses with horsemen. (23)
When the darkness of weapons had arisen, the Blessed Lord, seeing Rukmiṇī overwhelmed by fear, granted her freedom from fear, saying, "Do not be afraid."
The heroic Gada, younger brother of Baladeva, shaking his great bow,
entered the clash of the enemy forces like a lordly fire entering a forest.
With their limbs pierced by arrows and their armor shattered, the chariot-warriors fell upon the surface of the earth, their horses slain and their drivers killed.
O King, foot soldiers with severed legs, suffering from the pain of mace and arrow wounds,
fell upon the earth like trees struck down by the wind.
O King, some heroes mounted on horses, pierced by the arrows of the donkeys,
fell upon the field of battle along with their steeds like large wood-apples.
With their frontal globes split by arrows from donkey-faced creatures and torn asunder here and there,
they lay fallen upon the ground, shining like pieces of *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourds.
Then, seeing the army in flight, the mighty Śālva,
who was skilled in mace-fighting, struck Gada with his mace.
Struck by a mace, Gada— the archer who was an expert in the power of mace-fighting—
immediately abandoned the bow-fight and, in that moment, hurried with his mind.
When the battle had reached its height of distress, Gada, though fallen, rose up again;
he then took up that mace which had been given to him by his elder brother.
With that heavy and firm Kaumodakī mace, weighing a hundred thousand bhāras,
Gada struck Śālva as Indra strikes a mountain with his thunderbolt.
When Śālva had fallen to the ground, crushed by the blow of the mace, Pauṇḍraka, Jarāsaṃdha, Dantavakra, and Vidūratha [advanced]. (34)
Then four [warriors], filled with rage, rushed toward Gada;
the great hero Pauṇḍraka also [struck] the banner on Gada’s chariot.
He cut [Gada’s bow] with ten arrows, as if severing friendship with harsh words.
But Dantavakra, O lord of kings, crushed Gada’s beautiful chariot with his mace, just as one crushes a fine clay pot with a staff.
Likewise, Jarāsandha caused the horses to fall upon the surface of the earth, and Vidūratha, the king of Videha, struck down the charioteer with sharp arrows.
Then the powerful Baladeva, taking up a mace,
quickly struck Dantavakra in his terrifying and fearsome mouth.
Then, as Dantavakra was fighting, by the blow of a mace, that very tooth which was crooked even in his mouth fell indeed upon the ground. || 39 ||
Then, while Hari was accompanied by Rukmiṇī, he laughed at the enemy of the Daityas,
as well as at Pauṇḍraka, Jarāsandha, and the wicked Vidūratha.
Filled with rage, Baladeva quickly struck them with his mace;
all three fell in the battle, unconscious and drenched in blood.
Having drawn back the entire assembled army with his plow,
the mighty Baladeva, filled with rage, struck them with his mace.
For an extent of ten yojanas, chariots, elephants, horses,
and foot-soldiers were crushed and pulverized, lying upon the ground and having reached the earth.
Jarāsaṃdha and all the other kings, their lives now reduced to mere remnants of death,
fled and approached Śiśupāla, saying that their festival had utterly perished.
"O tiger among men, cast off this dejection!
Will there not be a hundred marriages for you on this earth through this one alone? (45)
"Having gone to Dvārakā this very day and having bound Rāma along with Aghava, we shall make the ocean-girdled earth devoid of Yādavas. (46)
Thus exhorted by his friends, the King of Cedi went to Candrikāpura;
thereafter, all the remaining kings departed for their respective cities.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Victory of the Yadus," within the section on Dvārakā of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā, in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva concerning the abduction of Rukmiṇī.
Hari Om Tat Sat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The venerable Nārada said:
Having heard of the abduction of Rukmiṇī and the defeat of his friends.
Rukmin made a vow in the hearing of all the kings.
Without having slain Kṛṣṇa in battle and without having recovered Rukmiṇī.
"I shall not enter Kuṇḍina; I tell you this as the truth."
Having spoken thus, he [bestowed] the divine armor, thick as a cloud formed from the waters.
That great warrior also wore a helmet made from the products of the Sindhu region.
A bow made of *sauvīra* wood and two quivers made of *śālī* and *lāṭaja* wood.
Having taken a sword from a Mleccha country and a shield made of *kūṭaja* wood. || 4 ||
The great spear of Yethara and the mace produced in Gurjarāṭa.
Holding an iron club made of tin and wearing finger-guards made of *kauṅkaṇa* leather, he had bound on arm-guards of iguana skin;
he wore a diadem and jeweled earrings.
Then Rukmī, whose armlets were made of gold, set his mind upon engaging in battle.
Having ascended the victorious chariot yoked with fleet-footed horses, he departed.
He followed behind Kṛṣṇa, leading two akṣauhiṇīs.
Seeing the army gathered once again, the immensely powerful Rāma—
Accompanied by Yadusena, he fought with her in battle.
"Stay! Stay! he cried, uttering these harsh words to the Lord of the Gods.
Rukmī reached his chariot, repeatedly twanging his bow.
Release my sister quickly, if you wish to live.
Otherwise, I shall immediately send you, along with your army, to the abode of Yama.
"Defiled by the curse of Yayāti, you have become a consumer of the remnants of cowherds' food."
Fearing Jarāsaṃdha, he fled from the presence of the Yavanas.
Having spoken thus, O Kṛṣṇa, he placed an arrow upon his bow from his quiver.
Drawing it back as far as his ear, he plunged it into the heart of Hari.
Even though struck, the Blessed One [heard] his resounding bowstring.
He swiftly cut it down with an arrow, just as Garuḍa seizes a serpent.
Having quickly set aside his bow and his gold-adorned bowstring, he departed.
But Rukmī struck Hari with ten arrows in the battle.
With a single arrow, Hari [struck] the bow together with its string.
He instantly cut through Rukmin, just as one cuts away the absence of qualities through knowledge.
Kṛṣṇa split that [arrow] in two at its midpoint with a futile shaft.
In that battle, Hari struck Rukmin with hundreds of arrows.
Then the King of Vidarbha, his bow having been severed, [hurled] a great spear of shimmering luster.
He hurled a spear at Hari, just as a sage does for the sake of higher knowledge.
The wielder of the mace, the elder brother of Gada, indeed struck her with his mace.
The great spear, having split into two, struck the charioteer of Rukma.
The heavy Kaumodakī mace, falling with great velocity.
He crushed that chariot along with its horses, just as a thunderbolt crushes a mountain.
Then that son of Bhīṣmaka also struck Hari with his own mace.
The Blessed One also pulverized her once again with his discus.
The powerful Rukmī, adorned with golden armlets, took up an iron club made of vaṅga metal.
He struck Śrī Hari on the shoulder and roared like a cloud in the battle.
Even when struck, the Blessed One was like an elephant smitten by a garland.
With that very same iron club, he struck him on the field of battle.
Struck by the iron bar, Rukmī’s mind became somewhat agitated.
Threatening Mādhava in battle, he indeed seized his sword and shield.
Having severed that sword with his shield, Hari seized his own sword.
With the tip of his sword, he cut through the great helmet and the tunic.
Even when these two were simultaneously severed by him in the battle, his hand-guards remained intact.
Seeing Rukmin standing nearby with his sword-hilt in hand, [he spoke].
Having seized him with his two staff-like arms, he threw him down upon the surface of the earth.
Hari stood upon him, just as a lion stands over a deer.
In his rage, he seized the sword named Nandaka, which possessed a cool blade.
Seeing him intent on killing her brother, Rukmiṇī was overwhelmed with fear.
Falling at her husband's feet, the virtuous lady spoke piteously.
Śrī Rukmiṇī said:
O infinite Lord of gods, abode of the universe, inconceivable Lord of Yoga, O Master of the world, you are [that].
O ocean of compassion, it is not right to kill my brother, Śālabhuja, who possesses mighty arms. || 28 ||
The venerable Nārada said:
His beloved was lamenting with terrors, her face parched by grief.
Seeing the virtuous lady with her throat choked [with emotion], Hari himself turned back.
Having bound it around his waist with a sharp-edged sword, he—
Hari performed the shaving of his beard and hair on one half of his face.
Having conquered two akṣauhiṇīs, Rāma arrived accompanied by his army.
He indeed beheld Rukmiṇa bound, deformed, and miserable.
Having released the bound one, the compassionate one spoke, rebuking Hari.
"O Kṛṣṇa, this which you have done is improper and is loathed by the world. (32)
This would indeed be a source of laughter for the noble people of Vaiśālī; for such a thing could not truly happen.
Since you have made her elder brother both deformed and chief [among the attendants]. || 33 ||
What will she say to you, too, out of concern for her brother's disfigurement?
Do not grieve, O auspicious lady; be composed, O lady of pure smiles. (34)
Noble daughter Mahābuddhi, do not grieve or be despondent.
I consider whatever is done at any time—whether pleasant or indeed unpleasant—to be [the result of] that.
The entire world would come under one's control, like a mass of clouds under the power of the wind.
Know that time to be Īśvara, Viṣṇu, the Lord of those who reckon.
This notion of "I" and "mine" is the cause of bondage for the world.
An entity devoid of those two is indeed liberation; of this there is no doubt. ||37||
There is no other bestower of pleasure and pain for a person than the delusion regarding the self.
Like enemies who are actually friends, they are created by the darkness of saṃsāra. ||38||
Thus was the son of Bhīṣmaka enlightened by the divine Rāma.
Casting aside her dejection, Rukmiṇī attained joy. || 39 ||
But Rukmī, abandoned by those two, had his own desires frustrated.
Remembering the disfigurement [he had suffered], he applied his mind to asceticism.
Dissuaded by his chief ministers, he did not go to Kuṇḍina again.
He built a supreme city named Bhojakaṭa for his residence. ||41||
Goviṃda, together with Rukmiṇī, Rāma, and surrounded by the Yadus, [departed].
O King, he set out for Dvārakā, sounding the drums of victory. || 42 ||
When a great festival had arisen in the city, [he took] Rukmiṇī, whose face was beautiful.
Hari himself married her according to the prescribed rites in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. ||43||
When the marriage of Hari, the Lord of Rukmiṇī, had taken place, Śrī Rukmiṇī adorned her golden palace.
Just as Amarāvatī belongs to Purandara, so did the meritorious Dvārāvatī shine. || 44 ||
Whoever listens with devotion to this wonderful account of the marriage of Bhaiṣmī, or causes it to be heard, [attains merit].
Right here, that very devotee, endowed with spiritual power, attains liberation as one who is liberated.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Marriage of Śrī Rukmiṇī," in the Śrī Dvārakākhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
The venerable Nārada said:
O King of Mithilā, hear now of the auspiciousness of Kṛṣṇa’s other wives.
It removes all sins, is meritorious, and is the supreme increaser of longevity. || 1 ||
The Syamantaka jewel was given directly by the Sun-god to Satrājit.
That jewel was requested by Śrī Kṛṣṇa from Ugrasena.
O King of Mithilā, Satrājit did not give it up out of greed for wealth.
He who daily produces eight bhāras of gold from his own self.
Then his brother Prasena, placing that jewel upon his neck, [departed].
Having mounted a horse from Sindh, he roamed the forest for the hunt.
He too was killed by a lion, and that lion was slain by Jāmbavān.
Having taken that jewel, Jāmbavān immediately went to his own cave.
His brother Maṇigrīva, having been slain by Kṛṣṇa, has gone to the forest.
"He has not come into the midst of his own assembly," Satrājit said.
The Blessed One, smeared with ill-repute by the citizens, went to the forest.
O high-minded one, come, behold Prasena’s horse and the lion! (7)
Having gone to the cave of the king of bears, Hari himself went to seize the jewel.
Having fought for twenty-eight days, he defeated the leader of the bears.
By him, the auspicious maiden Jāmbavatī was given to Hari.
O Indra among kings, Hari returned to Dvārakā together with the jewel.
The Lord Nirlāñchana gave the jewel to Satrājit.
Ashamed, with his face cast down and filled with fear, King Satrājit [offered] the jewel.
Having taken it back again, he gave it to that high-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
O Lord of Mithilā, he gave his daughter Satyabhāmā for the sake of peace.
Hari went to Indraprastha for the sake of assisting the Pāṇḍavas.
There, indeed, he who was affectionate toward his kinsmen dwelt for the months of the rainy season. ||12||
Once, Hari, having mounted his chariot together with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, [set out].
On the beautiful bank of the Yamunā, he went forth seeking game. ||13||
While Kālindī was performing austerities, desiring Śrī Kṛṣṇa as her boon, she was pointed out by the Pāṇḍava; taking her with him, he departed. ||14||
Having arrived at Dvārakā, [he beheld] the Kālindī, the daughter of the Sun, who is enchanting to the mind.
He married Mitravinda, the enchanting daughter of the King of Avanti, according to the prescribed rites, spreading supreme auspiciousness.
Just as the Blessed One carried off Rukmiṇī at her svayaṃvara.
Having subdued the seven bulls, he won Satyā, the daughter of Nagnajit.
Behold, Hari himself married her, who was the beloved of all the worlds.
But the Blessed Lord Hari [bestowed] the auspicious daughter of the King of Kaikeya.
He married her according to the prescribed rites, as one might wed the river Kālindī.
O King, Bṛhatsena gave his daughter Lakṣmaṇā, who was endowed with auspicious marks.
Having cut through the fish's snare, the Blessed Lord Hari seized it. ||19||
Likewise, there were one hundred and sixteen thousand princesses.
Having slain Bhauma, those beautiful women were brought forth from his suppression.
In a single moment, among those women in their inner apartments, there arose...
Assuming various forms through his own illusory power (māyā), he took hold of their hands in close proximity.
Each of those powerful ones [slew] ten sons of Kṛṣṇa one by one.
By means of the perfection of his entire self, he brought forth nine new [sons] from his father.
From Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīma, Pradyumna was the first-born.
This incarnation of Kāmadeva possesses all the characteristics of his father.
The merciless Śabara, having killed the youth, threw him into the ocean.
Even though he had entered the belly of a fish, that son of Hari did not die.
Having emerged from the belly of the fish, he was protected by his wife.
Having learned the news regarding his son by Kṛṣṇa's daughter, he, who had reached full youth, [acted].
Having slain that enemy Śambara, he was united with his excellent wife.
He went to Dvārakā, O King, and that deed of his was marvelous.
Having abducted the daughter of Sarukmin from the city of Bhojakata.
O King, that great chariot-warrior married her at the site of the svayaṃvara.
From him was born a son named Niruddha, endowed with the strength of ten thousand elephants.
This is the descent of Surajyeṣṭha, possessing the luster of an autumnal blue lotus.
For he is indeed the most perfect incarnation of the fourfold manifestation.
Thus is the wonderful and most auspicious account of the marriages.
It removes all sins, is meritorious, and is the supreme increaser of longevity.
I have told this to you, O King; what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Marriage of All the Queens," in the Śrīdvārakākhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva. || 8 ||
Bahulāśva said:
The city of Dvārakā is indeed blessed and renowned throughout the three worlds.
It is there that Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the most perfect, has made his dwelling.
The city of Dvārāvatī is renowned as having arisen from the very body of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
O Brahman, from where have you come here? Tell me, O Lord, at what time did you arrive?
Śrī Nārada said: "Excellent, excellent! You have asked well about the reason for coming to Dvārakā."
Having heard which, even a sinner who has slain the world attains purity. ||3||
There was a king named Śaryāti, a universal monarch and the son of Manu.
He ruled the kingdom on earth with righteousness for ten thousand years. ||4||
Uttānabarhis, Ānarta, and Bhūriṣeṇa—these are the three.
Śaryāti had sons who were the best among all upholders of dharma.
To Uttānabarhis he gave the eastern [quarter], and to Bhūriṣeṇa the southern.
And the king gave the entire western direction to Ānarta.
"This entire earth, made cool by snow, has been protected by me in accordance with righteousness."
You shall protect that [city] which was acquired by force by the most powerful one.
Having heard his father’s words, the middle son Ānarta [acted].
The wise man, as if smiling, spoke these words consisting of knowledge.
Ānarta said:
This entire earth was never protected by you in this manner.
O King, the Blessed Lord, the omnipresent one, is more powerful than what can be acquired by your strength. ||9||
The earth was protected by him alone as the lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The entire world was conquered by his splendor; no one is as powerful as Hari.
He alone creates, consumes, and protects the universe that he himself has fashioned.
He alone is Brahman, the supreme, the Lord who measures time for all who calculate it.
Having entered within all beings, he who is the refuge of all remains there by means of those very beings.
He is known as Viśva, the presiding deity of sacrifice, who is himself the most perfect. ||12||
Out of fear of whom this wind blows, and out of fear of whom the sun shines;
Out of fear of whom the god rains, and out of fear of whom death moves about; || 13 ||
The Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, who is most perfectly complete.
O King, worship with your whole being, free from egoism.
Nārada said:
Even though Śaryāti had attained knowledge, he was pierced by the arrow-like words of his son.
With his lower lip quivering in rage, he spoke to his own son, Ānarta.
Śaryāti said:
Go far away, you of wicked intellect! How can you speak as if you were my teacher?
"As long as my kingdom exists, you must not dwell upon this earth."
That Kṛṣṇa whom you have propitiated is also the maker of all assistance.
"Will the Blessed One himself indeed grant you a new earth? || 17 ||
Nārada said:
Thus addressed, the king of Ānarta, who bestows honor, then spoke to the king.
Wherever those two rule their kingdom, there shall be no dwelling for me. || 18 ||
Banished by his father, Ānarta also went to the shore of the ocean.
Having arrived at Velā, he performed austerities in the water for ten thousand years.
The Lord Hari is satisfied by devotion characterized by love.
Having granted him his own vision, he said, "Choose a boon."
Having joined his palms in reverence, Ānarta rose up quickly.
With his hair standing on end and overwhelmed by love, he bowed down at the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa.
Ānarta said:
Salutations to Vāsudeva, and salutations to Saṃkarṣaṇa as well.
Salutation to Pradyumna, to Aniruddha, the Lord of the Sātvatas. ||22||
O Lord, having been expelled by my father, I have come to you for refuge.
"Give me another piece of land where I may indeed have a dwelling. || 23 ||
By whose grace even Dhruva attained the supreme state.
Homage to that Blessed One, who removes the afflictions of those who bow before him.
The venerable Nārada said:
The Blessed One, who is compassionate toward the distressed, [beheld] Ānarta, who was dejected and miserable.
Being pleased, he spoke through Śrīmukha with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Blessed One said:
O King, what else remains for me to do in this world?
"Being fully satisfied by your devotion, I shall make those words of mine come true. (26)
Therefore, O scorcher of foes, [this is the way] to the divine world of Vaikuṇṭha.
I grant you a hundred yojanas of land and an auspicious cave.
The venerable Nārada said:
Having spoken thus to the King of Anarta, the Blessed One, who is compassionate toward his devotees, [departed].
And having uprooted it from Vaikuṇṭha, [he brought] a portion of the earth measuring hundreds of yojanas. ||28||
Having taken up the Sudarśana discus in the ocean of terrifying roar.
The Lord, the god, supported the King of Videha above him.
Ānarta indeed ruled his kingdom there for a hundred thousand years.
Accompanied by his sons and grandsons, O King, he attains the splendor of Vaikuṇṭha.
Having heard this, his father Śaryāti was indeed struck with wonder.
There was a land named Ānarta, so called by the grace of Ānarta.
Revata had a son, who was the offspring of the mountain Śrīśaila.
Having uprooted it with his own two hands, he cast it down among the Ānartas;
that mountain, though known by the name Revata, became known as Raivata.
Having constructed Kuśasthalī and ruled his kingdom, Raivata then [departed].
Having taken his own daughter with him, he went to the world of Brahmā.
Even regarding the marriage of Baladeva, that story was told by me.
Therefore, the gods know the meritorious Dvārāvatī to be the gateway to liberation. ||35||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Reason for Coming to Dvārakā," in the Śrīdvārakākhaṇḍa of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva.
The illustrious Nārada said:
Thus have I related to you the reason for my journey to Dvārakā.
It is meritorious and removes all sins; what more do you wish to hear?
Bahulāśva said:
The auspicious city of Dvārakā is a ground composed of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
O best of sages, tell me which among those are the principal holy sites (tīrthas).
The venerable Nārada said:
Having established the boundary of the sacrificial ground, extending as far as the sacred ford of Āprabhāsa.
O King, Dvārakā, which bestows liberation, extends for a hundred yojanas.
Upon seeing the city of Dvārakā, a man becomes Nārāyaṇa.
Even a certain donkey that died in Dvārakā became four-armed.
Beholding it, hearing its story, and sometimes saying, "This is Dvārakā," he would speak.
Even if one were to eat only grass, having seen [this], when death arrives, one goes to the supreme goal.
Once, the devotee Raivata was overwhelmed with the bliss of divine love.
Having looked at him and bestowed his vision upon him, Hari became tearful-faced.
From a drop produced from his eye, that great river Gomatī arose.
By the mere sight of whom one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin. ||7||
The man who wears upon himself the meritorious dust born on the banks of the Gomatī, [attains the highest state].
One is liberated from the sins committed over a hundred births; there is no doubt in this matter. ||8||
Even at the time of bathing, a man sometimes utters the name "Gomatī."
One certainly obtains the merit born of bathing in the Gomatī; of this there is no doubt. ||9||
When the sun is situated in Capricorn during the month of Māgha, one should perform the ritual bath at Prayāga.
The King of Videha obtains the merit born of a hundred horse-sacrifices.
A thousand times that merit is obtained when the sun is in Capricorn at the Gomatī.
Even the four-faced Brahmā is not capable of describing the greatness of the Gomatī.
And those stones which are at the Cakratīrtha in the Gomatī river—whatever they may be—
They all attain the state of being Cakras and should be worshipped with great effort. ||12||
One should perform a ritual bath on the twelfth lunar day at Cakratīrtha, which is marked by the sign of the discus.
For even one who is a vessel for sins goes to the feet of Cakrapāṇi.
Even a sinner who has fallen due to the sins committed throughout ten million lifetimes, [is purified].
Having reached the steps of Cakratīrtha, one may ascend to liberation.
Bahulāśva said:
For at Cakratīrtha on the great river Gomatī, one obtains the gift of auspiciousness.
O Mahāmati, tell me how that which is highly esteemed was born.
The venerable Nārada said:
In this very context, they cite this ancient history.
By the mere hearing of which, the supreme destruction of sin occurs. || 16 ||
The lord of Alaka, the king of kings, the master of treasures, the upholder of dharma, and the sovereign.
He commenced a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice on the northern lands of Kailāsa.
At his sacrifice, Viṣṇu himself indeed came from his own abode.
Brahmā, Śiva, the breaker of Jambha, Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures; ||18||
Vāyu, Yama, Ravi, Soma, and Kṣiti, the sovereign of all people.
The Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Siddhas all gathered there. ||19||
The celestial sages and likewise the Brahman-sages assembled there, O King.
His son was Nalakūbara, who became the lord of wealth.
He became Vīrabhadra for protection and Gajānana for the service of the virtuous.
Just as all the hosts of Maruts act as servers [of food]. ||21||
Devoted to righteousness, Bāhuleya performed the worship of the assembly hall.
Ghaṇṭānāda and Pārśvamauli are the two ministers of Kubera.
They became the two chief superintendents of charity, the most excellent among all those learned in the scriptures.
Thus, the sacrifice was performed according to the rules and became a supreme festival.
The high-minded king of kings had bathed in the final purificatory ablution of the sacrifice.
And he gave the supreme portion to the gods and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins. ||24||
Thus, when the sacrifice was complete and the eminent celestial sage was satisfied,
Then Durvāsas arrived, carrying a staff and an umbrella, and wearing matted hair.
He was wrathful, emaciated, with sandals on his feet, long-bearded, and lean-waisted.
The supreme one wears a seat of darbha grass, sacrificial fuel, a vessel, and a deerskin. ||26||
Having approached him as he arrived and having honored him according to the prescribed rite, [he spoke].
Terrified with fear, Kubera circumambulated him and prostrated himself.
Today my birth has become fruitful, and my wine too has become fruitful for me.
"O Brahmin, now that you have arrived, my sacrifice has become fruitful today."
Thus was the venerable sage Durvāsas gratified by him.
With a smiling face, he spoke of the nature of gods and humans.
You are the king of kings, righteous-souled, generous, and devoted to the Brahmins.
You have indeed performed the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, which is the cause of Viṣṇu’s satisfaction.
O Lord Vaiśravaṇa, I have never indeed requested anything from you anywhere.
Knowing you to be the best among givers, I make my request this very day.
I shall make your vow fruitful; I will grant you a true boon.
Otherwise, I shall surely reduce you to ashes by means of a most terrifying curse.
All nine treasures of the three worlds reside in your house.
Give them to me—blessings be upon you—for that purpose I have come.
Nārada said:
Having heard this, the king of kings, who was of generous disposition and noble intellect, [acted].
"Oṃ, accept it," said the Lord of the Guhyakas to him.
Thus, to the Lord of Treasures who was bestowing the hoards, the Superintendent of Gifts [spoke].
The sound of the bell and the one with the crest on his side spoke to those two who were deluded by greed. || 35 ||
The two said:
This Brahmin alone is greedy; what will he do with treasures?
"Grant him a hundred thousand divine [coins] as a livelihood, and likewise protect his future."
Nārada said:
Having heard those harsh words, Durvāsas became an embodiment of wrath.
He made his red eyes crooked with a frown of the eyebrows.
Like a cooking pot, the entire Brahmāṇḍa shook for two moments.
Seeing Dhanada bowing down before them, the sage pronounced a curse upon the two of them.
The sage said:
O great villain, Ghaṇṭānāda, you wicked-minded hunter!
Be like a crocodile; seize wealth, O you great villain! (39)
O Pārśvamauli, O Pāpabuddhi, you who are possessed by the intoxication of greed for wealth!
"O evil-minded one, since you act with the impetuosity of an elephant, become an elephant! (40)
The illustrious Nārada said:
Having given a curse to those two, the sage took the treasure from Kubera.
Duvasa then granted him another supreme boon, one that is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
And from this gift, may the nine treasures become twofold.
Having spoken thus, that treasure departed; oh, how great is the power of those possessed of intense splendor!

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Cakratīrtha," within the Narrative of Gomatī, in the Dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva, in the Śrī Dvārakā-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Nārada said:
The two ministers of Kubera were wretched, utterly deluded by the Brahmin’s curse.
There, Viṣṇu himself spoke directly to those two who had come to him for refuge.
The Blessed One said:
In a sacrifice associated with my worship, you two shall be joined with suffering.
Indeed, I am not at all able to set aside the words of the Brahmins. || 2 ||
May you two become a crocodile and a lion, for when there is a battle between you two.
Then, indeed, by my grace, you two shall return to your own true nature.
Nārada said:
Thus were those two ministers of the king of kings addressed by Hari.
The crocodile and the elephant became endowed with the recollection of their former births.
And on the Gomati, he became a crocodile for a hundred years due to the sound of a bell.
He was deformed, most terrifying, and constantly bore a fierce form. ||5||
The lordly elephant Pārśvamauli was in the forest of Mount Raivata.
He has four tusks, the luster of collyrium, and his back is elevated for a hundred bow-lengths.
With vañjula, kuraba, kunda, badara, vetra, and veṇu trees;
It was filled with *raṃbhā* trees, *bhūrja*, *vaṭa*, *kovidāra*, *asanā*, and *arjuna* trees. ||7||
With mandāra, pāṭala, aśoka, cūta, campaka, and candana [trees].
With jackfruit, udumbara, aśvattha, dates, and bījapūraka fruits. ||8||
It was beautifully adorned with *priyāla*, *āmrātaka*, *āmra*, and *kramuka* trees.
The great elephant roamed about in the vast forest of Raivata.
Once, in the month of Mādhava, Gajendra [emerged] from a mountain cave.
Accompanied by his followers, he went roaring toward that Gomatī Gaṅgā to bathe.
Having plunged for a long time into the waters, [he stirred them] here and there with his trunk-like trunks.
The king of serpents bathed all the young elephants with his trunk.
Even a mighty and powerful great crocodile staying there was impelled by fate.
With his body filled with rage, he seized the elephant by its foot.
By that very [means], the lordly elephant, arrogant with strength, was led to his house.
Having been drawn out and reached the exterior, he was again dragged back by him. ||13||
And the female elephants and their young were unable to carry him across.
Thus, as those two fought and dragged each other outside, they contended with one another.
Fifty-five years passed while the virtuous looked on.
Thus did that great elephant, having fallen into such dejection, remember his former births.
Taking refuge at the feet of Hari through devotion characterized by love.
Having fallen under the power of the noose of death, he remembered the divine Lord Śrī Hari.
The lordly elephant said:
O Viṣṇu, Lord of the gods, let there be salutation to You, the Black One (Kṛṣṇa), who assumes the form of Kṛṣṇa, the friend of Kṛṣṇa, and the body of Kṛṣṇa.
O Pūrṇaprabha, whose holy fame is supremely purifying, protect me, protect me, O Supreme Lord, from the noose of sin! 17.
Nārada said:
Thus Hari [the Lord] saw Hari [Viṣṇu], whose limbs were seized by the crocodile and who was thus recollecting Him.
Having understood this, he who is compassionate toward the distressed swiftly mounted his bird and rushed forward.
Having himself leaped down from the bird, he ran and hurled his discus.
When the wheel was obtained, it had already emerged from the head of the crocodile.
When dejection set in, it became as if separate from the body, like a forest.
Afterwards, the wheel fell into the lake of the Gomati river with a roar.
He indeed fashioned all those heaps of stones into the shape of wheels.
The Cakratīrtha, produced by the friction of its rim, brings about auspiciousness.
O King, by the sight of that wheel, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
The crocodile, having had its head severed, assumed its former form.
By the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, that elephant became possessed of a divine form. ||22||
Having circumambulated, bowed to Hari, and praised the Lord with palms joined in reverence, he remained there.
Those two ministers of Kubera returned once more to their own abode. ||23||
While the gods rained down flowers and raised shouts of victory.
The Blessed One himself went to his own abode, which is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
That best of men who hears this narrative of Cakratīrtha,
One obtains the fruit of bathing at Cakratīrtha; of this there is no doubt. ||25||
Whoever listens with a concentrated mind to this meritorious story of the elephant-seizer,
His bad dreams perish, and a good dream certainly comes to pass. || 25 ||

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Elephant and the Crocodile," within the account of the origin of Cakratīrtha, in the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva, in the Śrīdvārakākhaṇḍa of the glorious Gārgasaṃhitā. || 11 ||
The illustrious Nārada said:
Whoever gives a gift of gold at Śaṅkhoddhāra, the foremost of sacred fords (tīrtha), [attains great merit].
He shall attain the world of Viṣṇu, which is free from all calamities.
There was a great sage named Trita, a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa whose soul was tranquil.
In the course of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, he arrived in the lands of Ānarta.
Having seen the beautiful lake and bathed therein, he performed worship of Hari.
For its worship, a great conch shell endowed with beautiful characteristics [should be used]. 3.
Kakṣīvat, his disciple, stole it out of extreme greed.
Seeing that the conch had gone to Pūjā, the sage Trita spoke in anger: || 4 ||
May that conch by which my own conch was led away certainly become Śaṅkha.
Afflicted by the curse, Kakṣīvān himself became the form of a conch shell. ||5||
Having fallen at his feet, he said, "Protect me!"
Śānta, the son of Trita, quickly said: "O evil-minded one, what have you done?"
