O best of kings, he who hears even the life-story of Maruta [attains great merit].
His knowledge, accompanied by detachment and joined with devotion, arises. ||37||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Narrative of Maruta," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||1||
Bahulāśva said:
"How did the king duly perform the Rājasūya sacrifice?"
O Sage, speak this at length with Śrī Kṛṣṇa as your companion.
Śrī Nārada said:
Once, Ugrasena, having honored Kṛṣṇa in the Sudharmā assembly hall, [spoke].
Having bowed down, with a serene soul and palms joined in reverence, he spoke slowly.
Ugrasena said: "O Blessed One, I have heard from the mouth of Nārada about that which yields great fruit."
I shall perform that sacrifice known as the Rājasūya by your command. ||3||
Through service to your feet, [we have crossed] the great ocean of our former desires.
O Supreme Person, having trampled the world underfoot like a blade of grass, they are fearless.
The Blessed Lord said:
O King, O Lord of the Yādavas, you have deliberated rightly.
Through this sacrifice, your fame shall spread throughout the three worlds. ||5||
Then, having summoned the Yādavas in person, he assembled them all together in the hall.
O Lord, holding a betel-roll, cause him to make a vow.
All the Yādavas are my own portions, desiring to conquer both worlds.
Having conquered their enemies, they will come and seize the tribute of the quarters.
Śrī Nārada said: Then, having summoned Andhaka and the others, he sat upon the throne of Indra.
In the Sudharmā assembly hall, the king, holding a betel-roll in his hand, spoke.
Ugrasena said: "He who would conquer all the kings residing in Jambūdvīpa in battle..."
The wise one, wielding the bow of Śakra, eats that betel-roll. ||9||
Śrī Nārada said: While the kings remained silent,
the son of Śrī Rukmiṇī himself arrived.
O King of Mithilā, having bowed to the monarch, the high-souled enemy of Śambara took up the collection of betel leaves. 10.
Pradyumna said:
"Having conquered in battle all the kings residing in Jambudvīpa,"
And having taken the offering from them, I shall return by my own power.
Likewise, there was the act of approaching those who should not be approached, namely the tawny one (Kṛṣṇa), the Brahmin, and the preceptor.
May the murder of my own embryo befall me if I do not perform this deed. (12)
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard the words of the enemy of Śambara, the leaders of the hosts exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!"
While they were looking on, the best of the Yadus seized him as they spoke.
Having diligently awakened the preceptor of the Yadu clan, who was descended from Garga and others, for a brief moment;
He caused that ritual bath to be performed by sages with Vedic hymns.
Then Ugrasena applied a sectarian mark upon Pradyumna.
Having offered the oblation, all the leaders of the Yādava hosts paid their respects. ||15||
Ugrasena gave a sword to the high-souled Pradyumna.
The immensely powerful Baladeva himself bestowed the armor upon him. ||16||
Drawing from his two quivers those inexhaustible arrows, he took them out.
And having produced the bow Śārṅga, Hari gave it to him.
The divine crown and earrings, and the beautiful yellow garment.
Furthermore, the brave elder personally presented him with a parasol and two chowries. ||18||
The high-minded Vasudeva gave him a shield adorned with a hundred moons.
Uddhava personally presented him with an auspicious garland made of filaments.
Akrūra gave him a right-spiraling conch shell that bestows victory.
The sage Gargācārya gave this Śrīkṛṣṇakavaca yantra.
At that very moment, Śakra arrived, accompanied by the world-protectors and filled with curiosity.
Brahmā and Śiva arrived, surrounded by hosts of celestial sages.
The wielder of the trident gave a flaming trident to Pradyumna.
O great king, Brahmā gave him a ruby crest-jewel.
Pāśī [holds] the noose, and the wielder of the spear holds the spear that crushes enemies.
Vāyu [held] two divine fans, and Yama again presented a staff. ||23||
Ravi [wielded] a most heavy mace, and Kubera a garland of jewels.
The moon [shines upon] the moonstone, and the fire [upon] the iron bar.
And Kṣiti gave him two supreme sandals made of divine yoga.
The swift Bhadrakālī gave a spear to Pradyumna.
Richly adorned with gold, possessing lofty peaks, and yoked to a thousand horses.
It was fashioned by Viśvakarman himself, extending both inside and outside the cosmic egg.
It was equipped with a thousand wheels, possessed the speed of thought, and had a deep resonance.
Adorned with a network of anklets and small bells, and decorated with the tinkling sound of larger bells.
He gave him a great divine chariot, adorned with a thousand banners.
Śukra gave the victorious jewel made of gems to the high-souled Pradyumna.
Then conch shells and kettledrums resounded, as did cymbals, lutes, and other instruments.
With the sounds of mṛdaṅga drums and flutes, and filled with shouts of victory; ||29||
Accompanied by the sounds of the Vedas, parched grain, flowers, and showers of pearls.
The gods showered a rain of flowers upon Pradyumna.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Coronation of Pradyumna," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||2||
Śrī Nārada said: Then, having bowed down to Hari, Kārṣṇi paid homage to Ugrasena, Balarāma, and his preceptor.
Having received the command, he mounted his chariot and departed from Kuśasthalī.
Likewise, all his followers, the Yādavas headed by Uddhava, [did the same].
The Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, Madhus, Śūrasenas, and Daśārhas. ||2||
Likewise, all his brothers, headed by Gada, were urged on by Kṛṣṇa.
All of them, including their sons, their armies, and the great chariot-warriors headed by Samba, [were present]. ||3||
Wearing crowns and earrings, they were adorned with iron armor.
Endowed with the fourfold army, they set forth by the tens of millions. ||4||
With chariots bearing the emblems of a peacock, a swan, Garuḍa, a fish, and a palm tree as their banners.
[He was mounted] on [vehicles] resembling the solar disc and yoked with flickering horses. ||5||
With golden jars at their peaks and adorned with archways of pearls;
Exceedingly imitating the speed of the wind beyond that point.
With divine chowries being waved, adorned by circles of heroes;
The charming heroes shone, resembling the golden abodes of the gods.
Dripping with rut, variegated-faced, and adorned with nets of gold.
The great and formidable elephants had bells hanging from their high feet and were draped in crimson cloths. ||8||
The auspicious peaks of the lord of mountains [shone] like the lords of elephants distinguished by their quarters.
O King, elephants in the royal army were seen mimicking [the enemy].
Some are said to be auspicious, some are auspicious deer, and others are different.
Some originate from the Vindhya mountains, and some originate from Kashmir.
Some originate from Malaya, while others originate from the Snowy Mountains.
Some originate from Mount Maurya, while others arise from the forests of Kailāsa.
And there were elephants of the Airāvata lineage, possessing four tusks and adorned with flowing manes.
With three crests and possessing the luster of Garuḍas, they move upon the earth and in the sky.
There were ten million elephants equipped with banners and accompanied by ten million drums.
Accompanied by armies in the tens of millions and great ministers, they were adorned with circles of jewels. ||13||
Roaring like clouds, dark as rain-clouds, and adorned with *udumbara* trees at their nests;
They shone here and there in that army like makaras in the ocean.
Uprooting shrubs with their trunks, they cast them toward the solar orb.
Trembling the earth with their feet, they moistened the mountains with their rut.
They caused the difficult mountains, boulders, and other such things to fall upon the heads [of their enemies].
And such elephants as these shatter the strength of their enemies. ||16||
Horses emerged, O King—some from the Matsya country and some born in Kaliṅga.
The Auśīnaras, the Kauśalas, the Vaidarbhas, and the Kurujāṅgalas. ||17||
Those born in Kāmboja, those born in Sṛñjaya, the Kaikayas, and those originating from Kunti.
The Dāradas, Keralas, Āṅgas, Bāṅgas, and those born in Vikaṭa. ||18||
The Kauṅkaṇas, the Koṭakas, some Karṇāṭas, Gaurjaras, and horses.
The Sauviras, the Saindhavas, some of the Pāñcālas, and others from Arbuda. ||19||
And there were some from Kāśī, Ānarta, Gāndhāra, Mālava, and other regions.
Some originated from Mahārāṣṭra, some from Tailaṅga, and some from Jalasambhava. ||20||
Even of the Great-Souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is most perfectly complete.
Those who were staying in the stables for horses have all also departed.
And from Vaikuṇṭha, O King, the Śvetadvīpas and likewise the abodes of Ajita [proceeded].
Those who had arrived from the world of Vaikuṇṭha of Ramā have also departed. ||22||
Adorned with golden necklaces and captivating with strings of pearls.
They were attended by the great rays of their crest-jewels and possessed excellent retinues. ||23||
Adorned with chowries, their tails, faces, and feet shone with radiance.
Such horses as these are seen in the great army of the Yādavas. ||24||
With the speed of the wind and the speed of thought, they do not touch the earth with their feet.
O Maithila, even when the sutures are unripened and the bubbles have burst, [the fetus remains].
They move following mercury through nets and within those consisting of wool.
Even vast objects are seen without support within the waters, O King of Mithilā.
[He saw] boulders like tumors, river-fortresses, chasms, and clusters of palaces.
Those horses, being constantly restless, were leaping over [the ground]. ||27||
The gait of a peacock, a partridge, a curlew, a swan, and that of a wagtail;
O Lord of Mithilā, they were dancing here and there upon the earth. ||28||
Some were of excellent breed, with divine limbs, dark ears, and captivating beauty.
With yellow tails and the color of the moon, they emerged from the horse stable. ||29||
Others were born in the lineage of Uccaiḥśravas, descended from the horses of the Sun.
Rich in the sciences of the son of Āśvinī, they were dispatched by Varuṇa. ||30||
Some were dull in luster, while others were of variegated colors and captivating to the mind.
Resembling the *āśvinī* flower, they possess a golden luster and a green radiance. ||31||
Some, possessing the luster of rubies, were endowed with all the auspicious marks.
O King, millions upon millions of other horses also emerged. ||32||
The bow-wielding warriors in that army had attained renown in battle.
Others hold a spear, a trident, a sword, a mace, armor, and a noose.
O King, they rained down streams of weapons like the ocean at the time of universal dissolution.
They appeared like the elephants of the quarters, crushing their enemies in battle. ||34||
Thus, O King, did that vast army of the Yadus set forth.
Seeing this supreme marvel, all the gods and asuras were struck with wonder.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Departure of the Yādava Army," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||3||
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus did the heroes behold Pradyumna, the best among archers, surrounded by his army.
Ugrasena spoke to Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Baladeva.
Ugrasena said:
O Pradyumna of great wisdom, by the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, you have [returned] quickly.
Having conquered all the kings, you shall return to Dvārakā.
One who is intoxicated, negligent, insane, asleep, a child, an idiot, or a woman—
One who knows the dharma does not slay an enemy who has surrendered, who is deprived of his chariot, or who is terrified.
For the supreme duty of a king is indeed the removal of the suffering of those who are afflicted.
Thus, the slaying of those who have gone astray is the death of an assailant, which merits execution. ||4||
Whether a man, a woman, or even a eunuch, one who is self-conceited is base.
Lacking compassion for living beings, the killing of kings is no killing at all. ||5||
For a king who protects his subjects, the slaying of enemies in a righteous war is no sin.
The self-born Manu formerly spoke of the kings who were the first monarchs.
He who, having become fearless in battle, advanced with his foot placed forward, was deprived of life.
He shall go to the supreme abode, having pierced through the solar orb.
And he who, out of fear, desists from battle and abandons his lord in the midst of the fight; |||
That Kṣatriya who, having become [a mendicant], should wander [thus], shall go to the Mahāraurava hell. ||8||
For the king must protect the army, and the army indeed protects the king.
The charioteer should protect the warrior who has fallen into distress, and the warrior should protect the charioteer.
And you, all the Yādavas, are endowed with capability, strength, and vehicles.
May they protect Kārṣṇi, and may Kārṣṇi protect you all.
Cows, Brahmins, gods, the desires for righteousness, and the virtuous on earth—[these are the protectors].
They should always be worshipped by all humans who desire liberation. ||11||
The Vedas are the speech of Viṣṇu, the Brahmins are his mouth, and cows are the body of Hari.
The limbs are the deities themselves, and the vital breaths are known as the virtuous ones.
This Śrī Kṛṣṇa is Hari himself, the most perfect Supreme Lord.
But for those in whose hearts he dwells through devotion, victory is always theirs.
Śrī Nārada said:
They accepted the command of Ugrasena with their own heads.
All the Yādavas bowed down with their palms joined in reverence, O King.
To King Ugrasena, the heroic Vasudeva, Balarāma, and Hari.
The son of Kṛṣṇa bowed his head to the great sage Garga Ācārya. ||15||
O lord of men, when Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Baladeva had departed for the city, [the king remained].
Seeking to conquer the quarters, the son of Hari set forth together with the Yādavas. ||16||
Indeed, its royal highway was likewise four yojanas in length.
O Lord of Mithilā, it shone with all its pavilions made of gold.
The mighty Kṛtavarman was stationed at the head of the army.
Afterwards, Akrūra, the best among archers, set out accompanied by Dhvajinī. ||18||
After that, the minister Uddhava arrived, accompanied by five images.
After that, eighteen sons of Kṛṣṇacandra are recorded. ||19||
O King, those great chariot-warriors who were accompanied by a hundred akṣauhiṇīs departed.
Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Dīptimān, and Bhānu as well. ||20||
Sāmba, Madhu, Bṛhadbhānu, Citrabhānu, Vṛka, and Aruṇa.
Puṣkara, Vedabāhu, Śrutadeva, and Sunandana. ||21||
Citrabhānu, Virūpa, Kavi, and Nyagrodha.
After that, all of them, headed by Gada, set out at the command of Kṛṣṇa.
The Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, Madhus, Śūrasenas, and Daśārhas.
The number of Yādavas is said to be equal to the millions of arrows of the Seasons (Kāma).
O King, who on earth could calculate the number of that army? ||23||
Thus, as the Yadus and the kings were moving about,
they dragged along that great army.
The twang of the bow was joined by the "kuṃ" sound, as the kettledrums were struck with the "duṃ" sound. ||24||
With the trumpeting of lordly elephants, the neighing of lordly horses, and the fierce roars of heroes with their sturdy *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons;
With the sounds of their kettledrums, they roared like fierce clouds with the flashes of lightning. ||25||
The world-protectors, the elephants of the quarters, seemed as if deafened by the great roar of the circle of the earth as it shone forth.
Then, at once, the enemies, devoid of courage, fled from that difficult fortress; for how could they withstand the movements of those great-souled ones? 26.
But the tortoises, saying "What is this? and "Who are these people?", fled, crying out, "Whence do we come? Where are we going?"
"O Ordainer, where indeed does this calamity go?
For she has moved, moving together with all the worlds. (27)
Through the power of the sacrifice, Hari, the Supreme Lord,
brought down the burden of the earth from the King of Videha.
Salutations to that mountain-like Lord of infinite virtues, who was born in the lineage of Yadu as the possessor of the fourfold manifestation. 28.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Departure for the Purpose of Pradyumna’s World Conquest," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||4||
Śrī Bahulāśva said:
The son of Śrī Hari went in due order to conquer the Kaṅka countries.
O best of divine sages, tell me of his noble deeds.
Oh, how great is the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra toward His devotees!
When heard and meditated upon, it purifies even a multitude of sinful people. ||2||
The venerable Nārada said:
"Excellent, excellent is what you have asked; excellent is your stainless intellect."
The life-story of the devotees of Kṛṣṇa purifies the three worlds. ||3||
At that time, showers of rain fell from the clouds and all the dust of the earth was laid to rest.
O King, even if a poet were to count the virtues of the glorious Hari, he would not reach their end.
For its shadow is seen to extend for a distance of four yojanas.
Adorned by that white umbrella, the son of Rukmiṇī shone resplendent. ||5||
Surrounded by his own army, he [proceeded] in the chariot given by Śakra.
He went forth to conquer the Kaccha country, just as Śiva went to conquer Tripura. ||6||
The lord of the Kaccha country, Śubhra, went forth for the purpose of hunting.
Knowing that the army had assembled, he went to the city of Hālā.
Pradyumna's army arrived, trampling with the feet of their elephants.
O King of Mithilā, she pulverized the trees and brought down the regions.
The sky became blinded by those masses of dust that had been raised up.
All the people living in the marshy regions were seized with fear. ||9||
Then Śubhra, exceedingly delighted, [mounted] elephants adorned with golden garlands.
Having immediately led away five hundred horses as well as ten thousand more. ||10||
A load of twenty bhāras of gold has arrived before him.
Having offered the oblation, he quickly bowed down, binding his two hands with a garland.
Pleased with him, the enemy of Śambara gave him a garland of jewels.
Having established him in the kingdom, O King, for such indeed is the nature of the virtuous.
The powerful son of Rukmiṇī set out to conquer the Kaliṅgas.
Advancing like Indra with his clouds, he proceeded with his excellent army whose banners were fluttering. ||13||
The King of Kaliṅga, with his own forces and capable elephant-riders, [advanced].
He went forth to fight face-to-face with the high-souled Pradyumna. ||14||
Seeing that Kalinga had arrived, Aniruddha, the best among archers, [prepared himself].
With a single chariot, he fought against those armies in the presence of the Yādava. ||15||
And he struck the Kalinga king with a hundred arrows, and each of the charioteers with ten.
The hero struck the elephants while repeatedly twanging his bow.
And all their own enemies cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! to one another.
Āniruddha fought while Pradyumna looked on.
Some heroes were split in two by the torrents of Aniruddha’s arrows.
O King, the elephants had their heads split open, and the horses had their legs broken.
And chariots with their wheels shattered, their horses slain, and their leaders killed;
Charioteers and their drivers fell like trees before the winds. ||19||
O King of Mithilā, having seen that army fleeing, Kaliṅga [pursued it].
Mounted upon an elephant and with his armor shattered, he arrived in a state of rage.
He swiftly hurled a mace weighing seventy-two bhāras.
Felling the heroes with his elephant, the powerful one roared like a thundercloud.
Felled by the blow of a mace, his mind was somewhat agitated.
Seeing Aniruddha unharmed in the battle, the Yādavas were filled with rage.
At that very moment, they struck Kalinga with sharp arrows of shimmering luster.
Just as ospreys [attack] a powerful hawk year after year with their beaks. ||23||
Then Kāliṅga also, enraged, himself made his bow ready.
Making a clanging sound with his arrows, he repeatedly pulverized the other's shafts.
The powerful younger brother of Baladeva, taking up his mace, [advanced].
O King of Mithilā, he struck that elephant with his left hand.
By that crescent-shaped blow, the elephant was likewise shattered to pieces.
O King, like a boulder shattered by the blow of Indra’s thunderbolt.
Kāliṅga, having fallen down, seized a massive mace.
And then Gada struck both Kāliṅga and Gada himself with his mace.
A terrible battle indeed took place there between Kaliṅga and Gada.
The two maces, emitting sparks, were reduced to powder. ||28||
Having seized his mace, he struck down the King of Kalinga upon the field of battle.
He quickly dragged him with his own hand, just as Garuḍa seizes a serpent. ||29||
Pained by the blow of the mace, the bones of the King of Kaliṅga were crushed to powder.
He too came for refuge to the high-souled Pradyumna. ||30||
Having offered the bali-oblation, the King of Kaliṅga said: "O God of gods, you are the Supreme Lord."
Who could withstand one possessed by anger? Who would bow to you as a person bows to a wielder of the rod? Homage to you! (31)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Victory over Kaccha and Kaliṅga," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva, within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||5||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having thus conquered Kāliṅga, Pradyumna, the lord of the Yādavas, [proceeded further].
He went to the desert like a fire seeking water. ||1||
To Gaya, the lord of the region of Dhanva, who was endowed with mountain fortresses.
Having recognized him, the Lord of the Yādavas sent Uddhava.
Uddhava, the most excellent in intelligence, went in person to the mountain fortress.
Having entered the assembly, Gaya said: "Listen, O high-minded King! (3)
Ugrasena, the lord of the Yādavas, was a great king of kings.
Having conquered the kings of Jambudvīpa, he will perform the Rājasūya sacrifice. ||4||
He is the most perfectly complete, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself in person.
Hari became the minister of that lord of countless universes. ||5||
Indeed, Pradyumna himself, the best among archers, was sent by him.
Having quickly brought an offering to him for the sake of the welfare of the family. ||6||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard this, he became somewhat incensed, arrogant with the pride of his own prowess and heroism.
The very powerful king named Gaya spoke to Uddhava.
Gaya said:
"O high-minded one, I will not give him Bali without a fight."
In a short time, those like you, O Yadavas, have attained growth.
O King, having been addressed thus, Uddhava approached the enemy of Śambara.
And while all the Yādavas were listening, he indeed offered praise.
At that very moment, Rukmiṇī’s son arrived at Giridurga.
A terrible battle indeed took place with his Yādava troops.
And trampling the city-dwellers, the people of the earth, and the trees with his elephant feet.
Accompanied by two akṣauhiṇīs, Gaya set forth to fight. ||11||
There, chariot-warriors fought with chariot-warriors, and those mounted on elephants with elephant-riders.
Horsemen with horsemen, and heroes with heroes, [fought] one another.
They fought with floods of sharp arrows, as well as with shields, swords, maces, and spears.
With nooses, battle-axes, O King, śataghnīs, and bhuśuṇḍis; ||13||
And perceiving themselves to be surrounded by the Yadus, the heroic Gāyas were overcome with fear.
Abandoning each their own chariot, they all fled in the ten directions.
While his own army was fleeing, there was one of great strength named Gaya.
He went forth alone to fight, twanging his bow repeatedly. ||15||
The radiant son of Kṛṣṇa, however, [struck] the enemy's horses with arrows from his bow.
With one [arrow] he struck the charioteer, and with two he struck the raised standard.
And he struck the chariot with twenty arrows, and the armor again with five.
The one of great strength also cut his bow with a hundred arrows. ||17||
Gaya took up another radiant bow and [aimed it] at the son of Hari.
He struck him with twenty arrows and, being powerful, roared like a thundercloud.
By that blow in the battle, his mind became somewhat agitated.
Then Dīptimān seized a firm spear composed of light.
Having whirled her around, he hurled her at the high-souled one named Gaya.
She too, having pierced his heart, drank his great quantity of blood.
O King, Gaya also fell down on the field of battle and became unconscious.
And the radiant one, pulling that enemy by the throat with the tip of his bow—‖21‖
He went before Pradyumna, just as Garuḍa goes before the son of Kadru.
Then the drums of men and the drums of the gods resounded.
The gods rained down showers of flowers from the sky, and the kings [did likewise]. ||22||
At that very moment, O King, the son of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the enemy of Śambara, had his feet offered by him as well.
The high-souled one proceeded toward Avantikā, which was like a golden lotus to a bee. ||23||
Having heard that he had arrived, King Jayasena, the lord of Mālava, honored him.
O King of Mithilā, having brought the aged Subāli before that great-souled one, you were insulted by him, for he knew his [Subāli’s] power.
Having bowed down to Rājādhidevī, the sister of his father’s father, the high-minded son of Kṛṣṇa [departed].
Embraced by his two sons, Vinda and Anuvinda, he shone, surrounded by those born in the Mālava country.
Pradyumna, the best among archers, went to the city of Māhiṣmatī.
Together with the Yādavas and his own forces, he beheld the Narmadā river.
Shining with waves of water, it was like a tilaka mark of love.
Carrying a cluster of flowers like a crest-jewel upon her head. ||27||
It was surrounded by flowering cane and bamboo trees in full spring bloom.
...like the celestial river [Ganges], [filled] with gods both quivering and embodied. ||28||
On its bank, Pradyumna, the lord of the Yādavas, was stationed with his camps.
The Lord stood together with the Yādavas, like Indra among the gods. ||29||
O Great King, Indranīla was a wise ruler, the lord of Māhiṣmatī.
He dispatched his own messenger to the high-souled Pradyumna.
The messenger, having gone to the camp of King Pradyumna with palms joined in reverence, [spoke].
O King, he spoke these words there while everyone was listening.
The messenger said:
"By the wise son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of Hastināpura."
Established as an exceedingly powerful hero, to whom would he not give his strength?
If Suyodhana bestows wealth upon us according to our desires and not by force;
And you must fight; for indeed, a battle here would be fruitless.
Śrī Pradyumna said: "Just as Gaya and the King of Kaliṅga, though they were overcome, gave tribute, so too will he give tribute."
"This lord of Māhiṣmatī, a most eminent king among kings, does not recognize King Mahograsenaka. (34)
Śrī Nārada said:
Having been thus addressed, the messenger immediately went to the lord of Māhiṣmatī.
In the assembly, he related the words spoken by Pradyumna.
Seeing the formidable army of the Yadus, the lord of Māhiṣmatī [prepared for battle].
Five thousand elephants and one hundred thousand auspicious horses. ||36||
Having taken ten thousand victorious chariots, the king went forth.
Having quickly approached, he offered an oblation to the high-souled Pradyumna.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Victory over the Regions of Marudhanva, Mālava, and Māhiṣmatī," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||6||
The illustrious Nārada said: Then Pradyumna, of great prowess, having conquered the lord of Māhiṣmatī, [proceeded].
Leading a vast army, he marched against the King of Gurjara. ||1||
The powerful lord of Gurjara, a hero named Ṛṣya.
The son of Kṛṣṇa seized him with his army, just as a crocodile seizes a serpent.
Immediately after that, the mighty lord of the Yādavas took the sacrificial offering.
Leading a vast army, he then proceeded toward the lands of Cedi.
Damaghoṣa was the king of Cedi and the husband of Vasudeva’s sister.
Śiśupāla was his son, renowned as the enemy of Kṛṣṇa. ||4||
The one of great intelligence approached the mighty Damaghoṣa.
Having bowed, Uddhava, the most excellent of the wise, spoke to the one of great intelligence.
Uddhava said:
"O King, give tribute to that Ugrasena, the lord of the earth."
Having conquered the kings, he who shall perform the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having thus heard these words, the wicked son of Damaghoṣa...
With his lips quivering and intent on wrath, he spoke these words swiftly in the assembly.
Śiśupāla said: "Alas, the course of time is difficult to overcome; how wondrous is this world!"
Even for the ordinance that consists of time, there may be a degenerate age (kali) during the period of Prajāpati. ||8||
Where is the royal swan and where is the crow? Where is the fool and where is the wise man?
Servants shall conquer the sovereign universal monarch.
It is recorded that due to the curse of Yayāti, the Yadavas were deprived of their royal status and kingdom.
Having obtained even a very small kingdom, they overflow like rivers upon reaching water. ||10||
A king born of no lineage is indeed a fool, while one who is learned is the son of a scholar.
And one who was poor, having obtained wealth, regards the entire world as mere straw. ||11||
After how many days did Ugrasena attain the kingship?
That king was forcibly honored by his minister Vāsudeva.
His minister, Vāsudeva, fled swiftly out of fear of Jarāsaṃdha.
Having abandoned his own city of Mathurā, he went to the ocean for refuge.
It was previously proclaimed that even the cowherd Nanda had a son.
Vasudeva thinks: "This son of mine is devoid of shame. (14)
Since he was fair-complexioned from Vasudeva, why has he now become dark?
The Grandfather (Brahmā), though fair-complexioned, spoke these words with a sorrowful laugh: ||15||
Having defeated Pradyumna, his son, along with his army and the Yādavas.
I shall go to Kuśasthalī to make the earth free from Yādavas.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, he took up his bow and two quivers containing inexhaustible arrows.
Seeing him prepared to depart, the King of Cedi said to him: ||17||
Damaghoṣa said:
"Listen, my son, I shall speak; do not be angry, do not be angry."
If one performs an action impulsively, one indeed does not attain success. ||18||
For the attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, there is no means equal to forbearance (kṣamā).
Therefore, one should practice conciliation; there is no happiness equal to conciliation.
Conciliation shines through generosity, and generosity, in turn, shines through hospitable treatment.
In the same way, even hospitality shines forth only after it has observed a worthy quality in the recipient.
The Yādavas and the Caidyas are likewise remembered as their kinsmen and relatives.
I do not truly desire conflict between the Cedis and the Vṛṣṇis. ||21||
Śrī Nārada said: Although Śiśupāla was thus admonished by the wise Damaghoṣa, [he remained obstinate].
The great villain, somewhat dejected, remained silent for a while.
O King, Śrutiśravas was the queen of the king of Cedi and the auspicious sister of the son of Śūra.
Having approached her son named Śiśupāla,
she addressed him with perfect discipline.
Śrutiśravas said:
"O son, never give way to grief; may the Kali age never come upon the Yadus."
This maternal uncle of yours is indeed the son of Śūra, and Kṛṣṇa is his very brother’s son. ||24||
Those who are his sons gathered here,
headed by Pradyumna, are hundreds of great beings.
They are to be honored by me and by you, and should be cherished; they are certainly not fit for battle. ||25||
O father, with a compassionate heart, I shall go together with you to bring those who have gathered here.
With a mind long yearning to see him, such a time as this, filled with great festivals, will never come again. (26)
Śiśupāla said:
"Rāma and Kṛṣṇa are my enemies, and the Yādavas are also my enemies."
I shall cause all those by whom I have been insulted to be slain. ||27||
Indeed, in former times in the city of Kuṇḍina, it was by these two that I was insulted.
I have indeed chosen my marriage; Rāma and Kṛṣṇa are my lords.
If you two take the side of those Yādavas, [you will suffer].
Then, having seized you along with your father and bound you with firm shackles, [he will act]. ||29||
I cast my own parents into prison, just as Kaṃsa did.
Otherwise, if I were to kill him, my oath would be rendered void. ||30||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard those harsh words, when the King of Cedi had then departed in silence, [the sage spoke].
Having regained his own strength, he spoke all those words exactly as they had been uttered.
It consisted of an army, a division with banners, and was joined by a counter-akṣauhiṇī.
The army of Śiśupāla was indeed arrayed in four divisions.
Bahulāśva said:
"O Lord, tell me the number of the armies, beginning with Vāhinī."
For the seers know the past, the future, and that which lies beyond the present.
Śrī Nārada said:
[There were] a hundred elephants and a thousand chariot-warriors, joined by a hundred [others].
And ten thousand horses, as well as one hundred thousand foot soldiers. ||34||
The definition of a *senā* is small; twice that is a *caturaṅgiṇī*.
And four hundred elephants, as well as ten thousand chariots. ||35||
There were four hundred thousand horses and ten million foot soldiers.
Clad in iron armor, they were endowed with capable strength and mounts. ||36||
That army where there are heroes skilled in weapons and missiles is so described by the wise.
That same army, when doubled, is proclaimed as a *dhvajinī*. ||37||
A *dhvajinī* is known to be double that size; a *pṛtanā* was described previously [as being double a *dhvajinī*].
Even one who acts with rashness may be a hero; a vassal (sāmanta) is one who maintains a hundred heroes.
Supporting a hundred vassals, he was described as a "gajī" (an elephant-like leader) in battle.
In battle, the chariot-warrior should protect his charioteer, his horses, and his chariot.
He who protects an army with his arrows is called a mahārathin.
Protecting his own army and slaying the enemies on the field of battle. ||40||
He who always fights with an akṣauhiṇī is considered an atiratha. ||41||

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Journey to the Gurjara Kingdom and the Ācēdī Country," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||7||
Śrī Nārada said:
That Śiśupāla has departed from Candrakāpura together with his army.
Having disregarded those two parents, for such is the nature of the wicked.
And from Vāhinī and Dhvajinī, Dyumat and Śakti emerged.
Those two ministers, Pṛtanākṣa and Ūhiṇī, were as tawny as the color of a theatrical stage. ||2||
O King, Śiśupāla’s great army was like the ocean at the time of universal dissolution.
Having observed this, the young Kṛṣṇas came to cross over.
Afterward, the exceedingly powerful one named Dyumna followed, accompanied by his army.
Impelled by Śiśupāla, he fought together with the Yādavas. ||4||
And by the arrows of the two armies, a darkness arose on the battlefield.
Covering the sky with the rising masses of dust from the horses' hooves. ||5||
And horses, O King, were galloping toward the leaping elephants.
And elephants, wounded in battle, were throwing down their enemies with their feet. ||6||
They trampled [them] here and there with the blasts from their trunks.
Adorned with musk-paste, vermilion, and red blankets. ||7||
With arrows, maces, iron clubs, swords, spears, and javelins.
The foot soldiers fell with their limbs severed—their arms, legs, and knees cut apart.
O King, someone in that battle cut the horses in two with a sharp sword.
Some, having seized the tusks of elephants, went away with them in jars.
Crushing the minister and the elephant-riders like lions.
Those of great strength suddenly leaped over the herd of elephants. ||10||
Striking with sword-blows, they tore asunder the enemy soldiers.
Touched by horses, they are not seen; they appear like actors. ||11||
And seeing the onset of the enemy's army, Akrūra arrived.
He created a gloomy day with his arrows and the floods of shafts that issued forth from them.
And he covered Akrūra, as a cloud covers the sun during the rainy season. ||12||
Having severed that mass of arrows with his sword, the son of Gāndinī—
With his power, he struck that hero Dyumanta, who was overwhelmed with rage. ||13||
With his limbs shattered by that blow, he remained unconscious for two ghaṭikās.
Rising again, the powerful friend of Śiśupāla fought once more.
Then, having seized a heavy mace weighing one hundred thousand bhāras.
He struck Akrūra in the heart and roared like a thundercloud in the sky. ||15||
While Akrūra’s mind was somewhat agitated by that blow.
Then Yuyudhāna advanced, repeatedly making his bowstring resound.
With a single arrow, he effortlessly and swiftly severed his head.
When Dyumati had fallen in battle, his warriors indeed fled. ||17||
At that very moment, Śakti arrived, seeing the army in flight.
He suddenly hurled a spear at the wise Yuyudhāna.
And Yuyudhāna, with a flood of arrows, shattered that spear into a hundred pieces.
Being capable, he seized an iron club and struck Yuyudhāna.
Yuyudhāna, the friend of Arjuna, fell into a swoon for a moment.
At that very moment, the heroic and mighty Kṛtavarman arrived.
He indeed shattered even the chariot with its horses into pieces with his arrows, despite the opponent's power.
Although capable [of doing more], he nevertheless crushed that supreme chariot with his mace.
Kṛtavarman, abandoning his chariot, seized a spear in his rage.
Having felled him with his two arms, O King, he hurled him a distance of one yojana.
And when Śakti had fallen in battle, [the two others] were dispatched by Śiśupāla.
Those two ministers, tawny as saffron, were accompanied by an army of one akṣauhiṇī. ||23||
Discharging showers of arrows, they crushed their enemies in the battle.
They arrived, O Lord of Mithilā, like the wind and fire.
Beholding that formidable army, he who was equal to the father of the Lord of the Yādavas [prepared for battle].
Taking up his bow in the assembly, Pradyumna spoke these words: ||25||
Pradyumna said:
"I shall go before the people in the arena, which is tawny with dust from the fray."
And they were seen to be tawny-colored, possessing great strength and prowess. ||26||
The illustrious Nārada said: Having heard this, the mighty-armed and powerful Bhānu, son of Kṛṣṇa, [spoke].
Standing before them all, he spoke to his brother with wisdom.
Bhānu said: "O Lord, when the three worlds were seen by you as having come before you."
Then there will be no doubt that you will become free from all obstacles. ||28||
