"I shall do it," "I am doing it," and "This is mine and yours," so they have said.
Both you and I are happy and miserable, always deluded by ignorance.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti), not of the self (ātman).
By these, this world is pervaded, like a cloth woven with warp and woof. ||32||
Those established in sattva go upward; those characterized by rajas remain in the middle.
Those established in the practice of the lowest quality, being characterized by darkness (tamas), go downwards. ||33||
Just as the notion of a snake might arise toward a rope in the darkness due to its dark color.
Just as one perceives a mirage from afar as water, so too is this world perceived.
Know that coming and going is pleasant, just as it is for those who preside over a mandala.
And for men, that suffering is just like that of the inhabitants of hell.
The qualities of the body are like a dense row of clouds, as fleeting as death occurring day or night. ||35||
Just as the caravan [is ultimately unreal], so too the object of perception is indeed never anything at all.
Just as when a winged creature has left its nest, or as when one has crossed over from a boat. ||36||
Once knowledge has been obtained from the world in that manner, what further need is there for a mirror?
Likewise, having quickly established the path, the sage of equal vision should proceed. ||37||
Just as the moon [is reflected] in vessels of water, and as fire [is latent] in a heap of wood.
In the same way, the one Blessed One, the Supreme Self, is established as manifest. ||38||
Just as the great space exists both inside and outside a jar or a hut, so too does it exist within and without.
Likewise, the Supreme Self is untainted within embodied beings and amidst their own actions. ||39||
He who is a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, whose self is peaceful, who is established in knowledge, and who possesses dispassion;
The qualities do not touch him here, just as water does not touch the leaf of a lotus.
The man of wisdom, ever consisting of bliss, should move about in his body like a child.
He does not perceive his own clothing, like one intoxicated by the madness of wine. //41//
O King, just as an object within a house becomes visible at sunrise.
Having thus cast ignorance far away, one then directly perceives the vast reality.
Just as an object, which is the locus of many qualities, is perceived through various doors according to the sense faculties.
In that same way, Brahman is not brought [to conceptualization] by those who follow the paths of the scriptures and speak of it. ||43||
O King, some indeed declare this to be the supreme state of Viṣṇu.
Some indeed pervade Vaikuṇṭha, while others [pervade] that which is beyond it, the Peaceful.
Some call that Brahman Kaivalya, the supreme abode, and the imperishable.
The Imperishable, the supreme goal, Goloka, which is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). ||45||
Some who are conversant with ancient lore declare that the Nikuñja here is pure.
One attains it here through knowledge, dispassion, and devotion, and not from anything else. ||46||
Of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, of Hari, the Supreme,
the Lord of liberation, who is higher than the highest.
One shall go to the abode of Śrī Puruṣottama, reaching which the devotee does not return again. ||47||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having thus heard this knowledge of the Bhāgavata from the great sage, the son of Kṛṣṇa [Pradyumna]...
Having bowed with palms joined in reverence, he worshipped Agastya with devotion. ||48||

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Discourse on the Knowledge of Agastya and Kārṣṇi," in the section concerning Śrī Viśvajit within the glorious Garga Saṃhitā, during the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva, regarding the conquest of the lands of Uśīnara, Vidarbha, Kunti, and Darada.
Śrī Nārada said: Having bathed in the Kṛtamālā and the Tāmraparṇī, the Lord of the Yādavas [proceeded].
O King, he went to Rājapura together with the Yādava soldiers. ||1||
Śālva, the lord of Rājapura, having heard about the Yadus from my mouth, [acted].
He went quickly to meet the monkey leader Dvivida who had arrived. ||2||
For Dvivida was exceedingly enraged, a hero who had been aided by Mita.
The army of Śambara’s enemy advanced, shaking the surface of the earth.
He tore apart the banners, standards, and streamers with his claws and teeth.
[He saw] those joined with Kāśmīra blankets, [some] from the ocean, and adorned with gold. ||4||
Having swiftly mounted the elephants, he caused the chariots to be overturned.
He caused the horses to bolt by means of the knitting of his eyebrows and the sounds of his monkey-like cries.
When such a clamor had arisen, Pradyumna, the best among archers, [acted].
He arrived on his chariot, repeatedly twanging his bow.
Dvivida, intoxicated with pride, stepped out from near his chariot.
Shaking the parasol, the banner, and the horse-drawn chariot with his tail.
Pradyumna, seizing him by the neck with the tip of his own bow, dragged him along.
Then Kapi, becoming exceedingly enraged, struck him with his fist.
Pradyumna, having properly prepared the bow and other implements according to the prescribed rite, [stood ready].
Drawing [the bow] back to his ear, he struck him with an arrow. ||9||
Viśikhī, having whirled him around in the sky for a hundred yojanas, [cast him down].
Within half a watch, O king of kings, he caused it to fall upon Laṅkā.
That battle with the Rākṣasas lasted for two ghaṭikās.
Then Pradyumna, the best of the Yadus, struck down the Rākṣasas.
Causing the drum to resound, O King, he took tribute after having conquered.
Having seen the southern Mathurā, he ascended Trikūṭa.
He departed from Trikūṭa and went to the top of the Maināka peak.
From Maināka he went to Siṃhala and Caitya, and then returned again to Bhārata. ||13||
The lord of monkeys went slowly, step by step, to the Himācala mountain.
From the peak of the Himalayas, he went to Prāgjyotiṣapura. ||14||
Pradyumna, the lord of the Yādavas, [conquered] the sovereign of the Matsya country.
He went to the great field of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa at the construction of the bridge.
The ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, extending for a hundred yojanas.
Having observed this, the great hero, the son of Kṛṣṇa, approached the shore and stood there. ||16||
He summoned his own Yādavas, including Sāmba, Akrūra, and the others.
In the assembly, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the lords of yoga, spoke to Uddhava.
Pradyumna said:
"Bibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the island, resplendent with great luster, the ruler of Laṅkā, and the chief of the hosts of rākṣasas."
"O minister, tell the best of the Bhojas what you say; if he does not offer me tribute, speak it quickly! (18)
Uddhava said:
You are the God of gods, the Supreme among the Supreme Persons; indeed, you alone are Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, the Ultimate Reality.
O Lord, you ask me as if you were an ordinary person;
even for the best of yogis, your illusory power is difficult to overcome.
Brahmā and the others, constantly overwhelmed, bear his supreme command upon their heads.
O Infinite One, you alone are the manifest Puruṣa;
I am a servant of servants—what can I say to you?
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus addressed, while they were looking on, the blessed Lord Pradyumna, who is Hari, [departed].
Taking the leaf, O Lord of Mithilā, he wrote the message.
Offer a sacrifice to King Bhoja;
otherwise, listen to my words with force!
Having built a bridge with arrows released from my bow, I shall return accompanied by my hosts of troops.
Having written this and taken up his bow, he of fierce prowess—
Having fixed a feather upon the arrow, he drew it back as far as his ear.
It did not burst open clearly; there was no cracking sound, only the roar of lightning.
By that roar, the entire universe, along with the seven worlds and the subterranean realms, resounded.
An arrow released from his bow, illuminating the circle of the quarters.
In the midst of Vibhīṣaṇa’s assembly, the sound of a lightning bolt fell. ||25||
At that very moment, all the Rākṣasas rose up as if startled.
The wicked ones swiftly seized their weapons along with their scabbards. ||26||
Then, having extracted the leaf from the arrow and read it, Vibhīṣaṇa—
The immensely powerful lord of the Rākṣasas was struck with wonder in the midst of the assembly. ||27||
At that very moment in the assembly, Vibhīṣaṇa approached the preceptor Śukra.
Having prostrated and honored him with water for the feet and other offerings, he spoke with palms joined in reverence. ||28||
Bibhīṣaṇa said:
"O Blessed One, whose arrow is this, and who is this Bhoja king on earth?"
Tell me, you who possess direct divine vision, what is his power? ||29||
Śrī Śukra said: In this very context, they cite this ancient history.
O King, by the mere hearing of which, evil is pacified.
For in ancient times, the sons of Brahmā, Sanaka and the others, departed for heaven.
Wandering through the three worlds, they went to the divine realm of Viṣṇu. ||31||
Thinking the naked ones to be children, Jaya and Vijaya indeed [approached] them.
The two gatekeepers, stationed within the inner apartments, blocked the way with their staffs.
And they, enraged and longing for the sight of Kṛṣṇa, cursed those two.
May those two wicked Asuras indeed become purified through three births. ||33||
Thus cursed, they fell from their own abode onto the surface of the earth.
Those two sons of Diti were born, worshipped by the Daityas and Dānavas. ||34||
Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder, and Hiraṇyākṣa was likewise his younger brother.
The Blessed One, having become Yajñavārāha, lifted the earth from the waters.
He struck the immensely powerful Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa with his fist.
And Nṛsiṃha of fierce prowess [slayed] Hiraṇyakaśipu himself. ||36||
Indeed, he who acted as the companion of Kāyādhava tore him open in the belly.
Those two brothers, the sons of Viśravas, were born again from Keśinī.
Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa were the sole tormentors of all the worlds.
They both fell upon the field of battle with the arrows of Rāghava. ||38||
The two lords of the Rākṣasas, possessed of great speed, were seen by you along with their armies.
In this third birth, he was indeed born into a family of Kṣatriyas. ||39||
Śiśupāla and Dantavakra, both present there, were possessed of great strength.
He is the most perfectly complete, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself in person. ||40||
The Lord of Goloka, the master of countless universes, who is higher than the highest.
Hari himself was born in the lineage of Yadu for the sake of slaying those two.
The lord of the Yadavas, abounding in divine sports, shines resplendent in Dvārakā.
Mādhava [performed] at Yudhiṣṭhira’s great sacrifice and in the battle against Śālva. ||42||
He will slay Śiśupāla and Dantavakra; of this there is no doubt.
His son, the enemy of Śambara, set forth for the purpose of conquering the quarters. ||43||
He will conquer all the kings residing in Jambudvīpa.
When the gods had been conquered, the best of the Yadus [resided] in Dvārakā.
Ugrasena, the king of the Bhojas, will perform the Rājasūya sacrifice.
It is that very arrow, released from his bow with fierce force and impetuous speed, that has arrived here.
Marked with his name and surpassing the sound of lightning, it shone forth, illuminating the circle of Rākṣasas and the quarters of the sky. ||45||
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, that devotee of Śrī Rāma, Vibhīṣaṇa, then recognized Kṛṣṇa as Rāmacandra.
Having taken the offering, the leader of the host of demons returned to the army of Sunda’s enemy.
Then, descending from the great sky, he appeared with a body as long as a palm tree, possessing the luster of a shimmering cloud and eyes that were victorious.
Having circumambulated the son of Hari once more, he stood facing him with palms joined in reverence. ||47||
Vibhīṣaṇa said:
"Salutations to you, the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, the Creator."
Salutation to Pradyumna, to Aniruddha, and to Saṃkarṣaṇa. ||48||
Salutations to Matsya, to Kūrma, and to Varāha; salutations again and again!
Salutations to Śrī Rāmacandra; salutations again and again to the descendant of Bhṛgu. ||49||
Salutations to you, O Vāmana; salutations again and again to Nṛsiṃha.
Homage to the Buddha, the pure one, the remover of suffering, and the destroyer of the age of degeneration. ||50||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the bestower of honor worshiped the son of Śrī Hari.
With the sixteen modes of service, with supreme devotion, and with words full of tenderness.
Pleased with him, the enemy of Śambara granted him knowledge born of detachment.
They directly attain devotion that brings peace, which is characterized by difficult-to-attain love. ||52||
The great divine ruby crest-jewel bestowed by Brahmā.
In ancient times, Paulastya gave her a jewel necklace of radiant luster.
He then gave him the moonstone (candrakāntamaṇi) that had been given by Candra.
Clad in yellow garments, he is the supreme Pradyumna, the highest Lord manifest before one's very eyes. ||54||
Then Bibhīṣaṇa, having bowed to Pradyumna and offered him tribute, [departed].
The mighty lord of the rākṣasas, accompanied by his host, went to Laṅkā. ||55||

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Victory over Śālva, Matsya, and Laṅkā," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||13||
Śrī Nārada said:
Then, having beheld Ṛṣabha Hill, which is called Śrīraṅga, the son of Hari—
Kāma, the son of Kṛṣṇa, [reached] the city of Kāñcī and the Prācī, the best of rivers. ||1||
And having then crossed the Kāverī, he went to the region of the Sahya mountain.
Accompanied by the Yādavas, he was the Lord Hari himself in the form of Pradyumna. ||2||
He was coming toward the camps with his hair disheveled and naked.
An Avadhūta running along, his limbs well-nourished and covered with dust.
The children, running after him here and there with the sounds of their palms, [pursued him].
Making a great clamor and laughing, O Lord of Mithilā. ||4||
Having seen him, Karṣṇi, the best among the wise, spoke to Uddhava.
Pradyumna said:
"Who is this with a stout body, running like a child, a madman, or a ghost?"
Even when insulted by people, the great one, full of bliss, laughs.
Uddhava said:
"This one, known as a paramahaṃsa or an avadhūta, is a portion (kalā) of Hari."
The great sage Dattātreya himself, who is composed of eternal bliss. ||7||
By whose grace other kings attained supreme perfection.
Those who were the Yadus, Kāyadhavas, and others, headed by Sahasrārjuna; ||8||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard this, the enemy of Śambara bowed to and honored that sage.
Having seated him upon a divine throne, that best of the Yadus asked this: ||9||
Pradyumna said:
"O Blessed One, O Lord, please destroy the doubt that dwells within my heart."
Tell me truly about the world, the paths to Brahman, and the ultimate cause.
Dattātreya said:
As long as the sun is not seen, for that long is the purpose of the meteor.
When mastery over great bliss has been attained, what further need is there for the firebrand?
O virtuous one, the world persists only so long as that reality is not known.
Once the supreme Brahman has been attained, what purpose would the world serve? ||12||
Just as one sees the reflection of one's own face in a mirror, but not another's body.
In the same way, through knowledge, this individual soul [realizes] that which is higher than the highest, for the sake of the Pradhāna.
Just as every object is seen with the eye when the sun rises.
Likewise, upon the arising of knowledge, the reality of Brahman is [perceived] by the individual soul everywhere.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard this and then bowed to him, Pradyumna, the lord of the Yādavas, [spoke].
Accompanied by his army, he went to Vaikuṇṭhādri in the Draviḍa country. ||15||
The royal sage, the lord of Draviḍa, was truthful in speech and a knower of the essential principles of dharma.
Endowed with supreme devotion, he worshipped Pradyumna.
Having beheld the glorious Śrīśaila, the wonderful abode of Giriśa.
Then, O King, having beheld Skanda, he went to the Pampā lake.
The illustrious Lord of Dvārakā went to the Godāvarī and the Bhīmarathī.
Showing the sacred ford of Hari, he then went to Mount Mahendra.
To Rāma Bhārgava, the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas, who was staying on Mount Mahendra.
Having bowed and circumambulated him, the son of Hari stood there. ||19||
Rāma, having bestowed his blessing for the strength of the Yādavas, indeed—
O Indra among kings, he performed the worship with the yoga of the fourfold army. ||20||
Rice cooked with lentils, praleha, rudikā, and curd-based vegetables;
Śikhariṇī, avaleha, balakā, cakṣukheriṇī. ||21||
A *baṭaka* ball mixed with triangular sugar is called *madhuśīrṣaka*.
The pheṇikā, the upariṣṭa, and the śatapatra with its perforations. ||22||
Thus, those nectar-coils are known to bear the mark of a wheel.
Ghṛtapūra, Vāyupūra, and likewise Candrakalā are thus remembered. ||23||
And [he saw] curd-grounds and a circle of sugar-candy situated within a tube of camphor.
And there were moats filled with wheat, as well as those abounding in excellent fruit. ||24||
Dadhirūpa, Modaka, Śāka, and Saudhana.
Maṇḍakas, milk-rice, curd, and cow's ghee. ||25||
Fresh butter, whey, a small jar, and likewise thin pancakes.
Śaktikā, lasikā, and indeed suvṛt—these are the joints. ||26||
And with excellent fruits combined with sugar, one should offer various kinds of fruit.
Just as with delusion and enjoyments, and likewise with salt. ||27||
Astringent, sweet, bitter, pungent, and sour—thus it is of many kinds.
And indeed, these fifty-six [deities] are proclaimed as the enjoyers. ||28||
Resorting to yoga, Bhārgava reduced these mountains to dust.
When the army had been fed there, they were not lacking even in hands. ||29||
Having witnessed the power of Bhārgava as well, everyone was greatly amazed.
Then Pradyumna, together with the Yādavas, paid him homage.
O King, while everyone was listening, the son of Hari asked this.
Pradyumna said:
"O Blessed One, you have provided excellent food for everyone. (31)
O Lord, all prosperities and spiritual accomplishments are established within Your feet.
Among all devotees of Hari, which devotee is most dear to Hari?
Tell me this, O best of Brahmins, for you are the foremost knower of both the higher and the lower.
Paraśurāma said:
O Lord, do you not know? Yet you ask me as if you were an ordinary person.
You wander upon the earth, performing the gathering of people for their welfare alone.
He who is destitute of worldly possessions, who longs for the pollen of Hari’s lotus feet,
and who is solely intent upon hearing and chanting the glorious stories [of the Lord].
He whose mind is submerged in the waves of that ocean of beauty, beloved of the illustrious Moon-like Kṛṣṇa—he is declared to be a devotee. ||34||
He is self-controlled, great, affectionate toward all moving beings, peaceful, patient, exceedingly compassionate, and a true friend.
O Supreme Lord, he who is said to be the beloved of the illustrious Kṛṣṇacandra purifies the world from afar with the dust of his own feet. 35.
He who [desires] neither the entire sovereignty of Brahmā, nor the celestial abode of Mahendra, nor constant universal dominion over the earth, nor lordship over the netherworld;
Such a devotee does not desire the attainment of yoga nor rebirth; indeed, the dust of Your supreme feet is sufficient for him. ||36||
Free from possessions and detached from the fruits of their own actions, those great sages who are devotees of Hari attain that supreme state.
Devotees, being attached to the dust of Hari’s feet, enjoy [bliss], whereas others do not indeed know that happiness which is free from all dependence.
Neither Śambhu, nor Brahmā, nor Ramā, nor the son of Rohiṇī is known to Puruṣottama as dearer than his devotee.
Kṛṣṇa, the crest-jewel upon the hearts of his devotees, follows after his devotees and all the people of the world. 38.
Moving along after his own people, the Great-Souled One purifies the worlds, proclaiming his own devotion to the followers of Hari.
Therefore, to those who worship Him excessively, the Blessed Mukunda grants liberation, but never the yoga of sublime devotion.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard this, the lord of the Yādavas bowed down to the most excellent of the Bhārgavas.
O King, he went toward the eastern direction to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Victory over the Drāviḍa Country," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārada said:
Under the pretext of a world conquest, he repeatedly relieved the burden of the earth.
Then the Lord Pradyumna himself went to the region of Aṅga. ||1||
The lord of Aṅga, the master of the inner apartments, was captured by the Yādavas in the forest.
He, too, offered an oblation to that high-souled Pradyumna.
The lord of the Uḍḍīśa-Ḍāmara, with massive arms and great strength.
Intoxicated with pride, he did not give that offering to Pradyumna.
The hero Sāmba, son of Jāmbavatī, was sent by Pradyumna.
Armed with a bow, he set out alone in a chariot as radiant as the sun.
O King, he covered the city of Dāmara with a flood of arrows.
He covered the mountain on all sides with masses of frost, like a cloud.
Then the lord of the Ḍāmaras, having been overcome, joined his palms in reverence.
Having offered salutations, he presented an oblation to the high-souled Pradyumna.
The heroic lord of Vaṅga, Vīradhanvan, was intoxicated with pride.
Surrounded by an akṣauhiṇī army, Bali came forward to fight face-to-face.
Candrabhānu was the son of Hari, born while Pradyumna was looking on.
He shattered that army with arrows, just as one destroys friendship with wicked words. ||8||
And the pearls from the heads of elephants pierced by arrows.
They quivered and fell upon the earth like clusters of stars at night. ||9||
Many chariot-warriors, elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers fell down.
With their heads severed by his arrows, they were like pieces of a pumpkin gourd. ||10||
In a mere instant, a river of blood from that army indeed came into being.
It brings joy to the high-minded and causes fear to the terrified. ||11||
With headless trunks running about, adorned with golden armlets and earrings;
With crowns, bracelets, and weapons, the earth shone like the Great Pestilence.
Kūṣmāṇḍas, Unmādas, Vetālas, Bhairavas, and Brahmarākṣasas.
They seized their heads with speed for the sake of making a garland for Hara.
When the army had been thus struck down, Vīradhanvan arrived.
He quickly struck Candrabhānu with a mace that was like a thunderbolt.
Despite that blow from the mace, the son of Hari did not waver.
Candrabhānu, taking up a mace, struck him in the middle of his chest.
Pained by the blow of the mace, he fainted upon the surface of the earth.
He fell like a tree, vomiting blood from his mouth. ||16||
After a short while, the king, the sovereign of Vaṅga, regained consciousness.
He too went for refuge to the high-souled Pradyumna. ||17||
O King, when those two had given their strength, they went to the city of Vīradhanvan.
Having crossed the Brahmaputra, Pradyumna of immeasurable valor [proceeded]. (18)
Having taken up the image of Āśīmādhipati, the Lord of the Yādavas [departed].
Taking the offering, he went to Kāmarūpa together with the Yadus. ||19||
The lord of Kāmarūpa was Puṇḍra, who was highly skilled in the art of sorcery.
He went forth with his army to fight in the presence of Pradyumna.
A terrible battle indeed took place between the Āśīmas and the Yadus.
With arrows, axes, iron clubs, spears, swords, javelins, and darts. ||21||
Puṇḍra quickly created the Vidyās of the Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
Then, O Lord of Mithilā, the Guhyakas and Gandharvas [gathered] from all sides.
O King, flesh-eating Piśācas rushed about in the battle.
They repeatedly threw down embers by the tens of millions, again and again. ||23||
In a mere moment, that army vomited poison from their mouths.
Even venomous serpents arrived, hissing as they came. ||24||
Mounted upon donkeys, with tusks and curved faces, they were terrifying with their lolling tongues.
Then the Rākṣasas, devouring men in battle, rushed forward. ||25||
And there were yakṣas with lion-like faces and horse-like faces, O King.
Crying out, "Cut! Pierce! they rushed here and there with tridents in their hands.
In a mere instant, the sky was covered by masses of clouds.
For indeed, O King, there was darkness due to the dust raised by the force of the wind. ||27||
The Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, Madhus, Śūrasenas, and Daśārhas.
In that great battle, the best of the Yadus, having laid down their weapons, were struck with fear.
The son of Kṛṣṇa, seeking retaliation, took up the bow given by Kṛṣṇa.
O King of Mithilā, he discharged the great vidyā consisting of living beings with his arrows.
With his arrows, he [struck] the Piśācas, serpents, Yakṣas,
Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, clouds, and the darkness.
For he pierced those divine powers with his own powers, just as the sun disperses mist and clouds with its rays. ||30||
And with arrows, he caused Puṇḍra, along with his chariot and his mounts,
to whirl in the sky for two ghaṭikās.
He struck down his rival in battle, just as the wind strikes a lotus upon the earth. 31.
Then the Buddha, having approached him for refuge,
was immediately offered gifts.
Having given away hundreds of thousands of horses and tens of thousands of elephants, he bowed down before the son of Kṛṣṇa.
Then, O King, having crossed the Vipāśā with his armies, he reached the Śoṇa river.
The archer Pradyumna, the joy of the Yadus, went to the Kaikeyas.
The king of Kaikaya was the mighty Dhṛtaketu.
The great husband of Śrutakīrti, the sister of Vasudeva herself. ||34||
Dhṛtaketu honored that Yādava, Pradyumna.
O King, through supreme devotion, he was a knower of the power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Victory of Kaikaya," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||15||
Śrī Nārada said: Then Pradyumna, the joy of the Yadus, caused the kettledrums to resound from that place.
O King, he went from the Maithila country to your lands, which were filled with happiness. ||1||
The city shone with exceedingly tall golden palaces adorned with jars.
Having beheld Mithilā from afar, Mādhava spoke to Uddhava.
Pradyumna said:
"O minister, whose city is this that is now being seen by me?"
And the city shines with many palaces, like Bhogavatī.
Uddhava said:
O giver of honor, this city of Janaka is indeed named Mithilā.
The lord of Mithilā was Dhṛti; he was a great devotee of the Lord and a wise sage. ||4||
The best among all upholders of dharma, beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and dear to Hari.
Bahulāśva was his son, who from childhood was devoted to Hari.
The Blessed One will come to grant his own vision to him.
Bahulāśva the prince, and likewise Śrutadeva the twice-born.
The Blessed Lord Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, remembers Dvārakā intensely.
O Lord, he cannot be conquered even by the lords of the gods, much less by human beings.
Through supreme devotion and steadfastness, he brings Śrī Kṛṣṇa under his control. ||7||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard that, the Blessed One, the son of Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Uddhava, [departed].
Having made his own disciple Uddhava [his messenger], He arrived to see Dhṛti. ||8||
Indeed, it was for the purpose of testing the devotion of that king.
The son of Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Uddhava, beheld Mithilā.
The heroes, bearing shields and weapons, were adorned with garlands and forehead marks.
Where indeed everyone was chanting the names of Kṛṣṇa with a rosary.
And the names of Hari are written at every door for men.
Likewise, auspicious paintings of Śrī Kṛṣṇa were drawn. ||11||
And on every wall of the houses, O giver of honor, there were maces and lotuses.
Indeed, there are paintings of the ten incarnations and conch shells and discuses.
In this way, there were Tulasī temples in every courtyard and in every house.
Seeing thus the palaces and many people in Mithilā, he—
He beheld all the devotees adorned with garlands and forehead marks.
And [he saw them] covered with tilaka marks made of saffron, numbering twelve, applied according to the prescribed methods.
Their peaceful forms were anointed with the marks of Gopīcandana paste.
[He saw] Brahmins wearing the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and adorned with the temples of Hari. ||15||
And one should place the mace-mudrā on the forehead or above it, while reciting the name of Hari.
The discus, conch, lotus, tortoise, and fish [are held] in his two arms. (16)
Holding a bow and arrow, with the Śrī on his head and the Nandaka sword at his heart.
And then, O King, the son of Kṛṣṇa beheld a pestle and a plow.
In whichever street some men hear the Bhāgavata, [that place becomes sacred].
Others likewise [recite] the Itihāsa, the Bhārata, and the Harivaṃśa.
Sanatkumāra, Vasiṣṭha, Yājñavalkya, and Parāśara.
Who indeed recite the Saṃhitās of Garga, Paulastya, Dharma, and others? ||19||
The Brāhma, Pādma, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Laiṅga, and Gāruḍa [Purāṇas].
The Nāradīya, the Bhāgavata, the Āgneya, and that known as the Skānda.
The Bhaviṣya, the Brahmavaivarta, the Mārkaṇḍeya, and the Vāmana;
The Vārāha, Mātsya, Kaurma, and likewise that which is called the Brahmāṇḍa. ||21||
In every street and in every house, all the people were indeed hearing it.
Some indeed regard the poem of Vālmīki as the nectar of the life-story of Śrī Rāma.
Some twice-born ones indeed recite the Smṛtis, while others recite the three Vedas.
Some indeed perform the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, which is the source of all auspiciousness.
Who are those who repeatedly utter "Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa" and "Kṛṣṇa"?
Some dance and sing, being entirely devoted to the glorification of Hari.
With clay drums, cymbals, and musical instruments, enchanting with bronze lutes and vīṇās;
In every temple of Viṣṇu, the chanting of his praises is heard by the people.
Devotion endowed with the nine characteristics, which is characterized by love.
O King, the people of Mithilā perform [these rites] in every house within Mithilā. ||26||
Having thus beheld the city, the blessed Lord Pradyumna, Hari, [acted].
Having quickly reached the royal gate, he beheld the Lord of Mithilā.
In the assembly of the Lord of Mithilā, however, were Vedavyāsa and the sage Śuka.
Yājñavalkya, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and I, Bṛhaspati. ||28||
And there were other sages as well, appearing as if they were the very embodiments of the Vedas.
Proponents of the Dharma who are devoted to Hari are seen here and there. || 29 ||
There, the Lord of Mithilā remained steadfast, his face bowed with devotion.
O King, he performs the ritual worship of Bala’s sandals according to the prescribed rules.
This is the [work] named Japanmuktikara, concerning Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Baladeva.
Having seen him, he rose and paid homage to the celibate student together with his disciples.
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites with water for the feet and other offerings, the Lord of Mithilā [proceeded].
And with his palms joined in reverence, the king stood before him. ||32||
Janaka said:
Today my birth has become fruitful; my abode has been purified.
All the celestial rishis and ancestors are satisfied now that you have arrived.
But virtuous men like you on this earth are free from conceptual construction and possess equal vision toward all.
O Blessed One, they indeed wander for the sake of the ultimate liberation of the wretched. ||34||
The religious student said:
"You are blessed, O tiger among kings; blessed is your city of Mithilā."
All your subjects are blessed, being endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu. ||35||
Janaka said:
"This city is mine, yet I possess neither subjects, nor a home, nor wealth."
Indeed, wife, sons, grandsons, and all else belong to Kṛṣṇa alone.
He is the most perfectly complete, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself in person.
The Lord of countless universes shines resplendent in the abode of Goloka. ||37||
Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Puruṣa himself.
And likewise, Aniruddha alone became the fourfold manifestation on earth. ||38||
That which is committed by body, mind, speech, intellect, or the organs of sense.
O Brahmin, O great sage, that whiteness has been entrusted by me to him.
The religious student said:
"O illustrious Vaideha, best among those devoted to Viṣṇu!"
Kṛṣṇa, gratified by your devotion, will grant you oneness with Himself.
Janaka said:
"I am a servant of great-souled ones like you who are devoted to Kṛṣṇa."
"O Brahmin, devoid of any cause for it, I do not desire liberation or oneness."
The religious student said:
"O King, you practice causeless devotion, being yourself devoid of any motive."
And endowed with the characteristics of love, through devotional states that are free from the material qualities (guṇas). ||42||
The Lord Pradyumna himself set forth for the purpose of conquering the quarters.
"He has not come to your houses; this has caused me great doubt."
Janaka said:
"The Lord Pradyumna is Hari himself, the manifest inner controller."
O Lord, you are all-pervading, all-knowing, and eternal; what is there here that does not exist?
The celibate student said:
"O son of Kṛṣṇa, if you consider even through the vision of knowledge that [the Self] is here eternally [present],"
Then show me that God, like Prahlāda, who possesses divine vision.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard this, King Dhṛti, the great devotee of the Lord, [then spoke].
With his face filled with tears, he spoke in a faltering voice. ||46||
Janaka said:
"If my devotion to Śrī Hari has been made on this earth without cause,"
Then let the son of Hari, Kārṣṇi, manifest himself before me. ||47||
If I am a servant of the devotees of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, then may there be His grace.
If that state were present everywhere, then it would be a great fulfillment of one's desires. ||48||
Śrī Nārada said:
At that very moment, the son of Kṛṣṇa suddenly manifested, having instantly cast off his previous complexion and form.
While all the people were watching, that disciple, who was steadfast in devotion to Hari, became choked with emotion. ||49||
Possessing a dense radiance, with eyes as broad as lotus petals,
long arms, and enchanting to the worlds.
Clad in yellow garments, adorned with dark locks of hair, and possessing a beautiful, lotus-like face. ||50||
His divine form shone with the brilliance of his waistband and armlets, and he wore a crown and earrings as bright as the young sun in the winter season.
Beholding that son of Kṛṣṇa, King Dhṛti, with palms joined in reverence, prostrated himself fully with his eight limbs touching the ground. ||51||
Janaka said:
"Oh, how exceedingly blessed and fortunate am I! For you have indeed granted me the gift of your own vision."
"O Infinite One, born today as one equal to the son of Kāyādhava, I have fulfilled my purpose through my lineage from afar. (52)
Śrī Pradyumna said:
"O tiger among kings, you are blessed; you are a devotee who knows my power."
I have now come before you for the purpose of testing the state of your devotion.
O Lord of Mithilā, may you attain a form identical to mine this very day.
May there be abundant strength, longevity, glory, and fame in this world.
Śrī Nārada said:
He was honored by your father Dhṛti while the virtuous looked on.
O King, Pradyumna, who is compassionate toward his devotees, departed for his camp.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Janaka," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||16||
Śrī Nārada said:
Now, therefore, Pradyumna, whose banner bears the fish, set out to conquer the King of Magadha.
Surrounded by his own armies, he went quickly to Girivraja.
Having heard that Hari’s son had arrived specifically for the purpose of conquering the quarters, [the people came forth].
Jarāsandha, the lord of Magadha, indeed became greatly enraged.
Jarāsaṃdha said:
"All those Yādavas are insignificant, for their minds are disheartened in battle."
Today, those who have lost their senses have indeed set out to conquer the world.
Indeed, out of fear of me, Mādhava also abandoned his own city, Mathurā.
The father of that evil-minded one went for refuge to the ocean.
During the great rain, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa were forcibly reduced to ashes by me.
The two of them fled from the pursuit and took refuge in Dvārakā. ||5||
And having bound them, I shall bring both Sograsena and Kuśasthalī here.
I shall make this earth, girdled by the oceans, free of Yādavas.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the king departed from outside the city of Girivraja.
The powerful one was joined by twenty-three akṣauhiṇīs.
In her mouth, she holds cow-urine, vermilion, musk, and betel leaves.
With four-tusked elephants born of the lineage of Airāvata, whose ichor was flowing.
They felled many trees with the blasts from the trunks of their trunks.
The lordly King of Magadha shone with his elephants like Indra with the clouds. ||9||
And with chariots resembling the celestial abodes of the gods, equipped with banners and guided by horses.
O King, with the waving chowries, it possessed the splendor of the sound of a revolving wheel. ||10||
With horses swift as the wind, variegated in color, and fierce with rut.
With golden bands, necklaces, and the like, and with chowries held aloft by the rays of light from their crests; ||11||
Accompanied by heroic men clad in armor, who bore swords, shields, and bows.
In former times, the mighty lord of Magadha went forth accompanied by those equal to the Vidyādharas.
The quarters resounded with the "dhūṃ" cries of kettledrums and the twanging of bows.
The earth trembled, and the sky was shrouded by the dust raised by the armies. ||13||
That army of Jarāsaṃdha was like the fierce ocean at the time of universal dissolution.
O King of Mithilā, all the Yādavas were filled with wonder upon seeing this.
The Blessed Pradyumna, having beheld the ocean-like army of the lord of Magadha, [acted].
He blew his conch shell named Dakṣiṇa, granting fearlessness by saying, "Do not be afraid! (15).
Then the mighty-armed Sāmba [acted] while Pradyumna was looking on.
He fought with the king of Magadha, who possessed ten akṣauhiṇīs.
In that battle, elephants fought with elephants, and chariot-warriors with chariot-warriors.
Horses with horses and foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers, O Lord of Mithilā. (17)
A tumultuous, wonderful, and hair-raising battle took place.
As [the conflict] was between the Māgadhas and the Yadus, so it was between the Asuras and the Nirjaras.
Certain heroes mounted on horses, with spears in their hands, [roamed] here and there.
Mounted upon elephants, they crushed their enemies, with their weapons fixed upon the frontal globes of the tuskers. ||19||
Some, seizing Śakti who was the color of lightning, hurled her with force.
Those arrows, having pierced the armored enemies, entered the earth. ||20||
Some heroes, roaring, hurled chariot wheels at Kaurava.
They cut through the multitude of heroes, just as suns disperse the mist.
With bhindipālas, mallets, axes, swords, and spears.
And they fought in the sky with sharp spears, javelins, and swords.
And by tomaras, maces, and arrows, they were cut down upon the surface of the earth.
The heads of heroic elephants and horses fell down. ||23||
And headless trunks rose up there, striking down horses and men.
With swords in hand, they rush forward, terrifying in battle.
The heroes who had ascended onto the hero fell down with their arms severed.
Some horses upon other horses had their necks severed by arrows. ||25||
And the Vidyādharīs and Gandharvīs chose those who had gone into the sky.
Desiring heroic husbands, a great quarrel arose among them. ||26||
O King, some others, devoted to the dharma of the warrior class, gave up their lives in battle.
Never retreating even a single step from their position, they were always victorious in battle. ||27||
Having indeed beheld the orb of the sun, they went to the supreme state.
Indeed, they danced within the circle of the porpoises like actors.
Thus was the Magadhan army crushed by the great heroes along with Sāmba.
He fled while they were looking on, due to his devotion to Kṛṣṇa, as was auspicious.
Some indeed had their armor shattered, and others likewise had their bows cut asunder.
Fleeing and running away, they abandoned their swords and spears from their hands. ||30||
Seeing his own army fleeing, the lord of Magadha—
Making his bow twang, he arrived and granted them fearlessness, saying, "Do not be afraid."
Jarāsandha exerted his own strength against the bowstring.
For the great minister impels him, just as one drives an elephant with a goad. ||32||
He reached Sāṃbasta at that very moment with ten arrows discharged from his bow.
In the battle, he pierced the mighty lord of Magadha with arrows.
The bowstring, resounding with a terrifying friction like the surging waves of the ocean.
Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī, cut [them] off with ten arrows.
Taking up another bow, the immensely powerful Jarāsaṃdha—
With ten arrows, he cut through the bow of Sāmba right before him.
With four [arrows] he struck the four horses, with two the banner, and with three the chariot.
With one [arrow], Jarāsandha, the lord of Magadha, struck the charioteer. ||36||
With his bow broken, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed.
Then the exceedingly powerful Sāmba, having mounted another chariot, [proceeded].
Having taken up his exceedingly fierce bow and prepared it according to the prescribed rites, he—
Sāmba also shattered that chariot with hundreds of arrows.
Abandoning his chariot, Jarāsandha swiftly mounted an elephant.
He shone upon his elephant like Indra upon Airāvata, the elephant of the Lord of Magadha. ||39||
His limbs were variegated with colorful feathers, and he resembled Yama, the Ender of Time.
With an enraged mind, he urged the intoxicated elephant toward Sāmba. ||40||
The king of elephants took Sāmba along with his chariot, grasping him with his trunk-like proboscis.
Uttering distressed cries, he hurled it for nine yojanas.
Then, O King of Mithilā, when a great clamor arose among the armies of Sāmba, [the battle commenced].
And from the side of Pradyumna, Gada swiftly attained strength. ||42||
Dispelling the darkness like the sun rising from the mountain of sunrise.
The son of Vasudeva also struck Jarāsaṃdha’s elephant with his fist.
Śakra struck him with his thunderbolt, as if [striking] a mountain of lofty caverns.
The elephant, overwhelmed by the blow of the fist, fell to the ground. ||44||
He met his death, O King, and it appeared as if a miracle.
Jarāsaṃdha, having risen, swiftly seized his mace.
The powerful one suddenly struck him with his mace and roared like a thundercloud.
Despite that blow, the mace did not move from the field of battle. ||46||
Quickly taking up the mace, which was fashioned from a hundred thousand bhāras.
He struck Jarāsaṃdha and then let out a lion’s roar. ||47||
Afflicted by that blow, the powerful son of Bṛhadratha [fell].
Jarāsaṃdha rose up, seizing his mace along with the club.
O King, he angrily hurled it into the sky to a distance of a hundred yojanas.
The exceedingly powerful Gada also took the King of Magadha and caused him to be paraded around. ||49||
He indeed hurled it into the sky to a distance of a thousand yojanas.
The King of Magadha fell from the sky onto the Vindhya mountain.
Rising up, the exceedingly powerful one fought with him even by means of his mace.
At that very moment, Sāmba arrived, having seized the Lord of Magadha.
He dashed him against the surface of the earth with force, like one lion against another lion.
With one fist he struck Sāmba, and likewise with the second, Gada.
The King of Magadha struck him and swiftly roared upon the field of battle.
Afflicted by the blows of fists, Gada and Sāmba both fell unconscious. ||53||
At that very moment, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! suddenly arose upon the field of battle.
Pradyumna, the lord of the Yādavas, [departed] in a chariot adorned with an exceedingly lofty banner. ||54||
Accompanied by an akṣauhiṇī, he arrived and granted them fearlessness, saying, "Do not be afraid."
Jarāsaṃdha, taking up his mace which was fashioned from a hundred thousand bhāras, [rushed forward].
The lord entered among the army of the Yadus like a fire in a forest.
And many Saindhava horses, as brave as the sons of Rathaṅga.
O Indra among kings, he struck them down like a great elephant felling lotuses.
That entire army of Jarāsaṃdha has also assembled.
He struck the entire army of the Yadus from all sides with sharpened arrows.
Pradyumna, the fearless lord of the Yādavas, fought in the battle. ||58||
Felling his enemies with arrows, he repeatedly made his bow twang.
At that very moment, Baladeva arrived from the city of the Yadus.
He appeared there as well, while all the virtuous ones were looking on.
Having dragged the mighty lord of Magadha with the tip of his plow.
The immensely powerful Baladeva, filled with rage, struck him with his mace.
Chariots, horses, elephants, and infantry [extended] for a distance of one hundred yojanas.
Having fallen with their heads shattered, they all indeed met their end.
The drums of the gods resounded, and likewise the drums of men.
The gods showered a rain of flowers upon Baladeva.
Then there arose a great roar of "Victory! Victory! among the Yadus in their own army.
Then Pradyumna and the others, their afflictions gone, bowed down to Kāmapāla.
Thus, having conquered the lord of Magadha, the mighty Baladeva— ||64||
O King, the Blessed One, who is affectionate toward his devotees, departed for Dvārakā.
The wise Sahadeva, son of Jarāsaṃdha, [brought] a gift.
Having led [him] before the enemy of Śambara, he emerged from the mountain fortress.
There were one hundred thousand horses, two hundred thousand chariots, and likewise two hundred thousand elephants.
Having bowed to the son of Kṛṣṇa, he who knew his power gave him sixty thousand [cows].
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Victory of the Magadha King," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||17||
Śrī Nārada said:
Then the son of Kṛṣṇa, having arrived at Gayā and bathed in the Phalgu river along with his army, spoke.
He then set out once more to conquer other lands. ||1||
Having heard that Jarāsandha was defeated, other kings were then freed from their fear.
Afflicted by fear and having sought refuge, they indeed presented him with offerings. ||2||
From there, he went downstream to the holy Gomati and Sarayu rivers.
Then he went from the bank of the Bhāgīrathī to Kāśī. ||3||
The King of Kāśi, who was the rear-ally, was captured while out on a hunt.
Having heard of his great strength, he too offered him an oblation.
The powerful Pradyumna set out for Kośalā together with his soldiers.
O King, he stayed in the village of Nandigrāma, near Ayodhyā. ||5||
The Lord of Kosala and Nagnajit [departed] with horses, elephants, and chariots.
The knower of reality honored the enemy of Śambara with great riches.
Uttareśa is Dīpatama, the lord of Nayapāla, who is Gaja.
Viśāleśa and Barhiṇa—these indeed offered that tribute.
The lord of Naimiṣa was a devotee of Hari, knowing the power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having joined his palms in reverence, the king offered him an oblation.
Kārṣṇi went to Prayāga, to the Triveṇī which destroys all sins.
Having bathed, he, who knew the power of the King of Tīrthas, gave great gifts.
There were twenty thousand elephants and one million horses.
There were four hundred thousand chariots and ten billion cows there.
Adorned with a golden garland and clothed in golden garments.
Indeed, ten bhāras of gold and one hundred thousand pearls.
Two hundred thousand of the nine gems and one million garments.
And two hundred thousand new Kashmiri blankets. ||12||
The son of Kṛṣṇa gave [the land] to the Brāhmaṇas at Tīrtharāja, which is dear to Hari.
O King of Mithilā, there was a ruler of Kārūṣa named Pauṇḍraka.
Even he, the enemy of Kṛṣṇa, being apprehensive, honored the son of Kṛṣṇa (Arjuna).
And seeing Pradyumna arrived in Pāñcāla and Kānyakubja.
All the kings fell into fear, placing bolted bars upon every fortress.
All the Yādavas, afflicted by fear, fled from Viceru and took refuge in a place difficult to access. ||15||
The king who was the lord of the region of Bindu was long-armed and possessed great strength.
He arrived at the army to form a supreme alliance with the enemy of Śambara. ||16||
Dīrghabāhu said:
"All of you lords of the Yādavas have arrived as conquerors of the quarters."
Fulfill my heart's desire; may I be one whose mind is satisfied. ||17||
Even a glass vessel filled with water [is transparent] due to its being pierced by arrows.
Not even a single drop shall be lost; the arrow remains fixed there.
The bowl has not shattered into pieces; one must exercise dexterity with the hand within it.
"To those who fulfill my promise, I shall give these maidens. ||19||
All of you, O lords of the Yādavas, are experts in the science of archery.
I too have previously heard from the mouth of Nārada that they were possessed of great strength. ||20||
And while they were all struck with wonder, Pradyumna, the best of archers, [acted].
"So be it," he said in the assembly to the king who was the lord of Bindu-deśa.
Having firmly established two long bamboo poles and tied a cord between them.
For virtuous people who behold a water-filled glass jar tied with a string, [the reflection appears as if it were inside]. 22.
Having taken up his bow and observed that [target], the son of Kṛṣṇa fixed an arrow.
The arrow, having pierced the glass vessel, remained with its tip half-emerged in the middle. ||23||
From one side, by means of his face and arrow-heads, he was like the sun upon a cloud.
The arrow shone within the glass vessel; it was like a marvel. ||24||
A bowl that has become shattered is not a fit vessel, just like the fruit of the Trikuśa tree.
There was no movement, no trembling, nor even the emission of a drop. ||25||
The Lord Pradyumna again aimed at Bāṇa with a second arrow.
Having first abandoned everything, that king of Videha remained there.
Sāmba also, taking up his bow, took aim with five arrows.
And having shattered your glass vessel, they remained there with half of them spilled out. ||27||
Yuyudhāna, having taken up his bow, discharged a single arrow.
While they were all looking on, the vessel indeed shattered into pieces.
All the Yādavas and the enemy soldiers laughed aloud.
You are a great wielder of arrows here, just like Kārtavīryārjuna.
Are you Arjuna, or Bharata, or Rāma, or indeed the destroyer of Tripura?
Whether it was Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, or like Paraśurāma, the son of Jamadagni. ||30||
Aniruddha, the best among archers, placed another vessel upon it.
Then, having gone down and seen that, he swiftly discharged an arrow. ||31||
He too, having pierced the surface of the vessel, emerged from there as well.
Having tied that vessel above his five fingers, he placed it upon a stone in the sky.
The radiant one, taking up his bow, fixed a single arrow.
He too, having released an arrow that pierced the surface of the vessel, cast it forward.
And having struck the stone, he again took his stand there.
Even by the force of that arrow, not even a single drop was shed.
Indeed, throughout the coming and going [of the breath], not even a single drop was lost.
Then all those heroes, crying out "Excellent! Excellent!", [applauded him]. ||35||
Bhānu, having grasped his bow, looked [at it] with eyes closed.
While all the virtuous ones were looking on, he discharged an iron arrow from afar.
He too, having then broken that vessel and turned the vessel face downwards, made it into a bowl.
Turning his face upward once more, he remained there with half of his body emerged. ||37||
Even by the force of that arrow, not even a single drop was shed.
The bowl did not shatter; it was as if a miracle had occurred. ||38||
Thus were the eighteen great chariot-warriors who were the sons of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
They all broke their vessels, yet not even a drop of water was spilled. ||39||
The king, the lord of Bindudeśa, Dīrghabāhu, was greatly amazed.
To them he gave eighteen beautiful-eyed maidens whom he had created.
At the time of their wedding, conch shells, kettledrums, lutes, and other instruments [were sounded].
The Gandharvas sounded their songs and the hosts of Apsaras danced. ||41||
Above them were the gods, filled with shouts of victory.
Remaining in the heavens, they rained down showers of flowers and offered words of praise. ||42||
Sixty thousand elephants and likewise one hundred million horses.
Ten hundred thousand chariots and one hundred thousand female slaves.
The king gave four hundred thousand palanquins as a complimentary gift.
He sent them to Dvārāvatī; Kṛṣṇa, the best of the Yadus, shone forth. ||44||
Having reached Dīrghabāhu, he then proceeded to the Niṣadha country.
O Maithila, the heroic lord of Niṣadha was named Senajit.
He, too, gave a gift of welcome to the high-souled Pradyumna.
For thus it is said: "Bhadrādhipati is beloved by Śrī Kṛṣṇa and dear to Hari. (46)
Bṛhatsena honored the son of Hari along with his army.
Having reached Mathurā, Śūrasena, and Madhu with his army, [he remained there]. ||47||
Honored with words of welcome, the son of Kṛṣṇa returned once more to Mathurā.
Then, it is said, he circumambulated Mathurā along with its sacred groves.
[He saw] the cowherds, the cowherd women, Yaśodā, and King Nanda, the lord of Vraja.
Having bowed down to Vṛṣabhānu and Upananda, O King, the son of Kṛṣṇa shone with splendor.
And having repeatedly given tribute to King Nanda again and again.
Thus honored, he remained in Nanda’s cowherd settlement for several days.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Victory over the Māthura and Śūrasena Countries," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||18||
Śrī Nārada said:
Then the mighty-armed son of Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by his armies, [set forth].
Making the long-sounding drums resound, he of long-reaching speed marched against the Kurus. ||1||
And that army was bounded by a limit of twenty yojanas.
And the extent of those camps stood at ten yojanas.
Relying on a distance of five yojanas, the royal road follows its strength.
And there were thousands of market-stalls belonging to wealthy Vaiśyas.
Likewise, [he was skilled] in the examination of gems and in the business of dealing with clothing.
Glass-makers, weavers, dyers, and potters. ||4||
Likewise, there were makers of earthen vessels, makers of cotton, and makers of cloth.
Coin-smiths, painters, leaf-cutters, and barbers. ||5||
The artisans were weavers of fine cloth, makers of fine fabrics, and makers of leaf-ornaments.
Lac-makers, garland-makers, washermen, and likewise oil-pressers; ||6||
There were betel-leaf cleaners and artisans skilled in the craft of inlaying with variegated stones.
For those who break glass there are indeed [punishments] like those for those who burn food.
And of pearls and other gems, as well as fine jewels, there are those who pierce gems.
All these artisans are seen following in the king's path. ||8||
In some places, there were playful displays of Bhānumatī, employing the arts of illusion.
In some places actors were dancing, and in others, there was a battle between two bears.
In some places, however, there were female monkeys engaged in playful antics, accompanied by hand-drums and other musical instruments.
O King, in some places the sūtas, māgadhas, and bards sing.
And courtesans, adorned with twelve ornaments, perform a dance.
With their divine sixteen amorous graces, they captivate the minds of the celestial nymphs.
Even among his kinsmen and armies, there were great leaders in the city called Gajapura.
There was a commotion accompanied by agitation, caused by people who were distraught. ||12||
All the people fled, having bolted their doors shut within their houses.
A great clamor arose in every house and among every person. ||13||
The Kauravas, endowed with vigor, heroism, and strength, were universal emperors.
Even those lords of the earth, extending to the oceans, became exceedingly apprehensive.
Sent by Pradyumna himself was Uddhava, the most excellent in intelligence.
Having reached the city of the lord of the Kauravas, he beheld Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
From the mouth of this king, who was intoxicated with pride, there flowed [the scent] of elephants adorned with musk and saffron on their temples.
The courtyard of the temple was adorned by bees that were struck by the tips of the ears of elephants whose trunks were smeared with vermilion.
Together with Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Droṇa, Śalya, and Kṛpa, along with Bhūri, Bāhlika, Dhaumya, Śakuni, and Sañjaya.
[He was addressed] by Duḥśāsana, Vidura, Lakṣmaṇa, Duryodhana, Kṛpī’s son, and Somadatta. ||17||
Accompanied by Śrī Yajñaketu and others, they attended upon the lord of men with a ceremonial umbrella, white chowries, and a golden throne.
Having approached and attended upon the Lord of Hastināpura,
Uddhava bowed down and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to him while prostrate.
Uddhava said:
O best of kings, listen to what was spoken by Pradyumna.
Ugrasena was the lord of the earth, the sovereign of the Yādavas, and possessed of great strength. ||19||
Having conquered all kings, he will perform the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Dispatched by him with his armies was Pradyumna, the son of Rukmiṇī.
To conquer the great and formidable heroes, the kings residing in Jambudvīpa.
[He slew] the kings such as the Caidya, Śālva, Jarāsaṃdha, Dantavakra, and others. ||21||
The son of Kṛṣṇa has returned after conquering; offer him a great tribute.
And a gift should be given with the desire for the unity of one's kinsmen. ||22||
Let there be no strife among the Kurus and Vṛṣṇis, lest it come to pass.
Therefore, that which was spoken by him has been told to me; forgive it, O Lord of Men.
I shall tell you what I have to say regarding this messenger who is free from fault. (23)
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, having heard that, all the Kauravas were filled with indignation.
Arrogant with their valor, heroism, and pride, they spoke with their lips quivering. ||24||
The Kauravas said:
"Alas, the course of time is insurmountable; how wondrous is this world!"
Weak jackals run upon a lion in the forest. ||25||
Through our connection, they have received royal thrones bestowed by us.
But they are contrary to givers, just as serpents are to givers. ||26||
All the Vṛṣṇis were cowards, their minds distressed in battle.
For, devoid of shame, they have indeed set out to act in such a manner toward the Teaching. ||27||
And Ugrasena, being of little prowess, [conquered] the kings residing in Jambūdvīpa.
Having conquered Bali and brought him under his power, he will perform the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Where Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Droṇa, Duryodhana, and the others [are].
There you have been sent as a minister by Pradyumna, who possesses an evil mind. ||29||
Therefore, out of a desire for life, you must indeed go into the middle of the city.
If you do not go, we shall lead all of you to the abode of Yama.
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus was it spoken by the Kauravas, who were averse to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard this, Uddhava approached the enemy of Śambara and told him everything.
Having heard the words spoken by the Kaurava, Pradyumna, the best among archers, [replied].
Having seized his bow in return, his lower lip quivered with rage.
Pradyumna said:
"I shall slay the Kauravas, even though they are my own kinsmen, for they are arrogant with pride."
Just as a yogi [subdues] bodily afflictions through sharp arrows and restraints. ||33||
He who shall not pay tribute among the military hosts of the Yadus.
That man is not even the legitimate son of his father or mother compared to the Kauravas.
Śrī Nārada said:
At that very time, all the Yādavas—the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, and others—[gathered].
O King, filled with wrath, they marched toward Hastināpura with their armies. ||35||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Kauravas," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārada said:
At that very moment, all the Kauravas went forth, their wrath blazing.
Each joined by their own respective forces, they went forth to fight in the presence of Pradyumna. ||1||
They were equipped with victory banners and adorned with jeweled blankets.
Sixty thousand elephants, adorned with golden chains, marched forth. ||2||
Of those producing sounds through the friction of the great whirlpools of the ocean of dissolution.
Sixty thousand elephants emerged, accompanied by the sounding of kettledrums. ||3||
Elephants and oxen, adorned with large iron armor and mail-coats.
Two hundred thousand [beings], equipped with helmets, breastplates, and crowns, marched forth. ||4||
Adorned with golden bracelets, armlets, crowns, and excellent earrings.
And two hundred thousand mounted on elephants, clad in golden armor, marched forth.
They are clad in yellow robes and possess turbans that slope across [the forehead].
And two hundred thousand who were mounted on elephants, having won renown in battle.
Some wore red garments and were adorned with red ornaments.
They emerged on high, mounted upon elephants draped with red blankets. ||7||
Wearing black garments, they were surrounded by serpents clad in yellow cloth.
Some went forth wearing white garments, and some wearing pale-red garments.
And with chariots resembling the celestial abodes of the gods, adorned with banners bearing the lion-king.
Millions of kings went forth on extremely high [vehicles] with fluttering banners. ||9||
The kings [departed] with their limbs and members, as well as with restless horses from Sindh.
They went forth, equipped with weapons, on horses swift as thought and adorned with gold. ||10||
The heroes, clad in iron armor and helmets, sallied forth from all sides.
O King, they were like Vidyādharas, crowded together and intent on battle.
The bards, genealogists, and panegyrists sang the praises of the Kauravas.
With kettledrums, clay drums, tabors, and war-drums, resounding with the clamor of battle.
[He was carried] by [vehicles] yoked to white mounts and adorned with the lion-banner.
With fans having vajra handles, resplendent with the swaying of yak-tail whisks. ||13||
And it was four yojanas in extent, as beautiful as the orb of the moon.
Adorned with a beautiful parasol granted by kings. ||14||
Duryodhana shone forth in the great army, stationed upon his chariot.
Likewise, the other sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra stood, each stationed upon his own chariot.
And with parasols measuring four yojanas, from which pearls were suspended;
Together with Suratha, Atibhīṣma, and his preceptor Kṛpa.
And by Bāhlīka, Karṇa, Śalya, and the wise Somadatta.
And with Aśvatthāman, Dhaumya, and the archer Lakṣmaṇa. ||17||
And likewise by the hero Śakuni and by Duḥśāsana.
Likewise by Saṃjaya, by Tathā, by Sākṣāt, by Bhūri, and by Yajñaketu. ||18||
King Suyodhana shone like Śakra surrounded by the hosts of Maruts.
Two armies were dispatched from Indraprastha by the sons of Pāṇḍu.
And at that very moment, O King, the ally of the Kauravas arrived.
At that time, sixteen akṣauhiṇīs of the Kurus were then moving forward.
The earth shook, the quarters resounded, and the sky became pervaded by dust.
Like the sun emerging from the darkness, he shone forth amidst the dust raised by elephants, horses, and chariots.
Darkness fell upon the earth, and all the gods were filled with apprehension.
And here and there, trees were uprooted by the thrusting of elephants.
For a moment, the circle of the earth was covered by those heroic horsemen as they fell.
The armies of the Kurus and the Vṛṣṇis fought with one another.
Just as the seven oceans are agitated by sharp weapons at the time of dissolution.
Horses with horses, elephants with elephants, and chariot-warriors together with chariot-warriors.
Like hawks upon carrion, they are like foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers in battle.
The great ministers were matched by great ministers, the charioteers by charioteers, and the kings by kings. ||25||
Filled with rage, they fought with vigor like lions against lions.
With swords, spears, javelins, bhallas, pattisas, and mallets; ||26||
With maces, clubs, discuses, javelins, and bhindipāla missiles.
With *śataghnīs*, *bhuśuṇḍīs*, and axes of shimmering radiance. ||27||
Overwhelmed with rage, they severed heads with volleys of arrows.
When a darkness of arrows had arisen, Pradyumna, the best among archers, [acted]. ||28||
He fought with Duryodhana, repeatedly twanging his bowstring.
Aniruddha was indeed [conceived] by Bhīṣma, and Dīptimat by Kṛpa. ||29||
Bhānu was born from Droṇa, while Sāmba, the lord of men, was born from Bāhlīka.
Madhu fought with Karṇa, and Bṛhadbhānu indeed with Śala.
Citrabhānu was the son of Hari by the wise Somadatta.
O King of Mithilā, Vṛka was [ordained] by Aśvatthāman, and Aruṇa by Dhaumya.
Puṣkara was quickly struck by Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Duryodhana.
Vedabāhu, the son of Kṛṣṇa, [was slain] by Śakuni in a great battle.
In battle, Śrutadeva, the son of Hari, was slain by Duḥśāsana.
For thus did Sunandana fight with Sañjaya in battle. ||33||
Gada was greeted in person by Vidura, as was Bhūri by Sātvata.
O King, Akrūra fought in the battle against Yajñaketu.
Thus there occurred a great and tumultuous battle between them.
The son of Kṛṣṇa beheld the great army of Duryodhana.
Just as the Boar [lifted] the earth with his tusk and the ocean with his mass of arrows.
The temples of elephants, pierced by arrows, fall from the sky.
The pearls shone upon the earth like clusters of stars in the night sky.
With arrows, they struck down the chariot-warriors, the charioteers, and the chariots.
In that great battle, O Lord of Mithilā, he [overthrew them] with his impetuous forces, just as the wind fells trees.
Then Duryodhana arrived, repeatedly twanging his bow.
He struck Pradyumna with ten arrows in the battle.
The Blessed One Pradyumna, the lord of the Yādavas, cut them down.
Duryodhana, moreover, discharged ten arrows at his armor.
He deeply buried gold-feathered arrows, which, having pierced the armor, entered his body.
With thousands of volleys of arrows, he indeed struck down thousands of horses.
With hundreds of arrows, he cut down the other's bow together with its string.
The great hero and powerful son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra was the enemy of Śambara.
Then Pradyumna, having abandoned that chariot, quickly mounted another.
Having taken the bow given by Kṛṣṇa and having made it ready according to the prescribed rite, he [prepared for battle].
Having fixed a single arrow, he drew it back to his ear.
By the force of his staff-like arm, he indeed dragged that chariot down.
Having seized that chariot, Bāṇa whirled it around for two ghaṭīs.
He caused it to fall from the sky like a child dropping a water-pot;
by that falling, the chariot was instantly reduced to powder.
And all the horses, along with their drivers, met their death right before him.
Mounting another chariot, the mighty son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra [proceeded].
He struck Pradyumna with ten arrows in the battle.
Struck by them, the son of Hari was like an elephant struck by a garland.
And when the bow had been handed over to Kṛṣṇa, he likewise took up a single arrow.
Bāṇa, having taken him along with his chariot, ascended as far as the great sky.
Then Bāṇa, taking up a second arrow as well, departed in haste.
Just then, a third person arrived and led him into the courtyard of the temple.
And he [stood] near Dhṛtarāṣṭra with his chariot, horses, and charioteer.
He caused it to fall from the sky, as the wind causes a lotus bud to fall. ||50||
Having struck him down in battle, Bāṇa then approached the son of Kṛṣṇa.
By that fall, his chariot was shattered like a glowing ember.
Suyodhana fainted, vomiting blood from his mouth.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kaurava War," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārada said:
When Duryodhana had gone there, a great cry of lamentation arose.
Then Bhīṣma, the son of Gaṅgā and devoted to the gods, departed in haste. ||1||
While those Yadus were looking on, he repeatedly made the bow twang.
Blazing like a fire in a forest, he sought to reduce the Yadu host to ashes.
The best among all upholders of dharma, a great devotee of the Lord, and a wise seer.
By whom even Rāma, the leader of the hosts of heroes, was gratified in battle. ||3||
The Grandfather (Brahmā) has three heads, wears a crown, is fair-complexioned, and has white hair.
Just as a sixteen-year-old, wandering through the aftermath of battle by force, [acts]. ||4||
He struck down the great army of Aniruddha with arrows.
The elephants had their heads severed, and those horses had their necks split asunder. ||5||
With swords in hand, even the foot soldiers were split in two by shattered arrows.
By him, chariots were pulverized, their drivers, horses, and leaders slain. ||6||
The princes were with their faces turned downward or upward, and their feet severed.
With swords and bows in their hands, they fell with their arms severed. ||7||
Some indeed fell upon the surface of the earth with their armor shattered.
With fallen horses, heroic warriors, chariots, and elephants adorned with gold.
The circle of the battlefield shone like a forest with its trees felled.
Her teeth are weapons, her hair is arrows, her garment is a banner, and her breasts are swords.
O King, the earth, skilled in the art of chariot wheels, shone like Mahāmārī.
The army of chariots, horses, and men was produced from the flow of blood.
The river became a great abyss, like the Vaitaraṇī for men.
Kūṣmāṇḍas, Unmādas, and Vetālas were uttering a terrifying sound. ||11||
And having arrived for the sake of the sacrificial garland, they seized human heads.
Aniruddha, the best of archers, [departed] on a chariot adorned with many banners. ||12||
Seeing his own army fallen, the great warrior advanced toward Bhīṣma in the battle.
Resounding with a terrifying roar from the violent friction of the great whirlpools of the ocean of dissolution.
The son of Kṛṣṇa severed his bowstring with a single arrow.
With his sharp beak, O King, he was like Garuḍa seizing a female serpent. ||14||
Then the self-possessed Bhīṣma, taking up another bow, made it ready.
While everyone there was looking on, he discharged the Brahmā weapon in the battle.
Then, seeing that fierce splendor manifested, Mādhava—
For the sake of protecting his own forces as well, he himself took up the Brahmāstra.
Resembling twelve suns, they fought with one another.
Aniruddha burned the three worlds on the island; he indeed carried him away.
The best of the Yadus [struck] even the lightning-colored bow of Gangeya.
He cut them down with his arrows, as the sun dispels the mist with its rays. ||18||
Then Bhīṣma, having taken up a firm mace weighing a hundred thousand bhāras.
He sent it to Aniruddha and then let out a lion’s roar.
Having seized her with his left hand, like Garuḍa seizing a female serpent.
The Lord Pradyumna himself hurled his own mace at his heart.
Pained by the blow of the mace, he fell from his chariot in a swoon.
The son of Gaṅgā shone in the circle of battle like the sun emerging from the sky. 21.
Kṛpācārya also [bestowed it] right there upon the great-souled Aniruddha.
With his lower lip quivering in rage, he suddenly hurled a spear. ||22||
But Dīptimat, the son of Kṛṣṇa, O King, cut it down on the path.
One should sever friendship with a sharp-edged sword, as if with an evil word.
The mighty-armed preceptor Droṇa, filled with wrath, [stood] above the sun.
And repeatedly twanging his bow, he discharged the Pārvata weapon.
Mountains falling from the sky, pulverizing the enemy force.
O Indra among kings, by their falling, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose. ||25||
Then Bhanu, the son of Hari, took up the Vayavya weapon.
By that wind, all the mountains were indeed blown away from the battlefield.
Then Bāhlīka, filled with rage, took up the fire-weapon (vahnyastra).

There, Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī, took up the Pārjanya [bow].

Then Karṇa, abandoning Madhu, became filled with rage toward Sāmba.
He struck him with twenty arrows and, being powerful, roared like a thundercloud.
With his arrows, he caused Sāmba, along with his chariot, to wander for two ghaṭikās.
Having fallen back for another krośa, his mind was somewhat agitated. ||30||
Taking up his mace once more and abandoning the chariot, he approached him.
Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī, struck Karṇa with a mace.
Pained by the blow of the mace, he fell upon the surface of the earth.
O King, the heroic and mighty Karna fell into a swoon on the battlefield. ||32||
Sāmbo also, taking his own bow, mounted the chariot with speed.
He struck Śala with twenty arrows and Somadatta with five.
And he struck the son of Droṇa with ten arrows, and likewise Dhaumya with sixteen.
There he struck Lakṣmaṇa with ten arrows and Śakuni likewise with five.
And he struck Duḥśāsana with twenty arrows, and Saṃjaya separately with twenty.
He struck the king, whose banner was the sacrifice, with hundreds of arrows and hundreds of sharp shafts.
He struck with arrows in the battle and roared like a thundercloud, O mighty one.

Sāmba struck the heroes with five arrows each.
Having beheld the manual dexterity of Samba, the son of Jambavati.

All the Yadavas fled, filled with shouts of victory.

And two hundred thousand lordly elephants, distinguished by their two trunk-staffs. ||25||

A hundred droṇas of nectar and various kinds of fruits.
Of certain gems, gold, ornaments, and garments. ||36||

"Salutations to you, the Blessed One, the Great-Souled Puruṣa. (39)
