"I shall do this," "I am doing it," "O Lord, this is mine," and "this is yours"—thus they speak.
"I am happy," "I am joined with suffering"—thus the entire world of friends and people is deluded by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). ||47||
By performing improper actions through the qualities born of primary nature, time, disposition, and the body, a person becomes bound.
He perceives a child in a glass vessel, life itself in the sand, and a serpent in a thread, with his very eyes.
O Lord, today I have committed an offense out of folly, my mind deluded by your māyā.
Do not regard it as the work of a child, for like a father [toward his son], let such a thought never again arise in me even for a moment. (49)
May there always be for me supreme devotion to your lotus feet—that which they know to be most weighty.
Grant me knowledge conjoined with dispassion, which is the abode of Śiva, and grant me the highly praised association with your own holy ones. (50)
Śrī Nārada said:
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites this auspicious hymn of Pradyumna, [attains his desires].
In times of distress, Hari himself shall always be his companion.
To the Lord of Yakṣas who had spoken thus, the blessed Hari Pradyumna [replied].
Having said, "So be it," O King, he gave him a crest-jewel of ruby.
Having granted fearlessness by saying, "Do not fear," he gave him the play-umbrella along with the fly-whisks.
The Lord of the Yadus presented him with a lion-throne made of jewels.
Having circumambulated the son of Kṛṣṇa, the king of kings, the lord of wealth, [departed].
Having heard that the king of kings had been conquered by the high-souled Pradyumna, [he was filled with grief].
No kings fought with him, and they all paid tribute.
Then the mighty-armed son of Kṛṣṇa sounded many kettledrums.
Accompanied by his entire army, he went to the city of Prāgjyotiṣa.
Nīla, the son of the demon Bhauma, was subdued by his splendor.
Immediately he offered an oblation to that high-souled Pradyumna.
At the gate of the city of Prāgjyotiṣapura was a monkey named Dvivida. ||57||
In former times, that one of great strength was struck by the arrow of Pradyumna.
Rising up, overcome with rage, [he struck] with his teeth and harsh claws.
Having torn through the heroes and the horses, he roared with the knitting of his eyebrows.
Having bound the chariots with his tail, he cast them into the salt waters.
Seizing the elephants with his two arms, he violently hurled them into the sky.
Recognizing the monkey as his enemy, the son of Kṛṣṇa fixed an arrow upon his Śārṅga bow.
Having suddenly seized the reed and whirled it forcefully through the air, he—
As before, he caused the great monkey to fall in Kiṣkindhā.
Bāṇa returned again, quivering within Pradyumna’s quiver.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Victory over the Yakṣa Country," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||25||
Śrī Nārada said: Then [he saw] the supreme regions of Kārṣṇi, filled with divine trees and creepers.
He went [to those places] adorned with lakes possessing thousand-petaled lotuses. ||1||
And Pradyumna, of fierce prowess, was accompanied by a hundred akṣauhiṇīs.
Following the path indicated by the yakṣas, he went to the region of Kimpuruṣa. ||2||
There, at the foot of Mount Hemakūṭa, lies the city of Raṅgavallīpura.
The Kimpuruṣas spoke to him while Śambara’s enemy was listening.
The Kimpuruṣas said:
"Oh, how exceedingly blessed is the excellent city of Mathurā, wherein Hari, the Supreme Lord, resides!"
Oh, how perpetually blessed is the lineage of Yadu, for in it was born the protector of the entire universe! (4)
And blessed is that mansion of the hero’s son,
which has been made enchanting by the Lord of Goloka.
Most blessed is the supreme district of Mathurā, difficult even for the gods to attain, wherein Mādhava wandered. ||5||
The great forest, most blessed and enchanting,
where the infant Hari went from his father's house—
Indeed, Kṛṣṇa, his mouth full of milk, was cherished by Yaśodā as he moved about with the child Balarāma. ||6||
Vṛndāvana is most meritorious, resplendent with the dust of the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is higher than the highest.
Where Balarāma himself, along with the cowherd boys, wandered while tending the cows; there Hari also moved about. ||7||
He who indeed performs the pastime of giving, the pastime of honoring,
and the pastime of the divine dance with the beauties of Vraja;
In Vṛndāvana, where Kṛṣṇa wandered, whose glory even the three worlds sing. ||8||
Oh, how exceedingly blessed is Līlāvatī, the delight of Vṛṣabhānu, who shines with her own world!
He wandered with Kṛṣṇa in the forest on the banks of the Kalinda’s daughter, which was filled with the humming of bees. ||9||
Oh, how exceedingly blessed is the daughter of Kalinda, who was born from the left shoulder of Śrī Kṛṣṇa!
On the bank, crowded with the sound of the Milinda, a person attains the fulfillment of their purpose by touching that banyan tree. ||10||
That mountain which arose from the chest of Hari, named Govardhana, the king of kings among mountains;
He shines supreme within the circle of Vraja, by the sight of whom birth is no longer found again. ||11||
Oh, how exceedingly blessed is this enchanting earth, which shines upon the surface of the world with circles of fig trees!
Kuśasthalī is presided over by the pastimes of Vaikuṇṭha, just as a row of clouds in the sky is graced by flashes of lightning.
Wherein the Supreme Lord, the Puruṣa himself, shines forth resplendently, having assumed his fourfold manifestation.
Salutations again and again to that Hari, who bestowed the status of lord of kings upon Ugrasena and [the sovereignty] upon Kṛṣṇa. ||13||
Urged on by that wise king,
the great Makaradhvaja set out to conquer the world.
Having now beheld that which is difficult to see, we shall indeed have accomplished our purpose in every respect. (14)
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus, through his pure deeds, Hari made manifest the fame of the king, which illuminated the three worlds.
With those shimmering, sparkling, and rising rays mingled with the light of the full moon, he appeared like Mount Udaya emerging from the pure milk-ocean.
O King, having thus heard of his own stainless fame, Śambarāri, his body filled with extreme joy, bestowed wealth.
From them [came] armlets, necklaces of precious gems, and captivating crowns, jewels, earrings, and bracelets. ||16||
Subāhu, born of the Lunar dynasty, was the lord of Raṅgavallīpura.
Having bowed down, he also offered an oblation to the high-souled Pradyumna.
Pleased with him, the Blessed One Pradyumna, whose banner bears the fish, [appeared].
Having given his divine crest-jewel, the high-minded one asked this: ||18||
Śrī Pradyumna said: By whom was the name of Raṅgavallīpura also made manifest?
Tell this to me, O Subāhu; indeed, it was previously heard by you.
Subāhu said: "O King, in ancient times, the Ocean of Milk was churned by the gods and the asuras."
And fourteen jewels emerged from the churning. ||20||
From that [mouth], a beautiful jar filled with nectar emerged.
The lotus-eyed Hari beheld him directly with his own eyes.
And a drop from the joy of his eyes fell indeed into the water-pot.
From that tree arose what is proclaimed as Tulasī. ||22||
Madhusūdana gave it the name Raṅgavallī.
Here, in this Kiṃpuruṣa region, below Mount Hemakūṭa. ||23||
And where did he establish that garland of colors?
The great tree of the colorful vine always shines forth right here. ||24||
Thus, this city of Raṅgavallī became renowned by that name.
For here Hanumān is eternally present with the passionate ārṣṭiṣeṇa.
The high-souled one, a worshiper of Rāma, comes for the purpose of seeing him.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having thus heard this captivating Raṅgavallī, the enemy of Śambara—

Wandering alone in battle like fire in the forest.
Then Gada, having approached, [struck] that elephant Sumadotkaṭa.
Seizing him by the trunk, he cast him down upon the ground.

Suddenly overcome by fear, he himself joined his palms in supplication during the battle.

Thus, having conquered the Kimpuruṣa region, the mighty son of Kṛṣṇa [proceeded].

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Victory over the Kiṃpuruṣa-khaṇḍa," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||26||
Śrī Nārada said:
There is a region named Harivarṣa, endowed with every kind of prosperity.
O King of Mithilā, his boundary mountain was the actual Nishadha itself.
From within the forest, which was filled with the sounds of the twanging of heroes' bows, [he emerged].
The great vultures flew up, possessing bodies a krośa in size. ||2||
O King, all those with sharp beaks, including the Garuḍas, are long-lived.

In the army, due to the darkness, a great cry of "Alas! arose. ||4||
Then the mighty-armed son of Kṛṣṇa invoked the Tārkṣya weapon.
From his arrow emerged directly the Lord of Birds, Vainateya himself.
When the army was enveloped in darkness, the Lord of Birds [appeared].
Some he struck with the blow of his beak, and others with his wings that flashed with radiance.
Garuḍa struck down the vultures and kuliṅga birds to the surface of the earth.
Their pride shattered and their wings clipped, those birds were devoured.
Afflicted by fear, they fled in the ten directions even from Tārkṣya.
Then the mighty-armed son of Kṛṣṇa went to the territories of the Daśārṇas.

He gave an offering of excellent jewels to the high-souled Pradyumna.
The Lord Pradyumna is manifest, all-pervading, and all-seeing.
Out of a desire to gather the world together, he questioned that one of auspicious limbs.
Pradyumna said:

Tell me this, O King, Lord of the city of Niṣkauśāmbī.

"In ancient times, having slain Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Blessed One became Nṛsiṃha."
But Prahlāda, having come here, remained in Harivarṣa. ||14||

Therefore, O Great-minded One, I shall not cause your lineage to perish. (15)
Śubhāṅga said:
As he spoke thus, drops of tears of joy fell from his eyes.
O King, where those two fell, a lake was formed that became a source of auspiciousness. ||16||
Then, O King, having obtained the boon, Prahlāda was overwhelmed with joy.
The righteous-souled one, having bowed down with palms joined in reverence, spoke to Nṛsiṃha. ||17||

O Supreme Lord, tell me how I may be liberated from this debt to those two.
Nṛsiṃha said: "In this sacred ford born from the water of my eye, which is a source of auspiciousness,"
Perform your bath, O illustrious one; you shall be liberated from the ten debts.
Of one's mother, father, wife, sons, teacher, and deities.
And the debt to the Brahmins, to those who have sought refuge, to the sages, and to the ancestors.
He who, intent on insulting everyone, shall bathe in this great sacred ford;
He too is liberated from ten debts; there is no doubt in this matter. ||21||
Śubhāṅga said: Having bathed at the Daśārṇamocana tīrtha, Kāyādhava was freed from his debt.
Having become so, even today she comes from the Niṣadha mountain to bathe there.
At the Daśārṇamocana tīrtha, the region is called Daśārṇa.
Arising from its streams, this river is known as the Daśārṇeyā. ||23||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard that, the Blessed One, the son of Kṛṣṇa, together with all his attendants, [departed].
At the Daśārṇamocana tīrtha, he indeed performed ritual bathing and gave gifts.
O King, whoever should hear this story of the liberation of the Daśārṇas, [attains the highest goal].
He is also liberated from ten debts and shall become a partaker of liberation. ||25||

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Victory over the Daśārṇa Country," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||27||
The venerable Nārada said:

He went to the side of Śṛṅgavān, which was filled with various wonderful prosperities. ||1||

He who has gathered the great equipment, surrounded by hosts of divine sages.
That Guṇākara commenced the tenth horse sacrifice.

His son, Vīradhanvan, went forth to protect it. ||4||
Adorned with ten akṣauhiṇīs, he possessed fierce prowess.
The great hero wandered about, keeping his eye on the horse.
Vīra, Candra, Sena, Citragu, and King Vegavān.

Having prostrated before that king, the legitimate son of Guṇākara who possessed the splendor of the sun, he spoke as he sat upon his chariot.
Ugrasena was the lord of the earth, the ruler of Dvārakā, and the best of the Yadus.
Having conquered the kings of Jambūdvīpa, he will perform the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Urged by him, the hero Pradyumna, the best among archers, [set forth].
Having conquered that region of Bhārata as well as Kiṃpuruṣa, the king— ||14||

He, too, will offer tribute to the high-souled Pradyumna.
Accompanied by ten akṣauhiṇīs, he was honored even by Dhanada.
"You must present a gift to the high-souled Pradyumna."
Who on earth is capable of seizing the sacrificial animal taken away by him?
The Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra is his companion. || 17 ||
It would have been auspicious through gifts and honors, had there not been this war.
Vīradhanvan said:

On the delightful Śṛṅgavata mountain, Hari exists in the form of Varāha. || 19 ||
Whose service the Earth always performs with the highest respect.
In whose field Guṇākara performed penance, having meditated upon the God.
When ten thousand years were completed, Hari assumed the form of a boar.
Being satisfied, he said to the devoted king, "Choose a boon."
The king, overwhelmed with horripilation and love, bowed to Hari and said:
O Blessed One, there is no god, nor any other celestial being, nor even a human, who exists apart from you.
"May there be no one on earth who can defeat me; this is the boon desired by me."
Having said, "So be it," the Blessed One vanished right there.
Therefore, his liberation must be swiftly brought about by himself through his own glory.
If you do not [agree], I shall undoubtedly engage in a quarrel with you. || 24 ||
The venerable Nārada said:
O King, having been addressed thus by him, Uddhava returned to his own army.
He quickly related everything that had occurred in the assembly of the Yadus.
Śrutakarman, Vṛṣa, the hero Subāhu, Bhadra, and Ekalavya.
Śānti, Darśa, Pūrṇamāsa, Soma, and Vara as well; || 26 ||
For these are the sons of Kālindī, while Pradyumna looks on.
Surrounded by ten akṣauhiṇīs, they have come together to fight.
Together with the Uttarakurus and the Yadus of fierce prowess.
A tumultuous battle took place, like that of oceans clashing with oceans.
The foremost of warriors shone with their flashing, sharpened weapons.
In a mere instant, she who originated from blood assumed a fierce form.
O Indra among kings, it became a river a hundred yojanas in width.
Then the remaining people of Uttarakuru fled.
Just as when the autumn season has arrived, the masses of clouds disperse here and there.
Pūrṇamāsa, Mahāvīra, Kālindīnandana, and Bala.
He pulverized the chariot of Vīradhanvan with a flood of arrows.
Vīradhanvā, though deprived of his chariot, repeatedly twanged his bow.
He struck the mighty Pūrṇamāsa with twenty arrows.
Pūrṇamāsa split them in two at their midsections with his own arrow. ||33||
Then Vīradhanvan cut through his sounding bowstring.
O Indra among kings, he was struck by a single arrow, just as friendship is destroyed by a single ill-spoken word. ||34||
Quickly taking up a heavy mace weighing a hundred thousand bhāras.
The mighty Pūrṇamāsa struck Vīradhanvā. ||35||
Vīradhanvā, intoxicated with pride, was pained by the blow of the mace.
The son of Hari struck Pūrṇamāsa violently with his iron club.
Pūrṇamāsa, having risen, [reached] the mountain named Pavana.
Having uprooted [it] and stood there, the son of Śrī Hari held it with both hands. ||37||
Then, having whirled it around, he hurled it with great force toward the city of Vārāhī.
Vīradhanvan fell at Guṇākara’s sacrificial ground.
Fainting and his momentum broken, he vomited blood from his mouth. || 39 ||
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the city of Vārāhī as it was swiftly approached.
Then the celestial drums resounded, as did the drums of men.
Above Pūrṇamāsa, the gods rained down a shower of flowers.
Rising from the sacrifice, the king saw his son unconscious.
Having taken up his divine bow, he set his mind upon fighting.
The Hotṛ priest, the best among those who know the Dharma, the lord of sages, the all-knowing seer.
Seeing him prepared to depart, Vāmadeva said to him: || 42 ||
Vāmadeva said:
O King, for you do not know Hari, the most perfect one.
He who was born himself in the Yadu clan for the great benefit of the gods.
For the removal of the earth's burden and for the protection of devotees. || 43 ||
Having appeared in the Yadu lineage, he shines forth visibly in Dvārakā.
By that Kṛṣṇa, this son Pradyumna, the lord of the Yādavas, was produced.
He was impelled to conquer the world for the sake of Ugrasena’s sacrifice. || 44 ||
Guṇākara said:
Of the great-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is most perfectly complete.
O Brahmin, you who are the most knowledgeable among those who know both the higher and the lower, tell me the definition [of this].
Vāmadeva said:
In whom all splendors dissolve into his own splendor.
They call him Hari, the supreme, manifest, and most perfect.
The partial portion, the sub-portion, the portion, as well as the entry, and the digit—these are declared to be the full.
And he is remembered by Vyāsa and others as the sixth [incarnation], the most perfect one himself.
He is indeed Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the most perfectly complete; he is certainly none other.
Having arrived for the sake of a single task, he indeed accomplished ten million tasks.
The venerable Nārada said:
Having heard of Kṛṣṇa’s greatness, Guṇākara brought an offering.
Having cast aside his enmity, he arrived for the sake of seeing Pradyumna. || 49 ||
Having circumambulated the son of Kṛṣṇa, bowed down, and offered the sacrificial oblation, he then departed.
With his face filled with tears, he spoke in a faltering voice.
Guṇākara said:
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my lineage is auspicious.
Today, all sacrificial rites have become fruitful through the sight of you. ||51||
May devotion to your feet, characterized by the ultimate goal, always arise through association with the virtuous.
O Supreme Lord, O Infinite One, you alone are manifestly affectionate toward your own devotees; protect me, protect me! 52.
Pradyumna said:
Devotion conjoined with knowledge and dispassion is characterized by love.
May there be association with my devotees, and may there be prosperity here among the followers of the Bhāgavata.
The venerable Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the son of Kṛṣṇa, who is affectionate toward his devotees, was pleased.
He gave that horse fit for a horse-sacrifice to that king.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Victory over the Region of Uttarakuru," in the dialogue between Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārada said:
Then the mighty-armed Pradyumna, having conquered the Northern Kurus from afar, [proceeded].
The son of Kṛṣṇa indeed went forth to conquer the region named Hiraṇmaya.
There, the boundary mountain is long, and there is a stream named Srotas of shimmering luster.
Therein, Kūrma is Hari himself, whose teacher is Aryaman.
On the bank of the river Puṣpamālā, there was a great forest named Citravana.
Abundantly laden with the weight of flowers and fruits, it is naturally a treasure-trove of bulbs and roots. ||3||
There also dwell monkeys born of the lineages of Nala and Nīla.
O Lord of Mithilā, these were established by Śrī Rāmacandra during the Tretā age.
And hearing that roar of the army, those desiring battle came forth.
And in Pradyumna’s army, those overcome by rage rose up with the knitting of their brows.
O King, with their claws, teeth, and tails, they [attacked] elephants, horses, and men.
And having tethered the chariots with their tails, they forcefully hurled them into the sky.
The victory of Vijayadhvaja, the Lord, and the victory of Arjuna.
Then, having harnessed the chariot to its tail, some leapt up into the sky.
On the banner of the monkey-bannered one, there was the Lord himself, the Blessed One, the King of Monkeys.
Abounding in wrath and a friend of Phālguna, he [pervaded] the entire world in every direction. ||8||
And having bound them with his tail, he cast them down upon the ground.
Then all the servants of Śrī Rāma, having learned this, were filled with great joy. ||9||
O King, they all slowly bowed down to him from every side with their palms joined in reverence.
Some embraced him, while others sprang up with vigor.
Some monkeys kissed his tail, while others kissed his feet.
Having embraced them and touched them again with their own hands, those great heroes—
Having bestowed his blessing, the son of Añjanī then inquired after his welfare.
Having bowed to him, O King, all the monkeys went to Citravana.
Hanumān, moreover, vanished within the banner of Arjuna as well.
Then, from that region called Makara, Pradyumna, whose banner bears the fish, [emerged]. ||13||
He went forth together with the best of the Vṛṣṇis, repeatedly sounding kettledrums.
Then, on the side of Mount Makara, with the sounds of kettledrums, ||14||
It is said that millions of honey-bees, subsisting on honey, have flocked there.
The entire army was armored by them and filled with the trumpeting of elephants.
Then the mighty-armed son of Kṛṣṇa took up the wind-weapon (pavanāstra).
O King, struck by that wind, they too fled in the ten directions.
In that region, O King, all the people indeed have the faces of crocodiles.
Beyond that is the region of Diṇḍibha, where the people have elephant-like faces. ||17||
Thus, seeing various regions, he arrived at the territory of Triśṛṅga.
There too, Kārṣṇi saw men wearing horns.
On the side of Mount Triśṛṅga, there was a city adorned with gold.
It was divine, consisting of golden palaces, and adorned with walls of jewels.
With men of golden hue and women possessing the brilliance of lightning.
And with nāgas and nāga maidens, it was like the city of Bhogavatī.
On the bank of the Candrakāntā river stood the auspicious abode, resplendent with beauty.
O King, the son of Kṛṣṇa arrived like Śakra arriving at Amarāvatī.
There, the king named Mahāvīra was powerful and a friend of the gods.
Having heard of Bala’s strength from my mouth, he brought golden Bali [as tribute].
He worshipped Pradyumna again with supreme devotion.
The mighty-armed Lord Hari Pradyumna questioned him.
Tell me quickly, how is it that the splendor of all [the Buddhas] is like that of the moon?
Devasakha said:
[This was spoken] by Aryaman, the Lord of the Ancestors, regarding the Lord of the Earth who had assumed the form of a tortoise. ||24||
By that water with which his feet were washed, a great river was formed.
And descending from the peak of the White Mountain, O best of the Yadus.
The son of Manu named Pramēdha was appointed as the cowherd by his preceptor.
At night, suspecting her to be a lioness, he killed Kapilā when she had settled down.
Then, cursed by Vasiṣṭha, he fell into the state of a Śūdra.
His body afflicted by leprosy, he wandered about, visiting sacred pilgrimage sites. ||27||
When the son of Manu bathed in this river, his leprosy vanished.
He became liberated like the moon, and his bodily splendor shone forth.
And this river, known as Candrakāntā, became famous in the Golden Age.
For having bathed in that [river], the son of Manu was freed from his leprosy. ||29||
Then, O best of kings, we shall all perform our ablutions.
In beauty we shall be equal to the moon in this world; of this there is no doubt. ||30||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard this, the mighty-armed Pradyumna, together with the Yādavas, [acted].
Having bathed in the Candrakāntā river, he gave gifts many times over.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Victory over the Hiraṇmayakhaṇḍa," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||29||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having thus conquered the region of Hiraṇmaya, the mighty son of Kṛṣṇa—
He went to the delightful region of Ramyaka, which shone like the realm of the gods. ||1||
The mountain that serves as its boundary is the king of mountains, Nīla by name, manifest in person.
There, in the northern region, is the city named Bhīmanādinī.
There was a Rākṣasa named Kalaṅka, the son of Kālanemi.
In the Tretā Yuga, fearing Rāmacandra, he fled from battle. ||3||
Having come here to the city of Laṅkā, he dwelt together with the Rākṣasas.
He resolved to fight with ten million rākṣasas. ||4||
Mounted upon a donkey and black in color, he approached the strength of the Yadus.
A terrible battle indeed took place between the Yadus and the Rākṣasas.
Praghoṣa, Gātravan, Siṃha, Bala, Prabala, and Ūrdhvaga.
Saha-ojas, Mahāśakti, and Aparājita as well. ||6||
For these auspicious sons of Śrī Kṛṣṇa are indeed the delighters of Lakṣmaṇā.
He was encountered by all of them at once with sharp arrows of shimmering luster.
They destroyed the strength of the rākṣasas, as winds with the force of the wind disperse a cloud.
The Rākṣasas, who were fierce in battle, had their limbs cut and pierced by volleys of arrows. ||8||
Intoxicated with pride, they rained down tridents and mallets.
Then Kalaṅka arrived, devouring elephants and chariots.
He swiftly cast horses and men, along with their weapons and missiles, into his mouth.
And having raised the elephants by their feet, together with their attendants and their jeweled blankets.
Accompanied by the sound of bells, he forcefully cast them into the sky.
Praghoṣa, the son of Śrī Hari, took up the weapon of the Lord of Monkeys. ||11||
From that arrow emerged the mighty son of Vāyu in person.
The wind cast him a hundred yojanas into the sky, like a tuft of cotton.
Then, having recognized Hanumān, the lord of the Rākṣasas, Kalaṅka, [acted].
Making a great noise, he hurled a heavy mace weighing a hundred thousand bhāras.
The monkey leapt up with speed, and the mace fell to the ground.
Leaping up, the lord of monkeys repeatedly knit his brows.
Having struck him with his fist, he seized that crown of his.
Then Kalaṅka also took up his own trident against him. ||15||
As he was leaping up with great speed, the monkey fell upon the region of his back.
Then Hanumān, having thrown him to the ground with his two arms, [struck him].
Having brought him to a mountain of beryl, he threw him down upon it.
With his limbs crushed by the fall from the mountain, he was ground to pieces and met his death. ||17||
Then there arose a roar of "Victory! Victory! accompanied by the sound of conch shells.
The Lord Hanumān himself vanished right there. ||18||
The gods showered a rain of flowers upon Pradyumna.
Then the mighty-armed son of Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by his own army, [advanced].
He went to the human city of Manoharā, which was made of gold.
There, the forest of ultimate liberation was covered with wish-fulfilling trees and creepers.
It was adorned with yellow sandalwood trees, mandāra flowers, and pārijāta trees.
It was made fragrant by breezes mingled with the joy of the [celestial] lineage. ||21||
It was frequented by ketakī, campaka creepers, and kuṭaja trees.
It was surrounded by networks of flowering and fruit-bearing mādhavī creepers. ||22||
It was as beautiful as Vaikuṇṭha, filled with the songs of birds and swarms of bees.
It was five hundred yojanas in height and possessed beautiful peaks. ||23||
O King, it was adorned further and further down, extending for a hundred yojanas.
With male cuckoos, common cuckoos, peacocks, cranes, and parrots; ||24||
It resounded with the cries of ruddy geese, chakora birds, swans, and water-hens.
It surpassed the Nandana grove, which is richly adorned with flowers of every season.
O King of Mithilā, young fawns indeed sport together with tigers.
Where mongooses, having abandoned their enmity, dwell together with serpents. ||26||
There, ten thousand lakes resounded with the humming of bees.
With thousand-petaled lotuses and hundred-petaled lotuses of shimmering radiance. ||27||
Moving here and there, as if bliss itself were embodied.
Having seen that beautiful forest, the people of the city came forth.
Pradyumna himself, the omniscient poet, asked them what they desired. ||28||
Śrī Pradyumna said:
Whose is this beautiful city, and whose is this wonderful forest?
Speak quickly and in detail, O people of meritorious conduct! ||29||
The people said:
"O King, he who conducts himself in this manner is indeed Manu, the son of Vivasvat."
And on the delightful Mount Mānava, [he saw] Matsya, Nārāyaṇa, and Hari.
Having always bowed to the Present [Tathāgata], he performs extensive asceticism.
This is his delightful city, and this is his forest of ultimate liberation.
The earth and this mountain were likewise brought from Vaikuṇṭha.
All of you kings on earth are born of his lineage.
O King, indeed within the Solar dynasty and within the Lunar dynasty.
Śrī Nārada said:
And among all the kṣatriyas, he was their aged great-grandfather.
Having realized that Manu was Śrāddhadeva, the son of Hari was filled with wonder.
Having heard those words, he was immediately surrounded by his brothers and the Yadus.
Having ascended Mānavādri, he beheld Śrāddhadeva.
With a splendor like a hundred suns, he illuminated the ten directions with his radiance.
He is the embodiment of Mahāyoga, the King of Kings himself, appearing in a peaceful form.
And by Vedavyāsa, Śuka, and others, as well as Vasiṣṭha, Dhiṣaṇa, and the rest.
O Great King, they listened to one another as they heard the glory of Śrī Hari. ||36||
Kṛṣṇī, together with the Yadus, bowed down to him and remained there with palms joined in reverence.
Manu, rising up and recognizing the power of Hari, offered him a seat and spoke with a faltering voice. ||37||
Manu said:
Salutations to you, Vāsudeva; salutations to Saṃkarṣaṇa as well.
Salutation to Pradyumna, to Aniruddha, the Lord of the Sātvatas. ||38||
The selfless Puruṣa is you alone;
you are devoid of qualities and you are beyond Prakṛti.
Having always brought Pradhāna under your control by force through your qualities, you create, consume, and protect the universe. ||39||
Then, having abandoned all sense of separation and realizing that this entire world here is composed of mind, he [remained].
The Supreme Illusion, devoid of qualities, the primordial Person, the omniscient, the first Puruṣa, the eternal. ||40||
When this person has gone to sleep, he who remains awake— this world does not know him, the Being who is beyond.
I worship Him who, though seeing, is not seen by people, and who is both pure and yet possessed of impurity. 41.
Just as the sky, fire, and wind are not attached to a pot, nor to wood, nor to dust-covered objects;
In that same way, you are stainless with all virtues, just as a crystal might be exceedingly brilliant in its colors. ||42||
Through elliptical expressions, secondary indications, and paths of speech dedicated to the ultimate *sphoṭa*, one attains the supreme meaning and state.
It is not known even by the most excellent of wealthy men who speak rightly; how much less so by worldly people? (43)
Some say that on this earth the agent of action is time, while others say it is supreme yoga alone.
Some proclaim that which the knowers of the Vedanta call Brahman to be *vicāra* (investigation). ||44||
That which the qualities (guṇas) do not touch here, nor those born of time, nor the organs of knowledge, the mind, the intellect, nor the cognitive faculties;
"The Great Veda speaks thus," they say; therefore, all enter into that supreme state like sparks from a fire. ||45||
The wise declare that Hiraṇyagarbha, the supreme reality of the Self, is Vāsudeva.
Considering you to be such a one, the supreme among the best of men, I always wander about free from attachment. ||46||
The venerable Lord Pradyumna, Hari, having then heard those words of Manu, spoke.
With a gentle smile, he spoke to Manu with words that seemed as if they were utterly enchanting him.
Pradyumna said:
"You are our preceptor, the first king of the Kṣatriyas, and our grandfather."
"You are venerable to me; you are an elder, praiseworthy, and a bearer of the burden of Dharma. ||48||
O King, both you and your subjects must be protected and sustained by us in every way.
By you, divine austerity is being practiced; by that, the world attains happiness.
A virtuous person like you is to be sought; indeed, Hari himself is the Supreme Self.
Only the virtuous person, and not the sun, removes the inner darkness of men.
The venerable Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord Kārṣṇi took leave of him, bowed down, and departed.
Having circumambulated Manu, O King, he himself went down to the earth. 51.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Victory over the Land of the Mānavas," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||30||
The illustrious Nārada said:
Thus, having conquered the region of Ramyaka, the mighty son of Kṛṣṇa—
He went to Ketumāla in the eastern direction of Mount Sumeru.
O King of Mithilā, his boundary mountain was the very Mālyavat itself.
Where the Gaṅgā, known by four names, destroys great sins. ||2||
On the side of Mount Mālyavān lies a city that is full of amorous charm.
And it was adorned with jeweled walls and palaces, like the celestial city of the gods.
O King, where indeed dwell men whose splendor is equal to that of Kāmadeva.
Dark-complexioned like autumnal blue lotuses, with eyes resembling lotus petals. ||4||
Women wearing yellow garments, enchanting with garlands of flowers.
Where amorous women in the bloom of youth play with balls. ||5||
That breeze, fragrant with the body's scent, was made resonant by the humming of swarms of intoxicated bees.
It perfumes the region of the earth for a hundred yojanas in every direction. ||6||
The inhabitants of that city, who were deeply learned, came forth.
They sang the glory of Murāri and of Pradyumna as well, while he listened.
The inhabitants of Ketumāla said:
"There was indeed the primordial God, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, who lies upon the serpent Śeṣa as his bed and who removes the afflictions of the world."
Salutation to that Blessed One, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who was entreated by the best of gods for the protection of the world.
Having been born and having departed from his father's house, he— now in the body of an infant— liberated his parents and went to Nanda’s abode with the wife of Nanda.
Loved with affection and possessing great auspicious glory, he indeed dealt a fatal blow to Pūtanā. ||9||
As a child, he broke the cart while making his bed, and having struck down the Daitya, he placed that great marvel upon his back.
Having revealed his true form to his mother, he became adorned by Garga, who had described his beautiful fortune and splendor. ||10||
That boy, a thief of fresh butter, cherished by the people of Vraja, is dark-complexioned, possesses a captivating body, and is tender.
Breaking through, he devoured the vessel of curd;
though tied with a light cord by his mother, he shattered the two trees.
Wandering through Vṛndāvana together with the calves and cowherds, he struck down the demon Vatsāsura with kapittha trees.
Seizing the Daitya instantly with his two arms by the mouth of his donkey-like snout, he tore him apart like a blade of grass in the river.
And he, assuming the attire that enchants even Madana, herds many groups of calves with his children while sounding his flute.
He, whose body was that of a cowherd boy, protected the cowherds, the cows, and the calves who had been cast into the mouth of the demon Gopānagha, and he did so instantly.
The Knower of the Field, the Self, the Person, the Blessed One, the Infinite, the Full, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, the Primordial God.
Assuming that form and sporting among the boys of Vraja,
the unborn Kṛṣṇa wandered about, utterly bewildering Brahmā.
Seizing the powerful one named Kāliya with his strength, he suddenly hurled the mighty Dhenuka onto a palm tree.
He wandered about, drank fire, and swallowed his younger brother; that powerful one immediately slew Pralamba with a firm fist.
He who, wandering through the forest, sweetly sounding his flute, has his fame sung by the women of Vraja.
Having partaken of the food prepared by the wives of the brahmins on all sides, he carried off the divine garments of the excellent women.
And while the god was raining, desiring out of compassion to protect the cattle, he held up Govardhana like a child picking up a mushroom.
Holding Mount Kailāsa in one hand like an elephant holding a lotus, he was praised by the words of Indra, the Lord of Śacī. ||17||
Having shown the world both the divine and the supreme beyond darkness in the heavens, he protected Nanda from Varuṇa for the sake of his own kin.
Having entered the circle of the Śrī-rāsa dance, He took delight with the beautiful women of Vraja on the sandy bank of the Pulinda river.
Taking away the pride of those women who were arrogant because of their passion and youth, he—whose fame was sung by the women of Vraja—disappeared from sight.
Adorned with garlands and possessing a captivating form, Hari himself—the enchanter of Madana—appeared before those afflicted by the pain of separation. (19)
In Vṛndāvana, Viṣṇu, the primordial god, was [attended] by the wives of the Śabara chiefs, who were like the splendors of the heavens.
And he, adorned with armlets, earrings, and the ornate crest of a crown, rejoices, praised by the best of gods, upon the stage of the rāsa dance.
Having liberated Nanda, he bestowed upon the serpent king the divine jewel that grants liberation; and he, in turn, took it from Śaṅkhacūḍa.
Praised by the cowherds, he indeed struck Ariṣṭa— who had assumed the form of a bull—
after throwing him to the ground, killing him with his hand upon the horns.
Kaṃsa was seized by supreme fear, and by him the fierce Keśin was dispatched, possessing a body like a cloud thick with rain.
Having swiftly cast him off, Kṛṣṇa struck him with his glorious arm as he was rushing back toward him, the arm which had been placed in [the demon's] mouth.
He by whom the celestial being Vyoma—whose fortune and splendor had been extolled in many ways by Nārada—was deprived of his life by a superior foe.
The primordial God, whose great glory was described by Akrūra, who steals the hearts of the cowherd women distressed by their intense separation from Him.
Having shown his own true form to the son of Śvaphalka for his benefit, he vanished into the mass of water.
The Supreme Lord reached the grove of Mathurā there, and together with his forces, he beheld Mathurā along with the cowherds.
Wandering at his own will in Madhupura, Kṛṣṇa executed the washerman and then bestowed boons upon the weaver.
Having shown compassion for Mālavikā, he made the hunchbacked woman straight; and suddenly, while bending the bow, he broke it.
Having struck down ten princes at the gate,
and having killed, seized, and cast them down upon the arena floor, that lord of men—
Then Hari, having released Kaṃsa and his parents from their bonds, established Ugrasena as king in the city.
Having propitiated Nanda, who had performed many acts of charity, he summoned the Yadus, gratified them with great wealth, and made his announcement.
Having mastered the sciences, Kṛṣṇa bestowed [the kingdom] upon him, for he had made the offspring of Danuja-Pañcajana as good as dead by slaying him.
Having bestowed his grace upon the cowherd women, he then went with Uddhava and Akrūra to Hastināpura to see the sons of Pāṇḍu.
Having conquered the powerful son of Jarā, Kṛṣṇa reduced him to ashes by means of the Mucukunda glance, which was his own appointed time.
Having created a wonderful city for his residence here, Kṛṣṇa reportedly brought the daughter of Bhīṣmaka from the city of Kuṇḍina.
Through his son, he slew Śambara, the enemy, and having conquered the king of the bears in battle, he brought the jewel to the king.
And that Lord of Bhāmā, the Supreme Master, having taken the head of Śatadhanvan, carried away the daughter of Savitṛ.
Having subdued the bulls, Kṛṣṇa carried off Satyā, the daughter of the King of Āvantī, from the hall of the self-choice ceremony. ||30||
He carried off the auspicious daughter of the King of Kaikeya, as well as the daughter of Śrī Lakṣmaṇa, the lord of all that is auspicious.
Having conquered Bhauma along with his army in battle by means of multitudes of weapons, he also took away sixteen thousand excellent women.

Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard these words of his, the mighty Daitya was delighted.

The Lord Pradyumna himself, manifesting in a human form for his divine play.

Vṛka, Harṣa, Anila, Gṛdhra, Vardhana, and Annāda.

With his bow broken, having become a wolf, his horses slain and his charioteer killed.

At that moment, the delighted asura severed his bow in the battle.
Then Vṛka, that bull among the Yādavas, took up his mace.

He who is established in knowledge, who has resorted to supreme dispassion, and who is a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, even if he is free from worldly expectations;

those three qualities do not touch him on all sides.

Just as at sunrise all darkness dissolves and objects within the house become visible to people;

likewise, the supreme Brahman shines forth within the body.
Just as the supreme object, which rests upon the three guṇas, cannot be inferred by the senses through their separate paths; |||

Some call the supreme state Vaiṣṇava, while others call it the Supreme Lord beyond Vaikuṇṭha.
And some declare it to be peace, others call it the Great Beyond-darkness, and still others the Radiant Absolute.

Some sages attain a bower concealed by Kṛṣṇa’s own pastimes, and they reach His very feet. ||23||

Just as Kṛṣṇa was in the belly of Baka, and Vṛṣa was in the belly of Vṛtra.
Then, when a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose in the army of the Yadus, the King of Videha—
The powerful one, the younger brother of Baladeva, took up his mace, gadā.
He struck the exceedingly powerful Daitya named Vṛka on the head. ||38||
Then the Daitya, his head struck, shone with drops of blood.
Just as Mount Vindhya was [drenched] by the streams of water from the clouds, O King.
Phālguna, taking up his own sword, quickly struck at his feet.
With his feet severed, he fell upon the earth like a mountain whose wings have been clipped.
Aniruddha, having burst through her belly, emerged with his sword.
And he carried off that head, just as the slayer of Vṛtra [Indra] did with his thunderbolt. ||41||
Then, indeed, a cry of "Victory! Victory! arose among the Yadu army.
The drums of the gods resounded, and likewise the drums of men.
Above Aniruddha, the gods let fall a rain of flowers.
Indeed, this wonderful thing has been told; what more do you wish to hear? ||43||
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Daitya Vṛka," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||34||
Bahulāśva said: "O Sage, what a most wonderful battle has been fought by the son of Pradyumna!"
When the great Daitya Vṛka was slain, what happened next in the battle?
Śrī Nārada said:
Seeing the Daitya Vṛka slain, the great asura Kālanābha [attacked].
Mounted upon his lap, he repeatedly made his bow twang in the battle. ||2||
He struck Akrūra with twenty arrows and Gada with ten shafts.
[He struck] Arjuna with ten arrows and Yuyudhāna with five.
He struck Kṛtavarman with ten arrows and the son of Kṛṣṇa (Sātyaki) with a hundred arrows.
And Aniruddha with twenty, and Dīptimant with five. ||4||
And in that battle, the asura pierced Sāmba with a hundred arrows.
The heroes became overwhelmed by his arrows for a period of two ghaṭikās.
And the horses met their death on the field of battle, being ground to powder.
Seeing that dexterity of hand, the son of Rukmiṇī was pleased.
In the battle, he honored Kālanābha with well-spoken words.
Pradyumna, having taken up his own bow, fixed a single arrow upon it.
An arrow released from his bow struck that long-bodied creature in its chest.
Having lifted it up and whirled it around for a hundred thousand yojanas in the heavenly realm. ||8||
He caused it to fall from the sky into the ocean that resounded with a terrifying roar.
The Lord Pradyumna himself took up a second Bāṇa. ||9||
That Bāṇa also raised his great and powerful spear, Kālanābha.
Whirling him about, he forcibly threw him down in the city of Candrāvatī.
Kālanābha fell down, his mind somewhat agitated.
Then, having seized a heavy mace weighing one hundred thousand bhāras.
Having reached the battlefield, the king of the Daityas crushed the host of the Yadus.
With his mace, which was like a thunderbolt, he struck down elephants, chariots, horses, and heroes.
He struck them down with force, just as a great wind fells trees.
Lifting some up with both hands, he forcefully hurled them into the sky.
O King, they fell from the sky upon the earth like hailstones.
Then Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī, took up his mace.
He struck that Daitya, the great Asura Kālanābha, on the head.
A terrible battle with maces took place between those two on the field of combat.
The two maces, emitting sparks, were reduced to powder.
Taking up their weapons, those two stood ready for battle.
Then Kālanābha spoke to Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī.
I shall slay you with even a single blow; there is no doubt about this. ||17||
"Strike me first," Samba said in the battle.
Then Kālanābha struck Sāmba on the head with a mace.
Having taken up a mace upon his mace, Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī, [stood ready].
He struck the Daitya Kālanābha on the chest with his mace. ||19||
With his heart pierced by the mace, he vomited blood from his mouth.
Lifeless, he fell upon the surface of the earth like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt. ||20||
O King, there arose a cry of "Victory! Victory! and the acclaim of "Well done! from the virtuous.
The drums of the gods resounded, and likewise the drums of men.
Above Sāmbasena, the gods rained down a shower of flowers.
And the Vidyādharīs and Gandharvas danced and sang with joy. ||22||

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Daitya Kālanābha," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva, within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga Saṃhitā. ||35||
Śrī Nārada said:
When Kālanābha had fallen, a great clamor arose.
Mounted upon a camel, the Daitya Mahānābha arrived on the field of battle. ||1||
The illusory Daitya, the preeminent among demons, emitted fire from his mouth.
By that fire, the earth, the trees, and the ten directions were set ablaze.
For heroes, there are tunics, turbans, waist-bands, and body-protectors.
They blazed up, O Great King, like the downy tufts of the muñja grass flower. ||3||
[They were] born in the seaport cities, [distinguished by their complexions] yellow, reddish, white, and black.
With green, variegated, and fine powders, as well as those derived from saffron. ||4||
And there were elephants accompanied by blankets inlaid with gold and jewels.
O King, they blazed forth in battle like mountains with trees set ablaze by fire. ||5||
With crest-jewels, chowries, necklaces, and golden ornaments.
The horses leaping in battle were like deer fleeing from a forest fire.
Seeing the army afflicted by fear, the radiant son of Kṛṣṇa [acted].
In order to extinguish the fire of illusion, he took up the Parjanya weapon.
Clouds issued forth from Bāṇa like the masses of clouds at the end of an eon.
They rained down torrents of water, uttering a terrifying roar.
O Great King, through the downpour of rain, the monsoon season arrived upon the earth.
Male cuckoos, female cuckoos, peacocks, cranes, and so forth. ||9||
The frogs croaked with their songs, and the indragopa insects quivered.
O Lord of Mithilā, the sky shone with the rainbow and lightning. 10.
When the fire had thus been extinguished, the great asura Mahānābha [acted].
In his fury, he swiftly hurled a sharp spear at the radiant one.
The radiant son of Rohiṇī [the Moon] beheld Śūla approaching like a serpent.
He cut him with his sword in battle, just as Garuḍa seizes a serpent. ||12||
And they saw Daśanta and Udbhaṭa, the camel that was the mount of Mahānābha.
Radiant with his own sword, he struck him upon the field of battle.
With his neck severed by the sword, he fell to the earth, split in two.
The camel met its death while Mahānābha was looking on.
The great Daitya Mahānābha, having mounted an elephant with great speed, [set forth].
Then, with a trident in his hand, he advanced again, making the entire expanse of the sky resound.
Having mounted his radiant steed from Sindh, which was swift and dark-hued.
The son of Śrī Kṛṣṇa shone with a sword possessing the luster of lightning. ||16||
Leaping up from the surface of the earth by striking the horse with his heel.
He mounted upon the tip of the elephant's forehead, like Hari upon a mountain peak.
The radiant son of Kṛṣṇa [struck] with a sharp-edged sword.
Suddenly, he severed the head of Mahānābha from his body.
[He saw] the army of that evil-minded one raining down a shower of arrows.
The radiant one struck [them] with his sword, as a lion slays a herd of elephants. ||19||
Some were struck down by the sword, while the remaining Daityas fled.
The gods showered a rain of flowers upon the head of the radiant one. ||20||
The Kinnaras and Gandharvas sang, and the hosts of Apsarases danced.
The sages, the seers, and the gods praised the son of Śrī Hari.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Mahānābha," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||36||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard that Mahānābha was dead and seeing the army in flight, [he spoke].
The Daitya, mounted upon a Timiṅgila fish and possessing a tawny beard, arrived.
Then the Daitya Hariśmaśru, his lower lip quivering with rage, spoke.
He spoke harsh words while the Yādavas were listening.
Hariśmaśru said:
"All of you humans are indeed of limited prowess compared to my power."
Victorious with weapons yet truly wretched—what manliness is there in one such as you? ||3||
Is there anyone among you who is powerful enough to face me with nothing but his bare hands?
Let him indeed engage in a wrestling match, so that his manliness may be seen.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard these words of the Daitya and having beheld his formidable form, [he spoke].
They all became silent, praising one another. ||5||
While everyone was looking on, the powerful Bhānu, the son of Satyabhāmā, [acted].
Suddenly casting aside his weapons, he stood in the battle remembering Kṛṣṇa.
Having emerged from the timiṅgila, the mighty Hariśmaśru [emerged].
O King, he stood facing him, vigorously slapping his arms.
And having bound arm with arm, they both exerted forceful pressure against one another.
Like two elephants in the forest, they struck one another with their tusks.
That Daitya caused the sun to rise at a distance of one hundred yojanas.
O best of kings, with his two arms, he [seized] the lion by its strength, as a lion [seizes] another lion.
Then again, the son of Kṛṣṇa [slew] the great asura Hariśmaśru.
He suddenly raised [it] by force to a height of a thousand yojanas.
Placing his own arms around her neck and laying her upon his hip;
Having seized Bhānu, the king of the Daityas caused him to fall.
Bhānu, having placed him upon his back, [seized him] with the strength of his arms.
Seizing the Daitya by the shanks, he threw him down upon the ground.
Then, rising up once more, they stood there slapping their arms.
O King, those two powerful ones rushed forward swiftly, like a Garuda and a serpent.
The Daitya, having seized the Sun—the delight of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—by the strength of his arms, [carried him away].
Having grasped his two feet, he hurled him into the sky to a distance of a hundred thousand yojanas.
The sun fell from the sky with his mind somewhat agitated.
Like Prahlāda, he was protected from the mountain peak by the grace of Hari. ||15||
Having grasped Hari’s tawny beard, the son of Hari [seized] his long beard.
Then, having whirled it around, he hurled it into the sky to a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas.
Having fallen from the sky, he too was somewhat agitated in mind.
Placing his own beard in his mouth, he struck him with his fist.
O King, there was a hand-to-hand struggle for two ghaṭikās.
With his limbs crushed and his beard tawny, he [placed] the pressing-stone upon the head of Bhānu.
And Raktākṣa, frantic with rage, hurled it with great velocity.
Bhānu, having seized a tree, hurled it at his head.
He too, having seized a tree, hurled it at the head of Bhanu.
The great Daitya had a tawny beard, red eyes, and was overwhelmed with rage. ||20||
Having seized an elephant by its trunk, he struck Bhānu with it.
And Bhānu, having led another elephant away, seized that elephant by the trunk.
He struck the great Daitya Hariśmaśru firmly with his elephant.
Then, having seized that elephant as it was uttering cries of distress, he threw it down. ||22||
Having uprooted his two tusks, he struck Bhānu with them.
Bhānu said to Ākāśavāc: "Indeed, death resides in his *kūrca*. (23)
This great asura was abandoned by Śiva because of the boon granted to him.
Having heard these words, Bhanu ran forth, filled with rage. ||24||
Having clasped him with both arms, he repeatedly prostrated at his feet.
Having whirled it about, O Great King, while all the virtuous ones were looking on. ||25||
He cast him down upon the surface of the earth, as a child might throw a water-pot.
Having raised the beard from his face and having plucked it out with the strength of his hands, ||26||
He struck the great asura Hariśmaśru on the head with his fist.
Then, when the Daitya Hariśmaśru had met his death, the lord of men [acted]. ||27||
The drums of the gods resounded, and likewise the drums of men.
There arose a roar of "Victory! Victory! and the leaders of the gods danced. || 28 ||
O King, the delighted celestial beings caused a rain of flowers to fall.
Thus, the prowess of the sons of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is most wonderful. ||29||
I have related this meritorious account to you; what more do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Daitya Hariśmaśru," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||37||
Bahulāśva said:
Having learned that his brothers, Hariśmaśru and the others, were dead, the great asura—
O best of sages, tell me what Śakuni did first? 1.
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, when Hariśmaśru was slain, Śakuni was overwhelmed with rage.
Overwhelmed with grief for his brother, he spoke to the Daityas on the field of battle.
Śakuni said:
"O Paulomas and Kālakeyas, all of you listen to my words."
Oh, the power of destiny! By which reversal might not anything occur? ||3||
By my brother Kālanābha, Yama was [confronted] during the churning of the ocean.
Even he who was previously victorious has been slain here by men through destiny;
Śambara and Sūryajit were directly conquered by the son of Kṛṣṇa as a mere child.
Utkaca was also a conqueror of Śakra, possessing great strength, indeed great strength. ||5||
He too was killed by the boy Kṛṣṇa; this was heard from Nārada.
Formerly, during the churning of the ocean, while the asuras were looking on.
For even he by whom fire was conquered has been struck down, though he was full of joy.
Before whom Varuṇa formerly fled, terrified of battle. ||7||
Even he, the scorcher of beings, was slain by those of trivial prowess.
By whom Śiva was formerly gratified through his prowess in a great battle. ||8||
That wolf was indeed slain in this battle by the fierce Vṛṣṇis.
By my brother Mahānābha, Vāyu was conquered in heaven. ||9||
Even he has now been slain here by human Yādavas.
"Alas, O Fate! By whom the powerful son of Śakra was conquered in the heavenly realm! ||10||
He too, as well as Hariśmaśru, was struck down there by the men.
Therefore, I shall make this earth devoid of fear; this is my solemn oath.
By Jarāsaṃdha, Śālva, and the wise Dantavakra.
For I am indeed accompanied by you all and by my friend Śiśupāla.
And having been summoned by the Dānavas of fierce prowess who had heard [the news], they arrived.
Accompanied by the Asura Bāṇa, I shall go to conquer the gods.
Having conquered all the formidable and evil-minded Vṛṣṇis, beginning with Kārṣṇi;
Having bound the gods together with their wives, he threw them into the mouth of a cave on Mount Meru.
And [he honors] cows, Brahmins, gods, virtuous men, the Vedas, and ascetics.
Furthermore, [he honored] sacrifices, ancestral rites, those who practice endurance, and various teachers of sacred traditions. ||15||
I shall slay him, there is no doubt; thereafter I shall live in happiness.
Blessed is Kaṃsa, the one of great heroism, powerful and victorious over the gods.
On the surface of the earth, there exists no friend who is my supreme well-wisher.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus in the battle, the mighty Śakuni, the lord of the Dānavas, [flew up]. ||17||
The Daitya suddenly came forward to face Pradyumna as well.
Having taken up a great, firm bow weighing a hundred thousand bhāras.
Created by Maya, he indeed produced that twanging sound of the bowstring.
By the sound of the twang of his bow, the elephants of the quarters were deafened. ||19||
O King, many mountains collapsed and the oceans were agitated.
The entire universe resounded and the circle of the earth trembled.
The heroes, having ascended upon the hero, were greatly overwhelmed by the twang of the bowstring.
The elephants fled from the battle, leaping up, and the horses bolted in the fray.
Thus they all fled, suddenly overwhelmed by fear.
Then the heroes, headed by Gada, arrived, stationed upon their chariots.
Making their bows twang, those men of great strength and prowess [advanced].
Śakuni pierced Arjuna with ten arrows in the battle.
The wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, along with his chariot, fell four krośas from that place.
And Śakuni, intoxicated by the pride of battle, struck Gada with twenty arrows.
O King, he hurled him along with his chariot, making the entire circle of the sky resound.
With forty arrows, the hero struck Aniruddha, the foremost of archers.
O King, he pierced him along with his chariot, making the circle of the sky resound.
Aniruddha’s chariot, together with its horses, extended for sixteen krośas.
And Śakuni struck Sāmba in the battle with sharp arrows.
O King, Sāmba also, together with his chariot, [ascended] into the sky from the field of battle.
The King of Videha fell through a path of thirty-two yojanas.
Seeing the son of Kṛṣṇa (Sātyaki) arrived, Śakuni was filled with rage. ||28||
Suddenly, he struck him on the field of battle with a multitude of arrows.
O King, Pradyumna’s chariot was agitated for two ghaṭikās. ||29||
He fell upon the earth at a distance of a hundred krośas, like a struck water-pot.
Then all the Yādavas were struck with wonder upon seeing the power of Śakuni.
They struck the Daitya with various kinds of weapons, as elephants strike a mountain.
Gada was Arjuna, while Aniruddha was the son of Sāmba and Jāmbavatī.
Making their bows twang, they returned once more to the battle.
Then the mighty-armed son of Kṛṣṇa stood upon a chariot with the speed of the wind.
Making his bow twang, O King, he arrived at the field of battle.
Resounding with a terrifying friction from the collision of the ocean of universal dissolution.
The son of Kṛṣṇa cut Śakuni’s bowstring with ten arrows.
And with thousands of horses and hundreds of arrows, he struck the chariot.
With twenty arrows, he struck the charioteer down to the ground.
Then, having raised up the chariot, it was yoked with other horses.
Having placed another's son upon his chariot, the king of the Daityas mounted the vehicle.
O King, he fixed the whistling arrow upon his bow of fierce prowess.
Drawing a hundred arrows from his quiver situated at his back, he drew them forth.
Having placed [the arrow] upon his bow and drawn it back to his ear, he spoke to Manmatha: ||37||
Śakuni said,
"I shall cause the slaughter of all those who are intoxicated with pride, the foremost among our enemies."
"Afterwards, I shall destroy the army of the Yadus, who possess their own natural splendor. (38)
Pradyumna said:
"The youth of embodied beings always passes away by the power of time, like a shadow that flickers again and again even amidst happiness."
And likewise, suffering and happiness are like a line of clouds driven by the force of the wind across the sky, coming and going. (39)
For he waters the cultivation that has already been completed, just as a farmer cuts it down on all sides with a sickle.
For thus does Time, difficult to overcome, protect the multitude of people created by itself and then strips them of their virtues.
"I shall do this," "I am doing it," and "This is mine"— thus they speak.
"I am happy," "I am joined with suffering," "my kinsmen," "the world"—thus is one deluded by egoism, O Asura. (41)
Blessed are you, O tiger among kings, who emulates the sages with your words.
The intrinsic nature of men, which is distinct from the three qualities (guṇas), is difficult to abandon. ||42||
Śrī Nārada said:
While Pradyumna and the bird were thus conversing with one another in the battle,
O Lord of Mithilā, they fought like Śakra and Vṛtra standing against each other. ||43||
Thus, those arrows released from the bow were like the rays of the sun.
The son of Kṛṣṇa severed it with an arrow, just as one severs friendship with wicked speech. ||44||
Having seized that massive, heavy mace weighing a hundred thousand bhāras.
Śakuni, intoxicated by the pride of battle, struck Pradyumna on the head.
The Blessed Lord Pradyumna himself, with his mace which was like a thunderbolt, [struck him].
Just as a staff [breaks] a glass vessel, he shattered that mace into a hundred pieces.
Then the Daitya, overcome with rage, [hurled] a trident of shimmering luster.
He struck Pradyumna on the head while uttering a loud sound.
With his own trident, the son of Hari cut the [opponent's] trident into a hundred pieces.
The son of Rukmiṇī hurled a sharp spear at Śakuni. ||48||
With his heart pierced by the spear, his mind was somewhat agitated.
On the field of battle, he struck the son of Hari with a club.
Then, having led Yamadaṇḍa away, the powerful son of Rukmiṇī—
He reduced the Daitya’s most wonderful iron club to powder. ||50||
And he suddenly struck the restless horses with speed using the staff of Yama.
He caused the charioteer and the divine chariot to fall to the surface of the earth.
O King, when the chariot had been reduced to powder along with its horses, Sūta perished.
And the great Daitya Parigha, out of rage, seized a sword.
O King of Mithilā, the great hero Pradyumna also [struck him] with the staff of Yama.
He split that sword in two, just as Garuḍa rends a serpent. ||53||
With the staff of Yama, the son of Kṛṣṇa struck that Daitya upon his shoulder.
By that blow, Śakuni immediately fell into a swoon.
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa, overcome with rage, swiftly and especially struck down the army of the Daityas.
He struck down the great heroes like a forest fire consuming a forest.
The elephants, horses, chariots, and those attacking Daityas—
Mādhava struck him down with a rod of punishment like that of Yama.
With their feet severed, their faces severed, their limbs severed, and their arms severed.
The Dvaiteyas and Danujas were rendered unconscious and met their death in battle. ||57||
Having seen Pradyumna, who possessed the form of Yama and displayed terrifying prowess.
Abandoning their respective positions on the battlefield, some fled in the ten directions.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle of Birds," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||38||
Śrī Nārada said:
Śakuni, having risen again and seeing his own army crushed, [spoke].
O great king, he took up a bow weighing a hundred thousand bhāras.
Having fixed a sharp arrow upon his bow, he of fierce prowess.
O King, the powerful Śakuni, lord of the Daityas, spoke to the son of Kṛṣṇa in the battle.
Śakuni said:
"On the surface of the earth, action is paramount; action alone is the manifest teacher, the Lord, and the Master."
O King, by that very same action one experiences high and low status in this world; through it alone come victory and defeat. ||3||
For just as a calf finds its own mother among thousands of cows, so does he find her while the virtuous look on.
For indeed, whatever good or evil has been committed by anyone goes to that very person when they stand among men.
"Therefore, I shall conquer you, my enemy, through firm action; this is the oath I have made."
Therefore, perform an immediate remedy such that there may be no defeat for you on this earth. ||5||
Śrī Pradyumna said: "If you consider action to be the primary factor, then without time, no fruit exists."
And if an obstacle should arise at any point once the cooking has been completed, others always consider that to be the most powerful [time]. (6)
When there is a process of cooking, the means of cooking never arises without an agent.
Therefore, others say that the Creator is beyond this; O bull among the Daityas, listen now to [the views on] action and time.
Some indeed know yoga as being through non-yoga; for how could there be cooking in a pot without fire?
For indeed, everything—even yoga—becomes in vain without [the proper] time, just as action is futile when the agent is absent. (8)
Likewise, when yoga, action, the agent, and time are present, a ritual performed without Sāṃkhya becomes futile.
When one does not investigate the specific modes of cooking and so forth, then there can be no accomplishment of the cooking as it truly is. ||9||
Indeed, apart from the person of Brahmā who performs the rites of yoga, there is nothing at all.
I bow to Him, the most perfect portion, by whom the entire universe is known within the void.
Śakuni said:
"O Pradyumna, O mighty-armed one, you are the treasury of knowledge itself."
By the mere sight of you, a person attains the fulfillment of their purpose. ||11||
But those who, having attained non-attachment, constantly carry out their livelihood;
Indeed, even the four-faced Brahmā is not able to describe their greatness. ||12||
The illustrious Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the powerful Daitya Śakuni, a master of illusion and king of the Daityas, [departed].
Having been instructed by Maya the Daitya, he took up the Raurava weapon.
Mahoragas, biting snakes, and scorpions with virulent poison.
Crores of Garuḍas, Bāṇas, Nīlakaṇṭhas, and Kalāpins [were there]. ||14||
They displayed their entire strength, which had become intoxicated by their own hissing sounds.
Beholding the sons of Kṛṣṇa, the one of great intelligence took up the Garuḍa weapon.
Tens of millions of Garuḍas, Bāṇas, Nīlakaṇṭhas, and Kalāpins [were there].
And other terrifying birds emerged as he looked on. ||16||
He swallowed the foremost venomous serpents, along with the vipers, in battle.
With sharp beaks and large wings, they vanished from sight in an instant. ||17||
The Daitya, moreover, [employed] the Rākṣasa, Gāndharva, and again the Gauhyakī Māyā.
O King, Śakuni, intoxicated by battle, employed the Paiśācī weapon.
From those arrows emerged millions of spirits and likewise pretas.
Those terrible ones, appearing in black forms, indeed released the glowing coals.
Then, having recognized that demoniac illusion of the Piśācas, the fish-bannered god [Kāma]—
Desiring battle, the son of Hari fixed the Sattva weapon upon his arrow. ||20||
From that, O King, millions of Viṣṇu’s attendants emerged.
They destroyed that Piśācī illusion, just as Garuḍa destroys a female serpent. ||21||
The illusory Daitya, too, once again employed a Guhyakī illusion.
Millions of clouds, roaring and of terrifying form, have arisen.
They discharge excrement, urine, blood, fat, marrow, and bone.
Then, having understood the illusory power of the Guhyakī, the blessed Lord Pradyumna [acted].
O Great King, for the purpose of destroying that [weapon], he fixed the Kola-missile upon his bow.
Then Yajñavārāha, accompanied by his hosts, emerged with a gurgling roar. ||24||
Shaking his mane with speed, he struck the clouds with his sharp fang.
Tearing [his enemies] apart in battle, he shone like a mad elephant rending bamboo groves. ||25||
Then the Daitya employed the Gandharva illusion on the field of battle.
In the same way, no battle is seen there, nor are there millions of golden palaces. ||26||
They became adorned with garments and ornaments before the eyes of the virtuous onlookers.

Having recognized that Gandharva illusion was intended to bewilder him, the mighty son of Kṛṣṇa [Kārttikeya]...

The illusionist, that bull among the Daityas, employed a Rākṣasa illusion.

A great darkness fell upon the earth, like that of dense clouds at the end of a parārdha.

Maces, iron clubs, swords, bludgeons, and so forth were on all sides.

The hosts of Rākṣasas, with spears in their hands, cried out, "Cut! Pierce!"
And hundreds of Yātudhānas were devouring elephants and horses.

For with his sharp claws, he seized mountains along with their trees in the sky.

Having seized the hosts of Rākṣasas, he tore them apart with great speed.

Having torn apart lions, tigers, and boars with his sharp claws.
Viṣṇu hurled it into the sky, and there it disappeared once again.

O King of Mithilā, the great splendor of the hero, possessing the brilliance of ten million rising suns, is indeed conquering the ten directions.

He whose chest was beautiful with the excellent jewel Śrīvatsa, who had four arms, and whose large eyes were like lotuses.

Beholding the Lord, the Yadavas, filled with supreme joy, bowed down deeply with their palms joined in reverence.
O King of Mithilā, the gods, showering flowers, raised a great cry of "Victory! on all sides.

Śrī Nārada said:
After the bird Daitya had departed, the lotus-eyed Lord [spoke].
Having summoned all the Yādavas, beginning with Kārṣṇi, he spoke thus.
The Blessed Lord said: "Formerly, this Daitya Śakuni was on the northern side of Mount Sumeru."
Having renounced food for four yugas, he propitiated Śiva through austerity.
When four yugas have passed, the Lord Maheśvara himself [appears].
Being pleased, he granted his vision and said, "Choose a boon."
Then the Daitya Śakuni, having bowed down with his palms joined in reverence, spoke slowly.
With his hair standing on end and his eyes filled with tears, he spoke with a voice faltering with emotion. ||4||
O Lord, having died, may he be restored to life through contact with the earth.
O Lord, let my death not occur in the sky for even two ghaṭikās.
Having granted him two boons, Hara himself was addressed by the Daitya.
Having given the parrot situated in its cage to the Daitya, who stood with his face bowed, he spoke.
O sinless Daitya, always protect this Śuka, who is like Jīvaka himself.
And when he has died, O Asura, you yourself must know your own destruction.
Having thus granted him that boon, Rudra vanished from sight.
Therefore, his death will occur in the fortress once the parrot has died. ||8||
The venerable Nārada said:
Having spoken thus in the assembly of heroes, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, [remained silent].
Having quickly summoned Suparṇa, he spoke with a smiling face. ||9||
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, O Tārkṣya of great intellect, and go to the city of Candrāvatī.
[He saw] the army of the Daityas, crowded together and extending for a hundred yojanas.
With palaces that touch the sky and are enchanting with gold and jewels.
It was adorned with various groves and gardens by the foremost of the Daityas. ||11||
In the fortress, at the gateway, she was guarded by the foremost of the Daityas.
O King, in order to see her, Garuḍa assumed a subtle form.
Unobserved by the hosts of Daityas, he gazed upon the turrets of the palaces.
Flying up and flying up among them, he went to the palace of Śakuni.
Gazing at Śuka, the life-force of the Daitya, he remained there for a moment.
There, Śakuni, the foremost of the Daityas, was clad in armor for the sake of battle.
The hero, bearing various weapons, his mind filled with wrath.
Taking him by the hand, she said to her retinue, "O King, I am languid with intoxication."
Madālasā said:
"O King, all your brothers are indeed well-wishers and favorable toward you."
The preeminent and formidable Daityas were slain by their lord in battle. ||16||
Do not go to fight with the Yadus; the Blessed Lord Hari has arrived.
Give him an offering immediately, by which you shall indeed attain prosperity.
Śakuni said:
"I shall slay the Yadus with my armies; my brothers were killed by force."
By the boon of Śiva, there is no death for me even in the midst of the earth.
And on the auspicious mountain Pataṅga, in the subcontinent named Candra.
But my son Śuka currently exists in the form of a living being, O beloved. (19)
The parrot was protected day and night by the serpent Śaṅkhacūḍa.
No one knows this: how my death shall come to pass. ||20||
Śrī Nārada said: Then, having heard the news from Śuka, Garuḍa, the divine vehicle, [set out].
He then set his mind on going to that sub-continent named Candra.
Flying up with speed, Garuḍa reached the shore of the ocean.
Searching for the island named Candra, the bird wandered through the sky.
In the ocean, a hundred yojanas wide, resounding with a terrifying roar.
The king of birds reached Siṃhala, which was enchanting with its clusters of creepers.
There Garuḍa asked: "What indeed is his name among people?"
Hearing that this was Siṃhala, the bird Garuḍa flew up into the air.
O King, he reached Laṅkā on the peak of Trikūṭa with great speed.
Having reached Laṅkā, he then proceeded with speed toward Pāñcajanya. ||25||
Near the ocean where the Pāñcajanya conch resided, the powerful king of birds was hungry.
He violently seized the fish with his sharp beak.
And there, a single great crocodile was suspended, measuring two yojanas in length.
And Garuḍa, possessing fierce speed, [struck] him with his sharp beak.
With his strength, Garuḍa dragged him to the shore.
O King, their mutual attraction lasted for two ghaṭikās.
And Garuḍa, possessing fierce speed, [struck] him with his sharp beak.
He struck Dhṛṣṭāṅga on the back with his staff, like Yama, the King of Death.
Quickly casting off his crocodile form, he became a great Vidyadhara.
Having bowed to the glorious Garuḍa in person, he spoke with a smiling face. ||30||
The Vidyādhara said:
"Formerly, I was indeed a Vidyādhara named Hemakuṇḍala."
He went to the celestial realm to bathe in the Ākāśagaṅgā.
O best of sages, while Kakutstha was performing his ablutions there—
Having seized him by the foot, I sportively entered into the water. ||32||
Kakutstha also cursed me: "O evil-minded one, become a crocodile!"
Having been propitiated by me, he quickly became pleased and granted a boon. ||33||
By the blow of Tārkṣya’s beak, you shall be released from the state of being a crocodile.
O observer of noble vows, by your grace I am today released from his curse.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, when the Vidyādhara Hemakuṇḍala had departed for heaven, [the sage continued].
Thereupon, Garuḍa rose up into the expanse of the sky with his two wings.
And the bird reached the sub-continent named Hari with great speed.
There, Apāntaratamas performs extensive penance.
In that hermitage of the lord of birds, the moon-like wing indeed fell.
Seeing him, the sage Apāntaratamas spoke to Garuḍa.
"O bird, place one wing upon my head and then go as you please."
Having seized him by the head, the bird of Tarkṣya took him away and departed after carrying him for a fortnight.
He beheld many moons of various phases that were equal to it.
The sage Apāntaratamas spoke to Tārkṣya, who was greatly amazed. ||39||
For whenever the incarnation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa occurred, at those very times—
O bird, even a single wing of Garuḍa falls here constantly.
In age after age, may every single incarnation of Kṛṣṇacandra be my very own wing, placed upon the crown of my head.
Or, because of his infinity, they speak of him as having a beginning and an end; I bow with my head to that Kṛṣṇa. ||41||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard that, Tārkṣya was struck with wonder and, bowing down to that bull among sages, spoke.
He went to the island of Ramaṇaka, leaping from the vault of the sky.
Having also brought an offering for the serpents, he went to the island of Āvartaka.
There, having drunk the nectar from the divine vessel of nectar, Virāṭ became powerful.

O King, leaping up into the sky, he set his mind on proceeding to battle.

He is completely filled in heaven, on earth, and throughout the entire cosmic egg.

O King, that serpent-destroyer roamed through the sky for ten million yojanas.

Then, in the great battle, Garuḍa approached the side of Kṛṣṇa.
O King, the Daitya, with a dejected mind, went to the city of Candrāvatī.

The illustrious Nārada said:
Having summoned all the remaining Daityas, the powerful one, who was skilled in various modes of warfare, [prepared for battle].

O King, Śakuni, like a cloud, created a tempest of iron arrows.

Like two lions in a mountain cave, or like two elephants in rut in the forest.
Thus, those two fought with one another in the midst of the battle.
Śakuni urged Śrī Kṛṣṇa [to travel] one hundred yojanas.

Then, having become breathless, the Daitya fell upon the field of battle. ||26||
O King of Mithilā, by touching the earth, he regained his life in a mere moment.
Taking his own head with his hand, he placed it upon his own trunk.
He rose up to wage war, and that was like a marvel.
In this manner, the great asura was slain by Kṛṣṇa seven times.
By touching the earth, he became possessed of life and rose up again like Rāhu.
Alone, he was intent on bringing about the destruction of the Yādava clan. ||29||
The great Daitya, like a powerful fire, quickly entered the forest.
[He saw] great heroic elephants, equipped with their seven limbs, armed, and fierce.
Having grasped him with both arms, he hurled him a hundred thousand yojanas into the sky.
Having seized some elephants by the mouth and with both shoulders as well; ||31||
The Daitya shone in both his armpits like Rudra at the end of time with the fire of destruction.
In that great battle, the Daitya’s feet and hands were struck with terror.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the high-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

He instantly struck off the firm head of Śakuni,
just as the thunderbolt did that of Vṛtra in the great battle.
Having seized Śakuni in that great battle, he immediately cast him, dead, by force into the sky.
"O, the Lord of Śrī has spoken with his voice that he shall lift up the Yadus in heaven with his arrows!"— so he said.

Having thus heard the words of Hari, all those foremost of the Yādavas—

Śrī Nārada said:
When the remaining Daityas had fled from the field of battle, [the Lord acted].
Hari sounded the lutes, flutes, drums, and other instruments, as well as the kettledrums.

Taking the son of Śakuni onto her lap, Queen Madālasā—
