By the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, Madhus, Śūrasenas, and Daśārhas.
And accompanied by the gods, the king shone like Śakra at a sacrifice.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the most perfect Supreme Being, manifested at the sacrifice as the incarnation of the ritual itself.
He shone with his sons and grandsons, like the Supreme Self with its manifestations.
In that excellent royal consecration sacrifice (rājasūya), which was a great accumulation of the necessary requisites.
Having made Gargācārya his preceptor, King Yadu was indeed initiated.
Ten million were officiating priests, and ten million were consecrated initiates.
The Adhvaryus [recited] five hundred thousand [verses], and likewise the Udgātṛs, others.
Having consumed clarified butter, the fire-god’s streams of flame became like the trunks of elephants.
O King of Mithilā, O wise one, having encountered indigestion during that sacrifice, it became extraordinary.
Indeed, there were no living beings whatsoever in the three worlds who remained hungry.
Indeed, all the gods fell into a state of indigestion due to the soma. ||10||
The powerful Ugrasena, the leader of the Yadus, [married] Rucimatī as his lawful wife.
He performed the ritual bath at the conclusion of the sacrifice at the sacred ford of Piṇḍāraka.
He was bathed according to the prescribed rites with Vedic hymns by sages such as Vyāsa and others.
O King, just as a sacrifice shines with a beautiful sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). ||12||
The drums of the gods resounded, and likewise the drums of men.
The gods showered a rain of flowers upon Ugrasena.
And fourteen million elephants laden with burdens of gold.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, he gave a supreme sacrificial fee consisting of one hundred arbudas of horses.
Along with ten million pieces of the nine precious gems, together with great necklaces and garments.
To the sage Gargācārya, together with household utensils. ||15||
The high-minded Ugrasena, the lord of the Yādavas, gave [it].
There were a thousand elephants and likewise ten thousand horses.
He gave twenty bhāras of gold to each and every brahmin.
Just as the twice-born cast aside their vessels at the great sacrifice of Marutta.
Thus, being satisfied and joyful, they departed from the sacrifice of Ugrasena.
All the deities, being satisfied and having received their shares, departed for heaven. ||18||
The panegyrists, possessing abundant wealth, went home chanting cries of victory.
Rākṣasas, Daityas, monkeys, fanged creatures, and likewise birds. ||19||
The nāgas, their minds satisfied, all went to their respective homes.
Cows, mountains, clusters of trees, rivers, sacred fords, and oceans; ||20||
Those who were contented and had received their shares all went to their own homes.
The kings who were summoned with abundant wedding gifts. ||21||
Honored with gifts and respect, they too returned each to their own home.
Nanda and the other chief cowherds were honored by Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||22||
Delighted by the affection and the gifts, they all likewise went to Vraja.
This, O King, has been described to you—the mandala of the great sacrifice.
Where Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra resides, what indeed is not fruitful?
Those men who constantly hear this narrative and read it, ||24||
From these, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are produced. ||25||
May the Lord, the Supreme Ruler, the Sovereign, the Ancient Person, who is full, purify you.
Those men who listen to his wonderful story make their own lineage a sacred ford (tīrtha). ||26||
Through the power of the sacrifice, Hari, the Supreme Lord,
caused the burden of the earth to descend from the King of Videha.
Salutation to that mountain-like Lord of infinite virtues, who was born in the lineage of Yadu as the possessor of the fourfold manifestation. ||27||

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Festival of the Rājasūya Sacrifice," in the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bahulāśva within the Śrī Viśvajit-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||50||
Bahulāśva said: "O Brahmin, I have heard from your mouth this most wonderful and auspicious account."
Sweeter than a piece of nectar is this supreme, all-conquering fragment.
Even of the great-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is most perfectly complete.
To each of the sixteen thousand women, ten sons were born. ||2||
O sage, they had sons and grandsons by the millions.
If a wise man were to count the dust particles of the earth, he would not reach the end of the lineage of Hari.
Under Revatī, there was also the birth of the high-souled Baladeva Rāma.
How indeed may the birth of a son come to pass? Tell me this according to the truth. ||4||
Śrī Nārada said:
"Very well; I shall relate before you in every way the story of the Blessed Saṃkarṣaṇa, the elder brother of Acyuta, Balabhadra Rāma, the protector of desires. (5)
Then, on one occasion, the lord of sages and king of yogis named Prāḍvipāka, the preceptor of Duryodhana, arrived at the city called Hastināpura.
Honored by Suyodhana with the utmost respect and due hospitality, he took his seat upon a highly precious throne. ||7||
Having circumambulated him and prostrated, standing before him with palms joined in reverence, he recalled the doubt in his mind and spoke thus, "O Dhṛtarāṣṭra. (8)
For what reason and from which world did Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is Balabhadra himself, come to the earth at the request of whom? By him this city was turned on its side;
oh, tell me fully of the power of that teacher of mine, who instructed me in the use of the mace! ||9||
Prāḍvipāka said:
O Prince, best of the Kurus, hear the power of the foremost of the Yadus, by hearing which there shall be a supreme destruction of sins. (10)
At the end of this Dvāpara age, the earth, oppressed by the heavy burden of millions of demon hosts disguised as kings, assumed the form of a cow and went for refuge to the Self-born One. ||11||

Then that best of gods, accompanied by all the hosts of deities, placing the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha at their head, emerged through the opening in the upper shell of the cosmic egg—which had been split by the nail of the left big toe of the venerable Vāmana—and having beheld millions of multitudes of eggs in the primordial fluid, he reached the banks of the Virajā river.
Then, having beheld before him a circle of light consisting of countless millions of suns,
the Creator bowed and meditated; there he saw the infinite Saṃkarṣaṇa, possessing a thousand faces and characterized by the attributes of the qualities (guṇas), together with the gods.

Having arrived at that enchanting Goloka, which is crowded with the forests of Vṛndāvana, the Yamunā river, Govardhana Hill, groves, thickets, clusters of creepers and trees, and throngs of cowherds, cowherdesses, and cattle—all of which is coiled like a serpent by His enjoyment and is honored by all the worlds—He entered His own bower there, brought His command within, and beheld the manifest, most perfect Supreme Lord Himself, Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, the master of countless universes, the husband of Śrī Rādhā, possessing a dark-complexioned form, clad in yellow garments, wearing a forest garland, and holding a flute.

Having prostrated before Him—whose crown and earrings adorned His cheeks, whose lotus-face was radiant with locks of hair, and who shone everywhere with tinkling golden anklets, bells, bracelets, armlets, necklaces, the shimmering Kaustubha gem, and finger-rings, while millions of young suns blazed from all sides—Brahmā, accompanied by all [the gods], related the entire account of the burden upon the earth. ||14||

Having understood their request for the sake of removing the burden of the earth, the Blessed One gave instructions to his own people and all the gods exactly as they were, and spoke thus to Ananta, who has a thousand faces: ||15||
"O dear one, in the past you too, having been born of Devakī by Vasudeva, appeared from the womb of Rohiṇī; afterwards, I shall attain the state of being Devakī’s son. (16)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Cause of Baladeva’s Incarnation," in the dialogue concerning the prior ripening of Duryodhana's karma, within the Balabhadra-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||1||
Hari Om Tat Sat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Prāḍvipāka said:
Having been addressed thus, the thousand-faced one prepared to depart and remained seated in his own assembly hall.
At that very moment, the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas everywhere became bent with their necks bowed down. ||1||
Then the charioteer Sumati, having brought the divine chariot marked with the palm-tree emblem along with its horses, stood before him. ||2||
The mace that shatters enemy armies and the plow that subdues the Daityas quickly appeared before you, as did the armor named Brahmamaya.

Then, while everyone in that assembly of Śrī Balabhadra looked on, Śeṣa arrived from Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Ramā; being praised by sages such as Pāṇini and Pañcajanya, his thousand hoods shining like crowns, and being fanned with chowries by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, he offered praise to Ananta Saṃkarṣaṇa and merged into His form. ||4||

Then, having arrived from Ajitavaikuṇṭha, Śeṣa— the thousand-faced one, surrounded by Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Bahurūpa, Mahat, and others, and encircled by terrible *preta* spirits and *vināyakas*— approached the assembly, praised Ananta, and merged into him. ||5||

Then, having arrived from Śvetadvīpa, he was attended by his foremost attendants such as Kumuda and Kumudākṣa; he shone with a crown of a thousand hoods, possessed the luster of a white mountain, wore blue garments, had the brilliance of dark-blue locks of hair, and appeared formidable.
While everyone was looking on, he too became absorbed into that infinite form.

Then, at that very moment, Śeṣa arrived from the region of Elāvṛta, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of crores of female attendants and accompanied by the lords of Bhavānī; adorned with the circle of crests upon his thousand faces, and with his crown, bracelets, and armlets shimmering, he entered the assembly hall and merged completely into the infinite form [of Viṣṇu]. ||7||

Then, from thirty-two thousand yojanas beneath the netherworld (Pātāla), there arrived before the Blessed One the dark-complexioned Tāmasī-kala, personally adorned with a crown of a thousand faces like the orb of the sun, accompanied by great sages such as Vedavyāsa, Parāśara, Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra, Nārada, Sāṃkhyāyana, Pulastya, Bṛhaspati, Maitreya, and others.

He was resplendent, attended by lordly nāgas such as Vāsuki, Mahāśaṅkha, Śvetadhanañjaya, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Kuhaka, Kāliya, Takṣaka, Kambala, Aśvatara, Devadatta, and others, who held chowries in their hands; he was being anointed with pastes of musk, agallochum, saffron, and sandalwood by nāga maidens, while being celebrated in song by hosts of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and Vidyādharas, and followed and preceded by Hāṭakeśvara, Tripura, Bala, Kālakeya, Kali, and Nivātakavaca.

Accompanied by the eleven manifestations of Rudra, by Nābhi, Kāmadhenu, and Varuṇa following behind him, and resounding with the sounds of lutes, flutes, drums, cymbals, and kettledrums, the Lord of Serpents shone with swift movement like the King of Elephants; upon whose single hood this circle of the earth appeared like a mustard seed—he too arrived and merged into the body of the Great Infinite One. (8)
Having seen that wonder, all the members of his assembly and retinue, realizing him to be the most perfect one, became bowed down in reverence and filled with amazement. ||9||
Then the blessed Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, who has infinite faces and is infinitely vast, spoke to his attendants and the Siddhas.
"I shall go to the earth for the purpose of removing its burden; therefore, you shall be born among the Yādavas. (11)
"O charioteer of powerful and noble intellect, stay right here and do not grieve.
Whenever I, seeking battle, call you to mind, then you shall bring that divine chariot marked with the palm tree and come to my side. (12)
O Halā and Musalā, whenever I shall remember you both, at those very times appear before me in my city. 13.
O Varma, you too appear! O sages such as Pāṇini and others;
O millions of Rudras; O Lord of Bhavānī; O eleven Rudras; O Gandharvas!

O Vāsuki and other lords of the nāgas, O Nivātakavacas, O Varuṇa, O Kāmadhenu! All of you, always come and grant me your vision whenever I descend upon the earth in the land of Bharata within the lineage of Yadu. 14.
Prāḍvipāka said:
Having been thus commanded, they all returned to their respective abodes;
when they had departed, the Blessed One Ananta spoke to the groups of Nāga maidens.
I have understood your intention through my ascetic power: that you shall take birth in the houses of cowherds and grant me your vision. ||15||
"Perhaps one day, on the banks of the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā), at the very root of the sweetness of our pastimes, I shall perform the circle-dance (rāsa-maṇḍala) with you;
thus your heart's desire will bear fruit. ||16||
Then Kali, the king of the Nivātakavacas, with his hands joined in añjali at the feet of his master and having offered a garland of flowers, replied to the Blessed Lord.
"For I shall indeed do it; give me your command. "O Blessed One, wherever you go, there I too shall go;
for surely, by being separated from you, great distress will arise. "Indeed, [let us go] together."
Lead me; you are compassionate toward your devotees. ||18||
Thus entreated, the infinite Lord, being pleased, replied to King Kali, his own devotee: "Come happily with me here to Bharatakhaṇḍa, into the lineage of the Kaurava lords."
"Having become the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra by the name Duryodhana, you shall become a universal monarch; I will act as your ally and provide you with instruction in the art of the mace. (19)
Thus addressed, Kali paid him homage and returned to his own abode;
this very Kali has been born as you through the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, yet you do not remember your own self.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Mantra for Saṃkarṣaṇa’s Departure," in the dialogue between Prāḍvipāka and Duryodhana within the Balabhadra-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||2||
Hari Oṃ Tat Sat. May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Prāḍvipāka said:

Then Nāgalakṣmī, resembling the orb of ten million autumnal moons, seated upon a great chariot and adorned by a circle of ten million companions, arrived and spoke to her husband, the great Ananta Saṃkarṣaṇa, in the assembly hall. ||1||
O Blessed One, I too shall come to the earth together with you; distressed by separation from you, I cannot sustain my life. ||2||

Having beheld his beloved with her throat choked with tears, the Blessed Lord Ananta—the dispeller of the suffering of all devotees—spoke thus, like the elephant of Mahendra who restrains his coils: "So be it. ||3||
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, having become merged within the body of Revatī, you shall inhabit the world of mortals; do not grieve. 4.
Having heard that, Nāgalakṣmī replied: "Who is Revatī? Whose daughter is she?
Where does she dwell? Please tell me this clearly. Having heard that, the Blessed Lord Ananta, smiling, replied to his beloved.

In the beginning of creation, I was indeed born as the son of Kadrū to Kaśyapa by the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; holding the entire circle of the earth’s regions upon my single hood like a royal elephant holds a water-pot, I became resplendent everywhere beneath [the world].
Then, while I was present, the son of Cakṣus, the Manu named Cākṣuṣa of exceeding strength,
had the lotuses of his feet rubbed by the sovereigns of the regions of the seven continents;
his fierce commands were never transgressed by Indra and the other gods, and the staff-like arms of his enemies were shattered by the staff-like arms of his own fierce arms.
Adorned with all virtues, he became a sovereign emperor. ||7||
To that Manu there were sons beginning with Sudyumna.
From that sacrificial fire-pit, a daughter named Jyotiṣmatī was born. ||8||
Once, out of affection, Akṣuṣa asked his daughter, "Tell me, what kind of husband do you desire?"
She then said: "May he who is the strongest among all be my husband. (9)

Having heard that and knowing Śakra to be powerful, the king summoned him. To the wielder of the thunderbolt, who had arrived immediately at that very moment and stood before him, Manu respectfully offered a seat and spoke: ||10||
"Is there anyone more powerful than you, or not? Tell me the truth, if it is not forgotten. "Indeed, there is no dharma higher than truth," she said, for she was the Earth.
"I consider myself capable of enduring everything, except for a man devoted to falsehood. ||11||
Indra said, "I am not powerful; there is Vāyu who is more powerful than I.
With him as my ally, I shall accomplish the task. Having said this, he departed.
King Śakra summoned Vāyu and said, "There exists someone more powerful than you; speak the truth. (12)
Vāyu said,
"There are mountains more powerful than I, for they are not blown away by my force.
When Vāyu had spoken thus and departed, the king summoned the mountains and said:
"Tell us truly: who among you is powerful? ||13||
The mountains said, "By our support, the terrestrial region where we reside remains strong.
When the mountains had departed, the king summoned the circle of the earth and said, "Is there anyone stronger than you? Speak the truth. (14)
Having heard that, Bhūkhaṇḍa said,
"The venerable Saṃkarṣaṇa is more powerful than I."

Thus, this very Vāsudeva, the primordial deity, who is eternally infinite and an ocean of boundless virtues, possesses a thousand faces; he has a beautiful form like the king of serpents, a white radiance like Mount Kailāsa, and a brilliance equal to ten million suns. Shining with a loveliness that captivates ten million Cupids, his eyes are like lotus petals. He is celebrated by the songs of swarms of bees attracted by the pure, divine garlands upon the lotus-like pericarp of his heart, while being sung of by hosts of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and the best of the Vidyādharas. Worshipped by the multitudes of gods, demons, serpents, and sages, he remains resplendent, reigning supreme over all. ||15||
Upon a single head of whom I behold the entire circle of the earth’s regions, adorned with mountains, rivers, oceans, forests, and tens of millions of living beings.
By the mere recitation of whose name, even one who has destroyed the three worlds attains absolute liberation within the triple world. ||16||

Such is the power of the Blessed One: he is all-powerful, the cause of all causes, the Lord of all, possessed of boundless heroism, and established at the root of the Rasa; therefore, there is no one superior to him. ||17||
Mahānanta said: After the Lord of the Earth had departed having spoken thus, Cākṣuṣa’s daughter Jyotiṣmatī,
having understood the power of my sweetness and having received her father’s permission, went to the Vindhya mountain.
For the sake of attaining me, he performed the austerity of Brahmā for hundreds of thousands of years.

In the summer she was scorched by the heat of five fires; during the rains she bore all the falling torrents; and in the cold season, having immersed herself up to her neck in cold water, she became one who sleeps upon the bare ground. ||19||
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Narrative of Jyotiṣmatī," in the Balabhadra-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||3||
Hari Om Tat Sat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Mahānanta said:

Then, beholding Jyotiṣmatī—who resembled a hundred moons, possessed of fresh youth, beautiful, and yet ascetic—all of them—Indra, Yama, Kubera, Agni, Varuṇa, Soma, Sūrya, Maṅgala, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, and Śani—their minds deluded by lust ignited by her beauty, approached her hermitage and spoke to her. (1)
"O beautiful one with thighs like plantain stalks, you are blessed; for whose sake do you perform this penance? Your youth is not suited for austerity. Tell us your own heart's desire.
Having heard this, Jyotiṣmatī said: "The Blessed Ananta..."
"May my husband have a thousand faces; for this purpose I am performing penance.
Upon hearing these words, they all laughed individually, and among them, Indra spoke first as follows: ||2||
Indra said:
"O auspicious one, why do you practice this fruitless austerity when the king of serpents is ready to grant you a boon?"
Choose me, the king of the gods, Śatakratu, who has come to you of his own accord.
Yama said:
"Choose me, King Yama, who has come as the leader of punishment."
"You shall become my wife, the most excellent of all, in the world of the ancestors."
Dhanada said:
"O beautiful woman, know me indeed as the King of Kings, the Lord of Treasures."
O large-eyed one, worship him quickly and abandon your attachment to Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Agni said:
"Know me to be the mouth of all the gods and the foundation of all sacrifices."
Devote yourself to me, O large-eyed one, abandoning all other attachments.
Varuṇa said:
"Choose me, the world-protector who wields the noose, as the lord of the waters."
Behold, O beautiful lady, the vast majesty of the seven oceans!
Sūrya said:
"O son of Cākṣuṣa, I am indeed always the eye of the world and the one with fierce rays."
O excellent one, leaving behind your course through the netherworld, come to me, who am adorned with gold. ||8||
Soma said:
"I am the king of the twice-born, the lord of medicinal herbs, the lord of the constellations, and the maker of nectar."
I am indeed the bestower of strength upon women; worship me, O lady with the gait of an elephant! ||9||
Maṅgala said:
"This earth is indeed my mother, and my father is the Great Strider (Viṣṇu) himself."
O auspicious lady, having become one who desires abundant worldly existence, worship me, the source of all blessings. 10.
Budha said: "I am Budha, the wise one, a hero who increases the passion for women."
Having abandoned all the lords of heaven, do you take delight with me.
Bṛhaspati said:
"I am indeed Gīṣpati, Dhiṣaṇa, the preceptor of the gods, Bṛhaspati."
"O auspicious one, you consider me to be the manifest teacher of the gods in this world; therefore, worship me."
Śukra said:
"O high-minded one, I am Kāvya Bhārgava, the preceptor of the Daityas in person."
Having thus reflected upon your own highest good, become intensely devoted to me, O passionate lady. ||13||
Śani said:
"O blessed lady, I am the strongest of all, standing even above the gods."
Abandon your grief and choose me with a glance that turns the world to ashes.
Mahānanta said:
Then Jyotiṣmatī, having heard their words, her eyes reddened,
her lower lip quivering, and her eyebrows knitting in a frown, was like a mass of leaping flames from the rising fire of her intense rage.
He remembered me as the Supreme and became filled with supreme wrath. ||15||
By that [sound], the entire circle of the earth, even the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and everything beyond up to the world of Brahmā, trembled violently on all sides, and a great terror arose. ||16||
At that very moment, Śakra and the other gods, terrified by the fear of a curse and trembling, fell at her lotus feet with offerings in their hands;
they cried out, "Save us! Save us! and thus she was pacified by them.
Jyotiṣmatī cursed each of them individually. ||17||
Jyotiṣmatī said:
"O wicked one, you have come here to deceive me; become lame and keep your eyes cast downward!"
Become suddenly emaciated in body, with an exceedingly dark and loathsome appearance, subsisting on black māṣa beans and oil. (18)
O Śukra, become blind in one eye; O Gīṣpati, quickly become one designated as a woman here.
"O gentle one, they say that indeed your day is empty; no one ever goes there. (19)
May you become Mangala with the face of a monkey;
may you become the Moon afflicted with consumption.
O Divākara, may you have broken teeth;
O Pāśin, may your radiance belong to Añjanādharī. (20)
O Uṣarbudha, you shall become a devourer of all things;
O you who possess human nature, may your splendor be taken away.
O son of Vivasvat, may you quickly suffer the shattering of your great pride in battle against the powerful Rākṣasa.
O lowest of gods, having come here to abduct me, you stand reviling the Supreme Self with your words.
"Once you have gone to the bliss of heaven, some king will carry off your beloved and enjoy the pleasures of heaven for himself. (22)
Indeed, some Rākṣasa has forcibly seized you, who were bound by a noose and defeated in battle.
O Lord of Heaven, having come to the city of Laṅkā,
he will indeed cause you to be placed in a blind prison.
Śrī Mahānanta said:
Then, indeed, among the gods who had been cursed by her, Śakra also became enraged and cursed her in turn: "O wrathful one, even though Saṃkarṣaṇa is your husband..."
May there never be for you a festival celebrating the birth of a son, whether in this life or in another, at any time.
Having spoken thus, Śakra, overwhelmed by her splendor, departed for heaven along with all the hosts of gods. She then performed penance once more. ||24||

Then, having seen that austerity, Brahmā—the cause of the entire world—surrounded by Brahman-knowing brāhmaṇas such as Bṛhaspati and others, arrived from his own abode by means of a swan-vehicle. ||25||
Standing in the sky, he said to her: "O Jyotiṣmatī, daughter of Cākṣuṣa, your penance has become fruitful; by it you have attained perfection. I am highly pleased; choose a boon. (26)
Having heard that, he emerged from the water up to his neck, prostrated before Brahmā, and after offering praise with palms joined in reverence, spoke as follows.
"O Blessed One, if you are pleased, may the Blessed Saṃkarṣaṇa here become my boon with a thousand faces.
Having heard this, the bull among the wise replied: "Indeed, so be it."
"O daughter, although your desire is difficult to attain,
I shall nevertheless fulfill it this very day; for the Vaivasvata Manvantara has arrived, which is composed of thirty-six cycles of four yugas."
When the time comes, the blessed Saṃkarṣaṇa will be the bridegroom there.
Having heard that, Jyotiṣmatī said to Brahmā: "O God of gods, the Great Time (Mahākāla) is now present; my heart's desire must be fulfilled quickly, for you are capable of doing so.
Otherwise, I shall cast a curse upon you, just as one was given to the gods. (29)
Thus addressed, Brahmā, fearing the curse, reflected for a moment and spoke again:
"O princess, you shall become the daughter of that very King of Ānarta in Kuśasthalī."
Having granted her a boon, saying, "In that birth, a period of time equivalent to thirty-four yugas shall, for some reason, become like a single moment," Brahmā vanished right there.

Then she too took birth in the city of Kuśasthalī among the Ānartas as the wife of Revata. There, named Jyotiṣmatī Revatī, adorned with the jewels of beauty, generosity, and virtue, and possessing eyes like fresh autumn lotuses, she became marriageable. ||31||
Revaṇa, together with his wife, spoke with affection to her in the inner apartments, saying, "What kind of boon do you desire? Having heard these words, she then said:
"May he be the strongest among all; let that be my boon. (32)
Having heard this, King Revata, accompanied by his wife, took his daughter,
ascended a divine chariot, and having traversed the worlds to inquire after the powerful and long-lived one, went to the realm of Brahmā. ||33||
Having remained there for that moment, by that very moment, a period of time consisting of thirty-six yugas was produced in the world of mortals this very day.

O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, she exists this very day in the world of Brahmā; having become absorbed in her as an incarnation through spiritual penetration (āveśāvatāra), go to Dvārakā and rejoice.
Prāḍvipāka said:
Having heard these words, Nāgalakṣmī took leave of her husband Saṃkarṣaṇa,
went to the world of Brahmā, and entered into the body of Revatī.

Then the Blessed Saṃkarṣaṇa descended from the abode of Goloka, which is honored by the worlds, for the purpose of removing the heavy burden of the earth; this arrival of the Blessed Balabhadra has been narrated by me to you.
"O Prince, O Lord of the Kauravas, this [mantra] removes all evils and is a source of auspiciousness; what more do you wish to hear? ||36||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Episode of Revatī," within the "Episode of Jyotiṣmatī" in the Balabhadra-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||4||
Hari Om Tat Sat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Duryodhana said:
O lord of sages, I am indeed blessed; formerly I was a devotee of Saṃkarṣaṇa, and now I have been reminded by you of the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva.
Having heard here of the power and the most wonderful majesty of the two incarnations,
Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who formerly descended to the earth from their father’s city— let it be told how they went to Vraja and how they remained there unknown to the inhabitants of Vraja. ||1||
Prāḍvipāka said:
Now, once in Mathurā, the city of the Yadus, Ugrasena’s elder brother Devaka gave his daughter Devakī to Vasudeva; then, at the time of the departure of the bridegroom and the bride—
Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena, drove their chariot. ||2||

At that very moment, the divine voice said to Kaṃsa: "O wretch! The eighth child she bears shall indeed slay you. Hearing this, the great asura Kaṃsa, son of Kālanemi, took a sword in his hand and set out to kill his sister.
At that very moment, Vasudeva, having awakened him, said: "Do not kill her;
I shall deliver her sons to you, for from them your fear has arisen, as it has mine."
Having heard these words, Kaṃsa, who understood the essence of their speech, had the two of them imprisoned and became free from anxiety.
Then Vasudeva gave the first-born son of Devakī to Kaṃsa.
Knowing him to be a speaker of truth, Kaṃsa did not kill the child.
The movement of numbers is from left to right, and so it is with the gods; therefore, this person is an enemy,
for all the Yādavas are gods who desire your death—
due to these words of Nārada, he slew even a newborn child as soon as it was born.

Then a great hardship befell the Yadus who had fled out of fear of Kaṃsa. Now, the seventh embryo of Devakī was indeed the Lord Ananta. By the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Yogamāyā drew that splendor from Devakī’s womb and came to place it in Rohiṇī—the wife of Vasudeva—who, out of fear of Kaṃsa, was staying in Gokula. ||7||
Regarding this, there are these verses concerning Devakī’s seventh pregnancy, which increased both her joy and her sorrow:
He was brought to Vraja by Yogamāyā and placed within the womb of Rohiṇī.
"Alas! Where has the fetus gone? cried the people of Mathurā.
Then, in the month of Bhādrapada, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, under the Svāti nakṣatra, on a Wednesday, after five days had passed in Vraja.
And when the ascendant named Libra was occupied by five high planets at the midpoint of the day. ||9||
While the gods rained down a shower of flowers and the clouds released drops of water, [he departed].
The Lord was born from the wife of Vasudeva, illuminating the house of Nanda with His own radiance.
Nanda, performing the birth-rites for the infant,
gave a million cows to the twice-born.
Having summoned the cowherds, he spread a great auspiciousness through the songs of excellent singers. ||11||
Then, at that very moment, by His command, the eighth incarnation— the most perfect Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra— descended;
and at midnight, having placed Him in a cradle, He was born to the wife of Nanda.
While the world was fast asleep in yogic slumber, Vasudeva crossed the Yamunā, entered the great forest, placed his son upon the bed of Yaśodā, took that daughter, and returned home once more. 12.
Then, hearing the sound of a child's cry in the prison, Kaṃsa, terrified by his enemies, came and took the newborn girl and dashed her against the surface of a stone.
At that very moment, emerging from his hand into the sky and becoming Yoganidrā, she was praised by hosts of Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and Munis, and said this to Kaṃsa:
"O wicked one, where has your former enemy been born? Devakī and Vasudeva are merely wasting their efforts."
Having said, "You burn those who are distressed," she went to the Vindhya mountain.

Thus addressed, Kaṃsa was struck with amazement; releasing Devakī and Vasudeva, he summoned the demons Pūtanā and others, and issued an order to kill all infants—both those less than ten days old and those older. They did exactly as they were told.
Then Nanda also, having heard of the festival celebrating the birth of his son, held a great celebration; meanwhile, Rāma and Kṛṣ�a, who had arrived at Vraja under the pretext of fear of Kaṃsa,
remained unobserved by the inhabitants of Vraja through their own divine power (māyā), in order to bestow their grace upon them.
As soon as they were born, they performed wonderful infantile sports.
O Lord of the Kauravas, what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Birth Festival of Śrī Balabhadra and Śrī Kṛṣṇa," in the Balabhadra-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā. ||5||
Hari Om Tat Sat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Duryodhana said:
O Lord of Munis, Rāma—the infinite one of infinite pastimes—and Śrī Kṛṣṇa also shone after appearing upon the earth. Tell me His life story in brief; what did He do in Vraja?
What did he do in Mathurā, what in Dvārakā, what here, and what elsewhere? ||1||
Prāḍvipāka said:

Then, indeed, as soon as he was born, Śrī Kṛṣṇa performed wondrous pastimes, including the liberation of Pūtanā and the slaying of the demons Śakaṭāsura and Tṛṇāvarta; the manifestation of His universal form (viśvarūpa); the theft of the butter and the revelation of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa); the breaking of the pair of Yamalārjuna trees and other such deeds; the display of the illusory power of Durvāsas; the greatness and majesty of the names of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa as described by the venerable Garga Ācārya; and the narrative adorned with the marriage of Vṛṣabhānu’s daughter to the noble Ugrasena’s son [Kṛṣṇa] and the account of the Rāsa-maṇḍala. ||2||

Then, having arrived at Śrī Vṛndāvana and having slain the demons such as Vatsāsura and Bakāsura, He wandered through the forests of Vṛndāvana and other woods with the cowherds while tending the cattle. ||3||

Then, in the Tāla forest, the mighty Baladeva seized by his two staff-like arms the demon Dhenuka, who was striking him with his feet and making a harsh noise; having thrown him against a palm tree, he dashed him against the surface of the earth as he fell back again. He fainted.
With his head shattered by that immediate blow of the fist, he met his death. ||4||

Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa, having performed deeds such as the subduing of Kāliya and drinking the forest fire, engaged in pastimes that were to be narrated—pastimes consisting of the manifestation of Śrī Rādhā’s love, the testing of her affection, wandering in Vṛndāvana, the giving of gifts, honor, playfulness, and the expression of *hāva* and *bhāva*, as well as the story of the slaying of Śaṅkhacūḍa and the episode of Śiva and the Asura. ||5||
Then once, when the worship of the King of Mountains had been performed, Indra, whose strength was shattered,
rained down upon the region of Vraja with circles of Saṃvarta clouds. At that time, the Blessed One,
seeing Vraja distressed by fear, granted them fearlessness, saying "Do not fear," and with one hand—
Having uprooted the king of mountains along with its peaks, he held it like a child;
indeed, being only seven years old, he remained perfectly steady for seven days.

Then Indra, terrified with fear along with all the hosts of gods, bowed his head with his crown to the two glorious lotus-feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra; having offered praise and performed His consecration, the great king of the gods went to heaven together with Surabhi, the gods, and the sages. ||7||

Having witnessed that miracle of the lifting of Govardhana Hill, the cowherds were filled with wonder, and He showed them the glory of His power, such as the binding and releasing of the mountain. ||8||

Then Śruti, Rūpā, Ṛṣirūpā, the princess of Mithilā, the inhabitants of Kośala, the residents of Ayodhyā, Yajña, Sītā, Pulindakā, Aramā, Vaikuṇṭha, Śvetadvīpa, Urdhvavaikuṇṭha, Ajitapada, Śrīloka, and Acala; as well as her divine and non-divine companions, the gopīs of the three modes of nature, the women of Bhūmi, Gopa, Jālandharī, Barhiṣmatī, the celestial nymphs (apsarases), the inhabitants of Sutala, and the daughters of the serpent kings—along with these various groups of gopīs, Śrī Kṛṣṇa performed the rāsa dance in the circle of Vraja. ||9||

Once, while herding the cows with Balarāma, Śrī Kṛṣṇa engaged in childhood play with the cowherd boys at Bhāṇḍīra, characterized by the roles of rider and mount. There, the demon Pralamba, disguised as a cowherd, placed Rāma—who was victorious in play—upon his back during the sport and carried him away. 10.

Then, seeing him— who possessed a body like the lord of mountains— preparing to go to Mathurā, the mighty Baladeva, following behind in a rage, struck that great mountain on the head with his fist as if it were a wall; by that blow, its summit was instantly shattered.
Like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt, that Daitya fell to the earth. ||11||
Once, during the summer, while the cows and cowherds had gone into the Muñja forest,
a forest fire suddenly broke out and grew like the fire of universal destruction.
Then, seeing the cowherds who had come for refuge crying out "O Kṛṣṇa! O Rāma! Save us! Save us!", He commanded them, "Close your eyes; do not fear," and quickly drank up that fire.

Then, indeed, having led his herd of cows along with the cowherds to the bank of the Yamunā at Bhāṇḍīra, he arrived there in the Aśoka grove and partook of the meal brought by the wife of the sacrificer. ||13||
Then once, when King Nanda in Vraja was seized by Varuṇa, He shattered the pride of Varuṇa and showed Vaikuṇṭha— which is worshipped by all the worlds— to Nanda and the other cowherds. ||14||

Then, in the forest of Ambikā on the bank of the Sarasvatī, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, having touched with His glorious lotus feet— which are indeed worshipped by all the guardians of the worlds— the serpent Sudarśana who was swallowing Nanda, liberated him from the body of the snake. ||15||
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Balarāma, seized Vyomāsura—the friend of Kaṃsa who had assumed the form of a thief during a game of hide-and-seek—by his two staff-like arms;
spinning him around in the ten directions, he dashed him against the surface of the earth. ||16||

Likewise, having uprooted the demon Ariṣṭa, who had been dispatched by Kaṃsa in the form of a bull, He threw him down by his two horns. Then, at the command of Kaṃsa—who had heard the stories of Śrī Kṛṣṇa from the mouth of Nārada—Śrī Kṛṣṇa crushed Keśin, who had been sent forth, by thrusting His own arm into his mouth. In this manner, He suddenly performed many such divine pastimes with power within the circle of Vraja. ||17||

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pastimes of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa in Vraja," in the Balabhadra-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā, within the dialogue between Prāḍvipāka and Duryodhana.
Hari Om Tatsat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Prāḍvipāka said:
Now, O Prince, listen in brief to those deeds which Rāma and Kṛṣṇa performed in Mathurā.
Then Akrūra, dispatched by Kaṃsa, the son of Kālanemi, arrived at the district of Vraja to bring Rāma and Kṛṣṇa back. ||1||
Seeing the son of King Nanda intent on departing for that place, the multitude of cowherd women became distressed by the pangs of separation.

Having consoled them each individually, the Blessed Lord mounted His chariot with His army; while traveling toward the city of the Yadus with Akrūra, He revealed His own abode to the son of Śvaphalka within the waters of the Yamunā on the way.
Then, having stayed in the grove on the outskirts of Mathurā during the forenoon, he beheld the city of Mathurā from all sides in the afternoon.

Then the two ancient gods, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, assuming the attire of excellent actors for their divine play, wandered about displaying their own beauty—which surpassed ten million Cupids—and captivating the hearts of all; and the citizens and city women, desiring to see them, abandoned their tasks and ran after them like rivers flowing toward the ocean. ||3||
Then the Blessed One, with the tip of his hand, struck the washerman who was refusing to give him the clothes he had requested on the royal road while everyone looked on;
likewise, he bestowed his own likeness upon the tailor who was making the garments.

Then, under the pretext of taking sandalwood paste, he made the hunchbacked Sairandhrī Trivakrā straight and the most beautiful woman in the three worlds; thereafter, having addressed the Vaiśya people, he entered Dhanusthala accompanied by the boys of Mathurā. Thereupon, [he saw] a golden, variegated gate with seven bolts, thousands of times...

Beholding that Vaiṣṇava bow— which was impossible for men to carry, weighed eight hundred thousand *bhāras*, was held by the sacrificial pavilion, had been given to Kaṃsa by the descendant of Bhṛgu, and appeared like the serpent Śeṣa himself coiled up— he seized it by force. ||5||

Even as the people were watching, he playfully strung it and drew it back to his ear with his two staff-like arms; then, like an elephant breaking a stalk of sugarcane with its trunk, he snapped the bow in the middle.
With the twang of the breaking bow, the entire universe, along with the hollows of the seven worlds, resounded.
Then Tārā and the elephants of the quarters trembled; the entire circle of the earth’s regions shook like a vessel for only two ghaṭikās. ||7||

Then, in the afternoon, having approached the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa at the entrance of the arena and engaged in a brief bout of childish play, the boy seized him by his trunk, whirled him here and there, and dashed him to the ground like a water-pot. ||8||

Having thus slain him on the arena floor and shown his true nature to the people in Kaṃsa’s assembly hall, and having engaged in a wrestling match, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa threw Cāṇūra, Muṣṭika, Kūṭa, Śala, and Tośalaka onto the ground in front of Kaṃsa while everyone was watching. ||9||
Then, observing that deed of Kaṃsa as he boasted with harsh words,
Madhusūdana suddenly leapt up and ascended the very high couch.
Then, seeing him approaching swiftly like Death itself, Kaṃsa rose from his couch and, rebuking him with an agitated mind, quickly seized his sword and shield.
Hari suddenly seized Kaṃsa, who was equipped with shield and sword, by force with his two staff-like arms, just as Virāṭ seizes a venomous lord of serpents with the two parts of its mouth.
Then Kaṃsa, having forcibly emerged from Balarāma’s arm-bind like a serpent from the beak of a Tārkṣya bird,
fell with his sword and shield; yet rising once more, the two strong men,
crushing each other with speed upon the dais, shone like two lions on a mountain.
Then, as Kaṃsa was leaping up by force into the sky at a height of a hundred cubits, Kṛṣṇa,
springing up like one hawk seizing another, seized him. As that bull among Daityas was moving again here and there,
he who is the support of the three worlds grasped him with his two fierce, staff-like arms.
Having whirled him around, he threw him down upon the couch from the great canopy. ||13||
Then, from the stroke of lightning, the platform became like a grove of trees with its pole shattered.

Although that Vajrāṅga fell, he was somewhat agitated; rising suddenly, the Great-souled One fought with him once more. Again, the Blessed One seized him with his two staff-like arms, threw him onto a couch, mounted upon his chest, and immediately grasped his crown.

Seizing him by the hair, Sanātana— the support of all and possessed of infinite prowess— cast him from the dais onto the arena like a boulder from a mountain, and himself fell upon him with great speed.
By the impact of those two, the circle of the earth's surface sank down like a cooking pot, and the three staffs [of Mount Meru] suddenly trembled. ||14||

Then, while everyone looked on, Yadurāja dragged the deceased King of the Bhojas—who lay upon the ground like a lordly serpent—just as a lion drags its prey. At that very moment, a cry of "Alas! arose from the kings: "Oh, by his enmity, even Kaṃsa has attained a likeness to this Bhṛṅgin, just as a worm becomes like a bee! ||15||

Then, suddenly seeing Kaṃsa dead and beholding his younger brothers who had arrived bearing swords and shields, Balabhadra took up a mallet and struck them down on all sides. At that moment, the celestial drums resounded and a cry of victory arose from the gods.
The Vidyādharīs showered flowers, the Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras danced, and they sang. ||16||

Then, having consoled all his parents and released them, he gave the kingdom to Ugrasena; having received the sacred thread and mastered the sciences from Saṃdīpana, he returned his deceased son as the teacher’s fee,
killed Śaṅkha, and returning to Mathurā, while residing there, he dispatched Uddhava for the welfare of Vraja.

Again, having gone to Vraja himself and granted his vision to Rādhā and the gopīs, and having brought about the liberation of Ṛbhu in the midst of the rāsa dance, he shone once more as the Lord of Mathurā in Mathurā.
Rāma also ceased from that [battle] after having slaughtered the Kolas;
thus, thousands of purifying deeds occurred for those two in Mathurā. ||17||
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Pastimes in Mathurā," in the Balabhadra-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Hari Om Tatsat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Prāḍvipāka said:
Now, O Dhārtarāṣṭra, listen briefly to the pastimes of those two at Dvārakā.
Then, having overcome Jarāsandha who had arrived seeking friendship while Kaṃsa was absent,
and having constructed a fortress on the sea named Dvārakā, they settled their kinsmen there; and within a single night,
having caused Kāla to be slain at the sight of Mucukunda, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa once again—
Having reached Mount Pravarṣaṇa from there, they went to Dvārakā. ||1||
Then Raivata, having returned from the world of Brahmā and having duly given his daughter Ratnayutā to the powerful Balabhadra, departed for the forest named Badarī to perform austerities. ||2||
Then, while his enemies looked on, Śrī Kṛṣṇa carried away Rukmiṇī from the city of Kuṇḍina; likewise, having slain Bhauma, he took Jāmbavatī, Satyabhāmā, Kālindī, Mitravindā,
Nāgnajitī, Bhadrā, and Lakṣmaṇā.
He married one hundred and sixteen thousand princesses. ||3||
O King, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s first son by Rukmiṇī, the daughter of Bhīṣmaka, was an incarnation of Kāmadeva and was as beautiful as his father.
Therefore, Aniruddha was an incarnation of the Eldest of the Gods (Brahmā). ||4||
Then once, having taken a betel vine at King Ugrasena’s Rājasūya sacrifice,
Pradyumna, desiring to conquer the quarters, set out together with his Yādava brothers;
while performing the conquest of the nine divisions of Jambūdvīpa, he arrived near the mountain Kāmadugha.
He fought with the Gandharva king Pataṅga, the lord of the city of Vasantamālatī. ||5||
There, in that mace-duel, Gada, the younger brother of Baladeva, taking up his mace, struck Gadadhara with his own mace like a moth [into a flame]. He too struck him in the chest with great force;
thus the mace-duel between the two lasted for two ghaṭikās. Then—
From the blow of Pataṅga’s mace, Gada fell into a swoon for a moment in the battle. ||6||
Then, when a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, Balabhadra, resembling ten million suns, appeared;
drawing the entire army of the Gandharvas toward him with the tip of his plow, he struck them with his heavy mace upon it. By that, everything was simultaneously—
The army, along with its warriors, elephants, and chariots, was ground to dust. ||7||

Then Pataṅga, deprived of his chariot and terrified by fear, went to that city and once again formed a military array with the Yādavas to fight. Hearing this, the enraged Balabhadra [marched] toward the great city of the Gandharvas, which extended for a hundred yojanas.
Having suddenly ploughed up the entire land named Vasantamālatī with his plough,
Saṃkarṣaṇa swiftly dragged it toward the wish-fulfilling river.

Then, indeed, when the houses had collapsed and cries of "Alas! arose, the Gandharva Pataṅga, lord of the Gandharvas, beholding the entire city reeling like a boat tossed by the wind, joined his palms in reverence and was thus addressed:
"There are two hundred thousand celestial chariots fashioned by Viśvakarman, and four hundred thousand elephants."
Having brought as tribute a hundred billion horses and ten trillion loads of divine jewels, and having presented them to the powerful Bala, he circumambulated him and bowed down. ||9||
Then, for the sake of Samba’s liberation, Balabhadra arrived here; while you were looking on, Saṃkarṣaṇa himself tore open this city with the tip of his plow and drew forth the glorious Gaṅgā.
In that very same way, while the circle of the rāsa dance was being fashioned by the Naga maidens and the cowherd girls, he dragged the Yamunā with the tip of his plow.

Then once, a monkey named Dvivida, the minister of Sugrīva and friend of Bhauma, being urged by Nārada and desiring to fight Hari, descended to Mount Raivataka; having arrived there, he fought with his army for four *ghaṭikās*.
As he was striking with tree trunks, stones, and fists, Balabhadra struck him on the head with his club.
Again, having struck the one who had not died with his fist, the elder brother of Acyuta seized the fleeing man with his two staff-like arms,
threw him onto the ridge of Mount Raivataka, and struck him in the chest with a firm fist.
With its fall, the lord of mountains trembled like a water-pot with its handle broken. ||11||
Then indeed, O King, having heard of your preparations for war with the Pāṇḍavas today,
he departed from the city accompanied by Brāhmaṇas and citizens under the pretext of bathing at sacred fords;
having circumambulated Dvārakā and bathed at Siddhāśrama and Prabhāsa, he proceeded toward the west.

In that direction, having touched the Sarasvatī against its current, and having bathed at the various sacred fords (tīrthas) born in the Saindhava forest—namely Jambū, Mārga, Utpalāvarta, Arbuda, Hemavat, Sindhu, as well as Bindusaras, Tritakūpa, Sudarśana, Trita, Auśanasa, Āgneya, Vāyava, Saudāsa, Guha, Śrāddhadeva, and others—in the northern direction;

Having bathed in Kailāsa, Karavīra, Mahāyoga, Gaṇeśa, Kaubera, Prāgjyotiṣa, Raṅgavallī, Sītārāmakṣetra, Caitradeśa, Vasantatilaka, Daśārṇabhadrā, Kūrmatīrtha, Puṣpamālā, Citravana, Candrakāntā, Naiḥśreyasa, Manuparvata, Cakṣuḥkāmaśālinī, Kāmavana, Vedakṣetra, Sītāpṛthu-tīrtha, Tapobhūmi, Līlāvatī, Vedanagara, Gāndharva, Śakra, Bhīmarathī, the glorious Jāhnavī, Kālindī, Haridvāra, Kurukṣetra, Mathurā, and Puṣkara;
Then, having reached Śāmbhala and Saukara from there, and visiting other sacred fords (tīrthas), Saṃkarṣaṇa himself went to the Naimiṣa forest. ||12||
Seeing him arrive, the sages headed by Śaunaka rose and paid their respects, honoring him.
There, seeing Romaharṣaṇa—the disciple of Vedavyāsa—not rising to greet him, he struck him with a blade of kusha grass held in his hand. Seeing the sages crying out "Alas!
Alas!", even though he was a purifier of the world, he set his mind for twelve months on bathing at sacred fords (tīrthas) for the sake of purification and to win over the people.
There, a Daitya named Balvala, the son of Ilvala, appeared in the sky during the onset of the festival;

he was accompanied by a wind fierce with showers of dust and possessed a foul stench of pus, blood, excrement, urine, wine, and flesh. Then [he saw] one with a lolling tongue and a body like a thunderbolt.
Dark as a mass of crushed collyrium, with a beard terrifying like molten copper,
Bali was dragged from the sky by the tip of his plow and struck on the head with a mace by Balabhadra for the sake of Brahmā’s peace. From that blow, he fell lifeless from the sky like a water-pot.
Then the sages, being well-pleased, praised Rāma and, having bestowed infallible blessings,
consecrated him just as the gods did for the slayer of Vṛtra; permitted by them,
he [went] to the Sarayū, Kauśikī, Mānasa lake, Gaṇḍakī, and Gautamī rivers.

Having bathed and performed ablutions at Ayodhyā, Nandigrāma, Barhiṣmatī, Brahmāvarta, and other sacred sites, he went to Prayāga, the king of holy fords. There, he made a gift of ten thousand elephants. ||16||

Then, having bathed at Citrakūṭa, Vindhya, Kāśī, Vipāśā, Śoṇa, Mithilā, Gayā, and other holy sites, he went to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. There, he bestowed upon the Brāhmaṇas one hundred crores of cows, each adorned with golden horns and cloths, and individually laden with the weight of gold and jewels.

Thereafter, in due order, Saṃkarṣaṇa himself will establish sacred fords (*tīrtha*) in the southern direction, such as Mahendra Mountain, Saptagodāvarī, Veṇī, Pampā, Bhīmarathī, Skanda-kṣetra, Śrīśaila, Veṅkaṭa, Kāñcī, Kāverī, Śrīraṅga, Ṛṣabha Mountain, the Ocean, Setu, Kṛtamālā, Tāmraparṇī, Malaya Mountain, Kulācala, Dakṣiṇasindhu, Phālguna, Pañcāpsaras, Gokarṇa, Śūrpāraka, Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Nirvindhyā, Daṇḍaka, Revā, Māhiṣmatī, Avantikā, and others.
Then he will come to the slaughter for the sake of assisting you. ||17||

O Lord of the Kauravas, I have thus fully described this sacred account of Balabhadra’s life, which removes all sins, recounts his pilgrimage to holy sites, and is the cause of all auspiciousness; what more do you wish to hear? 18.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Pastimes at Dvārakā," in the section concerning Balabhadra within the Śrī Garga Saṃhitā, in the dialogue between Prāḍvipāka and Duryodhana.
Hari Om Tat Sat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Duryodhana said:
O tiger among sages, at what time did the blessed Balabhadra sport on the banks of the Kālindī with the serpent maidens and the gopīs?
Prāḍvipāka said:

Once, having mounted his chariot marked with the sign of the *hita* tree, he departed from the city of Dvārakā, filled with supreme longing to see the gods, and accompanied by King Nanda, Gokula, the cows, and the multitude of cowherds and cowherdesses.
Saṃkarṣaṇa arrived and was embraced by King Nanda and Yaśodā, who had long yearned for him;
having met with the cowherd women, the cowherds, and the cows, he dwelt there for two months of the spring season. ||2||
Then those aforementioned Nāga maidens became cowherd girls;

for the sake of attaining Balabhadra, they received the *Balabhadra-pañcāṅga* from Garga Ācārya and became accomplished through that very practice. Once, Baladeva was pleased by them on the banks of the Kālindī.
He began the *rāsamaṇḍala*. At that very moment, on the full moon day of Caitra, the full moon shone with a reddish hue, delighting the entire forest. ||3||

Cool, gentle breezes blew from all sides, enveloped by the masses of pollen from the nectar of lotuses. Indeed, the river born of the Kalinga mountains, with its gently rolling waves, made the pure sandy bank full of joy. And likewise, the land of Vraja became resplendent with clusters of bowers and groves, with the shimmering pollen of lovely sprouts and flowers, with the warbling of peacocks, cuckoos, and male kokilas, and with the sweet humming of bees. 4.

There, in the circle of the dance, he shone like the king of the Yakṣas surrounded by Yakṣīs, or like the king of cowherds surrounded by cowherd girls; his tinkling bells and anklets resounded, and he was adorned with shimmering jeweled bracelets, waistbands, armlets, necklaces, crowns, and earrings, while his dark garments were topped by lotus petals and his eyes were like the petals of pure lotuses.
Then the goddess Vāruṇī, sent by Varuṇa, made the entire forest fragrant as she descended from the hollows of the trees, which resounded with bees attracted by the scent of her burden of flowers.

Intoxicated by the wine he had drunk, his large copper-colored eyes like lotuses, his broad limbs moving with the agitation of the god of love, the decorative patterns on his cheeks dissolving from drops of perspiration born of the fatigue of dalliance, possessing the gait of a lordly elephant and adorned with arms like the trunks of great elephants, he—like a mad king of elephants accompanied by female elephants—stood upon the throne with a plow resting against it and a mace in his hand, resembling the full orb of ten million moons, while golden tinkling bells and anklets jingled as they moved with the clinking of rising jeweled ornaments.

The Lord, the Sovereign of the World, shone resplendently and took his delight with beautiful women who were adorned with bracelets, shimmering earrings, golden necklaces, auspicious neck-ornaments, finger-rings, and crest-jewels; and who, with their dark, snake-like braids, imitated the beauty of female serpents, and whose lovely cheeks were decorated with leaf-patterns. ||6||

Then, his lotus-like face covered with beads of perspiration arising from the fatigue of wandering and sporting in the forest on the banks of the Kālindī, he called out from afar to the Yamunā for the purpose of bathing and water-sports. When the river did not come, he became angry and, with the tip of his plow, dragged her along, as it is said. (7)
"Today you do not come to me even when summoned by me, having disregarded me; I shall surely split you, who act according to your own whims, into a hundred pieces with my club!
Thus rebuked, Yamunā, filled with great fear and trembling, fell at his feet and spoke.

O Rāma, Rāma, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Balabhadra, O mighty-armed one! I do not know your supreme prowess, on a single hair of whose head the entire circle of the earth is seen like a mustard seed. Not knowing your supreme majesty, I have sought refuge [in you].
You are worthy to consume me; you are affectionate toward your devotees. 9.
Thus entreated, Balabhadra then released the Yamunā;
like an elephant with its female mates, that king of cowherds plunged into the water with the gopīs.
Emerging again from the water, Yamunā suddenly presented blue garments, ornaments made of gold and jewels, and divine gifts to Balabhadra as he stood on the bank; indeed,
she distributed them individually among the groups of gopīs.
Having himself put on blue garments and donned a golden garland set with nine kinds of gems,
Balabhadra shone like Mahendra upon the lordly elephant.

In this manner, O Lord of the Kauravas, all the nights of spring passed while the Lord of the Yādavas was sporting. Even today, the Yamunā flows along a furrowed path as if to indicate the prowess of the Blessed Balabhadra, much like Hastināpura itself.
Whoever hears or causes others to hear this narrative of Rāma’s rāsa-dance cuts through the entire mass of their sins and attains that state of mutual bliss.
What more do you wish to hear? ||11||

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Rāma’s Play of Rāsa," in the section concerning Balabhadra within the glorious Garga Saṃhitā, in the dialogue between Prāḍvipāka and Duryodhana. ||9||
Hari Om Tat Sat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Duryodhana said:
"O Blessed One, please tell me out of your grace how the five-limbed *Balabhadra* [mantra] was given by Garga Ācārya to the group of cowherd girls; for you are omniscient. (1)
Prāḍvipāka said: O Lord of the Kauravas, once Garga Ācārya came from Mount Garga to the region of Vraja to bathe in the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā).

There, in a secluded grove on the banks of the Kālindī, where swarms of bees were intoxicated by the fragrance of the flowers and tender sprouts of trees and creepers swaying gracefully in the play of the wind, the daughters of the serpent-king, remembering their past lives, bowed down to Garga Ācārya, who was intent on meditating upon Śrī Rāma-Kṛṣṇa, and said: "We are here."
The cowherd girls asked about the means of service for the sake of attaining the glorious Balabhadra;
and having observed their supreme devotion, he bestowed upon that assembly of gopīs the paddhati, paṭala, stotra, kavaca, and the thousand names. What more [is there to say]?
Speak, for you wish to grasp that. ||2||
Duryodhana said:
"Tell me the path of Rāma, so that I may attain perfection."
O Brahman, you who are affectionate toward your devotees; O God who is my guru, salutations be to you! ||3||
Prāḍvipāka said:
"O best of kings, hear the rule for the path of Rāma."
By which the great lord Balabhadra becomes pleased. ||4||
The Lord, the Blessed One, the Sovereign of the World, possesses a thousand faces.
He is not attained by gifts nor by pilgrimages, but is attained through single-minded devotion. ||5||
Through association with the virtuous, one should quickly learn devotion indeed to Śrī Hari, the Guru.
He is declared a perfected one (siddha) in whom the characteristic of love has indeed arisen. ||6||
Rising during the Brahma-muhūrta and uttering the names "Rāma, Kṛṣṇa," he should perform his duties.
Having bowed to the Guru and to the earth itself, one should then place one's foot upon the ground.
Having sipped water and having remained in a secluded place upon a seat of kusha grass.
Placing his hands in his lap, he gazes at the tip of his own nose.
One should meditate upon the supreme Lord Hari, the eternal Balabhadra.
Fair-complexioned, clad in blue garments, heart-pleasing, and adorned with a forest garland. ||9||
Thus, he was constantly devoted to meditation for the sake of the pleasure of the Lord Halin.
Pure by performing the twilight devotions at the three times of day, observing silence, and free from anger. ||10||
Free from desire and devoid of greed, one should be free from delusion and truthful in speech.
Desiring to drink water twice, eating but once a day, and having conquered his senses. ||11||
Wearing linen garments, sleeping on the ground, and subsisting on milk-rice.
Thus, having conquered the group of six, one becomes single-minded.
Saṃkarṣaṇa Hari is always pleased with him.
He is the most perfectly complete, the manifest cause of all causes. ||13||
Thus has the ritual manual of Śrī Balabhadra been recounted by me.
O mighty-armed lord of the Kauravas, what more do you wish to hear? ||14||
Duryodhana said:
O Lord of Munis, O Master, tell me the Paṭala of the God of gods.
So that I may always perform service at those two lotus feet. ||15||
Prāḍvipāka said:
"Know that this secret chapter on power (balapaṭala) bestows spiritual accomplishment."
In a secluded place, it was given by Brahmā to the high-souled Nārada.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, the Kāmabīja follows thereafter.
Next to that is Kāliṃdībhedanapada, and after that is Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Having formed two [names] ending in the dative case, and having placed "svāhā" after them;
O King, this sixteen-syllable king of mantras was spoken by Brahmā.
Having become one who observes the vow, he should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and sixteen thousand times.
In this world and the next, he attains supreme accomplishment; of this there is no doubt. ||19||
Then, one should perform a great worship of the mantra that has been recited.
It is endowed with thirty-two petals and is radiant with a pericarp and filaments.
Having drawn a beautiful five-colored lotus on an auspicious sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila),...
Upon that, O King, one should place an auspicious golden throne.
In that [temple], one should worship the supreme image of Śrī Baladeva. ||21||

Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, the thousand-faced, the Great Infinite; svāhā! Having tied the topknot with this mantra, having bowed to Him from all sides, and having stood facing Him, one should bow down oneself. "Oṃ, victory, victory, O Ananta, Balabhadra, Kāmapāla, Tālāṅka, Kālindī-bhañjana; appear, appear and be present before me! With this mantra, one should perform the invocation (āvāhana).

Oṃ, obeisance be to you, O wielder of the plough, bearer of the plough and mace, son of Rohiṇī, blue-robed Rāma, lover of Revatī; obeisance be to you! With this mantra, one should offer the ritual services (upacāras), such as the seat, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), the bath, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), incense, lamps, the sacred thread, food offerings (naivedya), garments, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali), and the waving of lights (nīrājana).

"Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Vāmana, Trivikrama, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, Dāmodara, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Adhokṣaja, Puruṣottama, and Śrīkṛṣṇa. With this mantra, one should perform the worship of all the limbs, reciting: "I worship separately the feet, ankles, knees, thighs, hips, belly, sides, back, arms, neck, eyes, and head."

Then, one should [worship] Śaṅkha, Cakra, Gadā, Padma, Asis, Dhanus, Bāṇa, Hala, Musala, Kaustubha, Vanamālā, Śrīvatsa, Pītāmbara, Nīlāmbara, Vaṃśī, Vetra, Garuḍāṅka, Tālāṅka, Ratha, Dāruka, Sumati, Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Śrīdāman, and others, individually, with their respective name-mantras preceded by the Praṇava (Om), ending in the dative case, and joined with "namaḥ."

Having performed the worship [of the primary deity], one should likewise worship Viṣvaksena, Vedavyāsa, Durgā, Vināyaka, the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas), the planets (grahas), and others, all around the lotus in their respective places. Again, having worshipped Vaiśvānara according to the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice beginning with the sweeping of the ground (*parisamūhana*), one should offer twenty-five thousand oblations (*āhuti*) with the previously mentioned root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Likewise, one should offer eight thousand oblations with the twelve-syllable mantra, and eight thousand oblations with the four-fold manifestation mantra (*caturvyūhamantra*).

Then, having circumambulated the fire and paid homage to the preceptor (ācārya), one should honor him with costly garments, gold ornaments, copper vessels, a cow with its calf, and gold as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). Likewise, having honored the Brahmins with food and other offerings, and having given food to the people of the city, one should prostrate before the preceptors. He who thus remembers this according to the chapter on the ritual of power (balapaṭala) becomes endowed with success and prosperity both in this world and the next. This secret chapter on Śrī Rāma has indeed been described by me to you.
O King, it bestows all accomplishments; what more do you wish to hear? ||22||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Section on Ritual Manuals," in the dialogue between Prāḍvipāka and Duryodhana within the Balabhadra-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Hari Om Tat Sat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Duryodhana said:
O great sage of ancient fruition, [please recite] the hymn of praise to Śrī Baladeva.
Please speak to me directly that which bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
Prāḍvipāka said:
"The auspicious King of Hymns (Stavarāja) of Rāma, composed by Vedavyāsa."
O King, listen to that which bestows all perfections and grants liberation to men. ||2||
O God of gods, O Blessed One, O Protector of Desire, homage be to you!
Salutations to Ananta, to Śeṣa; salutations to you, Rāma, in person. ||3||
To the upholder of the earth, the full one, whose nature is self-sustained, the wielder of the plough.
Salutations eternally to you, Saṃkarṣaṇa, who possesses a thousand heads. ||4||
O Revatīramaṇa, you are indeed Baladeva, the elder brother of Acyuta.
O Halāyudha, O slayer of Pralamba, O Puruṣottama, protect me! ||5||
Salutations again and again to Bala, to Balabhadra, who bears the palm-tree emblem.
Salutations to you, who are clad in blue garments, who are fair-complexioned, and who are the son of Rohiṇī. ||6||
The enemy of Dhenuka, the enemy of Muṣṭika, the enemy of Kūṭa, and the slayer of Balvala.
You alone are indeed the enemy of Rukmī, the enemy of Kūpakarṇa, and the enemy of Kumbhāṇḍa.
You are the divider of the Kālindī and the dragger of Hastināpura.
The enemy of the two-fold [demon] is the lord of the Yadavas, the ornament of the circle of Vraja. ||8||
You are the slayer of Kaṃsa’s brother, the Lord who undertakes pilgrimages to sacred fords.
The preceptor of Duryodhana himself—protect me, protect me, O Lord! 9.
Victory, victory to you, O Acyuta-deva, higher than the highest,
yourself infinite, whose learning has reached the ends of all directions!
Salutations to you, the wielder of the mace, the powerful one who holds the plow, the bestower of boons upon the gods, sages, and lords of serpents. ||10||
The person who constantly recites this hymn shall attain the supreme abode of Hari.
In this world, all power belongs to him who subdues his enemies; his wealth consists of his own kinsmen, for they are his true wealth. (11)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the King of Hymns to Balabhadra," in the Balabhadra-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Hari Oṃ Tat Sat. May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Duryodhana said:
"The wise teacher Garga gave the armor to the cowherd girls."
O Great Sage, grant me this divine protection that provides all forms of defense. ||1||
Prāḍvipāka said: Having bathed in the water, wearing linen garments, seated upon a mat of kuśa grass, with purificatory grass in his hand, and having performed the ritual cleansing with mantras;
Then, having recollected and bowed to Balarāma, the elder brother of Acyuta, one should maintain [the practice] and become absorbed in the Dharma. ||2||
May the Lord of Goloka-dhāma, the Supreme Sovereign whose glory is pure, protect me among all beings.
May he who perceives the entire circle of the earth as small as a mustard seed protect me upon this very circle of the earth. 3.
May the wielder of the plow protect me in armies; may Halī always protect me in battle.
May Musalī protect me always in difficult places, and may Saṃkarṣaṇa, the primordial god, protect me in the forests. ||4||
May he who checks the current of the Yamunā and wears blue garments protect me always from the waters and from fire.
May Rāma protect me in the wind, Bala in the sky, and he of infinite form always in the great ocean. ||5||
May Śrī Vāsudeva protect [us] among the mountains,
and may the Thousand-headed one protect us in great disputes.
May the son of Rohiṇī protect me from diseases, and may Kāmapāla guard me in times of calamity.
May the enemy of Dhenuka always protect me from desire; may the slayer of Dvivida always protect me from anger.
May the enemy of Balvala always protect me from greed; may the enemy of the Magadha king indeed always protect me from delusion. ||7||
May the preeminent hero of the Vṛṣṇis always protect me in the morning, and may the Lord of Mathurā-pura always protect me in the forenoon.
May the Self-Ruler, accompanied by cowherds, protect me at midday; may He always protect me in the afternoon. ||8||
May the Lord of Serpents protect me always in the evening;
may He who is higher than the highest protect me at nightfall.
And at the full midnight, as well as at the time of dawn, may he of enduring valor protect me forever. (9)
May the Lord of Revatī protect me in the intermediate directions, the enemy of Pralamba in the cardinal directions, and the upholder of the Yadus below.
Above me is always Balabhadra, and likewise from afar and all around is indeed Baladeva.
May Puruṣottama, who is eternally within, and who sports like the lord of serpents without, protect me with his great power.
May Hari himself, the great Supreme Lord who is full, dwelling as the eternal inner self, protect me. 11.
He is the destroyer of the fear of gods and asuras, and the consumer of the fuel that is the accumulation of sins.
Know that Siddhāsana is the destroyer of the jar of obstacles and the supreme armor of strength. ||12||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Hymn and the Armor," in the Balabhadra-khaṇḍa of the glorious Garga-saṃhitā.
Hari Om Tat Sat; may this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Duryodhana said:
O great sage, this is the first ripening of the god Balabhadra.
Recite my thousand names, which are secret even from the hosts of gods.
Prāḍvipāka said:
"Excellent, excellent, O Great King! Excellent is your stainless fame."
That which you ask about is this supreme teaching spoken by Garga, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
I shall proclaim before you a thousand divine names.
It was given by Gargācārya to the gopīs on the auspicious bank of the Kṛṣṇā river. ||3||
Oṃ. Of this mantra of the *Śrī Balabhadra Sahasranāma Stotra*,

Garga Ācārya is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chanda*), Saṃkarṣaṇa the Supreme Self is the deity (*devatā*), "Balabhadra" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and "Revatī" is the power (*śakti*).
"Ananta" is the *kīlaka*; the application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of recitation (*japa*) for the pleasure of Balabhadra.
Then [he meditated on] the one in contemplation,
whose stainless crown was shimmering, who was adorned with tinkling bells and bracelets,
whose cheeks were framed by moving locks of hair, and whose lotus-face possessed the splendor of earrings.
I praise Kāmapāla, who is as beautiful as the snowy mountain, adorned with a sky of dark clouds, and possessing a great plow and mace. ||4||
Oṃ, Balabhadra, Rāmabhadra, Rāma, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Acyuta.
The god Revatīramaṇa, Kāmapāla, and Halāyudha. ||5||
Baladeva, the elder brother of Acyuta, is blue-robed and white-complexioned.
The slayer of Pralamba, the great hero, the son of Rohiṇī, possessed of great prowess.
Marked with the palm tree, wielder of the mace, wielder of the plow, Hari, the best of the Yadus, the powerful one.
Sīrapāṇi, Padmapāṇi, Laguḍī, and Veṇuvādana. ||7||
The hero who split the Kālindī, Bala, Prabala, and Ūrdhvaga.
Ananta is a portion of Vāsudeva; he has a thousand faces and is the self-ruling lord.
Vasudeva, the best of the Vasus, is the lord of the earth and the possessor of all wealth.
The best of the Yadus, the lord of the Yādavas, Mādhava, the beloved of the Vṛṣṇis. ||9||
Lord of Dvārakā, Lord of Mathurā, generous, honorable, and high-minded.
He is the Full, the Ancient, the Puruṣa, the Supreme Lord, the Highest God. ||10||
The most perfectly complete, the manifest Supreme Person, the Highest Puruṣa.
The Lord Ananta Śeṣa is eternal and transcends primordial nature (prakṛti). ||11||
The individual self, the supreme self, and indeed the inner self are eternal and immutable.
He who is the fourfold manifestation, the four Vedas, the four forms, and the four-footed. ||12||
The primary cause, primordial nature, the witness, the aggregate, the possessor of the aggregate, and the companion.
The great-minded one, whose friend is the intellect, has his mental egoism veiled. ||13||
The Lord of the senses, the divine self, is both knowledge, action, and bliss.
He is both non-dual and dual; he is formless and stainless. ||14||
Virāṭ, Samrāṭ, Mahaugha, Dhāra, Sthāsnu, and Cariṣṇumān.
The lord of serpents and king of snakes, adorned with a thousand hoods. ||15||
The lord of serpents, the serpent, the manifestation, the hisser, the shrieker, the master.
Maṇihāra, Maṇidhara, Vitalī, Sutalī, Talī. ||16||
Atala, Sutala, Pātāla, and Talātala;
Rasātala, Bhogitala, Sphuraddanta, and Mahātala. ||17||
Vāsuki resembles Śaṅkhacūḍa; Devadatta is like Dhanañjaya.
Kaṃbalāśva, Vegatara, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Mahābhuja. ||18||
His body intoxicated by the liquor of Varuṇa, his eyes reeling with intoxication.
Padmākṣa, Padmamālī, Vanamālī, and Madhuśravas. ||19||
Possessing the beauty of ten million Kandarpas, he was honored by the daughters of the Nagas.
Wearing anklets, a waist-belt, bracelets, and golden armlets. ||20||
Wearing a crown, adorned with earrings, bearing a staff, possessing a topknot, and marked by crescent-shaped ornaments.
He is Kali, the lover of Kali, Time, and the lord of the Nivātakavacas. ||21||
He is the destroyer, the one who causes dissolution, the fire of time, the cosmic dissolution, and the place of absorption.
The great serpent Pāṇini and Patañjali, the author of the commentary on the grammatical treatise. ||22||
Kātyāyana is Pakvimābha; Sphoṭāyana is Uraṅgama.
Vaikuṇṭha, Yājñika, Yajña, Vāmana, Hariṇa, and Hari. ||23||
Kṛṣṇa is Viṣṇu, Mahāviṣṇu, the all-powerful, and the knower of distinctions.
Haṃsa, Yogeśvara, Kūrma, Vārāha, and the sage Nārada. ||24||
Sanaka, Kapila, Matsya, Kamaṭha, and Devamaṅgala.
Dattātreya, Pṛthu, Vṛddha, Ṛṣabha, and the best of the Bhṛgus; ||25||
Dhanvantari, Nṛsiṃha, Kali, Nārāyaṇa, and Nara.
Rāmacandra, the lord of the Raghus, the sovereign of Kośala, the scion of the Raghu dynasty. ||26||
The descendant of Kakutstha, an ocean of compassion, a lord of kings, and endowed with all auspicious marks.
The heroic protector, son of Daśaratha, who increases the joy of Kausalyā. ||27||
The son of Sumitrā, Bharata, the archer Śatrughna, the scorcher of his enemies.
Equipped with a quiver, wearing armor, bearing a sword, holding arrows, and possessing a well-guarded chest. ||28||
Having bound on his leather arm-guards and finger-protectors, he was the one who shattered the bow of Śambhu.
The protector of sacrifice, the sustainer of sacrifice, and the slayer of Mārīca. ||29||
The enemy of the Asuras, the slayer of Tāṭakā, and the one who rendered Vibhīṣaṇa his ally.
The forest-dweller, the enemy of Virādha, was joyful and fulfilled his father’s word. ||30||
The sage, beloved of sages, made his dwelling in the Citrakūṭa forest.
Rāma, the slayer of Kabandha, whose hair is like a staff, is lotus-eyed. ||31||
The leader who wanders through the Mataṅga forest is the lord of Pañcavaṭī.
Sugrīva, the friend of Sugrīva, was delighted at heart by Hanumān. ||32||
The builder of the bridge, the enemy of Rāvaṇa, who was intent on burning Laṅkā.
The enemy of Rāvaṇa, seated upon the Puṣpaka chariot, was distressed by separation from Jānakī. ||33||
The glorious lord of Ayodhyā, the enemy of Lavaṇa, was honored by the gods.
He belonged to the solar and lunar lineages and was an expert in the playing of the flute.
The lord of the cows, the master of the cowherd host, the cowherd himself, surrounded by hundreds of cowherdesses.
The Lord of Gokula, the son of the cowherd, the protector of cows, the refuge of the herds of cattle. ||35||
The enemy of Pūtanā, the slayer of Baka, and the one who cast down Tṛṇāvarta.
The enemy of Agha, the enemy of Dhenuka, the enemy of Pralamba, and the Lord of Vraja. ||36||
The slayer of Ariṣṭa, the enemy of Keśin, and the destroyer of the demon Vyoma.
Drinking fire, drinking milk, and taking refuge in the creepers of Vṛndāvana. ||37||
The worthy son of Yaśomatī, the infant cherished by Rohiṇī.
Standing in the midst of the rāsa-circle, he is the ornament of the rāsa-circle. ||38||
Seeking the company of hundreds of cowherd maidens, he was intent on slaying Śaṅkhacūḍa.
The upholder of Govardhana, the conqueror of Śakra, and the protector of Vraja. ||39||
The excellent Vṛṣabhānu, Nanda, Ānanda, and the increaser of joy, Nandavardhana.
The son of King Nanda, the Lord of Śrī, the enemy of Kaṃsa, the slayer of Kāliya. ||40||
The slayer of Rajaka and Mushtika, the breaker of Kamsa’s bow.
